Bimergen Energy Corporation, a renewable energy project developer, focuses on the clean energy transition and providing critical grid stability through Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and solar development projects in the United States. It focuses on becoming a grid-balancing operator by developing, commercializing, and operating a diversified portfolio of BESS and solar energy projects. The company engages in the development and operation of BESS projects to mitigate energy imbalances and power deficits observed in markets with solar and wind energy generation. Additionally, it offers essential grid services, including frequency regulation, voltage support, and emergency backup during grid outages. The company also holds a portfolio of development projects that include approximately 3.6 gigawatts of alternating current power capacity. It serves traditional power transmission lines, offtakes, and utility companies in energy industry. The company was formerly known as Bitech Technologies Corporation and changed its name to Bimergen Energy Corporation in February 2025. Bimergen Energy Corporation is based in Newport Beach, California.

artigo.texto: Anatel confirma data center de IA com investimento de R$ 375 milhões na Telebras Agência reguladora porém, determina que, antes de qualquer contratação, seja formalmente identificada a fonte de recursos que financiará sua operação permanente da instalação. A Anatel formalizou nesta quarta-feira, 18 de novembro, a destinação de R$ 375 milhões para construir um data center de inteligência artificial que será operado pela Telebras. A decisão amplia as responsabilidades da estatal justamente quando seu balanço revela dificuldades para alcançar a independência financeira: nos primeiros nove meses de 2026, a companhia acumulou prejuízo de R$ 90,7 milhões e recebeu R$ 169,9 milhões em subvenções governamentais. Sem esse apoio, seu EBITDA ajustado teria sido negativo em R$ 32,9 milhões. O contraste entre a nova missão e a situação financeira da empresa está no centro do Acórdão nº 325/2026 (Nº 325 – Processo nº 53500.088928/2021-76), aprovado pelo Conselho Diretor da Anatel no último dia 4 e publicado agora no Diário Oficial da União. Embora autorize o investimento para construir a infraestrutura, a agência determina que, antes de qualquer contratação, seja formalmente identificada a fonte de recursos que financiará sua operação permanente. A exigência não é secundária. O governo informou dispor de até R$ 375 milhões para implantar a infraestrutura. O que ainda não foi demonstrado publicamente é quanto custará mantê-la funcionando e se as receitas da Telebras serão suficientes para sustentar essa nova responsabilidade sem ampliar sua dependência financeira da União. Ficou claro que o dinheiro proveniente dos saldos remanescentes do leilão do 5G poderá ser utilizado para implantar o empreendimento, mas não para custear sua operação. A Telebras fica responsável pelass despesas com energia elétrica, manutenção, atualização tecnológica, segurança e suporte. A Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz (EAF), responsável pela implantação, deverá transferir a infraestrutura à União e não poderá continuar financiando seu funcionamento.

artigo.texto: Congresso aprova crédito de R$ 34,9 milhões para data center do Serpro em São Paulo Falta agora a sanção presidencial para a liberação dos recursos. O Congresso aprovou na sessão desta terça-feira (17) o PLN 22/2026, que destina R$ 34,9 milhões em crédito suplementar ao Serpro. Os recursos serão aplicados pela estatal no data center modular de São Paulo, incluindo a execução de duas etapas do empreendimento e um aditivo contratual. O governo identifica três finalidades: execução da etapa 6, execução da etapa 7 e cobertura de um aditivo de serviços previsto para o projeto. Não se trata de uma destinação indiscriminada para equipamentos, software ou despesas administrativas. O crédito também utiliza recursos próprios da estatal, e não uma transferência adicional direta do Tesouro Nacional. A suplementação amplia a autorização orçamentária para realizar os investimentos, mas não significa, por si só, que o Serpro recebeu R$ 34,9 milhões em dinheiro novo.

artigo.texto: How GPUs Are Changing the Colocation vs. Private Data Center Debate GPUs are shifting the colo vs. private data center decision toward power, speed, utilization, and sustainability – not just location, scale, and cost. Traditionally, the main factors in deciding between colocation and a private data center were relatively straightforward: location, the scale of the infrastructure to be deployed, and future growth plans. By weighing those considerations, businesses could determine whether it made more logistical and financial sense to lease colocation space or invest in a data center of their own. In an era when GPUs have become a common component of data center infrastructure, however, the colocation-versus-private-data-center calculus has changed in important ways. Traditional considerations still matter, but organizations must now also account for factors that are unique to GPU-equipped environments. Here’s a look at how GPUs are reshaping the colocation decision, along with guidance on when colocation or a private data center may be the better fit. How GPUs Reshape the Colocation Decision GPUs, especially the high-performance accelerators used to support AI workloads, introduce several challenges that traditional data center infrastructure does not. One is power density. Historically, a typical data center rack consumed no more than about 10 kW. GPU-enabled servers can push that figure dramatically higher, often by a factor of 10. That shift creates demands around power delivery, cooling, energy sourcing, and utility interconnection timelines. Another is cost. GPU-equipped servers are significantly more expensive than standard servers, which makes utilization rates much more important from an ROI perspective. Idle or underused GPUs are costly assets. Speed to deployment is also a major factor. Many organizations pursuing AI training or inference initiatives are working on aggressive timelines. They cannot afford to wait years for a new facility to be built, commissioned, and connected to sufficient power. These are not the only considerations. Traditional factors such as total CapEx and OpEx, geographic requirements, and long-term capacity planning still matter. But in many cases, the power, cost, and deployment realities associated with GPUs outweigh the older decision framework, forcing businesses to reassess how they weigh colocation versus private infrastructure. How to Choose Between Colocation and Private Infrastructure for GPUs The right answer depends on several key questions. How Many GPUs Does the Business Need? The scale of GPU deployment matters. If only a small share of the organization’s infrastructure will require GPUs, GPU-specific concerns may not drive the overall decision. For example, if only 10% of planned servers will include GPUs, the choice between colocation and a private data center may still hinge primarily on broader considerations such as cost structure, location, and expansion capacity. If GPUs will make up a substantial portion of the environment, however, their power and cooling requirements become central to the decision. What Are the Business’s GPU Use Cases? How the organization plans to use GPUs is critical. For workloads such as AI model training, where GPU demand may be bursty rather than constant, colocation can make more financial sense. It may be more cost-effective to deploy in a facility already equipped for high-density infrastructure than to invest in a GPU-ready private data center that will sit idle for long stretches. By contrast, a private data center may prove more economical over time for organizations running GPU-intensive workloads continuously, such as large-scale AI inference. In those cases, the higher upfront capital investment can translate into lower long-term operating costs, especially if the organization can secure power more cheaply than a colocation provider, which may build a markup into power pricing. How Long Will It Take to Source Power for a New Data Center? If speed is a priority, colocation is usually the faster route. Building a new private data center can take years, especially if permitting delays emerge. Even after construction is complete, obtaining enough utility power to support a dense GPU deployment can take considerable time. In many markets, grid interconnection timelines have become a major constraint. Colocation providers, by contrast, may already have the power capacity, cooling systems, and operational readiness needed to bring GPU infrastructure online much sooner. How Important Is Energy Sustainability? Because GPUs consume far more power than conventional infrastructure, they also raise the stakes around sustainability. Colocation can offer an easier path to renewable energy, at least in the near term. Many providers already operate facilities backed by renewable energy contracts, low-carbon power mixes, or offsets. Achieving the same result in a private data center can be difficult, particularly in regions where renewable energy is limited or where building on-site generation is financially or logistically impractical. For organizations with aggressive sustainability targets, the difference may significantly influence the decision. Why GPUs Change More than Capacity Planning GPUs have not eliminated the traditional considerations involved in choosing between colocation and a private data center, but they have shifted the relative importance of these options. Power availability, deployment speed, utilization rates, and sustainability now play a much larger role in infrastructure strategy than they did in the past. The key is to evaluate not just how much infrastructure a business needs, but how GPU-driven workloads change the cost, timing, and operational realities behind that infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Public Pushback Complicates Data Center Buildouts Developers face closer scrutiny of utility costs, water use, and local benefits as community concerns complicate approvals and investment decisions. Public concern over electricity costs, water demand, and neighborhood impacts is pushing data center development toward tighter restrictions, including in states where leaders previously welcomed the investment. The shift is forcing developers to reassess whether expected permits, tax benefits, and utility arrangements will survive rising community resistance. In Pennsylvania, gubernatorial candidate Stacy Garrity initially praised Amazon’s $20 billion data center investment and urged the state to attract more projects before backing a pause on new development and stronger requirements. Gov. Josh Shapiro also moved from promoting investment and faster permitting to supporting stricter environmental standards and transparency requirements, according to Spotlight PA. Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley reversed his opposition to a moratorium during the campaign and ultimately backed a pause while supporting the elimination of the industry’s state sales tax exemption. After the election, he said he was considering requirements around resource-use disclosures, community support, and protections against shifting energy costs onto residents, according to an Associated Press report. If those exemptions disappear, developers could face higher equipment costs, larger bills for power infrastructure, and construction delays while new approval requirements take shape. November’s local ballot measures added to the pressure, with voters in multiple communities backing new restrictions on data center development. For developers, the immediate questions center on zoning decisions, utility agreements, and environmental approvals that could reshape both project timelines and costs. Sreenivas Duvvuri Venkata, research analyst for services at IDC, said developers now need to reassess which projects can realistically move forward. “Community acceptance has become material to timely execution of data center projects, alongside power availability, interconnection timelines, and environmental permits,” he told Data Center Knowledge. Venkata said builders should prioritize projects based on the constraints still to be resolved, not just on cost and capacity. Data center projects that broke ground between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026 waited an average of just over two years from announcement to construction, up from about 18 months for projects launched between early 2020 and mid-2025, according to GlobalData. Permits, Tariffs, and Grid Upgrades Can Reshape Project Timelines Different authorities control different parts of a project’s viability. Venkata pointed to state environmental permits and incentive agreements, utility commission decisions on tariffs and cost allocation, and local rezoning and conditional-use approvals as distinct exposure points. That means a project with land secured may still face unresolved questions about who will pay for grid upgrades or whether its planned generation equipment can operate as proposed. Developers need to map those decisions against procurement and construction commitments before locking in schedules. Alston Mason, president of energy solutions at Oldcastle Infrastructure, told Data Center Knowledge that on-site generation can introduce another permitting process. “They can have the power plan figured out and still be waiting on environmental permits for the equipment,” Mason said. “If that review takes longer, the project team has to evaluate what work can move forward in the meantime and adjust sequencing as more information becomes available.” Schedule changes also have to account for suppliers serving multiple markets. Recent Data Center Knowledge coverage of construction labor shortages highlighted the strain on specialized crews, reinforcing the need to align approvals with labor availability and equipment delivery capacity. “When you’re evaluating a site, the question is whether suppliers have the capacity to [deliver] the right components when construction timelines demand them,” Mason said. Developers Face Pressure to Put Commitments in Writing Residents want to know what a facility will require before construction begins, including where its water will come from and whether households could end up bearing higher electricity costs. Labor shortages and supplier constraints can further complicate scheduling, making it important to involve energy and water partners while designs are still flexible enough to address community concerns, Mason said. “If the developer is funding infrastructure upgrades that serve residents, like neighborhood roads and connectivity, people want to know what’s planned, who will benefit, and when,” he said. Publishing those commitments alongside power and water plans gives residents a way to track delivery and forces developers to reflect those promises in the project’s economics. “Enforceable commitments are key to winning approval,” Venkata said. Venkata said developers may face conditions that include full responsibility for utility costs, renewable energy requirements, closed-loop cooling, and limits tying projects to designated industrial sites. Reduced tax benefits, higher power costs, and long-term payment obligations can affect viability just as much as approval delays. Moving to another market does not eliminate those pressures. Developers still need to determine whether infrastructure, suppliers, and permitting schedules support the target opening date rather than assuming a more welcoming location is immediately buildable. “For an individual site, it still comes down to land, power, and water,” Mason said. “All three have to be available on a timeline the project can work with.”

artigo.texto: AI Workloads Hit by Power-Quality Issues at Data Centers Power quality, not just grid access, is limiting AI growth at US data centers, exposing weaknesses in internal infrastructure and monitoring. Electrical problems are constraining AI deployments at US data centers, with nearly a third of respondents to a Fluke survey saying power-quality issues have reduced their ability to deploy or operate high-density AI and GPU workloads. The survey, which polled 500 data center operators and professionals across the United States, suggests facilities are facing internal infrastructure constraints alongside the broader struggle to secure electricity from utilities. Just 36% of respondents said their electrical infrastructure is fully prepared for higher-density AI workloads, while 74% said insufficient power and grid capacity are moderately or severely limiting expansion. “The biggest risk is whether a data center’s internal infrastructure can reliably distribute and support that power at scale,” Michael Stuart, senior manager and technical fellow at Fluke, told Data Center Knowledge. Power, Cooling, and Cabling Failures Create Risks About three-quarters of respondents (76%) reported experiencing electrical or power-system issues. Separately, 79% said power-quality problems had contributed over the past year to delays, service disruptions, unplanned downtime, or serious near-misses. The figure groups operational failures together with incidents that did not result in an outage. It does not mean nearly four in five respondents experienced downtime. Stuart said weaknesses often emerge where power, cooling, and cabling systems intersect. Problems can include harmonics, voltage sags and swells, thermal hotspots, deteriorating cooling systems, and infrastructure connections that have not been adequately documented or verified. “Since each data center is so complex and diverse, determining weaknesses within facilities should be done on a case-by-case basis,” he said. Those conditions can limit the computing capacity a facility can support even after an operator has secured sufficient electricity. “If electrical, mechanical, and network systems aren’t performing to specification, operators may be unable to fully utilize the capacity they’ve already secured from the grid,” he added. Testing and Monitoring Before GPU Rollouts For operators preparing to install high-density GPU racks, Stuart recommends measuring power quality as close as possible to the GPU loads along the electrical distribution chain. The appropriate measurement points will vary by facility and may change during commissioning as actual load conditions become clearer. Electrical distribution and cooling also need to be evaluated together to establish whether they can sustain the intended workloads. “If measurements reveal that either system cannot reliably support the intended GPU workloads, operators should address those issues before proceeding with deployment,” Stuart said. The survey also identified gaps in operators’ ability to detect developing problems. Some 78% of respondents said they lacked comprehensive, continuous, real-time visibility across critical electrical systems. Another 15% said electrical problems were identified only after performance degradation, equipment failure, or downtime had already occurred. Stuart said operators should assess existing monitoring coverage to identify where additional visibility would most improve reliability. Potential areas include power distribution, backup power, batteries, and switchgear, although priorities will depend on each facility’s infrastructure and current monitoring capabilities. Labor Shortages Add Pressure to Maintenance Recruiting qualified electrical technicians has become harder for 57% of respondents, adding pressure to the teams responsible for installing, testing, and maintaining infrastructure. That hiring difficulty has not uniformly translated into slower expansion. Some 65% of respondents said skills shortages had not delayed infrastructure upgrades or new capacity. Still, Stuart said workforce constraints can contribute to localized delays, inconsistent installation practices, and additional work to correct problems or verify quality. “Not every problem is visible during an initial inspection; some only surface once electrical systems are operational,” he said. Stuart said qualified electricians should perform and validate the work, supported by testing and diagnostic tools to identify faults that may emerge after installation and help ensure long-term reliability.

artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. Rethinking High-Voltage Commissioning for AI Data Centers AI data centers are driving more direct high-voltage connections, making specialist HV commissioning essential for safe, reliable, and on-schedule delivery. The rapid global buildout of digital infrastructure to support the artificial intelligence boom is reshaping the design, construction, and commissioning requirements of data center projects. As computing capacity grows and rack densities rise to unprecedented levels, facilities are increasingly demanding power supplies measured in the tens and hundreds of megawatts. For many developments, securing that capacity means moving beyond conventional distribution networks and, where possible, connecting directly to high-voltage (HV) transmission infrastructure. Those connections can provide the capacity needed to support the next generation of AI facilities. They also significantly increase the complexity of the electrical environment. That raises both the difficulty and the risk for commissioning teams. Yet not every project fully acknowledges that the demands of HV data center commissioning extend well beyond conventional low-voltage (LV) certification and verification. HV infrastructure must be treated as a specialist engineering discipline, with its own competencies, testing methodologies, safety procedures, and assurance requirements. Incorporating it into an existing data center commissioning scope without appropriate specialist oversight risks leaving critical elements of the project insufficiently verified. The Changing Electrical Landscape Traditionally, data centers have relied on utility supplies delivered through distribution networks, with transformers stepping voltage down before electricity reaches the facility’s LV infrastructure. From there, uninterruptible power supplies, switchgear, and distribution systems provide the conditioned power required by critical IT loads. Now, the scale and nature of the AI boom are changing that equation. As AI data center development trends toward gigawatt-scale demand, local distribution networks in some markets cannot support new projects without major upgrades. That has contributed to extended approval processes and multiyear delays for some projects. Direct connections to higher-voltage networks, including 66kV, 110kV, and 150kV systems, are becoming an increasingly compelling alternative. However, connecting a data center directly to transmission infrastructure introduces additional complexity and cost. Substations, power transformers, HV cables, switchgear, protection systems, and utility interfaces all become integral parts of the critical power architecture. In many cases, some or all of those elements would have sat well outside the project boundary only a few years ago. From a commissioning perspective, that increases both the volume and the importance of the work required to bring a project from design through initial handover. Every HV element requires appropriate inspection, testing, and verification before energization, and commissioning that equipment brings its own risks and inherent complexities. HV Commissioning Requires Specialist Expertise HV commissioning differs fundamentally from conventional LV commissioning in both its technical requirements and its safety implications. At higher voltage levels, electrical hazards include arc flash, flashover, and fatal electric shock, even when personnel are exposed without direct contact with live conductors. The consequences of incorrect installation, protection settings, or switching procedures can be severe. Equipment failure during energization can damage expensive infrastructure, disrupt the wider electrical network, and cause significant project delays, in addition to the personal risk to teams working on the system. HV commissioning is its own discipline, with its own standards, testing methodologies, and safety protocols. It is not simply an extension of LV commissioning. The stakes are higher, and developers need to assess a project’s HV commissioning requirements during project planning rather than treating them as an extension of the broader electrical commissioning program. HV Commissioning from Installation to Verified Performance A structured HV commissioning program should define the inspection, testing, and acceptance requirements for every major component, supported by detailed inspection and test plans. The process begins with a comprehensive review of design documentation, equipment specifications, installation records, and manufacturer requirements. Site inspections then verify that equipment has been installed correctly, that connections and terminations are satisfactory, and that the installation reflects design intent. Individual equipment testing forms a substantial part of the program: - Power transformers require electrical testing to confirm insulation integrity, winding condition, and the correct operation of associated monitoring and protection devices. - HV cables and terminations must be tested to verify insulation performance and installation integrity. - Switchgear and circuit breakers need both mechanical and electrical verification, including checks of operating mechanisms, interlocks, contact resistance, and switching functionality. Any deficiencies identified during testing must be resolved and documented before the equipment progresses toward energization. - Protection-system verification means relays must be checked against approved protection studies and settings schedules, with secondary injection testing used to verify relay operation. - Grid-interface testing is particularly important because data center supply performance often depends on interactions among multiple systems delivered by different contractors and organizations. - Power-quality assessment forms part of this broader assurance process as well. artigo.texto: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers September 4, 2026 Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land. Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily. AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University. From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. An insatiable appetite for power Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that. And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. How the AI boom could slow climate progress All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels. One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone. And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal. Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries. Hidden water demand Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation. A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume. In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023. There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%. Data centers are making cities hotter Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas. Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy. Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%. Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts. First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities. On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants. One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year. Data centers take over large swaths of land Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. Repurposing natural and agricultural areas into industrial zones can threaten biodiversity and disrupt local ecosystems. In Hattersheim, Germany, for example, an 18-acre (7-hectare) parc

artigo.texto: This bill will fast-track the dirty data center buildout What's At Stake The Senate will soon vote on a bill that would fast-track the buildout of pipelines, mines, power plants, and dirty data centers. In exchange, it would sacrifice clean water, Tribal rights, public lands, and endangered species. Write to Congress today and tell them to oppose this destructive permitting bill. Not only does it threaten existing environmental protections, it would make it harder for future presidents to undo the harms caused by this administration. Delivery to U.S. Congress Important Notice Your message is delivered to a public agency, and all information submitted may be placed in the public record. Do not submit confidential information. By taking action, you will receive emails from Earthjustice. Change your mailing preferences or opt-out at any time. Learn more in our Privacy Policy. This Earthjustice action is hosted on EveryAction. Learn about EveryAction’s Privacy Policy. Why is a phone number or prefix required on some action forms? Trouble Viewing This Action? If the action form is not loading above, please be aware that ad blockers and VPNs may prevent the action form from displaying. Please add earthjustice.org as a trusted website in your ad blocker, and refresh this webpage. (Details.) If the action form still does not display, please report the problem to us at action@earthjustice.org with a screenshot image of the problem. Thank you! Your Actions Matter Your messages make a difference, even if we have leaders who don't want to listen. Here's why. You level the playing field. Elected officials pay attention when they see that we are paying attention. Read more. They may be hearing from industry lobbyists left and right, but hearing the stories of their constituents — that’s your power. Our legislators serve at the pleasure of the people who gave them their job — you. Make sure your elected officials know whose community and whose values they represent. When you contact your elected official, you’re putting a face and a name on an issue. Whether or not you voted for them, they work for you, for the duration of their term. Make sure your elected officials know whose community and whose values they represent. (Find your local, state, and federal elected officials.) Your action is with us in court. If a federal agency finalizes a harmful action, the record of public comments provides a basis for bringing them into court. Read more. Throughout each of the public comment periods we alert you to, Earthjustice’s attorneys are researching and writing in-depth, technical comments to submit — detailing how the regulation could and should be stronger to protect the environment, our communities, and our planet. We need you to join us — your specific experiences, knowledge, and voice are crucial to add to the Administrative Record through the comment periods. Lawsuits we file that challenge weak or harmful federal regulations rely on what was submitted during the comment period. The court can only look at documents that are in the Administrative Record — including the public comments — to decide if the agency did something improper. Your actions aid our litigation. Taking action and submitting comments during a comment period is substantively important. It’s the law. Federal agencies must pause what they’re doing and ask for — and consider — your comment. Read more. Many of us may have never heard of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), but laws like these require our government to ask the public to weigh in before agencies adopt or change regulations. Regulations essentially describe how federal agencies will carry out laws — including decisions that could undermine science, or weaken safeguards on public health. Public comments are collected at various points throughout the federal government’s rulemaking process, including when a regulation is proposed and finalized. (Learn about the rulemaking process.) These comments become part of the official, legal public record — the “Administrative Record.” When the public responds with a huge outpouring of support for environmental protections, these individual messages collectively undercut politicians' attempts to claim otherwise. What this means is each of us can take a role in shaping the rules our government creates — and ensuring those rules are fair and effective.

artigo.texto: US Energy Department Launches BattMan Consortium to Scale Domestic Battery Manufacturing The US Department of Energy on Oct. 28 unveiled a comprehensive national battery strategy and stood up a manufacturing consortium meant to push laboratory-stage storage technologies onto factory floors at home, with the aim of completing a domestic supply chain by 2030 and establishing American leadership in battery technology and production by 2035. The consortium, formally the Battery Manufacturing Accelerator and known as BattMan, is led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory alongside Oak Ridge, Argonne and the National Laboratory of the Rockies. Academic partners include the University of Washington, Binghamton University, the University of Alabama, Arizona State University and the University of Michigan-Dearborn. The initiative is also courting battery and materials manufacturers, and organizations interested in joining can apply through the program's website. The strategy, titled "A National Strategy for American Leadership in Batteries," was issued by the department's Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation. It targets the weak middle links of the supply chain: while investment has flowed into final assembly of cells and packs, the US still leans on outside suppliers for mining, refining and the processing of cathode and anode materials, electrolytes and separators. The plan sets six priority areas, spanning upstream and midstream investment, faster commercialization of research, manufacturing process innovation, storage deployment for grid modernization, strategic international partnerships and workforce development. Demand projections explain the urgency. The department expects US battery demand for transportation and energy storage to climb from 179 GWh in 2025 to roughly 707 GWh in 2035, nearly a fourfold increase, driven by electrified transport as well as soaring power needs from advanced computing and data centers and the push to harden the grid. Note: Demand figures are Department of Energy projections cited in the strategy. BattMan is the execution arm for the manufacturing piece of that plan. Its job is to close the gap between promising chemistries and commercial production, a stretch the department describes as a valley of death for lab breakthroughs. The consortium intends to pair what officials call "super intelligence" with advanced manufacturing in a coordinated, data-driven innovation ecosystem. "The advances we make today in battery manufacturing technology will determine America's energy security and economic competitiveness for decades to come," said Audrey Robertson, assistant secretary of Energy. Oak Ridge is contributing its Battery Manufacturing Facility research center and plans a smart test bed equipped with advanced sensing, real-time monitoring and data analysis to trial both wet and dry electrode processes. The accelerator also envisions autonomous pilot lines that fuse sensing, process monitoring and intelligent control, with the goal of an AI-based platform that catches production irregularities as they arise and adjusts parameters on its own to head off defects. "The BattMan Accelerator is exactly the kind of coordinated national effort that turns scientific breakthroughs into economic and energy security advantages," said Chins Chinnasamy, a distinguished R&D staff member who leads the consortium for Oak Ridge. The research agenda reflects persistent technical limits. Batteries store far less energy per unit of mass than petroleum-based fuels, and developers are chasing improvements on several fronts at once: safety beyond flammable lithium-ion cells, lower production costs, faster charging and reduced dependence on scarce raw materials. The accelerator hopes to ease the last of those by identifying battery materials among more abundant elements sourced domestically, sidestepping the critical minerals bottleneck that has complicated US cell production. The strategy's emphasis on midstream processing marks a shift from earlier federal support, which concentrated on cell and pack assembly. Building out refining and materials processing domestically would shorten a supply chain now exposed to overseas disruption, but it also sets up a collision course with allied suppliers in Japan and elsewhere that hold strong positions in battery materials and manufacturing equipment. How the US balances self-sufficiency against coordination with partners will shape procurement decisions for years. For investors, the program signals where federal attention and dollars are likely to flow: pilot-line automation, dry electrode processing, domestically abundant cathode chemistries and grid-scale storage for data centers. Companies able to plug into the national laboratory network may find a faster route from demonstration to production, while the emphasis on abundant materials could shift the competitive map away from chemistries that depend on constrained minerals. The 2030 and 2035 deadlines give the effort a scorecard, and the demand curve behind it gives the private sector a reason to stay engaged. artigo.texto: O Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) já credenciou 11 empresas para o fornecimento de equipamentos destinados a projetos de armazenamento de energia no Brasil. Entre as empresas já credenciadas pelo BNDES estão as brasileiras WEG, Moura, You.On e SecPower, além das empresas Canadian, BYD, Gotion, TBEA e Trina. A lista também passou a contar com a Windey Brasil, que está implantando uma fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento em Camaçari, na Bahia. O banco também reconheceu a Windey entre empresas para o desenvolvimento de software e firmware dos sistemas de gerenciamento de energia (EMS), que ainda conta com Moura, Automa e Reivax. O credenciamento permite que os fabricantes avancem na habilitação de seus equipamentos para acesso às linhas de financiamento do BNDES. A movimentação ocorre às vésperas dos leilões de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência (LRCap) com participação de baterias, previsto para 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. Uma das modalidades do certame, o Produto A, prevê a contratação de sistemas de armazenamento com exigências de conteúdo local, vinculadas ao credenciamento no CFI. Windey na Bahia A fábrica da Windey em Camaçari receberá investimento anunciado de R$ 100 milhões e ocupará uma área de aproximadamente 25 mil metros quadrados. A unidade terá capacidade produtiva prevista de 2 GWh por ano e deverá iniciar as operações em 2027. Será a primeira base de manufatura de sistemas de armazenamento da companhia fora da China, com produção destinada aos mercados brasileiro e latino-americano. A iniciativa também representa um movimento de entrada de fabricantes estrangeiros na cadeia industrial brasileira de baterias, em um momento em que o país busca ampliar a participação da indústria nacional no fornecimento de equipamentos para o setor elétrico. Em nota, o CEO da Windey Brasil, Ricardo Galvão, afirmou que a escolha da Bahia para sediar a primeira fábrica da companhia fora da China considerou a localização, a estrutura industrial e a presença de empreendimentos de energias renováveis no estado.

artigo.texto: A BYD aguarda a realização do leilão de reserva de capacidade para baterias para decidir se ampliará sua estrutura industrial ou construirá uma nova fábrica em Manaus, no Amazonas. A companhia mantém negociações com aproximadamente 70 empresas interessadas em adquirir sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês), mas considera a realização do certame e as exigências de conteúdo nacional determinantes para sua estratégia de investimentos no Brasil. Durante conversa com jornalistas após participar do 2º Fórum de Análise Setorial da Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE), Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente da BYD, afirmou que a ação civil pública movida pela Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica (Abeeólica) para suspender os leilões trouxe uma nova fonte de insegurança para os investimentos. Apesar da disputa judicial, o executivo disse não esperar o adiamento do certame, considerando a reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Em junho, a BYD anunciou investimentos de até R$ 500 milhões em baterias no Brasil, em um projeto relacionado à sua estrutura industrial em Manaus, com foco no atendimento ao mercado nacional. A unidade tem previsão para produzir até 10 GW. A companhia já havia questionado o índice mínimo inicial de nacionalização de 15% para sistemas de armazenamento de energia aplicável aos projetos que buscam habilitação nos leilões, por considerar o percentual baixo. Posteriormente, a fabricante passou a integrar a lista de empresas credenciadas pelo Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) para participação no certame. A definição sobre ampliar a capacidade existente ou construir uma nova unidade industrial dependerá das condições de contratação e das perspectivas de demanda no mercado brasileiro. Veículos elétricos como armazenamento Além dos sistemas estacionários, a BYD aposta no potencial das baterias utilizadas em veículos elétricos e híbridos plug-in para oferecer serviços ao sistema elétrico. Segundo Baldy, a frota brasileira desses automóveis já reúne quase 15 GWh de capacidade de armazenamento de energia, que poderia contribuir para o atendimento da demanda e para situações emergenciais. O executivo citou a atuação da empresa durante as enchentes no Rio Grande do Sul, quando 50 veículos foram enviados para auxiliar no fornecimento de eletricidade a estruturas do Corpo de Bombeiros e da Polícia Militar. Também mencionou aplicações para abastecer equipamentos hospitalares e assegurar o funcionamento de urnas eletrônicas. De acordo com Baldy, as baterias de 82 veículos perdidos nas inundações puderam ser reaproveitadas porque os sistemas de proteção impediram danos aos equipamentos. Outra oportunidade apontada pelo executivo é a possibilidade de os proprietários carregarem seus veículos nos períodos de energia mais barata e devolverem eletricidade à rede nos horários de preços mais elevados. Esse modelo, conhecido como vehicle-to-grid (V2G), permitiria maior participação dos consumidores no gerenciamento da energia e abriria novas oportunidades de negócios. Na avaliação de Baldy, a expansão dessas aplicações dependerá de avanços na regulamentação do setor elétrico, diante das mudanças no perfil de consumo provocadas pela eletrificação da frota.

artigo.texto: A eletrificação de automóveis, ônibus e caminhões pode movimentar mais de R$ 200 bilhões em investimentos no Brasil, segundo estimativa da BYD. A companhia aposta na redução dos custos operacionais dos veículos elétricos e na expansão da infraestrutura de recarga para impulsionar esse mercado, com planos de instalar mil carregadores ultrarrápidos no país até o fim de 2027. A projeção foi apresentada por Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente da BYD, durante o 2º Fórum de Análise Setorial da Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE). Na avaliação do executivo, o Brasil reúne condições para protagonizar uma das transições energéticas mais competitivas do mundo, devido à abundância de fontes renováveis e ao avanço das tecnologias de armazenamento. Baldy destacou que a decisão de compra dos consumidores é influenciada tanto por fatores relacionados à sustentabilidade quanto pela economia proporcionada pelos veículos elétricos. Segundo ele, rodar com um automóvel carregado na tomada de casa pode custar até nove vezes menos do que utilizar gasolina em um veículo a combustão. Mil carregadores ultrarrápidos até 2027 Como parte da aposta na expansão da mobilidade elétrica, a BYD pretende instalar mil carregadores ultrarrápidos no Brasil até o fim de 2027. A companhia lançou no país um equipamento com potência de 1,5 MW, associado a um banco de baterias que permite realizar recargas sem exigir uma infraestrutura de conexão à rede elétrica equivalente à potência máxima do carregador. O primeiro equipamento já está em operação em Brasília. Segundo Baldy, a tecnologia permite carregar a bateria de 50 kWh de um veículo de 20% a 80% em aproximadamente quatro minutos. A recarga de 10% a 97% pode ser realizada em cerca de oito minutos, proporcionando autonomia superior a 400 quilômetros, conforme o modelo. Na China, de acordo com o executivo, a BYD instalou 12 mil carregadores com essa tecnologia em um período de dez meses. A associação dos carregadores a sistemas de armazenamento é uma das alternativas para ampliar a infraestrutura de recarga, especialmente em locais onde a capacidade disponível na rede elétrica representa uma limitação. Ônibus elétricos têm custo de operação 65% menor Baldy também destacou o avanço da eletrificação do transporte coletivo em São Paulo, que já conta com mais de mil ônibus totalmente elétricos. Segundo o executivo, apesar dos desafios iniciais para adaptar as garagens e instalar os sistemas de recarga, os operadores que adotaram a tecnologia não demonstram interesse em retornar aos veículos movidos a diesel. Para a empresa, os ônibus elétricos apresentam custos de operação com eletricidade aproximadamente 65% inferiores aos gastos com diesel, além de despesas de manutenção cerca de 70% menores. A redução dos custos também começa a impulsionar a eletrificação dos segmentos de caminhões e veículos utilitários. O executivo mencionou ainda aplicações de baterias no transporte ferroviário. Os trens desenvolvidos pela BYD para o monotrilho da Linha 17-Ouro, em São Paulo, possuem sistemas próprios de armazenamento, que permitem continuar a operação até a estação seguinte em caso de interrupção do fornecimento externo de energia. Eletrificação pode reduzir emissões em São Paulo Além dos ganhos econômicos, Baldy destacou o potencial de redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa com a substituição de veículos a combustão por modelos elétricos. Como exemplo, citou a frota de São Paulo, que reúne mais de 12 mil ônibus e entre 3,8 milhões e 3,9 milhões de automóveis em circulação diariamente. Segundo estimativa apresentada pelo executivo, a substituição desses veículos por modelos elétricos poderia reduzir as emissões de carbono na cidade em aproximadamente 9 milhões de toneladas por ano. Baldy também mencionou o avanço da eletrificação nos serviços de transporte por aplicativo. De acordo com ele, uma empresa do segmento já possui quase 70% de sua frota eletrificada, sendo aproximadamente 62% composta por veículos da BYD. Para o vice-presidente da companhia, a combinação entre a expansão da infraestrutura de recarga, a redução dos custos de utilização e a disponibilidade de energia renovável deverá acelerar a eletrificação do transporte e ampliar as oportunidades de negócios no setor elétrico brasileiro.

artigo.texto: Por: Gustavo Estrella* A inteligência artificial deixou de ser apenas uma tendência tecnológica para se tornar uma força concreta de transformação econômica. Por trás dessa revolução, existe uma infraestrutura crítica que tem ganhado protagonismo recentemente: os data centers. E, junto com eles, cresce também um debate inevitável sobre energia, planejamento e competitividade. O avanço acelerado da IA generativa, da computação em nuvem e do processamento de dados está provocando uma corrida global por infraestrutura digital. Hoje, projetos que demandavam consumo de 20 megawatts já dão lugar a empreendimentos de 100 MW ou mais. Segundo projeções da Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação (Brasscom), a capacidade instalada de data centers no Brasil deve triplicar até 2031, passando de 1 GW para 3,1 GW, movimento que pode atrair cerca de US$ 92 bilhões em investimentos no país. Esse crescimento reposiciona o Brasil no mapa global da economia digital. O país já concentra cerca de metade do mercado latinoamericano de data centers e reúne vantagens competitivas importantes, matriz elétrica majoritariamente renovável, disponibilidade de energia limpa, conectividade crescente e capacidade territorial para expansão de infraestrutura. Em um cenário em que grandes empresas de tecnologia assumem metas cada vez mais rígidas de descarbonização, energia renovável deixa de ser diferencial e passa a ser requisito estratégico. O setor elétrico historicamente cresceu em linha com a demanda, acompanhando o desenvolvimento da economia, o aumento da população e a atividade industrial. Com a chegada e o avanço dos data centers, porém, entramos em uma nova dinâmica: o consumo de energia passa a crescer em ritmo muito mais acelerado, impulsionado pela digitalização, pela inteligência artificial e pela crescente necessidade de processamento de dados. Esse movimento representa, ao mesmo tempo, uma grande oportunidade e um desafio para o setor, que precisará acelerar investimentos e modernizar a infraestrutura elétrica para acompanhar esse novo patamar de demanda, garantindo segurança, confiabilidade e competitividade no fornecimento de energia. Diante dessa nova dinâmica, um ponto central permeia essa discussão: o crescimento dos data centers é indissociável do desenvolvimento coordenado da infraestrutura elétrica. Temos debatido este assunto com autoridades, operadores de data centers, investidores e especialistas sobre como alinhar o avanço da economia digital à capacidade energética do país. Nessas discussões, fica evidente que o principal gargalo não é a oferta de energia, mas a conexão à rede elétrica e o prazo de expansão da infraestrutura. Enquanto a demanda por conexão exige respostas em até 24 meses, projetos estruturantes do setor elétrico podem levar de cinco a oito anos. Essa diferença de velocidade desafia a competitividade do Brasil na disputa global por investimentos. Apesar de também desafiador, países da Ásia e os Estados Unidos já avançam em incentivos, segurança regulatória e aceleração de licenças. No Brasil, o debate começa a ganhar força a aprovação do PL 278/2026 (ReData), que prevê isenção de impostos federais para equipamentos de data centers. Nesse contexto, Campinas, uma das cidades de nossa área de concessão, desponta como um dos principais polos estratégicos para essa nova economia digital. A região reúne um ecossistema consolidado de inovação, universidades, mão de obra qualificada, infraestrutura logística e conectividade robusta. Soma-se a isso a disponibilidade energética e a presença de grandes corredores de transmissão, fatores decisivos para operações intensivas em consumo de energia. Para empresas de energia, esse movimento inaugura uma nova agenda estratégica. Na CPFL Energia, entendemos que o avanço dos data centers exigirá investimentos contínuos em redes, subestações, digitalização e planejamento integrado da infraestrutura elétrica. Por isso, ampliamos os investimentos em inovação, redes inteligentes e eficiência operacional para preparar o sistema elétrico para uma demanda cada vez mais intensiva em dados e inteligência artificial. O setor elétrico deixa de ser apenas fornecedor de energia e passa a atuar como viabilizador do crescimento econômico e digital do país. O debate sobre data centers não pode ser tratado apenas como uma pauta de tecnologia. Trata-se de uma agenda de desenvolvimento econômico, atração de investimentos, geração de empregos qualificados e modernização da infraestrutura nacional. O Brasil tem todos os ativos necessários para liderar esse movimento. O desafio agora é transformar potencial em capacidade de execução. Na CPFL Energia, estamos comprometidos em atuar como parceiros estratégicos dessa transformação, porque a nova corrida global da inteligência artificial também será uma corrida por energia. Os países que conseguirem alinhar expansão digital, segurança energética e sustentabilidade estarão mais preparados para liderar o próximo ciclo de crescimento econômico *Gustavo Estrella é presidente da CPFL Energia

Good morning. Andrew here. We’re getting ready for our annual DealBook Summit tomorrow. The past week has brought an avalanche of news, and you’ve sent us some extraordinary questions for our onstage interviewees, including Vice President JD Vance, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada, Elon Musk of SpaceX, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Christine Lagarde of the European Central Bank, Satya Nadella of Microsoft, the entrepreneur Hailey Bieber and many more.
We’ll have a special edition of DealBook tomorrow morning with information about how you can follow along all day. Now onto today’s news. (Was this newsletter forwarded to you? Sign up here.)
Nvidia’s next big test
Stock markets appear poised for more losses as the artificial intelligence sector, and Nvidia in particular, continued to weigh on investors.
The chipmaker is facing its latest crucible since the resignation last week of its leader, Jensen Huang: quarterly earnings. They will underscore the debut of Colette Kress’s era as interim C.E.O., with analysts ready to pepper her with questions about the health and future of the chipmaker, including whether her old boss might seek a comeback and whether she’ll turn off the investment spigot.
The latest:
Analysts want to know what lies ahead for Nvidia. That includes the true state of its China business amid questions about Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a data center company accused of smuggling Nvidia chips to China and who U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese asset. (Yesterday, the Trump administration moved to block China from gaining access to Nvidia chips via data centers based outside its borders.)
They will also want to know about efforts to find a permanent replacement for Huang, particularly as a “who’s who” list of Silicon Valley seeks to restore the former Nvidia chief to his position. Also potentially in favor of such a move: President Trump, who told reporters yesterday, “I would not mind that.”
Some analysts may also ask about the solidity of Nvidia’s chip sales after Huang’s departure, particularly after Elon Musk, a major customer, warned publicly that “at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”
All eyes will be on Kress, Nvidia’s former C.F.O., who, news reports suggest, had raised questions about the company’s increasingly expansive financial guarantees to A.I. businesses.
One challenge that may emerge for her is Huang’s two children, Madison Huang and Spencer Huang, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez, all of whom remain executives at the company. The Times reports that Kress — and many other executives — had clashed with Madison Huang, who essentially served as her father’s chief of staff.

artigo.texto: McDowell County residents raise concerns as data center moratorium nears expiration MCDOWELL COUNTY, N.C. (WLOS) — McDowell County residents are asking how a potential data center could affect local power, water and infrastructure as county leaders consider what rules might apply if a project moves forward. The county enacted a six-month moratorium on data centers in August 2026, which is set to expire in February 2027. Residents urged commissioners to extend the pause and put stricter regulations in place. The county cannot outright ban data centers, according to commissioners, but it can establish rules for a project. ASHEVILLE SETS 2 VIRTUAL INFORMATION SESSIONS ABOUT ITS DATA CENTERS STUDY "My hesitation is the lack of knowledge," resident Susan Elliott said. "I believe that once we began meeting in our group, we realized that there are many more things that we don't know than that we do know." Some residents said they worry there isn’t enough information to make an informed decision on regulations before the moratorium expires. Janice Whitson questioned whether the county’s infrastructure could support a data center while the region continues recovering from Helene. "My concern is, can we handle that from a data center? Is that possible, that our current system can handle it?" Whitson said. ASHEVILLE CITY COUNCIL APPROVES 1-YEAR PAUSE ON NEW DATA CENTER DEVELOPMENT Resident Melissa Biddix raised concerns about electricity use and potential effects on power costs. County officials said the planning board is considering requirements that could include studies of noise, water and power use, as well as buffers separating data centers from nearby homes, schools and businesses. The McDowell County Board of Commissioners is scheduled to continue its discussion Monday, Nov. 23, at 6:30 p.m. in the lower-level boardroom, McDowell County Services Building, 60 East Street, Marion, NC. The meeting is open to the public.

artigo.texto: LAS VEGAS, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- From November 17 to 19, 2026, HiTHIUM, a leading global energy storage technology company, showcased its integrated energy storage solutions and end-to-end delivery capabilities at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas. Organized around storage duration, the exhibition featured solutions spanning 2 to 8 hours, highlighting HiTHIUM's lithium-sodium technology portfolio, grid integration capabilities, and applications for AI data centers and microgrids. 8-Hour LDES: Unlocking Greater Lifecycle Value As renewable energy penetration increases across the United States, the duck curve is becoming more pronounced, particularly in solar-intensive markets such as California. Meanwhile, the rapid expansion of AI data centers and extreme weather events are driving greater demand for continuous power and grid resilience. These trends are strengthening the need for long-duration energy storage. In response, HiTHIUM presented its ∞Power 6.9+MWh 8h solution, featuring a native 8-hour architecture in a standard 20-foot container and powered by its self-developed ∞Cell 1300+Ah battery cell. Designed for a 25-year service life, the system achieves a DC round-trip efficiency of at least 96%. Compared with a 5MWh configuration, it requires approximately one-quarter as many battery cells per GWh, 27% fewer containers, and 68% less peak auxiliary power, helping improve overall project economics. Sodium-Ion Solutions: Broadening Technology Choices and Advancing Cost Competitiveness Lithium resource concentration and price volatility are important considerations for U.S. customers. Sodium resources are more than 400 times as abundant as lithium and are more evenly distributed. As sodium-ion production scales, its cost is expected to decline toward parity with lithium-ion, expanding customers' technology choices. HiTHIUM showcased its Next-Generation Sodium-Ion Energy Storage Solution ∞Power N4.0MWh, powered by its self-developed ∞Cell N785Ah sodium-ion battery cells. Designed for long-life energy storage applications, the solution features a cell cycle life of up to 20,000 cycles and a system design service life of 30 years. By advancing both lithium-ion and sodium-ion technologies, HiTHIUM is further expanding its energy storage technology portfolio and offering customers more options for diverse application scenarios. Grid Integration: Strengthening Local Validation Capabilities HiTHIUM also highlighted grid analysis and validation capabilities, including plant-level modelling, automated simulation, RMS and EMT benchmarking, hardware-in-the-loop verification and site measurement validation. Its SIT test platforms operate in Xiamen, Chongqing and Dallas; a European regional pre-commissioning platform is under construction in Spain and scheduled for completion in 2027. Expanding into AIDC and Microgrid Applications For AI data centers, HiTHIUM presented an integrated solution spanning battery containers, PCS, PPC, EMS and lifecycle services. Its portfolio includes LFP systems for durations above 2, 4 and 8 hours, as well as a sodium-ion option for durations above 2 hours. For cold-chain warehousing, food processing and industrial parks, HiTHIUM's ∞Power 1022kWh liquid-cooled storage cabinet-integrated with PCS, on/off-grid switching and EMS-enables PV-storage coordination and critical-load backup. It stores surplus solar or off-peak power and discharges at peak to cut costs; during outages, it switches off-grid to prioritize refrigeration and other critical loads while dynamically managing remaining loads such as EV charging. With integrated capabilities spanning product development, grid validation, and project delivery, HiTHIUM is committed to addressing the evolving needs of the North American market. Moving forward, the company will continue strengthening its local capabilities and delivering reliable, integrated energy storage solutions to support the region's energy transition.

artigo.texto: WEST RICHLAND, Wash. — Amazon gave West Richland residents a chance to learn more about its proposed data center project as the company faces growing opposition from people concerned about how it could affect the community. The open house took place at Enterprise Middle School and is expected to run until 8 p.m. The proposed data center campus near Lewis and Clark Ranch has drawn attention over its potential size, with plans calling for as many as 21 buildings across roughly 1,000 acres. Residents spoke directly with its experts and learn more about the proposal. But members of Tri-Cities Data Center Watch are used the event to push for more transparency and stronger protections before the project moves forward. "We're resource rich, and they want to come in here and utilize our water in our less expensive land. But the benefit to the community is not anywhere near as high as what Amazon's gonna get out of it. We're not going away. We're gonna fight for the quality of our community and the safeguards that we believe need to be in place," said Liz Emmens with Tri-Cities Data Center Watch. Emmens said her group is concerned about the project's potential demands on local water and electricity, along with noise, air quality and impacts on nearby neighborhoods. She also said the group previously asked Amazon to take part in a traditional town hall, where residents could hear questions and answers together, but the company declined. Amazon said it is aware of residents' concerns and is already working to address them. "When I say, we're here to listen. I mean, we're here to listen and we're here to take feedback and we're engaging with local leaders and stakeholders and residents from all walks of life, from all different perspectives. And all of that matters. All of that counts," said David Tanner with Amazon Web Services. Tanner said Amazon is still in the early stages of planning and does not have any timeline updates for the project. He said the initial phase could bring 120 to 150 permanent jobs, with more than a thousand at full buildout. Tanner also said Amazon would cover its own energy costs and any necessary grid infrastructure upgrades, while generating millions in property tax revenue for the area. The project remains strictly a proposal, and the city has previously said no data center development has been approved and no applications have been submitted.

artigo.texto: HOUSTON, Texas (KTRK) -- The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) has resumed approving data center permits before a community impact review ordered by Gov. Greg Abbott is finished, raising questions from watchdog groups about whether the state followed through on its commitment to pause the process. RELATED: Gov. Greg Abbott directs Texas environmental commission to halt all data center permits, office says Abbott directed the TCEQ to pause permits on Sept. 21 in a letter that also said data center projects must cover all electrical infrastructure costs, result in lower residential electrical bills, and complete audits by ERCOT and the Texas Water Development Board. But on Wednesday, the TCEQ said it has resumed its normal permit review processes, citing a notification that ERCOT had gathered information for the community impact review for pending data center projects. ERCOT told ABC13 the full findings from that review will not be complete until Dec. 10. Watchdog groups said the decision to lift the pause came without warning. "The public was under the understanding that we were waiting for ERCOT to complete its review that they said they would do on or slightly before December 10th. And there was no public notice. And we see just a bum rush of these permits being done by the TCEQ in this moment," Sam Law with FracTracker Alliance said. "I think that Texans were promised a pause on these data centers so that we could understand the community impacts, especially, but also other components of that audit that are not being provided in a transparent way by data center developers," Kathryn Guerra with Public Citizen said. ERCOT sent ABC13 a Nov. 5 update with preliminary findings showing that for medium load projects, 63% could not answer whether they were power self-sufficient and 70% could not answer questions on community impact. ABC13 asked whether permits being approved, including one for a site identified as Starbase Production, meet the requirements Abbott laid out in his September letter. No response had been received as of Thursday. ABC13 also asked for the completed audit from ERCOT, which said the audit will not be complete until Dec. 10. Groups fighting rapid data center growth in Texas said they believe the timing of the new approvals is tied to the recent election. "I think the election results showed this, but Texans really are concerned about data centers. And I think that the governor's idea to have a pause to do studies, it wasn't enough. It was beset by problems," Law said. "Now that we're past the election, we see that that is exactly what's happening. I don't think that comes as a surprise to anyone. The governor's directive was very flimsy. And I think if he intended for the data center industry to be regulated in a meaningful way, he would have called a special session and put a pause on these in a more formal and legal way," Guerra said. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa called for a moratorium on data centers during her campaign and has been outspoken about regulations. Abbott's office had not responded to a request for comment as of Thursday. SEE ALSO: Gov. Greg Abbott calls for data center penalties if not complying with state water laws

artigo.texto: Maharashtra Launches India’s First SO2 Emissions Trading Scheme 20 Nov 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share The Maharashtra government has launched India’s first sulphur dioxide (SO2) Emissions Trading Scheme in partnership with the Emissions Market Accelerator (EMA), seeking to reduce industrial pollution through a market-based system. The initiative follows the implementation and evaluation of the world’s first particulate matter (PM2.5) pollution market in Surat in 2019. EMA is a collaboration between the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab to expand emissions markets across the Global South. The Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB), which is implementing the scheme, has partnered with the University of Chicago Trust to incorporate artificial intelligence into environmental inspections. The launch came nearly seven months after the MPCB began mock trading for the SO2 market. Its proponents said the scheme could improve air quality for approximately 130 mn people in Maharashtra. Environment and Climate Change Minister Pankaja Munde said technology, including AI, would help the state monitor industrial pollution more intelligently while encouraging industry participation and supporting both environmental protection and economic growth. The scheme covers 17 industrial sectors. The MPCB will set emission limits for participating industries and distribute permits, with each permit authorising the release of a specified quantity of SO2. Industries must monitor and report their emissions through Continuous Emissions Monitoring Systems and surrender permits equivalent to their actual emissions at the end of each compliance period. Industries that emit less than their allocation can sell surplus permits, while those exceeding their limits can buy additional permits. This gives companies a choice between investing in emission-control measures and purchasing permits to meet compliance requirements. EMA said permit trading would create financial incentives for cleaner production and technological innovation. MPCB chairman Siddhesh Ramdas Kadam described the initiative as a major achievement for the state and said the approach was intended to develop alongside industry. EMA director Michael Greenstone said emissions markets could reduce pollution while lowering compliance costs and supporting economic growth. EMA co-chair Balaji Srinivasan said US emissions trading had cut pollution by 96 per cent, while J-PAL South Asia deputy executive director Tithee Mukhoppadhyay said the Surat pilot showed that pollution reductions need not harm economic growth. artigo.texto: Powering the Next Phase of AI Data Centers: The Changing Role of Batteries Higher compute density, volatile GPU workloads, and tight go‑live deadlines are reshaping AIDC power design — and redefining battery requirements for high safety and long‑term reliability. AI expansion is constrained not only by grid interconnection queues, but by power hardware’s ability to respond to sudden, large load fluctuations without compromising safety or uptime. The IEA projects global data center electricity demand will nearly double from 2025 to 2030, hitting 950 TWh, with AI facilities driving most of that growth. Grid bottlenecks and power equipment supply chains remain key constraints for developers. For operators, the challenge is more than securing megawatts. Infrastructure must handle rapid load swings, sustain consistent performance over years, and fit real site layouts. This shifts battery evaluation away from simple nameplate energy capacity toward balanced assessment of reliability and safety. From static backup to dynamic‑duty hardware Traditional data center batteries were built for steady‑state outage backup. AI training and inference create fast power spikes and frequent shallow cycling that existing standards poorly capture. Conventional SOC/SOH algorithms, calibrated for stable float conditions, drift heavily under millisecond load turbulence, creating hidden reliability risks. This mismatch between test protocols and real AIDC operating conditions is a central finding from the Ampace AIDC Battery Solutions White Paper. Ampace recommends procurement teams prioritize three capabilities underpinning reliable, safe AIDC operation: high‑rate bidirectional charge/discharge, tolerance to frequent shallow micro‑cycling, and stable current sharing across large parallel battery arrays. Rated kWh alone is insufficient. Ampace stresses operators need proof of both reliable power performance and inherent safety under the thermal, cycling and ageing stress their facility will actually see. This balanced performance is enabled by Ampace’s high‑power semi‑solid-state LFP architecture, which delivers high rate capability while reducing free electrolyte to lower thermal risk. Regional backup rules mask tough performance demands Many North American AIDC projects adopt a five‑minute end‑of‑life backup specification. A common misconception is that shorter backup windows make batteries easier to qualify. Ampace’s analysis shows EOL‑5min requirements demand sustained high‑power output after years of float and dynamic cycling; fresh nameplate capacity tells little about usable power and reliability at end of life. Multi‑cabinet deployments add risk: uneven ageing and current drift can reduce real usable reserve during an outage, undermining both reliability and safety margins. Layered storage: separate critical backup from grid services There is no universal storage design for AI facilities. UPS batteries remain mission‑critical backup, while site BESS and rack‑side storage can deliver peak shaving, renewable integration and demand response where market rules allow. Ampace’s whitepaper advises designers to draw clear boundaries between non‑negotiable backup duties and secondary flexibility use cases early in architecture planning, so grid services never erode the safety and reliability margin of outage reserve. Faster deployment calls for factory‑integrated power blocks Compressed build timelines favor prefabricated power assemblies. Integrating batteries, BMS, thermal controls and fire containment at the factory surfaces interface issues before shipment and cuts on‑site commissioning risk. Ampace’s design approach centers pre‑validated factory power blocks to lock in consistent safety and reliability for hyperscaler and colo deployments. Fast delivery delivers no value if unresolved integration gaps delay acceptance. Safety validation must match installed conditions Cell stability is foundational, but thermal runaway propagation across dense cabinets is the bigger system‑level concern that threatens both uptime and safety. UL 9540A LSFT large‑scale fire testing is built to generate installation‑specific safety data for designers and code authorities. Few UPS battery vendors have published full LSFT results under zero‑clearance dense cabinet layouts. Ampace's safety engineering was further demonstrated through an LSFT of its PU100 UPS battery system, conducted in accordance with UL 9540A Edition 6. The test was conducted in a facility with a 3 m ceiling height and involved zero side-by-side cabinet clearance, 20 millimeters of back-to-back clearance and all cabinets at 100% state of charge. These results apply only to the tested configuration. Ampace reminds engineering teams that safety testing must align with final physical layout to preserve the intended reliability and safety design margin. AI data center battery decisions must be workload‑led, not datasheet‑led. Teams need to define dynamic duty cycles upfront, validate end‑of‑life power capacity, model cross‑cabinet ageing and demand safety evidence matching their installation. Ampace’s core position: the true benchmark for a battery system is consistent high safety and reliable performance under your site’s real‑world stress. About the Author Ampace Ampace is a global innovator in lithium-ion battery technology and energy storage solutions, empowering the next generation of data center and AI infrastructure. Leveraging its integrated capabilities in cell development, battery manufacturing, and system integration, Ampace delivers high-safety, high-reliability battery solutions for data center UPS and Battery Backup Unit (BBU) applications, supporting the evolving power demands of mission-critical infrastructure.
