artigo.texto: NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WTVF) — As data centers continue to expand across Tennessee, residents and local leaders in communities are pushing back. But when it comes to stopping or limiting these facilities, local governments may have less power than many residents expect. Communities across Tennessee have raised concerns about data centers moving into their neighborhoods. In Nashville, city leaders have paused new data center development for now. In Montgomery County, officials passed new zoning rules limiting the size and scope of the facilities. But attorney David Raybin says local governments face significant legal hurdles when trying to block or restrict data center development. "Local governments are ill equipped to deal with this," Raybin said. Raybin explained that Tennessee's legal framework gives data center developers considerable leeway. "Tennessee is very pro-business. We have a lot of statutes that say — you have the right to use the property as you want," Raybin said. At the state level, Tennessee Finance and Administration Commissioner Jim Bryson chairs the state's AI Advisory Council, a group working to help government officials understand the implications of artificial intelligence infrastructure — including data centers. "Data centers are a big issue right now," Bryson said. "Data centers can have a huge economic impact. They also need to understand what the drawbacks are and what the opportunities are — and then they can make an informed decision." The AI Advisory Council is expected to release a statewide action plan before the end of the year. But Bryson says the council's role is to inform lawmakers, not to dictate policy. "If we can provide information that will lead the general assembly to making some legislation, that would be good. But we don't anticipate making any recommendations on legislation," Bryson said. As Tennessee lawmakers return to Nashville in January, data center legislation is widely expected to come up. The central question will be whether the state legislature gives cities and towns more authority to regulate data centers — or whether more of those decisions get made at the state level. artigo.texto: Loudoun supervisors on Tuesday approved a 12-month pause on processing legislative data center applications. The vote came after over 90 minutes of public comment from community members both supporting and opposing the pause. The proposal originated in July from Supervisors Juli E. Briskman (D-Algonkian) and Laura A. TeKrony (D-Little River) who originally asked for a data center moratorium in Loudoun. County Attorney Leo Rogers said the board did not have the legal authority to implement a moratorium on a particular use. However, he said the state code does set 12-month deadlines for the review of legislative applications—applications that require action by the board rather than solely a staff-level review—and that they could implement a pause during that time period. That clock starts when an application reaches the Planning Commission for review, Rogers said. 12-month Pause Details Tuesday night’s resolution applies to legislative applications with the exception of those within specialized tax districts, such as the county’s Rt. 28 Tax District, which is set to expire in December. The resolution states that the board will not act on any data center or substation application beginning Sept. 15 until it completes its work on Phase Two of the Data Center Standards and Location updates to the Zoning Ordinance and comprehensive plan. Those regulations have been under development for nearly two years as the board works to establish new standards for the industry. Substations deemed necessary for “grid reliability” will be exempted and may be scheduled for public hearings. In the meantime, the county staff will continue to accept applications, which will stay in a backlog. Applications that are nearing the 12-month deadline will be taken up if the applicant refuses to extend the review timeline. After the pause timeframe has expired, or after the new regulations are adopted, applications in the backlog will be scheduled for a public hearing with a maximum of five proposals heard during a single meeting at a time. Public Comment Speakers supporting the pause cited concerns with the industry’s impact on the community including noise, emissions, environmental impacts and the need for new transmission lines. Residents in western Loudoun pointed to the Valley Link transmission line that is planned to be built across Short Hill Mountain and near Lovettsville. “By pausing data center development, you are addressing the root cause of the so-called grid reliability issue behind future transmission lines, because we know that whatever happens with Valley North, there's going to be another transmission line coming right behind it,” Ashley Warmeling said. Attorney Woody Turner, whose firm represents numerous communities pushing back against transmission lines, pointed to a week of tech difficulties from some of the country’s largest companies including Microsoft, United Airlines, Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Zelle. “Perhaps the technology sphere should take a pause and figure out what their problems are before they go crazy with new applications,” he said. “But here in Loudoun County, we've been enduring a land use and electrical planning failure for some time. That's also cause for alarm, and it's time for the county and the data centers, who we would like to see them be our partners if they would just join us, take a pause and fix the things that are broken.” Many speakers urged the board to implement the pause and take time to ensure that any new approvals be made with proper mitigation in place to ensure residents are protected. “I am here to support a meaningful temporary pause,” Loudoun Coalition of HOAs and Condo Associations Chair Ben Keethler said. “Loudoun County has experienced extraordinary growth in this industry, bringing significant economic benefits, but also unintended consequences extending well beyond individual facilities. Despite its best efforts, the county has often found itself responding to challenges after they emerge, rather than having the appropriate regulatory framework in place beforehand.” Supporting a pause ensures any new growth happens with an appropriate regulatory framework, he said. Those opposing the pause included several representatives from the data center industry who said the change would harm their businesses, costing them investments they have been working on for years. Changing the rules in the middle of the applications will give Loudoun a bad reputation, they said. “Moratoriums send a signal that an area is closed for business, for data centers, for the trade unions and schools that are training and growing the construction and operational workforce, for the many local businesses that provide goods and services that support the data center industry, and for other significant economic development projects,” Data Center Coalition Virginia Government Affairs Director Nicole Riley said. Loudoun has a good reputation for predictable decisions and fair, well-planned development, Riley said. “[That] would be undermined by a moratorium, creating uncertainty for businesses, property owners, workers, and residents who rely on the county's established processes,” she said. Some speakers said there is no real difference between a moratorium and a pause. “To be clear, a pause is a moratorium, and to be doubly clear, a moratorium is not permitted under Virginia law,” Land use attorney Colleen Gillis said. “I know from conversations that I have had with clients that that will change,” she said. “[Loudoun] will no longer be predictable and fair, and there will be lawsuits that will be filed. Don't pause. Please don't pass the moratorium. I'm saying that not just in my professional role, but as a taxpayer.” Some speakers said the pause would reduce the board’s ability to negotiate deals like the recent announcement from County Chair Phyllis J. artigo.texto: Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (POWERGRID) has extended the bidding schedule for its proposed 50 MW/200 MWh standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) project at the Talaricheruvu Renewable Energy (RE) Project in Andhra Pradesh. According to a corrigendum issued on November 18, 2026, the revised deadline for online bid submission is November 25, 2026, at 11:00 AM. The bids will now be opened on November 25 at 11:30 AM, against the earlier schedule of November 18. The extension applies to Package AP-BESS-13, which falls under POWERGRID's larger plan to set up 1,250 MW/5,000 MWh of four-hour battery energy storage capacity across Andhra Pradesh. What Are The Revised Tender Dates? As per the revised schedule, bidders can purchase the tender documents until November 23, 2026, at 11:55 PM. The online bid submission deadline has been moved to November 25, while the technical and other bid details will be taken up following the revised opening schedule. The tender document fee is Rs 25,000, while the earnest money deposit (EMD) is listed as zero. The bidding documents are available through POWERGRID's PRANIT e-procurement portal under RFX number 5002005819. POWERGRID's BESS Project Targets Grid-Scale Storage The 50 MW/200 MWh project is designed as a four-hour battery storage installation. POWERGRID's scope of work includes the design, supply, erection, testing, commissioning, operation and maintenance of the battery energy storage system. The project is part of Andhra Pradesh's broader 1,250 MW/5,000 MWh BESS programme, which is being divided into multiple procurement packages. These installations are intended to add energy storage capacity to the state's power infrastructure and support the integration of renewable energy into the grid. The latest corrigendum changes the bidding timeline for AP-BESS-13, while the overall project capacity and scope remain as specified in the original tender. What Does The Project Mean For Andhra Pradesh? With a storage capacity of 200 MWh, the Talaricheruvu project will be able to store electricity and discharge it over a four-hour period, helping manage differences between power generation and consumption. Battery storage can help address the variability of solar and wind generation by storing surplus electricity when generation is high and supplying it during periods of lower renewable output or higher demand. It is also part of POWERGRID's larger 1,250 MW/5,000 MWh BESS project in Andhra Pradesh. If implemented across the planned capacity, the programme would provide a larger pool of dispatchable storage to support renewable energy integration, peak demand management and grid balancing.

A receita do terceiro trimestre de 2027 também mais que dobrou em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior, para US$ 115,8 bilhões, acima da previsão de US$ 108,9 bilhões da Factset. A empresa ainda reportou um aumento expressivo nas receitas do segmento de data centers, totalizando US$ 107,6 bilhões, também mais do que o dobro do registrado no mesmo período do ano passado. A empresa informou que 92% de suas vendas continuaram a ser de sua unidade de data center, que inclui a receita de seus chips de inteligência artificial (IA). No guidance, a Nvidia elevou sua previsão para o trimestre atual, afirmando que agora espera vendas de US$ 130 bilhões e margens brutas entre 71% e 2%. artigo.texto: Data centers se tornam alvos estratégicos de guerra Infraestrutura de computação é responsável pela comunicação e funcionamento em diversos serviços essenciais. Gerando resumo Quando uma coluna de fumaça e fogo subiu nos arredores de Sasovo, a quase 500 quilômetros de Moscou, a conclusão de que mais um bombardeio ucraniano chegava às pontes, fábricas ou bases aéreas russas parecia óbvia. A estrutura atingida, porém, era menos evidente: dezenas de metros quadrados de computadores capazes de armazenar dados de um país inteiro. O bombardeio gerou falha em sistemas de pagamento, de transporte e de delivery. Com um impacto gigante e poucas maneiras efetivas de defesa, os data centers entraram no mapa estratégico de alvos militares e devem ser cada vez mais visados nas guerras pelo mundo. Em março deste ano, o Irã lançou um ataque com drones Shahed a duas estruturas da AWS, serviço de nuvem da Amazon, nos Emirados Árabes Unidos, tirando do ar serviços como atendimento telefônico e armazenamento em nuvem. De acordo com a UNIDIR (Instituto das Nações Unidas para Pesquisa sobre Desarmamento), organização pertencente à ONU, esse ataque foi o primeiro registro de uma ofensiva deliberada a um data center como estratégia de guerra. No ataque à Rússia, o problema foi maior. Na segunda semana de outubro, a Ucrânia lançou drones para destruir a infraestrutura de dois dos parques de data centers da Yandex. Em Moscou, São Petersburgo e Novosibirsk, milhões de pessoas tiveram dificuldades em acessar e-mails, e-commerce, aplicativos de transporte, de bancos e de entretenimento. O impacto para o país foi tão significativo que o presidente Vladimir Putin aprovou um decreto em 2 de novembro permitindo que as empresas pudessem armazenar seus dados em instalações estrangeiras temporariamente. Os países mais buscados, segundo empresas de tecnologia da Rússia, são os aliados Cazaquistão e Belarus. No mesmo decreto, Putin também determinou que todos os data centers privados reservem 10% de sua capacidade para atividades estatais. Em uma nação que convive com sanções ocidentais e não possui nenhuma das empresas tradicionais de tecnologia, a Yandex ficou conhecida como “Google da Rússia”, por oferecer um serviços semelhantes aos da gigante americana. “Quando nossos ataques atingiram os centros de dados da Yandex, de repente ficou um pouco mais fácil respirar em muitas plataformas de mídia social”, disse Zelenski em um discurso após os ataques, no início de outubro. “Muitas pessoas perceberam isso. Houve menos ódio, menos divisão e menos provocações.” O movimento foi uma resposta a um ataque anterior da Rússia a uma infraestrutura de data centers e de telecomunicações nos arredores de Kiev, no final de setembro. Na época, além da rede de internet, outros serviços como sinais de emissoras de TV, transporte e sistemas de segurança. O bombardeio matou ao menos três pessoas na capital ucraniana. Além do leste europeu e de países do Golfo, o Irã também sofreu ataques contra data centers em março, em uma operação atribuída aos EUA e Israel. O centro de dados do banco estatal Bank Sepah, em Teerã, foi atingido por um míssil. A instalação era supostamente utilizada pelas forças iranianas para processar pagamentos do exército e da Guarda Revolucionária. Esses ataques deixaram bem claro que esse tipo de infraestrutura é, agora, um alvo militar em estratégias de guerra de diversos países. Não apenas por afetar o desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial (IA) e interromper serviços, mas porque os parques são, frequentemente, erguidos em algum tipo de parceria com o governo dos países, e não apenas comerciais. Os data centers são realmente uma infraestrutura crítica, exatamente como estradas, pontes ou qualquer outra coisa. Connor Martin, pesquisador do Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) “Eles são centrais para o poder econômico de um país e os próprios governos usam alguns desses data centers para vários serviços. Mesmo os data centers ‘comuns’ são completamente vitais para muitos dos serviços logísticos dos quais todos dependemos”, afirmou Connor Martin, pesquisador em Relações Internacionais do think tank americano Council on Foreign Relations (CFR). A ideia de mirar data centers como alvos militares, mesmo que de forma isolada, deu um salto neste ano, mas não é exatamente nova. Quando a Rússia iniciou a guerra com a invasão no território ucraniano em 2022, os data centers do outro lado da fronteira já eram atacados. Foi quando a Ucrânia começou a migrar o processamento de dados de diversos serviços para fora do país. Mas, naquela época, os data centers não entravam em uma lista de alvos tão críticos quanto usinas de energia, por exemplo. “O governo ucraniano tem sido muito aberto e público sobre o papel que essas empresas de tecnologia desempenharam em manter a resiliência e a sustentabilidade da infraestrutura digital. (A migração de dados) foi um momento-chave nessa discussão”, afirmou Hugo Rosemont, pesquisador sênior do departamento de Estudos de Guerra da King’s College University, em Londres. Caros para construir, fáceis de atacar Gigantes, os parques de data centers ocupam dezenas ou centenas de quilômetros quadrados em áreas afastadas de centros urbanos. O alto consumo de energia para o funcionamento dos computadores gera calor residual - de acordo com um estudo da Universidade do Arizona, nos EUA, um data center de grande porte, com potência de cerca de 36MW, por exemplo, dissipa a mesma quantidade de calor do que o funcionamento elétrico de 40 mil residências. O rastro térmico deixado por esses complexos os torna um elemento fácil de identificar com equipamentos relativamente simples. Eles brilham como árvores de Natal nas imagens térmicas de satélite e são facilmente detectados por drones térmicos. artigo.texto: A nova regra do Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos que passa a exigir licença para a venda de chips avançados de inteligência artificial (IA) ao Brasil não deve inviabilizar os projetos de data centers no País, mas tende a afastar investidores. A avaliação é da Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Software (Abes). “Essa política não necessariamente vai causar um problema no curto prazo, mas ela vai causar uma inibição de investimentos”, disse Marcelo Almeida, diretor de relações governamentais da entidade. Segundo ele, a medida deve afetar não só o que é importado diretamente dos EUA, mas também os chips produzidos na Ásia com tecnologia americana, que entram no alcance da norma. De janeiro a outubro deste ano, o Brasil importou US$ 7,2 bilhões em circuitos integrados e microconjuntos eletrônicos, categoria que inclui os chips, segundo dados do Comex Stat, sistema do Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC). O valor já supera em 29,8% o total do ano passado, que foi de US$ 5,55 bilhões. A Ásia, sem contar o Oriente Médio, respondeu por 96,5% das compras de chips do Brasil neste ano. Para Almeida, a regra parece ser mais uma iniciativa americana “com medo da expansão tecnológica protagonizada pela China”. O Brasil, segundo ele, foi incluído por ser classificado como de risco elevado de desvio de tecnologia. Como em outras decisões recentes do governo americano, faltam evidências que justifiquem a medida, na sua avaliação. Mais burocracia para o Redata O diretor diz que a medida chega num momento ruim, em meio à regulamentação do Redata, o regime especial de tributação para serviços de data center. Segundo Almeida, o presidente afirmou que deve sancionar a regra nos próximos dias. “Você vai ter que estabelecer mais um elemento de burocracia no processo já atrasado do Redata”, disse. “Um inibidor, sem dúvida nenhuma.” As empresas brasileiras que investem em infraestrutura tecnológica devem ser as mais prejudicadas, segundo Almeida. Big techs americanas como Amazon, Google, Microsoft e Oracle, que têm operações de data center no Brasil, também devem ser afetadas, mas em menor grau. A regra dispensa de licença as vendas a empresas com sede nos EUA, desde que quem envia os chips informe as remessas ao governo americano. Trunfo do Brasil “Eu acho que não inviabiliza”, disse Almeida sobre o Redata. Para ele, o Brasil mantém a atratividade em especial por causa da sustentabilidade, “um motor muito poderoso para gerar atratividade de investimentos”. Na sua avaliação, nenhuma regra dos EUA consegue substituir essa vantagem competitiva brasileira. Os data centers viraram tema de disputa nas eleições de meio de mandato americanas, por causa de estruturas antigas, que consomem muita energia e desperdiçam água por não terem circuito de resfriamento fechado, lembrou Almeida. “Não é o que a gente tem no Brasil. Nós temos data centers mais modernos que cuidam dessa questão de sustentabilidade ambiental.” Alternativas chinesas aos chips americanos já são usadas no País. Segundo o diretor da Abes, há estruturas de grande processamento no Brasil com tecnologia da Huawei, por exemplo. Para ele, porém, esses fornecedores não conseguem atender ao volume de demanda e não devem funcionar como substitutos. A regra A norma, divulgada nesta segunda-feira, 16, como regra provisória com efeito imediato após sua publicação, exige licença para exportar, reexportar ou transferir chips e computadores avançados de IA para Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia. O governo americano classifica esses países como de risco de desvio maior que o normal. Os pedidos serão analisados caso a caso, levando em conta a eficácia do controle de exportações de cada país e a cooperação com o Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão do Departamento de Comércio. O objetivo declarado é impedir que empresas chinesas usem data centers no exterior para ter acesso remoto a chips americanos. A Associação Brasileira da Indústria Elétrica e Eletrônica (Abinee) disse, em nota, que está avaliando os eventuais impactos da norma. artigo.texto: DENVER—An effort to keep data centers off America’s public lands stalled a key vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA, S. 5653) in the Senate Wednesday night. Oregon Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley objected to a time agreement for amendment votes on the permitting bill after senators controlling the debate left Wyden’s amendment to ban data centers on public lands off their list of potential votes. “Republicans are blocking a simple vote on my amendment to ban data centers on public lands,” Wyden wrote on X. “Republicans are too afraid to stand up to Trump even though Americans overwhelmingly voted to rein in data centers.” On Wednesday, just hours before Wyden’s data center amendment hit the Senate floor, 115 conservation, community, and faith groups sent a letter to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins calling for an immediate moratorium on new commercial data centers on public lands. The Trump administration, they wrote, is moving ahead without first resolving whether this new industrial use is legally authorized on public lands. At least 17 data center campuses and 13 related infrastructure projects have been proposed on more than 24,000 acres of public land in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Wyoming, according to Bureau of Land Management records. Backers of BAAJA are making clear the AI industry would benefit from the bill. In separate remarks this week, Senator Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma and House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie of Kentucky pitched the permitting bill as essential to continuing the AI data center boom. Armstrong, the former CEO of pipeline giant Williams Companies and a key BAAJA negotiator and supporter, told the Senate on Tuesday that “nowhere is that connection between infrastructure and affordability more important than when it comes to the tremendous growth that we’re seeing from data centers.” If the bill fails, he warned, “our data center and artificial intelligence leadership will follow them right out the door.” A day later, Guthrie told an energy industry audience that removing provisions sought by Senator Mike Lee of Utah would make “the deal fall apart.” Lee’s provisions would curb the use of the National Historic Preservation Act to review projects, a change Tribal nations have opposed. Guthrie tied keeping the bill intact to the growth of AI, warned against local data center moratoriums, and said that for data centers, “The answer is to build more energy.” Armstrong also told colleagues the bill requires data centers to pay “100 percent of all grid upgrade cost.” That same day, BAAJA’s lead sponsors filed a manager’s amendment exempting facilities used primarily for “internet access” or telecommunications from those cost requirements. An Earthjustice analysis found the exemption could reach cloud platforms like Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud, along with AI service providers, calling it “a significant loophole in the ratepayer protection provision.” The sponsors’ offices say the language is meant to cover home internet providers. An energy attorney told Politico it “does create new bases for disputes over what’s covered and what’s not.” Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, who is co-sponsoring BAAJA, also has a personal stake in the data center boom. He holds between $2.1 million and $8.6 million in shares of companies tied to data centers, including NVIDIA and Oracle, according to Forbes, which ranked him first among senators with data center-linked investments. Oracle Cloud is among the services Earthjustice says could escape the bill’s cost requirements under the new exemption. The latest developments around BAAJA’s impacts on data centers undermine arguments from Whitehouse and BAAJA’s other Democratic co-author, Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who still disingenuously claim that BAAJA “does not permit data centers on public lands.” The push to pass BAAJA comes just two weeks after voters across the country approved dozens of local ballot measures restricting data center development. The Center for Western Priorities released the following statement from Communications Director Kate Groetzinger: “BAAJA supporters are finally saying the quiet part out loud, admitting the bill weakens protections for public lands and sacred sites so tech companies can build and power AI data centers faster. And the one provision meant to protect families from paying for data centers’ energy costs now has a massive loophole. Voters just rejected data center growth. This lame-duck Congress is not listening.” Learn more: - Is the Trump administration illegally authorizing data centers on public land? – Westwise - Senator Armstrong says BAAJA would speed data center buildout – Center for Western Priorities on Instagram - Coalition of 115 Groups Calls for Immediate Data Center Moratorium on Public Lands – Common Dreams - Guthrie warns permitting bill could ‘fall apart’ with too many changes – Politico Pro - Green groups decry new data center ‘loophole’ in permitting bill – Politico Pro - BLM Data Center Tracker – Center for Western Priorities Feature image: Utah Data Center located in Bluffdale, Utah and run by the National Security Agency; Source: Swilsonmc, Wikimedia

artigo.texto: $3.26 million in SpaceX AI data center revenue will be pumped back into the City of Memphis — up to $25,000 on offer to low-income residents for repairs and home improvements The city is making its first major investment through the Community Benefit Ordinance, using a portion of the tax generated by SpaceX AI's Colossus 1 facility for the benefit of residents. The City of Memphis has announced that it will make its first major investment as part of its new Community Benefits Ordinance. The fund will use revenue generated by taxing SpaceX AI's Colossus 1 facility to fund various initiatives within the South Memphis neighborhoods around that data center. The fund will help with the costs associated with housing, neighborhood improvements, and services, with the first $2 million allocated for the Memphis HOPE Initiative — a new home repair assistance program that helps residents make vital repairs as well as improvements that will make their homes more accessible. The HOPE Initiative will provide low- and moderate-income homeowners and even renters with up to $25,000 for qualifying repairs and improvements. Eligible improvements include structural repairs as well as plumbing, heating, and air conditioning repairs. Roof repairs and replacement, accessibility improvements, and some exterior improvements like painting, fencing, and landscaping are also eligible. Funds will be provided as a deferred, interest-free, forgivable loan with zero monthly payments. Any required lien will be recorded after repairs are completed and forgiven after three years. SpaceX AI's Colossus 1 data center became fully operational in May 2025, packing 220,000 GPUs and 300 megawatts of compute capacity. A year later, in May 2026, it was announced that Anthropic had signed a lease that would see it take over the entire facility in an effort to ease usage bottlenecks across Claude's paid-for ecosystem. The company said that the additional compute afforded by Colossus 1 would enable higher Claude Code limits, the removal of throttling for Pro and Max customers, and increased API request limits for Claude Opus models. But none of that will matter to those benefiting from the Community Benefits Ordinance, of course. The full breakdown of the $3,259,282 allocation includes: - $2 million for home repair assistance - $309,282 for community grants supporting public safety, youth, workforce development, and other services - $250,000 for paid neighborhood cleanup and beautification jobs - $250,000 for property board-ups and demolitions - $150,000 for blight mitigation and remediation - $125,000 for cooling and air quality equipment for residents - $100,000 for environmental education - $50,000 for grants to health care-focused organizations - $25,000 for Memphis City Beautiful Today's news comes hot on the heels of SpaceX AI CEO Elon Musk telling employees that the company will increase the power capacity of its data centers by 7x to 10 gigawatts by late 2027. The move would see those data centers rake in between $300 billion and $500 billion per year, according to Musk. Perhaps notably, the claim also comes as SpaceX's market capitalization dropped by nearly $570 billion in less than two months. artigo.texto: 17 Novembro 2026 No último dia de agosto, o Instituto de Pesquisa em Direito e Tecnologia do Recife (IP. Rec) e o Instituto Teramar, entre outras 34 instituições, publicaram uma nota pública em que alertavam o Governo Federal sobre os riscos do Redata, o programa que concede benefícios fiscais para a instalação de data centers no Brasil. O primeiro ponto do documento dizia que, antes de estimular uma nova onda de empreendimentos, o Brasil precisaria estabelecer regras para a expansão, avaliar os impactos já observados nos territórios e definir onde e sob quais condições essas infra estruturas poderiam operar. A entrevista é de Maria Carolina Santos, publicada por Marco Zero, 04-11-2026. A mobilização não teve efeito: 15 dias depois, o presidente Lula sancionou sem vetos a lei que criou o Redata. E, consequentemente, abriu o Brasil para o mercado dos data centers – que estão sendo rejeitados pela população dos Estados Unidos, o país com mais estruturas do tipo. Doutor em direito, com foco em Inteligência Artificial, o advogado André Fernandes, fundador e diretor IP.rec – Instituto de Pesquisa em Direito e Tecnologia do Recife, acompanhou de perto a tramitação do Redata em Brasília e a falta de diálogo dos entes públicos com a sociedade civil organizada. Em entrevista para a Marco Zero, o advogado fala sobre o trâmite da lei e de como os data centers podem se tornar mais um problema socioambiental para o Nordeste. Eis a entrevista. Entre a nota de agosto, assinada pelo IP.rec e outras organizações, e a lei sancionada, vocês conseguiram mudar alguma coisa no texto? Não. Na nossa leitura, o texto piorou. O Senado alterou um termo sobre a origem da energia: onde se falava em fontes limpas, entrou “baixa emissão”. A troca veio de uma emenda do senador Laércio Oliveira e foi feita como emenda de redação, que no processo legislativo serve para corrigir uma vírgula fora do lugar ou uma palavra imprópria, sem mudar o sentido. O relator, senador Cid Gomes, é do Ceará, que hoje é uma das fronteiras dessa discussão no Brasil. Ele apresentou a mudança como mera emenda de redação, e a Mesa Diretora da Câmara registrou formalmente que aquilo alterava o conteúdo. Isso aconteceu porque há um lobby muito forte do setor de gás para entrar como fornecedor dos data centers. Ao incluir a baixa emissão, abre-se espaço para essas outras fontes, num Redata que era mais restritivo. O resto foi votação simbólica e acordão, justamente para evitar rediscutir. Se o Senado alterasse o texto substancialmente, ele teria que voltar para a Câmara, que foi a casa iniciadora do projeto. Como o Nordeste fica com o Redata? Vamos ter mais data centers aqui do que em outras regiões? O Redata confirma uma tendência global que apontamos há uns três anos. Os data centers nunca querem jogar dentro das regras: querem benefícios, flexibilizações, retirada de obrigações. Quando o primeiro se instala com essas concessões, vem uma série de projetos a reboque. Mesmo sem o Redata, vemos todo mês o anúncio de dois ou três grandes projetos. Há três anos, praticamente só tínhamos o caso de Caucaia, no Ceará. Depois descobrimos o de Eldorado do Sul, no Rio Grande do Sul. No Ceará já são cinco projetos em tramitação, além do data center do TikTok, que está em construção. Sabemos de projetos no Delta do Parnaíba, no Piauí, em área de preservação. Sabemos de projetos na Paraíba, de medidas do governo do Rio Grande do Norte para atraí-los e de casos no interior de Pernambuco. No Nordeste, os data centers estão vindo na esteira das renováveis. Essa conexão foi feita de maneira estratégica: onde há parques solares ou eólicos, há tentativas de implantar data centers. É o caso da Usina São Clemente, no interior de Pernambuco. Soubemos que há um projeto para um data center lá. Qual a diferença entre um data center e um data center para inteligência artificial? Data center é um centro de dados. Conversando com pessoas leigas, já me perguntaram se tinha a ver com shopping center. Não tem: é um galpão industrial gigantesco cheio de computadores. Existem data centers voltados à conectividade, que garantem velocidade e estabilidade da internet e reduzem a latência, que é o tempo de resposta a uma requisição. Isso é muito útil para aplicações de internet das coisas ou cirurgia remota. Eles consomem muita energia, mas não precisam ser gigantescos. Podem ser distribuídos, no que chamamos de processamento federado, e funcionar em prédios dentro das cidades. São os data centers de borda, ou edge. O data center de IA, que chamamos de hiperescala, muda essa lógica. A inteligência artificial demanda grande poder de processamento e uso intensivo de infraestrutura computacional. Estamos falando de áreas equivalentes a 40, 60, 70 campos de futebol, ocupadas por galpões de concreto cheios de computadores. Quando você vê um vídeo no celular, ele esquenta. Imagine então um galpão com centenas de milhares de aparelhos assim, todos ligados e quentes. O data center também tem um efeito econômico complicado. Hoje os componentes de computador, especialmente placas de vídeo e memórias RAM, estão muito caros e faltam no mercado. As empresas de IA estão comprando tudo, inclusive a produção futura, com dinheiro de investimento especulativo. O data center de hiperescala também exige uma fonte de energia dedicada. Não é como um prédio na cidade ligado à rede pública. E, apesar de todo o argumento das energias renováveis no Brasil, essa fonte de energia para um data center não pode ser intermitente. Quando o vento muda, quando é noite ou está nublado, a produção de usinas eólicas e solares cai. Então os data centers não vão usar apenas a energia das eólicas? Não. Esse argumento é falso, porque eles precisam de energia 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana. O raciocínio puramente econômico, que ignora direitos humanos, tem sua verdade: existe uma oportunidade porque há excesso de energia no Nordeste e o data center pode ser uma alternativa. artigo.texto: Beyond Announced Megawatts: Metlen's Lillian Kasa on Delivering AI Infrastructure Key Highlights - Announced capacity is not deliverable capacity. Data center projects require more than available land and ambitious power commitments. Infrastructure, permitting, financing, and customer deployment must converge on a credible schedule. - Oil and gas offers a development playbook. Metlen's Lillian Kasa argues that AI infrastructure developers should manage project pipelines as portfolios, progressively reducing uncertainty and concentrating capital on the most viable opportunities. - Speed requires commercial discipline. Staged commitments, clearly allocated risks, and power architectures designed around customer requirements can help developers move faster without exposing themselves to unjustified investment. For an industry racing to build infrastructure at unprecedented scale, the most consequential question may no longer be how many megawatts can be announced. It is how many can actually be delivered—and which projects deserve the investment required to get there. As hyperscalers, neoclouds, and data center developers assemble increasingly ambitious capacity pipelines, the distinction between potential and execution has become central to the economics of AI infrastructure. Announcements routinely involve hundreds of megawatts or gigawatts. But behind those numbers lie unresolved questions about power availability, equipment procurement, customer commitments, construction schedules, and financing. For Lillian Kasa, Head of Energy and Data Center Infrastructure Origination for North America at Metlen, these are not simply obstacles to be overcome in pursuit of speed. They are the fundamental questions that determine whether an infrastructure opportunity is worth developing in the first place. In a new episode of the Data Center Frontier Show, Kasa joined DCF Editor in Chief Matt Vincent to examine how developers can distinguish viable projects from speculative pipelines, allocate capital under uncertainty, and build commercial structures capable of supporting the next generation of AI computing infrastructure. The conversation follows Kasa's participation at September's Data Centre West conference in Calgary, where she moderated a panel on Solving for Power. As DCF reported in its Data Centre West 2026 conference analysis, the industry is increasingly discovering that power availability and delivery certainty—not simply land or market demand—determine which projects can proceed. Kasa brings an additional perspective to that conversation: years spent in offshore oil and gas exploration, where capital-intensive investment decisions must routinely be made with incomplete information. Her argument is that AI infrastructure development can benefit from much the same discipline. The Difference Between Announcing Power and Delivering It "When I hear an announcement involving hundreds of megawatts or gigawatts, I really want to understand where those megawatts are, when they'll be available, and what's actually been secured," Kasa told Vincent. An announcement, she explained, can represent widely different stages of development. It might involve an identified site, an interconnection application, or a generation project still years from commercial operation. There is nothing inherently wrong with announcing early-stage opportunities. Every infrastructure project begins somewhere. But the distinction between identifying potential capacity and demonstrating deliverability is becoming increasingly important. Indeed, that distinction was also at the center of DCF's recent Trends Summit analysis, From Announcements to Delivery: What Separates Real AI Data Center Projects From the Rest, which examined the widening gap between ambitious development pipelines and projects with credible paths to construction. A credible project requires land control, a workable pathway to power, permitting, infrastructure equipment, a clear customer requirement, and the commercial commitments needed to justify substantial investment. More importantly, these elements must converge on one realistic development schedule. "You could have a great site and a viable power solution, but if those timelines don't line up, you still don't have a deliverable project," Kasa said. That scheduling challenge is particularly acute in AI infrastructure. AI hardware and computing architectures are advancing at extraordinary speed, while the electrical systems supporting them operate on much longer development cycles. Substation upgrades, transmission expansion, and new generation infrastructure can take years to engineer, permit, procure, and construct. As DCF has examined in its reporting on transmission as a defining constraint for AI data centers, these infrastructure timelines are increasingly shaping where and when new computing capacity can be deployed. A developer may secure an attractive parcel of land and identify a technically feasible power solution, only to discover that the electricity cannot be delivered when the customer needs to deploy its computing equipment. The result is a growing premium on evidence: not simply how much capacity a developer controls or proposes, but how much can realistically be energized within a customer's required timeframe. What AI Developers Can Learn From Offshore Exploration Kasa's proposed framework comes from an industry accustomed to managing enormous financial commitments amid significant uncertainty. Before joining Metlen, she spent much of her career at Equinor, including work involving offshore oil and gas exploration. Such projects can require substantial investment in seismic analysis, subsurface studies, and drilling before the commercial value of a resource is established. The objective is not to eliminate uncertainty before making a decision. That is rarely possible. Instead, developers progressively invest in the information needed to decide whether the next commitment is justified. "

artigo.texto: - Flatiron Energy develops, builds, owns, and operates utility-scale battery storage across the Eastern U.S., with a 24 GWh portfolio, following significant expansion under Hull Street Energy - Rising electricity demand, retiring power plants, and state-backed storage programs are driving demand for firm capacity that supports grid reliability and ratepayer affordability - EQT will support Flatiron’s management team in delivering its contracted projects and scaling its presence, drawing on EQT’s deep expertise across energy and digital infrastructure STOCKHOLM, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — EQT is pleased to announce that EQT Transition Infrastructure (“EQT”) has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Flatiron Energy (“Flatiron” or the “Company”) from Hull Street Energy (“HSE”). Founded in 2021, Flatiron develops, builds, owns, and operates utility-scale energy storage projects across New England, New York, and the Mid-Atlantic power markets. The Company develops projects in dense, capacity-constrained areas, where storage supports grid reliability at times of peak demand. Since HSE’s initial investment in 2022, Flatiron has expanded its portfolio by nearly ten-fold to 24 GWh of capacity, been awarded 6 GWh of long-term contracts, and is in construction on 2 GWh of batteries – including the largest urban energy storage project in the world. In Flatiron’s markets, electricity demand is growing rapidly as older power plants retire and more renewable generation connects to the grid. This dynamic increases the need for battery projects, which store power when it is plentiful and deliver it when the grid needs it. As a result, energy storage capacity is expected to grow in these markets from 2 GWh operating in 2026 to 108 GWh in 2035. EQT will support Flatiron’s management team as the Company delivers its contracted projects, helps communities meet their energy needs, and expands into new markets. EQT intends to invest in the Company’s team and capabilities, drawing on its deep experience of building energy storage platforms and significant expertise across energy and digital infrastructure. EQT has over $100 billion in digital and energy infrastructure assets, with over 260 GW across operating, under-construction, and pipeline energy assets, and a portfolio over 100 data centers, making EQT one of the largest data center developers globally. The acquisition is made through EQT Transition Infrastructure, a strategy that applies EQT Infrastructure’s industrial experience and sector expertise to scale emerging but proven businesses supporting the transition to a decarbonized, more resource-efficient economy. It builds on EQT’s investments in battery storage, including Statera Energy in the UK and Ju:niz Energy in Germany. Benjamin Bygott-Webb, Partner, EQT, said: “Battery storage has become essential to keeping the grid reliable and electricity affordable, as an ageing grid, a changing generation mix and rapidly growing power demand continue to put the system under strain. Flatiron has secured scarce, well-located sites and built a strong record in the communities where it operates. Building on EQT’s deep experience investing in critical infrastructure, our expertise in scaling energy platforms and the opportunities for collaboration across the EQT infrastructure portfolio, we look forward to supporting the Flatiron team as they deliver their projects and bring more firm capacity to the region.” Rob Brink, Chief Executive Officer, Flatiron Energy, said: “We started Flatiron with the mission to bring reliable energy where it’s needed most, in the communities that rely on it every day. EQT is an exceptional firm with a strong track record of scaling platforms in the energy transition, and we couldn’t be more excited to partner with them on our next stage of growth. My co-founders and I are incredibly grateful to HSE, whose unwavering support and belief in our strategy brought us to this point.” Sarah Wright, Founder and Managing Partner, HSE, said: “This transaction underscores HSE’s approach to identifying attractive opportunities and creating long-term value in a rapidly growing and decarbonizing power sector. HSE is highly selective about the management teams we back, and Flatiron is an excellent illustration of why this matters. Because the Flatiron team has a strong track record in the sector and a rigorous, fundamentals-driven approach to setting strategy, they have been able to deliver material growth and value accretion. HSE has appreciated the collaborative partnership with the team as they worked to build the project portfolio and establish Flatiron as an industry leader.” The transaction is subject to customary conditions and approvals. It is expected to close in Q4 2026. Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP acted as legal counsel and Santander acted as financial advisor to EQT. Kirkland & Ellis LLP acted as legal counsel and Guggenheim Securities, LLC acted as financial advisor to the Company. Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath LLP acted as legal counsel to HSE. https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBM.resumo: A Astella, empresa do Grupo ABL dedicada a data centers, cloud e infraestrutura digital, iniciou suas operações com o objetivo de transformar Curitiba (PR) em um importante polo de conexão de uma rede nacional e internacional de centros de processamento de dados. A estratégia combina expansão regional, conectividade global, infraestrutura energética e serviços voltados à crescente demanda por processamento de inteligência artificial (IA). Agnaldo Lopes, presidente do Grupo ABL, detalhou o plano de expansão, que prevê investimentos de aproximadamente R$ 1 bilhão no longo prazo. A primeira unidade, inaugurada em 11 de novembro, recebeu R$ 50 milhões em investimentos destinados à modernização de uma estrutura de 8.800 metros quadrados e 16 pavimentos, que anteriormente abrigou operações de empresas como GVT e Vivo. O data center começa a operar com capacidade de 3,5 MW, expansível para 5 MW, conforme a demanda dos clientes e a disponibilidade de energia. Os recursos foram provenientes da geração de caixa do grupo e de aportes dos acionistas. Segundo Lopes, o aproveitamento de uma estrutura existente permitiu reduzir significativamente os custos de implantação em comparação com a construção de uma unidade do zero A próxima etapa prevê investimentos de aproximadamente R$ 300 milhões entre 2027 e 2028 para implantação de seis novas localidades. Conectividade internacional e integração de data centers Um dos principais diferenciais da estratégia é a parceria com a Megaport, empresa especializada na interconexão de data centers e provedores de serviços digitais. A plataforma permitirá integrar a unidade de Curitiba a uma rede internacional com presença em mais de 1.200 data centers, ampliando as possibilidades de conexão, troca e replicação de dados entre diferentes mercados. "Curitiba será um dos pontos dessa rede. Vamos estar conectados ao mundo por meio desses mais de 1.200 pontos. É diferente de simplesmente contratar um provedor de internet. Estamos falando de conexão entre data centers, troca de dados e replicação de informações", explica Lopes. A infraestrutura deverá viabilizar serviços de baixa latência, distribuição de processamento e redundância operacional. A localização de Curitiba, fora dos principais polos de concentração de data centers, especialmente São Paulo, também é considerada uma vantagem competitiva. Segundo o executivo, testes realizados pela empresa apontaram latência de conexão com os Estados Unidos até cinco vezes menor do que determinadas rotas utilizadas para acessar a infraestrutura da AWS. A rede também poderá atender organizações localizadas em regiões mais distantes dos grandes centros tecnológicos, como o Acre, sem exigir necessariamente a implantação de grandes estruturas locais. Curitiba será o centro de uma rede nacional A unidade paranaense terá papel estratégico na administração da rede, concentrando atividades de gestão, monitoramento, suporte técnico, segurança e operação. A proposta é distribuir processamento e armazenamento de acordo com as necessidades geográficas e operacionais dos clientes. O portfólio contempla serviços de colocation, nuvem privada, cloud híbrida, conexão com provedores de nuvens públicas e edge computing. "Nosso foco é nacional. Estamos começando pelo Sul, mas a rede que estamos construindo permitirá atender clientes em todo o Brasil. O cliente poderá escolher se quer manter seus dados somente em Curitiba ou distribuí-los por todos os pontos da nossa estrutura", afirma Lopes. A interligação permitirá implementar ambientes de contingência e recuperação de desastres (Disaster Recovery), além de ampliar a disponibilidade de aplicações e serviços. A expansão será modular, acompanhando a contratação de clientes e o crescimento da demanda, evitando investimentos antecipados em capacidade sem ocupação definida. Entre os projetos regionais, destaca-se a implantação de um data center em Macapá (AP), que deverá operar no modelo off-grid, com geração de energia integrada à infraestrutura de processamento. Nesse formato, a unidade geradora e o centro de dados serão instalados no mesmo terreno, reduzindo a dependência da rede convencional de distribuição. "Nos outros projetos, vamos trabalhar com o modelo off-grid. O data center será construído junto com a unidade geradora de energia. Macapá será um projeto assim", confirma o executivo. Em Maringá (PR), o grupo também dispõe de uma operação de geração de energia e de uma área que poderá receber um novo data center. A implantação dependerá da evolução dos planos de expansão e das condições de conexão com a concessionária. Infraestrutura preparada para inteligência artificia A crescente demanda por inteligência artificial está entre os principais vetores de negócios da Astella. A unidade de Curitiba foi projetada para suportar cargas computacionais de alta densidade, com sistemas de refrigeração líquida e soluções específicas para racks que exigem maior capacidade de dissipação térmica e consumo energético. A empresa já mantém negociações comerciais e estima que a capacidade disponível poderá estar integralmente contratada em aproximadamente oito meses. Um dos primeiros clientes utilizará a estrutura para processamento e treinamento de modelos de IA, no modelo de colocation. Nesta fase inicial, os investimentos estão concentrados na infraestrutura física, energética e operacional. A aquisição de servidores, equipamentos de processamento e GPUs ocorrerá progressivamente, conforme a evolução dos contratos. No médio prazo, a companhia também avalia desenvolver uma operação própria de cloud e processamento com GPUs, ampliando sua participação no mercado de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial. Para essa etapa, considera utilizar mecanismos de financiamento do programa Redata, especialmente para a aquisição de equipamentos tecnológicos. Soberania digital e segurança cibernética A soberania dos dados é outro componente central do posicionamento da Astella. A empresa pretende atender organizações públicas e privadas que precisam manter informações armazenadas e processadas no Brasil, com maior controle sobre a localização dos dados e os fluxos de comunicação. "Nosso objetivo é criar um modelo de negócios no qual os dados das empresas e do governo permaneçam no Brasil e trafeguem dentro do Brasil", afirma Lopes. Nesse contexto, o Grupo ABL iniciou, há aproximadamente oito meses, um processo de credenciamento junto ao Ministério da Defesa para obter o reconhecimento da empresa como estratégica de segurança. A iniciativa busca fortalecer sua atuação como provedora de infraestrutura nacional para organizações com requisitos específicos de controle e proteção de ativos digitais. A segurança cibernética integra a arquitetura da operação, que prevê soluções de proteção contra ataques distribuídos de negação de serviço (DDoS), firewalls e mecanismos de prevenção a ameaças, implementados com o apoio de parceiros especializados. O grupo já acumula experiência nesse segmento desde 2015, quando implantou sua primeira infraestrutura de nuvem privada em Curitiba, utilizando tecnologia da Palo Alto Networks. A nova unidade foi concebida com referência ao padrão Tier III, contemplando requisitos de disponibilidade, continuidade operacional e proteção dos dados. "Qual é a preocupação do cliente? Primeiro, o servidor não pode parar. Precisamos garantir alta disponibilidade. Ninguém pode roubar seus dados. É isso que estamos trabalhando para oferecer", destaca o executivo. Expansão e geração de empregos A operação de Curitiba iniciou suas atividades com aproximadamente 25 colaboradores, além de oito profissionais vinculados à usina de energia. Com o aumento da ocupação e a entrada de novos clientes, Lopes estima que o quadro de funcionários poderá crescer pelo menos 50%.

artigo.texto: TAYLORS — The wave of data center discontent sweeping the country has finally made it to Greenville County. Data center opponents showed up in force at Greenville County Council’s Nov. 17 meeting, demanding officials reject a rezoning on Wade Hampton Boulevard that would allow a small-scale data center inside an existing storage facility. Opponents — ranging from former council members to high school students — packed a standing-room only meeting, lofting signs that read “SAY NO TO DATA CENTERS” and “AMEND LAND DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS.” More than 1,600 people had signed a petition against the center by the time of the meeting. Many said they weren’t opposed to all data centers. Yet they raised concerns about water pollution, noise and electricity use, and they said the county must create rules to prevent harm to neighboring homes and businesses before allowing new data centers. “How are we protected?” asked Lynn Ramirez, who said the county had fallen behind in providing modern regulations.“Until this council can protect residents from the impacts of these projects by updating their own zoning guidelines to reflect current reality, I urge you to vote no.” Representatives for the developer, Prime Group Holdings, did not speak at the meeting. Previously, company CEO Robert Moser said the facility would be almost entirely self-contained and would have little impact on neighbors. County Council members voted unanimously to send the proposal back to its planning and development committee, effectively postponing the issue until more guidelines can be created. “I’m not an expert on this, and I don’t know if any of us are,” Councilmember Steve Shaw said. “But the applicant needs to explain this to the public.” Data centers are the subject of growing opposition across the United States. Counties and cities throughout South Carolina have passed moratoriums temporarily blocking them. In neighboring Spartanburg County, officials are embroiled in a months-long fight over a $2.8 billion, 457-megawatt data center that has sparked environmental concerns. Opponents consider data centers a serious threat to their quality of life. Advocates argue those concerns are overblown and say the centers are necessary and valuable infrastructure. Data centers have been built in the Upstate for years. At one time, officials welcomed them with open arms as a source of investment and job creation. But as artificial intelligence grows and massive “hyperscale” data centers make headlines, the public has turned against them. Moser said the project was technically not a data center, describing it as an “inference point” to provide “low-latency inferences” for local technology. In other words, it would allow artificial intelligence systems to process information more quickly. It’s faster because it’s nearby rather than hundreds of miles away, Moser said. That can be important for sensitive technology, like robotics used for surgery. Moser said his company, Prime Storage, a subsidiary of Prime Group Holdings, is renovating its storage facilities to house inference points. The storage facility in question is on nearly 5 acres on Wade Hampton Boulevard in Taylors. The large, windowless brick building is steps from Texas Roadhouse restaurant and behind a neighborhood. Moser said the company won’t change the footprint of the building or use local water or sewer services. Residents would not be able to hear anything outside of the property, according to Moser, and it would use about 5 megawatts of energy, which officials said was a relatively small amount. “It's a very low impact, high, high beneficial infrastructure to be deployed,” Moser said at an Oct. 19 public hearing. But residents said nothing prevents the company from changing its mind later on and building a larger data center. That’s because the county lacks any updated regulations for these centers. Rezoning the property from a commercial district to a services district would open the door to a range of industrial uses and potentially much larger data centers. Rachel Fox, who organized the petition and lives near the site, said there are too many unknowns to approve the rezoning. She asked how it would affect her and her neighbors and what would happen if developers decide to build a larger facility. “It is all well and good … to tell us it won't impact our water, our air quality, our noise. But if there is no legal accountability for when promises are not kept, then all we have are words,” she said. Council members quickly agreed that data centers need guardrails and that the rezoning should be postponed. Some suggested the county form a committee or taskforce to come up with regulations. Councilmember Frank Farmer said he’s already drafting such an ordinance. The council initially suggested postponing the rezoning for 30 days, to which the crowd began shouting “no” and asking for more time. After the vote, Council Chair Benton Blount told the crowd that council members hadn’t developed any coordinated plan beforehand to shelve consideration and that the decision was swayed by their concerns.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de eletrodutos metálicos intermediários: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de eletrodutos metálicos intermediários até 2035, impulsionada pela demanda de data centers e pela modernização da rede elétrica Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de eletrodutos metálicos intermediários, o setor chega a 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de suprimento mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de eletrodutos metálicos intermediários (IMC) representa um segmento crítico da indústria de infraestrutura elétrica, conciliando resistência mecânica, proteção contra corrosão e eficiência de instalação para aplicações comerciais, industriais e de infraestrutura. Em 2026, o mercado se recupera das rupturas de cadeia de suprimentos do pós-pandemia e vem sendo remodelado pela aceleração dos investimentos em infraestrutura, pela modernização da rede elétrica e pela rápida expansão de data centers e da automação industrial. O IMC, alternativa de parede mais fina e mais leve que o eletroduto metálico rígido (RMC), é preferido onde se exige proteção conforme as normas, mas a facilidade de instalação e o custo pesam na decisão. A demanda deriva principalmente de novas construções e dos ciclos de investimento de capital, com a demanda de reposição desempenhando papel secundário. A estrutura do mercado reúne fabricantes multinacionais, especialistas regionais e distribuidores atacadistas de material elétrico, todos sujeitos a códigos de construção e normas elétricas rigorosas, como o National Electrical Code (NEC) nos Estados Unidos e padrões equivalentes em outros países. Este relatório oferece uma avaliação abrangente do estado atual do mercado, de seus fundamentos, da dinâmica competitiva e de sua trajetória até 2035, sintetizando dados de produção, consumo, fluxos comerciais e preços para apresentar uma visão holística do ecossistema global de IMC. O cenário-base para o mercado global de eletrodutos metálicos intermediários até 2035 prevê expansão moderada, porém constante, com o crescimento da demanda estreitamente ligado à construção comercial, aos gastos de capital da indústria e aos investimentos públicos em infraestrutura. Espera-se uma aceleração gradual em relação à base de 2026, à medida que as principais economias avancem em programas de modernização da rede elétrica, ampliem a capacidade de data centers e atualizem a infraestrutura de serviços públicos. América do Norte e Ásia-Pacífico devem permanecer as maiores regiões consumidoras, sustentadas pela adoção exigida por normas em edifícios comerciais e instalações industriais. A Europa deve crescer em ritmo mais lento, limitada por mercados de construção maduros, mas apoiada por investimentos na transição energética. América Latina e Oriente Médio e África oferecem potencial de alta com o desenvolvimento de infraestrutura, embora a volatilidade cambial e as restrições de financiamento possam conter o crescimento. Do lado da oferta, a volatilidade dos preços das matérias-primas, sobretudo aço e alumínio, segue como risco relevante, enquanto a capacidade industrial deve se ajustar gradualmente à demanda. O cenário-base não considera grandes rupturas regulatórias e projeta trajetória estável para os gastos com construção, resultando em taxa de crescimento anual composta de aproximadamente 3,5% a 4,5% no período de previsão, com o índice de mercado alcançando cerca de 140 em 2035 (2025=100). Vetores e restrições da demanda Principais vetores de demanda - Aceleração da construção de data centers e da expansão da infraestrutura de computação em nuvem, que exige infraestrutura elétrica robusta para distribuição de energia e gestão de cabos. - Modernização da rede elétrica e atualização da infraestrutura de serviços públicos, incluindo a implantação de redes inteligentes e a integração de energias renováveis, o que impulsiona a demanda por sistemas de eletrodutos duráveis. - Crescimento da construção comercial em economias emergentes e atividade de reforma em mercados desenvolvidos, apoiados por exigências normativas de segurança elétrica. - Automação industrial e ampliação de plantas fabris, contextos em que o IMC oferece proteção mecânica à fiação em ambientes agressivos. - Programas governamentais de investimento em infraestrutura, especialmente em transportes, tratamento de água e prédios públicos, que especificam eletrodutos metálicos para sistemas elétricos. - Maior rigor das normas elétricas e de construção, que exigem sistemas de eletrodutos aprovados para proteção da fiação em ambientes comerciais e industriais. Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - Volatilidade dos preços de matérias-primas, sobretudo aço e alumínio, que pressiona as margens dos fabricantes e pode levar ao adiamento de compras. - Concorrência de outros tipos de eletroduto, como o eletroduto metálico flexível (EMT) e os eletrodutos não metálicos (PVC), que podem ser preferidos em certas aplicações por custarem menos ou serem mais fáceis de instalar. - Desaceleração da construção comercial em mercados-chave devido à incerteza econômica, aos juros elevados ou à redução dos gastos de capital. - Rupturas na cadeia de suprimentos e desafios logísticos, incluindo gargalos de transporte e mudanças na política comercial, que afetam a disponibilidade e os prazos de entrega. - Escassez de mão de obra qualificada no setor de instalações elétricas, o que pode atrasar projetos e conter o crescimento da demanda. artigo.texto: - Coal - 2 min read Maharashtra announces India’s first sulphur dioxide emissions trading market The scheme aims to reduce industrial air pollution by allowing participating plants to trade emission permits. The Maharashtra government on Tuesday announced India's first statewide sulphur dioxide (SO2) emissions trading scheme in partnership with the Emissions Market Accelerator (EMA), an initiative of the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL). According to the official press release, the scheme, to be implemented by the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB), aims to reduce industrial air pollution by allowing participating plants to trade emission permits. Around 130 million people are expected to benefit from improved air quality across the state. Under the proposed market mechanism, plants that can reduce SO2 emissions at a lower cost will have an incentive to make greater reductions and sell their surplus emission permits to plants facing higher pollution-control costs. “Our approach is not to control, but to grow together with industry. Without the active participation of the industries, and the support of our knowledge partners, the University of Chicago, the Emissions Market Accelerator and J-PAL, this would not have been possible,” said Siddhesh Ramdas Kadam, Chairman of MPCB. The initiative builds on the particulate matter (PM2.5) emissions trading market launched in Surat, Gujarat, in 2019. The research collaboration involving the Gujarat Pollution Control Board, J-PAL South Asia and EPIC India demonstrated that emissions trading could reduce air pollution while lowering compliance costs for industry. MPCB to develop AI-assisted inspection framework Separately, MPCB and the University of Chicago Trust, through the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago India (EPIC India), have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to advance data-driven environmental regulation using artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning. Under the collaboration, the two institutions will jointly develop and pilot an AI-assisted inspection framework using data shared by MPCB. The system will help the Board identify industries more likely to be non-compliant. The partnership will also include knowledge-sharing sessions for MPCB officers and inspectors on AI and environmental data analytics. Evidence from the pilot will inform its potential expansion across Maharashtra.

artigo.texto: KANSAS CITY, Mo. — KSHB 41 reporter Isabella Ledonne reports on stories in Overland Park, Johnson County and topics about government accountability. Share your story idea with Isabella. — Evergy wants to build a $4.5 billion power plant generator in Buchanan County, Missouri near St. Joseph to increase energy supply for the Kansas City metro. The energy company says demand has gone up across the board with all customers, but many neighbors in Kansas City are skeptical the new plant is being driven solely by data center growth. "Why are we building these?" one Missouri resident asked during Tuesday night's public hearing. WATCH | KC neighbors speak out on Evergy's proposed power plant amid data center growth That's been the main question during two night's of Evergy's public hearing with the Missouri Public Service Commission for the $4.5 billion new power plant. Dozens of Missouri residents, including many from Kansas City, packed the room on Monday night to share their concerns on how the power plant may impact their lives and electric bills. "We should not be asked to pay the bills for these massive data centers," Cody Boston said. "We went up [to St. Joseph on Monday night] because we recognize that struggle and that problem relates directly to us as well." Kansas City neighbors who have been tracking data center growth, like Boston with the KC Data Center Watch Dog group, see the proposed 1,400 megawatt power generator as a supply for the data center energy demand. "We do not want this," Boston said. "We know it doesn't benefit us, and I hope that they deny this application." But Evergy says it's the opposite, and that the new power generator is necessary to supply power to all customers in both Kansas and Missouri. "Is this plant primarily for large format user customers and if it's not, then why do we need this plant?" KSHB 41 News reporter Isabella Ledonne asked. "This power plant would be built even without the data centers. It was needed without the data centers," chief customer officer Chuck Caisley said. "Now, it's large enough that it's going to accommodate some of that [data center] load, but it's not dedicated to any one data center or caused by any one data center." According to Caisley, 25% of the proposed plant's power will be supplied to Buchanan County and the remaining 75% will be delivered to the Kansas City metro. "That [75%] has nothing to do with data centers," Caisley said. "That is just providing them the power that they need to keep the grid reliable in the way that they have expected to have their power delivered to them." Under Evergy's agreement with Missouri and Kansas, data centers pay 20% more than regular customers and pay for all infrastructure upgrades upfront for their portion of needed energy. "The proportion of this power plant that's going to serve [data centers], they are going to pay entirely for that," Caisley said. But regular neighbors will still pay for the portion they're expected to use, as Evergy reports a 8.2% population growth in the Kansas City metro. "[Regular customers] are using their air conditioner more, they're using computers more, they're around more during the day," Caisley said. "That growth, coupled with data centers, is what's causing the need for us to build these plants." Evergy states bills are lower because of data center payments and any rise in bills is attributed to inflation. "People should not expect a huge spike in their bill, our costs going to go up generally in line with inflation," Caisley said. "Inflation this year is around 3.5%. That's probably a good benchmark for people to think about in terms of us just staying kind of a pace of inflation." But some Kansas Citians still find it hard to believe data centers are a net positive for electric bills. "How much of the power is actually going to benefit residents versus these large load users, the data centers?" Boston said. The Missouri Public Service Commission will have the final say on whether Evergy gets the green light for the proposed power plant in Buchanan County. —

artigo.texto: Texas lieutenant governor-elect Vikki Goodwin, a Democrat who campaigned extensively against what she described as the data center development "crisis" in the Lone Star State, named an active data center lobbyist to her transition team, records reviewed by the Washington Free Beacon show. Goodwin, a four-term state representative, announced her 14-member transition team on Tuesday. Though she emphasized that the team includes both Democrats and Republicans, its reliance on lobbyists is perhaps more notable. Eight of the 14 members are registered lobbyists, including Leticia Van de Putte, who served for more than 20 years in the Texas House and Senate as a Democrat before launching a lobbying firm. Van de Putte—the transition team's co-chair—boasts a number of active clients, most notably Vantage Data Centers, a global data center developer. The company is behind a $25 billion data center campus in Shackelford County, Texas, known as "Frontier." Vantage announced the project in August 2025, saying it would help "meet unprecedented AI demand" and cement Texas as "a strategic, global AI hub." Four months later, in January, it retained Van de Putte on a year-long contract with an anticipated compensation of up to $114,429.99, records show. Texas has indeed become a global hub for data center and AI infrastructure in recent years, though Goodwin campaigned against the industry during the 2026 midterm elections, calling for a "pause on new data center construction" and accusing Republicans of spending "billions on water projects to enable big-tech data centers, instead of prioritizing drinking water for families." She also held a "Data Center Accountability Press Conference," during which she called for a special legislative session to address what she called "the data center crisis." "I, Representative Vikki Goodwin, pledge to protect Texas water and put the people and animals of Texas first," she said. "As Lt. Governor, I will prioritize bills that regulate data centers and protect our water, land, health, and access to electricity." The presence of a data center lobbyist on Goodwin's transition team suggests that the Democrat's crusade against AI infrastructure had more to do with politics than policy. A University of Texas poll released in late June found that a majority of Texans oppose data center construction in their community; Goodwin held her "Data Center Accountability Press Conference" three weeks later. In addition to Van de Putte, Goodwin's transition team includes Tommy Williams, a Republican who served in the Texas House and Senate before advising Gov. Greg Abbott on fiscal policy. He has an active lobbying contract with utility company NextEra Energy, which announced a "strategic energy and technology partnership" with Google to develop "new gigawatt-scale data center campuses" and "accelerate AI growth and transform the energy industry" in December. Van de Putte, meanwhile, also represents Natura Resources, a Texas-based nuclear energy company that says it's working to meet "the unprecedented power needs created by rapid data center expansion." It's unclear if Williams's work with NextEra involves data centers. Williams, Goodwin, and Van de Putte did not respond to requests for comment. Van de Putte, Williams, and the six other lobbyists who make up a majority of Goodwin's transition team will now be tasked with helping the Democrat "build a great staff" and ensure "the Senate will operate effectively," as she put it during a recent press conference. The team's executive director, longtime operative Angela Hale, is also a registered lobbyist. Texas ethics rules do not bar lobbyists from serving on a transition team, as members of such a team are considered advieors rather than employees. If Goodwin were to hire any of the lobbyists as full-time staffers in her official office, they would have to stop lobbying.

artigo.texto: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has expanded its partnership with the Government of Bangladesh to develop five additional solar and battery energy storage projects, taking the total planned capacity under the programme to more than 1,000 MW across six projects. The initiative aims to attract private investment, increase renewable energy generation and strengthen Bangladesh’s energy security by reducing dependence on imported fuels. Under the expanded programme, ADB will provide transaction advisory services for the five additional projects, building on its existing support for the 130 MW Sonagazi solar photovoltaic project in Feni District. The expanded initiative will be implemented through three phases and is expected to mobilise more than $1 billion in private sector investment. The programme will support Bangladesh’s renewable energy targets of generating at least 20% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030 and increasing the share to 30% by 2040. The projects are expected to improve access to reliable renewable electricity while creating opportunities for domestic and international investors to participate in the country’s clean energy sector. The first phase will focus on the 130 MW Sonagazi solar project, which will include a 26 MWh battery energy storage system. The tender for the project is expected to be launched within 2026. As the first project under the partnership, Sonagazi will establish a framework for project development, procurement and implementation for the remaining five projects under phases two and three. ADB will work with Invest Bangladesh and the Bangladesh Power Development Board to assess the suitability of government-owned land for the additional projects. Its advisory support will cover the complete project development process, including project preparation, technical and financial assessments, market consultations, tender document preparation and assistance with competitive bidding and contract awards. ADB Country Director for Bangladesh Qingfeng Zhang said the expanded partnership would help create a scalable market for clean energy investment. He highlighted the importance of stronger project preparation, competitive procurement processes and an investment-friendly environment to attract capital, technology and expertise. Invest Bangladesh Chair Ashik Chowdhury said the government aims to accelerate private sector participation, particularly foreign direct investment, in renewable energy projects. He added that the partnership with ADB would help expand clean energy capacity, diversify the country’s energy mix and strengthen long-term energy security. The memorandum of understanding was signed by Mostafa Kamal, Member (Additional Secretary) of the Public–Private Partnership Division at Invest Bangladesh; Afroza Sultana, Secretary of the Bangladesh Power Development Board; and Qingfeng Zhang of ADB. The expanded initiative represents an important step in Bangladesh’s efforts to develop large-scale solar power and battery storage infrastructure. By combining international advisory expertise with private sector investment, the programme aims to establish a structured pipeline of renewable energy projects and support the country’s transition towards a more diversified and sustainable electricity system.
