artigo.texto: A Casa dos Ventos recebeu pelo Porto do Pecém, em São Gonçalo do Amarante, a primeira carga das turbinas eólicas do complexo eólico Ibiapaba, que vai gerar a maior parte da energia do data center da ByteDance, dona do TikTok, no Ceará. O navio Star Louisiana atracou na segunda semana de novembro com pás de 89,5 metros de comprimento, o início da entrega das 75 turbinas que a empresa contratou da chinesa Envision Energy para o parque. O complexo fica na Serra da Ibiapaba, nos municípios de Tianguá, Carnaubal e Guaraciaba do Norte, e reúne dois parques: Tianguá III, com 25 turbinas, e Serra de Ibiapaba, com 50. Cada máquina da Envision tem 8,4 megawatts de capacidade, e a Dois A Engenharia, responsável pelas obras civis, a considera a mais potente já instalada no Brasil. Em operação, o Ibiapaba vai gerar energia equivalente ao consumo de 800 mil residências, de acordo com a construtora. >> Siga o canal da Movimento Econômico no WhatsApp A Casa dos Ventos fechou a compra das turbinas em janeiro de 2026, num acordo de 630 megawatts (MW) com a Envision que inclui 30 anos de operação e manutenção das máquinas pela fabricante. Operados com inteligência artificial (AI), os equipamentos são do modelo Galileo AI, que estreia no Brasil com esse projeto. A potência do complexo varia entre as fontes: a Dois A informa 589 MW instalados, enquanto o contrato das turbinas e o anúncio do fornecimento de energia ao data center, em maio, falam em 630 MW. A operação em Pecém movimentou quase 5 mil toneladas de carga, distribuídas em 370 unidades. O lote inclui cinco turbinas eólicas completas, com 15 pás e torres divididas em cinco partes, com segmentos de 15,4 a 26,8 metros. O Porto do Pecém classifica as pás como uma das maiores já movimentadas no terminal. O mesmo navio desembarcou mais seis pás eólicas para outros projetos da região, que não foram identificados, o que eleva o total a 21 pás. Vieram ainda equipamentos de grande porte da China e da Índia. Energia do parque vai abastecer o data center do TikTok A energia do Ibiapaba já tem comprador. Em maio de 2026, a Omnia, plataforma de data centers do Pátria Investimentos, assinou com a Casa dos Ventos um contrato de US$ 2 bilhões por 20 anos. O acordo segue o modelo de autoprodução de energia, em que o grande consumidor participa da geração da eletricidade que usa, mecanismo que permite tarifa mais competitiva. O complexo cearense responde pela maior parte do fornecimento. A parte complementar do consumo vem do parque eólico Dom Inocêncio, no Piauí, também da Casa dos Ventos. A primeira fase do data center da ByteDance, no Complexo do Pecém, prevê 200 MW de capacidade de tecnologia da informação, com demanda estimada em cerca de 300 MW de energia. As obras começaram em janeiro de 2026, e a operação está prevista para o terceiro trimestre de 2027, com expansão gradual até 2029. Descarga é a primeira de cinco operações de grande porte O Complexo do Pecém, que administra o porto, apresenta a chegada do Star Louisiana como a primeira de cinco operações de grande porte. O comunicado, divulgado nesta quinta-feira (19), não detalha as outras quatro, nem as datas, as cargas ou os clientes envolvidos. Para o presidente do Complexo do Pecém, Max Quintino, o porto “está preparado para atender às demandas de uma indústria cada vez mais sofisticada e estratégica”. “Mais do que movimentar grandes equipamentos, estamos contribuindo para viabilizar investimentos, fortalecer a cadeia produtiva das energias renováveis e ampliar as oportunidades de desenvolvimento econômico para o Ceará”, afirma. Nem o porto nem as empresas divulgaram o valor do investimento no Ibiapaba ou o prazo para a chegada das demais turbinas. O comunicado também não informa quando o parque deve começar a gerar energia. artigo.texto: Juniper Green Energy Limited has commissioned 94.77 MWh of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity through its wholly owned subsidiary, Juniper Green Stellar Private Limited. The commissioning was completed on November 19, 2026, marking another step in the company’s expansion of its energy storage portfolio. The newly commissioned battery storage capacity will initially operate on a merchant basis, allowing the company to sell electricity directly in the power market. The company also retains the flexibility to shift the capacity to a long-term Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) in the future, depending on market conditions and available opportunities. With this commissioning, the total operational capacity of Juniper Green Energy Limited and its subsidiaries has increased to approximately 2,844 MWp of renewable energy capacity and around 698 MWh of battery energy storage capacity. The company disclosed the development to the National Stock Exchange of India Limited under the stock symbol JNPR. Juniper Green Energy Limited, formerly known as Juniper Green Energy Private Limited, is headquartered in New Delhi and has its corporate office in Gurugram, Haryana. The company continues to expand its renewable energy portfolio while increasing its focus on energy storage solutions. Battery storage systems play an important role in supporting renewable energy integration by storing electricity when generation is high and supplying it when demand increases. The merchant-based operation of the newly commissioned capacity will provide Juniper Green Energy with exposure to market-based electricity prices while maintaining the option of securing long-term contracted revenue through future PPAs. The addition further strengthens the company’s operational BESS portfolio and supports its broader clean energy expansion strategy. artigo.texto: BNZ, an independent power producer (IPP) developing and operating next-generation multi-technology renewable projects, has announced the start of construction works on its battery energy storage systems (BESS) at the Rinaldone and Camposcala projects, located in the Lazio region, Italy. Both infrastructures represent the technological hybridization of the photovoltaic plants BNZ already operates in the region: Rinaldone, with a capacity of 45 MWp, and Camposcala, with 53 MWp. Each of these new battery systems features a power capacity of 27 MW (108 MWh) and a 4-hour duration, allowing energy to be stored during solar production peaks and fed into the grid during periods of highest demand. Construction of the Rinaldone project is being carried out by Grupotec, while works at Camposcala are being delivered by Elecnor, with the objective of commissioning both facilities before year-end. In the words of Luis Selva, CEO of BNZ: "The start of construction of the storage systems at Rinaldone and Camposcala marks a decisive step in our consolidation as a fully-fledged (alt.: comprehensive / integrated) energy operator in Italy. Hybridizing our assets with BESS technology is a cornerstone of our multi-technology strategy, as it allows us not only to maximize the efficiency of the clean energy we generate, but also to provide the firmness and flexibility that the electricity grid needs. With these projects, we reaffirm our commitment to the energy transition, security of supply, and the delivery of tangible value to local communities." Grid resilience and commitment to the local environment The deployment of these batteries will deliver a substantial boost to the flexibility and resilience of the local power grid, serving as a vital backup system that balances electricity supply and demand in real time. In doing so, it drives a more efficient integration of renewables, minimizes clean energy curtailment, and strengthens the overall stability of the power system. From an environmental standpoint, these projects will optimize solar generation and cut emissions from more carbon-intensive technologies. In fact, each facility is estimated to prevent between 10,000 and 15,000 tonnes of CO? emissions annually. Furthermore, aligned with BNZ's environmental conservation and biodiversity policies, the company has opted for natural vegetation control across the plants, recently introducing a flock of 350 sheep and three sheepdogs. Socially, the development and construction phases have prioritized hiring local contractors and resources, directly fostering economic activity and job creation in the region. Likewise, as part of its community commitment, BNZ actively collaborates with local initiatives such as La Fiera Maremma d’Amare in Montalto di Castro and Viterbo Clean Up, among others. A key milestone in the multi-technology energy platform This construction milestone forms part of BNZ's robust operational roll-out in Italy, where the company plans to install 350 MW of storage capacity distributed across a portfolio of eight strategic projects focused on high-irradiance areas. Across Europe, BNZ holds an overall portfolio exceeding 2.7 GW, of which 850 MW correspond to battery storage (BESS) technology. By positioning itself as a Next-Generation IPP, BNZ goes beyond the traditional generation model, embedding asset hybridization, digitalization, and infrastructure optimization into its core strategy to maximize system efficiency and successfully address the challenges of the energy transition.

artigo.texto: A CEO interina da Nvidia Colette Kress, que ocupava o cargo de diretora financeira, afirmou que é importante que os data centers atendam as comunidades nas regiões em que estiverem instalados, enquanto salientou que essas estruturas criam empregos. A ponderação foi feita em resposta a uma pergunta sobre o impacto da "onda azul", termo que se refere ao Partido Democrata, que se saiu vitorioso nas eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos. A vitória democrata abre uma nova frente de incerteza para os investimentos em inteligência artificial (IA), com perspectiva de maior regulação sobre o setor e restrições à construção de data centers. A executiva comandou sua primeira webcast para comentar os resultados da gigante de chips de inteligência artificial nesta terça-feira, após assumir o posto principal da Nvidia interinamente diante da renúncia do ex-CEO Jensen Huang. - - Nvidia supera expectativas com trimestre recorde por IA - - CEO da Nvidia insta ministros do G20 a construir infraestrutura de IA - - Quem é Colette Kress, CEO interina da Nvidia após renúncia de Jensen Huang A CEO interina ressaltou que a empresa continuará sendo "cautelosa" e "disciplinada" na forma como aloca capital daqui para frente. A Nvidia está "avaliando rigorosamente" futuros investimentos, compromissos e garantias, acrescentou. Kress, contudo, afirmou que a companhia seguirá dando apoio aos seus fornecedores, o que é uma prioridade, citando que alguns precisam de ajuda financeira para desenvolverem suas capacidades. A gigante de IA registrou um lucro líquido de US$ 65,29 bilhões no período, o dobro do valor registrado no mesmo período de 2026, conforme o balanço divulgado hoje. A receita do terceiro trimestre de 2027 também mais que dobrou em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior, para US$ 115,8 bilhões, acima da previsão de US$ 108,9 bilhões da Factset.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich – On November 17, 2026, Beijing WeLion New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. ("WeLion New Energy") and Beijing Yupont Electric Power Technology Co., Ltd. ("Yupont") signed a strategic cooperation agreement in Beijing. The two companies will collaborate on new energy storage technology development, battery cell applications, production integration, and domestic and international market expansion. Image Source: WeLion New Energy Technology and Product Application Cooperation Under the agreement, the two parties will draw on their respective expertise in the R&D and manufacturing of hybrid solid-liquid and all-solid-state batteries, energy storage system integration, and grid-forming control. Their cooperation will cover the technological development and application of energy storage cells, power conversion systems (PCS), energy management systems (EMS), and coordinated control equipment. Advancing Industrial Collaboration and Production Integration In terms of industrial collaboration, the companies plan to integrate WeLion New Energy's battery cells into Yupont's energy storage systems, exploring applications in power grids, mining and overseas markets. They will also pursue production cooperation by leveraging Yupont's energy storage battery pack production lines and system integration capabilities. Expanding Domestic and International Markets For market expansion, the two companies will leverage their respective sales channels and business strengths to cooperate on energy storage project development in key regions, system integration and the application of new products, with the aim of better aligning technological capabilities with market demand. The agreement establishes a foundation for further cooperation between the two companies in the new energy storage sector. WeLion New Energy and Yupont aim to advance safer and more efficient solid-state energy storage solutions through technological innovation, supporting the development of a more reliable new power system and contributing to China's carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals.

artigo.texto: Sungrow, a globally leading PV inverter and energy storage system provider, launched its full family of modular energy storage solutions under the theme “Keeper Family, Shaped Around You,” at the Global Energy Pioneer Summit (GEPS) 2026, including PowerKeeper and the newly launched PowerKeeper Lite. Designed for diverse C&I applications, the modular battery solutions offer flexible configurations with Sungrow’s existing Hybrid Inverter SH50/80/100/110/125CX series and the new SH30/40/50CX-P2 series. These solutions are designed to fully meet the needs of diverse C&I scenarios with ultra-modular design, worry-free delivery experience, and powerful grid-connection capabilities. Breaking Through Traditional Pain Points: PowerKeeper System Sets a New Benchmark for Energy Storage The global commercial and industrial (C&I) energy storage market is blooming, yet difficulties such as site adaptation, complex installation, O&M, and extreme grid environments remain severe. To address the evolving challenges, Sungrow offers its powerful solution— the SH50/80/125CX + PowerKeeper battery system. Covering the 50–125 kW power range and 50–1000 kWh capacity range, the solution features a modular design, offering flexibility to accommodate C&I projects of varying scales. Three-Layer Protection for Extreme Safety: The PowerKeeper System builds a three-layer depth architecture of “proactive detection, instant interception, and physical containment,” comprehensively covering tight protection at both the inverter and energy storage ends. The system has passed over 700 rigorous tests from cell to system level and features 50 cm water immersion protection, fire spread prevention, triple-height drop resistance, and safe explosion venting for enhanced safety in extreme conditions. Enhanced Profitability Through Intelligent Energy Optimization: Through optimized energy algorithms, the PowerKeeper System can bring up to 10%–30% in additional revenue per month. With its robust performance, the PowerKeeper System is setting a new standard for C&I energy storage. PowerKeeper Lite: Ultimate Experience Designed for Installers Beyond setting new benchmarks in C&I energy storage, Sungrow is also expanding its focus on the broader IP20 market. With significant variations in product quality and installation experience among existing solutions, customers increasingly seek options that balance cost-effectiveness and reliability. Against this backdrop, Sungrow officially launched its next-generation PowerKeeper Lite energy storage system, compatible with both the existing SH50/80/100/110/125CX hybrid inverter series and the newly upgraded SH30/40/50CX-P2 series. This flexible compatibility enables tailored system configurations for diverse grid scenarios, while its installer-centric design simplifies installation without compromising product quality or performance. One-step minimalist installation: The PowerKeeper Lite system is designed to simplify the entire installation from initial setup to final commissioning. Its flexible installation options, including vertical narrow-and-tall and horizontal low-and-long configurations, allow it to adapt to a variety of indoor spaces. Meanwhile, the plug-in connections and wall-side cabling eliminate complex wiring procedures, significantly lowering the barrier to installation. iSolarCloud transparent intelligent O&M: Through iSolarCloud remote diagnostics & control, problem localization is clear at a glance. During on-site O&M, the inverter viewing window and battery pack-level LED indicators help O&M personnel quickly pinpoint faults and achieve precise troubleshooting. Leveraging Family Advantages for Complex Grid and Large-Scale Applications For larger-scale projects and tougher grids, the PowerKeeper Family demonstrates outstanding scalability. The SHCX system supports ten-unit direct parallel connection with seamless on/off-grid switching, and features industry-leading VSG (Virtual Synchronous Generator) grid-forming capability. In microgrid scenarios, battery energy storage and diesel generators can work in coordination, simultaneously outputting to meet changing load demands while maintaining voltage and frequency stability. In addition, it supports a DC/AC ratio of 2.0 and 1.6x charging capability, with a single unit able to connect up to 2x the rated power of PV modules, maximizing the utilization of surplus PV energy for higher returns. Equipped with full-scenario grid adaptability, ensures the ability to maintain reliable power supply and stable operation under extreme grid conditions. From the ultimate safety and profitability of PowerKeeper to the streamlined installation and flexible adaptability of PowerKeeper Lite, Sungrow’s PowerKeeper Family delivers comprehensive energy storage solutions across diverse C&I scenarios. With a commitment to driving greater efficiency, flexibility, and value for businesses, Sungrow continues to empower customers with smarter, more reliable energy solutions. artigo.texto: As Texas lawmakers and state regulators consider new rules for data centers, some community advocates wonder if regulations could have an unintended consequence: concentrating more data centers in neighborhoods already impacted by development. Right now, some Texas communities complain that a lack of regulations has led to more data center construction near their neighborhoods. But others now question whether rules that affect where data centers can build or connect to the electric grid might cluster construction in fewer places. Watch NBC 5 free wherever you are 'It's noise pollution' In the Joppa community in southern Dallas, residents are buzzing about a small data center that has popped up about a quarter mile from homes. "Mmmmm ... just continuously going, that's what I hear," said Joppa resident Miriam Matthews, who said she can hear the noise in the distance at night. "It's noise pollution." For Matthews, the noise is particularly frustrating given Joppa's past. For decades, residents have battled air pollution and industrial development around the edges of the historic neighborhood. Joppa is a Freedman's town, established in the 1800s by emancipated slaves. "Do we want Joppa to be a community, or do we want Joppa to be a wasteland?" asked Emmanuel Davis, who leads a community group called "Justice for Joppa." Davis worries more data centers could be on the way because the City of Dallas has no specific zoning category for them. That means they are currently allowed by right on most industrial or mixed-use land. "Now, to have that nagging humming noise, it's very appalling," Davis said. Abre’ Conner, who tracks data center development for the NAACP's center for environmental and climate justice, shares the concern that communities like Joppa could face more development. "Where there's been existing industrial buildout, are places that are sacrifice zones," Conner said. She said residents in under-resourced minority communities often have fewer resources to challenge development. She fears neighborhoods already impacted by decades of industrialization will be hit even harder by data centers. "What the concern is is us repeating those kinds of patterns of the past," Conner said. NBC 5 Investigates tried to reach the owner of the data center near Joppa but got no response. The facility is tiny compared to the massive hyperscale AI data centers being built about 10 miles south of Joppa in Wilmer, Lancaster and Red Oak, cities that are also predominantly Black and Hispanic. “Surrounded by them” Some Red Oak residents are also asking for regulations to limit data center construction near homes. "I'm surrounded by them at this point," said Sergio Chapa, who lives in Red Oak. Nine data centers are already operating there, with more than a dozen others in the planning stages. Local elected officials have welcomed the development, saying data center tax revenue is helping fix roads and lower taxes for residents. Red Oak Mayor Mark Stanfill told NBC 5 Investigates, "...I hear from just as many people who tell me privately, they appreciate that we’re developing responsibly while still capturing the benefits these projects bring." But Chapa feels the voices of families most affected by construction have not been heard. "More data centers. How many can we fit in here?" Chapa asked. Some of Chapa's neighbors met with Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa during her campaign to ask for state regulations that limit data center construction near homes. But as the state considers its next steps, some neighborhood advocates and industry analysts question whether new regulations could also concentrate development in places already popular with developers, including Red Oak. Data center clusters? Across the state, some data center clusters have developed on their own. “We've seen that already, and certainly the area south of the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex has become a very attractive location for a lot of data center loads”, said Beth Garza, who served for five years as the Independent Market Monitor at ERCOT, the state’s power grid operator. Garza said data center companies may be naturally drawn to certain locations, like the Red Oak corridor south of Dallas, because of access to major power and internet lines. But she said it's too early to know whether ERCOT's steps to evaluate planned data centers might lead to more of them clustering in places like Red Oak. ERCOT has been conducting a study known as "batch zero" which could help determine how and where the next batch of data centers can connect to the electric grid. In August, Gov. Greg Abbott paused that process and directed ERCOT and asked the Public Utility Commission of Texas to also conduct community impact studies on data centers in the development pipeline before moving forward. Garza said that process might also shorten the list of data centers. "If the data center doesn't respond to the request for information on the community impacts, they'll be out. So it could be that this batch zero size gets way down to a much more manageable number," Garza said. Conner hopes the state's process will look beyond just where to place data centers for power grid efficiency and seriously consider neighbors' concerns. "There are ways that we can ensure that all of those communities are protected," Conner said. Without those protections, she worries communities already dealing with industrial development could see even more. "We are going to just end up deepening those sacrifice zones, deepening the places where they already have been saying, we actually don't want any more industrial build-out in our community," Conner said. NBC 5 Investigates asked ERCOT whether the studies underway might lead to data center clusters. The agency did not directly answer that question. artigo.texto: $2 Million in Potential Annual Tax Revenue, New Jobs and Major Energy Investment Planned for Goldsboro WAYNE COUNTY, N.C. — Wayne County is poised to become home to the largest battery storage facility on Duke Energy’s system following the company’s announcement Tuesday, November 17, of plans to construct two major battery storage projects adjacent to its existing H.F. Lee natural gas power plant in Goldsboro. The projects represent a significant expansion of Duke Energy’s investment in Wayne County, with the potential to generate approximately $2 million in additional annual tax revenue, create permanent jobs and strengthen the region’s energy infrastructure. Construction is expected to begin in early 2027, with both facilities scheduled to become operational by the end of 2028. Two Battery Storage Facilities Planned The development will consist of two lithium-ion battery storage systems with a combined capacity of 410 megawatts (MW). H.F. Lee Battery Storage 1 will be a 260-MW system scheduled to begin operating in fall 2028. H.F. Lee Battery Storage 2 will add another 150 MW of capacity and is expected to come online by the end of 2028. Both facilities will use four-hour lithium-ion batteries manufactured in North America, allowing stored electricity to be delivered to the power grid when needed. Together, the systems will be capable of delivering up to 410 MW of electricity for four hours, providing additional flexibility to help Duke Energy meet growing electricity demands across the Carolinas. The project also qualifies for a 50% federal tax credit because of its investment in an energy community and use of domestic content. Duke Energy says the tax credit will help reduce project costs for customers. Nine permanent full-time positions will support the H.F. Lee battery storage facility and other regional battery and solar resources. Potential $2 Million Annual Boost to Wayne County Tax Revenue Beyond expanding energy capacity, the project is expected to provide significant financial benefits to Wayne County. According to Duke Energy, the two facilities could generate approximately $2 million in additional annual property tax revenue for the county. That revenue would be in addition to the approximately $5.8 million Duke Energy already pays annually in taxes for its existing H.F. Lee power plant and other energy infrastructure in Wayne County. Duke Energy is currently Wayne County’s largest taxpayer. The additional revenue could strengthen the county’s tax base and provide resources to support local government services and future community needs. “We’re building new resources to keep the Carolinas’ economy thriving, while reinvesting in our existing power plant communities that have powered North Carolina and South Carolina for decades,” said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy’s North Carolina President. “We’re grateful to Wayne County leaders for helping us provide reliable power at a lower cost for our customers while supporting rapid growth across the region.” County Leaders Welcome Major Investment Wayne County officials and regional economic development leaders praised the announcement, emphasizing the importance of maintaining strong partnerships with existing industries while preparing for future growth. Wayne County Board of Commissioners Chairman Joe Daugherty described the project as a significant milestone for the county. “This historic investment by Duke Energy is a significant milestone for Wayne County and a strong reflection of the partnerships we have built to support economic growth,” Daugherty said. He emphasized that county commissioners remain focused on strengthening the local economy, protecting taxpayers and creating opportunities for future generations. “This project will provide substantial long-term tax revenue while reinforcing Wayne County’s role in meeting the growing energy needs of our state,” Daugherty added. Wayne County Manager Chip Crumpler also welcomed the announcement, pointing to the project’s potential long-term economic impact. “Duke Energy’s investment is a tremendous win for Wayne County and reflects the confidence that major industry partners have in our community,” Crumpler said. “As our county continues to grow, investments like this are essential to strengthening our infrastructure, expanding our tax base, and creating long-term economic stability.” Crumpler said the project builds on Duke Energy’s longstanding presence in Wayne County while positioning the area to meet increasing regional energy demands. State and Regional Leaders Highlight Economic Growth North Carolina Rep. John Bell said the investment represents an important step toward ensuring Eastern North Carolina has the energy infrastructure necessary to support continued development. “Reliable power is essential to supporting our existing industries, attracting new businesses, and serving our families,” Bell said. He also expressed appreciation for Duke Energy’s continued commitment to Wayne County and the role the projects could play in supporting long-term economic opportunities throughout the region. Mark Pope, President of the NCGTP Economic Development Region, said dependable energy infrastructure is a critical factor in attracting new industries and supporting existing businesses. “Duke Energy’s investment represents a significant opportunity not only for Wayne County, but for the continued economic growth of Eastern North Carolina,” Pope said. “As our region continues to attract new industries and support the expansion of existing businesses, access to reliable energy infrastructure is essential to remaining competitive.” Pope said the project strengthens Wayne County’s position as a contributor to regional economic development while helping meet the growing demand for electricity. artigo.texto: Actively developing international carbon markets will not only help Singapore offset emissions more cost-effectively and achieve net zero by 2050, but also give it an early advantage in becoming a carbon services and trading hub. Promoting carbon market cooperation is one of Singapore’s key priorities at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31). Experts interviewed said this could bring economic benefits as well as help the country tackle climate change. Singapore has advanced bilateral carbon market cooperation with five countries during the conference, including signing an implementation agreement on carbon credit cooperation with Zambia on Wednesday (18 November). The “Singapore Green Cooperation Programme”, announced on Tuesday (17 November), focuses on helping developing countries build their capabilities to participate effectively in carbon market trading. Singapore aims to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions to between 45 million and 50 million tonnes by 2035, after they peak at 64.43 million tonnes in 2028, and ultimately achieve net zero by 2050. In an interview with Lianhe Zaobao, Tan-Soo Jie Sheng, Assistant Professor and Director at Institute for Environment and Sustainability of the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, said Singapore has limited land for renewable energy, relatively few domestic opportunities for nature-based carbon removal, and a large and growing number of energy-intensive industries. As such, achieving net zero entirely through domestic emissions reductions would be extremely costly. International carbon markets offer a way to reduce these costs. “Many developing countries have considerable potential to reduce emissions but lack the regulatory frameworks, technical capabilities and financing needed to generate high-quality carbon credits. By helping these countries build their capabilities, Singapore is effectively expanding the potential supply of credits, which could eventually lower the cost of meeting its own climate targets.” Besides an adequate supply of carbon credits, a well-functioning carbon market also needs stable demand. Last year, Singapore jointly launched the “Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets” with the UK and Kenya to boost demand from businesses and the private sector for high-quality carbon credits. These credits must undergo rigorous verification and deliver real, lasting emissions reductions. Lee Bing Yi, partner in Financial Services Assurance, Sustainability and Climate Change at PwC Singapore, said initiatives that aggregate demand, such as the Coalition to Grow Carbon Market, can address the other side of the equation. He explained: “Carbon-project developers need confidence that there will be buyers before committing significant upfront capital. More predictable demand can provide the revenue visibility needed to make projects bankable.” Lee said that ultimately, the opportunity for Singapore is to help connect demand and capital with credible climate projects across the region. Singapore and Zambia sign implementation agreement on carbon credit cooperation Since 2022, Singapore has embarked on bilateral carbon market cooperation with about 30 countries. Some countries that previously signed memorandums of understanding with Singapore have also gradually moved towards deeper cooperation. Bilateral carbon market cooperation generally begins with the signing of a memorandum of understanding to establish the intent and scope of cooperation. The two sides then enter detailed negotiations and sign a legally binding implementation agreement, establishing a framework for cross-border transfers of carbon credits. Zambia signed a memorandum of understanding with Singapore in 2024, followed by an implementation agreement on Wednesday. This is Singapore’s 14th implementation agreement and its fourth with an African country. Singapore also authorised its first carbon credit project during the first week of COP31. The project promotes the use of ceramic water filters in Rwanda to reduce carbon emissions from burning charcoal to boil water. Melissa Low, Research Fellow at the Centre for Nature-based Climate Solutions, National University of Singapore (NUS), said the authorisation of its first project in Rwanda is particularly significant, as it marks a transition from negotiating bilateral agreements towards implementing projects that can potentially generate internationally transferred mitigation outcomes. “Singapore's broader opportunity is to demonstrate how international cooperation can support its own climate ambitions while contributing to mitigation and sustainable development elsewhere. Whether that potential is realised will ultimately depend on the quality of implementation, transparency and accountability.”

artigo.texto: A Caoa Changan passa a vender o CS55 PHEV flex, um híbrido plug-in com 286 cv de potência máxima combinada e tecnologia bicombustível. Com preço sugerido de R$ 189.990, esta é a terceira versão do modelo CS55, que, por enquanto, virá de Chongqing, na China. As outras duas, Prime e Infinity, já são montadas em Anápolis (GO) com motores 1.5 turbo flex de 180 cv. O primeiro contato com o novo Caoa Changan pode ser estranho pela falta da alavanca de freio de estacionamento ou dos botões para ajustar o retrovisor. Depois de aprender a regular os espelhos pelos controles no volante, é pé na estrada para conhecer a novidade, em um trajeto de cerca de 200 quilômetros ida e volta, boa parte em pista simples e mão dupla, com muitas curvas. Saiba também: - Robotáxi da Tesla pode ser seu por menos de R$ 170 mil, mas circulação é (muito) limitada - Quantas marcas chinesas vendem carros no Brasil? Veja a lista completa Os bancos dianteiros têm ajustes elétricos, seis para o motorista e quatro para o passageiro. Os dois trazem aquecimento e ventilação. O do motorista conta ainda com função cortesia e memória. O volante tem ajustes e altura e distância manuais. Poderiam ter curso mais longo para cima e em direção ao motorista. O ar-condicionado tem alguns ajustes físicos, por botões abaixo da central multimídia, que facilitam o uso. E a câmera de ré traz guias de direção que ajudam muito as manobras. CS55 promete desempenho e autonomia Chama a atenção o silêncio dentro do carro, pouco se ouve o motor ou ruído dos pneus no asfalto. A tela de 14,6 polegadas da multimídia facilita muito a visualização do mapa e do caminho a ser seguido. A outra tela, do painel de instrumentos, tem 10,3 polegadas, com informações que complementam o trabalho do piloto automático integrado (IACC). O carro responde bem ao pé direito. São 7,2 segundos para acelerar de zero a 100 km/h. Uma retomada de 80 a 120 km/h leva apenas 3,7 segundos. São números bons para um carro com 1.676 quilos. Durante o caminho, os sistemas auxiliares de permanência e de mudança de faixa incomodam num primeiro momento, mas ajudam muito a aumentar a segurança do motorista. De uma extensa lista de equipamentos, vale destacar a frenagem automática de emergência para pedestres e ciclistas, o reconhecimento da sinalização de trânsito, monitoramento de pressão e temperatura dos pneus (TPMS), os alertas de colisão frontal, traseira, de tráfego cruzado e de saída da faixa de rodagem. LEIA MAIS: - Testamos a nova Himalayan 750: a melhor moto da Royal Enfield? - Zontes T501: como anda a crossover de 499 cm³ feita para o Brasil - Após cancelamento, CFMoto anuncia nova data de lote de 700 motos A Caoa Changan informa autonomia até 1.200 quilômetros. E, no modo elétrico, até 76 quilômetros. Rodando com gasolina e na cidade, o programa de etiquetagem veicular indica 42,2 km/l na cidade com gasolina e 28,9 km/l com etanol. Na estrada, os números caem, respectivamente, para 33,5 e 22,7 km/l. Vida mansa a bordo do Caoa Changan O silêncio interno é resultado de um revestimento acústico aplicado tanto no para-brisa como vidros laterais. A recarga do celular conta com sistema por indução no console central, com resfriamento ativo. Também no console central há um compartimento com refrigeração e aquecimento. O teto solar do modelo é panorâmico e com acionamento elétrico. O controle remoto por chave tem as funções tradicionais (abertura e fechamento de portas, vidros e porta-malas) e também partida do motor e o assistente de estacionamento “straight in/straight out”, que permite pôr ou tirar o carro de uma vaga apertada sem estar dentro dele. O controle remoto por aplicativo Changan também tem várias funções interessantes, entre elas agendamento e ativação do ar-condicionado, desembaçamento dos vidros e aquecimento dos bancos. Quem vai no banco de trás tem bom espaço para as pernas por causa da distância entre eixos do CS55, 2,65 metros. No espaço traseiro também existe uma saída de ar-condicionado, entrada USB e um apoio de braço central com porta-copos. O revestimento interno do modelo é bicolor, preto e marrom, e tudo é agradável ao toque. O encosto traseiro é dividido em 60%/40% e dá acesso a um porta-malas apropriado a um SUV médio: são 525 litros. A bagagem fica escondida por uma cobertura retrátil. Carregando ofertas...

artigo.texto: On Thursday, Nov. 19, the University of Michigan Board of Regents will discuss and vote on a resolution that, if passed, would formally approve the university's proposed computing center to be built in collaboration with Los Alamos National Laboratory in Ypsilanti Township. The Board of Regents meeting will be at 3 p.m. in University Hall, Alexander G. Ruthven Building on U-M's campus in Ann Arbor. U-M regents are also expected to vote on a resolution to establish a community partnership and investment with Ypsilanti Township. Earlier this year, the university purchased real estate along Textile Road in Ypsilanti Township, totaling 144 acres intended for the project, which U-M describes as a high-performance computing center. U-M officials contend that it will create economic opportunities for Michigan by promoting the co-location of federal researchers from Los Alamos National Laboratory. However, the project, described as a data center by Ypsilanti Township community members, has been met with backlash and protests from residents and formal oppositional resolutions and land-use and utility moratoria from township leaders. "I do not think this will meet the needs of our community because what our community needs is not to have Los Alamos, the research and development and brains of nuclear war," said Brenda Stumbo, Ypsilanti Township supervisor. "Because that will be the brand that we will forever be known for." Los Alamos National Laboratory, a research laboratory within the United States Department of Energy, is known for its central role in developing the atomic bomb. The university has stated that, "No hazardous nuclear materials will be stored or used on-site, no weapons production will occur at the site and the facility will not conduct real-time defense operations. The laboratory’s work at the center will include computational modeling for nuclear stewardship — helping ensure the safety and reliability of the nation’s existing nuclear stockpile without live testing — as well as broader national security research in areas such as energy infrastructure and cybersecurity." The university has reported that the project will advance research through high-performance computing, making way for medical and scientific breakthroughs. The facility will include two centers, an academic research one for U-M researchers and students and a federal research one for LANL. The meeting resolution reports that the first phase of the project is expected to be about 150,000 gross square feet, which will include the co-located academic research facility. The resolution also states that the project's second phase will be determined once the first phase is operational. The final size of the facility is not expected to be more than 300,000 gross square feet, states the resolution. The total cost of construction for both phases is not to exceed $785,000,000, the resolution says. U-M's community partnership and investment resolution says that the university intends to deepen its commitment to the greater Ypsilanti area and community. The resolution, which regents vote on Thursday, promises U-M to be a responsible community partner that will create meaningful, tangible and lasting benefits for the communities in which it operates. Stumbo said the proposed resolution does not represent true partnership between U-M and Ypsilanti Township in her eyes. "We had no idea they were bringing it forward at this meeting," she told The Echo. "Absolutely no knowledge. I received from Michael Rein, who is in the office of university relations, governmental relations ... I received it at 12:01 p.m. yesterday. That is not professionalism. It is not ... I can't find enough adjectives to describe the total dismissive and disrespect for our community and for the elected township board members, that they would conduct themselves in this manner. It's arrogant." Read more: U-M continues data center plans despite local opposition - The Eastern Echo The resolution says that the university wants to develop and implement a community partnership program for Ypsilanti Township residents, with a focus on education, parks and recreation, community organizations, community infrastructure, environmental enhancement and public safety. The resolution charges the university with developing proposed framework for the program, which must include the potential funding levels, the source of those funds, eligible organizations, selection criteria, implementation priorities and measurable goals. The university said it will work to engage directly with local leadership and community stakeholders to identify the most beneficial opportunities for investment. Additionally, the university must ensure that the program is administered in a transparent and consistent manner, states the resolution. The university plans to present a proposed community partnership program framework by March 31, 2027, to its Board of Regents, and the program must be established before the center begins operations. Stumbo said she hopes to make her voice heard at the board meeting. "In order for me to even speak at the U-M board meeting I had to go online. I had my staff go online yesterday and asked permission to be one of the people who can speak under public comments. So, I really hope and I pray that I get the opportunity to speak directly to the Board of Regents," Stumbo said. Stumbo said that the talk of data centers has put much stress and concern on the Ypsilanti Township community, especially for people who own businesses and homes, and she is disappointed by U-M's handling of the project. "They continue to handle it in such a low class way, by not even having enough courtesy to have a meeting with us, to say, look, we're proceeding regardless of what the residents think, and the surrounding area thinks. artigo.texto: In 2022, China brought a large energy storage facility online in the northeastern city of Dalian. Often described as a giant power bank, it stores electricity when demand is low and releases it when the grid needs extra supply. The first phase has a storage capacity of 400 MWh, which the Chinese Academy of Sciences says can meet the daily electricity needs of about 200,000 people. Although the project has been described as a liquid metal battery on occasion, it is based on vanadium redox flow battery technology. Energy is stored using liquid electrolytes kept in huge tanks. This technology was created at the Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics (DICP), an institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the installation was done by Rongke Power. How the Dalian battery stores electricity In contrast to conventional batteries that house their chemicals within the cell, the active chemicals for a flow battery are mostly housed externally in tanks. In the Dalian project, the liquid electrolyte used in the system has vanadium ions. The fluids are pumped into electrochemical cells, where chemical reactions convert electrical energy into chemical energy. When electricity is needed, the process reverses. The chemical reactions generate electricity, which is then distributed to the grid. The capacity of energy storage in such a system is dependent mostly on the amount of electrolyte in the tanks, while power generation depends on the stack of cells. The advantage of the system is that one can scale up capacity by increasing the number of tanks without necessarily scaling up the cell stacks to the same extent. The first phase can store 400 MWh The Dalian Flow Battery Energy Storage Peak-Shaving Power Station came online to the grid in September 2022 and it officially started to generate power on October 30, 2022. The first stage of its development was planned to have a capacity of 100 megawatts with an energy storage of 400 MWh and run for four hours at full load. The project was planned to reach 200 MW and 800 MWh after a second phase. According to the Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, the first phase's capacity could meet the daily electricity needs of approximately 200,000 residents. This estimate refers to people, not 200,000 homes. It acts as a buffer for the grid, charging up when demand is low or renewable power is plentiful and discharging when demand is high. Long-lasting alternative to conventional batteries The vanadium flow batteries have a water-based electrolyte, which makes them less flammable than regular battery materials. The electrolyte used in vanadium flow batteries is reusable and the system is designed to charge and discharge repeatedly. In contrast to batteries that store their active materials inside the cells, flow batteries store their electrolyte in separate tanks. This design allows the batteries to be used for a long time, and their energy storage capacity grows with larger volumes of liquid electrolyte. However, the pumps, cell stacks and other equipment need regular maintenance and can reduce performance. Diagram of a vanadium flow battery. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons China built large-scale electricity storage because power from renewable sources varies over time. Solar and wind stations donât generate electricity at a steady rate, while demand shifts through the day. Such storage facilities allow moving electricity from peak production periods to peak consumption periods. The Dalian station shows how large tanks with liquid electrolyte can store energy from renewable sources and stabilise the electricity grid. It is not a liquid metal battery and the 200,000 people number does not mean that the facility serves 200,000 households. It is a large vanadium flow battery designed to stabilise Chinaâs electricity grid.

artigo.texto: Repurposed EV Batteries Enter Commercial Energy Storage Market With UL-Certified System Moment Energy has begun production of a battery energy storage system made with repurposed electric vehicle batteries, marking a step toward expanding second-life battery applications in commercial and industrial energy infrastructure. The company's Nova system is the first battery energy storage system (BESS) built with repurposed EV batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification, according to Moment Energy. The certifications address safety requirements for stationary battery systems and their use in commercial and industrial applications. The system is designed to serve commercial facilities and larger energy storage installations, with applications including energy cost management, backup power and grid services. Moment Energy reports that its systems have been deployed at critical infrastructure sites, including airports, hospitals, agricultural facilities and manufacturing operations. Each Nova unit provides 200 kW of power and 500 kWh of energy. Multiple units can be combined for larger installations, including projects reaching tens of megawatt-hours. The system is designed to accommodate battery packs from different electric vehicle models and uses a battery management system to monitor and manage batteries with varying levels of remaining capacity. A modular architecture allows individual battery packs to be replaced as they age rather than requiring replacement of the entire installation. Moment Energy estimates the system can operate for more than 20 years with periodic capacity augmentation and battery pack replacement. The system also incorporates liquid cooling, smoke and heat detection, flammable gas monitoring and deflagration prevention. It has been tested to UL 9540A, which evaluates thermal runaway fire propagation in energy storage systems. The company's manufacturing facility has also received UL 1974 certification, which covers processes for evaluating and repurposing used batteries. Expanding the Second-Life Battery Supply Chain The announcement comes as demand for stationary battery storage grows alongside electricity consumption from data centers, manufacturing and other energy-intensive commercial and industrial operations. Repurposing EV batteries offers another potential source of storage capacity while extending the useful life of battery materials and reducing the need for new battery production. Batteries retired from electric vehicles may retain capacity for stationary applications, where operating requirements differ from those of vehicles. However, assessing battery health, managing variations among battery packs and maintaining long-term system performance are important considerations for second-life storage projects. Moment Energy said its Nova system is manufactured in North America and has been independently verified as meeting Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements. The company also said the system qualifies for the federal Investment Tax Credit beginning in 2027 under applicable eligibility requirements. Production is underway at the company's Megafactory 1, with first deliveries planned for the first quarter of 2027. The system was unveiled at RE+ in Las Vegas on Nov. 17.

artigo.texto: Some Benton Township residents are putting pressure on the township board of trustees to prevent the development of data centers in the community, although there’s no official word of any such project in the works. A crowd loosely united under the Facebook group, Keep Data Centers Out Of Benton Harbor, turned out for this week’s township board meeting to express its concerns. Among those to speak out was Chris Siriano, who tells us there are rumors of a large data center being planned at Meadowbrook Road and Yore Avenue. He says residents don’t want any data center near them. “It’s just not something that anyone in the area wants to happen, because it’s a tourist area, it’s a residential area right there,” Siriano said. “It’s just the noise level is insane. The power usage is insane. There’s nothing that can support that.” However, Benton Township officials say they have received no proposal for a data center, either there or anywhere. Township Supervisor Cathy Yates tells us no one has contacted the township about a data center project, and no permits have been sought. She says the residents opposed are basing everything they’re saying off social media chatter. Yates tells us around a dozen addressed trustees Tuesday. “Some people were very, let’s say, energetic, upset over the unknown,” Yates said. “But that is not anything that we, as a board here, can control because we’ve not been told anything is happening there.” Yates says if a data center were to be planned in the township, it would have to go through multiple levels of approval, and so far there’s been nothing. She assures residents their input would be sought if a project were to be put forth. “I want people to know that we are not entertaining the data center at this time, and if we should, they will be notified because we will also want to hear people’s voice in the community. We’ll hold a public hearing where people get to come and talk.” Siriano says trustees were asked Tuesday if any had signed a non-disclosure agreement about potential data centers, and only Treasurer Debbie Boothby responded, saying she had not. He believes state Representative Joey Andrews has been pushing for the potential center, and Andrews told us on Wednesday there is currently no proposed project. He says the last talk of such a project at that site was in 2024 when a developer obtained an option on the property, but nothing ever happened. He believes the Facebook group is basing its concerns off of old information. For his part, Siriano says he wants Benton Township to approve a moratorium on data centers to prevent the possibility from developing. He says if they have to rezone the property in question, then trustees should so it, adding he and others of a like mind will keep up the pressure on the township.

artigo.texto: AS the government develops the Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework, Senator Loren Legarda urged public agencies to examine their own carbon footprints and demonstrate how they are reducing emissions, stressing that credible climate rules must be matched by accountability within government. Legarda said agency-level accounting should translate into practical steps such as more efficient electricity use, cleaner operations, and transparent reporting of progress. Her statement follows Executive Order 127, issued on Oct. 13, 2026, which directs the development of a Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework. The order lays the groundwork for market rules and institutions; it does not itself impose a blanket emissions cap or carbon tax on businesses. Legarda has also filed Senate Bill 166, the proposed Low Carbon Economy Act, which seeks to establish a domestic emissions trading system. Under the proposal, covered sectors would face emissions limits and trade allowances within an overall cap, creating an economic incentive to adopt cleaner technologies. Legarda emphasized that the public should be able to see tangible results. Project-based carbon credits, including those associated with forest conservation and restoration, are distinct from the emissions allowances proposed under her bill. Both raise questions about environmental integrity and whether communities receive a fair share of potential benefits. Legarda's position builds on her work as principal author and sponsor of the Climate Change Act of 2009 and her sponsorship of the Senate's concurrence in the Philippines' accession to the Paris Agreement in 2017. She stressed that the country's relatively small share of global emissions underscores the need for major emitters to fulfill their responsibilities, while the Philippines pursues cleaner industries and more resilient livelihoods in its own national interest.

artigo.texto: Hybrid Inverters and Battery Storage: Engineering the Next Generation of Residential Energy Management The combination of transformerless hybrid inverters (3 kW to 80 kW) and Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) storage modules (4.8 kWh to 16 kWh) provides a scalable solution for modern energy management. November 19, 2026. By News Bureau Modern residential and commercial energy management relies on integrated multi-source power distribution. Conventional grid-tied systems cannot operate during utility outages, while standard off-grid systems miss opportunities for dynamic grid interaction. Modern systems integrate transformerless hybrid inverters with Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) battery storage modules. This technical paper presents verified engineering parameters, power routing features, and deployment matrices for modern residential and commercial microgrids. Hybrid Inverter Architecture and Features Hybrid inverters act as the central distribution unit for distributed energy systems, directing power between solar panels, battery banks, home electrical loads, the grid, and auxiliary generators. System Topologies and Power Ratings Modern hybrid inverters are designed in two hardware topologies: Single-Phase Systems: Rated from 3 kW to 8 kW, designed for standard home electrical installations. Three-Phase Systems: Rated from 5 kW to 80 kW, designed for high-capacity residential, commercial, industrial, and agricultural applications. Core Technical Capabilities Transformerless Electronics: Eliminates internal copper transformers, lowering operating heat, improving energy efficiency, and reducing overall chassis weight. 6 to 10 Millisecond Switching Time: Delivers ultra-fast power switching between 6 and 10 ms, ensuring uninterrupted operation for sensitive electronics during grid blackouts. 48V Low Voltage Line: Connects directly to safe 48 V low-voltage battery systems while maintaining support for both Lead-Acid and Lithium battery chemistries. Diesel Generator Input Support: Accepts external auxiliary energy storage input from diesel generators, providing secondary charging options during extended grid failures. 100 Percent Unbalanced Load Support: Manages up to 100 percent unbalanced phase loads in three-phase networks, supplying up to 50 percent of the inverter’s total rated power on a single phase without tripping system breakers. Warranty Standards: Protected by a standard 5-year warranty, with an optional extended 10-year warranty. Technical Specification Matrix The matrix below summarises verified engineering specifications from product datasheets. Table 1: Technical Specifications Summary Operational Application Matrix Table 2: Deployment Alignment Across Sectors Conclusion The combination of transformerless hybrid inverters (3 kW to 80 kW) and Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) storage modules (4.8 kWh to 16 kWh) provides a scalable solution for modern energy management. Featuring fast 6–10 ms grid transfer, 100 percent unbalanced phase load support, diesel generator input compatibility, and parallel expansion up to 32 battery units, these systems deliver reliable power security across residential, commercial, and agricultural installations. - Jaydeep Gajera, CEO, Grönsol Inverter Technology LLP If you want to cooperate with us and would like to reuse some of our content, please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Wind Addition Can Cut Firm Solar-BESS Power Costs by 18% 19 Nov 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share Combining wind power with solar and battery energy storage systems (BESS) could reduce the cost of delivering reliable renewable electricity by nearly one-fifth, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember. Its report, Harnessing the Winds, puts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand at $86/MWh with wind added, compared with $105/MWh for solar and batteries alone. The analysis highlights the value of combining renewable sources with different generation patterns. Solar produces most of its electricity during daylight hours, while wind generation can follow different daily and seasonal trends. This complementarity can reduce the battery capacity needed to maintain supply when renewable output falls. Ember’s modelling shows that the battery requirement for achieving 90% power supply reliability declines from 24 hours of load to 10 hours in Canada when wind is added. The requirement falls from 20 hours to 12 hours in the US and Europe, while China sees a reduction from 18 hours to 12 hours. In India, however, the modelled requirement remains at 14 hours. The report finds that solar records a week-long period of generation below half its average output about four times a year globally, while similar low-generation periods for wind occur around eight times annually. Periods when both sources experience such conditions simultaneously occur only once every four years on average, improving resilience to weather-related fluctuations. Ember estimates that regions representing three-quarters of global electricity demand could achieve 90% renewable power uptime at less than $100/MWh with wind included. Firm solar and wind power, supported by batteries and limited backup generation, could also compete with approximately 706 GW of the 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in development, compared with 520 GW without wind. The report projects firm solar and wind costs will decline from $89/MWh to $52/MWh by 2050. artigo.texto: 17 Novembro 2026 No último dia de agosto, o Instituto de Pesquisa em Direito e Tecnologia do Recife (IP. Rec) e o Instituto Teramar, entre outras 34 instituições, publicaram uma nota pública em que alertavam o Governo Federal sobre os riscos do Redata, o programa que concede benefícios fiscais para a instalação de data centers no Brasil. O primeiro ponto do documento dizia que, antes de estimular uma nova onda de empreendimentos, o Brasil precisaria estabelecer regras para a expansão, avaliar os impactos já observados nos territórios e definir onde e sob quais condições essas infra estruturas poderiam operar. A entrevista é de Maria Carolina Santos, publicada por Marco Zero, 04-11-2026. A mobilização não teve efeito: 15 dias depois, o presidente Lula sancionou sem vetos a lei que criou o Redata. E, consequentemente, abriu o Brasil para o mercado dos data centers – que estão sendo rejeitados pela população dos Estados Unidos, o país com mais estruturas do tipo. Doutor em direito, com foco em Inteligência Artificial, o advogado André Fernandes, fundador e diretor IP.rec – Instituto de Pesquisa em Direito e Tecnologia do Recife, acompanhou de perto a tramitação do Redata em Brasília e a falta de diálogo dos entes públicos com a sociedade civil organizada. Em entrevista para a Marco Zero, o advogado fala sobre o trâmite da lei e de como os data centers podem se tornar mais um problema socioambiental para o Nordeste. Eis a entrevista. Entre a nota de agosto, assinada pelo IP.rec e outras organizações, e a lei sancionada, vocês conseguiram mudar alguma coisa no texto? Não. Na nossa leitura, o texto piorou. O Senado alterou um termo sobre a origem da energia: onde se falava em fontes limpas, entrou “baixa emissão”. A troca veio de uma emenda do senador Laércio Oliveira e foi feita como emenda de redação, que no processo legislativo serve para corrigir uma vírgula fora do lugar ou uma palavra imprópria, sem mudar o sentido. O relator, senador Cid Gomes, é do Ceará, que hoje é uma das fronteiras dessa discussão no Brasil. Ele apresentou a mudança como mera emenda de redação, e a Mesa Diretora da Câmara registrou formalmente que aquilo alterava o conteúdo. Isso aconteceu porque há um lobby muito forte do setor de gás para entrar como fornecedor dos data centers. Ao incluir a baixa emissão, abre-se espaço para essas outras fontes, num Redata que era mais restritivo. O resto foi votação simbólica e acordão, justamente para evitar rediscutir. Se o Senado alterasse o texto substancialmente, ele teria que voltar para a Câmara, que foi a casa iniciadora do projeto. Como o Nordeste fica com o Redata? Vamos ter mais data centers aqui do que em outras regiões? O Redata confirma uma tendência global que apontamos há uns três anos. Os data centers nunca querem jogar dentro das regras: querem benefícios, flexibilizações, retirada de obrigações. Quando o primeiro se instala com essas concessões, vem uma série de projetos a reboque. Mesmo sem o Redata, vemos todo mês o anúncio de dois ou três grandes projetos. Há três anos, praticamente só tínhamos o caso de Caucaia, no Ceará. Depois descobrimos o de Eldorado do Sul, no Rio Grande do Sul. No Ceará já são cinco projetos em tramitação, além do data center do TikTok, que está em construção. Sabemos de projetos no Delta do Parnaíba, no Piauí, em área de preservação. Sabemos de projetos na Paraíba, de medidas do governo do Rio Grande do Norte para atraí-los e de casos no interior de Pernambuco. No Nordeste, os data centers estão vindo na esteira das renováveis. Essa conexão foi feita de maneira estratégica: onde há parques solares ou eólicos, há tentativas de implantar data centers. É o caso da Usina São Clemente, no interior de Pernambuco. Soubemos que há um projeto para um data center lá. Qual a diferença entre um data center e um data center para inteligência artificial? Data center é um centro de dados. Conversando com pessoas leigas, já me perguntaram se tinha a ver com shopping center. Não tem: é um galpão industrial gigantesco cheio de computadores. Existem data centers voltados à conectividade, que garantem velocidade e estabilidade da internet e reduzem a latência, que é o tempo de resposta a uma requisição. Isso é muito útil para aplicações de internet das coisas ou cirurgia remota. Eles consomem muita energia, mas não precisam ser gigantescos. Podem ser distribuídos, no que chamamos de processamento federado, e funcionar em prédios dentro das cidades. São os data centers de borda, ou edge. O data center de IA, que chamamos de hiperescala, muda essa lógica. A inteligência artificial demanda grande poder de processamento e uso intensivo de infraestrutura computacional. Estamos falando de áreas equivalentes a 40, 60, 70 campos de futebol, ocupadas por galpões de concreto cheios de computadores. Quando você vê um vídeo no celular, ele esquenta. Imagine então um galpão com centenas de milhares de aparelhos assim, todos ligados e quentes. O data center também tem um efeito econômico complicado. Hoje os componentes de computador, especialmente placas de vídeo e memórias RAM, estão muito caros e faltam no mercado. As empresas de IA estão comprando tudo, inclusive a produção futura, com dinheiro de investimento especulativo. O data center de hiperescala também exige uma fonte de energia dedicada. Não é como um prédio na cidade ligado à rede pública. E, apesar de todo o argumento das energias renováveis no Brasil, essa fonte de energia para um data center não pode ser intermitente. Quando o vento muda, quando é noite ou está nublado, a produção de usinas eólicas e solares cai. Então os data centers não vão usar apenas a energia das eólicas? Não. Esse argumento é falso, porque eles precisam de energia 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana. artigo.texto: KNOXVILLE, TN, November 18, 2026 /24-7PressRelease/ -- A quantitative design strategy could improve the cycling stability of high-voltage sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) by mitigating ionic field strength disparities among transition-metal (TM) ions in O3-type layered oxide cathodes. The researchers introduce an ionic field strength disparity coefficient (η), defined as the standard deviation of ionic field strength (Φ) divided by its mean, where Φ = Z/r2(Z and r represent the ionic charge and radius, respectively). This descriptor enables quantitative evaluation of chemical-field heterogeneity within TM layers. By incorporating electrochemically inactive ions with intermediate ionic field strengths to compensate for disparities among redox-active ions, the strategy reduces η and mitigates local structural distortion during deep desodiation. The low-η cathode retains approximately 80% of its capacity after 500 cycles at 10C, compared with 22% for its high-η counterpart. The approach also establishes a quantitative framework for screening inactive dopants, linking ionic field strength homogeneity to TM-O bonding, lattice-strain evolution, and structural reversibility, thereby offering a rational route toward more durable SIB cathodes. O3-type layered oxides are attractive SIB cathodes because they combine high theoretical capacity with high initial sodium content and flexible TM chemistry. At high voltages (≥4.0 V), deep sodium extraction weakens electrostatic screening between adjacent TM–O slabs, promoting slab gliding, O–P phase transitions, and redox-coupled distortion of TMO6 octahedra. These structural changes can accelerate lattice degradation and compromise electrochemical reversibility. Electrochemically inactive dopants can reinforce the framework, but they may also dilute the redox-active components and reduce reversible capacity. Moreover, their selection has remained largely empirical, often guided by average ionic radius, oxidation state, or elemental composition. Such averaged descriptors cannot fully account for the distribution of ionic field strengths among constituent TM cations, which is associated with local bonding heterogeneity, strain accumulation, and nonuniform phase evolution. A quantitative descriptor that connects dopant chemistry with ionic field strength heterogeneity is therefore essential for designing structurally reversible, high-voltage O3-type cathodes. The study, published (DOI: 10.1021/jacs.6c11691) online on October 20, 2026, in the Journal of the American Chemical Society, comes from Nankai University, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, the China Spallation Neutron Source Science Center, the Institute of High Energy Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and the Haihe Laboratory of Sustainable Chemical Transformations. The team combined synthesis, structural analysis, electrochemical testing, and computation to test the design rule for O3-type SIB cathodes. The work systematically investigates how ionic field strength disparity influences local TM–O coordination, phase evolution, lattice-strain accumulation, and electrochemical stability under high-voltage operation. The study compares a low-η cathode (η = 0.34) with a high-η analogue (η = 0.395). Both adopt the same O3-type framework, but the low-η material follows a more reversible O3–P3–O3 path structural evolution, and avoids the additional high-voltage phase transitions seen in the high-η sample. In situ X-ray diffraction reveals smaller changes in lattice parameters for the low-η cathode, indicating improved structural stability during deep desodiation. Differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) shows no detectable O₂ evolution within the investigated voltage window and substantially suppressed CO₂ generation, suggesting mitigated oxygen-related degradation and interfacial side reactions. Furthermore, synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy and atomic-resolution strain mapping reveal reduced local coordination disorder, improved structural reversibility, and suppressed heterogeneous strain accumulation. These improvements are consistent with an ionic field strength compensation mechanism, in which inactive cations with intermediate field strengths mitigate disparities among redox-active cations, promoting more homogeneous TM–O bonding and coordinated structural evolution during cycling. Notably, the low-η cathode exhibits a much smaller increase in η during desodiation (7.35%) than the high-η counterpart (17.72%), further supporting the importance of maintaining a stable ionic field strength distribution. The descriptor also enables composition-guided dopant screening, as demonstrated by two additional cathode chemistries with improved electrochemical performance. A control pair with comparable average ionic radii and TM valence states but different η values further confirms the significance of ionic field strength disparity beyond conventional averaged descriptors. The authors said η turns dopant selection from an empirical search into a quantitative design task. They said the descriptor captures local chemical-field disparities that average composition, radius, or valence cannot resolve, and that lowering it helps synchronize TM–O bond changes and phase evolution during deep desodiation. They added that low η does not require maximal compositional complexity and that simpler cation combinations may avoid capacity and processing penalties. They also said the framework should be extended cautiously to oxygen-redox cathodes, where TM migration and lattice-oxygen loss add separate failure modes. The approach could accelerate cathode development for stationary storage and high-voltage SIBs by narrowing dopant candidates before costly cell testing. Because η is calculated from formal valence, ionic radius, and cation fraction, it can be adapted to other multicomponent O3-type layered oxides. artigo.texto: ROTTERDAM, Netherlands, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Netherlands is approaching a major change in its residential energy landscape. From 1 January 2027, the country's net metering scheme (salderingsregeling) will officially end, changing how households with solar panels manage the electricity they generate and consume. According to market data, approximately 36% of residential addresses in the Netherlands had registered solar PV systems in 2024, up from 33% in 2023. Residential solar installations reached a combined capacity of 11,672 MWp, representing approximately 40% of the country's total installed solar capacity. Once net metering ends, households will no longer be able to offset electricity fed into the grid against electricity purchased from it. Instead, surplus electricity will receive separate compensation from energy suppliers. Meanwhile, feed-in charges (terugleverkosten) have already become an additional cost for many solar households. This shift makes maximising solar self-consumption increasingly important. SAMDUO highlights the role of accessible home energy storage and intelligent energy management in helping households make better use of their existing solar installations. SAMDUO's Nex E6000 and Nex E6000H home energy storage systems are designed to store surplus solar electricity for later use. Their plug-in design offers an accessible option for households looking to add storage to existing solar setups without necessarily undertaking a complete system overhaul. Compatibility and installation requirements depend on the existing configuration. The SAMDUO P1 Meter helps households monitor electricity consumption and energy flows. Combined with AI Mode, the system considers solar generation forecasts, household consumption, battery state of charge and dynamic electricity prices to optimise energy scheduling. The end of net metering marks a new phase in household energy management. SAMDUO aims to advance home energy solutions beyond standalone storage towards a smarter, more connected and data-driven energy ecosystem, empowering households to manage their energy and make greater use of the solar electricity they generate. About SAMDUO SAMDUO is a home energy brand developing intelligent energy solutions for European households. Built on an industrial foundation with more than two decades of experience in precision manufacturing, power and energy storage, SAMDUO combines engineering, product design and intelligent energy management to help households store, manage and use energy more proactively. Home Energy Intelligence for every home. Own Your Power.

artigo.texto: Ampace Highlights AIDC Battery Safety and Semi-Solid-State Technology for AI Data Centres At Data Centre World Paris, Ampace showcased its PU200 UPS battery system, built with semi-solid-state cells. Recent large-scale fire testing of the PU100 provides evidence of the company's approach to system safety. PARIS, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- At Data Centre World Paris 2026, Ampace showcased how it designs batteries for a critical moment in an AI data centre: when the mains supply fails and the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) must immediately carry the load. Its PU200 battery system combines high-rate discharge capability with a compact cabinet for facilities where space for backup power is limited. Ampace develops the cells, modules and complete battery systems used in its data centre portfolio. Its engineers work from the requirements of the installation back to the cell itself. The power a UPS must deliver guides cell design, the heat generated during discharge informs thermal management, and the space available in the facility shapes the cabinet. Safety and reliability are design priorities at each stage. Battery safety, from cell design to large-scale fire testing A UPS battery can spend long periods on standby before it is called on to deliver high power within seconds. Ampace designs its cells with low internal resistance to limit heat generation during high-rate discharge and support reliable power delivery until an alternative supply takes over. To assess how a complete battery system behaves under fire conditions, Ampace subjected its PU100 UPS battery system to large-scale fire testing under the sixth edition of UL 9540A. The PU100 met the applicable test criteria. For data centre operators evaluating battery fire risk, the results provide evidence of how the tested system performed under those conditions. Semi-solid-state cells for high-power backup The PU200 brings Ampace's semi-solid-state lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cell technology into a UPS battery cabinet. Its cells support the short, high-power discharge required during a supply interruption, while the compact cabinet gives operators more flexibility when allocating floor space in an existing facility or planning a new modular data centre. A detachable battery management system simplifies access for servicing. Ampace's AIDC Battery Solutions White Paper explores the evolving role of UPS batteries in AI data centre power architectures beyond traditional backup power. Ampace will continue to work with European data centre operators and industry partners to support power infrastructure needs.
