artigo.texto: MULTIFIT Advances Solar Storage Solutions as a Global Leading Energy Storage Inverter Manufacturer BEIJING, BEIJING, CHINA, November 20, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Making Solar Generation More Flexible Through Energy Storage As solar power becomes a larger part of the electricity mix, using generated energy beyond daylight hours is an increasingly important system requirement. As a Global Leading Energy Storage Inverter Manufacturer, MULTIFIT focuses on inverter technology and photovoltaic equipment that connect solar generation, battery storage, and electricity consumption. An energy storage inverter does more than convert power: it coordinates energy flows, supports battery charging and discharging, and helps a solar installation respond to changing generation and load conditions. Solar panels generate electricity according to available sunlight, while household and business demand follows a different daily pattern. Production may exceed immediate consumption around midday, then decline in the evening when electricity use remains high. Battery storage can retain part of the surplus for later use. The inverter provides the electrical interface for this process, converting DC electricity from photovoltaic modules and batteries into AC electricity for compatible loads and managing charging according to the system design. As solar projects combine generation and storage, compatibility among PV input, battery voltage, output configuration, protection, and communication becomes essential. MULTIFIT's inverter and photovoltaic equipment portfolio addresses these system requirements. MULTIFIT's Experience in Photovoltaic and Storage Equipment Established in 2009, MULTIFIT is a manufacturer of photovoltaic power generation systems and green energy equipment. Headquartered in Beijing, the company operates a production base in Shantou, Guangdong Province, and develops products under the Vmaxpower and MULTIFIT brands. Its business covers research and development, manufacturing, sales, photovoltaic system design, installation, cleaning, and operation and maintenance. A complete storage installation depends on more than an inverter. Solar modules, batteries, controllers, protection devices, and connected loads must work as a coordinated system. MULTIFIT's portfolio includes hybrid and off-grid inverters, solar panels, batteries, controllers, photovoltaic systems, and cleaning equipment. The company reports more than 60 independent intellectual property rights and over 40 product certifications. Its management and product credentials include ISO9001, ISO14000, OHSMS28001, CE, and FCC. MULTIFIT also reports sales in more than 100 countries and regions. These certifications reflect MULTIFIT's focus on product quality, manufacturing management, and the requirements of international photovoltaic markets. Energy Storage Inverter Design and Product Applications MULTIFIT's energy storage range includes hybrid inverter solutions designed to work with photovoltaic input and battery storage. One example is the Vmaxpower MULT8KH3 three-phase hybrid inverter. It supports lithium and lead-acid batteries within a stated voltage range of 125â600 V and provides CAN and RS485 communication interfaces. The listed enclosure protection rating is IP65. These specifications define the conditions for system integration. The MPPT range determines the suitable PV operating voltage, while battery voltage and chemistry affect storage compatibility. Three-phase output suits installations using three-phase distribution, and CAN/RS485 interfaces support communication with compatible equipment. IP65 protection is relevant where dust and water exposure are considerations, subject to installation guidance. MULTIFIT also offers all-in-one solar and lithium battery energy systems, including the M-ESS3200W stackable energy storage system. Its published configuration combines a 3,200 W inverter with an integrated lithium battery and solar charging functions. The listed battery energy is approximately 8.0 kWh. An integrated format can simplify equipment arrangement where a coordinated inverter-and-battery package is preferred. Sizing must reflect energy use, peak load, backup duration, and solar generation. Alongside storage-focused products, MULTIFIT supplies off-grid inverters and inverter-chargers for different system arrangements, including installations that may incorporate utility or generator input. Not every inverter supports the same grid connection, battery configuration, or operating mode. Selecting equipment according to the intended system architecture helps avoid mismatches among the PV array, battery bank, AC loads, and available power sources. Supporting Residential, Commercial, and Off-Grid Systems Residential rooftops, flat roofs, and carports can accommodate photovoltaic modules where site conditions permit. Battery storage retains part of daytime generation for later household use, making inverter capacity, battery energy, load profile, and backup requirements interdependent design factors. Workshops and other commercial or industrial buildings can use rooftop PV to supply part of their electricity demand. Storage may shift solar energy to periods of lower generation; its value depends on tariffs, load schedules, system size, and grid rules. MULTIFIT supplies inverters, batteries, panels, and related system services for these projects. Remote villages, islands, beaches, and other locations with limited grid access may use PV generation and batteries for independent power. artigo.texto: Os investimentos globais em inteligência artificial continuam exigindo volumes elevados de capital, especialmente em chips, infraestrutura e centros de processamento de dados. Para Arthur Frota, sócio-fundador da AFPAR, esse movimento pode abrir uma nova frente de oportunidades para startups brasileiras capazes de transformar essa infraestrutura em aplicações voltadas a problemas concretos das empresas. Segundo o executivo, a discussão não deve se limitar ao avanço das big techs ou ao volume de recursos aplicado na corrida pela IA. O ponto central está em identificar quais partes dessa cadeia podem gerar novos negócios no país. “As Big Techs que estão liderando a corrida da IA vêm pagando um preço alto por conta dos pesados investimentos necessários ao avanço da tecnologia. Mas a IA é um foguete que não dá ré. E a pergunta certa para as startups brasileiras não é se vamos participar da evolução da IA, mas sim quais serão as oportunidades que podemos explorar nessa cadeia para criar novos unicórnios”, reflete. Redata pode ampliar atração de investimentos Frota também aponta o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, o Redata, como um possível catalisador para a entrada de capital estrangeiro no país. O programa prevê incentivos fiscais para instalação de centros de processamento de dados, acompanhados de contrapartidas relacionadas a pesquisa e desenvolvimento e à destinação de parte da capacidade ao mercado brasileiro. Para o empresário, porém, atrair os projetos representa apenas uma parte do desafio. “Atrair o projeto é a parte fácil. O desafio é criar condições para que a injeção de capital não só aconteça, mas permaneça. Isso passa por dar conta do aumento exponencial da demanda energética, definir regras claras para a implantação dos data centers e oferecer previsibilidade de retorno aos investidores”, diz. Na avaliação de Frota, infraestrutura disponível não significa automaticamente desenvolvimento de um ecossistema tecnológico. “Não adianta ter uma autoestrada muito bem pavimentada se não se constrói uma cultura para seu uso nas corporações e as startups não desenvolvam soluções que se tornem indispensáveis, atacando dores reais do mercado”, assinala. Oportunidade está em fazer a IA funcionar nas empresas É justamente na aplicação que o executivo enxerga uma das maiores oportunidades para startups e empresas de serviços especializados. Conhecimento sobre sistemas utilizados no país, particularidades regulatórias e operacionais de diferentes setores e capacidade de implantar ferramentas no ambiente real das empresas podem se tornar diferenciais importantes. “Conhecer os sistemas usados no país, entender as particularidades de cada setor e conseguir colocar uma aplicação em funcionamento são conhecimentos pelos quais um cliente está disposto a pagar. Há espaço para quem instala infraestrutura, para quem desenvolve tecnologia e para quem ajuda outras empresas a aplicá-la”, diz. Nesse cenário, a vantagem não estaria apenas em desenvolver modelos próprios de inteligência artificial, mas em conseguir integrar soluções já existentes aos processos das organizações. Dados continuam sendo um dos principais gargalos Para Frota, a qualidade e a integração das informações disponíveis são determinantes para que projetos deixem a fase experimental e passem a produzir impacto financeiro. Levantamento da Deloitte com 501 lideranças nos Estados Unidos, em organizações que ao menos testavam agentes de IA, mostrou que 72% relataram falta de dados unificados e acessíveis. “Já há algum tempo que os dados são o novo petróleo, mas agora com a IA eles ganharam protagonismo absoluto e precisam ser integrados. Se o histórico de vendas está em um sistema, as devoluções em outro e os custos de entrega e tributários em planilhas distintas, a IA não consegue entregar resultados tangíveis e o ROI fica comprometido. A IA precisa receber os critérios adequados à decisão que está sendo tomada. E isso só se resolve com as pessoas que conhecem a operação na mesa”, explica Arthur Frota. O executivo também defende que projetos de IA sejam tratados como processos permanentes, sujeitos a ajustes conforme regras, sistemas e fontes de informação mudam. “O processo muda, uma fonte de informação é substituída, uma regra passa a valer de outra maneira. A aplicação precisa acompanhar essas mudanças para continuar sendo útil. É essa sustentação ao longo do tempo que separa quem entrega tecnologia de quem entrega lucratividade”, diz. Retorno precisa aparecer na operação Do ponto de vista de quem investe em tecnologia, Frota defende uma análise objetiva dos resultados. A aplicação ajudou a comprar melhor? Reduziu o tempo para reunir informações? Diminuiu erros ou retrabalho? Essas perguntas, segundo ele, ajudam a separar projetos de demonstração de iniciativas com impacto efetivo. “Os benefícios precisam ser comparados com os custos de implantação, operação e manutenção. Começar pequeno, com uma análise preparada para revisão humana, permite aprender sem exigir uma reconstrução completa da operação”, constata. A formação profissional também aparece como parte dessa equação. “Precisamos de gente que consiga entender uma dúvida de negócio, trabalhar com os dados e avaliar uma entrega. Conhecimento técnico e experiência de operação precisam caminhar juntos. Universidades, empresas e profissionais precisam se alinhar para oferecer uma formação que prepare talentos para esta nova realidade. E isso é pra ontem”, alerta. Para Frota, a próxima geração de empresas brasileiras de IA pode surgir justamente dessa combinação entre conhecimento local, capacidade técnica e aplicação prática. “Minha aposta é que podemos desenvolver startups relevantes fazendo a IA funcionar nas condições reais das empresas brasileiras. Quem conseguir ajudar um cliente a resolver um problema importante terá uma oportunidade de construir um negócio. artigo.texto: Cumberland County data center project will not proceed after sales agreement expires CUMBERLAND COUNTY, Pa. (WHP) — A data center proposal that faced a lot of opposition from neighbors has been pulled after its sales agreement expired, officials confirmed on Monday. Pennsylvania Data Centers will not seek a renewal of its sales agreement of the proposed data center in Monroe Township. In the past, the project faced pushback from neighbors and surrounding small businesses, such as Ashcombe Farms and Greenhouse. Residents and people from surrounding areas have mixed reactions to the renewal not moving forward. Brant Gift, a retired teacher from Franklin County, said: “A lot of people will, you know, be disappointed in that, that they, came to fruition.” Warren Hardman, who lives in Monroe Township, said: “I’m a little on the relief side. You know, slightly disappointed.” Martha Nagel, from Cumberland County, said: “I’m not sure they’re we’re ready for them here in Pennsylvania. Taking up our rural. That’s what we know, what we’re known for, our rural countryside and our farms and the beauty and everything of it,” Nagel said. Nagel said she is concerned about the impact data centers could have on the rural areas. PREVIOUS | 'We are not in support:' Monroe Township farm opposes proposed data center project Monroe Township Supervisor Tim Thompson said a representative from Meadows of Ashcombe Limited Partnership confirmed the sales agreement between the two parties expired, and Pennsylvania Data Centers will not seek a renewal. It was originally proposed to be developed on the 800 block of West Granthan Road and the 1400 block of Williams Grove Road. Hardman, who has lived in Monroe Township his whole life, said the area holds a lot of memories for him. “I’m glad you know. Yeah. So, let’s keep the farmland the way it is,” Hardman said. However, Hardman said he also understands the need for more jobs and economic growth. “If we do 17 jobs for a massive data center, that’s not a that’s not a good return on investment in terms of the land use. But, yeah, I mean, right there again. We need to increase the economy and create jobs. And that’s a, you know, which seem to be the way the economy’s going,” Hardman said. The “No Data Center” signs could be seen throughout the area near Ashcombe Farms and Greenhouse, which borders the proposed site. “They’re vehemently protesting against the data centers. I think that it’s a good thing and we need to find alternative energy sources to support the data centers,” Gift said. Pennsylvania Data Centers also invested in the PAX-1 project in Middlesex Township. A legal battle is currently unfolding over that proposal to fight its development. READ MORE | Judge hears arguments over controversial PAX-1 data center: 'This is like algebra' CBS 21 reached out to the developer for a statement on the expiration of the sales agreement, but they refrained from commenting. The owner of the land says there are no current plans for future use.

artigo.texto: Proposed Wade Hampton Boulevard data center would use 5 megawatts, far less than Spartanburg County projects Councilman Frank Farmer says the Prime Storage site is not one of the large-scale data centers making national headlines GREENVILLE COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - A proposed data center on Wade Hampton Boulevard in Greenville County would require about 5 megawatts of power, which Councilman Frank Farmer said is comparable to the electricity demand of a Walmart. The owner of the Prime Storage facility wants to rezone the property to build the data center. The site is next to Texas Roadhouse and near several homes. Recent coverage of large data centers across the country, including projects in Spartanburg County, has raised concerns about bringing similar developments into local communities. Farmer said data centers vary in size and function. “No data center is the same. They’re like fingerprints. Every single one’s different,” Farmer said. How the power use compares Farmer said the data centers receiving national attention are large artificial intelligence facilities, and the proposed project is not necessarily one of them. Here is how the proposed power requirements compare with other data center projects in the region: - Prime Storage, Wade Hampton Boulevard: About 5 megawatts - Valara, South Pine Street: At least 475 megawatts - Tyger River Industrial Park: Four proposed data centers, each projected to require about 50 to 65 megawatts Farmer said the Prime Storage project would use about as much power as a Walmart or a typical manufacturing facility. “I know five megawatts sounds big,” Farmer said. “Spartanburg, they’re dealing with 65 megawatts.” Farmer said the proposed facility would also use a closed-loop cooling system that would need to be filled about once a year with water from a facility outside Greenville County. “This is a super small scale data center. This isn’t one that uses gobs of electricity or water,” Farmer said. Farmer described the project as a low-latency data center. That means information would not have to travel as far, helping speed up data processing. What rules apply now? Farmer said the property’s proposed S-1 zoning includes protections against noxious fumes from diesel generators and requires noise to remain within the property line. Those protections are part of the zoning requirements, he said, but the county does not have an ordinance that applies specifically to all data centers. Farmer said he has been working on a countywide data center ordinance for about six months. It would be the county’s first ordinance specifically addressing data centers. He said he is gathering input from Georgia Tech representatives, industry leaders, policy experts and environmentalists. The proposed ordinance could address water use, noise, power consumption and limits on expansion, Farmer said. Residents’ concerns Residents who spoke during Tuesday’s Greenville County Council meeting raised concerns about the project, including the potential for expansion. “There’s nothing to stop them from moving outside of that building, clearing off all of those trailers and boats, and going into those storage containers as well,” one resident said. “We will have no ability to hold this company ... from building a much larger data center,” another resident said. Farmer said he understands the concerns of residents who live behind the proposed site. “There is a neighborhood behind it, and I totally understand why they would be worried,” Farmer said. “They don’t want their quality of life being impacted. I don’t want their quality of life being impacted.” What happens next Greenville County Council unanimously sent the rezoning proposal back to the Planning and Development Committee to consider additional safeguards for nearby residents. The proposal will undergo further review and require additional votes before moving forward. Farmer said that once a draft of the county’s proposed data center ordinance is ready, officials plan to hold public workshops to gather input from residents, industry representatives and other stakeholders. artigo.texto: Xcel Energy Advances 135.5-MW Battery Storage Project in Minnesota Xcel Energy has received battery units at its Blue Lake site in Minnesota, marking a construction milestone for a battery energy storage project that is part of the company's broader plan to expand energy storage capacity across the state. The Blue Lake project is part of Xcel Energy's strategy to diversify its electricity generation resources while maintaining service reliability and managing customer costs. Along with two planned projects in Becker, Minnesota, the company expects to have more than 735 megawatts (MW) of battery energy storage capacity operating in Minnesota by the end of 2027. The portfolio would be the largest in the Upper Midwest. "For more than a century, energy companies have generated electricity when customers need it and delivered it almost immediately. Battery storage changes what's possible. It allows us to store energy and dispatch it when it's needed most, giving us a powerful new tool to maintain reliability, support growing energy needs and make the most of the diverse resources that power our system," said Bria Shea, president of Xcel Energy–Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota. Battery energy storage systems store electricity when it is available and return it to the grid when demand increases. Advances in storage technology have also made it possible to install systems at existing energy facilities, such as Blue Lake, allowing utilities to use existing infrastructure while incorporating new technologies. The Blue Lake facility will store energy generated across Xcel Energy's Upper Midwest system, including electricity from wind, solar, nuclear and natural gas resources. The 135.5-MW facility will include 132 battery units capable of storing and delivering electricity for up to four hours. At full output, the system is expected to provide enough electricity to power approximately 125,000 homes during periods of peak demand. "The Blue Lake project demonstrates how battery storage is becoming an increasingly important part of grid operations," said Justin Meagher, Xcel Energy battery storage project manager. "These systems can respond quickly to changing conditions, store energy when it's available and provide electricity when customer demand is high. That flexibility helps us operate the electric system more efficiently while continuing to deliver reliable service to customers." The Blue Lake Battery Energy Storage System is expected to begin serving customers in 2027.

But Southampton Township officials, including Solicitor George Morris, spent the Oct. 20 governing body meeting assuring residents that the plan “does not allow for a data center on that site.” Resident Michael Kent, however, has attended previous Southampton committee sessions calling for a complete and explicit prohibition on data centers in the municipality, similar to edicts passed earlier this year in neighboring Pemberton and Medford townships. Kent, in attending the Oct. 20 session and mentioning the future of the Diamond Lumber site was a concern for him, said he was seeking an “articulate answer” as to “why we don’t feel the need to have ordinances specifically outlawing data centers when other townships like Pemberton and Medford, of course, are running to do so.” “Does what we have in place have enough teeth to prevent that type of development?” he asked. artigo.texto: The University of Michigan’s Board of Regents will vote on proceeding with the development of the planned Ypsilanti Township data center during Thursday’s monthly meeting. Ahead of the Board convening, project officials hosted a press conference to discuss recent developments, such as the project’s updated timeline and financing. The discussion was moderated by Paul Corliss, assistant vice president for public affairs and communications, and featured project lead Steve Ceccio; Robert Green, project director in the office of the executive vice president; Patricia Hurn, interim vice president for research and innovation; and engineering professor Karthik Duraisamy. If the resolution is approved during the Nov. 19 Board meeting above-ground construction is expected to begin in late 2027. The first phase of construction will cover an approximately 150,000 square-foot facility. Renderings of the potential facade of the data center were presented during Tuesday’s press conference. Ceccio said the goal of the facility’s exterior is to blend into the natural landscape. “If you look at the facade we’ve tried to make, it’s an industrial motif, but we try to have it blend into the environment,” Ceccio said. “We have a natural landscaping to harmonize with the land that’ll be abutting the river.” Construction will occur in two phases, and the total size of the development will be approximately 290,000 square feet. Approximately 50,000 square feet will be dedicated to University research, with the remaining 240,000 square feet to be utilized by research tenants, such as Los Alamos National Laboratory. Ypsilanti Township residents have vocalized a number of concerns in recent community forums regarding the data center’s impacts on their quality of life. A common concern among many has been the facility’s noise output. According to Green, the development would have the same sound output restrictions as any other campus facility, which is 61 decibels during the day and 55 at night. A normal conversation averages about 60 decibels, whereas the typical data center averages an output between 45 to 55 decibels at the property line. “We expect to test noise levels during commissioning and to continue monitoring after the facility opens to ensure noise levels are within the acceptable standards,” Green said. “The final model and design will determine the full spectrum of mitigation measures that we’ll install.”’ In an interview with The Michigan Daily, Green said noise mitigation efforts have been increased due to resident feedback. “We’re taking standards that are above and beyond what you would see with a typical facility of this nature to make sure that we are distancing those noise-producing elements of the facility away from the public access areas or away from the roadways or property lines,” Green said. “We’re taking additional measures to screen those with berms, trees, and then following up on that, we’ll be using our monitoring and modeling to see if that isn’t sufficient, then we’ll look at engineered sound barriers to, again, mitigate that noise emission.” Residents have expressed concerns during community feedback sessions about the data center’s potential to draw water from or discharge water into the Huron River. According to Green, the facility does not plan to draw or discharge water from the river. He also said they are looking to reduce potable water use. “Our model estimates that the peak water demand would be up to 650,000 gallons per day under the most demanding weather conditions and with roughly one-third of that water-drawn amount discharged back into the sanitary sewer system after its uses in the cooling process,” Green said. “We are also evaluating options to reduce the potable water use.” The University will continue to conduct environmental impact and acoustic studies during the next phase of project development. Additionally, the next phase will include the completion of design developments and construction documents, as well as refining utility plans. The first phase of construction is estimated to cost approximately $450 million. According to documentation submitted to the Board, the project will be supported by a grant provided by the state of Michigan, which totals up to $100 million and is contingent upon the development being built in Ypsilanti Township. Supplemental funding will come from “university bond proceeds with debt service paid from a combination of rental payments and general fund resources.” The first phase of construction is estimated to be completed in fall 2031. Hurn said she believes this development is necessary to keep the University competitive with research advancements. “We want to be able to meet our mission, which is to serve the public,” Hurn said. “There is no way that our research will be able to do that if we don’t move to be able to accelerate our capacities for research computing.” Hurn added that these data center developments have the opportunity to impact a variety of fields across the University. “One of the things that’s so important about this expanded capacity is, first of all, that it’s going to cut across all fields — medicine, engineering, climate science, some aspects of social and behavioral science — but all of these things are going to be taking on bigger and more complex problems than we’ve ever been able to work on before,” Hurn said. Daily News Editor Alexa Cheaney can be reached at acheaney@umich.edu.

artigo.texto: DCF Video: CoolIT's 3 MW CDU Brings Smart Monitoring and Fanless Cooling to AI Infrastructure As AI infrastructure moves toward higher rack densities and increasingly liquid-cooled architectures, the next challenge is not simply removing more heat. It's ensuring that the cooling systems themselves remain reliable, efficient, and capable of protecting increasingly valuable computing hardware. At the 2026 OCP Global Summit in San Jose, CoolIT Systems Director of Marketing Charles Robison gave Data Center Frontier a close-up look at several technologies addressing that challenge, including the company's new 3-megawatt CHx 3000 coolant distribution unit (CDU), integrated coolant health monitoring, and a fifth-generation cold plate loop designed for fanless servers. The demonstration comes at a significant moment for CoolIT, which was acquired by Ecolab for approximately $4.75 billion in July 2026. On November 16, Ecolab formally introduced its new integrated AI cooling platform at SC26 in Chicago, placing the CHx 3000 and its embedded 3D TRASAR technology at the center of a broader strategy combining liquid cooling hardware, fluid management, and digital monitoring. Looking Inside the CHx 3000 The CoolIT CHx 3000 is a liquid-to-liquid CDU rated for 3 MW of cooling capacity at a 3°C approach temperature difference, with a specified flow rate of 4,500 liters per minute. Designed for high-density AI deployments, the unit incorporates Ecolab's 3D TRASAR technology to continuously monitor the condition of the circulating coolant. In the video, Robison points directly to the sensor array that makes the integration possible. "3D TRASAR, and you can see the array of sensors here, allows coolant health monitoring," Robison explains. "It allows people to see real-time what's going on with the coolant. So before it goes out of spec, they know what's happening and they can address it." The distinction is important. Traditional cooling monitoring typically emphasizes temperature, pressure, and flow. Ecolab's technology adds visibility into fluid chemistry and contamination, allowing operators to identify deteriorating conditions before they compromise the system. According to a November 10 technical report from CoolIT, the integrated monitoring system tracks parameters including glycol concentration, pH, turbidity, conductivity, and differential pressure. These measurements can help identify conditions that contribute to corrosion, biological growth, and restricted flow through cold plate microchannels. Robison describes the monitoring capability as another layer of reliability for high-density liquid cooling infrastructure. Opening the CHx 3000 enclosure, he also walks through the unit's mechanical architecture, identifying its pumps, large 25-micron filters, heat exchanger, and control system, all accessible from the front of the CDU. Cold Plates Push Toward Fanless Servers The second part of the demonstration moves from the CDU to the server itself. Robison highlights a fifth-generation cold plate loop developed for a server OEM, describing it as a high-performance design intended to remove the need for conventional server fans. "What's unique about this cold plate design is there's—it's a fanless design," he says. "So we're doing 100% heat capture through this cold plate loop." That claim reflects a larger transition underway in AI server thermal design. As processor power demands climb, liquid cooling must increasingly address not only CPUs and GPUs but also memory, networking, storage, and power components that traditionally relied on airflow. In a September 2026 technical discussion of fanless AI servers, CoolIT described near-total liquid heat capture as an increasingly practical requirement for very high-density systems. The company identifies less than 1% of server heat remaining for air cooling as an achievable engineering target, while acknowledging that literal 100% capture is difficult to establish. The underlying direction is clear: as liquid cooling takes on virtually the entire server heat load, eliminating server fans becomes increasingly feasible. Robison concludes the walkthrough with CoolIT's range of cooling fluids, spanning pure water and multiple propylene glycol-based formulations. The display underscores another aspect of the company's expanding portfolio: matching coolant selection and fluid management to the requirements of increasingly sophisticated direct liquid cooling systems. From Cooling Capacity to Cooling Intelligence For DCF, the OCP demonstration also provides a useful continuation of our recent tour of CoolIT's manufacturing and R&D operations in Calgary, where Robison showed how the company is scaling production and testing for megawatt-class cooling infrastructure. The latest demonstration moves that story forward, illustrating how greater cooling capacity, continuous fluid monitoring, and increasingly comprehensive server-level heat capture are beginning to converge. With Ecolab's newly announced platform bringing these technologies together, the industry is moving toward an approach in which coolant quality, thermal performance, and operational reliability are managed as parts of the same system. For AI data centers increasingly defined by the density and value of the compute they house, that integration may prove as consequential as the next increase in CDU capacity. artigo.texto: JA lança ecossistema de energia solar e armazenamento de mesma origem em Chengdu AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 17 de novembro de 2026 CHENGDU, China, 17 de novembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A JA apresentou seu ecossistema de energia solar e armazenamento de mesma origem no evento “ORIGIN — Lançamento do ecossistema de energia solar e armazenamento da JA” em Chengdu, reunindo representantes de associações do setor, instituições de pesquisa, clientes e órgãos de certificação. Guiado pela abordagem de integração de sistemas fotovoltaicos e de armazenamento de mesma origem da JA, o ecossistema alinha energia solar, armazenamento de energia, gestão inteligente de energia e atendimento ao cliente desde o início, em vez de reunir, posteriormente, produtos desenvolvidos separadamente. Em seu discurso de abertura, o presidente da JA, Yang Aiqing, afirmou que uma integração mais estreita entre energia solar e armazenamento de energia é um próximo passo natural à medida que ambos os setores amadurecem. Os clientes precisam de mais do que equipamentos de alto desempenho: precisam de sistemas de energia confiáveis e fáceis de gerenciar, projetados de acordo com suas necessidades. Começar pelo valor para o cliente pode reduzir os custos de coordenação e melhorar os resultados gerais. Liu Shuo, presidente do centro de marca e marketing da JA, observou que excelentes módulos solares e equipamentos de armazenamento não garantem automaticamente um sistema excelente. Compatibilidade, despacho e responsabilidade devem ser considerados na fase de design. Com base em 21 anos de experiência na fabricação de painéis fotovoltaicos, a JA estruturou sua abordagem em torno de origem, sinergia e convergência, conectando P&D conjunto, operações coordenadas, pré-comissionamento conjunto antes do envio e serviço unificado. Guo Yafei, copresidente do centro de operações regionais da JA, descreveu três capacidades essenciais: controle e despacho unificados, gestão coordenada de energia verde e serviço unificado. Fundamentadas em um modelo de P&D de três gerações, essas capacidades reúnem uma arquitetura de hardware unificada, uma plataforma de software e um processo de comissionamento. A JA estima que, em comparação com sistemas montados separadamente, sua abordagem pode melhorar a eficiência do sistema em 2% a 3%, reduzir o tempo de implantação e comissionamento em 20% a 30%, diminuir os custos de gerenciamento do ciclo de vida do projeto em 30% e reduzir os custos de operação e manutenção em 10% a 20%. A JA ESS também apresentou soluções baseadas na integração de sistemas fotovoltaicos e de armazenamento de mesma origem, combinando os produtos desenvolvidos pela JA com a inteligência em nível de nuvem, borda e dispositivo. Elas abordam oito áreas de aplicação: centros de dados com IA, projetos de grande escala para serviços públicos, instalações comerciais e industriais, agricultura, sistemas integrados de energia solar, armazenamento e carregamento, microrredes conectadas e desconectadas da rede, mineração e energia residencial. A JA destacou as implementações na Itália, no noroeste da China, na República Democrática do Congo e na Mongólia Interior. Para um projeto comercial e industrial típico, a modelagem da JA indica um período de retorno do investimento 28,3% menor e um aumento de 36,5% na taxa interna de retorno (TIR). Bai Yiqi, da TÜV Rheinland Greater China, apresentou planos para desenvolver padrões para verificar o valor de sistemas integrados de energia solar e armazenamento, abrangendo desempenho em nível de usina, coordenação do sistema, confiabilidade do ciclo de vida e valor do ativo, bem como um relatório técnico conjunto com a JA. Na mesa-redonda do setor, os participantes defenderam uma mudança de paradigma, passando da conexão de dispositivos individuais para o projeto e gerenciamento de sistemas integrados, apoiados por objetivos compartilhados, responsabilidades claras e padrões de avaliação consistentes. Olhando para o futuro, a JA planeja levar seu ecossistema de energia solar e armazenamento de mesma origem para mais de 180 países e regiões por meio de uma rede de mais de 5.000 parceiros, ajudando os clientes a obter benefícios de energia limpa mais eficientes, confiáveis e mensuráveis. img alt=”” src=”https://rt.prnewswire.com/rt.gif?NewsItemId=PT98450&Transmission_Id=202611171144PR_NEWS_LATAM____PT98450&DateId=20261117″ style=”border:0px; width:1px; height:1px;” /> Tópicos Relacionados: Novos Produtos/Serviços, Serviços Públicos, Concessionárias de Energia Elétrica, Produtos e Serviços Ambientais, Energias Alternativas, Ambiental, Social e Governança, Tecnologia Verde A OESP não é(são) responsável(is) por erros, incorreções, atrasos ou quaisquer decisões tomadas por seus clientes com base nos Conteúdos ora disponibilizados, bem como tais Conteúdos não representam a opinião da OESP e são de inteira responsabilidade da PR Newswire Ltda

artigo.texto: Despite the hot topic of data centers in Virginia and nationwide, so far companies have yet to eye Halifax County as a destination. Halifax County Planning and Zoning Administrator Detrick Easley said in a recent interview that he has not received any requests to move a data center into the county. “I know a big topic in the county has been data centers,” Easley said. “I’ve seen a couple of posts. But I currently have not had anyone reach out to me about data centers.” Though there are no data center requests yet, the county is still working on a new ordinance, starting with a work order with the Berkeley Group. “We have a work order with the Berkeley Group because we don’t know about data centers,” he explained. “All we know is what we hear about the water and the noise,” he continued. “So, we felt like we weren’t educated enough, so we hired the Berkeley Group to go out and research, go to all locales and research the pros and the cons.” After that research has been done, the county may ask the Berkeley group to help create a new ordinance. “But the rumors that we have data centers coming here, they found that’s not factual,” he said. “That is not true.” Along with working on the data center ordinance, the county is also working on an ordinance for small modular reactors and battery storage. “It’s a new wave of energy,” Easily explained. “So we also have a working group working on the ordinance for SMRs.” He said there has been some interest in bringing small modular reactors to Halifax County, but they take up less land than data centers. “You wouldn’t know they were there, and that’s the way we want it,” Easley said. Easley explained that battery storage is a new wave right now to help store energy made by solar farms. “Once you get solar and solar starts making all this energy, if you don’t have the grid mass to put this solar in power, you’re losing it,” he said. “So we have a couple of developers looking now to site battery storage facilities in the county,” he explained. “They’re better because they are more compact and take less land. So, solar might take 1,000 acres, battery might only need 50 acres.” Emily Barber is a staff writer for The Gazette-Virginian. Contact her at ebarber@yourgv.com.

artigo.texto: State environmental regulators have resumed reviewing data center permits, bringing an end to an earlier directive from Gov. Greg Abbott ordering a pause on permit approvals related to data center projects. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality received notice on Friday from Abbott’s office that officials at the state’s electric grid had completed gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers — one of multiple issues Abbott asked grid officials and electricity regulators to evaluate. “The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations,” TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said in a written statement. In August, Abbott had called on the Electric Reliability Council of Texas and electricity regulators to audit all data centers trying to connect to the grid, as well as gather information about tax incentives, power use, water use and potential neighborhood impacts. Abbott at that time paused approval of any grid interconnections for data centers while the audit was completed. In his Sept. 21 letter to TCEQ calling for the environmental permitting pause, Abbott said the agency needed to wait until ERCOT “completes its review.” Environmental advocates at Public Citizen, responding to the news of the resumed permits, called on TCEQ commissioners to resign. “The TCEQ is asserting that ERCOT has concluded its assessment of the community impacts of data centers, and without sharing those results with communities or detailing how the TCEQ will incorporate the findings into permitting decisions, agency leadership has begun unilaterally issuing data center permits,” said Kathryn Guerra, the TCEQ watchdog campaign director for Public Citizen, in a statement. Intense opposition to data centers had been growing all year in communities across the state, where Democrats and Republicans alike fought projects they worried would destabilize the electric grid, lead to more pollution from new gas-fueled power generators and guzzle up water in a state with serious drought concerns. TCEQ handles permits related to air pollution at facilities and stormwater runoff on construction sites. The agency faced criticism in October from Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance. The groups noticed that some data center-related construction permits were being cleared anyway — counter to Abbott’s order. TCEQ said it suspended the permits and then it shut down its entire automated electronic filing system and required physical applications be submitted for staff to review. Then in a staggering upset on Nov. 3, Abbott lost his reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who on the campaign trail vowed to keep data center approvals paused until legislators pass new state laws. Neither Abbott’s office nor Hinojosa’s media team on Tuesday immediately responded to a request for comment. “Texans are tired of this political theatre,” said Sam Law, researcher at FracTracker Alliance, in a written statement shared by Public Citizen. “We need real leadership, transparency, and a true moratorium on data center development.” ERCOT provided an update on its review of community impacts to electric regulators at the Public Utility Commission of Texas on Nov. 5. ERCOT reported receiving responses from 93% of 465 projects, which provided enough information for “a statistically meaningful analysis for the final report.” ERCOT officials plan to report their full findings to the PUC on Dec. 10 and discuss them at the next PUC open meeting Dec. 17. artigo.texto: The Hood County Commissioners Court voted 5-0 to find a third party expert to address safety concerns regarding the Apache Hill battery energy storage system (BESS) in response to a risk analysis of the facility. The analysis was conducted by Dr. Andy Wolford, who founded Risknology, a safety consulting and risk assessment firm, in Houston in 1994. Wolford and other community members have previously voiced concerns about the BESS’s location adjacent to the Rainbow’s Promise daycare off Mambrino Highway. The Apache Hill BESS project by Vitis Energy features 96 Sungrow Power Titan 2.0 battery energy storage system containers and is expandable to 120 containers. Wolford said the site density is comparable to 1,000 Tesla car batteries. The BESS is located 200 feet from the daycare. The site is intended to provide 200 megawatts of power and 400 megawatt hours of energy. “That’s about a fifth of one of the Comanche Peak nuclear reactors,” Wolford said. Wolford filed a peer review of the facility with the developer of Apache Hill BESS in June 2026, and this was forwarded through the Hood County fire marshal to the company’s fire protection and engineering contractor. In September, the contractor responded to Wolford’s critique. “I had 16 key issues for them to address,” Wolford said. “They addressed one and stated that the other 15 were invalid and they weren’t going to do anything about it.” Wolford issued a rejoinder challenging the consulting firm’s response. Because the industry and fire codes governing it are new, “it’s not backed up by operational experience and accident history,” Wolford said. Summit Fire Consulting, which performed safety studies for Apache Hill, and Risknology disagree on the safety concerns, Wolford said. “I boiled this down to three primary reasons,” Wolford said. “Number one, the lab testing was done incorrectly.” He noted that the testing was done in China and was “performed incorrectly with propagating errors.” The testing results also influenced the design of the equipment, he said, adding, “they’re wrong, and they need to be redone.” Second, “the most significant hazards that the fire company was supposed to identify, they did not,” Wolford said. He identified these as container-to-container fire propagation risk and toxic vapor cloud dispersion. A third concern, Wolford said, is that the consulting company ranked the risks “unreasonably low,” adding that “the rankings are very biased and extremely low risk, which achieves no further engineering work if you meet a risk tolerance.” Wolford’s recommendations to the commissioners court were “first and foremost” for Hood County to not issue a certificate of occupancy “until all deficiencies are resolved,” to have the county fire marshal’s office seek a response from Summit regarding Risknology’s findings, to define resource needs for county fire departments to respond to BESS facilities and to contract with a third party expert to arbitrate between Summit and Wolford’s findings. That report would empower the fire marshal to act according to third party findings. He added that the cost of resources needed to respond to BESS incidents should be paid for by those operating BESS facilities and not by the taxpayers. Wolford said the risk to children should be considered. “Do we really want a crisis involving a large number of children who are a disadvantaged evacuation population — they’re vulnerable?” he said. Wolford said that Hood County is worth requiring responsible risk management over minimum compliance, adding, “Are we wise enough to recognize that something brand new, unproven and hazardous needs extra scrutiny?” Precinct 2 Commissioner Nannette Samuelson asked County Attorney Matt Mills if the county had received a response from communication sent to the Public Utility Commission, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality or the Attorney General “regarding risks at Apache Hill.” Mills said he was not aware of any response. Samuelson said the West fertilizer plant explosion (in 2013) was an example of “a lot of safety standards being bypassed” before a tragedy occurred. Precinct 1 Commissioner Kevin Andrews asked how higher standards can be required. “What can we do just in our world?” Wolford asked. “I think the first thing that we need to do is give (County Fire Marshal) Jeff (Young) the ability to respond however he needs to whatever pressure that the developer puts on him. It’s clear to me it’s their expectation that they’re going operational next month. … So we have to give our fire marshal the ability to either let that happen or not.” Andrews said he did receive a response from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas saying ERCOT was monitoring and following developments with the BESS. “What I don’t want to happen is for the standards to get revised due to an accident at Apache Hill,” Samuelson said. Messages left with Vitis Energy and Summit Fire Consulting seeking comment were not returned by press time.

artigo.texto: O governo de Mato Grosso do Sul tirou 8 ações orçamentárias do Plano Plurianual PPA 2023-2027. As iniciativas descontinuadas abrangem áreas como o suporte à ciência e tecnologia, o empreendedorismo e a infraestrutura rural, incentivos aos setores de mineração e bioindústrias, apoio a feiras comerciais, articulação de atenção básica, concessão de aterros sanitários e gestão operacional. Por outro lado, a administração estadual tem focado na estruturação do mercado de carbono, algo que a gestão de Eduardo Riedel pretende consolidar como prioridade estratégica para os próximos anos. Para operacionalizar esse mercado e impulsionar a agenda verde, o Poder Executivo criou no PPA a Ação 6288 – Estruturação, Desenvolvimento e Valoração de Ativos Ambientais, sob responsabilidade da Secretaria de Estado de Meio Ambiente, Desenvolvimento, Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação (Semadesc) e vinculada à Companhia Gestora de Ativos Ambientais de Mato Grosso do Sul S.A. (MS Ativos Ambientais). A nova ação incluída no PPA garante o aporte orçamentário necessário para que o Estado possa mensurar, precificar e negociar títulos ecossistêmicos e créditos de carbono. A iniciativa fortalece diretamente a meta de transformar Mato Grosso do Sul em um território de "Carbono Neutro" até 2030, criando mecanismos financeiros capazes de atrair investimentos privados alinhados à conservação ambiental. No que tange às exclusões orçamentárias, a Semadesc concentrou a maior parte das exclusões, somando seis ações operacionais descontinuadas na revisão do planejamento público. O Apoio ao Desenvolvimento Pautado em Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação (CT&I) teve seu encerramento motivado pela reorganização do fomento à pesquisa e inovação dentro das instâncias estaduais competentes, segundo consta na mensagem enviada por Eduardo Riedel à Assembleia Legislativa. Da mesma forma, a a ação que trata de “Produtividade, Competitividade e Empreendedorismo Rural” foi desativada após ter suas metas absorvidas por programas transversais de desenvolvimento econômico e extensão rural. Já o Fomento Econômico e Tecnológico dos Setores de Mineração, Energias Renováveis e Bioindústrias deixou de figurar como rubrica autônoma para adequação à nova matriz de incentivos da pasta. Além disso, o “Apoio a Espaços de Comercialização”, voltado ao suporte de feiras e pontos de venda, foi integrada a ações de fortalecimento do comércio regional e da agricultura familiar. Ainda no escopo da Semadesc, o governo descontinuou a Articulação de Ações de Serviços de Atenção Básica, encerrando uma linha de apoio a serviços comunitários após o reordenamento das atribuições setoriais. Fechando o conjunto da pasta, a uma das ações de Apoio à Infraestrutura às Propriedades Rurais, focada em intervenções físicas no meio rural, foi retirada do quadro de ações prioritárias fixadas para 2027. Na Secretaria de Estado de Infraestrutura e Logística (Seilog), o Poder Executivo cancelou uma ação: a Concessão de Aterro Sanitário por meio de Consórcios Públicos. Criada originalmente para estruturar modelos regionalizados de destinação final de resíduos sólidos urbanos em parceria com consórcios municipais, a iniciativa foi descontinuada do PPA em razão da readequação dos projetos estaduais de saneamento e infraestrutura. Por fim, na Secretaria de Estado de Turismo, Esporte e Cidadania (Setesc), a inativação alcançou a Ação 6267 (Gestão e Eficiência Operacional). Trata-se de uma rubrica de apoio administrativo interno cujas rotinas e processos operacionais foram absorvidos e integrados aos programas continuados de gestão e manutenção da máquina pública estadual. Para além disso, a Setesc deve ser eliminada da estrutura administrativa, conforme proposta também enviada à Assembleia Legislativa. Revisão do PPA na Assembleia Para além do detalhamento das alterações nas ações, a Segunda Revisão encaminhada pela Mensagem nº 47/2026 apresenta um panorama global sobre a arquitetura do Plano Plurianual (PPA 2024-2027), instituído pela Lei Estadual nº 6.158/2023. O PPA é o instrumento basilar do planejamento de médio prazo que orienta a confecção da Lei de Diretrizes Orçamentárias (LDO) e da Lei Orçamentária Anual (LOA). Sua metodologia desdobra-se em três dimensões integradas: a dimensão estratégica, que condensa o Mapa Estratégico, a visão de futuro, os valores e as diretrizes gerais; a dimensão tática, responsável por traduzir a estratégia em entregas efetivas à sociedade por meio de 28 Programas Finalísticos; e a dimensão operacional, que detalha os projetos e atividades executados pelas unidades gestoras. A visão panorâmica do plano reafirma o compromisso de Mato Grosso do Sul em se consolidar como um "Estado inclusivo, próspero, verde e digital", pautado pelos valores de probidade, moralidade, comprometimento, resolutividade e empatia. artigo.texto: Oak Ridge's AI Factory Moment: Lux, Nuclear Power, and the Next Data Center Frontier Key Highlights - ORNL’s 4,032-GPU Lux system opened to scientific users as the first dedicated AI factory supporting the DOE’s Genesis Mission. - Oak Ridge is attracting billions of dollars in proposed nuclear generation, uranium enrichment, fuel manufacturing, and recycling projects. - TVA’s Clinch River SMR has received a construction permit but awaits a final build decision, while Kairos Power advances a Google-backed demonstration reactor. - DOE is seeking private AI data center development on federal land, but no Oak Ridge developer has been publicly selected. - Power availability, licensing timelines, and skilled-worker shortages remain key constraints on the region’s ambitions. Oak Ridge, Tennessee, has spent more than eight decades at the intersection of American scientific ambition and national energy priorities. Now, a major new supercomputing deployment is bringing the historic center of nuclear research into sharper focus as a potential proving ground for the infrastructure technologies that will define the AI era. On November 16, during the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago, the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) announced that its new Lux supercomputer had opened to scientific users, becoming the first dedicated AI factory supporting the DOE's Genesis Mission. The system debuted at No. 14 on the latest TOP500 supercomputer rankings, recording 220.79 petaflops of performance on the High Performance Linpack benchmark. Developed in partnership with AMD and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), Lux represents a significant addition to the computing resources available at Oak Ridge. But its importance extends beyond another entry on the global supercomputing rankings. The system arrives as the surrounding region experiences a surge of nuclear energy investment, advanced fuel manufacturing, research infrastructure development, and federal initiatives aimed at connecting artificial intelligence with the nation's future energy systems. According to HPE's November 16 technical announcement, Lux is built on HPE ProLiant Compute XD685 infrastructure, equipped with AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs, AMD Pensando networking technology, and the AMD ROCm software stack. The direct-liquid-cooled platform incorporates HPE Juniper Networking technology, including Ethernet switches supporting 800-gigabit connectivity, addressing the network performance, thermal management, and GPU utilization challenges associated with large-scale AI computing. The system comprises 504 compute nodes and 4,032 GPUs, according to ORNL's Lux system documentation. Its architecture is designed to support both traditional high-performance computing and AI workloads, including model training, inference, and scientific applications that combine simulation, experimental data, and machine learning. Its TOP500 performance score measures conventional high-performance computing capability rather than AI training throughput, but the underlying architecture offers a useful view of how AI and scientific computing infrastructure are beginning to converge. Lux is also intended to provide a flexible, multi-tenant computing environment. Approximately half of its annual allocation of 3.5 million node-hours will support the Genesis Mission, while the remaining capacity is reserved for proprietary partner access, including AMD's development and testing work. The mission itself is intended to accelerate discovery in fields including fusion energy, critical materials, manufacturing, and scientific modeling by combining AI, advanced computing, and experimental research. Among the initial research directions is AI-driven forecasting of water availability, river temperatures, and streamflow, with applications for hydropower and thermoelectric generation in the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) region. Other work addresses fusion technology, materials development, and computational methods that could help improve the performance and efficiency of future energy systems. For the data center industry, Lux offers an immediate example of the convergence occurring between AI computing, high-density liquid cooling, high-performance networking, and energy research. What makes its arrival especially significant, however, is the wider industrial transformation already underway around Oak Ridge. The same region that now operates one of the nation's newest AI computing systems is also attracting billions of dollars in small modular reactor development, nuclear fuel enrichment, advanced manufacturing, fuel recycling, and related infrastructure. In parallel, DOE is pursuing the development of privately operated AI data centers on portions of its Oak Ridge Reservation. Taken together, the developments suggest that Oak Ridge could become an important center for technologies that will eventually be deployed at AI data centers well beyond Tennessee. From Manhattan Project Infrastructure to a New Energy Development Campus For much of its history, Oak Ridge has been associated with the Manhattan Project and the subsequent development of America's nuclear research and production capabilities. Established during World War II, the community became home to major facilities for uranium enrichment, nuclear materials processing, scientific research, and ultimately high-performance computing. Today, that legacy is being repurposed for a new generation of industrial development. The former K-25 uranium enrichment complex, once a critical part of the nation's atomic weapons program, has been transformed into the East Tennessee Technology Park (ETTP), where extensive environmental cleanup and redevelopment have made former federal property available for commercial use. At an October 27 gathering in Oak Ridge, federal officials and nuclear industry representatives highlighted more than $15 billion in announced nuclear-related projects across the region

artigo.texto: Electricity prices and reliability are on the minds of all Pennsylvanians. A recent study found that the region’s electricity grid is getting stretched to its limits, and as a result, prices have been on the rise. Pennsylvania could also start experiencing more than a dozen electricity shortfalls — and potential blackouts — annually by 2030 because of this stress on the grid. Unfortunately, with new data centers and more extreme temperatures on the horizon, energy use will continue to rise, making the strain on our grid even greater. In response to this energy demand spike, dozens of new fossil fuel projects are being proposed that would bring more air and climate pollution to our state. This includes a gas plant near Pittsburgh that would become the largest power plant of its kind in the nation — and could, by some estimates, emit 17 million tons of air and climate pollution annually. Instead of finding cheap and clean alternatives to tackle the challenge, the U.S. Department of Energy is keeping old fossil fuel power plants open that should have been retired. Here in Pennsylvania, two aging power plants that produce considerable climate emissions were kept open past their retirement date to help meet energy demand. Pennsylvania doesn’t need to keep open dirty power plants to meet the region’s energy demands. Instead, we can pair clean, renewable energy such as wind and solar with battery storage systems. This allows us to power the state and the nation with pollution-free electricity and avoid massive price hikes that some energy companies foist on consumers when electricity demand is highest and most urgent. Much like we use batteries in our everyday lives to power our TV remote or our kids’ newest toy, utility-scale batteries can also store and then supply the extra electricity needed to meet our energy demand. One of the great things about battery storage is that it allows us to capture and store extra electricity being produced from solar energy on the sunniest days. Then, in moments when the grid is strained and energy demand is high, that extra energy can be sent to the grid, providing consistent renewable power throughout the day. Red and blue states alike are taking full advantage of these benefits: Texas currently has approximately hundreds of times the battery capacity as Pennsylvania, much of which is paired with new solar developments. This buildout is in response to the 2021 winter storm Uri, which forced dayslong blackouts and resulted in hundreds of deaths across the state. Since that extreme cold, the huge investment in battery storage has helped to keep the grid up and running in subsequent winter storms and intense heat waves. In California, battery systems paired with solar arrays have been so efficient at saving and delivering energy to the grid that natural gas generation in the state has decreased, helping to reduce pollution while still meeting energy demand. With 21,000 megawatts of battery storage capacity, California has been able to use its wind and solar energy — even when the wind isn’t blowing and the sun isn’t shining — to power the state. Sadly, Pennsylvania currently isn’t taking advantage of this technology. A recent study by the PennEnvironment Research & Policy Center showed that Pennsylvania has seen little measurable growth in battery storage over the past decade. This is despite the fact that the cost of battery storage has been rapidly and substantially declining, like many other clean energy technologies. When we combine this with maximizing clean renewable energy, it can deliver real results for Pennsylvania. With batteries already being paired with renewables across the country, promoting storage here in Pennsylvania will help us take the next major step in renewable electricity production. The good news is that a proposal that would require utility companies to utilize more battery storage passed the Pennsylvania State House earlier this fall with bipartisan support. This legislation, state House Bill 2380, would allow utilities to capture excess energy produced and deploy it to our electricity grid when it’s stretched thin. If these batteries are paired with sources such as wind and solar, we can also power Pennsylvania with more clean, renewable energy. The Pennsylvania Legislature should pass this commonsense and bipartisan proposal as quickly as possible next session. Getting this bill to the governor’s desk is one of the best ways that Pennsylvania can protect our health and our climate — and keep the lights on. State Rep. Nikki Rivera, a Democrat, represents the 96th House District. Belle Sherwood is a climate and clean energy advocate for PennEnvironment.

artigo.texto: WASHINGTON – The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices. The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths. Recommended Videos The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year. The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act. Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote. Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no. Industry groups back bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more. However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals. “Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project. Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate. Democrats push for amendments A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands. Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels. “Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said. Majority Republicans stymied Merkley's effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.” The bill's sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process," he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators. “I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said. Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill. “In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government. “Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said. The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation. The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years. “We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said. Co-sponsor calls bill ‘the floor, not the ceiling’ for legislative action on climate Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some

artigo.texto: The calls are coming into Martin, Bertie and Chowan counties regularly asking what the data center restrictions are. The answer at this time is “no, we have no restrictions.” However, that is changing rapidly. The key may be rapidly. Three counties — and the municipalities within — lack of an ordinance is a signal the “plains are open.” The topic of ordinance conversation for the past few months, data centers are causing anxiety among residents. Edenton's town council recently adopted a 60-day moratorium on Data Centers. The council's action — a firewall, if you will — prohibits a data center deal maker from making a data center deal that is not the right for town. In September, Bertie Planning Board Chair Gayle King presented a draft ordinance to the Bertie County Commissioners. King, a Louden, Va. transplant, familiar with the onslaught of data centers in Louden, presented a draft ordinance prohibiting approval of new centers without strict development criteria. King experienced the Loudoun Data Center explosion and relocated to Merry Hill. According to estimates, Loudoun County has approximately 240 Data Centers in operation or in the planning stages. While the $1.3 billion estimated tax revenue received from these operations is astronomical, what it has done to the county, in King's words is, “tragic.” She does not want that to happen here. Neither does the town of Edenton nor Chowan County. While the Bertie County Commissioners took the idea of an ordinance or a moratorium under advisement, they have yet to act on a Data Center ordinance. The Edenton Town Council was a bit more prudent adopting a resolution placing a 60-day moratorium on Data Centers. Chowan County is also addressing the concerns and potential problems the county could face. Chowan County Commissioner Larry McClaughlin has been researching the topic for months, reaching out to those in the community that may know more than he does on the subject. McLaughlin explained while he was recently campaigning for his county commission reelection bid residents raised Data Center questions. On Nov. 23, the Chowan County Commissioners will hold a meeting to discuss and possibly adopt a one-year data center moratorium. McClaughlin suggested the town of Edenton and the county adopt the same or similar ordinances to solidify a united front to the data center deal makers. McLaughlin’s suggestion is worth reviewing and may make sense for Bertie and Martin County Commissioners to do the same. Knowledgeable residents suggest timing is most important. King stressed the point if there are no ordinances or restrictions, data deal makers can purchase property, put the shovel in and move forward with a plan, if the county’s and town’s do not have an ordinance in place to prohibit such a move. While data centers could be a financial lifeline for towns, counties and residents, ordinances need to be rapidly adopted outlining data center requirements. Aside from this, officials should call on knowledgeable, experienced data center professionals, many living within the area, to offer input into the process.

artigo.texto: After months of packed meetings, petitions, a lawsuit and a recall election, the latest chapter in Urbana’s data center fight ended on Tuesday, Nov. 17, not with a final vote, but rather an empty spot on the agenda. Hours before Urbana City Council was scheduled to hold a third and final reading on a proposed settlement and Memorandum of Understanding with developer Thor Equities LLC, the company withdrew the agreement. With nothing left to approve, vote down or table, council members formally removed the resolution from the agenda, filling the room with applause and cheer. Despite pulling the agreement, Thor Equities said it is not abandoning the project and remains open to talks with incoming and current local leaders. Meanwhile, city officials said they will continue addressing the dispute through the courts. Thor Equities’ federal lawsuit against the city, members of city council, and the Building and Zoning Appeals Board remains active. With voters having just passed a charter amendment banning new large-scale data centers along with a vote to recall longtime Mayor Bill Bean, city officials and residents are now left asking the same question: What’s next? Where it started The pushback over the proposed project, originally planned for land south of Ohio 55 and west of U.S. 68, traces back to early 2025 when members of city council passed Ordinance 4621-25 to allow data centers in the city’s M-1 Light Manufacturing District, according to city records and previous coverage. Later that year, council also approved a Community Reinvestment Area tax abatement agreement for the project. For many residents, the scale of the plans did not hit home until February 2026, when Thor Equities submitted a site plan application and city staff read the project description aloud during a council meeting. Opposition organized quickly as a response. Residents, educators and local groups raised alarms over water usage, risks to nearby wells, noise levels, diesel backup generators and the site’s proximity to Cedar Bog Nature Preserve and Urbana City Schools. Under the mounting public pressure, council reversed their course throughout the spring: - March 3: Before an overflow crowd, council voted 6-1 to pass Resolution 2727-26, placing a 12-month moratorium on new data centers through March 2027 and creating a citizen-led Data Center Moratorium Committee to study regulations and environmental impacts. - April: The city’s Building and Zoning Appeals Board ruled against Thor Equities’ site plan application. Later that month, council voted unanimously to start the process of repealing previous zoning changes. - June 16: Following a unanimous recommendation from the Planning Commission, council voted unanimously to pass Ordinance 4635-26, removing data centers as a permitted use in the M-1 district. Lawsuits, mediation and the ballot box Just three days after members of council repealed the zoning changes, Thor Equities filed a federal lawsuit against the city, members of city council, and the Building and Zoning Appeals board. In subsequent public letters and statements, city officials and speakers cited Thor’s claimed damages at more than $115 million. Around the same time, citizens launched two petition drives — one to place a city charter amendment on the Nov. 3 ballot banning new data centers drawing 7.5 megawatts or more, and another to recall Mayor Bill Bean, who had supported bringing the project to Urbana and later backed a negotiated settlement. Following court-ordered federal mediation in September, city officials introduced Resolution 2740-26 the following October to approve a settlement and MOU with Thor Equities. Under the proposed terms outlined by Bean in an open letter, Thor would have dropped its legal claims and agreed to fund an environmental study as well as make up to $50 million in payments to the city without a tax abatement. Rather than passing the agreement, members of council stalled the issue. Over multiple meetings in October and into early November, members repeatedly delayed a final vote —including an Oct. 20 meeting where a 4-3 vote to table the resolution fell short of the two-thirds supermajority required under council rules, pushing the measure to a second reading on Nov. 3. That Nov. 3 meeting took place on Election Day and was hosted inside the Urbana Junior High cafeteria, where hundreds of residents turned out to publicly oppose the deal. Resident Richard Barker provided members of council with excerpts from the proposed MOU, citing the agreement as having “layers of protection for them, and nothing for residents, the city, or the county.” At the polls that same day, voters approved the charter amendment banning data centers by roughly 77.25% and roughly 73% voted to recall Mayor Bean. Council pushes back on Thor’s exit By the time council met on Tuesday night for what would’ve been the third reading of the MOU, Thor Equities had pulled the agreement, releasing a statement from Global Chief Operating Officer Melissa Gliatta claiming the company had repeatedly tried to meet with city leaders without hearing back. “Withdrawing this agreement is not walking away from Urbana. Our preference has always been to sit down with the community’s leaders and build something together,” Gliatta said in the statement, adding that the offer remains open to the mayor-elect, council, the school district and local partners. “We still believe this project can deliver lasting benefits for Urbana’s schools and residents. We are ready to talk whenever city leaders are.” Several council members pushed back against that claim during the meeting, saying the company had waited far too long to engage with the public. Councilwoman Amy Jumper said she would “take the blame” for declining to have Thor make an appearance, citing her reasons for telling them to not come as it was simply too late.
