artigo.texto: O boom de data centers de IA no México está se acelerando, e a demanda de energia do setor deve chegar a 1,73 gigawatt (GW) até 2031, ante cerca de 279 megawatts (MW) de capacidade instalada em 2026. A Amazon Web Services e o Google Cloud já montaram infraestrutura em Querétaro, enquanto desenvolvedoras preparam instalações maiores para computação em nuvem e cargas de trabalho de IA. Querétaro respondeu por 78,7% da absorção líquida de data centers em quatro grandes mercados da América Latina, segundo o estudo da CBRE referente ao primeiro trimestre de 2026. O próximo desafio do México é entregar a infraestrutura elétrica necessária para uma nova expansão. Estimativas do setor apontam 205 MW em construção e outros 205 MW de fornecimento de energia previstos até o início de 2027, embora ainda não haja um cronograma completo para o pipeline de desenvolvimento até 2031. Demanda de energia: a demanda de eletricidade dos data centers do México pode chegar a 1.730 MW até 2031, ante uma base de 279 MW de capacidade instalada em 2026, segundo os dados divulgados. A projeção abrange o setor de data centers como um todo, e não apenas a IA. Necessidade de expansão: a diferença entre a base divulgada e a projeção é de 1.451 MW. Trata-se de uma comparação baseada em projeções, e não de um pipeline de obras confirmado nem de uma escassez de energia. Crescimento na América Latina: Querétaro registrou 213 MW de absorção líquida no estudo da CBRE do 1T26, o equivalente a 78,7% do total combinado de São Paulo, Querétaro, Santiago e Bogotá. Escala do investimento: o setor de data centers do México projeta cerca de US$ 82,5 bilhões em investimentos diretos e indiretos até 2031, incluindo US$ 20,63 bilhões em investimento direto. Riscos de infraestrutura: a capacidade de transmissão, as subestações e as conexões à rede podem determinar quando as novas instalações entrarão em operação, sobretudo em Querétaro. A expansão dos data centers no México foi além dos anúncios de investimento. O Google Cloud inaugurou sua região em Querétaro em dezembro de 2024, seguido pela Amazon Web Services (AWS) em janeiro de 2025. A AWS lançou três zonas de disponibilidade e pretende investir mais de US$ 5 bilhões no México ao longo de 15 anos. Essas instalações permitem que as empresas armazenem dados localmente, reduzam a latência e acessem serviços baseados em nuvem. A demanda vai além das empresas de tecnologia e alcança instituições financeiras, fabricantes e outros negócios que dependem cada vez mais da infraestrutura em nuvem. A IA também está mudando a forma como os data centers mexicanos são construídos. Em setembro de 2026, a ODATA anunciou que a instalação e os testes da tecnologia de refrigeração líquida estavam em andamento em sua unidade QR03, em Querétaro, para dar suporte à computação de alta densidade. Os racks de servidores preparados para IA costumam exigir de 100 a 200 quilowatts (kW), ante 10 a 15 kW dos racks de TI convencionais, segundo a avaliação da OCDE de 2026. A maior densidade de potência pressiona mais a distribuição elétrica e os equipamentos de refrigeração. Querétaro atraiu investimentos em larga escala por causa de sua conectividade consolidada, da atividade industrial e da proximidade com as redes norte-americanas. A CloudHQ desenvolve um campus de seis edifícios perto do aeroporto de Querétaro, projetado para comportar uma capacidade de computação expressiva, com infraestrutura elétrica de alta tensão no próprio local. Esses projetos refletem tanto a demanda já consolidada por nuvem quanto a expectativa de maior adoção de IA. A projeção de 1,73 GW do México, porém, abrange o setor de data centers como um todo, e não apenas a computação de IA. O setor de data centers do México projeta cerca de US$ 82,5 bilhões em investimentos diretos e indiretos até 2031. Desse total, US$ 20,63 bilhões, ou aproximadamente 25%, correspondem ao investimento direto projetado. Os outros US$ 61,89 bilhões cobrem os investimentos esperados nos setores de apoio. A estimativa mais ampla engloba atividade econômica além das instalações dos data centers, como construção, infraestrutura elétrica, equipamentos e serviços de tecnologia. Ela não representa US$ 82,5 bilhões já comprometidos ou gastos. A Associação Mexicana de Data Centers (MEXDC) também alertou que suas projeções econômicas não são uma lista de projetos individuais já confirmados. Fontes: projeções de investimento da MEXDC divulgadas pela Câmara de Comércio México-China e entrevista da diretora executiva da MEXDC, Adriana Rivera, em novembro de 2026. O setor de data centers do México espera que a demanda de energia chegue a 1.730 MW até 2031, cerca de 6,2 vezes a base de 279 MW de capacidade instalada divulgada para 2026. A diferença entre a base divulgada e a projeção é de 1.451 MW, mas esse número não representa um pipeline de obras confirmado nem uma escassez de energia. Capacidade de computação instalada e demanda projetada de energia não são, necessariamente, medidas idênticas. A MEXDC identificou 205 MW em construção, com conclusão prevista para o fim de 2026. A diretora executiva, Adriana Rivera Cerecedo, também espera o fornecimento de energia para outros 205 MW de demanda de data centers no primeiro trimestre de 2027. Fontes: entrevista do presidente da MEXDC, Juan Carlos Mondragón, em novembro de 2026, e perspectiva de energia da diretora executiva da MEXDC, Adriana Rivera, de 4 de novembro. O número de 1.451 MW é uma comparação aritmética entre a base divulgada e a projeção. Capacidade instalada, obras em andamento e fornecimento de energia não são, necessariamente, medidas intercambiáveis. Os dois marcos de curto prazo somam 410 MW, o equivalente a 23,7% da demanda projetada para 2031. Eles não podem ser somados automaticamente à base de 279 MW para calcular a capacidade futura em operação. A MEXDC não divulgou um cronograma completo, projeto a projeto, que estabeleça quando toda a demanda projetada será atendida. A Comissão Federal de Eletricida

artigo.texto: Demand for data centers continues to put the pedal to the metal, driven in part by artificial intelligence and the need for more computing capacity. But as developers look for places to build, their attention is on rural America rather than traditional tech hubs. Pinion principal Quint Shambaugh says it’s not just about acreage, but access to the infrastructure needed to support these large-scale facilities. “In North America the primary market data center supply reached 10,903 megawatts in the first half of 2026. That is up over 30 percent from the previous year and vacancy, so open spaces in data centers, still remained under 2 percent. So lots of them are getting built. The ones that are getting built are full and then even to add to that, 80 percent of new construction, so construction that isn’t even up and running yet, that capacity is already sold so it is pre-leased. So a data center currently right now that’s not on the market and that’s getting built, 80 percent of it is already pre-leased.” What does it take to power these data centers? The scale and density of newer builds need a lot of energy. “So AI workloads are driving dramatically higher, and power densities are driving dramatically higher, too. With some AI high-density racks consuming as much as 80 to 100 homes amount of electricity. So with one rack in one data center, it can consume that much energy. And the U.S. data center industry is expected to require roughly 30 gigawatts of new power demand annually to support continued AI growth. So when we look at this, really the core issue is power availability and it is really the dominant constraint of this entire industry.” That’s why access to power infrastructure, water, and land is making rural areas attractive. “Rural assets are becoming exceptionally strategic and are something that these companies are very interested in. Site selection increasingly depends on a combination of power access, transmission infrastructure, fiber connectivity, water resources, and land that you can develop on. All these assets are commonly found in rural America as you all know, and developers are pursuing locations beyond traditional areas and traditional hubs because of grid constraint.” But even when all the assets are in place, there are other challenges that impact whether a project moves forward. “Industry studies are consistently showing that delays in power delivery, permitting, or stakeholder alignment can be more impactful than the actual cost of the site itself. So it’s not the land that’s holding people up, it’s the actual communities that are slowing down these projects. As we recently saw in the midterm elections, I think it was 40 out of 41 ballot initiatives went against data centers. So the two biggest constraints right now, number one is power, but number two is community constraints.” As data center development continues to expand, rural areas with the right mix of infrastructure and resources are expected to remain at the center of site selection discussions.

artigo.texto: The development of next-generation electric vehicles, portable electronics, and advanced energy-storage systems calls for lithium metal batteries that combine high energy density with long-term cycling stability. However, conventional lithium metal anodes face two major challenges: producing uniform ultrathin lithium foils at scale and preventing uneven lithium deposition and continuous lithium consumption during battery operation. Addressing both limitations, a research team has developed a screen-printing strategy that integrates patterned lithium arrays with a chemically reinforced interphase. The resulting ultrathin anodes demonstrate promising performance in both liquid- and solid-state lithium metal batteries, offering a practical approach to high-energy-density battery design. Why This Innovation Matters Ultrathin lithium anodes can substantially reduce inactive lithium mass and increase battery energy density. Yet molten lithium spreads poorly on copper substrates, making it difficult to manufacture uniform, defect-free ultrathin foils. During cycling, unstable interphases and non-uniform lithium deposition further accelerate lithium consumption and dendrite formation. These problems become particularly serious when the lithium inventory is limited. Therefore, achieving scalable fabrication while maintaining stable electrode-electrolyte interfaces is essential for practical high-energy-density batteries. Innovative Design and Mechanism The research introduces a mask-assisted screen-printing method that forms regularly distributed lithium microdiscs on copper rather than relying on continuous molten-lithium coating. By controlling the dimensions and spacing of the patterned arrays, the researchers produced anodes with equivalent lithium thicknesses of 10-28 µm, overcoming the limitations imposed by poor lithium wettability. Meanwhile, Mg(TFSI)2 is introduced into molten lithium to generate a multicomponent nanocomposite containing inorganic species such as LiF, Li3N, Li2S, and Li-Mg compounds. These components provide lithiophilic nucleation sites and contribute to an inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase. Together, the discrete architecture and modified interphase promote uniform lithium deposition, reduce mechanical stress, and suppress dendrite growth and parasitic reactions. Outstanding Performance The Li@Mg(TFSI)2 array anodes demonstrate excellent electrochemical stability. In liquid-electrolyte full cells paired with LiFePO4 cathodes, the system maintains a specific capacity above 130 mAh g-1 and Coulombic efficiency exceeding 99.8% over 260 cycles. With high-loading cathodes, the anodes also support stable cycling for up to 120 cycles. The calculated stack-level energy densities reach 504 Wh kg-1 and 1071 Wh L-1 for the 20 µm-equivalent anode configuration. Applications and Future Outlook Importantly, this strategy is compatible with both liquid- and solid-state battery systems. In solid-state cells, the spaces between lithium microdiscs accommodate volume changes, while the reinforced interphase helps maintain stable electrode-electrolyte contact. The successful integration of ultrathin lithium arrays with high-loading cathodes highlights the potential of this approach for future high-energy battery technologies. By combining scalable electrode fabrication with interfacial and structural engineering, this work offers a promising route toward more energy-dense and durable lithium metal batteries.

artigo.texto: Ford Starts Michigan Battery Cell Output With CATL-Licensed Technology Cells from the $3 billion plant are shipping for Fathom pickup prototypes. Ford plans to ramp production next year. Ford began battery-cell production in Marshall, Michigan, in October and has started shipping cells for prototypes, a step toward bringing lower-cost lithium iron phosphate batteries into future U.S. vehicles. The shipments are headed to prototypes of the Fathom, Ford’s small electric pickup. The roughly 2 million-square-foot facility represents a $3 billion investment. Ford is in the early stages of certifying its manufacturing processes as it prepares to increase output. The project is part of Ford’s effort to adopt lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, cells for U.S. vehicles. The battery chemistry originated in the United States but was commercialized largely in China. Ford licensed technology and manufacturing support from Chinese battery maker CATL to help establish LFP production more quickly. Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced development projects, said the company needs to move quickly to produce affordable electric vehicles in the United States. He described CATL as the best supplier to provide the technology and help Ford learn how to make LFP cells. The Marshall plant is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells per minute, equivalent to 20 gigawatt-hours of annual capacity for electric vehicles and energy storage. That is below Ford’s earlier plan for as much as 40 gigawatt-hours a year, amid a pullback in electric-vehicle plans at Ford and across the industry. The facility is highly automated, and Ford says its planned production pace will help reduce battery costs. It also has room to add capacity if needed. The project has drawn criticism from some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford’s ties to CATL. In September, Duffy wrote to Ford CEO Jim Farley, expressing concern that the company’s ties to Chinese businesses could harm Ford and the U.S. auto industry. The White House praised Ford’s domestic jobs and manufacturing the following day. Ford plans to ramp up cell production next year. The Fathom pickup is expected to launch in the fourth quarter of 2027.

artigo.texto: During the November 17, 2026, Board of Supervisors meeting, the majority of the Board voted to pause action on legislative data center and electrical substation applications for up to 12 months, the maximum allowed by Virginia law. A previous legal opinion from the Loudoun County Attorney indicated that a moratorium to stop all data center approvals is not legal. The Board made the pause retroactively effective as of September 15. The Board’s reason for considering pausing action on legislative applications is to allow time for the county to complete the ongoing review of current data center policies and regulations. The project proposes amendments to the Loudoun County 2019 Comprehensive Plan and Loudoun County Zoning Ordinance pertaining to data center standards and locations. Amendments to the comprehensive plan and zoning ordinance have the potential to impact existing and new legislative applications for data centers. That project is expected to wrap up in the summer of 2027. The Board’s pause will end when the Board adopts comprehensive plan and zoning ordinance amendments as part of the Data Center Standards and Locations project. Under the terms of the pause, the Board's final votes on data center and substation applications would be deferred for up to one year. Virginia law requires action on such legislative applications within one year. The one-year period begins at the time applications are first submitted to the Planning Commission. During the Board’s pause, developers may continue to submit applications that propose or would allow for data center and substation uses. County staff will continue to review applications and schedule the Planning Commission’s public hearing; however, the Board’s intent is to pause any Board of Supervisors public hearings and Board votes on such applications until after the Data Center Standards and Locations project is complete. The pause would not cause any applications to become inactive. The Board’s action has the potential to impact 33 legislative applications that are currently active. The Board may consider exceptions to the pause for legislative applications that involve electric grid reliability or if the statutory period for a decision is about to expire. The action does not apply to legislative applications for properties located within the Route 28 Tax District. The Board’s action does not impact applications that are subject to administrative processes. The Board previously approved an end to by-right data center development, requiring all data center projects to come before the Board for a vote through the county’s special exception process. More information about the Board’s adopted resolution on pausing action on legislative applications for data centers and substations is available in the Board’s November 17 staff report. Additional information about data centers is available on Loudoun County’s website online at loudoun.gov/DataCenters and information about various transmission line initiatives is available at loudoun.gov/TransmissionLines. # # #

artigo.texto: Quick summary - Hundreds rallied at the state Capitol Wednesday for passage of the POWER Act, which would regulate data centers. - The bill’s Senate sponsor said the bill is a “big solution” for a “big problem.” - The legislation would, among other things, require big tech companies to pay for the energy used to power giant data centers. SPRINGFIELD — Hundreds of residents and environmental advocates rallied at the state Capitol Wednesday to urge lawmakers to regulate data centers. The residents came via bus, car and Amtrak from around the state to call for passage of the POWER Act, a bill that would require data centers to pay to create the energy they consume, mandate transparency around water use, limit noise levels and diesel generator use, ensure local community benefit agreements, and more. The bill failed to progress during the spring legislative session, but advocates hope to see it passed during the veto session. “Illinoisans are tired of fighting alone for basic protections without help from the state legislature,” said Lori McKiernan, a Springfield community organizer and Sierra Club member. “Time is up. Our legislators must take action on data centers.” Over the summer break, lawmakers have been meeting with environmental advocates, organized labor and representatives of the data center industry to negotiate the details. The Senate Energy and Public Utilities Committee was set to hold a hearing on the POWER Act at 4:30 p.m. Wednesday. Sen. Ram Villivalam, D-Chicago, is the lead sponsor of the Senate bill. He called the roughly 1,000-page bill a “big solution” for a “big problem,” and described the legislation as the “most comprehensive data center legislation in the nation.” “You’re here because this matters,” Villivalam told the crowd. “When something affects your families, your homes, your neighbors, and of course our bills, your voices deserve to be heard.” Battling big tech Data centers have existed for years in Illinois, housing servers and hardware that store data and power the digital world, supporting email, video streaming and other web services. But in recent years, as major technology firms race to create generative artificial intelligence, they have begun to build hyperscale data centers — massive buildings and campuses that sometimes consume the energy of a small city. Their actual and projected energy consumption have driven up energy costs for regular residents and small businesses. The rally comes shortly after the release of two reports from state agencies proposed delaying the planned closures of 11 fossil fuel plants, as required under the state’s landmark energy bill, in order to guarantee enough energy supply to meet the growing demand. But environmental advocates don’t want to see the state’s landmark climate goals delayed to power hyperscale data centers. “Big tech, they’re counting on us to be intimidated by their big money. They’re counting on us to be overwhelmed by the fight in front of us,” Illinois Environmental Council organizer Cate Caldwell said at the rally. “But as I look at this crowd today, I think big tech should be intimidated by us.” There won’t be a vote this week, but lawmakers could take up the issue when they return for their final days of the veto session next month. Capitol News Illinois is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news service that distributes state government coverage to hundreds of news outlets statewide. It is funded primarily by the Illinois Press Foundation and the Robert R. McCormick Foundation. artigo.texto: Ulaanbaatar, November 20, 2026 /MONTSAME/. Dr. Namkhairinchen M., Director of the Policy and Planning Department at the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change of Mongolia, participated in a meeting of partner countries under the Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM), where he presented Mongolia’s policies, legal reforms, achievements and objectives in international carbon market cooperation and outlined the country’s position on future collaboration. Organized by the Government of Japan on the sidelines of the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), the meeting was held on November 17 in Antalya, Türkiye. Ministers and senior officials from countries including Japan, India, Mongolia, Oman, Palau and Ukraine attended the meeting to discuss the implementation of the Paris Agreement, the development of international carbon markets and ways to expand cooperation in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. During the meeting, Dr. Namkhairinchen emphasized that Article 6 of the Paris Agreement is not only a mechanism for carbon markets but also a strategic tool for mobilizing climate finance, accelerating technology transfer and promoting sustainable development. He noted that Mongolia adopted the Law on Climate Change in July this year, establishing the legal foundation for carbon markets, climate finance, greenhouse gas management, transparency and accountability. The country is also developing relevant regulations, methodologies and institutional arrangements, he said. Mongolia became Japan’s first partner country under the Joint Crediting Mechanism in 2013. Since then, the two countries have implemented projects and programs in renewable energy and energy efficiency, promoted private-sector participation and strengthened national capacity, the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change reported. Mongolia expressed its intention to continue cooperation with Japan and expand carbon market partnerships with the Republic of Korea, Singapore and Switzerland, with a view to attracting investment, facilitating technology transfer and supporting sustainable development. Mongolia also highlighted its commitment to establishing a robust system for authorizing, registering and reporting carbon market activities, applying corresponding adjustments and preventing double counting. Such a system would support the country’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), safeguard environmental integrity and ensure transparency, helping develop a reliable carbon market that earns international trust. Carbon markets are economic mechanisms through which carbon credits and emissions allowances are bought and sold to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and combat climate change.

artigo.texto: [Ibase Gaming FY2026 Q3 Earnings Call] First Three Quarters Revenue Only NT$98.73 Million, Loss of NT$4.54 Per Share — Taiwan's Ibase Gaming Bets on ASEAN 20MW Energy Storage and AI Optical Communications for 2027 Transformation Taiwan's Ibase Gaming (6441.TW) has fallen into a slump. In an online earnings call on November 18, the company reported financial results for the first three quarters of 2026: cumulative revenue of just NT$98.73 million (approximately $3.0 million), less than half of the NT$235 million (approximately $7.1 million) posted for all of 2025 and a steep decline from NT$540 million (approximately $16.4 million) for all of 2024. Cumulative gross loss reached NT$105 million (approximately $3.2 million), with after-tax net loss of NT$242 million (approximately $7.3 million) and a loss per share of NT$4.54. This marks the second consecutive year of losses for Ibase Gaming, with no sign of the losses narrowing. "This has indeed been a challenging year for Ibase Gaming," Liao Yi-chung, special assistant to the chairman, said in his opening remarks, acknowledging that the company faces short-term operating pressure while also building the foundation for its next phase of growth. Financial Highlights at a Glance Three Headwinds Combine to Turn Gross Margin Negative Liao attributed this year's weak performance to three factors. First, demand in the U.S. unregulated gaming market has been weak, contracting at least 40% to 50% this year, with customers adjusting both procurement volumes and schedules. Second, existing products are gradually reaching the end of their life cycles, while the next-generation Gaming PC platform still requires customer testing, system integration and validation; during the transition between old and new products, mass-production ramp-up has fallen short of expectations. Third, revenue has fallen rapidly, but fixed operating costs cannot be reduced proportionally in a short period, dealing a severe blow to gross margin and operating profit. "When revenue falls rapidly, existing fixed operating costs cannot be adjusted in tandem, which relatively increases the cost burden," Liao explained. The financial statements show that Ibase Gaming's gross margin for the first three quarters of 2026 was -107%, a marked deterioration from -10% for all of 2025 and far worse than the positive 21% gross margin in 2024. It is worth noting that although cumulative revenue for the first three quarters fell sharply year over year, monthly revenue disclosures show that third-quarter 2026 revenue was about NT$60 million (approximately $1.8 million), up 25.3% from the same period in 2025, indicating that the revenue decline was concentrated mainly in the first half. October revenue of NT$30 million (approximately $910,000) was up 456.3% year over year, also hinting at a recovery from a low base. Still, cumulative revenue for the first three quarters was only NT$98.73 million, and returning to 2025 levels for the full year will remain difficult. Short-Term Debt-Servicing Capacity Flashes Warning Signs Amid the operating losses, Ibase Gaming's financial structure has also deteriorated. As of the third quarter of 2026, total assets had fallen to NT$1.563 billion (approximately $47.5 million), while total liabilities climbed to NT$760 million (approximately $23.1 million), raising the liabilities-to-total-assets ratio from 31% at the end of 2024 to 48%; shareholders' equity fell to NT$803 million (approximately $24.4 million). The current ratio plunged from 150.52% at the end of 2024 to 80.56%, while the quick ratio dropped from 80.71% to 31.90%. "This reflects that the company is indeed facing some management pressure on working capital and short-term liquidity," Liao acknowledged. Going forward, in addition to improving revenue and profitability, the company will place greater emphasis on the efficiency of capital deployment, including inventory management, project payment terms and control of accounts-receivable cash flow. New Businesses Emerge as Bright Spots: ASEAN 20MW Energy Storage and AI Optical Communications Orders Secured Despite the weak core business, Ibase Gaming delivered tangible results in its new business initiatives, providing one of the few bright spots at the earnings call. In the energy business, the company secured an ASEAN 20MW industrial energy storage project this year, extending from pure equipment supply to site demand analysis, project planning and third-party vendor integration — an important milestone in entering large-scale energy storage system integration. In AI optical communications, Ibase Gaming established Guangchi Technology in 2026 to enter bonding and assembly contract manufacturing for silicon photonics thermal components, and has already won orders from a major U.S. client. Liao said this business "is no longer just an early-stage technology deployment, but has begun to enter the stage of actual manufacturing and commercialization," adding that the company is actively expanding capacity and plans to extend into the assembly and testing of finished high-speed optical communications modules. In addition, Ibase Gaming is advancing a modular AI computing center (AIDC) solution that integrates AI servers, energy storage, power management and cooling systems, and is currently in talks with several potential clients. Liao, however, was cautious about this business, stressing that project amounts are usually high and that the company "will certainly be prudent and then some." Three Directions for 2027 in a Push to Return to Profit Looking ahead to 2027, Liao outlined three operating directions: improving business commercialization efficiency, improving the operating profit structure, and strengthening cash flow management. artigo.texto: The Port Angeles City Council has voted to extend the citywide moratorium on data centers for an additional six months, to end by September 1, 2027. Council's action requires additional steps including a public hearing and schedule for the extension. The moratorium pauses the acceptance, review and approval of permit applications for facilities whose principal use is digital data processing, storage, management or transmission. The City will use this time to study the potential impacts of data centers, engage with the community, and determine how data centers should be regulated locally. To learn more about what the moratorium and regulatory development process means for Port Angeles, please see the below Frequently Asked Questions. Data Center Moratorium 1. Are data centers allowed in Port Angeles? Not currently. The Port Angeles City Council has adopted a moratorium, or temporary pause, on the acceptance, review and approval of permit applications for facilities whose principal use is digital data processing, storage, management or transmission. 2. Why did the City Council adopt a moratorium on data centers? The moratorium provides the City with adequate time to study the potential impacts of data centers, thoroughly engage the public on this topic, and ultimately establish regulations that provide predictability for future economic development efforts while protecting the health and safety of our residents and environment. 3. How long will the moratorium last? The moratorium was first adopted by City Council on September 1, 2026, for a period of six months. On November 17, 2026, City Council authorized extension of the moratorium for an additional six months, to end by September 1, 2027. Council's action requires additional steps including a public hearing and schedule for the extension. 4. What happens to new data center applications during the moratorium? Data center applications will not be accepted or move forward through the City’s permit review process while the moratorium is in effect. 5. Does the moratorium permanently prohibit data centers in Port Angeles? No, the moratorium does not predetermine whether data centers should or shouldn’t be allowed. Instead, the moratorium is a temporary pause that will give the City time to establish appropriate regulations for data center facilities. Regulatory Development 6. What regulations are already in place for the construction of data centers in Port Angeles? The Port Angeles Municipal Code does not specifically define data centers as a land use. During the moratorium, the City will develop regulations and standardized permitting processes that address this type of facility. That said, numerous codes are already in place that regulate environmental impacts, including the State Environmental Policy Act (SEPA), Critical Areas protection, and the City’s Shoreline Master Program. Substantial state and federal regulatory requirements are also in place that can work to mitigate known potential impacts of data centers including the protection of air, water, stormwater, wastewater, and prevention of toxic contamination. 7. What are the goals of the regulatory development process? The City seeks to establish predictable standards for stand-alone or larger-scale facilities whose electrical demand, infrastructure needs, cooling systems, or operational impacts may differ substantially from other commercial and industrial uses. 8. What are some considerations when developing regulations? The City is studying the potential impacts of data centers to the environment, local utilities, and surrounding land uses. Some considerations include the water and electrical demand for this type of development, potential impacts to ratepayers, fire and emergency access requirements, noise compliance and multiple other potential environmental impacts. Former McKinley Mill Site 9. What is the City’s role in the redevelopment of the McKinley site? The former McKinley Mill site is comprised of two adjacent lots: one owned by McKinley and one owned by the City of Port Angeles, which is currently leased to McKinley. For the redevelopment of this site, the City of Port Angeles is involved in three separate roles: one as a property owner for the City-owned lot, one as the regulatory authority for land use, environmental, and other permits, and finally as the purveyor of electric and water utilities. Considering the City’s obligation to provide all customers with electrical utilities in our jurisdiction, the City has provided a letter to Candelaria indicating that under certain conditions protective of other rate payers, the City can provide electricity to the site. 10. Who makes the decisions regarding the City’s roles? Any new lease or sale of the City-owned lot would require City Council approval. Land use decisions generally lie within the purview of the Director of Community and Economic Development and/or the Hearings Examiner. Electric and Water contracts would have to be approved by City Council. 11. Has the City received any data center applications for this site? No formal permit applications have been submitted. The City of Port Angeles has received a letter from Candelaria Industries with conceptual ideas which did not include data center components. A subsequent presentation was provided to City Council by Candelaria Industries on October 20, 2026. 12. What cleanup or remediation would be required at this site? According to the original lease agreement, the obligation is for the lessee to surrender the property in as good an order as it was when the City signed the lease in 1967. The City expects that obligation to be honored with any redevelopment. Public Participation 13. Can I provide feedback to the City on the topic of data centers? Yes, feedback is highly encouraged. artigo.texto: Here’s What’s Next for Missoula Data Centers Missoula County is moving closer to stricter rules on data centers. But it could be another year before permanent rules are in place. Last week, county commissioners accepted a new staff report finding that data centers have "very real impacts" on public health, safety, and the environment. The report names more than a dozen potential concerns, including those brought up in public hearings, such as noise, water use, and climate change. That vote gives staff the go-ahead to begin working on permanent rules, although there could still be some delays in the process outside the county's control. Eye on the Legislature The report also raised the question of whether Montana's "Right to Compute Act" could override any local zoning policies, with staff suggesting it could be best to wait until after the Legislative session to see if there's a change in state law. That may mean the county could have to extend the current moratorium on data centers for an additional year. "No gap" promise for data center controls Commissioner Dave Strohmaier promises the county will keep the situation under control until a final policy is in place. "To give folks some level of comfort, there will be no gap," Strohmaier said in support of the motion. "Either we have permanent zoning in place by the end of this moratorium period or the more likely case in a separate action, from today is that we will extend the moratorium. So again, there will be no gap." READ MORE: Missoula County Considers Data Center Zoning Advocates are also urging commissioners to push state regulators to ensure data centers, not residential ratepayers, cover the cost of their massive power and transmission demands. And the county says it intends to play a role in power rate setting by the Montana Public Service Commission. 5 Montana Towns Companies Are Targeting For New AI Data Centers Gallery Credit: Chris

artigo.texto: Os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias têm ampliado sua gama de aplicações no setor elétrico. No Brasil, um dos exemplos mais recentes é o da Agropecuária Larssen, no oeste do Paraná, na qual a Weg implantou, em parceria com a integradora Lenz, dois sistemas BESS associados à geração fotovoltaica. A principal instalação utiliza um sistema BSCW400, da WEG, com 300 kW de potência e 645 kWh de capacidade de armazenamento, conectado a uma usina fotovoltaica de 300 kW. O equipamento atende uma granja com capacidade para produzir 70 mil ovos por dia, cuja continuidade do fornecimento de energia é particularmente importante. Em caso de falha na rede, o BESS assume as cargas em aproximadamente 40 milissegundos, evitando uma interrupção perceptível na operação. O segundo sistema tem 100 kW de potência e 215 kWh de capacidade. Juntos, os dois sistemas somam 400 kW de potência e 860 kWh de armazenamento. Além de funcionar como fonte de emergência e backup das instalações, a bateria pode ser carregada com energia solar nos períodos de menor tarifa e utilizada posteriormente no horário de ponta, reduzindo a necessidade de compra de eletricidade mais cara da rede. Outra aplicação está em Uberlândia (MG), na qual a BYD forneceu baterias para um projeto desenvolvido pela Cemig em parceria com a Alsol Energia Renováveis. O sistema tem 1,26 MVA de potência máxima e 1,36 MWh de capacidade de armazenamento e opera integrado a uma usina fotovoltaica. Diferente da aplicação na Agropecuária Larssen, em Uberlândia o BESS atua junto à geração fotovoltaica para mitigar a intermitência da fonte renovável. A solução usa baterias LiFePO4 da BYD para armazenar energia solar e liberá-la posteriormente, aumentando a flexibilidade e deslocando o consumo para momentos mais adequados. Essa capacidade aumenta a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico e pode facilitar a integração de fontes variáveis, como solar e eólica, ao aproximar a oferta de energia do perfil de consumo. Em uma escala maior, a ABB participou do desenvolvimento de um BESS da Universal Power Solutions Inc. (UPSI), em Limay, na província de Bataan, nas Filipinas. O empreendimento tem potência de 50 MW capacidade e foi projetado para reforçar a confiabilidade e a estabilidade da rede elétrica. Nesse caso, o papel da bateria é diferente. Em vez de atender principalmente a um consumidor individual ou armazenar a energia de uma usina solar, o sistema funciona como infraestrutura de suporte à rede, podendo armazenar energia e disponibilizá-la em momentos de maior necessidade. A solução fornecida pela ABB utiliza arquitetura modular e pré-engenheirada, com sistemas de baterias, gerenciamento de energia, inversores, transformadores,equipamentos de média tensão e proteção e controle. A expansão das aplicações também vem acompanhada de novos modelos de negócio. Além da venda tradicional, a empresa oferece o modelo BESS-as-a-Service, assumindo projeto, instalação, comissionamento e manutenção, enquanto o cliente paga pelo serviço. A proposta busca reduzir a barreira do investimento inicial e permitir que empresas utilizem o armazenamento para reduzir custos de energia, gerenciar picos de demanda, aumentar a resiliência do fornecimento e aproveitar melhor a geração renovável.

artigo.texto: - NORTH AMERICA EDITIONAustraliaNorth AmericaWorld POSCO said it will now work to improve the production stability and sales competitiveness of its lithium business to drive profitability. South Korea’s POSCO Group, trading under POSCO Holdings (NYSE:PKX,KRX:005490), has signed a long-term agreement to supply lithium to Contemporary Amperex Technology (SZSE:300750,HKEX:3750) (CATL), the world’s largest electric vehicle battery maker, covering 2026 to 2028 with deliveries already underway. POSCO did not disclose volumes, pricing or which of its operations will supply the material. CATL accounts for about 40 percent of the global EV battery market and supplies major automakers in China and abroad, according to POSCO. The steelmaker has expanded its lithium business using the raw-material sourcing and development capabilities it accumulated in steel, along with a production base built on high-quality lithium resources it secured early. It said the CATL agreement will strengthen its sales base in China, the world’s largest EV battery market, and reinforce its position in the global lithium market. POSCO linked the agreement to the strategy of Chang In Hwa, CEO of POSCO Holdings, which centers on preemptively securing high-quality resources and building long-term partnerships with leading global customers. The supply pact follows a run of partnerships CATL has announced since September with companies further down the battery value chain. On October 10, CATL and SERES Group signed a long-term strategic cooperation agreement in Chongqing. SERES’ AITO brand has used CATL batteries in every model since launch, with cumulative deliveries above 1.2 million units, and will continue to do so across its full lineup. The companies will also accelerate the second phase of their “Plant in Plant” project at the SERES Super Factory, which is planned to reach 10 to 12 gigawatt hours of annual capacity and bring combined capacity across both phases above 20 gigawatt hours. On November 2, CATL agreed to develop customized aviation power batteries for Blue Vector’s SKYLA V30 aircraft, with Blue Vector naming CATL its exclusive battery partner. In late Q3, CATL signed a memorandum of understanding with Kuehne+Nagel covering the electrification of CATL’s transport flows in Europe and a battery-swapping pilot for heavy-duty trucks, provided by Qiji and slated to launch in China in 2026. artigo.texto: Mintech will jointly develop diagnostic equipment with Terra Leader for use in solid-state battery manufacturing processes. Mintech said on Nov. 17 that it signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Terra Leader, a company specializing in digital pressure control, to develop and commercialize diagnostic solutions for solid-state battery manufacturing. The two companies will combine Mintech's electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) technology with Terra Leader's precision pressure-control technology. EIS analyzes internal battery resistance to assess battery condition and performance. Solid-state batteries use solid electrolytes instead of liquid electrolytes, making the contact condition between electrodes and electrolytes an important factor affecting performance. Technologies that maintain uniform pressure during manufacturing and precisely analyze the condition of electrode-electrolyte interfaces are therefore critical. The companies plan to develop an integrated solution that performs temperature and pressure control alongside electrochemical analysis in a single piece of equipment. The goal is to improve manufacturing efficiency and measurement reproducibility by analyzing battery cells without transferring them to separate equipment, while maintaining their manufacturing conditions. Mintech plans to expand its battery diagnostics business, which has primarily focused on lithium-ion batteries, into the solid-state battery sector. It will pursue commercialization targeting global battery manufacturers and materials companies.

artigo.texto: POSCO Group has signed a long-term lithium supply agreement with Chinese battery manufacturer CATL. POSCO Group said on November 18 that it had signed a contract to supply lithium to CATL over three years, from 2026 through 2028. The company did not disclose the supply volume or contract value, citing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) with the customer. Deliveries under the contract have already begun. CATL holds approximately 40% of the global electric vehicle battery market and supplies batteries to major automakers worldwide. The long-term agreement gives POSCO Group a stable customer base in China, the world’s largest electric vehicle battery market. POSCO Group has expanded its customer base in China from battery materials producers to battery cell manufacturers. In August, the group also agreed to cooperate on lithium supply with Ronbay Technology, China’s largest producer of ternary cathode materials. The companies agreed to collaborate on supplying lithium produced from ore and brine, as well as recycled lithium recovered from spent batteries. POSCO Group is also expanding its lithium production capacity. POSCO Holdings completed the upstream processing facilities at its second brine-based lithium plant in Argentina in October. Including its first plant, the group’s annual production capacity in the country has increased to 48,000 metric tons. The company plans to complete downstream processing facilities at the Yulchon Industrial Complex in South Jeolla Province in 2027 to convert lithium carbonate into battery-grade lithium hydroxide. Lithium is a core business under POSCO Group’s “Triple Core” strategy announced in July. The group plans to establish annual lithium production capacity of 173,000 metric tons by 2033 and generate more than 1.8 trillion won in operating profit from its lithium business by 2035.

artigo.texto: PIERCE TOWNSHIP, OH. — The halls of the Pierce Township Center overflowed with residents looking to listen and participate in a conversation on the future of data centers in their community. After getting through all the other agenda items, trustees were able to discuss the final two motions. Both were written by Trustee Allen Freeman, who explained the action the trustees would take. "We've pushed it back to the zoning commission with more definition of what we want to try to see. And what that is, is that we've asked them to give us changes to our code that would prohibit data centers inside of Pierce Township. The second motion does the same thing; it just prohibits small nuclear power plants," Freeman said to me after Wednesday's meeting. After the first motion passed, Freeman explained to residents that this is only a first step. “This is the beginning step of the process; this is not the end, this is the beginning. So, it clarifies what we want the zoning commission to go and do," Freeman said. Watch to see the data center decisions made by Pierce Township Trustees Wednesday night: Data centers have been the subject of many township discussions in just the last few months. “I want to help the zoning committee, and I want to help you all with the ability to show that the property that has been proposed for a data center is not appropriate," Pierce Township Resident Lisa Harris Hollister said Wednesday night. The resident was referring to a San Francisco-based company that proposed a 300-megawatt data center in Pierce Township earlier this year. A Crane Data Centers representative presented to the Pierce Township Zoning Commission on Sept. 1. The project includes three 200,000-to-300,000-square-foot buildings on 300 acres of wooded hillside across the street from the now-closed Walter C. Beckjord Generating Station. Pierce Township has a moratorium on data center construction through May 31, 2027. On Oct. 6, the zoning commission met at the Locust Corner Elementary School gymnasium. Several residents shared their concerns regarding data centers in Pierce Township with the commission. After the meeting, resident Kathy Cummins spoke with me about why she thinks a data center isn't right for that space. “This particular site that we're talking about is already a polluted site," Cummins said. And her worries stretch beyond that. “Environmental, it's noise, pollution, you name it," Cummins said. One resident did stand behind data centers. “I don’t think it’s right. I don’t think it’s a good idea to just ban something," he said. Freeman's original motion had a 250 megawatts or greater threshold written, but he removed that number and changed his motion during Wednesday's meeting. The trustee explained to me why he made that change. "There are data centers, there are the commercial-type data centers that are used by hospitals and banks and others, and we don't really want to eliminate those. Those have been around for 50 years or more, so we don't really want to work through those. But it's really the hyperscale that we want to really focus on and those are the ones we would like to have prohibited from Pierce Township. They just don't fit into the character of the township," Freeman said. Freeman explained what the next step will look like. "The zoning commission is going to have a December meeting. So, during that meeting, they'll start to organize around, as they've already said to me before they left, they'd like to have a consultant on board, so that's going to start to have that discussion of how we're going to go about doing that," Freeman said. The next zoning commission meeting is Dec. 1, and the next board of trustees meeting is Dec. 9.

artigo.texto: Key Takeaways - BYD started in a rented factory in Shenzhen and entered the auto industry through an acquisition in 2003. - BYD has produced more than 19 million NEVs, and its exports rose 93.75% year-on-year in the first 10 months of 2026. BYD (HKEX: 1211) marked its 32nd anniversary on Wednesday with a look back at how it grew from a battery maker in Shenzhen into an automaker with factories in Thailand and Brazil. In its anniversary article, BYD traced its origins to November 18, 1994, when more than 20 people started the business in a rented factory in Shenzhen. The company entered the lithium-ion battery industry in 1996. In 2003, BYD entered the auto industry by acquiring Xi'an Qinchuan Automobile. It launched its first mass-produced car, the F3, in 2005, followed by the F3DM plug-in hybrid sedan in 2008. BYD then expanded into commercial vehicles. It entered the new energy bus market in 2009 and built an electric bus factory in Lancaster, California, in 2013. In 2015, BYD unveiled a strategy covering the entire new energy vehicle (NEV) supply chain and a range of markets. It broadened its electrification efforts beyond passenger cars, buses and taxis to include logistics, ports and mining. As NEV output rose, BYD began building passenger cars overseas. Its 5-millionth NEV rolled off the production line in August 2023. In 2024, BYD completed its first overseas passenger car factory in Rayong, Thailand, where it produced its 8-millionth NEV. On November 18 that year, cumulative NEV production reached 10 million vehicles. BYD began production at its Brazilian factory in 2025, and its 14-millionth NEV rolled off the line there. All 8 of the company's roll-on/roll-off car carriers entered service that year. Earlier this month, BYD announced that its 19-millionth NEV had rolled off the production line, 124 days after it produced its 17-millionth. Chairman and president Wang Chuanfu said on Tuesday at the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen that BYD had produced more than 19 million NEVs in total. Wang said BYD's Thai factory can produce 150,000 vehicles a year and employs about 6,000 people, more than 95% of them local hires. The company also plans to expand local sourcing and research and development in its overseas markets. BYD exported 1,513,154 NEVs in the first 10 months of 2026, up 93.75% year-on-year. Over the same period, its sales in China fell 27.81% to 2,108,590 vehicles, while global sales declined 2.16% to 3,621,744 vehicles. In March, BYD unveiled its second-generation Blade Battery and new flash charging technology. According to the company, the technology can charge a battery from 10% to 70% in 5 minutes and from 10% to 97% in 9 minutes.

artigo.texto: UK battery company AceOn has launched a range of 12 V sodium-ion battery packs for applications including solar street lighting, roadside equipment, medical devices and remote telemetry, which is UN38.3-certified . The StamiNa+ Core range comprises four packs from 10 Ah to 30 Ah, equivalent to 120 Wh to 360 Wh, and is now available to order following completion of UN38.3 transport testing. UN38.3 is the section of the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria covering the transport safety testing required before rechargeable lithium and sodium batteries can be shipped. Tests include altitude simulation, thermal cycling, vibration, shock, external short circuit, impact or crush, overcharge and forced discharge. AceOn said certification allows it to ship the StamiNa+ Core packs to OEMs and system integrators in the UK, Europe, Africa and other markets. The packs are rated to discharge between –40°C and +70°C and charge between –20°C and +60°C, with a claimed cycle life of 5,000 cycles to 70% remaining capacity. That low-temperature performance is one of the areas where sodium-ion developers are increasingly targeting applications traditionally served by lead-acid batteries. BESTmag reported in September that Aeson was promoting sodium-ion as an alternative to lead-acid for automotive starter and auxiliary batteries, while Clarios, Altris and InoBat have validated sodium-ion cold-cranking performance down to –40°C. AceOn said the new range is aimed at applications where conventional lead-acid batteries can struggle in extreme cold and where lithium-ion chemistry may create safety or supply-chain concerns. The company said it is also seeing interest from the defence sector. All four packs use 32140-format cylindrical sodium-ion cells in a 4S configuration and incorporate an AceOn-designed battery management system providing overcharge, over-discharge, over-current and short-circuit protection, as well as cell balancing. The range comprises two 10 Ah/120 Wh packs, a 20 Ah/240 Wh pack and a 30 Ah/360 Wh model. Maximum current is 5 A for the 10 Ah packs and 10 A for the larger variants. AceOn has also developed a dedicated 15.6 V, 5 A charger for the range. The charger and integrated BMS were designed in-house. The company’s work with sodium-ion dates back to 2017, when it integrated Faradion pouch cells into a modified SolarSDS off-grid solar system. AceOn said that early project provided field experience with the chemistry and led to subsequent development of its own sodium-ion battery management technology, including work on a zero-volt BMS. Sodium-ion cells can tolerate deeper discharge than many lithium-ion chemistries and can use aluminium current collectors on both electrodes rather than requiring copper on the anode side. AceOn said its cells contain no lithium or cobalt and use sodium compounds derived from abundant materials including salt and soda ash. The launch follows growing commercial activity in the 12 V sodium-ion market. BESTmag reported last year that Unigrid had launched a sodium-ion platform as a drop-in replacement for conventional 12 V starter batteries. AceOn is also expanding sodium-ion assembly in Africa. Its new facility near Kampala, Uganda, includes a 3,000 sq ft battery assembly and training centre as well as BMS research and development. The site is intended to supply locally assembled StamiNa+ packs to East African markets. AceOn co-founder and CEO Mark Thompson said: “We first put sodium-ion cells into one of our solar systems back in 2017, when most people had never heard of the chemistry. It proved to us that sodium-ion could do a real job in the field. Nine years on, StamiNa+ Core is a certified range we can ship anywhere in the world. “Solar street lights, roadside signs, medical devices and remote telemetry all need batteries that work in the cold, last for years and don’t depend on cobalt or lithium. That is exactly what these packs are built for, and we’re ready to talk to OEMs and integrators now. “We want to be a leader in sodium-ion pack technology. Our team designs the BMS and charger in-house, we’re now assembling packs in Uganda, and we want to work with cell manufacturers around the world to take this chemistry into every market that needs it.” Photo: AceOn’s StamiNa+ Core range comprises four UN38.3-certified 12 V sodium-ion battery packs from 10 Ah to 30 Ah, alongside a dedicated charger. The packs are rated to discharge at temperatures as low as –40°C. Credit: AceOn.

artigo.texto: LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam powers on battery energy storage system - Official operation of battery marks a key milestone towards operating the factory on 100% renewable energy. - The system is the first of its scale in Vietnam. - The renewable energy solution supported by battery storage and LEGO Manufacturing Vietnams 12,400 rooftop solar panels are expected to avoid the equivalent of 20,000 tonnes of CO2e annually in the first five years of operation¹. LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam has powered on its battery energy storage system, developed in partnership with VietnamSingapore Industrial Park (VSIP), marking a key milestone in the companys ambition to operate its Vietnam factory using renewable energy. Jesper Hassellund Mikkelsen, Senior Vice President of Asia Operations and General Manager of LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam, said: This is an exciting step for the LEGO Groups sustainability ambitions in Vietnam and around the world. By bringing together innovative technology and strong collaboration with our partners, we are turning our renewable energy ambitions into reality and demonstrating what is possible when industry works together. Nguyen Phu Thinh, General Director of VSIP, said: We congratulate LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam for taking a pioneering step in adopting large-scale renewable energy solutions and demonstrating that ambitious sustainability goals can be translated into tangible action. The DPPA between the LEGO Group and VSIP is not only a significant milestone for both organizations, but also a powerful testament to how industrial developers and manufacturers can jointly create a new paradigm for sustainable manufacturing. As part of Vietnams first large-scale renewable energy solution for industrial use, LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam operates its own on-site rooftop solar panels alongside a direct Power Purchase Agreement (DPPA) with VSIP. Under this framework, electricity generated from VSIPs rooftop solar and integrated Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) is delivered directly to the factory via a dedicated transmission line. When generation exceeds demand, VSIPs battery stores the excess power and releases it as needed, ensuring a continuous and highly reliable renewable energy supply. Combined with the existing 12,400 rooftop solar panels on the factorys rooftops, the battery energy storage system is expected to cover approximately 75% of the factorys total electricity demand during the first five years of operation and help avoid approximately 20,000 tonnes of CO₂e emissions each year². LMV is exploring additional power purchase agreements to address the remaining 25% electricity demand and support its continued transition towards renewable energy. Opened in April 2025, the LEGO Groups Vietnam factory has been designed to support the companys long-term growth in the region, while advancing the companys sustainability ambitions. Facts about the battery energy storage system - Agreement type: Direct Power Purchase Agreement (DPPA) with VSIP, signed September 2025 - System: Integrated rooftop solar and battery energy storage solution operated by VSIP, supplying renewable electricity directly to LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam - Forecast renewable coverage: Combined, solar generation and battery storage are expected to support 75% of the factorys electricity demand with renewable energy. - CO2e reduction: Approximately 20,000 tonnes of CO2e per year (based on Vietnam grid emission factor of 0.561 tCO2e/MWh), including the contribution from LEGO Manufacturing Vietnams existing rooftop solar system. Facts about LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam - Jobs: For a full list of job openings, visit our career page or follow LEGO Careers and see how you can build your career. - Employees: 1,350 - Land: 44-hectares, size of 62 soccer pitches - Buildings: Five buildings that cover approximately 150,000 m2 and include office spaces, energy centre, moulding, packing buildings, a high bay warehouse and other buildings critical to factory operations. - Precision manufacturing: All LEGO factories follow the same blueprint, using high-tech equipment to produce bricks with 1/10th of a hairs width precision. - Location: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Environmental Sustainability Initiatives - Renewable energy: LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam is supported by Vietnams first large-scale renewable energy solution specifically designed for industrial use. The factorys renewable electricity supply is delivered through on-site rooftop solar panels and an adjacent energy centre combining large-scale solar generation with battery energy storage. Until all remaining energy needs can be accounted for through power purchase agreements, renewable energy certificates will be used. - Paper-based bags: The packaging line at LEGO Manufacturing Vietnam packages LEGO bricks in new paper-based bags, which replace single-use plastic bags. - Zero waste to landfill: The factory shares the same ambition as all LEGO operations to generate zero waste from factories which is sent to landfill. - Certification: LEED (Leadership in Energy & Environmental Design) Platinum and Gold certifications have been issued for the factorys main buildings, covering energy, water and waste. - Materials: In 2025, renewable and recycled sources accounted for 52% of the materials purchased to make LEGO® bricks, up from 33% in 2024, primarily through the use of the mass balance approach. - Investment: Sustainability investments increased by 20% in 2025 compared with 2024, and by more than three times compared with 2022. ¹ Avoided emissions are estimated using Vietnams 2026 electricity emission factor. Actual avoided emissions may vary as the emission factor changes over time. ² Based on Vietnams current grid emission factor. artigo.texto: According to SNS Insider, the global Activated Carbon Market is entering a period of accelerated expansion as governments strengthen drinking water standards, industrial operators improve pollution control and manufacturers adopt advanced adsorption technologies. The global activated carbon market was valued at USD 5.31 billion in 2025, is estimated to reach USD 5.77 billion in 2026 and is projected to expand to USD 12.15 billion by 2035, registering a CAGR of 8.63% during 2026–2035. Demand is increasingly influenced by regulatory measures addressing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), volatile organic compounds and industrial contaminants. Activated carbon remains an important filtration material because its porous structure enables adsorption of impurities from liquids and gases. Market development is also shifting toward reusable filtration media, carbon reactivation services and specialized grades for pharmaceutical manufacturing, chemical processing, energy storage and environmental remediation. Asia Pacific dominates global consumption and production, while North America and Europe are strengthening investment in advanced treatment infrastructure. Through 2035, suppliers offering certified filtration materials, reliable feedstock sourcing and reactivation capabilities are positioned to benefit from recurring industrial and municipal demand. Market Size and Forecast Demand Drivers and Constraints Primary Demand Drivers - Stricter drinking water standards: PFAS monitoring and treatment requirements are increasing demand for granular activated carbon across municipal water systems. - Industrial pollution control: Chemical plants, power facilities and manufacturing operations use carbon filtration to manage emissions, solvents and wastewater contaminants. - Expansion of water infrastructure: Urbanization and industrial development are encouraging investment in municipal and industrial purification systems. - Growing reactivation demand: Regeneration of spent carbon offers opportunities to reduce material consumption and establish recurring service contracts. - Specialty industrial applications: Pharmaceuticals, food processing, mining and energy storage are expanding the range of activated carbon applications. Potential Growth Constraints - Volatility in coal, wood and coconut shell raw material prices. - High energy consumption during carbon activation and reactivation. - Competition from membrane filtration and ion exchange technologies. - Trade barriers affecting international material sourcing. - Certification requirements and lengthy procurement cycles for drinking water applications. Demand Structure by Type Powdered Activated Carbon (2025 Market Share: 47.36%) Powdered activated carbon dominated the market with a 47.36% revenue share in 2025, supported by its rapid adsorption performance and widespread application in municipal water treatment, pharmaceutical purification, food processing and industrial emissions control. Its fine particle structure enables effective removal of dissolved organic compounds, taste-related impurities and selected contaminants. Municipal utilities frequently use powdered grades for seasonal treatment requirements, while industrial operators employ them in chemical purification and mercury capture. Through 2035, established processing infrastructure and recurring consumption are expected to sustain demand. Current trend: Continued demand from municipal water treatment and industrial purification. Major trends: Seasonal contaminant treatment, powdered carbon injection, pharmaceutical purification and optimized adsorption efficiency. Granular Activated Carbon (Forecast CAGR: 9.62%) Granular activated carbon is estimated to see the highest compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 9.62%, over 2026-2035. It is capable of being used in fixed-bed filtration systems and therefore is ideal for drinking water purification, PFAS elimination, groundwater cleanup and industrial gas purification. In contrast to powder activated carbon, granular activated carbon has the capacity to be thermally reactivated, which improves economics through the lifecycle. Current trend: Accelerating installation of granular filtration systems for contaminant removal. Major trends: PFAS treatment, carbon reactivation, fixed-bed filtration and reusable adsorption media. Demand Structure by Raw Material Coal-Based Activated Carbon (2025 Market Share: 43.84%) Coal Activated Carbon generated 43.84% of total revenue in the market in 2025, retaining its leadership due to the presence of production capacity and suitability for commercial use. Coal activated carbon is used in municipal water treatment, industrial gas purification, wastewater treatment, and emissions management. Production capacities are present in China, the USA, and Europe. Future demand from 2026 until 2035 will be determined by investments in filtration and raw material costs. Current trend: Stable industrial consumption supported by large-scale manufacturing capacity. Major trends: Water purification, industrial emissions treatment, raw material optimization and production efficiency. Coconut Shell Activated Carbon (Forecast CAGR: 9.84%) Coconut shell-based activated carbon is expected to grow at a CAGR of 9.84% through 2035, supported by demand for hard, microporous, low-ash filtration materials. These characteristics make it suitable for drinking water purification, gold recovery, food processing and selected pharmaceutical applications. Indonesia, the Philippines, India and Sri Lanka represent important supply markets. Growing interest in agricultural by-product utilization creates opportunities for producers, although seasonal shell availability and processing costs remain important commercial considerations. Current trend: Increasing preference for coconut shell-derived filtration materials. Major trends: Biomass utilization, specialty adsorption grades, gold recovery and sustainable feedstock sourcing. artigo.texto: A Cirion Technologies anunciou nesta quarta-feira, 18, a Datrix, nova marca da empresa para atuar no setor de data centers. A operação assume a gestão dos 12 complexos da Cirion na América do Sul, incluindo as unidades em São Paulo, Curitiba e Rio de Janeiro. Em comunicado, a Cirion destacou que a Datrix representa um novo passo na estratégia de crescimento no segmento de infraestrutura digital na América Latina. A marca busca fortalecer a presença regional da companhia e ampliar as capacidades de infraestrutura nos países em que mantém operações. Na relação com o mercado, a subsidiária deve atuar para atender hyperscalers, provedores de nuvem, empresas regionais e globais, plataformas de conteúdo e novas demandas de infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA). Além do Brasil, a Datrix conta com data centers na Argentina, no Chile, no Peru, na Colômbia e no Equador. A operação ocorrerá no modelo neutro (carrier-neutral), possibilitando que o cliente se conecte a diversos provedores de rede e tecnologia, com liberdade de escolha, informou a Cirion. "O papel da América Latina na economia digital das próximas décadas será definido pela infraestrutura que construímos hoje. A Datrix foi criada não apenas para sustentar esse futuro, mas para ajudar a moldá-lo", afirma Santiago Londoño, CEO da Cirion Technologies, em nota. "Nossa nova marca reflete tanto a força do nosso legado quanto a nossa ambição para o futuro", afirma o CEO da Datrix, Nelson Fonseca. "A Datrix dá a essa experiência um foco claro no que vem pela frente: o rápido crescimento da nuvem e da inteligência artificial na América Latina", complementa.

artigo.texto: Fight over Vineland data center noise stays alive as judge denies lawsuit dismissal Vineland residents say loud, metallic noises are impacting their quality of life. This story is part of the WHYY News Climate Desk, bringing you news and solutions for our changing region. From the Poconos to the Jersey Shore to the mouth of the Delaware Bay, what do you want to know about climate change? What would you like us to cover? Get in touch. A New Jersey Superior Court judge cleared the way this week for a class-action lawsuit against a hyperscale data center accused of emitting jarring noises. Residents who live near the Vineland data center complain about loud humming and buzzing sounds that allegedly disrupt their sleep, induce stress and prevent them from enjoying their yards. “We’re like prisoners inside the house,” said Tiffany Leone-Vespa, who lives about a mile from the facility but is not named in the complaint. The 300-megawatt data center is being developed by DataOne for the Nebius Group to support infrastructure for artificial intelligence as part of a $17 billion deal with Microsoft. This week, Judge James Swift denied a motion to dismiss the case during a hearing attended by a couple dozen residents, as well as virtual attendees. The lawsuit alleges DataOne has failed to soundproof the data center’s engines and cooling systems. The plaintiffs, which include three residents who live near the data center, allege the noise, likened to that of a hovering helicopter, prevents them from enjoying their homes, and worry it will lower their property values. Video obtained by WHYY News from residents less than 2 miles from the property depicts loud metallic and droning noises in the daytime and evening. Attorney Laura Sheets said 1,000 residents within 1.5 miles of the data center could be eligible for the class-action lawsuit. She believes the case is among the first of its kind in the U.S. “At the end of this case, we want the noise to stop. We want proper noise abatement,” Sheets said. “And, we want [residents] to be compensated. We are alleging that not only is it interfering, for the last year and a half, with their ability to use and enjoy their property, but that it’s causing major damage to their property values.” Leone-Vespa said the noises have become so intense that they vibrate her house. She said she keeps her windows closed and has hired a landscaper to mow her lawn so she can avoid going outside. Still, the noises distract her during the day and keep her awake at night. “I hear it all day long, I go to sleep with it, and then wake up to it again in the middle of the night,” Leone-Vespa said. Ryan Suppi, who lives about 1.5 miles from the data center, said the sounds, which he likens to a loud lawn mower, prevent him from getting adequate sleep. “I’ve been there 19 years. My kids grew up there. It’s been a quiet, peaceful place and we want it to go back to that way,” said Suppi, who is not a plaintiff in the case but hopes to be included in the class. “If I play loud music at 11 o’clock at night, the police are going to come to my house and tell me I have to turn it off. It should be no different for any company after a certain hour.” During the hearing, defense attorneys Mark Makhail and Ben Klein argued that residents are experiencing temporary construction noises that pose a mere annoyance. They said that until construction is complete, it can’t be determined whether the sounds are unreasonable. Although the data center is under construction, at least three data rooms operate 24/7, according to the lawsuit. Last month, environmental regulators in New Jersey fined DataOne more than $1 million for operating 62 natural gas-powered generators without a permit. Natural gas generators emit carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and other combustion-related pollutants. Sheets said she believes the metallic noises residents are hearing come from the generators. DataOne has said the engines will be replaced with Bloom Energy fuel cells, which turn natural gas into electricity through an electrochemical reaction. The company said the technology is much quieter and emits fewer emissions. However, the installation timeline is unclear. During the hearing, Swift said his responsibility was not to determine whether the accusations are true or the cause of the noise, but to determine whether the allegations can be sued over. He argued that the allegations constitute a public nuisance and that the data center has a duty to mitigate noise. Swift also denied the defendant’s request to strike the class-action component of the lawsuit. He rejected their notion that because noise doesn’t travel uniformly, it would require 1,000 “mini trials” to examine individual factors. Defense attorney Makhail denied a request for comment after the ruling. The defense must now file an answer to the allegations, and both sides will begin to swap evidence to build their cases. Residents like Stefanie Bartiromo, who is not mentioned in the complaint, say they hope the case could lead to compensation. Bartiromo hopes to be included in the class. She said even though she loves her home of almost 20 years, the noise and potential environmental impact of the data center is enough to consider leaving. “I want to be able to enjoy my house. I didn’t plan on moving, but if it gets worse, I might have to,” Bartiromo said. “You’re stuck in limbo. You want to improve your house, but should I put money into it if I’m just going to be forced out?” Get daily updates from WHYY News! artigo.texto: FRANKLIN COUNTY, Va. – Franklin County supervisors want another round of expert input on data centers, saying they still have questions about power use, water systems, environmental impacts and potential tax revenue. The board discussed next steps after an informational panel in October. One supervisor said the discussion left uncertainty about how much additional electricity closed-loop cooling systems may require. “There were varying degrees of information about the uptick in power usage from closed loop systems,” the supervisor said. Supervisors want a second panel that could include an environmental engineer and someone who has built and operated a data center. They also raised questions about how localities track equipment inside data centers for tax assessments. Supervisor Bonnie Law said she would like to hear directly from people with experience building and owning the facilities. “I would like to talk to people that have actually built the structures. The good, the bad, the ugly,” Law said. The board also discussed possible tax benefits. A supervisor cited Mecklenburg County, saying data centers occupy about 1% of its real estate and generate more than 45% of its tax revenue. The figure was presented during the meeting as an example for the board to consider. Supervisor Lorie Smith said the board must weigh potential revenue against its responsibility to residents. “We can be wooed by the money, of course. But we’ve got a fiduciary job to do on behalf of our citizens,” Smith said. The board also discussed finding its next county administrator. Supervisors have decided to consider both internal and external candidates and are weighing whether to hire an executive search firm. They are aiming for a decision around the end of March, with the timing subject to change as the process moves forward. Brian Carter, the county’s chief financial officer and deputy county administrator, was appointed interim county administrator on November 18. Smith said the search should include public engagement and focus on finding someone committed to Franklin County.
