artigo.texto: Ford Motor (NYSE:F) has commenced production of low-cost battery cells at a new plant in Michigan, US, using technology licensed from Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL) (HKG:3750). The cells are made with a lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) chemistry and are being shipped to a plant in Louisville, Kentucky, to be used for the company’s forthcoming Fathom midsize electric truck. Ford’s Vice President of advanced development projects Alan Clarke has spoken to the media about the use of CATL battery technology, noting that it is the fastest way for the company to build affordable electric vehicles (EVs) in the US. “CATL being the biggest in the world, it means that they’re the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn how to produce LFP cells,” Clarke says. The move has drawn criticism from the US Government, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy saying in September that the agency was “deeply alarmed” by the company’s use of licensed technology from CATL. As previously reported, LFP batteries are gaining global momentum due to their long-life attributes, low cost, and high-safety characteristics. In 2025, LFP batteries accounted for over 55% of all EV batteries globally, up from nearly 50% in 2024. Unlike nickel-manganese-cobalt chemistries, LFP batteries rely on lithium carbonate rather than hydroxide. The chemistry has traditionally been concentrated in China and is popular in more urban markets rather than for longer-range vehicles. While LFP usage is not as widespread in the US, more than 50 gigawatt-hours of battery manufacturing capacity was redirected towards LFP production in 2025, across several companies including Ford and LG Energy Solution. Ford Motor’s Fathom is expected to launch in early 2027, joining the Mustang Mach-E in the company’s line of consumer EVs. As recently reported at Benchmark Week 2026 in Shanghai, CATL is focused on industry collaboration and sharing its expertise through global partnerships. As US automakers balance geopolitical pushback against the need for affordable EVs, licensing established LFP technology highlights how global partnerships remain central to scaling North America’s battery manufacturing and EV industry. Mato Grosso do Sul quer que os programas estaduais de conservação ambiental tenham prioridade na venda de créditos de carbono à aviação civil internacional. O governo apresentou a proposta durante a COP31, em Antalya, na Turquia. Segundo o secretário estadual de Meio Ambiente, Artur Falcette, o governo federal abriu um canal de negociação e se comprometeu a ouvir os estados na definição das regras. O pedido trata principalmente dos créditos do REDD+ Jurisdicional, mecanismo ligado aos resultados de conservação e redução do desmatamento em escala estadual. Além da equipe do Ministério do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, participaram da reunião representantes do Consórcio Brasil Verde e do Centro Brasil no Clima. Na avaliação de Falcette, a aviação internacional já oferece uma das poucas fontes regulares de demanda por esses créditos. O secretário defende que a receita das vendas financie a preservação dos biomas e o combate ao desmatamento. Ele também alertou que, se a regulamentação demorar, Mato Grosso do Sul pode perder a oportunidade de acessar esse mercado dentro dos prazos previstos. Cooperação entre União e estados Na mesma reunião, as três instituições discutiram uma proposta de cooperação técnica nas áreas de clima, biodiversidade e combate à desertificação. Pelo modelo em debate, o ministério ofereceria orientação técnica e capacitação. Já o Consórcio Brasil Verde reuniria as demandas dos estados, enquanto o Centro Brasil no Clima coordenaria as ferramentas de acompanhamento das políticas estaduais. Para o governo de Mato Grosso do Sul, as negociações também interessam ao programa MS Carbono Neutro 2030. A expectativa é que a venda dos créditos ajude a financiar a restauração ambiental e a redução das emissões no estado.

artigo.texto: Com atuação da alta à baixa tensão, passando pelas disciplinas de hidráulica e combate a incêndio, o Grupo Planem oferece soluções de engenharia de ponta a ponta para um dos maiores hyperscalers (empresas que oferecem serviços em grande escala) do mundo. O projeto, ainda em sigilo, será o primeiro campus de data centers da empresa no Brasil. O escopo cobre todo o ciclo de energia a partir do ponto de entrega da concessionária, incluindo a subestação turn-key de 138 kV/34,5 kV, a distribuição em média e baixa tensão, além das subestações abaixadoras. A atuação também contempla os sistemas hidráulicos e de combate a incêndio, além da interface técnica com a concessionária. Ao concentrar disciplinas sensíveis sob responsabilidade única, o Grupo Planem minimiza riscos de integração e fortalece a confiabilidade do conjunto. A complexidade da obra exige coordenação precisa. Além disso, os prazos impõem um desafio adicional, pois demandam frentes de trabalho simultâneas e lideranças dedicadas ao planejamento e à logística — itens fundamentais para esse desafio. Outro ponto, não menos importante, é o apagão de mão de obra que o país vem enfrentando. O Grupo Planem já atua há algum tempo com estratégias para reter e qualificar suas equipes, com remuneração acima do mercado, o que tem a ajudado a vencer desafios com prazos curtos. BIM, Primavera P6, scanner 3D, registros georreferenciados, checklists eletrônicos e inspeções técnicas de processos apoiam a precisão, a produtividade e a rastreabilidade dos serviços. O comissionamento, com testes FAT, SAT e IST, validam o desempenho conjunto dos sistemas em condições reais e cenários de falha. Com essa combinação de integração técnica, planejamento, tecnologia e controle, o projeto evidencia o know-how do Grupo Planem para atuar em data centers e outros empreendimentos de infraestrutura crítica, nos quais confiabilidade e execução disciplinada são requisitos essenciais.

artigo.texto: The Jacksonville City Council will consider a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center construction while looking into whether the massive computer server facilities should be regulated differently than other developments. Council members Jimmy Peluso and Moné Holder have filed the legislation, which would pause the acceptance, review and approval of applications for data center development. The council members say that will give the city a chance to draft new zoning and safety policies for potential future hyperscale data centers. “We’ve seen other counties proceed with different kinds of moratoriums and sort of lead from the front on this, and I wanted Jacksonville to be a part of it,” Peluso tells Jacksonville Today. “We have a lot of natural resources here in Florida, so I imagine that at some point we would see more and more data center interest from national groups. And I just want to make sure that we have a plan.” There’s been public pressure on state and local governments nationwide to restrict or ban data centers, as the artificial intelligence boom has accelerated their development. The facilities can consume a lot of water for cooling and electricity, putting a strain on local utility supplies. A CBS News report on Nov. 18 cited a Harvard University study that says hyperscale data centers in the U.S. collectively consumed 1.8% of all U.S. electricity between 2024 and 2025. Peluso and Holder’s bill calls for a task force led by city staff from the Office of Economic Development, Public Works, Environmental Quality Division and the Planning Department to study best practices for local data regulation, as well as do a comprehensive review of the potential effects on: - Water supply and wastewater treatment capacity - Electrical grid capacity and infrastructure requirements - Land use compatibility - Community impacts regarding utility affordably and reliability - Other environmental considerations The moratorium would not apply to any existing data centers or their expansions approved. If the bill were to pass, Duval County would become the fourth in Northeast Florida to pass a data center moratorium, joining St. Johns, Nassau and Clay. Lake and Volusia counties have also passed pauses in data center development. Florida statute prohibits local cities and counties from enacting an all-out ban on data center development. But Senate Bill 484, signed into law this year by Gov. Ron DeSantis, keeps zoning, permitting and land use rulemaking on data centers under local control. That includes temporary moratoriums. Peluso notes the one-year timeline of the bill — straddling the current city council and the next, which will be elected in the spring of 2027 — will allow both crops of city lawmakers a chance to influence policy around data center development in Duval County. “As a county and a city and as a state, we need to come to grips with what is the future of planning in this new era of AI and technological advancements,” Peluso says. What regulations could do Under the proposed law, the city could consider code requirements like land buffers, noise reduction and energy loans and permit criteria for how much water a data center can consume, Peluso says. “We want to make sure that we are not going to be caught unawares by some massive project that just sort of shows up,” he said. According to Peluso, the city also needs guardrails on for data center owners who want to scale up. He proposes a scenario where a landowner has a 10 megawatt data center that sits on land with a legal use permit to add another 20 megawatts of computing power over a decade. “What if you slowly build up to it? How do we prepare ourselves, or better, have a plan in place in the event that somebody does try to do that?” Peluso said. Holder, who served on the Jacksonville Planning Commission before her election to city council, says data centers should have their own land use category in the city’s zoning code. She notes that Duval County does have small data centers. Nearly all are part of mixed-use buildings that include offices and retail, and not the large-scale, multi-acre stand-alone centers that have gained national attention. “But if we are thinking about bringing in data centers that that is their primary use, then we need to figure out how we zone that in and how we make sure that they’re placed in areas that don’t have negative impacts on residents and other surrounding areas of the city,” Holder tells Jacksonville Today. When Holder campaigned this summer in a special election for her at-large council seat, she said the common theme from the Beaches to Baldwin was concern about data centers, including their noise, heat pollution and water use. She said people are generally worried about where data centers might be located, “especially some communities that have been historically redlined or have had things come into their neighborhoods that had negative environmental impacts. They’re wondering if they’ll be first in line for something like that,” she says. In October, Holder held a public meeting on data centers that she says informed the development of the bill she filed this week. People asked Holder if a recent string of JEA rate increases had been caused by data centers. JEA interim CEO Jody Brooks said during a board meeting this week that the utility is experiencing “unprecedented rising costs” in part because data center growth is putting strain on supply chains. Brooks said copper prices were up 45% as of Nov.13 and aluminum was up 85% year-over-year. “Increasing demand on transformers, switch gears, conductors, electrical steel and manufacturing capacity nationwide — we’re already experiencing that even though we haven’t landed a data center in our territory,” Brooks said. artigo.texto: MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL. The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors. The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China. The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL. Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible. "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells." The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing. Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production. Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry. Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed. The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

artigo.texto: 17/11/2026 - 13:00 As restrições dos Estados Unidos à exportação de chips de inteligência artificial podem atrasar projetos de data centers no Brasil e adiar parte da demanda por equipamentos da WEG (WEGE3), avalia o Bradesco BBI. O banco considera a notícia negativa para a fabricante de motores e equipamentos, mas mantém suas projeções, a recomendação equivalente à compra e o preço-alvo de R$ 62 por ação. A dimensão do impacto ainda é incerta e dependerá das características de cada projeto. Restrições a chips podem adiar investimentos em data centers Desde 16 de novembro, fornecedores precisam de autorização do governo americano para exportar ao Brasil determinados processadores utilizados em data centers. As exigências alcançam componentes fabricados fora dos Estados Unidos quando desenvolvidos com tecnologia americana. O objetivo de Washington é impedir que empresas chinesas utilizem operações em outros países para contornar as restrições tecnológicas impostas à China. A regulamentação do Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) citada na análise classifica Brasil, Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia como países com risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal desses componentes para China e Macau. Para o BBI, as exigências podem desacelerar a implantação de projetos no momento em que o governo brasileiro tenta atrair investimentos por meio do programa ReData. Como a WEG fornece equipamentos para esse mercado, eventuais adiamentos poderiam postergar encomendas. O banco ressalta que as regras não representam uma proibição total das exportações para o Brasil. Há exceções para operações ligadas a empresas americanas. O efeito dependerá da estrutura societária dos projetos, dos usuários finais dos chips e das aplicações pretendidas. Dados da Abinee, citados pelo BBI, mostram que as importações brasileiras de semicondutores atingiram US$ 6,8 bilhões entre janeiro e setembro, avanço de 51% na comparação anual. JPMorgan eleva preço-alvo da WEG para R$ 66 Em sua análise sobre a companhia, o JPMorgan reiterou a recomendação overweight, equivalente à compra, e elevou o preço-alvo da WEG de R$ 56 para R$ 66 ao fim de 2027. O novo valor representa um potencial de valorização de aproximadamente 30% em relação aos níveis considerados no relatório. A expectativa do banco é de aceleração do crescimento, sustentada principalmente pelos negócios de transformadores, sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS) e motores elétricos. Exposição internacional favorece a WEG com real mais fraco O JPMorgan destaca a proteção natural da companhia diante da desvalorização do real. Mais de 60% das receitas da WEG são geradas fora do Brasil, com cerca de 30% provenientes da América do Norte. Pelos cálculos do banco, cada depreciação de 5% do real acrescenta aproximadamente 4% ao EBITDA projetado da empresa. Após incorporar um cenário de câmbio mais depreciado, o JPMorgan elevou em 6% sua estimativa de EBITDA para 2027. A projeção passou a considerar crescimento de 27% nessa linha. O banco prevê receitas e lucro líquido acima do consenso de mercado em 2027 e 2028. Banco vê desconto nos múltiplos de WEGE3 Na avaliação do JPMorgan, a ação da WEG negocia a múltiplos atrativos, com desconto de aproximadamente 15% em relação à média histórica do período pós-pandemia. Os analistas argumentam que a companhia tende a se beneficiar da exposição ao dólar e da menor dependência do ciclo econômico brasileiro. Esses atributos, associados à percepção de qualidade da empresa, sustentam a visão favorável do banco para WEGE3. artigo.texto: CATL hosted a business luncheon in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Fourth ABAC Meeting. Founder Robin Zeng said the battery maker had built 2,520 battery swap stations across 200 Chinese cities by the end of September, tying swapping to fast charging and vehicle-to-grid. The release, as issued by CATL Shenzhen, November 14, 2026 — On the sidelines of the Fourth ABAC Meeting of 2026, CATL hosted a luncheon in Shenzhen under the theme “Zero-Carbon Asia-Pacific, Together We Lead.” Business leaders from manufacturing, finance, consulting, digital technology and other sectors across the Asia-Pacific, together with representatives of international organizations and academic institutions, came together over lunch to share perspectives on zero-carbon technologies and the reshaping of energy systems amid the global energy transition, and on new pathways for green development in the region. Dr. Robin Zeng, Founder, Chairman and CEO of CATL, delivered the welcome remarks. Francis De Jaeger, Programme Officer in the Project Facilitation and Support Division of the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), and Yang Lei, Deputy Dean of the Institute of Energy at Peking University, shared their insights with guests. Robin Zeng shared CATL’s practical experience in battery swapping and low-altitude mobility, highlighting their potential to advance the energy transition across the Asia-Pacific. In battery swapping, CATL had established 2,520 battery swap stations across 200 cities in China as of the end of September, integrating battery swapping, super-fast charging, vehicle-to-grid (V2G) interaction and station-to-grid interaction. In low-altitude mobility, eVTOL aircraft are already being used to transport supplies to offshore oil platforms, completing a 150-kilometer journey in 58 minutes. The world’s first five-aircraft eVTOL formation flight covered 133 kilometers in 47 minutes. At the luncheon, the full version of the report “Key Enablers for the Energy Transition: The ‘Storage +’ Paradigm for System Integration” was officially released. Led by IRENA and jointly developed by more than ten companies and organizations, including CATL, the report explores cross-sector collaboration in advancing the energy transition. The Global Initiative for Energy Storage (GIFES), an industry-led collaborative mechanism established under the IRENA framework, also announced the results of its inaugural Global Energy Storage Flagship Project Selection. Several CATL-supported projects were recognized as regional best practices, including Supernode BESS in Australia, Malgarida & El Romero in Chile and MGEN CARMEN BESS in the Philippines.

artigo.texto: From emission pricing to green investment incentives Within the framework of the 31st Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), Vietnam launched its Carbon Market Information Portal, marking another step forward in perfecting the infrastructure and operational mechanisms of the market. The public disclosure of information on policies, regulations, and trading activities is expected to facilitate access to the market for businesses and investors, while also promoting the mobilization of resources for emission reduction activities. Previously, on June 29, 2026, the Vietnam Carbon Exchange officially launched at the Hanoi Stock Exchange, along with the commissioning of the National Registration System for Greenhouse Gas Emission Quotas and Carbon Credits. The gradual completion of the market's components lays the foundation for transparent trading, establishes a carbon pricing mechanism, and encourages businesses to invest in emission reduction solutions. According to the plan, approximately 511 million tons of CO₂, equivalent to the approved emission quota, will be allocated on a pilot basis during the 2025-2026 period to 110 facilities in three sectors: thermal power, iron and steel production, and cement. These are all energy-intensive industries with a high demand for production line modernization and the adoption of emission reduction technologies. Including these facilities in the quota allocation mechanism not only increases their responsibility for emission control but also forces businesses to reassess the long-term effectiveness of their investments. According to Mr. Bui Duc Hieu, Deputy Director of the Climate Change Department, carbon credits are not only a tool for managing emissions but also an incentive for businesses to innovate technology, use energy efficiently, and invest in emission reduction solutions. However, for the market to play this role, perfecting the legal framework and technical infrastructure needs to go hand in hand with improving the quality of emission measurement, reporting, and assessment, as well as the capacity of businesses to participate. When emission costs are factored into production calculations, businesses have more incentive to innovate technologically, save energy, and improve investment efficiency. Units maintaining energy-intensive production lines may face increased compliance costs; while businesses that proactively improve processes and reduce emissions will have an advantage in cost control and production organization. This also encourages capital flows towards clean technology projects, efficient energy use, and sustainable production development. Furthermore, the carbon quota and credit trading mechanism opens up the possibility of generating additional revenue from emission reduction results that meet the conditions for recognition and transfer . Although this revenue depends on regulations, trading capacity, and market price fluctuations, the prospect of commercializing emission reduction results can become a factor for businesses to consider when developing investment plans. Through this, the carbon market gradually links environmental goals with economic benefits, creating further incentives for businesses to transform their production models towards low emissions. Market transparency to unlock capital flows. Along with the establishment of carbon pricing mechanisms, the ability to mobilize resources for emission reduction projects is becoming a matter of concern. The demand for investment in technological innovation, improved energy efficiency, and the use of clean fuels is growing, while many businesses still face difficulties in balancing capital, especially for projects with high initial costs and long payback periods. The development of the carbon market is therefore expected to create additional financial incentives, supporting businesses in implementing the green transition process. According to John Robert Cotton, Director of the Energy Transition Partnership (ETP) for Southeast Asia at UNOPS, very few countries have been able to transition from establishing a legal framework to operating a mandatory carbon market in such a short time as Vietnam. He believes that carbon pricing is crucial in incorporating emission costs into businesses' financial calculations, thereby creating incentives for investment in emission reduction. Notably, from 2029, when the quota auction mechanism is expected to be implemented, the market could generate additional budget revenue for reinvestment in emission reduction activities in industry. Besides domestic resources, international cooperation also opens opportunities to mobilize financing for green transition. Through cooperation mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, projects that meet emission reduction requirements can access financing from the international carbon market. However, the ability to attract capital depends on the quality of the project, the transparency of emission reduction results, and compliance with transaction standards. While the carbon market opens up opportunities to mobilize resources, the ability to convert these opportunities into actual investment capital still depends on the financial efficiency of each project. From a credit perspective, Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, said that Vietnam needs approximately US$368 billion in additional investment capital by 2040 to adapt to climate change, enhance resilience, and reduce emissions, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP per year. Specifically in the electricity sector, the investment needs for developing power sources and grids in the 2026-2030 period, according to the revised Power Development Plan VIII, are estimated at around US$136 billion. The large scale of capital indicates the need to mobilize diverse resources, with bank credit continuing to play a crucial role for green transformation projects. Mr. Bui Minh

artigo.texto: The Duxbury Planning Board is looking to offer next year’s Town Meeting up to six new or updated zoning laws, including regulations for battery energy storage systems, members announced this week. On Monday at the Selectboard’s meeting at Town Hall, Planning Board Chairwoman Kristin Rappe said members of her committee had been meeting weekly to ready the zoning alterations for the March 13, 2027 Town Meeting. One of the more consequential proposals is a new bylaw to regulate battery energy storage systems. Known as BESS, these systems use lithium-ion batteries to store electricity, most often produced from renewable sources, and release it to the power grid when the energy is needed during peak usage hours. In Duxbury, a plan to put a BESS on residentially zoned land on West Street last year caused an uproar with hundreds of residents objecting to it. Proponents did not move forward with that project, but the experience showed the Planning Board that it needed to find a way to regulate BESS, since the state’s clean energy regulations require the town to address these systems. While the town can’t prohibit BESS in Duxbury, it can pass a law that sets town standards to protect the health and safety of residents, said Rappe. Passing regulations does not mean the town is welcoming these systems, said Selectboard member Brian Glennon. The proposed bylaw would establish regulations for siting a BESS on land in town. These include setbacks and screening required for when the system is built, safety mechanisms for when it is running and a decommissioning and financial surety for when it would no longer be in service. Many battery energy storage systems are large and take up multiple acres. One of the newest and the largest is in Medway and was completed this year. That site is 10.6 acres with the BESS taking up 5.2 acres and producing 250 MW, according to the state Department of Public Utilities. Duxbury’s proposed BESS zoning law could limit these systems to lots that are at least 250,000 square feet, or nearly six acres. This is because the system would be required to have 200-foot setbacks on all sides with a minimum lot size of 500 by 500 feet. The locations would also be required to have a perimeter buffer and fencing, access roads large enough for fire trucks and a water cistern and fire hydrant. Also, no BESS could be sited in the Dunes, Flood Hazard, Wetlands Protection, Aquifer Protection or Waterfront Scene Area overlay districts. Rappe said the Planning Board studied other towns’ regulations before writing its own. Also, board members kept two principles in mind for the new rules: They must not endanger the health, safety and welfare of residents and they must protect the environment. In addition, the new zoning proposal needed to meet three tests, she said. These include adoption at Town Meeting, approval by the state Attorney General and being defensible in court. “There is a very long list of things we’ve done to try to make sure that Duxbury and its citizens are kept safe,” she said. “The consequences of not passing it are that we have no local regulations, no control, and it could be sited almost anywhere.” This bylaw is not to encourage BESS in town but to have a process to regulate them if they are proposed, said Rappe. The Planning Board held a public information session on BESS on Nov. 16. Selectboard members had a few questions for the Planning Board on the BESS bylaw but they praised the effort so far. “Great job,” said Glennon, “You’ve done a lot of hard work on this.” “We need to put something in place even if we abhor to have to do this,” said Selectboard Vice Chairman Fernando Guitart. “When it comes to town, at least we have some measure of control, so that’s going to be the key selling point. We have to convince Town Meeting.” In addition to the BESS bylaw, the Planning Board is proposing five other law changes. One of the less complicated proposals includes updates to certain sections of the town’s current zoning law to ensure the language is consistent with changes to Chapter 40A, the state law that regulates local zoning bylaws. That law was updated in July. A second proposal amends the existing Flood Hazard Area Overlay District as specified by the Massachusetts Department of Conservation and Recreation. According to Rappe, this action will not affect residents’ flood insurance. The board is also proposing to update over 60 definitions and terms in the zoning bylaw. Many are language updates such as changing the term “Board of Appeals” to “Zoning Board of Appeals” or changing “Chairman” to “Chair.” There are two other more substantial zoning bylaw changes. One is to update the Inclusionary Housing section to encourage more affordable housing and the other would replace the Residential Conservation Cluster zoning with something called the Open Space Residential Development District. Any zoning bylaws proposed for Town Meeting will be reviewed by both the Selectboard and Planning Board at public hearings before the meeting.

artigo.texto: Supply Runs from 2026 to 2028, Expanding POSCO’s China Market Presence While the Deal Follows Recent Agreements With SK On and Longbai Group POSCO Group has signed a long-term contract to supply lithium for electric vehicle batteries to China’s CATL for three years from 2026 to 2028. Photo provided by POSCO Group. POSCO Group is strengthening its penetration of the Chinese market by signing a long-term lithium supply contract with China’s CATL, the world’s largest electric vehicle battery manufacturer. Following a lithium supply contract with SK On and business cooperation with China’s Ronbay Group earlier this year, the group is expanding its global lithium sales network by securing CATL as a client. POSCO Group announced on Nov. 18 that it has signed a contract with CATL to supply lithium required for electric vehicle battery manufacturing for three years from 2026 to 2028. Supply under the contract is currently underway, and the specific supply volume and contract amount have not been disclosed. CATL is a company that holds approximately a 40% share in the global electric vehicle battery market and supplies batteries to major automakers in China and other countries. Through this contract, POSCO Group plans to expand its lithium sales base in China and strengthen long-term transactions with global battery manufacturers. Currently, POSCO Group is expanding its production capacity centered around the Hombre Muerto salt lake in Argentina, which it acquired in 2018. In 2024, the group completed the construction of its first lithium hydroxide plant with an annual production capacity of 25,000 tons, and additionally completed the upstream process of its second plant in October. The second plant can produce 23,000 tons of lithium carbonate annually, and POSCO Group plans to link this with a subsequent process scheduled to be completed in South Korea in 2027. Once the domestic subsequent process is completed, the group will have a lithium hydroxide production system with an annual capacity of 50,000 tons, including the existing first plant. The group is also operating domestic lithium production facilities utilizing Australian ore. POSCO Pilbara Lithium Solution, a joint venture between POSCO Holdings and Australia’s Pilbara Minerals, has built a lithium hydroxide production facility with an annual capacity of 43,000 tons at the Yulchon Industrial Complex in Gwangyang, South Jeolla Province. Along with the expansion of its production base, the group is consecutively signing long-term supply contracts with battery companies. In February, it signed a contract to supply up to 25,000 tons of lithium to SK On by 2028. This volume is sufficient to produce batteries for approximately 400,000 electric vehicles and will be utilized in SK On’s electric vehicle battery business in Europe and North America. Following this, in August, the group signed a strategic business agreement with Chinese cathode material company Ronbay Group in the fields of lithium supply and waste battery recycling. The two companies are pursuing cooperation to supply recycled lithium, as well as Argentine brine lithium and Australian ore lithium. The group has secured supply contracts not only for lithium raw materials but also in the cathode material business. In September, its battery materials affiliate POSCO Future M signed a contract to supply lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials worth approximately 1.1 trillion won (about $825 million) to SK On. The supply period is from 2027 to 2029. Based on this, POSCO Future M plans to respond to the battery materials market for energy storage systems (ESS) as well as electric vehicles.

artigo.texto: Ford Ships First LFP Cells From Michigan Battery Plant as CATL-Licensed Technology Lands in the U.S. Ford Motor has begun shipping the first batch of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic cells from its BlueOval battery plant in Marshall, Michigan. The cells will go to the company's Louisville, Kentucky, assembly plant for use in its next-generation Fathom electric pickup. Ford disclosed the milestone in an announcement Wednesday local time, marking the formal entry of the highest-volume U.S.-owned automaker into battery manufacturing. "Ford is officially in the battery business," CEO Jim Farley wrote that day on social media platform X. He said the company is building the capacity to supply batteries for more affordable EVs and will apply the same LFP technology and manufacturing expertise to Ford's newly established energy storage business. The roughly $3 billion plant, with about 2 million square feet of floor space, began producing cells in October and is now shipping them. According to Ford's figures, the cell assembly line can produce 40 cells per minute, which the company says makes it one of the fastest LFP prismatic cell assembly lines outside China. The plant has planned annual capacity of about 20 gigawatt-hours, half the earlier plan, mainly because EV demand has grown more slowly than expected. Ford also said the plant can further raise output in the future if needed. The plant is still in the early stages of certifying its production processes. Ford plans to ramp up cell output in 2027 ahead of the Fathom pickup's expected launch in the fourth quarter of that year. Beyond cells, the company plans to bring the plant's battery pack line into operation in 2027, completing the production chain before the new vehicle goes on sale. Design, control systems and manufacturing expertise accumulated along the way will also be used to prepare energy storage battery production at Ford Energy's Glendale, Kentucky, site. Technology licensed from CATL, cost target below $30,000 For Ford, building its own battery capacity is aimed directly at lowering the cost of its next-generation EVs. Reports say the Fathom is planned to start below $30,000 to attract traditional combustion-pickup buyers, and cheaper batteries are key to hitting that target. LFP batteries use no nickel or cobalt, helping control material costs while offering good cycle durability. Ford is also using prismatic cells that integrate directly into the chassis layout, letting the battery pack take on part of the body's structural role and further cutting structural costs. The LFP technology used at the Ford plant is licensed from CATL (300750.SZ). Alan Clark, Ford's vice president of advanced development programs, told reporters this week that this is Ford's path to building affordable EVs in the U.S. as quickly as possible. "If we want to be able to build affordable electric vehicles in the United States, we have to do it as fast as possible. CATL is the largest battery manufacturer in the world, so they're the best supplier to provide us with this technology and help us master LFP cell production," he said. The plant is owned by Ford but uses technology licensed from CATL, an arrangement that has drawn scrutiny from some U.S. lawmakers and government officials. According to South Korean media reports, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote to Farley in September saying the department was "deeply concerned" about the Michigan plant's reliance on CATL-licensed technology. Ford responded that rivals are still importing finished Chinese-made batteries, whereas Ford is building its own battery production base on U.S. soil, which internalizes the supply chain. The company expects to qualify for federal battery manufacturing tax credits as normal because it meets domestic production requirements, despite the licensing dispute. Ramp-up and industry impact On the timeline, the key milestones for Ford's battery business are concentrated in the next two years: Note: Compiled from Ford's announcement and public reports. The global auto industry is accelerating its shift from nickel-based batteries to lower-cost, more durable LFP batteries. Ford's move into mass production means a U.S. automaker has connected the manufacturing chain for LFP cells on American soil, though the technology still comes from a Chinese company. Whether this model can be sustained under regulatory pressure will influence the battery localization paths chosen by other U.S. automakers. For the battery industry, Ford's choice also reflects the hard demand for low-cost batteries in affordable EVs. South Korean battery makers are expanding their lower- and mid-priced product lines, including LFP, mid-nickel and lithium manganese-rich (LMR) chemistries: LG Energy Solution is converting existing equipment at the Spring Hill, Tennessee, plant of its Ultium Cells joint venture with General Motors to EV LFP battery lines, while Samsung SDI and SK On are also moving toward mass production of mid-nickel batteries with reduced nickel content. Still, with automakers prioritizing cost cuts on affordable models, the relatively pricier South Korean-made nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries are unlikely to be widely displaced in the near term. The pace of the Ford battery plant's ramp-up, the Fathom's final pricing and the realization of U.S. federal tax credits will be the three key variables for judging the success of Ford's battery business. artigo.texto: Democrats Plan Grid Rule Overhaul; Data Centers Could Pay $35 Billion More in Power Bills Over a Decade After winning majorities in both chambers of Congress, the U.S. Democratic Party is pushing a federal permitting overhaul, one aim of which is to accelerate federal environmental review of various energy projects so that data center operators can more easily obtain power. But the overhaul contains another layer of design: Democrats want data centers to bear the extra costs of connecting to the grid themselves, rather than passing those expenses on to utility companies and other ratepayers. According to a report by Cnyes, a consulting firm Grid Strategies estimates that federal-level grid rule changes alone could force data centers to pay an additional $35 billion (approximately NT$1.2 trillion) over the next decade; if states make full use of other provisions in the bill, they could collect a combined additional $13.6 billion (approximately NT$450 billion). Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse said that once the bill passes, the situation in which data centers "free-ride" on the power system will end. He noted that going forward, when data centers connect to the grid, they must bear the resulting extra costs themselves and cannot pass the expenses on to utility companies, leaving other ratepayers to foot the bill. The legislation has drawn sharply divided reviews in Washington. Some environmentalists opposed to the permitting bill criticize it as effectively a "gospel" for tech companies that could accelerate the buildout of natural gas-fired data centers; supporters see it as the starting point for Democrats taking a tougher stance on artificial intelligence companies. Note: Amounts are based on Grid Strategies' report estimates; NT$ conversions use reference exchange rates. How the new rules will be implemented remains subject to many variables. Texas is home to one of the largest concentrations of U.S. data centers, but the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) has no jurisdiction over Texas's main grid, raising questions about whether federal rules can be applied uniformly. In addition, utility regulators in some states still need to work out the details and establish how transmission costs will be allocated. Another key unknown is whether higher power bills will prompt tech companies to exit the public grid. Dozens of planned off-grid data center projects have already emerged in the industry, using generation methods that include less efficient gas turbines and even converted jet engines. Related analysis indicates that if data centers supply their own power with such facilities, greenhouse gas emissions would be 31% to 90% higher than connecting to the public grid. Opponents are also concerned about knock-on land-use effects. Aaron Weiss, executive director of the nonprofit environmental group Western Priority Center, believes the new bill could trigger a data center construction boom across American land, and that once it takes shape, it will be difficult to reverse. From an industry perspective, the overhaul has a two-sided effect for data center operators. Faster permitting would help shorten timelines for securing power and ease the supply bottlenecks constraining artificial intelligence computing expansion; but if grid connection costs must be borne by the operators themselves, large operators' operating expenses will rise markedly, and their cost structure could shift from one-time construction spending to long-term power bill burdens. For utilities and ordinary ratepayers, if the new system is implemented, it is expected to ease the upward pressure that data center electricity use puts on power prices. The market's next focal points are whether the bill's provisions can address grids beyond federal jurisdiction, such as Texas's, and how quickly state regulators allocate transmission costs. If power bills become too heavy a burden and the share of tech companies turning to self-built generation rises, that will simultaneously affect demand for natural gas equipment, the logic of data center site selection, and discussions of related emissions rules. artigo.texto: A national ballot could let up to 375,000 hectares of New Zealand farmland into the emissions trading scheme (ETS) by the end of 2050 if every hectare on offer is taken up, Federated Farmers has warned. The group wants the country’s next government to scrap that ballot and extend last year’s limits on whole-farm conversions to all eight classes of farmland. In a column on Tuesday, Richard Dawkins, the group’s meat and wool chair, said five of the six parties it asked before the election had committed to stopping the incentives that drive whole farms into permanent carbon forestry. National, the senior partner in the current coalition, was the only one with a cross beside its name, as the country waits to learn who will form its next government. “But it was a brake, not a stop,” Dawkins said of last year’s Climate Change Response Amendment Act. Whilst he credits the law as a step forward, he warns the scheme can still make converting a whole sheep and beef farm to exotic trees more attractive than producing food. As Wood Central’s election guide showed, the parties went into the vote with plans ranging from National keeping forestry in the scheme with a carbon price floor held until 2031, to Labour pausing new forestry registrations during an urgent review, and the Greens taking forestry out of it altogether. Carbon forestry compass: where New Zealand’s parties stand Hover over or tap a party to read its policy and how it answered Federated Farmers. Hover over or tap a party on the compass. Positions follow each party’s stated policy on forestry in the emissions trading scheme, ordered by how far it would go, from keeping today’s rules on the left to taking forestry out of the scheme on the right. The points are evenly spaced and are not scored. The six parties are the ones Federated Farmers asked in its 2026 voter guide whether they would commit to stopping the incentives that drive whole farms into permanent carbon forestry, with answers as it reported them. Wood Central takes no political stance on the 2026 New Zealand general election and invites all parties contesting it to provide a contribution to the masthead. Carbon forestry compass: hover over or tap each party to see where it stands on forestry in the emissions trading scheme, and how it answered Federated Farmers. (Graphic Credit: Wood Central) For now, farmers can register up to 25 per cent of their land in Land Use Capability (LUC) classes 1 to 6 as exotic forest in the scheme, on a scale that ranks farmland from 1, the most versatile, to 8, the most limited. Yet Dawkins said another 15,000 hectares of class 6 country can go in every year through the ballot, over and above that allowance, whilst classes 7 and 8 sit outside the restrictions altogether. Indeed, the first ballot this year was more than twice oversubscribed, he said, with applications covering 12,079 hectares for the 5,500 on offer, and the year's second ballot closed on Friday. That 375,000 hectares, he warned, comes before the 25 per cent allowance or any class 7 and 8 land is counted. And it is a fight Dawkins has taken onto the land, too, with his column picturing him and vice chair Simon Cameron taking a break from cutting down pine trees in Gisborne this year. Yet National's Forestry Minister, Todd McClay, told a farmer debate in the Waikato during the campaign that it was "the first full year that the sale of valuable farmland for conversion to trees has stopped." Dawkins is not convinced. He said National's cross was hard to reconcile with the party's own promise to stop large-scale conversions. Already, sales have slowed sharply since the peak years of 2021 and 2022, with Beef + Lamb New Zealand counting an initial 15,743 hectares of sheep and beef farmland sold into forestry last year, Wood Central reported in August. Back in August last year, Dawkins warned that the real threat lay in the hill country, saying class 6 and 7 land "is not 'marginal land' as it's often described by foresters." Foresters, for their part, have long argued the opposite, with Matt Wakelin, president of the New Zealand Forest Owners Association (FOA) when the limits were announced, warning that much of the country's class 6 land was ill-suited to food production but ideal for planting trees. Restricting it, he said, would push planting onto marginal or less productive land, which "will have an impact on future timber and fibre supply, jobs and forestry's ability to support New Zealand in meeting its climate change obligations." More recently, the FOA's chief executive, Dr Elizabeth Heeg, said planting intentions had fallen since the whole-farm rules took effect, with the outlook for new commercial forests this year cut by more than two-thirds from the 60,000 hectares planted in each of the previous two years. Uncertainty over the scheme was "dampening long-term investor confidence in the forestry sector," she said in January. At the same time, Dawkins cited Simon Upton, the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, who has called for a fundamental rethink of the ETS and forestry's role within it. Upton described the scheme as "essentially rudderless" in his Adrift report in August. Before polling day, Dawkins took his case straight to National in a column, writing that the party "needs to strengthen its restrictions, not just stand by them." artigo.texto: Ford Begins U.S. Battery Cell Output With CATL Technology at $3 Billion Michigan Plant Ford Motor has begun making battery cells in the United States, using technology licensed from China's CATL, as the automaker pushes to put cheaper lithium iron phosphate batteries into its next generation of electric vehicles. The cells are being built at a roughly 2 million-square-foot plant in Marshall, Michigan, about 100 miles west of Detroit, at a cost of $3 billion. Output started last month and the cells are now shipping, the company said Wednesday. They will go into prototypes of the Fathom, a midsize electric pickup that CEO Jim Farley has positioned as competitive with Tesla and Chinese rivals. The project represents a milestone for Ford, the largest producer of U.S. vehicles, and a step toward wider use of LFP chemistry in American-made cars. The technology was developed in the United States but was largely commercialized in China, where it now underpins much of the world's low-cost EV supply. Ford says the Marshall site can turn out 40 cells a minute, equal to 20 gigawatt-hours a year for vehicles and its energy storage business. That is half the 40 gigawatt-hours once planned, a reduction the company attributes to a pullback in EV demand across the industry. The plant is highly automated, and Ford said it is still certifying its processes, with cell production set to ramp up next year ahead of the Fathom's expected launch in the fourth quarter of 2027. Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology was the quickest route to affordable EVs. "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells." The arrangement has drawn criticism in Washington. In September, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies, which the agency said could harm the automaker and the broader U.S. auto industry. Ford dismissed the letter as a "wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines" and pointed to its construction of a domestic battery plant while competitors keep importing cells from China. The White House followed the letter a day later by praising Ford for its American jobs and manufacturing. The scrutiny comes as Washington tightens its review of Chinese links to U.S. companies, even while President Donald Trump meets this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Ford said it still expects the project to qualify for a federal tax credit for battery manufacturing. For the industry, the start of cell production at Marshall offers a test of whether U.S. automakers can adopt Chinese-developed LFP know-how at home without running afoul of policymakers. Several carmakers are shifting to the chemistry because it costs less than nickel-based cells and is considered more durable, a combination that matters as buyers weigh affordability. Ford's ability to scale the plant toward its original capacity, and to secure incentives, will shape how quickly that shift reaches American assembly lines. artigo.texto: POSCO Signs 3-Year Lithium Supply Deal With CATL, Securing China's Battery Giant POSCO Group has signed a long-term lithium supply contract with China's CATL, the world's top player in the global electric vehicle battery market. According to POSCO Group on the 18th, the two companies agreed to a three-year contract to supply lithium used in EV battery manufacturing from 2026 through 2028, and shipments under the agreement are already underway. Specific volumes and the contract value were not disclosed. The deal gives POSCO Group a stable sales channel in China, the world's largest EV battery market. CATL holds about 40% of the global EV battery market and supplies batteries to automakers in China and around the world. A POSCO Group official said the two companies "agreed to work together to solidify a long-term partnership and build a stable raw material procurement system." Lithium is a core material directly tied to battery production costs, and its price is highly volatile, making stable sales channels critical for producers and raw material supply chain management critical for battery makers. The contract extends the strategy Chairman Chang In-hwa has emphasized: securing quality resources preemptively and diversifying global customers. POSCO Group has expanded its lithium business based on the raw material procurement and development capabilities it built in the steel business. After securing mining rights to Argentina's Hombre Muerto salt flat in 2018, it completed a 25,000-ton-per-year lithium hydroxide Plant 1 there in 2024, and in October it finished the raw material production facilities for brine lithium Plant 2. That site produces 23,000 tons of lithium carbonate a year, which is brought to the Yulchon Industrial Complex in Gwangyang, South Korea's South Jeolla Province, and refined into battery-grade lithium hydroxide. The Yulchon refinery, targeted for completion in the first quarter of next year, will have a capacity of 25,000 tons per year. Once completed, Argentina's brine-based lithium hydroxide capacity will rise to 50,000 tons per year. Adding the 43,000 tons of ore-based capacity secured at the Yulchon complex by POSCO Pilbara Lithium Solution, a joint venture with Australia's PLS Group, brings total capacity to 93,000 tons per year. POSCO Group plans to build Plants 3 and 4 in Argentina to expand local brine-based lithium product capacity to 100,000 tons per year by 2033. Note: Argentina Plant 2 produces 23,000 tons of lithium carbonate a year, which is brought to Yulchon and refined into lithium hydroxide. POSCO Group previously signed a long-term lithium supply contract with South Korea's SK On in February. It will supply up to 25,000 tons from this year through 2028, with the volumes destined for EV battery projects in Europe and North America. With a long-term customer among South Korean battery makers and now the global No. 1, POSCO Group's lithium sales channels span South Korea, China, Europe and North America. The contract illustrates how both raw material producers and demand-side companies are prioritizing supply chain stability amid growing lithium price volatility. POSCO Group aims to boost the profitability of its lithium business by expanding capacity and increasing long-term supply contracts with global battery makers. However, with volumes and value undisclosed, the specific impact of the deal on earnings has yet to be determined. artigo.texto: ETRI Uses Cross-Server Memory Sharing to Ease AI Data Center Expansion Bottleneck A technology has emerged that could ease the memory shortage that has become a bottleneck for expanding artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. By letting an entire data center share the memory installed in each server, the approach could provide immediate relief from the current memory supply crunch. South Korea's Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute (ETRI) said on the 19th that EMP, its in-house cross-server memory sharing software, is being piloted at the University of Southern California (USC) Center for Advanced Research Computing. The center operates a high-performance computing (HPC) cluster of about 500 servers. EMP is system software that links servers in a data center over ultra-high-speed networks, allowing one server to borrow spare capacity from another when its own memory runs short. Its key feature is that it can push past the memory limits of individual servers without adding separate hardware. The test results are notable. A server with only 448 gigabytes (GB) of its own memory completed a large-scale genomic analysis requiring about 1.8 terabytes (TB) after EMP was applied, borrowing roughly three-quarters of the memory it needed from other servers. Performance per unit of memory improved by as much as 2.3 times. With demand for AI training and data processing surging, data center operators face a heavy burden in securing massive amounts of memory. Equipping every server with memory sized to peak demand drives up upfront investment, while idle memory sits unused when workloads are light. ETRI expects EMP to reduce this inefficiency and raise utilization of existing equipment. Still, the technology is unlikely to fundamentally reduce new memory demand. Performance was found to decline somewhat when borrowing another server's memory compared with using local memory. Ko Kwang-won, head of ETRI's AIDC Research Division, said, "Its significance lies not so much in raising the efficiency of a single memory as in sharing memory across multiple servers," adding, "From a hyperscaler's perspective, it amounts to gaining a temporary stopgap before new memory arrives." He added, "These days it takes a long time to secure memory, and this technology can put out the immediate fire," but "companies that need to boost data center performance will ultimately bring in more memory." Industry watchers see the technology helping accelerate the buildout of AI data centers. Because memory supply is a key variable in data center construction, the ability to operate resources flexibly should make supply forecasting considerably easier. The pilot was conducted at USC's request. ETRI plans to broaden the scope of testing with USC researchers to include genome assembly, protein analysis and weather forecasting. Drawing on operating experience gained at a large US data center, it will expand deployment to South Korean high-performance computing centers, universities and research institutions, and pursue commercialization. "Based on our US pilot experience, we will develop this into a core system software that raises resource utilization efficiency at South Korean AI data centers," Ko said. ETRI said inquiries about adoption are continuing from other universities and departments after news of the large US data center pilot spread. The technology is drawing attention because it arrives as a structural shortage of memory semiconductors persists. As AI server expansion gathers pace, demand for server memory including high-bandwidth memory (HBM) has surged, and data center operators cannot guarantee memory procurement schedules even as they draw up expansion plans. Analysts say that if cross-server resource sharing is commercialized, it could serve as a buffer that helps pace near-term expansion. On November 19, the topic "CATL calls police on Li Auto" trended on social media, pushing the pair once regarded as a model of supply-chain partnership into the center of public debate. Although both sides still publicly call each other "strategic partners," the cracks are clearly visible — from capacity fulfillment and recall liability to the full rollout of self-developed batteries. The conflict became public in September 2025. According to a report by Yijian Auto, during the production ramp-up of the Li Auto i8, Li Auto staff and a logistics fleet arrived at CATL's Liyang plant to collect goods but were blocked outside the factory grounds. At the time, the i8 was underperforming market expectations, and Li Auto wanted to pause battery production, while CATL demanded that it take delivery of all batteries produced, with inventories at one point exceeding 10,000 units. The batch was later reported to have quality problems and delivery was suspended, leaving large numbers of trucks stranded on the road outside the plant. CATL called police, citing suspected disruption of traffic order and safety-production risks. What truly pushed the relationship to the brink was the Li Auto MEGA fire and recall incident. In November 2025, a MEGA caught fire, and the investigation pointed to a coolant anti-corrosion defect that carried a risk of thermal runaway. Li Auto planned to recall more than 11,000 vehicles. At a meeting with CATL, the battery maker suggested addressing the issue at a single point rather than conducting a large-scale recall, saying "there's no need; this matter can be played down." When Li Auto executives asked whether CATL would share liability if another spontaneous fire occurred, CATL did not respond. Financial reports show Li Auto lost 1.1 billion yuan (approximately $165.0 million) due to the recall, but insiders say the actual cost exceeded 2 billion yuan (approximately $300.1 million), all funded from the company's cash flow. The supply shortfall was equally striking. In the fourth quarter of 2025, Li Auto placed orders for 8,000 i6 battery packs with CATL but ultimately received only 4,000, with CATL citing insufficient capacity. The i6 had accumulated about 40,000 orders at the time; hampered by the battery shortage, only 29,000 were delivered in 2025, with nearly 10,000 orders forced to be postponed to 2026. A battery executive at an automaker said a supplier capacity deviation of within 15% is acceptable, but more than 50% constitutes a massive supply failure. CATL has its own explanation. At its third-quarter 2025 earnings call, company executives said that due to short-term capacity constraints, some orders had to be diverted to peer companies. Data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) shows that in September 2025, China's domestic passenger vehicle retail sales reached 2.241 million units, a record high, of which battery-electric retail sales were 838,000 units, up 32.3% year on year. Mid-to-high-end BEV models priced above 200,000 yuan (approximately $30,000) accounted for 20% to 25%, precisely CATL's main battleground. That month, about 50 to 80 passenger vehicle models were equipped with CATL batteries, with lithium iron phosphate accounting for 70%. Li Auto's response was to accelerate in-house development. At an August 26 second-quarter earnings briefing, Li Auto Chairman Li Xiang further clarified that starting in the second half of the year, self-developed batteries would gradually be installed across all models. On September 7, Li Auto announced that its self-developed batteries had been installed in the L8, L6 and i8, with full coverage of all models to follow; the new-generation MEGA and the all-new i9 would use CATL batteries for their first deliveries before fully switching to self-developed batteries, while the 2026 i6 would use self-developed batteries across the lineup. Capacity anxiety had long troubled management. According to insiders, Li Xiang was anxious about battery capacity almost every day during that period. artigo.texto: Upper St. Clair meeting to address zoning changes for potential data centers Upper St. Clair is hosting a meeting Thursday night at its municipal building to discuss proposed zoning changes that could allow data centers in the township. The possibility of a data center in the township has raised concerns among some residents, including Dr. Gretchen Kreizenbeck, who recently learned about the township reviewing a proposed zoning text amendment to Chapter 130 of the township code. She said the township is being proactive. "According to Pennsylvania law, no municipality or township can actually ban data centers altogether, so I believe this is probably one of the best ways to minimize it," Kreizenbeck said. Currently, the township code does not specifically define or regulate data centers. The proposed changes would define data centers and establish strict operational, environmental, and safety standards. To clarify, there is no data center being developed or proposed at this time in Upper St. Clair. The township stated that by proactively creating these standards, it aims to ensure that any future proposals are regulated and compatible with surrounding properties. "We are going to the meeting to learn about it, and to understand how we can work together to make our area safe as well as, I think, the broader area safe," Kreizenbeck said. artigo.texto: Giant Batteries Replace Gorgas Coal-fired Power Plant A utility-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) is a large-scale rechargeable battery installation connected to the electric grid that stores electricity and discharges it when needed, according to Alabama Power Company. The utility now has its first site operating in the Walker County town of Parrish. The company says the facility was able to become operational in October, six months ahead of schedule. From Coal to Cells The first-of-its-kind BESS in Alabama is located on the 7-acre site of the former Gorgas coal-fired power plant, built in 1917. That plant was shut down in 2019 due to federal environmental regulations and high compliance and retrofit costs. The battery storage facility replacing it is generally a net environmental benefit by helping grids use more renewable energy and cut fossil-fuel emissions. The property has now been repurposed to boost Alabama Power’s reliability during peak power needs, such as high HVAC usage during extreme summer heat or winter cold. Gorgas BESS construction manager Cameron Key said in an Alabama Power release that the giant batteries are charged during nonpeak times so they can be accessed when needed. “This facility is designed to support our peak loads, to be able to put that additional power out that’s needed.” Megapack Muscle The company describes the facility as providing a totally different way for Alabama Power to be ready to supply power for customers in emergency power situations. The Tesla Megapacks, large-scale, pre-assembled rechargeable lithium-ion battery systems, are connected to 46 medium-voltage transformers and linked through a control house to a switchyard that ties directly into Alabama Power’s high-voltage grid. The Gorgas BESS is capable of storing 150 megawatts of electricity, enough to power roughly 9,000 homes for two hours. The system can charge in just over two hours, enabling it to absorb excess energy when demand is low and discharge when the grid needs support, particularly during peak usage times. Alabama Power is developing additional storage and hybrid projects at the Clearview Solar and Battery Energy Storage Facility in Macon and Bullock counties. One side benefit of the batteries, according to company officials, is that the battery storage facilities will help Alabama absorb surging data center power demand. artigo.texto: Key Takeaways - BAIC Motor aims to free up capital through the sale, while its parent is working with CATL to bring more models onto the battery maker's swap network. - The assets have an appraised value of about 278 million yuan ($41.4 million). BAIC Motor (HKEX: 1958) plans to sell assets tied to 112 battery swap stations through a public tender to free up capital tied up in non-core assets. Its wholly owned subsidiary, BAIC Powertrain, plans to submit a notice of the proposed sale to the China Beijing Equity Exchange (CBEX) by the end of November, BAIC Motor said in a Hong Kong stock exchange filing on Tuesday. BAIC Powertrain plans to sell its entire interest in the assets, which include inventory, fixed assets, construction in progress and intangible assets used in station operations. A September 30 appraisal using the cost approach valued the assets at about 278 million yuan ($41.4 million), excluding tax, about 1.54% above their unaudited book value. The listing price will be at least as high as the appraised value ultimately filed with the authorities. The winning bid will determine the sale price. At the time of the filing, BAIC Powertrain had yet to identify a buyer or sign a sale agreement. BAIC Motor estimates that a sale at the appraised value in 2026 would lift its consolidated profit for the year by about 3.52 million yuan after transaction costs. BAIC Powertrain plans to use the proceeds to fund its operations and development. The proposed sale comes as BAIC Motor's parent, Beijing Automotive Group (BAIC Group), expands its battery swap partnership with CATL (HKEX: 3750). BAIC Group said in October that it would bring compatible models from several of its brands onto CATL's Choco swap network and make dealership sites available for new swap stations. The partners aim to serve 1 million vehicles. On November 13, BAIC Group's Arcfox brand launched a LiDAR-equipped battery swap version of the Beta S3 and a battery swap version of the Beta T1. Both use CATL's battery swap system for passenger vehicles. Arcfox said it would offer a battery swap version of every model in its lineup next year. Battery swap stations are expensive for automakers to build and maintain, BAIC Group chairman Zhang Jianyong said at the launch. Battery makers can benefit from economies of scale in both construction and operation, he said. BAIC began researching battery swap technology in 2011, making it one of the first automakers in China to invest in the field, Zhang said. He said BAIC Group and CATL would draw on their respective strengths to build China's first battery swap network capable of serving about 1 million vehicles. ($1 = 6.7118 yuan)

artigo.texto: Global electricity use by data centers could double by 2030 and stretch power grids, potentially delaying new projects, the International Energy Agency warned. Data centers could consume around 1,000 terawatt-hours of electricity a year by 2030, according to the IEA, which added that tight supply chains, local opposition and limited grid capacity could slow construction. The warning is part of the IEA's Stated Policies Scenario, in which the agency forecasts are based on measures that have been put forward but have not yet been adopted. Texas, Virginia, Finland and the U.K. The IEA cites large data center project pipelines in Texas, Virginia, Finland and the U.K. In several regions, the combined capacity of data centers waiting to connect exceeds current peak demand. Without grid upgrades, power networks could become more congested and less reliable, the IEA said. New projects could face longer waits to connect, while generators could be forced to cut output when the grid cannot meet demand. Peak electricity demand is projected to rise 40% to 50% by 2035, according to the IEA. Under the Stated Policies Scenario, grids should be expanded by 26 million kilometers of new lines by 2035, while about 16 million kilometers of existing lines need to be replaced or refurbished. Supplies of copper, cables and transformers are already tight, the IEA said. Grid spending could rise 75% Under the Current Policies Scenario, which is based on energy policies and regulations already in place, grid spending is projected to rise 75% over the next decade. The agency says power networks are "one of the biggest energy investment stories of the next decade." The scenario projects that renewable power generation will grow 85% more in the next decade than in the previous one. Solar photovoltaics would become the world's largest source of electricity from the late 2030s Electricity would account for nearly 30% of global final energy consumption by 2035, up from 23% in the IEA's main scenarios. Energy security adds urgency The IEA said the 2026 energy crisis could accelerate electrification as countries seek to reduce their reliance on imported oil and gas. Electrification can reduce exposure to imported fuels, but it also makes a reliable power grid more important. Before the Iran war, an average of 20 million barrels of crude oil and oil products a day transited the Strait of Hormuz in 2025 — about 25% of global seaborne oil trade. The strait also carried nearly 20% of global LNG trade. "The pressures of the current crisis must not obscure the choices that will shape energy security, sustainability and prosperity for the decades to come," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said.

The announcement came as ASEAN leaders met in Manila, where energy security has been high on the agenda. Addressing regional leaders, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said her country’s “hydro-tanks” would be available for use under the proposed initiative for cooperation on oil stockpiling. The regional bloc has previously called for “unimpeded” passage through the Strait of Hormuz, which was closed following US-Israeli strikes on Iran. Under the Japanese POWERR Asia initiative, ASEAN nations would be able to use Japan’s excess storage capacity for crude oil. “We have suggested to utilize our crude oil stockpiling facilities in Japan, which is not utilized,” Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs press secretary Toshihiro Kitamura told reporters on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit. “By utilizing those unused facilities in Japan, we can stockpile the other countries’ crude oil and in case of crisis... It’s a kind of joint stockpiling system,” he said. Japan has 254 days’ worth of oil reserves, he said, while at the outbreak of the Middle East war in February some ASEAN countries had less than a month’s worth. An ASEAN-backed study for joint stockpiling of oil has also recommended using facilities in Thailand and Indonesia, but Kitamura said a final decision had not been made. “It’s under specific discussion,” Kitamura said. “But as a government in Japan, we are ready to work with ASEAN countries to utilize our own facilities.” Longer term, Tokyo plans to assist ASEAN states to build their own “stockpiling facilities.” “I think this is very important in order to prepare ourselves for future possibilities, crises,” he said. Philippine Secretary of Energy Sharon Garin said a memorandum of cooperation signed with Japan on Monday included assistance to “put up many more facilities to store more oil, whether [that] is diesel, gas or crude oil,” in the archipelago nation. “What this means is the Philippines will be more prepared in ensuring there is adequate oil for our homes and businesses, whatever the situation is,” Garin told reporters. “With our reserves in place, we would be better positioned to support our transport, markets, and industries,” she said.
