artigo.texto: Spain's government is seeking to tighten restrictions on one of Europe's fastest-growing data center booms, as the country's Socialist prime minister prepares to fight an election. Investors like Amazon, Microsoft and Blackstone-backed QTS are on tenterhooks. The measure, which doesn't need parliamentary approval, could be approved by Pedro Sánchez's cabinet by next week, and is widely expected to pass ahead of the Nov. 29 elections. It could potentially cost one of Europe's fastest-growing tech regions billions of dollars in investment. The government first introduced the decree in August, partly in response to concerns over energy demand and prices. After fierce opposition, it put forward a revised version on Oct. 26, but the proposal still includes strict renewable-energy requirements. "These requirements could pose insurmountable barriers and act as an effective moratorium," S&P said in an October report. The proposed rules would require 80% of electricity used by data centers to come from renewable sources matched hour by hour, with projects potentially losing grid access if they fail to comply. Projects already in development or awaiting grid connections would also be subject to the rules, with a five-year transition period to comply. Data center buildout faces public backlash Data center build-out has quickly become a prominent political issue around the world. In the U.S. midterm elections, CBS exit polls found data centers were a major influence for more than half of voters. In Spain, concerns over the water and energy demands of data centers are increasingly part of the election debate as the country faces mounting pressure to expand its electricity grid to meet the demand. CBRE estimates that while developers have announced 10.5 GW of data center capacity across Spain and Portugal, only about 4.5 GW is currently considered realistically deliverable because of grid, permitting and infrastructure constraints. Alberto Nadal, the opposition center-right Popular Party's deputy secretary for the economy, has said a conservative government would repeal the decree. Recent polling shows the Popular Party leading, with several seat projections putting the PP and far-right Vox together above a parliamentary majority. Aragón at center of debate Aragón, a landlocked region in the country's northeast, governed by the Popular Party, has emerged as one of Europe's fastest-growing digital infrastructure hubs and is at the center of opposition to the draft rules. The region has attracted investors with fast-track permits, abundant renewable energy and land, and international cable connections. Aragón president, Jorge Azcón, wants to turn it into the "Virginia of Europe," referring to the U.S. state with the world's highest density of data center sites. Aragón is set to receive more than 60 billion euros ($66 billion) in data center and digital infrastructure investment over the next decade. But concerns are growing among residents over noise, water use and pressure on the electricity grid. Investment versus resources Pilar Alegría, leader of the Socialist Party in Aragón, told a Nov. 15 rally that the election would be decisive for the region's future and for protecting its natural resources. She highlighted the Ebro River, which runs through Aragón, and raised concerns about the resources used by data centers in a region vulnerable to drought. Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, speaking the same day, sought to reassure investors. "It would be a mistake to squander that advantage through poor planning or regulation that creates uncertainty for investors," Feijóo said. Eva Valle, Aragón's economy minister, has also called for the decree to be scrapped. "It is necessary to halt the approval of this decree, which abounds in harmful conditions placed on the sector," she said at an AWS-organized event on Oct. 27, accusing the government of pursuing "a political agenda." Amazon Web Services and Microsoft have said their investment plans in Aragón remain unchanged, while urging Spain to provide long-term legal certainty and regulatory predictability. Google has already put a multibillion-euro data center project on hold pending greater regulatory certainty, according to a report in Spanish newspaper El Mundo, which cited anonymous sources. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. SpainDC, which represents the data-center industry in the country, said the decree would give the group's members the most restrictive data center framework in the European Union and could put 80% to 90% of investment at risk. "We are going to use all the institutional, regulatory and legal avenues at our disposal" to challenge the decree, said SpainDC president Emilio Díaz.

artigo.texto: The town doesn’t have a stoplight for traffic — and, as the November 3 election showed, it doesn’t have a red light for data centers either. It was the only place in the country where voters approved one of these facilities, and it wasn’t close: the margin was 3 to 1. The tale is a clue to the future of data centers around the country. Applied Digital, a Dallas-based data center company, wants to build a $3 billion facility in the Harwood area. It would be the largest such facility in the state, covering 1.8 million square feet, the equivalent of 31 football fields. The company had told voters that the alternative was putting the center next door in Fargo, and that convinced Harwoodians that “we might as well get the tax benefits and the tax revenue from it,” as Mayor Blake Hankey put it. He expected the city would get $1.65 million, six times its existing total property tax revenue. And then there were the promised 200 new jobs for the region. Harwood stood in sharp contrast with the rest of the country. Gallup found in March that 71 percent of those surveyed were opposed to data center construction. NBC’s exit polling on November 3 found that data centers were a crucial factor for 69 percent of people voting for Congress. It was little wonder that some of the biggest champions of the centers scurried for cover, including Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro (a Democrat who won big anyway) and Texas Governor Greg Abbott (a Republican who lost by a stunning margin), and who just a year before had proclaimed the state would be the “epicenter of AI development.” Analysts are still sorting out this stunning result, but several things are clear. Local residents didn’t like the idea of big developers draining local water, putting contaminated water back into the ground, gobbling up enormous amounts of electricity, and putting noisy complexes not far from their homes. Frightening warnings that AI is lurking to control us, perhaps somehow building the capacity to kill us all, surely didn’t help. Six in ten Americans are afraid of riding in self-driving cars. It’s broadly ironic that the revolt against technology has happened at precisely the time Americans have become more dependent on the devices in virtually everyone’s pocket. But that’s not all that’s jingling in pockets. A Brookings analyst projected that by 2032, data center and related investment will total $10.3 trillion. That, the Wall Street Journal said, would be “the biggest economic get in US history,” far greater than the Gilded Age railroads or the interstate highway system. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google combined for more than $720 billion in data center investment this year, three times the amount just two years ago. In Texas alone, data center construction accounts for more than one-fourth of the state’s gross domestic product. That sets up a looming dilemma. Harwood voters showed what a green light looks like, but just about everywhere else, voters flashed red. In Texas, Abbott hit a yellow caution light, calling for an audit of planned water and energy usage before giving new centers the green. But Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa wants red, calling for a complete ban until “laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans.” That won’t be easy to do. Democrats won the state house for the first time in 24 years, but Republicans have a comfortable 19-12 margin in the state senate and that’s going to make it hard for the legislature to pass anything restricting data centers. Hinojosa has promised executive action to shut down data center construction, but she can’t do that unilaterally. She’d have to rely instead on three separate regulatory commissions, including the agency regulating the state’s Electric Reliability Council, which is still struggling to right itself after the 2021 weather disaster that almost shut down the state’s whole power grid. The governor gets to make appointments to those commissions, but vacancies occur on a rotating basis and she won’t be able to get controlling appointments for several years. Moreover, appointments to some commissions require senate confirmation, and that’s going to be tough with Republicans holding the upper chamber. And then there’s the tsunami of cash and potential construction jobs building up in every corner of the state. Add the zoning issues lurking in the background. In Texas, for example, cities and towns have zoning power but counties don’t, so if a data center developer plans a project just outside a city limit, there might be nothing to stop it except the property owner’s agreement to sell the property. All these complications make it much harder for the light to stay red for long. One investment bank estimates that perhaps only 2 to 4 percent of planned data centers will ultimately be stopped. With so much money at stake, Harwood’s green light is ultimately the most likely signal to find.

artigo.texto: Guest Opinion A friend called and suggested looking at a video from the All Indian Governors Council, which represents 19 New Mexico pueblos, that outlines their opposition to the Senate’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. The main objection: Tribes lose a seat at the table and the measure will make it harder to protect sacred lands from development. To read more articles by Mark Trahant, go to: Marktrahant.substack.com. Yesterday the Senate voted on another procedural bill and continues to consider amendments. The final vote could still come this week and then the bill would move to the lame duck House. What’s the rush? Why not wait for the next Congress where the bill could actually go through a legitimate process? The champion of the bill, New Mexico Democrat Sen. Martin Heinrich has said: “This is the closest we have come to actually finding something that can get signed into law, and I’m not going to wait.” Or have hearings. Or listen to communities. Or look at the data. Just pass the damn thing. There is a lot going on below the surface. One of the sponsors pitches is that the permitting bill will make it easier to develop clean energy. But the trade off is it will also make it much easier to build data centers. And to develop more fossil fuel projects. So many reasons to make this legislation a no go. Timothy Noah of the The New Republic says “the problems in this nearly 500-page bill are too numerous to fix through the amendment process or in House-Senate conference. It needs to be ripped to pieces so that Congress’s new Democratic majority, which will have much more leverage over the finished product, can start afresh.” He says Heinrich was ticked off because of the tactics used against the SunZia Wind and Transmission project. “When I raised preservationists’ complaints about BAAJA with Heinrich (Whitehouse’s office didn’t reply to my query), he told me (again, via email): “I have listened to Tribes’ concerns and worked to codify in statute the federal government’s obligation to consult with Tribes under Section 106.… Still, I recognize there is more work to do, and I am committed to continuing to worsk with Tribal leaders and my colleagues to strengthen consultation beyond this bill.” Heinrich is right to suggest that such discussions can’t be conducted on the fly while the bill is days away from Senate passage. But Native Americans are hardly the only preservation-minded groups opposed to BAAJA. The National Trust for Historic Preservation said last week in a prepared statement that it “remains strongly opposed to” BAAJA, which “retains provisions that give federal officials broad discretion to subordinate historic preservation to other considerations.” If, as Heinrich says, “There is more work to do,” why not do it before BAAJA is allowed to become law, rather than at some unspecified future date?” A study released this week by led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative show that over the course of a year, hyperscale data centers —the largest and most powerful class of data centers, supporting services such as cloud computing, large language model training, and global deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) tools—are powered mostly by fossil fuels and use as much electricity as entire U.S. states. “While data centers are known to require significant electricity to run, few studies have examined this topic facility by facility, estimating not just how much electricity each HDC uses, but what fuels generated this electricity. For this study, the researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 HDCs across the U.S. and estimated annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used Environmental Protection Agency data to attribute carbon emissions to each HDC based on the mix of power plants in its regional grid. “The study found that these HDCs, depending on how hard they were running, together used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity—with the upper estimate approaching the amount some states, such as Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. During the study period, HDC electricity demand corresponded to approximately 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption, and was associated with about 25.7 million metric tons of CO2—an amount two to three times higher than an earlier estimate for 2018. “Today, electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely much higher than they were during the study period, the researchers say. “What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Guidi said. “The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.” “The study also found that roughly 54% of the electricity powering the HDCs was generated by fossil fuels—mainly natural gas (38%) and coal (15%)—and about a quarter of the electricity was in grid regions dirtier than average.” And we need to build these data centers faster, why? It’s also clear that the markets are starting to see the dangers of over capacity (that will be followed by a bust.) The growing scandal involving the U.S. government and Nvidia is part of this complexity. The Wall Street Journal reported today that Jensen Huang saw the threat of public support shifting and wanted to create a superfund to speed things up. A few firms pledged $500 million to make bigger deals, faster. Only, no. But the promise was short on substance. To date, no capital has actually been deployed, according to people familiar with the matter. artigo.texto: Sam Altman disse em 16 de novembro de 2026 que as pessoas devem poder comprar bastante RAM para seus computadores. No fórum Silicon Valley & The World, da Semafor, ele também manteve seu argumento condicional: durante uma escassez, compartilhar memória em centros de dados poderia permitir um uso mais contínuo. Altman ainda elogiou a experimentação com computadores em casa. Quando a memória está escassa, a ideia de compartilhá-la é um argumento sobre eficiência na alocação; não substitui a escolha de ter RAM no próprio computador. O que Altman disse sobre a RAM dos usuários? Altman afirmou que as pessoas devem poder comprar muita RAM para seus PCs. A fala esclareceu comentários anteriores em que ele criticou o baixo uso da memória em computadores pessoais, mas não abandonou sua defesa de avaliar como a memória escassa poderia ser aproveitada. A distinção é importante: defender uma forma de distribuir um recurso limitado não equivale a defender restrições à compra de memória. Altman também disse que considera positiva a possibilidade de as pessoas experimentarem com seus computadores em casa. Por que ele defende compartilhar memória durante uma escassez? O argumento de Altman é que memória reunida em centros de dados poderia ser compartilhada e usada com mais continuidade do que a memória instalada em dispositivos pessoais, que pode ficar ociosa em certos momentos. Ele apresentou isso como uma possibilidade de eficiência quando há escassez, não como uma medição comparativa de uso. Há uma diferença prática para quem quer executar inteligência artificial no próprio computador: o processamento local depende do hardware do usuário, enquanto o argumento de Altman considera a memória compartilhada em centros de dados. Ele reconheceu que essa possibilidade tem contrapartidas e que a eficiência teórica não precisa determinar a decisão no mundo real. A memória é um entre vários gargalos de infraestrutura Ao falar sobre as necessidades da OpenAI, Altman citou diferentes restrições em momentos distintos: memória, montagem de racks, capacidade de centros de dados e outros componentes. Assim, a memória aparece como uma parte de um conjunto de desafios de infraestrutura. Em 1º de outubro de 2025, a OpenAI anunciou que Samsung Electronics e SK hynix planejavam acelerar a expansão de capacidade, com uma meta de iniciar o processamento de até 900 mil wafers de DRAM por mês. A cifra descreve um objetivo anunciado, não uma produção já alcançada. A OpenAI detalhou o plano e as parcerias.

artigo.texto: Em breve o Paraná poderá entrar na disputa por novos data centers. Um projeto de lei, aprovado na Assembleia Legislativa do Estado do Paraná (Alep) estabelece diretrizes para incentivar a instalação e a expansão de Data Centers no Estado. O Projeto de Lei 55/2026 cria o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (PRODATAPR). A iniciativa reúne propostas voltadas ao desenvolvimento da economia digital, à atração de investimentos privados, à geração de empregos especializados e ao aproveitamento das vantagens competitivas do Paraná. O foco é a produção de energia renovável e na conectividade. Data Centers Os Data Centers são estruturas essenciais para o funcionamento da economia digital. Neles são armazenadas e processadas grandes quantidades de informações utilizadas por empresas, governos, instituições financeiras, hospitais, universidades e plataformas. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial, essas instalações ganharam importância estratégica na disputa mundial por investimentos tecnológicos. De acordo com a justificativa do projeto, o PRODATAPR tem o objetivo de consolidar o Paraná como polo estratégico de Data Centers na América Latina, gerando empregos qualificados e fomentando a cadeia produtiva de tecnologia. O texto autoriza o Governo do Estado a conceder benefícios fiscais às empresas beneficiárias do Programa. A proposta estabelece diretrizes para estimular novos empreendimentos, ampliar a infraestrutura de telecomunicações e incentivar parcerias entre empresas, universidades e centros de pesquisa. Outro diferencial é a preocupação com a sustentabilidade. O projeto incentiva a utilização de fontes renováveis de energia, o aproveitamento do biometano, o uso racional da água e a adoção de tecnologias sustentáveis de resfriamento dos equipamentos. Expansão A aprovação ocorre em um momento de expansão do setor no Brasil. Em setembro de 2026, foi sancionada a Lei Federal nº 15.504, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). A legislação federal prevê incentivos tributários condicionados a compromissos de sustentabilidade, investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento e utilização de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão. A iniciativa foi proposta pelos deputados Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (PP) e Bazana (PSD). “A inteligência artificial, a computação em nuvem e os serviços digitais dependem de uma infraestrutura robusta de processamento de dados. Temos energia, universidades, profissionais qualificados e um ambiente favorável à inovação. Queremos transformar essas vantagens em investimentos, empregos e oportunidades para os paranaenses”, ressaltou a deputada Maria Victoria. Já o deputado Luiz Fernando Guerra destaca a importância do planejamento. “Com esse projeto, o Paraná terá diretrizes para planejar a expansão dos data centers, dar mais previsibilidade a quem pretende investir e identificar os empreendimentos estratégicos para o Estado. Para operar e manter essas estruturas, as empresas vão precisar de profissionais preparados. Por isso, a proposta incentiva parcerias com universidades e centros de pesquisa para qualificar mão de obra e ampliar as oportunidades de trabalhar com tecnologia em diferentes regiões do Paraná”, afirma o Guerra. “Queremos que o Paraná aproveite seu potencial em energia renovável e conectividade para atrair investimentos que gerem oportunidades para a população. Como coautor desse projeto, defendo que a expansão dos centros de dados fortaleça também as empresas locais, estimule a formação profissional e leve empregos qualificados ao interior. É uma forma de preparar o estado para as novas demandas da economia e ampliar as possibilidades de desenvolvimento dos nossos municípios”, defendeu o deputado Bazana.

artigo.texto: Salt Lake City has moved swiftly to pass a six-month moratorium on new data centers in the face of a project unfolding in the Northpoint neighborhood. The City Council approved the temporary land-use restrictions late Tuesday with a 6-0 vote with one member absent, after altering its meeting agenda at the eleventh hour Monday to add the item, which passed without a public hearing. The ordinance removes data centers as an allowed use in manufacturing and business park districts for 180 days — the maximum period for such a ban allowed under state law. City officials are directed to use the six-month interim, according to the council’s vote, to draft new development and zoning rules to address the impacts from data center projects on energy and water usage as well as propose ”mitigation measures for impacts from noise, heat, lighting and any other issues identified.” Mayor Erin Mendenhall earlier Tuesday called the step “a healthy pause.” The mayor said the city’s land-use rules “never contemplated these massive data centers” and that issues around their water usage alone are “tremendously in flux as that industry is evolving rapidly.” Many first learned last week of Florida development company Qlevr LLC’s applications for a state air-quality permit and city building clearance in pursuit of constructing a one-story, $105 million data center at 2258 W. 2950 North. The proposed Northpoint data center is to be powered, documents indicate, by the standard electrical grid and would be located on what is now an open lot directly south of and across 2200 West from multiple homes, not far from the fragile fringe of the Great Salt Lake. The city — which like the rest of Utah, faces longstanding drought conditions — recently passed a permanent 200,000-gallon daily cap on water consumption for non-residential land uses. This pause, Mendenhall said, would allow for the hard work of researching and adjusting the city’s zoning and development rules “make sure what happens here is reflective of our capacity.” The city’s newly approved ordinance has been justified in part by a finding that a proposed data center “would pose physical harms to nearby residents in the form of impaired air quality, significant adverse construction impacts, noise pollution and light pollution.” The ordinance also says that the ban is needed to protect the city’s water resources, prevent residents’ electricity bills from rising and ensure that data center projects are subject to public input. A representative from the city’s nonprofit Westside Coalition, Anthony Washburn, praised the council’s move, “due to the potential for the project to negatively impact community health and the environment in the Northpoint area.” Attempts by The Salt Lake Tribune to contact officials at Qlevr for more information and comment have so far proved unsuccessful. Following Tuesday’s vote, council member Victoria Petro, whose west-side District 1 spans the area, pointed to dire neighborhood impacts from sprawling warehouses in that area that were approved before the city’s zoning rules had a chance to catch up as a reason for instituting a data center ban now. “A huge part of the concern I have with data center policy,” Petro said, “is that this is a sector of the economy that has been allowed to run free without the input of the neighbors.” She said she was making the interests of Northpoint residents her top priority, while placing second those of migratory birds seeking refuge along the Great Salt Lake’s shores. Capitol Hill and Avenues council member Chris Wharton also said that a recent Salt Lake County moratorium on data centers only applied in the county’s unincorporated areas, prompting leaders of Utah’s capital to step in.

artigo.texto: Brazil, China, EU-Led Carbon Market Coalition Launches Working Groups, Sets 2027 Priorities - COP31 Declaration adopted: OCCCM representatives adopted the Coalition’s COP31 Declaration at a meeting in Antalya. - Working Groups launched: Members and Observers launched the Coalition’s Working Groups and set strategic priorities for 2027. - Membership grows: The voluntary, member-led initiative counted 13 Members and 34 Observers as of 16 November 2026. Representatives of the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets (OCCCM) adopted the OCCCM COP31 Declaration at a high-level meeting in Antalya. The same meeting launched the Coalition’s Working Groups and set its strategic priorities for 2027. Those priorities apply to a group that counted 13 Members and 34 Observers as of 16 November 2026. The Declaration reaffirms the Coalition’s ambition to become a key point of reference for international cooperation on compliance carbon markets. These are government-mandated carbon pricing systems, such as emissions trading schemes. The text also commits the Coalition to work closely with existing initiatives and fora. Brazil convened the High-Level Ministerial Meeting as Chair, with China and the European Union as Co-Chairs. The meeting also welcomed new participants to the initiative. The OCCCM treats these markets as a policy tool for Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), or national climate plans, under the Paris Agreement. It aims to build mutual understanding of carbon pricing mechanisms and to explore convergence and long-term interoperability. However, the Coalition did not name the new Working Groups, the new participants or the content of its 2027 priorities. What’s New Since COP30 The OCCCM launched at COP30 in Belém as a voluntary, member-led international partnership. Its stated goal is to accelerate collective climate ambition and action while keeping greenhouse gas cuts cost-effective. “The momentum gained by the Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets since its COP30 launch proves that climate action can stay the course with close partnerships among countries and stakeholders. One year later, our growing Coalition counts 13 Members and 34 Observers and begins the implementation of its work programme. Strong membership, capable and experienced observers, and a results-oriented work programme will enable the Open Coalition to set trends and become the central point of reference on effective carbon pricing and high-quality carbon credits. The latter is an EU priority for next year, as the European Commission prepares a proposal to ensure the availability of high-quality international carbon credits that can count towards the EU’s 2040 climate target,” said Kurt Vandenberghe, the European Commission’s Director-General for Climate Action and OCCCM Co-Chair. artigo.texto: O Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente de Campinas (Comdema) convidou três instituições de ensino e pesquisa para avaliar os possíveis impactos da construção de um mega data center na Fazenda Pau d'Alho, em Barão Geraldo. Os ofícios foram publicados no Diário Oficial desta quarta-feira (18) e buscam ampliar a análise dos efeitos do empreendimento sobre o meio ambiente e as atividades científicas na região. Os convites foram enviados à PUC-Campinas, ao Centro de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento em Telecomunicações (CPQD) e ao Centro Nacional de Pesquisa em Energia e Materiais (CNPEM). A Unicamp já participa das discussões, por meio de professores de diferentes áreas. O complexo é um projeto da Terranova, ligada à gestora de investimentos Actis, e poderá alcançar 400 megawatts (MW) de capacidade até 2029. Quando foi anunciado, em agosto, esse valor correspondia a 40% da capacidade de processamento de dados em operação no Brasil. O Comdema afirmou que também está organizando um grupo de trabalho (GT) com especialistas em tecnologia, energia, recursos hídricos, legislação e saúde. A expectativa é apresentar um primeiro relatório técnico em até 90 dias, para ajudar o conselho a avaliar o empreendimento. Em nota, a Terra Nova negou que o projeto vá consumir 3,24 milhões de litros de água por dia e afirmou que seguirá as normas ambientais. Segundo a empresa, as obras ainda não começaram e o primeiro prédio deve entrar em operação em 2028. Leia o posicionamento completo abaixo. 🔎 Quais são as preocupações? Projeto do data center em Campinas (SP) — Foto: Terranova Os data centers são grandes instalações que abrigam servidores responsáveis por armazenar e processar informações, inclusive para sistemas de inteligência artificial. Como funcionam continuamente, esses equipamentos precisam de muita energia e de refrigeração para evitar o superaquecimento. No caso de Campinas, o Comdema quer esclarecer principalmente: - Água: o conselho apontou uma estimativa de consumo de até 3,24 milhões de litros por dia em determinadas condições de refrigeração. - Energia: a alta demanda de eletricidade e os possíveis efeitos sobre a infraestrutura regional. - Calor: a possibilidade de aumento da temperatura no entorno do empreendimento. - Ruídos e vibrações: possíveis interferências em equipamentos científicos sensíveis. - Resíduos eletrônicos: o descarte de baterias, processadores e outros componentes. - Impactos urbanísticos: a compatibilidade do complexo com o planejamento ambiental da região. Em agosto, a Terranova afirmou que utilizará um sistema de refrigeração com água circulando por pequenos tubos próximos aos servidores. Segundo a empresa, a tecnologia funciona em circuito fechado, sem evaporação da água utilizada no processo, o que reduziria o consumo hídrico. 🔬 Por que as instituições foram convidadas? Vista aérea do laboratório Sirius, em Campinas — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV Uma das principais preocupações é a proximidade do empreendimento com o CNPEM, onde funciona o Sirius, um acelerador de partículas utilizado em pesquisas científicas. Segundo o conselho, os equipamentos exigem condições rigorosas de estabilidade, e vibrações provocadas pelas obras ou pelo funcionamento do complexo poderiam interferir nas atividades. Por isso, o CNPEM foi convidado a contribuir com estudos sobre esses possíveis efeitos. O CPQD poderá ajudar na avaliação da eficiência energética, dos sistemas de refrigeração e do descarte de resíduos eletrônicos. Já a PUC-Campinas foi chamada para colaborar com análises sobre os impactos ambientais e urbanísticos. A Unicamp participa do grupo por meio de pesquisadores de diferentes áreas, e a Reitoria também demonstrou interesse em acompanhar os trabalhos, segundo os ofícios. Questionamentos sobre o projeto A instalação do complexo já havia sido questionada pelo Comdema em agosto, quando o conselho pediu a suspensão dos licenciamentos da subestação de energia. Entre as preocupações estavam o consumo de água e energia, os possíveis impactos ambientais e a concessão de autorizações separadas para a subestação e o data center. Em setembro, o Ministério Público de São Paulo (MP-SP) instaurou um inquérito civil para apurar os impactos e a regularidade do projeto, após receber três denúncias, incluindo uma do próprio conselho. Na época, a Prefeitura de Campinas informou que apenas a subestação havia recebido autorizações e que as demais etapas do empreendimento continuavam em análise. A administração afirmou que os procedimentos adotados seguiram a legislação municipal. A Terranova também declarou, em setembro, que cumpria as exigências legais para avançar no licenciamento. A empresa destacou as contrapartidas previstas, como a preservação de áreas verdes, a construção de vias públicas e a implantação de estações de tratamento de água e esgoto. O projeto prevê investimento inicial de US$ 500 milhões e geração de aproximadamente 3 mil empregos, diretos e indiretos. A primeira fase está prevista para 2027. O que diz a empresa? "A TERRANOVA acompanha com respeito o trabalho do Comdema e das instituições de pesquisa de Campinas, e está à disposição para o diálogo técnico ao longo do desenvolvimento do projeto. O projeto do campus tem como compromisso atender à legislação e às normas aplicáveis para ruído, vibração, calor e resíduos. O objetivo é que a energia venha 100% de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, como prevê a lei federal dos data centers (REDATA, Lei nº 15.504/2026). O volume de 3,24 milhões de litros de água por dia indicado não corresponde ao projeto do Campus Campinas. O resfriamento funciona em circuito fechado, sem captação de rios ou poços e sem resfriamento evaporativo, que é o tipo de sistema que demanda grandes volumes diários de água. No primeiro prédio, o circuito é abastecido uma única vez, com cerca de 1.040 m³ de água de reuso transportada por caminhão-pipa, sem uso da rede pública, e na operação só repõe pequenas perdas. artigo.texto: Digital Infrastructure World (DIW) has announced its first 85 speakers for its inaugural conference, scheduled for February 2–4, 2027, at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center in San Jose, California. The event, originally planned as a two-day conference, has expanded to three days to accommodate growing industry interest. Produced by CloserStill Media in collaboration with the Open Compute Project Foundation (OCP), the conference is designed to bring together the computing and physical infrastructure communities responsible for supporting large-scale AI deployments. Organizers report that companies represented by early registrants account for approximately 80 gigawatts of AI infrastructure buying capacity. The conference is expected to attract approximately 2,500 attendees representing as many as 500 organizations. The initial speaker lineup includes representatives from AMD, Arm, AWS, Broadcom, Crusoe, Digital Realty, Google, Intel, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Oracle, Schneider Electric and Siemens. Keynote presentations will feature executives and technology specialists from Broadcom, Google, Keysight Technologies, NVIDIA and Oracle. Connecting the Rack to the Grid The conference program is organized into four technical tracks addressing the relationship between advances in AI computing and the infrastructure required to support them. The Rack track, led by OCP, will examine the development of 1-megawatt rack architectures, including silicon diversity, in-rack power distribution, open hardware designs and advanced cooling technologies. The Cluster track will address networking, optical connectivity and computing architectures needed to connect individual racks into large-scale AI systems, including environments supporting up to one million GPUs. The Data Center track focuses on the facilities infrastructure required to support higher-density computing, including liquid cooling, elevated facility water temperatures, 800-volt DC and medium-voltage electrical distribution, and prefabricated construction approaches. The Energy track will examine grid interconnection, on-site generation, battery storage, nuclear power and strategies for meeting the electrical requirements of gigawatt-scale data center campuses. Discussions will also address the challenge of managing fluctuating AI workloads and their impact on power infrastructure. The programming reflects the growing interdependence of IT architecture, electrical infrastructure and facility design as AI deployments move toward megawatt-scale racks and multi-gigawatt development pipelines. Open Compute Project Collaboration A central component of the event is the participation of the Open Compute Project Foundation, which will organize a colocated OCP Tech Day and lead discussions involving open computing architectures and AI infrastructure design. The collaboration supports OCP's Open Systems for AI Strategic Initiative, which seeks to accelerate the development and deployment of scalable AI infrastructure through greater coordination among technology manufacturers, cloud providers and infrastructure operators. "Scaling AI Data Centers requires more than advances in computing performance," said George Tchaparian, CEO of the Open Compute Project Foundation. Fran Pennella, vice president of the U.S. Digital Infrastructure Portfolio at CloserStill Media, said the expanded conference format reflects the need for greater collaboration between organizations developing AI computing technologies and those responsible for powering, cooling and operating data center facilities. The event will open February 2 with a keynote presentation and welcome reception, followed by two days of conference sessions, exhibits and industry networking on February 3–4. Exhibitors and participating companies include Vultr, Hydra Host, Ecolab, Munters, Camus Energy, DriveNets and Quantum Computing Inc. Registration is open at digitalinfrastructure.world.

artigo.texto: Smartphone batteries have become an important part of the buying decision, especially for people who spend hours gaming, watching videos or scrolling through social media. With the iQOO 15, the company is focusing on battery life through its fourth-generation silicon anode technology. The smartphone comes with a 7,000mAh battery, and iQOO claims that it can deliver up to 10.5 hours of continuous gaming, 32.6 hours of video streaming and 22.6 hours of social media usage on a single charge. But what exactly is silicon anode technology, and how does it help a smartphone battery last longer? To understand this, it is important to know how a smartphone battery works. A battery has two main parts called the anode and cathode. During charging and discharging, lithium ions move between these two parts to store and release energy. Most traditional smartphone batteries use graphite in the anode. Silicon, however, can store more lithium ions than graphite. This means it has the potential to hold more energy in the same amount of space. This is where silicon anode technology comes in. By using silicon-based materials in the battery's anode, manufacturers can increase energy density. In simple terms, a battery can store more power without necessarily becoming much bigger. However, silicon also has a limitation. It expands and contracts during charging and discharging, which can affect battery life and stability over time. Battery makers therefore have to work on ways to manage this expansion. The fourth-generation technology used in the iQOO 15 is designed to improve energy density and battery performance. However, iQOO has not publicly explained every material change that separates this generation from earlier versions. The phone also uses second-generation semi-solid battery technology, which the company says helps maintain stable performance across temperatures ranging from -20°C to 40°C. According to iQOO's laboratory figures, the 7,000mAh battery can offer up to 10.5 hours of continuous gaming. For people who mainly use their phones to watch videos, the company claims up to 32.6 hours of continuous video streaming. Social media users can also get up to 22.6 hours of usage, according to the company's figures. These numbers are based on iQOO's internal testing and should not be treated as guaranteed everyday battery life. Actual results will depend on factors such as screen brightness, network strength, gaming settings, background applications and the type of content being played. The phone also supports 100W wired FlashCharge and 40W wireless charging. It includes bypass charging, which allows power to go directly to the phone's system instead of charging the battery while gaming. This is d esigned to reduce battery heat during long gaming sessions. Another feature is Battery Life Extender mode. The company says this helps users return to their previous activity when the phone is connected to a charger after its battery runs critically low. The iQOO 15 also features Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor and an 8K vapour chamber cooling system. These features are meant to support demanding tasks such as gaming while helping manage heat. artigo.texto: Much attention has been given to artificial intelligence, cloud computing and the technology driving the modern economy. Those topics certainly deserve discussion. Yet for local residents, the more important question is far simpler: What do these projects mean for our communities? The answer begins with jobs and investment, but it does not end there. The arrival of large-scale data centers represents one of the most significant private investments ever contemplated in this region. Drawn by reliable electric power, strategic location, available land and access to major markets, technology companies are increasingly viewing West Virginia as an attractive destination for future development. The benefits begin long before a facility becomes operational. During construction, hundreds and potentially thousands of local and regional workers may be employed in site preparation, building construction, utility installation, electrical work and equipment deployment. These projects create opportunities for heavy equipment operators, electricians, steel workers, concrete specialists, truck drivers, engineers, surveyors and countless others. Once operational, the facilities create a new layer of highly skilled employment opportunities, including data center technicians, network engineers, facility operators, security professionals, maintenance personnel and management staff. These positions typically provide competitive wages, specialized training and long-term career opportunities. Data centers represent extraordinary concentrations of private investment. The land, buildings, electrical infrastructure and equipment associated with these facilities collectively create a property tax base unlike anything most communities have previously experienced. Once placed on the tax rolls, those assets generate recurring revenue year after year. Where does the data center revenue go? Economic development projects are often measured by the number of jobs created. While employment matters, residents should also ask another important question: Where does the revenue go? The answer is straightforward. Tax revenues generated by these facilities are distributed through existing state and local systems and ultimately support essential public services. Those revenues benefit public schools, county government, emergency services, public safety operations, infrastructure improvements, and important statewide initiatives. The combined Monarch and Tamarack developments in Mason County are expected to generate approximately $231.2 million annually in property tax revenue. Of that amount, more than $90 million would support county schools, nearly $47.5 million would flow to county government and more than $7 million would support Fire and EMS services. Additional funding would support statewide initiatives, including the Personal Income Tax Reduction Fund, the Economic Enhancement Grant Fund and improvements to West Virginia's electric grid. Putnam County's proposed Google development, while smaller in scale, would still generate approximately $40.9 million annually in property tax revenue. Local schools would receive approximately $17.4 million each year, the County Commission more than $8.2 million, and Fire and EMS services approximately $1.6 million, with additional revenues supporting statewide priorities. Combined, these projects are projected to generate more than $272 million in annual property tax revenues. For Mason County schools alone, the projected annual distribution exceeds $90 million. Putnam County schools stand to receive more than $17 million annually. These are investments in classrooms, teachers, educational technology, facilities, and opportunities for future generations. County governments would gain resources that could strengthen emergency services, improve infrastructure, address deferred maintenance, expand recreational opportunities and better prepare for future growth. Perhaps most importantly, this revenue stream is not a one-time payment or a temporary grant. It is generated year after year for as long as the facilities remain in operation. This is no longer simply a discussion about technology projects or industrial development. It is a discussion about whether West Virginia can position itself to capture the benefits of one of the fastest-growing sectors of the modern economy. Reasonable questions should be asked. Citizens deserve transparency. Public officials should be held accountable for the decisions they make. Those principles are fundamental to good government and responsible economic development. At the same time, it is important to recognize opportunity when it appears. Years from now, the success of these projects will not be judged by the size of the facilities or the sophistication of the technology they contain. They will be judged by whether they helped build stronger schools, safer communities, better public services, greater economic opportunity, and a higher quality of life for the people who call Mason and Putnam Counties home. That is the true promise of this moment. It is a once-in-a-generation opportunity, and one worthy of thoughtful consideration. Clark S. Barnes, of Scott Depot, is a former state senator and president of the Heritage Hills Development Corporation.

artigo.texto: By Hervé Jeannin, co-rapporteur for the EESC opinion on the potential of the sodium battery manufacturing sector Europe’s energy transition requires an industrial base capable of delivering it. Batteries power electric mobility, facilitate the integration of renewable electricity and help households and businesses manage their energy consumption. Our ability to manufacture them will shape Europe’s competitiveness and energy security. Yet intense international competition and dependencies on materials, components and equipment are weakening this essential industry. As co-rapporteur for the European Economic and Social Committee’s opinion on sodium battery manufacturing, I am convinced that sodium technologies offer a tangible opportunity to strengthen Europe’s capabilities while making better use of its own resources. Beyond lithium: what makes sodium batteries different? Today, lithium-ion batteries dominate the global market, powering everything from smartphones to electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Their production is heavily concentrated in Asia, particularly China, which leads in battery manufacturing and the processing of key materials. Sodium-ion batteries offer an emerging alternative: they use sodium instead of lithium, reducing reliance on certain critical raw materials. Although they generally store less energy for the same weight, they could be cheaper to produce and are particularly promising for stationary energy storage and more affordable electric vehicles. China is already investing heavily in this technology, making it essential for Europe to develop its own manufacturing capacity before another strategic dependency takes hold. Sodium batteries: an opportunity for Europe Sodium is abundant in Europe. Suitable battery chemistries can reduce dependence on lithium, cobalt and nickel, while the hard carbon used for anodes can be derived from wood or agricultural waste. The EESC highlights the possibility of producing sodium batteries entirely from European raw materials. Turning this potential into strategic autonomy requires European capabilities across the entire value chain, from processing to recycling, and, above all, strong political commitment to driving the development of European solutions encompassing both raw materials and manufacturers. Sodium should complement lithium-ion technologies. Each application calls for a different balance between energy density, cost, safety and durability. Sodium-ion batteries generally have slightly lower energy density, but weight and size matter less for stationary storage than for electric vehicles. Storing renewable electricity for households, businesses and grids therefore represents a particularly relevant market opportunity. Public support must reflect technological maturity. Sodium-ion batteries offer prospects for deployment in the nearer term; sodium–saltwater systems require further research, particularly into solid electrolytes, to explore their potential for marine applications and longer-term storage. Our opinion also identifies the possibility of using sodium recovered from desalination by-products, linking water resilience to energy storage, subject to technical and environmental assessment. From innovation to industrial production The immediate challenge is industrial scale-up. A laboratory breakthrough alone does not create a competitive factory. Companies must demonstrate the reliability of their solutions, secure customers and finance production equipment. Small businesses often struggle to shoulder these risks. The EESC therefore calls for an updated industrial roadmap for lithium and sodium batteries, coordinated by the European Battery Alliance, with targeted investment support and cooperation with research and technology organisations. Investing in Europe’s battery industry The EESC’s opinion on the Battery Booster strategy makes a specific request: broaden funding to cover chemistries beyond lithium and explicitly include sodium. Support should reach SMEs, suppliers and recyclers alongside cell manufacturers, and should not be limited to electric vehicles. Critical chemicals, electrolytes and European-made machinery also deserve investment. Dependence on imported inputs and equipment leaves vulnerabilities that building more cell factories alone cannot resolve. Affordable energy, predictable permitting procedures and timely funding are essential. The EESC calls for stronger and better-targeted funding for the Battery Booster strategy in the next EU Budget. Our opinion on sodium advocates an overall budget of at least EUR 220 billion for FP10. International cooperation must help build lasting European expertise. Both opinions call for technology transfer; the Battery Booster opinion recommends making state aid, public procurement and subsidies conditional on technology transfer and local content. Investment must strengthen European research (80% of current projects are not launched for lack of funding in Europe), skills and suppliers, while ensuring that requirements for products entering the EU market are applied fairly. Sustainability, jobs and regional development Circularity must be built in from the outset. Ecodesign should facilitate disassembly and materials recovery, while production should minimise energy consumption and the use of hazardous substances. Recycling requires economically viable facilities, harmonised collection and the efficient transport of used batteries to authorised facilities within the single market. Materials recovery capacity must grow in step with production. Industrial ambition must also benefit workers and regions. The Battery Booster opinion makes job quality and compliance with EU standards conditions for public support. Adequate staffing, training, investment in prevention and effective inspections are essential. Workers must be involved in identifying risks arising from new processes. artigo.texto: Long-duration battery project will support energy resilience in the Winterhaven area IMPERIAL– The Imperial Irrigation District (IID), in partnership with the Fort Yuma Quechan Indian Tribe and CMBLU Energy, has secured $7.2 million in grant funding from the California Energy Commission for the Echo Sands Community Resilience project, according to a recent IID press release. The funding will support a 1 MW / 10 MWh long-duration energy storage pilot at IID’s Pilot Knob Hydroelectric Plant near Winterhaven. The release said the project is designed to strengthen energy reliability and resilience for the Quechan Tribe and surrounding communities during extreme heat and other disruptive events. “This funding reflects the value of strong partnerships,” said IID Board Chairwoman Karin Eugenio in the release. “Working with the Quechan Tribe helped make this opportunity possible and will support greater energy resilience for communities in eastern Imperial County.” The Fort Yuma Quechan Indian Tribe is a key partner in the project, helping ensure the pilot reflects the resilience needs of the Tribe and surrounding Winterhaven communities, the release said. Tribal participation will include project planning, community engagement and identifying critical facilities that could benefit from greater energy resilience. “Reliable energy is essential to the safety and well-being of our people,” said Fort Yuma Quechan Indian Tribal President Jonathan E. Koteen in the report. “We appreciate this partnership and the opportunity to advance a project that will strengthen resilience for the Quechan people and our neighboring communities.” The pilot will use CMBLU Energy’s SolidFlow technology, marking IID’s first deployment of a non-lithium long-duration battery storage system. The technology uses non-flammable, aqueous materials and is designed to avoid thermal runaway, allowing IID to evaluate an innovative energy storage option with community safety in mind. According to the release, results from the pilot will help IID evaluate the technology's performance and determine whether larger-scale applications may be appropriate in the future. IID will continue working with the Quechan Tribe, CMBLU Energy and other project partners as the project moves forward, per the report.

artigo.texto: Key Takeaways - The plant's assembly lines can produce 40 cells per minute, making them among the fastest prismatic LFP battery lines outside China. - The project, which uses CATL-licensed technology, achieved commercial mass production after navigating setbacks including US political scrutiny and a downsizing. Ford Motor's (NYSE: F) plant in Michigan has rolled out its first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells using technology licensed from CATL (HKEX: 3750), marking the US auto giant's official entry into battery manufacturing. The prismatic LFP cells, produced at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall, Michigan, are headed to the Louisville Assembly Plant to power prototypes of the Fathom electric pickup truck, Charles Poon, vice president of hardware engineering at Ford, said in a statement on Wednesday. With commercial-scale deliveries from the wholly owned and operated plant, Ford will become the first automaker to introduce LFP batteries for the mainstream US consumer automotive market, helping push pure electric vehicle (EV) prices lower. To significantly reduce vehicle cost and weight, Ford chose proven technology from CATL, the world's largest battery maker, and integrated the prismatic LFP battery pack directly into the vehicle design as a structural chassis component. The plant's assembly lines can produce 40 cells per minute, making them among the fastest prismatic LFP battery lines outside China, and use AI image recognition technology to pursue a low defect rate at the parts-per-billion level. Following the shipment of the first cells, Ford plans to bring a supporting battery pack plant into operation in Marshall in 2027 to prepare for the official launch of the Fathom electric pickup. Manufacturing experience gained from the on-schedule launch of the Michigan plant is helping a battery energy storage system plant in Glendale, Kentucky, prepare for its start of production in 2027, Ford Energy president David Carroll said on Thursday. The bumpy partnership began in February 2023, when Ford initially announced a $3.5 billion investment to build a plant with an annual capacity of 35 gigawatt-hours (GWh), with CATL providing technology licensing and operational support. After US Republican lawmakers questioned whether federal subsidies could indirectly flow to CATL, the project was temporarily halted in 2023 before restarting in November of the same year with investment and annual capacity cut to $2 billion and 20 GWh, respectively. Facing policy headwinds such as the early termination of US federal EV tax credits in September 2025, Ford recorded $19.5 billion in related asset impairment charges in December 2025, but kept the LFP project and decided to expand into the energy storage business. Ford announced in June this year that the plant had completed full-process trial production of its first cells and was conducting tests under CATL standards, and has now achieved the official roll-out and shipment of automotive power cells within the year as planned.

Jeff Bezos is set to carry Google’s A.I. chips into orbit: Google has booked a dedicated launch on Blue Origin’s heavy-lift New Glenn rocket for Project Suncatcher, its space computing project. The flight is targeted for the first quarter of 2029, Travis Beals, the project’s lead, has just announced in a blog post. New Glenn is to deploy satellites into sun-synchronous orbit, each with roughly the capacity of a data center rack. From Prototype to Heavy Lift With Project Suncatcher, Google wants to move A.I. infrastructure into space and tap the virtually unlimited solar power available in orbit. Mr. Beals calls the project a “long-term moonshot” and the dedicated launch with Blue Origin “a crucial milestone” on its road map. The companies have not disclosed how many satellites will fly or what the launch costs, the trade publication Via Satellite reported. Until now, Suncatcher has operated on a small scale. In the fall, a SpaceX rideshare mission carried a first prototype satellite into orbit, built together with the Earth-imaging company Planet. It carries four of Google’s A.I. chips, known as tensor processing units, which run the open model Gemma. Two more test satellites are planned for next year to check whether the chips can be linked by laser. The New Glenn launch would be a first step toward larger satellite swarms. Less Dependent on SpaceX With Blue Origin, Google gains a second major launch partner. For the prototype, it still had to rely on SpaceX, a company in which Google holds a stake but which plans to operate its own A.I. data centers in orbit from 2028. Google says the deal builds on its ongoing work with other satellite and launch partners. The race for computing power in space is well underway. Besides SpaceX, the start-up Starcloud is working on orbital data centers, and Nvidia has already unveiled space-grade A.I. chips. The motivation is the same everywhere: On the ground, A.I. data centers face long waits for grid connections and growing opposition from residents, while solar panels in sun-synchronous orbit can generate up to eight times more power than on Earth, according to Google. Does It Pay Off in Space? Whether orbital data centers will ever pay off remains an open question. By Google’s own calculations, launch costs would have to fall below $200 (about 180 euros) per kilogram by the mid-2030s for computing in orbit to compete with data centers on the ground. Mr. Beals himself recently told NPR that he did not see it becoming cheaper to compute in space within the next five years. Cooling is another hurdle: In a vacuum, the chips’ waste heat has to be radiated away through heavy radiators, which is why the prototype can only compute for 15 minutes at a time. The rocket also still has to prove itself. New Glenn has flown only a handful of times, and on its third flight in April its payload ended up in the wrong orbit, Spaceflight Now reported. That leaves a little more than two years until Google’s planned launch.

artigo.texto: Support WBUR Kraft-backed data center proposal met with opposition from Sutton residents Residents in Sutton, Massachusetts expressed outrage at a planning board meeting Monday over a proposal to build $16 billion data center campus in their town. The proposed project is backed by The Kraft Group, which owns the New England Patriots. The data center campus would span 10 buildings and draw 900 megawatts of electricity, according to a town memorandum on the project. If built, it would be the among largest data centers in the country. Because the town currently has no zoning laws related to data centers, Sutton’s planning board is exploring options to add a bylaw for data centers to be built in the town. Town officials said at the meeting that the campus would bring in nearly $28 million in tax revenue each year, which could lower the tax bill of an average single-family home and help close the town’s growing budget deficit. But residents in attendance said they are worried about the data center’s impact on the environment, public health and home values. Shawn Buzzell, who has lived in Sutton for three years, stood outside the town hall collecting signatures on a petition before the meeting. He said the petition, which had more than 300 signatures as of Monday night, calls for a special town meeting for residents to vote on the petition’s definition of data centers and prohibit their construction in Sutton. He said he’s against the proposed data center because he’s concerned that it will put residents at risk of higher electricity costs and noise pollution. “They’re sticking them in the middle of people’s neighborhoods,” Buzzell said. “They wedge these in there and it’s not because it’s the right place to put it, it’s because it’s the cheapest place to put it. They end up ruining a lot of people’s lives, destroying quality of life, destroying household resale value, just so they can make themselves a little bit more extra money, and that’s not fair.” Crystal Smith, a Sutton resident for 15 years, said she has been following the news about data centers, but never expected one to be built in the “tiny town” of Sutton. “We don’t have the space for that, we don’t have the resources for that and it would impact way too many things here,” Smith said. About 75 residents attended Monday night’s planning board meeting. Some held signs that read, “NO DATA CENTERS” and “NO DATA CENTERS IN SUTTON.” Others chimed in during the meeting, voicing their disapproval of the project. WBUR reached out to The Kraft Group for comment, but did not receive a response in time for publication. In a memorandum outlining the project, the town said the proposal is tentative. Applications with the town have yet to be filed and "important details on power, water, equipment and site impacts are still to come," the memo reads. Gov. Maura Healey signed an executive order in September requiring data center projects to get local approval before they can obtain state permits. Under the order, data center projects are also required develop energy resources to support their operation or to create a "Ratepayer Protection Fund" if they can't supply their own power infrastructure. The proposed data center would draw 900 megawatts of power, roughly the amount of electricity required to power 450,000 homes.

(“Kandi” or the “Company”, collectively with the consolidated subsidiaries, the “Group”) (NASDAQ GS: KNDI), a global innovator in intelligent equipment and a technology-driven platform company, today announced its unaudited financial results for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Nine Months of 2026 Financial Highlights Net revenues increased 38.5% year over year to $82.1 million. Revenue from off-road vehicles and associated parts increased 33.5% to $74.0 million, compared with $55.4 million for the same period of 2025. Net income was $5.6 million, or $0.57 per basic and diluted share, compared with a net loss of $6.3 million, or $0.75 per basic and diluted share, for the same period of 2025. Cash and cash equivalents, restricted cash, and certificates of deposit totaled $291.3 million as of September 30, 2026, compared with $211.9 million as of December 31, 2025. Through the retailer’s retail network, Kandi aims to broaden its market reach, strengthen brand awareness, and create new sales opportunities for its core North American business. Meanwhile, we further advanced Rawrr Inc.’s integration into the Group, leveraging synergies across R&D, manufacturing, supply chain and distribution to lay the groundwork for upcoming product launches and future growth. “Our new businesses in energy and intelligent equipment also made meaningful progress in commercialization. China Battery Exchange secured new orders from CATL, while advancing equipment production, project deliveries and capacity expansion. We are pleased that this business began contributing revenue in the third quarter. Looking ahead, we will remain focused on customer needs and confirmed orders as we advance the commercialization of our emerging businesses. “As Kandi continues to upgrade its product portfolio and advance the commercialization of its battery-swapping equipment, we observe opportunities to build a more diversified base for sustainable growth. artigo.texto: Blenden Township unable to reach decision on controversial battery energy storage system BLENDON TOWNSHIP, Mich. (WOOD) — The Planning Commission of Blendon Township met Wednesday night to decide on a controversial battery energy storage system, known as a BESS. Neighbors worry about proposed battery energy storage system in Blendon Township The Wednesday meeting regarding the facility developments lasted nearly three hours, with outraged residents and town commissioners ultimately unable to reach an agreement. The project was initially proposed by Key Capture Energy, which has been trying to develop a 100-Megawatt BESS for the past 15 months. Commissioners ended up splitting their votes three to three on the decision for approval, which has left the project in limbo. Throughout the entire process, residents have been concerned about the environmental impact of a BESS. They called attention to the risks of a fire at the BESS and how the facility could have long term impacts on the area and its farms. Key Capture Energy says that the BESS would be safe and highly regulated, but commissioners expressed reservations over what a potential fire could mean for nearby property values, pointing to fires that have broken out at other BESS facilities. Advertisement "Any type of development has a risk of fire loss of a larger than typical compared to a home, or as our counterparts experienced the common amount of hazardous chemicals that could contaminate the environment during and after a failure," Planning Commissioner Ben Van Zweden said at the Wednesday meeting. "I consider their submission being conclusive that they did not address failure with this is a possibility. There have been fires at BESS facilities, so there should be data on that." Key Capture Energy says that a nearby Van Buren substation makes Blendon Township an ideal location for the project. "The biggest benefit is a stable and reliable electric grid," said Chris Linsmayer, director of public affairs and community relations at Key Capture Energy. "So the way that these work is they store energy at periods of low demand, typically when prices are low and then that energy is available to dispatch back onto the grid." The commissioners are now working on revisions to the BESS application and are planning to bring those to the next board meeting. One option Key Capture Energy says they would consider is going to the state to seek approval through Public Act 233, which reduces local control over land-use decisions and would potentially giveo the Michigan Public Service Commission the authority to approve the project. Residents of Blenden Township as well as commissioners shared their unease about what that path would mean for the town and if it would be benefitted at all based on agreements made with Key Capture Energy.o Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. artigo.texto: - Solar installations keep growing, and the market enters a new stage India has steadily accelerated solar project construction, and solar has become a major part of its renewable energy development. According to data published by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE), cumulative installed solar capacity reached 174.55 GW as of October 31, 2026, of which ground-mounted utility-scale capacity was about 127.33 GW. From April to October 2026, India added about 24.29 GW of solar capacity, including about 3.50 GW in October alone. Annual additions also show the pace of development. In FY2025–26, India added 44.61 GW of solar capacity, up roughly 87.2% from 23.83 GW in FY2024–25, which indicates a clear acceleration in project development and construction. As electricity demand grows and the energy mix continues to transition, solar demand keeps expanding. Beyond large ground-mounted plants, rooftop solar, commercial and industrial distributed generation, and hybrid energy projects are becoming additional sources of new demand. Under the PM-Surya Ghar rooftop scheme, about 6.526 million households had benefited as of early November 2026, and cumulative rooftop installations reached about 19.1 GW, further boosting the distributed solar market. Still, rapid capacity growth places greater demands on grid infrastructure and power absorption. As solar accounts for a larger share of the power mix, how well generation growth matches transmission capacity will directly affect whether new projects can connect to the grid and perform as expected. - Growing capacity and grid absorption constraints highlight the need for energy storage As solar capacity expands, some regions of India have begun to face a mismatch between renewable output and grid acceptance capacity, and solar curtailment is drawing growing attention. Solar curtailment refers to situations where a solar plant can generate electricity but part of that output cannot be delivered to the grid because of insufficient transmission capacity, supply-demand mismatches, or dispatch restrictions. For solar projects, curtailment reduces actual electricity sales, affects returns on investment, and may weaken the incentive to develop future projects. According to Grid Controller of India data submitted to Parliament by the MNRE, solar curtailment reached 8,133 GWh from April to June 2026, with 2,417 GWh in April, 3,235 GWh in May, and 2,481 GWh in June. This shows that while solar capacity has grown rapidly, grid transmission and absorption capacity has not fully kept pace with generation, and the power supply-demand mismatch is becoming more visible. As more solar projects come online, expanding transmission capacity and building supporting energy storage will become key directions for reducing curtailment and improving solar utilization. Transmission delays are also affecting renewable grid connections. In the first quarter of 2026, India lost about 300 GWh of renewable generation due to transmission constraints, roughly two-thirds of the renewable curtailment in interstate grid projects over the same period. In addition, some transmission projects are behind schedule, and about 20 GW of renewable projects face grid connection delays of more than four months. This points to a continuing gap between renewable project development and grid construction. Against this backdrop, energy storage has become an important complement for improving solar absorption. Battery energy storage systems (BESS) can store electricity during solar peak output and release it at night or during demand peaks, shifting power across time periods to ease the timing mismatch between generation and consumption. According to the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) statistics on energy storage projects as of August 31, 2026, about 3.03 GW / 9.08 GWh of BESS projects are in operation, about 28.21 GW / 79.92 GWh are under construction, about 7.32 GW / 24.13 GWh have been awarded, and about 18.31 GW / 63.53 GWh are at the tendering stage. These figures show that India has a large pipeline of storage projects, but projects under construction, awarded, or in tendering are not the same as storage capacity already in operation. Looking at project progress, India’s BESS pipeline has grown substantially, but operating capacity remains limited, with projects under construction and at the tendering stage making up the bulk of the pipeline. The focus of the storage market is gradually shifting from project planning and tendering toward construction, grid connection, and actual operation. As storage projects come online, their role in easing peak-period supply-demand imbalances, improving solar utilization, and strengthening grid regulation will become more apparent. In addition, on July 31, 2026, the Indian government approved the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana, which plans to develop 5,000 MW of floating solar paired with at least two hours of storage, corresponding to about 10,000 MWh. The project will be implemented over FY2026–27 to FY2030–31, further reflecting India’s direction of combining solar generation with storage. Overall, the growth focus of India’s solar market is extending from new capacity additions to grid transmission, absorption, and storage support. Transmission construction progress and the commissioning of storage projects will be important factors affecting the actual generation performance of solar projects and future market demand. - Localization policies continue to advance, and DCR and ALMM are reshaping module procurement While expanding solar capacity, the Indian government has also continued to promote domestic solar manufacturing, aiming to reduce reliance on imports and build a domestic supply system covering more segments of the industrial chain. India currently drives industrial localization mainly through the Domestic Content Requirement (DCR), the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM), and the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schem

artigo.texto: Rare look inside Port Washington's $15M AI data center project drawing mixed reactions A $15 million AI data center project in Port Washington, developed by Vantage in partnership with Oracle and OpenAI, is under construction and drawing both community curiosity and criticism. 12 News got a rare look inside one of the largest AI data centers in the country. Get an exclusive look behind-the-scenes in the video player above. The 672-acre site, with an additional 1,000 acres reserved for expansion, is larger than the entire Village of Whitefish Bay. The construction site sees 3,500 workers daily, and Port Washington Mayor Ted Neitzke has been leading van tours of the site to engage locals and address concerns. “Our restaurants are thriving, and our bars are thriving, and our hotels are thriving, and our downtown businesses are thriving,” Neitzke said during one of the tours. The project The first phase of the project includes four data center buildings, each with a footprint large enough to hold two Lambeau Fields. “This is one of the four data center buildings being built here. 800 thousand square feet each,” Neitzke said. “It’s comparable to other data centers that are being built across the country. But definitely as someone who has been in construction for a large part of my life, this is definitely fantastic to watch and build,” he added. Vantage says the center will be operational by early 2028, providing internet and cloud services while storing, processing, and distributing data. “Almost everything you’re seeing here is manufactured, made, or fabricated here in Wisconsin. So it’s not just a Port Washington thing. It’s statewide,” Neitzke said. The project is expected to bring significant tax benefits to the community, transforming agriculturally zoned land assessed at a few million dollars into a site valued at $120 million. This increase is anticipated to support the majority of city services for Port Washington. Responses after tour Tour participants shared their impressions of the project. “It’s really something else,” one attendee said. “I didn’t know what the Vantage Center was really for. And now I know a lot more, so that’s good,” another participant said. When asked if they thought the project was positive for the area, they replied, “Sure. Sure.” Al Poull, whose family has lived on a nearby farm for 126 years, acknowledged the changes brought by the project. “Things change, you know? It’s just the way it is,” Poull said. Criticism Despite the enthusiasm from some locals, the project has faced criticism and opposition. One contentious meeting resulted in the arrest of three women. Clean Wisconsin and other groups have raised concerns about the environmental impact of AI data centers and the power plants required to support them. Video below: Data center dust and noise fight continues near Port Washington “Wisconsin is incredibly vulnerable right now to AI data centers,” a Clean Wisconsin representative said. “When you have something as large as what’s going on in Port Washington, that will be vastly bigger in terms of energy needs than anything Wisconsin has ever seen before, where so much has to be given to that, these are resources we all rely on. That needs to be a conversation that needs to happen well before right now when the construction is going on and it’s almost done,” the representative added. Neitzke acknowledged the unexpected backlash. “Surprised? Yes. Caught off guard is probably the better way to describe it. Did not see that coming,” he said. Transparency The mayor has emphasized transparency during the tours, addressing concerns about water usage, power supply, and electricity rates. “It does not use a lot of water. Power is protected, your electricity rates do not go up,” Neitzke said. He believes the data center is a transformative project for the community. “I really believe that data centers are the newest of all the utilities. And a utility is something everyone needs, right? Clean water, clean sidewalks, electricity, and now information,” Neitzke said. Neitzke has also been advising elected officials across the country on how to navigate similar projects. “Right now, local communities are in an amazing position to negotiate. And I don’t know why anyone wouldn’t. As you saw out there, I mean, it’s an amazing project,” he said. Construction on the data center began in December 2022 and is scheduled to be completed by 2028.
