artigo.texto: Brian Fellon is senior vice president at Xpansiv, a market platform for energy and environmental commodities. Winter Storm Fern hit Texas in January 2026 with extreme cold and hazardous precipitation. But unlike Winter Storm Uri in 2021, the lights stayed on. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas’ post-event report captured how the grid remained intact without Energy Emergency Alerts, public conservation calls or systemwide outages. During Fern, ERCOT’s battery energy storage resources were indispensable for covering peak-demand reserves, while all resource types contributed to meeting broader system demand. The critical lesson is that grid performance is highly dependent on coordinating nascent technologies and real-time operations with legacy generation assets. That lesson is now being tested at scale across the country. The U.S. electricity sector is undergoing its most abrupt transformation since deregulation. After nearly two decades of flat demand, load growth is accelerating from data centers, transportation and industrial electrification. The forward demand curve has never been this steep, and ERCOT's long-range planning assumptions contemplate peak load reaching more than four times today’s record levels. Across the PJM Interconnection footprint, forecasted load growth is raising expectations that tens of gigawatts of new supply may be needed over the coming decade to maintain system reliability. This demand jump is colliding with aging grid infrastructure, constrained transmission, record-long interconnection queues and a shifting policy landscape. These factors are reconfiguring wholesale power markets and revaluing baseload and dispatchable generation, while establishing battery storage as essential grid infrastructure. Batteries are often described as a foundational solution because they respond instantly, start and stop without thermal plants’ mechanical constraints, and uniquely shift energy from off-peak to on-peak periods. In practice, the grid does not simply benefit from batteries as fixed capacity in the conventional sense. It benefits from dynamic, flexible battery storage systems that are specifically configured to accelerate responsiveness, along with the telemetry, data feeds, market interfaces and 24/7 readiness required to perform under normal and stressed conditions alike. That distinction matters as storage scales, owners compete for arbitrage opportunities and electricity markets evolve. In organized wholesale markets, dispatch is not a single daily event. It’s a sequence of day-ahead scheduling, intraday adjustments and real-time dispatch, translated into 5-minute price intervals. For chemically-constrained assets like batteries, timelines are crucial because spot market decisions are inseparable from current and future state-of-charge, known as SoC. Every megawatt discharged at a given time affects what can be delivered later. Fortunately, policy and market design are adapting to support this reality. FERC’s Order No. 841 requires ISOs/RTOs to remove barriers to storage participation and adopt participation models that recognize storage’s physical and operational characteristics. That mandate expanded the range of products storage can provide, with more options for revenue production. Although not governed by FERC, ERCOT went even further than Order 841. In December 2025, ERCOT implemented Real-Time Co-optimization Plus Batteries (RTC+B), which co-optimizes energy and reserves in real time while accounting for what battery resources can actually deliver. One month later, during Winter Storm Fern, ERCOT credited RTC+B with helping redistribute ancillary services across the system during a localized transmission emergency. The same change that helped ERCOT lean on batteries during Fern also changed how those batteries earn revenue. As these rules open new ways for storage to participate, the mix of market products that pay off keeps shifting. The new paradigm, and what’s needed Market participants and grid operators need timely, accurate information about what a battery can deliver under variable constraints. Unreliable data or inconsistent operations aren’t theoretical problems, because they show up directly in project economics after commercial operations begin. Similarly, optimization only creates value if it’s converted into timely, accurate and compliant market submissions. There has never been a greater need for validated bid and offer workflows, automated checks against asset constraints and market rules, reliable ISO/RTO connectivity, clear audit trails, and the ability to rapidly adjust trades as forecasts, prices, outages and SoC conditions change. The same need for accuracy and coordination extends into real-time operations. Wholesale markets and grid conditions don’t simply pause at 5 p.m. when the workday ends for most electricity consumers. Scarcity pricing, forced outages and weather disruptions often happen during off-hours. Sophisticated storage operators utilize defined escalation pathways, telemetry monitoring and situational awareness tools to coordinate instantly when grid conditions require immediate support. A practical checklist for battery owners and operators includes: - Treat data and telemetry as mission-critical infrastructure. Validate data quality and latency end-to-end, not just at the device level. - Run multi-market playbooks, not single-product strategies. Markets change; build the adaptive capability to shift with them. - Treat market submission as a core operating capability. Whether built in-house or outsourced, deploy resilient controls, versioned workflows and exception handling. - Operationalize SoC discipline. Establish SoC guardrails tied to existing obligations, revenue targets and forecast uncertainty. Review after-action performance during unforeseen events. ERCOT has shown what adaptive market design can deliver. Other markets should follow. Operators can only do so much on their own. Market rules decide how

artigo.texto: The Harvard-led study estimates that 403 of the nation's largest data centers consumed 1.8% of U.S. electricity and accounted for about 0.5% of carbon dioxide emissions, while finding that the electricity supplying those facilities was less carbon-intensive than the national average. The findings estimated that the hyperscale data centers consumed approximately 82 terawatt-hours of electricity and were associated with 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions between May 2024 and April 2025. The research showed over 50 percent of electricity came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The findings come as data center development supports growing demand for AI and cloud computing while prompting scrutiny of electricity consumption, environmental effects, and infrastructure requirements. AiAi Holdings Ceo, Todd Furniss says the 3 areas of concern: are the source of power, how will they distribute the electricity and the community impact. Out of approximately 5500 data centers nationwide, the 403 where labeled "hyperscale" facilities, meaning they are built for rapid expansion, high power density, automated operations, and repeatable designs that can be deployed across multiple regions. Furniss highlighted the study covers around 10 percent of all U.S. data centers, and not all facilities require the same amount of power. He says the findings also showed about 20 percent of the data centers use nuclear power which is good because it alleviates pressure on the grid. "The bad is- the nuclear plant can produce so much electricity, that the community residents don't get the benefits of lower costs of that production." He said. He says data center developers are actively looking at small modular reactors as an option. "The question is- how do you get through the red tape of developing those centers and making sure they 're safe and secure in whatever area they are." Furniss added. Furness says, meanwhile, businesses are left hanging in the balance as they need data centers to help them run more efficiently. "Let us figure out how to work with you but at the end of the day I need the compute capacity in order to compete on the global stage-economically." The AiAi Ceo says open dialog should continue to allow for an exchange of ideas. He says he questions whether the public can remain calm and levelheaded to reach an agreement. As far as the data centers output numbers and environmental footprint- the study's author, points to further research as it is needed to fully measure the community impact. "Decisions about where data centers go and how they're powered are critical environmental and public health decisions, and they should be made with good data," Francesca Dominici, the study's corresponding author, said in the release.

artigo.texto: Open house event sheds light on proposed battery energy storage system in Sandcut TERRE HAUTE, Ind. (WTWO/WAWV) — Concerned residents from Sandcut got the chance to learn more about a proposed battery energy storage system that could be coming to the area. The event was an open house-style event where people could go from station to station to speak with officials from the NextEra Energy Resources group that is in charge of the proposed project. Taylor Christian is the lead project manager for NextEra Resources, and he mentioned what the battery energy storage system actually is. "Energy storage is essentially a grid reliability mechanism," Christian said. "It stores energy whenever the demand is low and the supply is high. Then it puts that energy back onto the grid whenever you see periods of higher demand and lower supply." Officials said this project is just for energy purposes. "This is not tied to any Vigo County data center or any Vigo County, any other development in Vigo County really. This is an energy source project that we're proposing in Vigo County." Dustin Houser is a resident of Sandcut who came to the open house, and he mentioned that there are several concerns with this proposed project. "The largest concerns that I have are noise pollution, light pollution and environmental concerns," Houser said. "The animals are going to get driven off in our area, which we've had even bald eagles coming back in our area. So, we don't want them to go away." Another concern residents have is the possibility of the batteries catching fire. "When they catch fire," Houser said. "They release a lot of chemicals in the air and they can't put the fire out. They have to let the fire burn out itself. Smoke will linger; there's been reported fires that have lasted up to 17 days, and they have to evacuate the area because of the hazardous materials that are in the air." This is just a proposed project at this time, but Sandcut residents hope changes can be made. "The commissioner's office needs to understand and undo the rezoning that they just did," Houser said. "Residents live out in the country for a reason. We like the quiet. We like the dark. We enjoy looking at the agriculture." Officials with NextEra Energy Resources said this proposed project can bring 175 jobs to the area during construction and millions of dollars in tax revenue to the area. artigo.texto: A Halma plc (LSE:HLMA) reportou um aumento de 22,5% no lucro operacional ajustado, atingindo £345,4 milhões nos seis meses encerrados em 30 de setembro de 2026, superando as expectativas dos analistas. O crescimento dos lucros foi impulsionado pela maior demanda por tecnologia de data center e pela melhoria das margens operacionais. O grupo britânico de tecnologia para segurança, saúde e meio ambiente gerou uma receita de £ 1,43 bilhão, um aumento de 15,8% em relação aos £ 1,24 bilhão do mesmo período do ano passado. O crescimento orgânico da receita, excluindo aquisições, alienações e variações cambiais, atingiu 12,3%. O lucro operacional ajustado subiu de £282 milhões no ano anterior, superando a previsão dos analistas, compilada pela própria empresa, de £332,3 milhões. O lucro ajustado antes de impostos atingiu £327,7 milhões, superando as expectativas do mercado de £310,8 milhões, enquanto o lucro ajustado por ação de 66,24 pence superou a previsão consensual de 63 pence. A Halma manteve sua previsão para o ano inteiro, apoiada pela demanda contínua em todos os seus negócios e por uma entrada de pedidos que permaneceu acima da receita. A margem operacional expande para 24,1% A margem operacional ajustada da Halma aumentou para 24,1%, ante 22,8% no ano anterior, representando uma melhoria de 130 pontos base. A empresa atribuiu o aumento à gestão disciplinada de custos, a uma combinação de produtos favorável e às contribuições de aquisições com margens operacionais mais elevadas. O período do ano anterior incluiu um lucro extraordinário de £ 9,3 milhões associado a um contrato de licenciamento de marca registrada. Excluindo esse benefício dos números comparativos, o lucro operacional ajustado aumentou 26,4%, enquanto a margem operacional do ano anterior foi de 22,3%. Nessa base comparativa ajustada, a melhoria da margem foi de 180 pontos base. A maior rentabilidade refletiu tanto o crescimento da receita quanto a contribuição de atividades com margens mais elevadas, particularmente nas operações de fotônica da empresa. Receita do setor de fotônica se beneficia da forte demanda por data centers A divisão de fotônica da Halma, que fabrica tecnologia de comutação óptica, registrou um crescimento orgânico de receita de aproximadamente 30% durante o primeiro semestre. A demanda foi impulsionada pelo investimento contínuo em infraestrutura de data centers, onde switches ópticos são usados para gerenciar as comunicações e a transmissão de dados. A empresa informou que um grande cliente de data center representou 22% da receita total do grupo, em comparação com 19% no mesmo período do ano passado. O aumento da contribuição destaca a crescente importância da demanda relacionada a data centers para o desempenho geral da Halma. A administração indicou que a demanda dos clientes por produtos de comutação óptica permaneceu forte, sustentada por pedidos de compra recorrentes que normalmente cobrem períodos de seis a doze meses. No entanto, Halma reconheceu a possibilidade de restrições de oferta, visto que a demanda continua a aumentar. A empresa continua monitorando a capacidade de produção e a disponibilidade de suprimentos, em resposta às necessidades dos clientes. Empresas do setor de saúde registram crescimento orgânico de receita de 5,8% A Halma reportou um crescimento orgânico de receita de 5,8% em seu negócio de Saúde durante o primeiro semestre. O desempenho da divisão contribuiu para a expansão da receita do grupo como um todo, juntamente com um crescimento mais forte na área de fotônica e contribuições de aquisições. No Reino Unido, a receita orgânica aumentou 2,4%, refletindo uma taxa de crescimento mais moderada do que a alcançada pelo grupo no geral. O portfólio diversificado da Halma abrange tecnologias de segurança, monitoramento ambiental e saúde, proporcionando exposição a uma ampla gama de mercados industriais e comerciais. A empresa continua buscando crescimento por meio de uma combinação de investimento orgânico e aquisições de empresas de tecnologia especializadas. A conversão de caixa melhora para 85% A Halma reportou uma conversão de caixa de 85% durante o primeiro semestre, em comparação com 79% no mesmo período do ano passado. Essa medida reflete a proporção do lucro operacional ajustado convertido em caixa. Embora a conversão de caixa tenha melhorado em relação ao ano anterior, permaneceu abaixo da meta da empresa de 90%. Halma atribuiu a diferença ao momento dos fluxos de caixa e ao investimento adicional em capital de giro. A administração espera que a conversão de caixa para o ano fiscal completo seja de aproximadamente 90%, em linha com a meta estabelecida. A empresa continua a equilibrar o investimento na expansão dos negócios com seus objetivos de geração de caixa. Halma conclui aquisições recordes de £516 milhões no primeiro semestre A Halma concluiu seis aquisições durante o semestre encerrado em setembro de 2026, com um gasto total que atingiu o valor recorde de 516 milhões de libras. As transações incluíram a compra da Dreampath, especialista francesa em sistemas de patologia, representando a maior aquisição da história da Halma. Após o término do período de relatório, o grupo concluiu duas aquisições adicionais por um valor combinado de aproximadamente 55 milhões de libras esterlinas. As transações fazem parte da estratégia de longa data da Halma de expandir seu portfólio por meio de aquisições de empresas especializadas que atuam nos mercados de segurança, saúde e tecnologia ambiental. A dívida líquida aumentou para 966,1 milhões de libras no final de setembro, em comparação com 769,1 milhões de libras no final de março de 2026. O aumento refletiu a atividade de investimento do grupo durante o primeiro semestre, incluindo seu programa de aquisições. Dividendos provisórios aumentados em 7% A Halma anunciou um aumento de 7% em seus dividendos provisórios, para 10,30 pence por ação, em comparação com 9,63 pence no mesmo período do ano passado. artigo.texto: Largest U.S. data centers use as much electricity as some states and countries, study finds The largest U.S. data centers collectively consume roughly as much energy as some individual states and even some countries, according to new research from Harvard University. Researchers found that so-called hyperscale data centers, which occupy as much space as several football fields, consumed 82 terawatt-hours of electricity, or 1.8% of all U.S. electricity, between 2024 and 2025. That's roughly the equivalent of what a state like Missouri uses or a nation like Denmark. Combined, the facilities also produced 26 metric tons of carbon dioxide. Harvard scientist Gianluca Guidi, the lead author of the paper published in Nature Sustainability this week, told CBS News that it took two years to analyze the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of 403 hyperscale data centers between May 2024 and April 2025. The study likely understates the centers' estimated energy consumption, given the swift pace of AI construction across the U.S., he added. "The data stops in April 2025, which in AI time is basically ancient history," Guidi said. There are now more than double that number of large-scale facilities operating in the U.S., with an additional 2,000 planned or under development. "The industry is growing faster than anyone can track it," Guidi added. Factories that never sleep The study highlights AI's dependence on data centers and their outsized impact on the environment. Guidi explained why the facilities are such heavy electricity users. "Every email you send, every photo you post, every show you stream, every question you ask of any generative AI software goes through a building like this," he said of the windowless facilities housing tens of thousands of computers that run around the clock. The machines generate a lot of heat and require constant cooling. "So it's basically a factory that never sleeps," Guidi said. Although he's excited about AI's capabilities and considers himself a proponent of the technology, Guidi called for more transparency in assessing when and how facilities are built, along with their impact — before data centers are built. "The evidence shouldn't show up after the buildings do, and neither should the public's voice," he said. "There are better ways to build this, maybe that cost more, maybe they take longer. So we have to ask ourselves: Are we confusing what's possible or what's profitable with what's actually good for society?" To that end, he issued a challenge to hyperscalers like Amazon, Meta and Microsoft. "We've proven we can build AI really fast. Now, let's prove that we can build it right," he said. Negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Turkey earlier this week launched a voluntary pledge calling on companies and governments to power AI with cleaner energy. "We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet-heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the pledge's launch. "Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse." So far, the pledge has failed to attract signatures from the U.S. tech companies that are driving the AI buildout.

artigo.texto: This story was produced in partnership with the Pulitzer Center’s AI Accountability Network and is the first of a yearlong Capital B investigation into how data centers are reshaping Black communities around the world. By the time Zakiya Mabery learned that a $2 billion data center was planned just a 10-minute walk from her house, officials had already approved it. The 200-acre facility in Augusta, Georgia, was first authorized in 2022 without a public hearing that would’ve allowed the community to voice their concerns. Just months before the facility known as Project Eisenhower came to be, Mabery bought her home in a new housing development called Hayne’s Station. Since then, two-thirds of the people who’ve moved into the community have been Black. “We would’ve never purchased a house if we knew a data center was coming,” she said about the project that began construction earlier this year. Mabery’s experience exposes the racial divide in America’s data center boom — not just in where facilities are built, but in who gets a chance to question them. Majority-Black communities are more than two times more likely to host a data center than majority-white ones and far less likely to receive the chance to hear about the projects before they’re approved or offer their opinion through public comment. “It seems like [processes] are being built to silence citizens,” Mabery said at an Augusta Planning Commission meeting this past summer. In recent years, dozens of AI data centers in communities home to hundreds of thousands of Americans have been approved without a public hearing. For Black communities, the data center boom is extending a familiar pattern of environmental racism that has plagued families for generations. Black communities are hosting infrastructure that generates wealth elsewhere. Meanwhile, they live with the pollution and disinvestment that undermines economic opportunity and contributes to poor health outcomes and premature deaths in their neighborhoods. The stakes are growing as tech companies pour hundreds of billions of dollars into new infrastructure. President Donald Trump has pulled the levers of government in favor of these companies as he’s cast AI dominance as a competition the United States cannot afford to lose to China. His administration has ordered agencies to exempt data centers projects from federal environmental review and to revise federal rules to accelerate their construction. At the same time, he has pushed federal agencies to limit the opportunities for public comment as the building boom reaches communities already carrying generations of industrial burdens. The opportunity for residents to speak their mind is consequential to the outcome of a data center project. On average, communities that have received a hearing before construction are nearly 80% white on average. Those without one are roughly 60% people of color. When communities have received a public hearing, data centers have been blocked 66% of the time. When they don’t, they’re approved 80% of the time, according to Zoned Out, a tool created by researchers at Harvard University. “We know disparities already exist in our communities, and now in the case of data centers, we’re seeing the targeting that happens without any say. It is systemic injustice,” said Aino Halonen, a former AI worker who led the Harvard study. The racial disparities showed up during November’s midterm election. More than 40 jurisdictions nationwide allowed voters to decide if they wanted data centers in their communities via ballot measures. White residents made up an average of over 83% of the population in these places, compared with less than 5% for Black residents. The racial divide behind the data center boom In Georgia, Mabery and her neighbors want a voice in what happens to their homes, health, and finances. Data centers have increased PM 2.5 air pollution, which Black Americans die from at the highest rate in the U.S. The pollution can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular disease. It is linked to asthma attacks, strokes, dementia, and cancer. Carbon emissions from data centers are also connected to the intensification of climate change. America’s largest data centers are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of climate change-causing carbon dioxide emissions annually — more than emissions from entire countries like Kenya and Guatemala. “These are not emotional concerns. This is where we live. We invested here. We live and bear the impact here,” Augusta resident Charles Zabel said about the data center. “We ought to have a voice in this. So far, we have not had a meaningful voice in this discussion. Representation does not mean protecting a project. Representation means protecting the people who already call this place home.” Researchers at George Washington University Law School joined American University researchers to analyze the placement of more than 5,200 data centers in the U.S., finding the major racial divide in where they’re found. Researchers accounted for income, population density, home values, and proximity to major power lines, and compared neighborhoods within the same state to test whether economics or geography explained the racial disparities in where data centers were located and the benefits the communities received. Even after those adjustments, neighborhoods with larger Black, Latino, and Asian populations remained most likely to have these negative experiences with data centers. “Even when you control for all of that, race stands out,” said Dhanaraj Thakur, director of the Fair Technology Initiative at George Washington University. “I think it’s important to show that this is not some anecdotal thing that’s happening in a few cities like Memphis or elsewhere,” he added. “It’s actually happening across the country.” The difference often comes down to zoning. artigo.texto: Um estudo publicado na Nature Sustainability estimou que 403 centros de dados hiperescaláveis identificados nos Estados Unidos usaram de 68 a 99 TWh de eletricidade entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025 — o equivalente a 1,5% a 2,2% do consumo elétrico total do país. A estimativa foi relatada pela Ars Technica e não corresponde apenas a centros de IA: os pesquisadores não conseguiram separar a computação de IA dos serviços tradicionais oferecidos por esses locais. O resultado é uma estimativa modelada, não a soma de leituras diretas de cada instalação. Terawatt-hora (TWh) mede energia consumida ao longo do tempo; megawatt (MW), usado para indicar a capacidade elétrica dos centros, mede potência. Antes de comparar números de consumo de data centers, confira se eles abrangem o mesmo tipo de instalação e o mesmo período. O que a estimativa de consumo dos data centers dos EUA abrange A conta considera 403 centros hiperescaláveis identificados no país durante um período de um ano, de maio de 2024 a abril de 2025. Além de não isolar a carga de IA, a amostra pode incluir instalações que nem sequer são centros de dados de IA. A seleção começou com 675 instalações candidatas. O estudo reteve 403 após excluir locais sem capacidade elétrica informada ou cujas características de construção, refrigeração e conexão elétrica não puderam ser verificadas. Cada centro incluído tinha, em média, cerca de 40 MW de capacidade elétrica; esse valor não é o consumo anual de energia. Emissões estimadas e fontes de eletricidade A Ars Technica relatou que a geração da eletricidade estimada corresponde a 21 milhões a 31 milhões de toneladas de CO₂, cerca de 0,5% das emissões de CO₂ dos EUA provenientes de combustíveis fósseis. Segundo a reportagem, o cálculo considera a intensidade de emissões da geração elétrica na região da rede que atende cada instalação. A estimativa de emissões não inclui a geração de energia no próprio local, fora da rede. A mistura de geração elétrica atribuída aos centros incluídos foi de 54% de fontes fósseis, principalmente gás natural, 25% de fontes renováveis e 21% de energia nuclear. Quais dados do estudo estão disponíveis ao público A página do estudo informa que os dados de cada instalação são restritos por um acordo de uso. Já as exportações agregadas por estado e por autoridade de equilíbrio da rede, além do código de análise, são públicos. Os registros públicos não incluem identificadores, endereços e coordenadas das instalações nem atributos comercialmente sensíveis. A página do estudo na Nature Sustainability descreve esses limites de acesso.

artigo.texto: US Energy Storage Installations Cross 200 GWh: Report Energy storage installations reached 48.3 GWh in 9M of 2026 November 18, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights The U.S. has surpassed 200 GWh of cumulative energy storage installations with 14.3 GWh of energy storage capacity added in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026, according to the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 released by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. The country’s cumulative storage capacity is expanding as grid operators, and energy buyers increasingly deploy storage to reduce energy costs and strengthen grid reliability. Installations during the first nine months (9M) of 2026 totaled 48.3 GWh. Utility-scale storage accounted for most additions in Q3, with 12.2 GWh deployed. Commercial and industrial storage installations totaled 1.3 GWh, while residential storage additions stood at 746 MWh. The report raised its forecast for cumulative U.S. energy storage deployments by 2030 by 3.7% to 708 GWh across grid-scale and behind-the-meter segments. Texas led utility-scale energy storage deployments through 9M, adding 12.3 GWh. Arizona and California followed, adding 7.7 GWh and 6.8 GWh, respectively. Eleven states surpassed their previous year’s annual energy storage installation records. These were Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois. According to a recent SEIA analysis, the rapid deployment of solar and energy storage contributed to a 42% decline in average wholesale electricity prices in Texas and a 51% decline in California between summer 2021 and summer 2026. Pete Tillotson, Senior Analyst at Benchmark Minerals, noted that states are moving from targets to centralized procurements. Across utility mandates and bulk capacity contracts, energy storage pipelines are growing because of both investment appetite and flexibility requirements. Manufacturing Capacity Battery manufacturing capacity in the U.S. also expanded during the period. A new battery cell manufacturing facility commenced operations in Tennessee in July, followed by another facility in Indiana in October. These additions brought the country’s total battery cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, representing a 50% increase. SEIA also called on the U.S. Congress to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which it said would accelerate energy storage deployment, reduce project costs, and expand access to lower cost and reliable electricity. The U.S. added 4.7 GW/17.2 GWh of utility-scale battery energy storage systems in Q2 2026, taking cumulative operational capacity past the 50 GW milestone, according to the American Clean Power Association. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, more than 16% of the utility-scale solar capacity added in the U.S. through September 2026 was co-located with operational battery storage, compared to just 2% in 2017.

The electric SUV is establishing its presence across Asia-Pacific, Europe and the Middle East, marking another addition to BYD's growing global passenger vehicle portfolio. Introduced internationally in 2026, the ATTO 3 EVO is marketed in Asia-Pacific countries including Singapore, Australia and New Zealand. Its presence also extends across the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Austria, Switzerland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Poland and the Czech Republic, as well as Israel. The 100 kW front-wheel-drive configuration is powered by a permanent magnet synchronous motor producing 310 Nm of torque. BYD's 60.48 kWh Blade Battery supports a WLTP-rated driving range of up to 420 kilometres on a single charge. DC fast charging of up to 105 kW adds flexibility for longer journeys and everyday use. The vehicle has a distinct exterior design, with revised front bodywork and contemporary detailing. Inside, an 8.8-inch digital instrument display presents driving information, while the steering-column-mounted gear selector creates a cleaner centre-console arrangement and a more open cabin. Digital features include a 15.6-inch intelligent infotainment touchscreen, smartphone connectivity, wireless charging and digital key functionality. An eight-speaker Dirac HD sound system further contributes to the cabin experience, bringing entertainment and connected functions together in an accessible layout. Safety technologies include Automatic Emergency Braking, Adaptive Cruise Control, Blind Spot Detection, Lane Keeping Assist and Rear Cross Traffic Alert. A 360-degree camera supports visibility when parking and manoeuvring. Multiple airbags, Electronic Stability Control and ISOFIX child-seat anchorages provide additional occupant protection. Designed for everyday practicality, the five-seat SUV offers luggage capacity expandable to 1,340 litres when the rear seats are folded. Ventilated front seats, electrically adjustable seating and a panoramic sunroof add comfort for drivers and passengers. Through its combination of electric performance, charging capability, intelligent safety and convenience features, the ATTO 3 EVO broadens BYD's international electric SUV offering. The 100 kW model is one configuration within the wider international range. Its combination of motor output, battery capacity and charging capability is intended to support driving requirements, while the SUV format provides space and flexibility for everyday use and travel.

artigo.texto: Restrições de chips dos EUA ao Brasil afetam data centers O governo dos Estados Unidos, sob a administração de Donald Trump, incluiu o Brasil em uma lista de países que passam a ter restrições para importar chips avançados destinados a data centers. A medida, anunciada pelo Departamento de Comércio, vale mesmo quando os semicondutores são fabricados fora da jurisdição americana. A partir desta segunda-feira (16), fornecedores precisarão de autorização do governo americano para enviar os processadores a empresas brasileiras, com pedidos analisados caso a caso. Além do Brasil, a relação inclui Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia. Segundo a norma, esses países apresentam risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal dos chips para China ou Macau — alvos de embargos junto com Rússia, Irã, Coreia do Norte, Síria e Cuba. O objetivo é evitar que empresas chinesas usem sedes no exterior para treinar modelos de inteligência artificial com uso de chips restritos a Pequim. Risco de desvio para China Os territórios classificados como elevado risco de desvio, assim como o Brasil, abrigam grandes complexos de processamento de dados ligados a big techs orientais, como ByteDance (dona do TikTok), Tencent (dona do WeChat), Alibaba e Huawei. A norma norte-americana exige que empresas dos cinco países solicitem licenças de exportação dos EUA para os chips mais avançados, em um esforço para reduzir o contrabando desses produtos. “A regra foi elaborada para garantir que as restrições existentes ao acesso a tecnologia norte-americana sensível não possam ser contornadas por meio de acordos de computação remota envolvendo data centers em países terceiros”, afirmou o Departamento de Comércio em comunicado. A medida busca fechar brechas que permitiam o uso indireto de tecnologia americana por entidades sob embargo. Prazos e isenções previstos Os produtos já enviados estão isentos das novas normas por 30 dias. Os fornecedores que prestam volume relevante de serviços de computação avançada para o grupo sob embargo têm 90 dias para obter uma licença junto ao Escritório de Indústria e Segurança do Departamento de Comércio. As novas restrições não se aplicarão a sistemas usados por varejistas online e empresas de mídia social, que, segundo o departamento, não representam a mesma ameaça à segurança nacional. Em janeiro de 2025, nos últimos dias do governo Joe Biden, os Estados Unidos já haviam incluído o Brasil em um grupo intermediário de países com acesso limitado a chips avançados de inteligência artificial. A classificação previa cotas para a importação desses componentes. A nova regra amplia o controle, passando de cotas para licenciamento individual. Impacto para o setor de tecnologia A exigência de licenças caso a caso pode afetar a expansão de data centers no Brasil, especialmente aqueles que dependem de chips de última geração para processamento de inteligência artificial. Empresas brasileiras que operam grandes infraestruturas de nuvem e serviços de IA podem enfrentar atrasos e custos adicionais para obter os componentes necessários. O Departamento de Comércio não detalhou os critérios exatos para aprovação das licenças. Para o comércio e a indústria do interior paulista, a medida pode ter efeitos indiretos, uma vez que a digitalização de processos e o uso de serviços em nuvem dependem de data centers eficientes. A disponibilidade limitada de chips avançados pode impactar a oferta de serviços de computação em nuvem no país, com possíveis reflexos em custos para empresas de todos os portes. A fonte não detalhou estimativas de impacto econômico. A decisão americana reforça a tendência de controle tecnológico em um cenário de disputa geopolítica. O Brasil, como destino de investimentos em data centers, terá de se adaptar às novas exigências para manter o fluxo de importação de semicondutores avançados. A medida pode estimular o desenvolvimento de alternativas locais ou a busca por fornecedores de outros países, mas a fonte não detalhou planos nesse sentido. Perguntas Frequentes Por que os EUA incluíram o Brasil na lista de países com restrições para comprar chips para data centers? O Brasil foi incluído porque, segundo a norma, apresenta risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal desses chips para China ou Macau, que são alvos de embargos. Quais outros países estão na lista de restrições dos EUA para compra de chips para data centers? Além do Brasil, a lista inclui Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia. O que os fornecedores precisam fazer para enviar chips avançados para o Brasil a partir de 16 de junho? A partir de 16 de junho, os fornecedores precisarão de autorização do governo americano para enviar processadores avançados a empresas brasileiras, com pedidos analisados caso a caso.

artigo.texto: Berea unanimously passes data center moratorium Year-long measure stops city from accepting, processing or approving data center applications and permits BEREA, Ky. (WKYT) - The city of Berea adopted a year-long data center moratorium by unanimous vote Tuesday night, becoming the latest municipality in Kentucky to adopt some form of data center moratorium. The decision gives the city another year to decide the permanent future of data centers. What the moratorium does During the moratorium, the city will not accept, process or approve data center applications or permits. Public comments before the vote The unanimous vote came after a handful of public comments in which residents raised concerns about draws on resources such as water and power. Council member comments Council member Katie Startzman was one of the driving forces behind the legislation. “I haven’t heard from one person who is in favor of data centers unless they were someone who was a lobbyist for the industry. So I think it’s pretty clear where people stand,” Startzman said. She has seen what surrounding cities and towns have done with their moratoriums and believes they are a tool to more closely study the issue before making a decision that affects residents. She said the entire council was in agreement on that. “This was not something that was challenging for us to come to consensus on. I think we all pretty immediately agreed that data centers have no place in Berea,” Startzman said. Advocate reaction Katie Dapkus has been advocating against data centers across central Kentucky. She is optimistic seeing other cities adopt similar moratoriums. “I think it’s sort of a domino effect. All of our elected officials are being lobbied hard, but the people were sort of left in the lurch, and I think people are collectively waking up to what’s happening and demanding more from our leadership,” Dapkus said. What’s next One sitting council member said he hopes the next council is bold enough to enact a complete ban if that is what Berea residents want to see. The future of data centers in the city has yet to be determined. Other communities with regulations Berea joined nearby towns and cities, including London, Nicholasville, Versailles and Winchester, that have some form of data center regulations in place. Woodford County is the only county in the area to enact a total ban. Copyright 2026 WKYT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Power grids in Texas and eastern Australia can soon receive a major boost in energy storage capacity as operators work to manage fluctuations in solar generation. To bridge this gap, global renewable developer X-ELIO is deploying five utility-scale battery installations across both regions. Four of the facilities will be built in Texas, where grid operators face their tightest supply margins during evening hours. “In both markets, the systems will shift midday solar output into the evening peak—addressing Texas’s tightest supply hours after sunset and supporting coal retirement goals in New South Wales,” said the company in a press release. The fifth installation will be constructed in New South Wales, Australia, where stored renewable energy is needed to support regional coal retirement goals. Balancing grid supply and demand By capturing excess midday solar output and releasing it during peak demand, the systems will provide dispatchable electricity. This capability helps grid operators balance supply and demand in real time. As a result, the batteries will strengthen overall network reliability and reduce the need for fossil-fuel peaking power plants. To build the five sites, X-ELIO has signed supply agreements with e-STORAGE, the energy storage solutions division of Canadian Solar. The combined capacity of the projects totals 590 MW / 1.43 GWh DC. Canadian Solar announced the multi-region deals at one of North America’s largest clean energy industry events. More from Energy See All All five installations will utilize e-STORAGE’s SolBank 3.0 technology. The units do not rely solely on external suppliers for core components. Instead, they are constructed using battery cells manufactured directly at Canadian Solar’s own facilities. Alongside the battery enclosures, e-STORAGE is supplying the power conversion systems and plant controls needed to connect the units to local transmission networks. These components are designed in a smart way. They can work together to regulate power output and maintain grid stability during rapid shifts in demand. Equipment shipments currently underway Deployment is already in its early logistical stages, with equipment shipments currently underway. The five projects are scheduled to enter commercial operation across a two-year window in 2027 and 2028. Beyond delivering the physical hardware, e-STORAGE will remain involved in the day-to-day performance of the assets. Each contract includes a 22-year long-term service agreement (LTSA). These agreements lock in ongoing maintenance and operational support across the full lifespan of the batteries. Jeff Roy, President of e-STORAGE, noted that the deal marks the beginning of a global partnership with X-ELIO. He described the developer as a sector leader with a strong twenty-year track record in renewable energy. “Having them place their trust in e-STORAGE’s products and team for the next 22 years is a positive reflection of our ability to successfully deliver projects across multiple regions with varying complexities,” concluded Roy.

artigo.texto: A Assembleia Legislativa do Paraná (Alep) aprovou na terça, 17 de novembro, o Projeto de Lei 55/2026, que cria o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (PRODATAPR). A proposta autoriza o governo estadual a conceder benefícios fiscais a empreendimentos de infraestrutura digital. O ponto em aberto para a sociedade é o custo desses incentivos e quais contrapartidas serão exigidas das empresas. Assinam a proposta Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (Progressistas) e Pedro Paulo Bazana (PSD). Segundo a Assembleia, o objetivo é atrair investimentos privados, estimular empregos especializados e aproveitar a oferta paranaense de energia renovável e conectividade. Os centros de dados processam e armazenam informações usadas por serviços digitais, instituições financeiras e aplicações de inteligência artificial. A expansão dessa infraestrutura pode demandar eletricidade e sistemas de refrigeração, com diferentes consumos de água conforme a tecnologia adotada. Por isso, a simples promessa de investimentos não substitui a avaliação do impacto ambiental e fiscal de cada projeto. O texto divulgado pela Alep incentiva fontes renováveis, aproveitamento do biometano, uso racional da água, tecnologias sustentáveis de resfriamento e parcerias com universidades e centros de pesquisa. Diretrizes, porém, não são equivalentes à divulgação de metas mensuráveis, fiscalização, empregos efetivamente contratados ou valores de renúncia tributária. O debate relevante, portanto, é se eventuais benefícios serão vinculados a investimentos verificáveis, formação profissional, transparência das renúncias e critérios públicos de consumo energético e hídrico. Esses parâmetros precisam ser examinados nos atos que regulamentarem o programa e nas concessões concretas de incentivos. A informação disponível confirma a aprovação legislativa relatada pela Assembleia, mas não comprova a sanção da proposta nem a concessão de qualquer benefício a uma empresa específica. artigo.texto: Madison County presents first draft of ordinance to regulate data centers Madison County has begun sharing a draft of a zoning ordinance that would regulate data centers in the county. As IPR’s Thomas Ouellette reports, that draft includes a ban of so-called “hyperscale” projects. Audio Transcript The ordinance would outright ban any facility that’s more than 40 acres in size. It also heavily regulates smaller data centers. Bryan Stumpf, with the engineering firm hired by the county, says banning all data centers is difficult because they currently exist throughout the county. “People aren’t upset about the data centers that are like at the hospital and the school system computers,” he said. “People don’t have an issue with that it’s the hyperscale data centers that have that excessive draw on electricity and water and other concerns that way.” Read More: Delaware County residents want a data center moratorium Under the drafted ordinance, commercial data centers would be capped at that 40 acre size with a required power need of no more than 20 megawatts. It would need to provide written guarantees from a power company that it can handle the facility’s power needs. It would also be required to make a water management plan that identifies sufficient water supply sources and minimizes consumption. Several rounds of water monitoring are also required through both the pre- and post-construction process with additional sampling being done every six months while the facility is operational. The ordinance also provides for environmental protection. No more than 10 percent of any data center can be located on designated prime farmland. If the property has not been used for 12 consecutive months, all data center components must be restored for reuse or removed by the owner within one year. Read More: Over half of Indiana counties now restrict data centers Regulation for energy storage systems is also included in the drafted ordinance. The draft is still being updated. Madison County passed a one-year moratorium on data center projects in August for time to write the regulations. Thomas Ouellette is our reporter and producer. Contact him at thomas.ouellette@bsu.edu.

artigo.texto: Patrocinado por: Jensen Huang, fundador da Nvidia, no evento da empresa que antecedeu a CES 2026, em Las Vegas. Foto de arquivo (AFP/AFP) Repórter de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 17 de novembro de 2026 às 18h44. Em meio às incertezas após a saída de Jensen Huang, a Nvidia divulgou seu primeiro balanço sem o fundador no comando. Os embarques do sistema Vera Rubin NVL72 começaram no trimestre encerrado em 25 de outubro de 2026, e a receita de data centers atingiu US$ 107,6 bilhões, alta de 110% em um ano. A receita total foi de US$ 115,8 bilhões e a empresa prevê US$ 130 bilhões para o próximo trimestre. Em meio às incertezas que permeiam o futuro da Nvidia desde a saída de Jensen Huang, a empresa entregou números que mostram que a demanda por sua infraestrutura de inteligência artificial segue firme. A estreia do Vera Rubin ajudou a companhia a mais que dobrar a receita de data centers no trimestre encerrado em 25 de outubro. A divisão faturou US$ 107,6 bilhões, alta de 110% em um ano, segundo o balanço divulgado nesta terça-feira, 17. O resultado era aguardado como um teste. É o primeiro balanço desde que o fundador deixou o comando, em uma semana em que a Nvidia chegou a perder cerca de US$ 600 bilhões em valor de mercado. A diretora financeira Colette Kress acumula a cadeira de CEO interina, e coube a ela apresentar os números a investidores que ainda tentam entender quem vai definir a estratégia da maior fornecedora de chips de IA do mundo. A receita total foi de US$ 115,8 bilhões, alta de 103% em um ano, acima do teto de cerca de US$ 110,2 bilhões projetado pela própria empresa em agosto. O lucro líquido subiu 105%, para US$ 65,3 bilhões. Os data centers responderam por mais de 90% do faturamento, o que reforça a dependência da Nvidia em relação aos gastos de big techs e laboratórios de IA com infraestrutura. A Nvidia disse que o Vera Rubin NVL72 teve o aumento de produção mais rápido de sua história. O sistema reúne 72 unidades de processamento gráfico Rubin e 36 processadores Vera em um único rack, para treinar e rodar modelos de inteligência artificial. O perfil Wall St Engine afirmou no X que o Vera Rubin gerou quase US$ 20 bilhões em receita no trimestre de estreia. O comunicado de resultados confirma o início dos embarques, mas não discrimina esse valor. Em agosto, Kress estimava que a plataforma responderia por cerca de 20% da receita de data centers no trimestre, mas a estimativa não equivale ao valor realizado. Na nota financeira, a Nvidia também atribui o avanço da divisão às vendas de processadores Vera separados e ao crescimento do Blackwell Ultra, da geração anterior. Ou seja, a nova plataforma chega sem canibalizar, por ora, a demanda pelos chips que ainda estão nas linhas de montagem dos clientes. A troca de geração tem custo. A margem bruta contábil ficou em 74,8%, ante 75% no trimestre anterior. Na nota a investidores, a empresa atribuiu a queda de 0,2 ponto percentual à fase inicial de produção do Rubin, período em que o volume ainda não compensa os gastos de fabricação. Para o quarto trimestre fiscal, a Nvidia prevê receita de US$ 130 bilhões, com margem de variação de 3% para mais ou para menos. A projeção cobre um trimestre com uma semana a mais e não inclui receita de computação para data centers na China. A empresa espera margem bruta entre 71% e 72%. A previsão de margem abaixo do patamar atual indica que a empresa espera mais pressão de custos à medida que o Rubin ganha escala. Para o mercado, os próximos meses vão mostrar se a Nvidia consegue sustentar esse ritmo sem Huang e quem será escolhido para sucedê-lo de forma definitiva. É a geração de sistemas da Nvidia para treinar e rodar modelos de inteligência artificial. O NVL72 reúne 72 unidades de processamento gráfico Rubin e 36 processadores Vera em um rack. A Nvidia registrou receita de US$ 115,8 bilhões no trimestre encerrado em 25 de outubro de 2026. Os data centers responderam por US$ 107,6 bilhões. Glossário Vera Rubin Geração de sistemas da Nvidia para treinar e rodar modelos de inteligência artificial. O NVL72 combina 72 unidades gráficas Rubin com 36 processadores Vera. Data centers Instalações que abrigam servidores, redes e sistemas de armazenamento. São usadas, entre outras aplicações, para treinar e rodar modelos de inteligência artificial. Blackwell Ultra Geração anterior de chips de IA da Nvidia, que segue em produção e ajudou a impulsionar a receita de data centers ao lado do Vera Rubin.

artigo.texto: Philippines joins global carbon trade coalition The Philippines has joined an 18-country coalition seeking to expand high-integrity carbon credit markets, as governments at the COP31 climate talks ongoing at Antalya, Turkey, pushed for policies to attract more private financing for climate action. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) said the country joined The Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets alongside Colombia, Egypt and Ireland, bringing the group's membership to 18. Mobilizing climate finance Environment Secretary Juan Miguel T. Cuna said the Philippines would endorse the Antalya Statement as part of its efforts to mobilize climate finance and develop a national carbon market framework. “As we implement Executive Order (EO) 127 and develop our national carbon market framework, we recognize that private investment must complement public finance to accelerate climate action and sustainable development,” Cuna said. “Government leadership is essential to provide the policy certainty, transparency, and integrity that give corporate buyers the confidence to invest in credible climate solutions,” he added. EO 127 was issued on 13 October 2026, directing the DENR to establish a national carbon market policy framework for voluntary markets even as its seeks to mobilize climate finance, attract green investments, and speed up progress toward national greenhouse gas reduction targets Ministers convened in Antalya The coalition, with support from the Türkiye COP31 Presidency, convened ministers in Antalya on 16 November to discuss policies that could stimulate demand for carbon credits and encourage private investment. The meeting followed the release of the Antalya Statement, which was backed by 17 countries, and a Policy Playbook outlining measures governments can adopt to develop carbon credit markets. Colombia, Ghana and Peru signed the statement, while Colombia and the Philippines joined the coalition. UN Framework Convention on Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said high-integrity carbon markets could help limit the extent and duration of global warming beyond the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold. Race against time “We are in a race against time to keep the overshoot of the 1.5C limit as small and as short as possible... High-integrity carbon markets can play a critical role and so can this Coalition,” he said. The initiative seeks to help mobilize private financing to address a $1.3-trillion climate finance gap. Carbon credit markets can channel additional private funds toward climate programs, complementing public financing and supporting countries' climate and development goals. Policy Playbook welcomed Three advance market commitment groups — Action for a Resilient Climate Coalition, Emergent and Kinetic Coalition — welcomed the Policy Playbook and urged governments to implement its proposed policy measures. The coalition also released a compendium of policy actions taken since COP30. These include planned carbon market guidance in the United Kingdom, an expanded carbon certification scheme in France, Canada's support for carbon removal credits and new carbon market regulations in Zambia.

artigo.texto: Minneapolis data center ordinance vetoed by mayor MINNEAPOLIS (FOX 9) - The Minneapolis mayor vetoed a data center ordinance that was passed by the city council last week, saying that last-minute changes to the ordinance would result in "a de facto ban" on data centers in the city. Data center ordinance vetoed by Minneapolis mayor What they're saying: Mayor Frey said he objects to the council's proposed changes to primary zoning and requiring overlay districts for each proposed data center site. He also said "a strong commercial tax break" is needed to support the "robust social programs to support residents." "We have an opportunity to provide an important regulatory framework, embrace economic progress, and alleviate a tax burden for our residents," Mayor Frey said. "We should do that." Dig deeper: Downtown Council CEO Adam Duininck called for a veto of the ordinance earlier this week, citing the sale of the Sleep Number building for $235 million, eight times its previous value of about $30 million. Duininck credited the AI data center for that increase in value. "We want to try to make things easier for people to invest money in the city, it should be a clear process, a clear timeline," said Duininck. Minneapolis data center ordinance The other side: The Minneapolis City Council passed the data center ordinance 7-6. One of the compromises that was made after the full ban failed to pass was the overlay district. This measure means that any new data centers would need to be approved by the council, and that they would only be added to existing buildings instead of having new ones built. The ordinance also required a mandatory disclosure of energy, water and generator use, and that data centers not be the primary use of the building. The ordinance also barred data centers from the first or second floor, called for a sound attenuation plan and required a decommissioning plan if a site stops operating. Data centers larger than 50,000 square feet would also have had to enter an Xcel Energy program and pay a premium for renewable energy credits, according to Chowdhury. The Source: This story uses information shared in a letter from Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey and previous FOX 9 reporting.

artigo.texto: What if a drone's legs could do more than support its weight—and also store energy? Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have developed a structural battery electrode that remains stable even when fitted into curved structures, such as drone legs. By making it possible to integrate energy storage into a device's frame, the technology could help make drones and robots lighter and extend their operating times. On November 18, KAIST (President Choongsik Bae) announced that a research team led by Professor Il-Kwon Oh of the Department of Mechanical Engineering had developed a monolithically integrated lithium-sulfur (Li-S) battery cathode by growing nickel cobalt selenide (NiCo₂Se₄) nanowires directly on woven carbon cloth. Made from interwoven carbon fibers, the carbon cloth serves as a mechanical robust, flexible, and electrically conductive foundation for the electrode. By growing ultrafine nanowires directly on its surface, the researchers created an electrode that combines mechanical robustness with reliable electrical conductivity. For drones and robots, maximizing energy storage while minimizing weight and space is a major engineering challenge. Conventional designs use separate batteries and structural frames, limiting opportunities to reduce overall weight and volume. Structural batteries offer a promising alternative by allowing components to both support mechanical loads and store energy. In a drone, for example, the landing legs could serve as structural supports while also functioning as part of the energy storage system. Turning this concept into a practical technology requires batteries that can conform to different component shapes. Drone legs and robotic frames often feature curved surfaces and hollow, tubular structures, making conventional flat battery designs difficult to integrate. The KAIST team therefore focused on developing an electrode suitable for installation within these non-planar structures. The researchers selected lithium-sulfur batteries, which use sulfur as the cathode material and offer the potential for high energy storage capacity at a relatively low weight. The cathode is one of a battery's two electrodes and plays a central role in the electrochemical reactions involved in charging and discharging. Despite their advantages, lithium-sulfur batteries face several challenges. Sulfur has poor electrical conductivity, and intermediate compounds known as lithium polysulfides can dissolve and migrate away from the electrode during operation. This phenomenon can reduce battery performance by disrupting the electrochemical reactions needed for efficient energy storage. Conventional electrode fabrication methods present an additional challenge. Active materials are typically applied to a conductive substrate as a coating, which can detach under repeated bending or mechanical stress. Such detachment can disrupt electrical pathways and compromise electrode performance. To overcome these limitations, the team grew nickel cobalt selenide nanowires directly on the carbon fiber surfaces. Nanowires are extremely thin, wire-like structures measured on the nanometer scale, with one nanometer equal to one billionth of a meter. Nickel cobalt selenide, a compound containing nickel, cobalt, and selenium, helps facilitate sulfur-related electrochemical reactions while also helping to capture lithium polysulfides and limit their migration. This approach creates a tightly integrated structure in which the nanowires are firmly anchored to the carbon fibers rather than simply deposited as a separate coating. The direct connection helps maintain continuous electrical pathways, even when the electrode is bent. The electrode demonstrated excellent mechanical durability in bending tests. After 1,000 bending cycles at a radius of just 2.5 mm, the nanowires remained firmly attached to the carbon fiber surfaces, with no visible damage or structural collapse. The results demonstrate the electrode's ability to maintain its structural integrity under repeated bending, an important requirement for integration into tightly curved spaces. The researchers then incorporated the electrode into a lithium-sulfur pouch cell to evaluate its feasibility for integration into various non-planar structures. They integrated the cell into oval and square structures, as well as a drone-leg component, and successfully powered a light-emitting diode (LED). These demonstrations confirmed that the battery could supply electricity when integrated into structures with different geometries. To further evaluate as a structural battery, the team also evaluated battery performance under external mechanical loads. When installed inside a cylindrical structure, the battery retained 99.8% of its initial voltage even under a load sufficient to fracture the surrounding structural frame. In a separate loading test, an LED powered by the battery remained illuminated without interruption or flickering. The study represents an important step toward extending structural battery technology beyond the flat configurations that have dominated previous research. By demonstrating a structural battery electrode capable of operating within curved and hollow structures, the researchers have opened up new possibilities for integrating energy storage into components with complex geometries. Looking ahead, the technology could be combined with load-bearing composite materials to create drone legs and robotic frames that provide both structural support and energy storage. Such composites typically combine materials such as carbon fibers and resins to achieve high strength at low weight. Integrating batteries into these components could make more efficient use of the limited weight and space available in drones and robots. However, further research will be needed to determine how much weight could be saved and how significantly flight times or operating durations could be extended in practical appli

artigo.texto: Expansão de data centers na UE enfrenta resistência local A União Europeia quer triplicar sua capacidade de data centers nos próximos cinco a sete anos, como parte de um esforço para reduzir a dependência das grandes empresas de tecnologia dos EUA e construir capacidades próprias de IA na Europa, segundo a Euronews. Na Irlanda, Polônia, Dinamarca, Finlândia, Espanha, Países Baixos, França e Reino Unido, moradores e ativistas ambientais foram às ruas para exigir a paralização do desenvolvimento de novos projetos. Owen Espley, coordenador do Stop Dirty Data Centres.eu, disse ao Euronews Verify que os críticos se preocupam com os efeitos sobre a terra e a água, com as necessidades substanciais de energia dos data centers e com a possibilidade de que esse consumo de energia desvie o fornecimento da moradia. Michael Winterson, secretário-geral da European Data Centre Association, também participou do programa. Metas climáticas e custos de energia A UE se comprometeu a se tornar o primeiro continente climaticamente neutro do mundo até 2050. Os ministros da UE mantêm seu compromisso com a transição verde apesar da disparada dos preços da energia e das preocupações com o fornecimento. No entanto, os eleitores querem energia mais barata agora, enquanto muitas medidas destinadas a proporcioná-la levarão muito mais tempo para compensar. Os resultados de pesquisas citados no episódio indicam que 76% das pessoas nos Países Baixos, 72% na França e 68% na Alemanha duvidam que seu país faça progressos significativos rumo ao net zero. Nos Países Baixos, 54% afirmam que as políticas ambientais deixaram as pessoas comuns em situação pior. Ines Pereira, do Euronews Verify, explorou esse equilíbrio político com Sven Haremling, chefe de clima da CAN Europe. Haremling sugeriu que as pessoas gostam de ouvir a verdade sobre o que precisa mudar, desde que alguém trabalhe com elas em soluções e as regulamentações governamentais mudem de acordo. O Euronews Verify é transmitido ao vivo na TV, no site da Euronews e em plataformas digitais todos os dias úteis às 18h40, no horário de Bruxelas, com duração de pouco menos de 11 minutos.

artigo.texto: Effingham County commissioners approve OpenAI data center site plan despite opposition Effingham County commissioners approved the site plan for Project Camellia, an OpenAI data center, after a three-hour meeting where residents voiced concerns about its impact on the community. Effingham County commissioners approve OpenAI data center site plan despite opposition Effingham County commissioners approved the site plan for Project Camellia, an OpenAI data center, after a three-hour meeting where residents voiced concerns about its impact on the community. Effingham County commissioners approved the site plan for Project Camellia, a proposed OpenAI data center development along Effingham Parkway and Gateway Parkway, during a three-hour meeting Tuesday night. After the vote, many opponents of the data center walked out of the room, upset that they were not allowed to speak during the site plan discussion. District 2 Commissioner Roger Burdette explained that the item was not a public hearing. “Well, a site plan like this, we’ve already been over the same thing several different times. It’s not like a public hearing. Different things are public hearings, some things aren’t. This is one of those things that just aren’t,” Burdette said. The vote moves Project Camellia forward despite opposition from residents, some of whom held signs and voiced concerns about the development’s impact on the community. “This is a project on 1,400 acres. And you’re going to give us 400 jobs on that amount of space for this amount of money for all these negatives? It just doesn’t make sense to me,” Zach Springer, an opponent of the project, said. One woman in the audience expressed frustration, saying, “Shame on all of you. This is our community. You cannot compare this data center to any other data center, because it’s the biggest in the world. They don’t know how loud it’s gonna be.” Commissioners had previously delayed the vote to address concerns, including noise protections for nearby neighborhoods and whether the developer would commit to a proposed 20-foot earthen berm. Burdette said he is satisfied with the developer’s commitments. “They went beyond. We have a lot of great standards in place. It was important for me to hear that I’m going to get the extra buffer, I’m going to get the extra berm, I’m going to protect the residents in any way possible. Another great point they brought up was double sizing the ponds and make sure we take care of the water,” Burdette said. In addition to approving the site plan, commissioners tabled a decision on a possible moratorium for future data center developments until Jan. 19, citing residents’ concerns about the wording of the proposal.

artigo.texto: Reno, Nev. (Nov. 18, 2026) – With the rapid proliferation of the digital realm and a growing artificial intelligence sector, data centers are spreading across the world. Nevada is one of the fastest-growing data center regions in the U.S. and globally due to abundant land, cost-competitive energy, and an attractive tax and regulatory environment. This explosive growth offers both opportunities and challenges due to the water and electricity required to operate these centers. DRI scientists Erik Henzl and Sean McKenna produced a comprehensive report: Data Center Water and Electricity Consumption in Nevada to inform the public and policy makers about this rapidly growing sector of the state's economy. First published in early 2026, an updated appendix has been added to the report as of Nov. 18, 2026. The new appendix uses new information from NV Energy's 2026 Integrated Resource Plan to project the water and electricity needed to support future data center growth through 2036. According to Data Center Map , more than 75 data centers are currently in operation, under construction, or planned in Nevada. "Nevada has the potential to be a central player in the increasingly digital world, but there are challenges that must be resolved to ensure that other stakeholders and priorities are balanced with the increasing demands of rapid data center expansion," said report author Sean McKenna, Senior Program Developer and Hydrologist at DRI. The report offers estimates of water and electricity use that are calculated based on the size of proposed and under-construction data centers in the state and average resource use for existing and new technologies. The uncertainty around exact water and power usage remains a challenge for understanding their impact. Because the information is not available, the report does not include the resource use of Nevada's existing data centers. Nevada's data center market has grown rapidly over just two years. Between 2024 and 2026, there has been a 180% increase in data center capacity requests and a 70% increase in data center load growth across the state. Data centers currently comprise just 5% of NV Energy's sales, but this number is expected to rise to 64% by 2046. To put the state's data center growth in context, that is roughly equivalent to the state's net electricity generation in 2024, or the energy demand of 5 million homes. It is also nearly double the total energy required to power all electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles in the nation in 2025. The water needed to support these new data centers is also examined, with estimates provided for both on-site, direct water use and the water required for their energy production. On-site water use is highly dependent on the cooling technology being used by each data center, and this information is not made available by the owners and operators. The report provides estimates based on available and emerging cooling technologies and their water efficiency. Despite the rapid growth of data centers in the state, advancements in cooling technologies result in a lower range of estimated direct water use than was provided in the initial report. However, the estimated water needed for electricity generation increases from the initial report, as driven by the large increase in the power required for new data centers. Direct water use for new data centers in the state by 2036 is estimated at approximately 12,770 acre feet, or 4 billion gallons, per year. The full range for this estimate is between 4,257 and 63,850 acre feet/year (between 1.4 and 20 billion gallons/year). By 2036, DRI's estimate for the annual indirect water demand linked to Nevada's new data center power requirements is approximately 21,283 acre feet/year (roughly 7 billion gallons). This is roughly equivalent to the annual water use of 64,000 American households. To read the full report, visit https://www.dri.edu/datacenters/. To view the updated Storymap with highlights from the report, as well as additional context, maps, and visuals to facilitate understanding of the information produced by DRI's Communications Team, visit Data Centers in Nevada . ------------- Can't get enough DRI science in your life? Support DRI with a donation , attend one of our events, or sign up for our monthly newsletter . More information: The full report with the updated appendix is available at https://www.dri.edu/datacenters/ To see highlights from the report from DRI's Communications Team, view the Storymap: Data Centers in Nevada Study authors include: Erik Henzl and Sean McKenna About DRI We are Nevada's scientific research institute, founded in 1959 to empower experts to focus on science that matters. We work with communities across the state — and the world — to address their most pressing scientific questions. We're proud that our scientists continuously produce solutions that better human and environmental health. Scientists at DRI are encouraged to follow their research interests across the traditional boundaries of scientific fields, collaborating across DRI and with scientists worldwide. All faculty support their own research through grants, bringing in over $6 to the Nevada economy for every $1 of state funds received. With more than 600 scientists, engineers, students, and staff across our Reno and Las Vegas campuses, we conducted more than $59 million in sponsored research focused on improving peoples' lives in 2025 alone.

artigo.texto: EQT to Acquire Energy Storage Developer Flatiron Energy The acquisition will give EQT ownership of Flatiron’s energy storage portfolio across New England, New York, and the Mid-Atlantic November 19, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights EQT Transition Infrastructure, an investment strategy of EQT focused on businesses supporting the transition to a decarbonized and more resource-efficient economy, has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire utility-scale energy storage developer Flatiron Energy from Hull Street Energy. Simpson Thacher & Bartlett acted as legal counsel to EQT, while Santander served as its financial adviser. Kirkland & Ellis acted as legal counsel to Flatiron, and Guggenheim Securities served as the company’s financial adviser. Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath acted as legal counsel to Hull Street Energy. The transaction remains subject to customary conditions and approvals and is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. Financial terms were not disclosed. Founded in 2021, Flatiron develops, builds, owns, and operates utility-scale energy storage projects across New England, New York, and the Mid-Atlantic power markets. Hull Street Energy initially invested in Flatiron in 2022. Since then, Flatiron has expanded its portfolio nearly tenfold to 24 GWh of capacity. The company has also secured 6 GWh of long-term contracts and has 2 GWh of battery storage projects under construction. Following the acquisition, EQT plans to support Flatiron in delivering its contracted projects and expanding into additional markets. EQT also plans to invest in the company’s team and capabilities. Rob Brink, Chief Executive Officer, Flatiron Energy, said, “We started Flatiron with the mission to bring reliable energy where it’s needed most, in the communities that rely on it every day. EQT is an exceptional firm with a strong track record of scaling platforms in the energy transition, and we couldn’t be more excited to partner with them on our next stage of growth. My co-founders and I are incredibly grateful to HSE, whose unwavering support and belief in our strategy brought us to this point.” The acquisition will be made through EQT Transition Infrastructure, a strategy focused on businesses supporting the transition to a decarbonized and more resource-efficient economy. EQT has previously invested in battery storage companies, including Statera Energy in the United Kingdom and Ju:niz Energy in Germany. Corporate M&A activity in the energy storage sector increased 35% YoY, with 27 transactions announced in 9M 2026, up from 20 in the same period in 2025, according to Mercom’s recently released 9M 2026 Funding and M&A for Energy Storage report. In July, Zenobē, an owner and operator of grid-scale battery storage, has acquired Bavaria-based battery energy storage developer sdp energie. According to Zenobē, this acquisition is expected to gain access to a 1.75 GW pipeline of transmission-connected battery storage projects across six sites in Germany
