artigo.texto: A IA precisa de mais do que algoritmos: Jean Pierre Lessa e Santos Ferreira explica o papel dos datacenters AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 18 de novembro de 2026 Por trás de cada resposta de um modelo existem prédios de servidores, energia e refrigeração que definem custo e velocidade. Para um CTO como Jean Pierre Lessa e Santos Ferreira, o tema é diário e a expressão “nuvem” cria uma imagem confortável e enganosa: a computação em nuvem acontece em galpões reais, com servidores, cabos, geradores e sistemas de refrigeração. Em um contexto de inteligência artificial, a natureza física do processamento de dados retornou ao epicentro do debate, uma vez que a formação e operação de modelos demanda um aumento substancial na demanda por energia e por equipamentos especializados. A compreensão do funcionamento dessa infraestrutura é fundamental para auxiliar os gestores na tomada de decisões mais precisas e eficazes em relação a custos, desempenho e riscos. Nesse contexto, o conceito de migração para a nuvem, o impacto das GPUs no projeto dos datacenters e os critérios para definir o local de execução de cada carga de trabalho tornam-se aspectos centrais para o planejamento tecnológico. Da máquina local ao datacenter: o caminho de uma aplicação na nuvem Os provedores estruturam sua infraestrutura de forma regionalizada, com cada região composta por zonas de disponibilidade, ou seja, data centers autônomos equipados com energia, rede e sistema de refrigeração independentes. A distribuição de uma aplicação em mais de uma zona permite que ela continue funcionando quando uma delas falha, garantindo assim as promessas de alta disponibilidade. No decorrer de mais de 25 anos de carreira em tecnologia, período em que a infraestrutura migrou de servidores próprios para a nuvem, Jean Pierre Lessa e Santos Ferreira ocupou posições de CTO, CIO e VP. A mudança implicou em alterações na rotina das equipes, que passaram a se dedicar ao desenvolvimento de arquiteturas tolerantes a falhas e ao acompanhamento da fatura como indicador técnico, em vez de adquirir e instalar máquinas. A localização é um fator relevante. A distância física entre o usuário e o servidor influencia a latência, e a região escolhida define sob qual legislação os dados ficam armazenados, o que é um fator relevante para os setores sujeitos à LGPD e às regras de residência de dados. Energia, refrigeração e GPUs redefinem os limites da infraestrutura de IA Os modelos de inteligência artificial (IA) dependem de processadores gráficos, também conhecidos como GPUs. Esses dispositivos apresentam maior potência e geram mais calor por rack em comparação com os servidores tradicionais. Muitos datacenters projetados para cargas convencionais precisaram revisar a distribuição de energia e adotar soluções como refrigeração líquida para acomodar esses equipamentos sem comprometer a estabilidade. A aplicação prática de IA em larga escala, liderada por Jean Pierre Lessa e Santos Ferreira como Diretor de Tecnologia, torna esse debate concreto para qualquer empresa. Cada nova funcionalidade com modelos de linguagem ou de previsão consome capacidade de processamento, que deve ser devidamente planejada, contratada e monitorada. Além disso, a escassez de GPUs em determinados períodos transforma a disponibilidade em fator estratégico. O conceito de eficiência energética não se caracteriza como um mero detalhe, mas como um requisito indispensável. Quanto mais eficiente o datacenter, menor o custo por consulta. Técnicas como compressão de modelos, cache de respostas e escolha de modelos menores para tarefas simples reduzem o consumo sem afetar a qualidade do resultado. Como distribuir cargas entre nuvem e infraestrutura própria Em síntese, não há uma resposta única para tal questão. Cargas com demanda variável e necessidade de crescimento acelerado geralmente se beneficiam da nuvem pública, enquanto sistemas estáveis, com volume previsível e exigências rígidas de controle, frequentemente são mais econômicos em ambiente próprio. O modelo híbrido combina as duas lógicas e exige atenção redobrada à integração e à segurança entre os ambientes. O repertório de Jean Pierre Lessa e Santos Ferreira, que combina profundidade técnica e visão de negócio, auxilia na organização dessa escolha por meio de perguntas objetivas: qual é a variação de demanda, qual a latência aceitável, que dados devem permanecer em determinado território e quanto custa manter o ambiente por todo o seu ciclo de vida. A decisão de construir ou adquirir infraestrutura segue o mesmo raciocínio. A revisão periódica dessa escolha é essencial para evitar que a arquitetura fique presa a decisões antigas. A infraestrutura que atende bem hoje pode deixar de atender quando os modelos de IA crescerem. Portanto, o planejamento de capacidade deve tratar energia, refrigeração e custo como variáveis de projeto desde o primeiro desenho. artigo.texto: The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) lifted a permitting pause on data centers this week that Gov. Greg Abbott had previously ordered. In September, Abbott, in a letter to the TCEQ, directed the state agency to “halt all permits sought by data centers.” The order followed Abbott's directives to the Public Utility Commission (PUC) and Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to “thoroughly audit” data centers seeking connection to the Texas grid, as well as the order to the Texas Water Development Board to “compel data centers to comply with water use reporting requirements.” The TCEQ permit pause was intended to last until ERCOT completed its review of data center projects. The state agency regulates certain environmental permits and assesses the environmental impacts of water quality, air pollutants, and wastewater relating to data center projects. Following its November 17 decision to lift the pause, the TCEQ told The Texan in a statement, “TCEQ has been notified that ERCOT has gathered information for the community impact review for pending data center projects. The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations.” In other data center-related news, state Sen. Charles Perry (R-Lubbock) filed legislation related to water consumption and the creation of a new regulatory framework for data centers after the Texas Legislature's bill pre-filing period opened on November 9. Senate Bill (SB) 338, authored by Perry, joins the chorus of new House and Senate filings aimed at regulating data centers in the state. The newly filed bills address data center regulations ranging from prohibiting tax abatements to repealing sales and use tax exemptions. Perry’s bill specifically aims to establish “new safeguards for water consumption, transparency, and the impact of data center development on Texas communities,” according to his press release. The legislation garnered support from 15 bipartisan co-authors. Perry cited a September hearing as a major impetus for drafting the bill: “At our hearing in September, we heard from Texans who are concerned about what these developments mean for their water, their property, and their quality of life.” He called the concerns “legitimate,” adding that “Texans should not have to sacrifice their water resources or the peaceful enjoyment of their own homes to accommodate a new development." Regarding water, the legislation seeks to establish “new standards for future data center developments” and require companies to implement water-efficient cooling techniques, according to the press release. About water usage by data center companies — a topic that has been shrouded in uncertainty due to a lack of data from the data centers themselves — Perry stated, “We cannot responsibly plan for Texas' future if we do not even know how much water these facilities are using or where that water is coming from." During the aforementioned hearing, the PUC reported that only 155 out of 377 data center companies reported water usage information. SB 338 also seeks to further regulate the tax incentives that counties and cities provide data center companies, and revise abatement conditions to include water-related stipulations. The bill states that a Texas city cannot offer a property tax abatement to a data center that covers more than 50 percent of the property’s otherwise taxable value in a given year. It also states that the Jobs, Energy, Technology, and Innovation Act agreements that data center companies have with school districts — 10-year property tax limitation contracts with a local school district, a company, and the Governor’s office — would be limited by the same water and environmental stipulations. Texas Policy Research (TPR) stated that the bill’s “cooling mandates, siting rules, and disconnection penalties single out one industry for treatment no other large user faces, and they leave the real cost question unaddressed.” TPR concluded, “Texas should stop subsidizing data centers, stop singling them out, and do the harder work of building the power and water supply a growing state needs.” According to research from Power Hopper — a Texas electricity broker that also maintains a public repository tracking Texas legislative filings — data centers and large load users were the most frequently cited in electricity-related bill filings between November 9 and November 13.

artigo.texto: Relatórios Relatório da IEC defende critérios mais abrangentes para avaliar a sustentabilidade dos data centers de IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveO PUE revela a eficiência da sobrecarga, mas não a demanda absoluta nem a intensidade… Ver mais - O PUE revela a eficiência da sobrecarga, mas não a demanda absoluta nem a intensidade de carbono do fornecimento de energia de uma instalação. - O quadro de Contribuição Total abrange quatro dimensões, mas ainda carece de um método para torná-las comparáveis. - A flexibilidade da resposta à demanda depende de quem controla as cargas de trabalho e a maioria dos operadores não tem visibilidade sobre a computação de terceiros. A Comissão Eletrotécnica Internacional (IEC) propõe uma abordagem mais ampla para avaliar a sustentabilidade dos data centers de IA. Anunciado em 17 de novembro, seu Documento estratégico sobre centros de dados sustentáveis e briefing para lideranças apresenta uma estrutura de «Contribuição Total», que considera a pegada ambiental de uma instalação, bem como sua relação com a rede elétrica, a produtividade econômica e os serviços públicos. A ideia central é avaliar um data center como parte de um sistema mais amplo. O consumo de eletricidade e água continua sendo uma medida essencial, mas a IEC quer que os relatórios também indiquem se uma instalação pode contribuir para a resiliência da rede e oferecer serviços digitais úteis. A organização criou um Grupo Estratégico de Normas para Centros de Dados, responsável por desenvolver métricas consistentes, protocolos de elaboração de relatórios e mecanismos de garantia. Trata-se de um roteiro estratégico para avançar na padronização. O anúncio não estabelece uma fórmula global de pontuação já concluída nem uma exigência vinculante para que todos os data centers adotem sistemas de resfriamento sem consumo de água. Por que o PUE não conta a história toda A Eficiência no Uso de Energia (PUE, na sigla em inglês) mede a energia total consumida pela instalação dividida pela energia usada pelos equipamentos de TI. Um PUE de 1,2 significa que a instalação consome 20% mais energia do que os equipamentos de TI, por si só. Um menor consumo adicional pode indicar maior eficiência no resfriamento e no fornecimento de energia, mas essa proporção não revela a demanda absoluta de eletricidade da instalação nem a intensidade de carbono da energia que a abastece. A IEC já publica a ISO/IEC 30134-2:2026, que define o PUE e estabelece como medi-lo, calculá-lo e relatá-lo. A nova iniciativa aborda uma questão mais ampla: como incluir indicadores desse tipo, referentes a uma instalação, na avaliação de resultados ambientais e sociais. Mesmo uma instalação de grande porte com excelente PUE pode impor uma demanda significativa a uma rede com capacidade limitada. Duas instalações com proporções semelhantes também podem ter necessidades de água muito diferentes ou oportunidades distintas de reutilizar calor. A eficiência dentro de um edifício e a sustentabilidade em uma região estão relacionadas, mas medem aspectos diferentes. Os quatro componentes da «Contribuição Total» O anúncio da IEC organiza a estrutura proposta em torno de quatro dimensões interligadas: - Energia e integração à rede: resposta à demanda, apoio à resiliência da rede e integração de novas fontes de geração renovável ou instaladas no local. - Gestão ambiental e dos recursos: consumo de energia, uso de água, emissões de carbono, circularidade, resfriamento avançado e recuperação de calor residual. - Produtividade econômica e digital: relação entre o consumo de recursos e contribuições como o aumento da produtividade possibilitado pela IA, a transformação digital e o emprego qualificado. - Resiliência social e regional: apoio à saúde, às comunicações, ao governo e a outros serviços essenciais, além do desenvolvimento regional. O próximo desafio é tornar essas dimensões comparáveis. Um benefício para a economia digital de um país não resolve automaticamente a escassez de água em uma localidade. Uma avaliação confiável precisa mostrar onde ocorrem os impactos, quem recebe os benefícios e como as alegações são medidas, em vez de condensar todos os aspectos envolvidos em uma pontuação favorável. A flexibilidade da rede tem limites práticos Em uma contribuição anterior da IEC para a plataforma AI for Good da ITU, a organização descreveu o próximo documento como uma forma de identificar lacunas de sustentabilidade e segurança na padronização. A IEC ressaltou a importância de tratar os data centers como participantes ativos dos sistemas de energia e de examinar o resfriamento, o uso de água, o lixo eletrônico e as emissões ao longo do ciclo de vida. A resposta à demanda pode tornar essa relação mais proveitosa: uma instalação ajusta seu consumo de eletricidade em coordenação com as condições da rede. No entanto, a possibilidade de participar depende das restrições operacionais e de quem controla as cargas de trabalho. O relatório «Impulsionando a inteligência artificial» da IEA afirma que o gerenciamento ativo das cargas computacionais ainda é raro. Muitos operadores atendem terceiros e têm visibilidade ou controle limitados sobre as tarefas executadas em suas instalações. A IEA considera que a troca padronizada de informações entre clientes de serviços de computação, fornecedores de infraestrutura e redes elétricas é importante para viabilizar a flexibilidade. Para a iniciativa da IEC, isso torna mais significativo relatar a capacidade real do que simplesmente classificar um complexo como «capaz de apoiar a rede». Evidências úteis mostrariam que parte da demanda pode ser alterada, por quanto tempo e sob quais compromissos de serviço. Resfriamento líquido e consumo de água são questões distintas O anúncio da IEC destaca o resfriamento líquido e por imersão, a distribuição de energia em corrente contínua e a qualidade da energia para a infraestrutura de IA como áreas que precisam de normas. artigo.texto: New U.S. export rules could slow Southeast Asia's data center boom by tightening access to advanced AI chips and targeting the region's role in providing computing power to Chinese companies. According to an interim rule released Monday by the Commerce Department, data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will need a U.S. government license to purchase advanced AI chips, including those from Nvidia. Facilities already serving large Chinese customers will have 90 days to apply for a license or face future export restrictions, the rule said. The region has seen a surge in data center construction to house the semiconductors needed to train and develop artificial intelligence models. U.S. restrictions on China's access to Nvidia's most advanced chips have pushed Chinese technology firms, including Alibaba Group and ByteDance, to rent computing capacity in overseas data centers. About 75% of China's overseas AI compute was forecast to be concentrated in Southeast Asia by the end of 2026, according to October estimates by the Institute for Progress, a Washington-based think tank. The buildout has come under greater scrutiny as Washington presses ahead with the investigation into Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang left the company that he co-founded in 1993 after reports of several alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy who is believed to facilitate billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips into China. The new restrictions will likely make building and operating these data centers "slower and costlier," said Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations. The rules could undercut the business model of neoclouds — newer cloud providers built around AI computing — in the region, she said. Operators are likely to face more rigorous regulatory and national security requirements, said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. Greater scrutiny over investment into these projects could also weigh on Asian economies that have benefited heavily from the region's data center build-out. Who are most exposed? Malaysia stands to lose the most from the new restrictions, analysts say, given the scale of capacity being built in Johor and the sector's reliance on Chinese customers. More than half of Malaysia's data center capacity is in colocation facilities with Chinese firms accounting for "a sizeable share of these workloads," said Leah Fahy, senior China economist at Capital Economics. Restricting access to overseas cloud facilities would weaken the commercial case for further expansion and ultimately weigh on investment from both Chinese and U.S. companies, Fahy said. "Any resulting slowdown in investment would add to the drag from an anticipated cooling in the global AI export cycle," she said, potentially knocking 0.2 percentage points off Malaysia's GDP growth forecasts through 2028. Thailand, which has more than 60 data centers operating and about 30 under construction, is also bracing for tighter scrutiny. Thailand's vice minister for commerce, Kirida Bhaopichitr, told CNBC's JP Ong in Manila on Sunday that the country would scrutinize data centers importing high-end chips and "crack down" on those that re-export them to third countries. New projects that fail to secure U.S. approval for advanced chips may "not be able to complete construction," the vice minister said, though existing facilities providing AI services could be less affected. Governments in the region have signaled compliance with the U.S. requirements. "We will have to discuss with the U.S. to make sure that the chips are coming," and are allowed for use in data centers operating in Thailand, Bhaopichitr said. Malaysia's investment, trade and industry minister, Johari Abdul Ghani, said Tuesday, "If you want to be in the game, you have to follow U.S. regulations." Singapore, meanwhile, has said it plans to negotiate "trusted access" to advanced AI chips for its companies. Narrower gate The rule, however, exempts U.S.-linked firms, leaving a narrow route for Chinese companies to continue renting advanced computing power through American cloud giants, analysts said, though they might exercise caution. "Potentially, U.S. firms may receive an advantage," Chong said. "There is a significant risk that Chinese companies will pivot from renting compute from data centers in Southeast Asia, to renting compute from data centers in Virginia," said Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and former National Security Council official. He urged Washington to close that loophole before it is exploited. Bhattacharya said some high-end capacity may also shift to Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, though constraints on power and land may restrain how much those markets can absorb. Chinese technology companies have already begun looking for alternative sources of computing power outside of Southeast Asia. CNBC reported earlier this month that Chinese developer Moonshot AI tried to access Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. artigo.texto: Oregon volcano could help power Google data centers A proposed geothermal project near Central Oregon’s Newberry Volcano could supply electricity for Google’s data centers in The Dalles, drawing on heat deep beneath the ground. Google has agreed to buy 50 megawatts of electricity from Project Obsidian, which is being developed by Quaise Energy. The company said power could become available as early as 2030, although the project’s timeline remains uncertain. FOX 12 NOW spoke with Eric Burns, a research hydrologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, about how geothermal energy works, the challenges of extracting it and the potential risks of drilling near a volcano. How would the project generate power? Geothermal energy draws on heat beneath the Earth’s surface. In volcanic areas, magma can bring heat closer to the surface, making those places attractive for geothermal development, Burns said. Newberry is a shield volcano, and researchers are still studying how heat is distributed underground there, he said. Previous drilling has shown a heat resource exists in the area. Burns said the project’s target zone is in the upper 4 to 5 kilometers underground — roughly 2.5 to 3 miles — though drilling to those depths can be expensive. Enhanced geothermal systems generally use wells to reach hot rock and create pathways that allow fluid to move through it. The fluid picks up heat underground and carries it to the surface, where the heat can be used to generate electricity. Burns said developers can use different methods to create those pathways, including fracturing or chemical stimulation. He said he had not seen all of Quaise’s plans and was describing his understanding of the proposed approach, not confirming the project’s final design. In its announcement of the Google agreement, Quaise said the project’s initial phase would use conventional drilling. A later phase is expected to use a technology called millimeter-wave drilling. What about earthquakes and water? Burns said two questions surrounding geothermal development are whether underground work could cause earthquakes and whether it could contaminate water. Creating fractures changes conditions underground and can produce seismic activity, he said. He also said monitoring and engineering can help manage risks, but did not say they would eliminate them. The interview did not establish specific monitoring requirements for Project Obsidian. Asked whether the project could cause an eruption, Burns said he is not a volcanologist. He said he saw no reason to believe the planned work would cause a massive eruption and described that risk as probably very low. His comments were not a site-specific volcanic risk assessment. Could geothermal energy also cool data centers? Data centers need electricity to run their systems and energy to keep equipment cool, Burns said. While Project Obsidian is intended to generate electricity, other geothermal technologies can use the relatively stable temperatures in shallow ground to help heat or cool buildings. Some systems can also store seasonal heating or cooling underground for later use, he said. Those technologies are separate from the proposed deep geothermal power project; Burns did not say Google planned to use them at its data centers. What comes next? Burns said a 2008 USGS assessment found Oregon had favorable geothermal potential, but development in the state had lagged behind places such as Nevada. He said some enhanced geothermal projects in Nevada were already supplying power, though relatively few such systems were operating. That limited track record makes it difficult to predict precisely how a new project will perform or when it will come online, Burns said. He pointed to engineering and cost as important challenges, including whether developers can access underground heat affordably. Copyright 2026 KPTV-KPDX. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Grupo Algar cria empresa independente na Amazônia para escalar negócios de carbono e bioeconomia Sob liderança de Luciana Di Paula, nova Algar Florestas gerencia 145 mil hectares em Portel (PA) e mira dobrar de tamanho combinando créditos ambientais, cacau agroflorestal e movelaria certificada Após atuar por cinco décadas na região amazônica, o Grupo Algar transformou sua operação florestal em uma empresa 100% independente. Batizada de Algar Florestas, a nova unidade de negócios nasce como um braço autônomo dentro do conglomerado para gerenciar uma área superior a 145 mil hectares no município de Portel, no Pará, com a meta de dobrar seu faturamento e quadro de colaboradores a partir da monetização da floresta em pé. Para comandar o processo de expansão, a companhia escolheu a executiva Luciana Di Paula como diretora-presidente. Segundo ela, a separação societária e operacional (modelo de spin-off) busca dar agilidade para atrair investimentos e escalar Soluções Baseadas na Natureza (SbN) sem ampliar a pressão extrativista sobre o bioma. "A nossa operação na Amazônia existe desde a década de 1970, o que nos deu tempo para errar, aprender e amadurecer. Transformar a Algar Florestas em uma unidade de negócios independente é um reconhecimento dessa maturidade", explica Luciana. "Essa é a principal mudança de paradigma que queremos mostrar ao mercado: nosso crescimento não vem do aumento da pressão extrativista, mas da agregação de valor e da prestação de serviços ambientais. Em vez de tirar mais da floresta, nós extraímos mais valor do que já é conservado e manejado de forma regenerativa." Mercado de carbono e créditos de biodiversidade A estratégia de crescimento apoia-se em dois pilares centrais: os serviços ambientais e a bioeconomia produtiva. Na frente climática, a carteira de créditos de carbono da empresa já inicia operando com R$20 milhões movimentados e projeta capturar cerca de 200 mil toneladas de CO² equivalente por ano, podendo alcançar a comercialização de até 30 milhões de toneladas ao longo do ciclo do projeto. Os projetos são auditados sob o padrão internacional VCS (Verra) com o selo CCB (Climate, Community & Biodiversity), certificação que exige comprovação de benefícios sociais e ambientais paralelos à captura de gases de efeito estufa — rigor técnico que rendeu à iniciativa o prêmio de Melhor Projeto de Carbono do mundo pela Environmental Finance em 2025. "Não vendemos expectativa; vendemos projetos certificados. Vemos as exigências do mercado global como algo extremamente positivo, pois separam as boas práticas das falsas promessas", afirma a executiva. Ampliando a tese de financiamento ambiental, a companhia lançou durante a 17ª Conferência das Partes da Convenção sobre Diversidade Biológica (COP17), realizada na Armênia, um ativo voltado especificamente à fauna e flora: o Crédito de Biodiversidade. O projeto capitaliza o monitoramento contínuo da vida silvestre já realizado na área, atestado pelo Selo Onça-Pintada. "Enquanto o crédito de carbono foca na mitigação climática, o Crédito de Biodiversidade é focado na proteção e regeneração da vida silvestre de um bioma. Os compradores são empresas globais e nacionais com compromissos Nature Positive, que buscam ir além do Net Zero e querem investir de forma mensurável e auditada na preservação de ecossistemas complexos", detalha Di Paula. Cacau agroflorestal e verticalização com design No eixo da bioeconomia, a empresa utiliza o cultivo de cacau como ferramenta de recuperação de áreas degradadas no passado. Inserida em Sistemas Agroflorestais (SAFs), a frente de restauração tem potencial para produzir até 100 mil toneladas anuais de amêndoas. "A produção de cacau na Algar Florestas não concorre com a floresta nativa; ela é a ferramenta de recuperação. Nós utilizamos o plantio consorciado com outras espécies para recuperar áreas que foram antropizadas, devolvendo a cobertura vegetal, melhorando o solo e gerando um produto de alto valor comercial, sem derrubar uma única árvore", ressalta a presidente. Já o manejo florestal certificado pelas normas internacionais FSC e PEFC abastece uma cadeia verticalizada por meio da Pacajá Móveis, marca própria dedicada à movelaria de alto padrão. O portfólio inclui peças assinadas pelo design brasileiro, como a Cristaleira Igarapés, projetada pelo Studio Érico Gondim e selecionada para a mostra do 36º Prêmio Design do Museu da Casa Brasileira. "Ao transformarmos a madeira certificada em mobiliário de alto padrão, nós verticalizamos a cadeia. A margem de valor agregado sobre o móvel finalizado é infinitamente superior à venda da madeira bruta, maximizando nosso retorno financeiro por metro cúbico manejado", pontua. Impacto social nas comunidades de Portel Atualmente, a operação emprega mais de 60 trabalhadores diretos e 600 indiretos, números que devem dobrar com o plano de expansão. O programa socioambiental da unidade envolve diretamente 15 comunidades locais em Portel, combinando geração de renda, capacitação técnica e fomento a cadeias como piscicultura, avicultura e horticultura — atuação que rendeu à companhia a Comenda Arucará, concedida pela prefeitura municipal, e destaque no Prêmio ESG. "A premissa do selo CCB que possuímos é justamente o benefício direto à comunidade. O negócio só para em pé se a comunidade crescer e prosperar junto conosco", diz Di Paula.

artigo.texto: Salt Lake adopts 180-day pause on data center development SALT LAKE CITY (KUTV) — The Salt Lake City Council adopted a temporary ordinance pausing data center development in the city for up to 180 days, giving officials time to study regulations for the industry. The council plans to use the pause to consult with residents, industry representatives, experts and other levels of government. From there, the council "intends to initiate formal petitions to amend the Salt Lake City Code to adopt zoning regulations pertaining to data centers." The 180-day period is the maximum allowed under state law, Councilwoman Victoria Petro said. The vote comes after permit applications for a proposed data center in Salt Lake City’s Northpoint area drew opposition from nearby residents. The ordinance will temporarily pause any progress on that and any other data center projects on Salt Lake City land. Dennis Bangerter, who lives across the street from the proposed site, said he believes development approvals are moving too quickly. “We’re just kind of caught in the middle of a puzzle that they’re trying to do too many things,” he said. Chris Souther, who lives nearby, said he has noticed more noise and air pollution as the neighborhood has changed. He says that has impacted more than just the quality of life, but also property value. "My life savings is gone because the city decided to commercialize to make a bigger tax base for themselves," Souther said. Petro said residents have not had enough input into the development of the data center industry. “You can’t leave our neighbors out of it,” she said. “You have to engage them.” Petro represents the area and said residents’ concerns about noise, light, energy use and water use will be part of the council’s review. “I am constantly working against clocks trying to preserve the sanity for my neighbors who want to stay," Petro said. Petro said the council will seek input from residents, experts and other stakeholders during the pause. She hopes the city will develop “an evidence-based, truth-based way to regulate an industry that could either be beneficial or harmful.” But Petro cautioned that the city may have limited ability to stop the Northpoint project. She said it is already vested and the landowners have the zoning they need. “We will struggle to even play defense,” Petro said. “The only way we can be sure things will be different is if our constituents and every other stakeholder comes to the table and finds a path forward.” Petro said the council is not inherently opposed to data centers, but is concerned about the speed of development, lack of information, and potential harm to residents, the environment and wildlife. “We are hostile to abuses of our environment and our neighbors that could make a project like this detrimental for time to come,” she said. _____

artigo.texto: Filiais da Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust Inc. (BXDC) assinaram em 11 de novembro de 2026 um acordo com entidades ligadas à Amazon para adquirir 75,1% de cada uma de duas joint ventures imobiliárias. As empresas conjuntas deteriam 13 data centers com capacidade total de 647 MW de potência de TI. A Blackstone anunciou o acordo em 16 de novembro: o valor bruto agregado informado para o portfólio é de US$ 5 bilhões, e o fechamento era esperado para o quarto trimestre de 2026, sujeito a condições. O documento protocolado na SEC detalha os termos da operação. Para entender o negócio, separe três papéis: participação nos imóveis, gestão das joint ventures e locação dos data centers. O que a BXDC pretende adquirir O acordo prevê que a BXDC fique com 75,1% de cada joint venture; as partes ligadas à Amazon manteriam os 24,9% restantes. No conjunto, as empresas deteriam nove edifícios no norte de Indiana e quatro no Mississippi. A taxa de capitalização inicial informada para a operação é de 7,0%. A compra envolve participações em empresas que deteriam os imóveis, não a transferência da operação de serviços de nuvem da AWS. O arranjo prevê que a Amazon continue como locatária do portfólio. Como seriam o financiamento e a locação A BXDC esperava aportar US$ 1,9 bilhão em recursos de seu IPO e levantar cerca de US$ 2,5 bilhões em novos empréstimos hipotecários non-recourse para cobrir as necessidades restantes da transação, inclusive custos. Esses valores descrevem o financiamento previsto no acordo. Os imóveis seriam alugados integralmente à Amazon Data Services, Inc. por contratos triple-net. O prazo inicial médio ponderado seria de 12 anos; com todas as extensões, o prazo médio ponderado chegaria a 32 anos. As extensões são opções, não uma garantia de que serão exercidas. O contrato prevê reajuste anual de 2,75%, e Amazon.com, Inc. garantiria as obrigações de pagamento do aluguel. Quem ocuparia os data centers e quem administraria as joint ventures A Amazon seria a locatária, enquanto o membro da empresa conjunta ligado à BXDC administraria os negócios e assuntos de cada joint venture. As partes locatárias ligadas à Amazon teriam direitos de aprovação sobre determinadas decisões importantes e fundamentais, conforme os termos do acordo protocolado na SEC. O contrato, portanto, trata separadamente da ocupação dos imóveis e da gestão das empresas conjuntas. Prazo e condições de fechamento Ao anunciar o acordo em 16 de novembro, a Blackstone informou que esperava concluí-lo no quarto trimestre de 2026, condicionado ao cumprimento das condições de fechamento. O contrato estabelece 31 de dezembro de 2026 como prazo-limite, sujeito a prorrogações. Se uma das partes deixar de concluir a operação quando estiver obrigada a fazê-lo, poderá haver uma taxa de rescisão de US$ 150 milhões, conforme as condições do contrato. A Blackstone apresentou a expectativa de fechamento junto com o anúncio da operação.

artigo.texto: The rapid expansion of data centers is adding pressure to the U.S. power grid heading into winter, as electricity demand climbs and extreme weather threatens to strain supplies. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) warned in its new winter reliability assessment released on Wednesday that electricity demand continues to rise rapidly, driven in part by the growth of data centers and other large industrial loads. The increase comes as a strengthening El Niño climate pattern raises the prospect of extreme winter weather that could push some regions' power systems closer to their limits. “While the resource outlook has improved, the unpredictable weather of El Niño and rapid load growth present unique challenges this winter,” NERC President and CEO Jim Robb said in a press release announcing the assessment. “We anticipate operators will need everything in their tool kit—including requests for emergency support—to maintain reliable operations.” Read More on U.S. Newsweek reached out to NERC by email for comment on Wednesday. How Is Data Center Growth Affecting the U.S. Power Grid? Electricity demand is expected to increase in 21 of the 23 regions assessed by NERC this winter, reflecting widespread growth in power needs across much of North America. While data centers are not responsible for all the growth, NERC identifies their expansion alongside large industrial loads and broader electrification as factors driving demand higher. The challenge is that the grid must be able to meet that additional demand even during periods of extreme weather, when households and businesses may also be using considerably more electricity. However, data centers could also play a role during a grid emergency. If electricity supplies fall short, or are expected to, grid operators in areas with large loads can seek emergency authority from the Department of Energy to direct those customers to switch to backup generators as a last resort, reducing demand and helping avoid an energy shortfall. U.S. Power Grid Regions With ‘Elevated’ Risk This Winter The report found that several parts of North America could face reliability challenges under stressed conditions this winter. Quebec, the Canadian Maritimes and parts of the U.S. Southeast are classified as at elevated risk, while New England faces concerns tied to limited natural gas supplies and parts of the central U.S. face localized transmission constraints. No region was classified as high risk. The picture has shifted since last winter, when the Pacific Northwest and several other regions were among those facing elevated concerns. NERC’s assessment can change from year to year as electricity demand, available generation, imports and transmission conditions evolve. Where Is Data Center Growth Occurring Fastest in the U.S.? Despite growing pushback from some state leaders, including Texas Governor Greg Abbott and New York Governor Kathy Hochul, data center development continues to expand rapidly across the U.S. Major projects are underway in states, including Texas, Virginia, Utah, Ohio and Louisiana, as companies race to build the infrastructure needed to meet rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Atlanta has overtaken Northern Virginia as the country's biggest market for data centers under construction, while Texas has emerged as a major center of the broader boom. El Niño Could Threaten U.S. Power Grid This Winter Despite growing demand from data centers, the greater uncertainty this winter comes from extreme weather, as El Niño increases the potential for disruptive cold, ice and storms in parts of the country, including southern areas less accustomed to severe winter conditions. Extreme cold can put power grids under pressure in several ways. Electricity demand rises as homes and businesses use more energy for heating, while freezing temperatures and ice can disrupt power plants, fuel supplies and other grid infrastructure. artigo.texto: Here’s How Much Electricity Powerful Data Centers Use A new study reveals the environmental costs of hyperscale data centers—most of which are powered by fossil fuels such as coal and natural gas. Across the country, large data centers have become a charged political issue. But basic information, including how much energy they use and how much pollution they emit, has been largely lacking. A paper recently published in the journal Nature Sustainability documents the consumption and output of the largest and most powerful data centers across the United States. Those roughly 400 hyperscale centers use almost as much electricity in a year as massive, mature industries like steel and aluminum and even as much as all the collective homes, businesses, and facilities in some individual states. “It's pretty extraordinary—a few hundred buildings are consuming as much as an entire state,” says Gianluca Guidi, a data scientist at Harvard’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the study’s lead author. Most of the electricity comes from burning fossil fuels, causing the combined centers to emit more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) a year, the study found. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas largely responsible for climate change. (Solar panels that plug into your wall are about to be everywhere.) Hundreds more hyperscale data centers, each of which contain tens of thousands of computer servers that power the artificial intelligence industry and cloud computing, are planned or under construction, so their electricity demands are poised to grow significantly, Guidi says. “Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step,” Gina McCarthy, the former administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, said in a statement. The researchers calculated the number of hyperscale centers using a database from a commercial research company along with satellite imagery documenting their size. Then, using the research company’s information along with their own calculations of size and operating hours, they estimated annual electricity consumption for each facility. Finally, data from the Environmental Protection Agency revealed the mix of electricity sources used by utilities serving each center. The study covers the year between May of 2024 and April 2025. Collectively, the centers required between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity (a terawatt is a trillion watts) during the study year. Roughly half, 54 percent, came from fossil fuels, including natural gas (38 percent) and coal (15 percent). Another 21 percent used nuclear energy, and a quarter employed hydropower, solar, wind, and other renewables. Prior to this calculation, the last estimate quantifying hyperscale centers’ energy consumption published in a scientific journal appeared five years ago, using data from 2018. It calculated cumulative energy use then at 23 terawatt hours. “This was before the AI boom rapidly expanded the number of these centers. Our data shows it’s now at least three time higher,” says Francesca Dominici, a Harvard data scientist and coauthor of the paper. The earlier research also found carbon emissions were roughly three times lower than they are now. The implications of this much electricity consumption go beyond the strain many electric grids are currently experiencing. The study authors say their future research will study how much these data centers take a toll on human health. Research clearly links emissions from fossil-fuel-based energy generation with changes to the climate, as well as health harms like lung and heart disease. Even low levels of chronic exposure to pollution, including from fossil-fuel power plants, damages the heart, according to a study published in July in the journal Radiology. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) scans that had been performed in more than 11,000 Canadians concluded those living in areas with higher fine particulate pollution have more calcium plaque and artery obstruction. This occurred even in places where the particulate matter fell below allowable government standards. “There was no lower level at which we didn't see an association, which indicates there may be really no safe level of air pollution exposure,” says Kate Hanneman, a cardiac radiologist at the University of Toronto, who conducted the research. (Debunking three myths about air pollution.) Exposure to emissions from coal-powered plants—some 15 percent of the hyperscale centers’ energy consumption—may be particularly harmful, says Corwin Zigler, an environmental scientist at Brown University. Older people exposed to its sulfur-dioxide-laden pollutants have especially high death rates, Zigler reported in Science in 2023. In recent years, coal plants have installed technologies reducing their emissions, but “still, the burden is not zero,” Zigler says. The Nature Sustainability study found very large data centers are concentrated in specific parts of the country, with four states—Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—consuming more than half of the electricity use reported. This concentration means some locations bear more burden than others. Research published last year by the same authors, examining computer centers mining for bitcoins, found higher concentrations of particulate pollution in some regions of the country. Some of that pollution remained close to the data centers, but other particulates appeared hundreds of miles away, thanks to wind and atmospheric patterns that disperse them. Similarly, coal power pollution impacts health far from the plant locations. “If you live in Boston, some of that pollution you're breathing came from Ohio or Kentucky or Missouri or Indiana,” Zigler says of his research. artigo.texto: THE Philippines is strengthening its participation in Southeast Asia's emerging carbon markets through private-sector engagement with the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF), contributing to regional efforts to promote carbon market integrity, cooperation, and climate finance. Aboitiz Foundation, representing the CarbonPH Coalition and the Philippines Nature-based Solutions (NbS) Group, is joining the ACCF as an Observer and participating in the signing of its Memorandum of Collaboration (MoC) at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye. The engagement provides an opportunity to bring Philippine perspectives and experience to regional discussions on carbon market standards, financing, and cross-border cooperation. It also highlights the growing role of Philippine private-sector initiatives in advancing forest restoration, nature-based climate solutions, and sustainable investment opportunities. The signing coincides with the renewal of the ACCF's Memorandum of Collaboration for another two years, reaffirming regional commitments to developing connected, transparent, and high-integrity carbon markets across ASEAN. "ASEAN has the natural capital and economic dynamism to become a significant player in global carbon markets. Through the CarbonPH Coalition and our work in nature-based solutions, we hope to contribute Philippine perspectives and practical experience to this regional effort,” said Ginggay Hontiveros-Malvar, Aboitiz Chief Reputation and Sustainability Officer and President of Aboitiz Foundation. “Our aim is to help build a carbon market where integrity attracts investment, climate action creates economic opportunity, and communities share in the value being created,” she added. The Philippines' participation builds on ongoing private-sector efforts to strengthen the country's emerging carbon market ecosystem through industry collaboration, knowledge-sharing, and capacity building. Among these initiatives is the CarbonPH Coalition, which brings together stakeholders to explore opportunities for credible carbon market development and nature-based climate solutions. Complementing these efforts, both CarbonPH Coalition and NbS Group have a long-term nature-based solutions initiative focused on forest restoration, biodiversity conservation, watershed protection, community development and recommended governance frameworks. These efforts highlight the Philippines' potential to develop nature-based carbon projects that support environmental protection, attract climate financing, and create economic opportunities for local communities. They also provide practical experience that Philippine stakeholders can bring to regional discussions as ASEAN works toward a more connected and credible carbon market. Established in 2024, the ACCF brings together carbon market organizations from Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Thailand, alongside the ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets, to strengthen regional coordination and advance the development of high-integrity carbon markets. Under its 2026–2028 strategy, the framework is prioritizing broader ASEAN representation, alignment with international standards, stronger market infrastructure, and technical cooperation to support credible carbon financing and cross-border market development. This representation creates an avenue for Philippine private-sector stakeholders to contribute local perspectives, share practical experience, and learn from regional carbon market initiatives. For the Philippines, the engagement marks another opportunity to strengthen regional partnerships, support the development of credible carbon market mechanisms, and attract investment in climate solutions that benefit both the environment and local communities. As ASEAN advances cooperation on carbon markets, Philippine private-sector participation can help connect regional climate financing opportunities with local conservation efforts, sustainable livelihoods, and long-term environmental resilience. artigo.texto: Flow battery manufacturers are expanding grid-scale energy storage capacity as utilities seek alternatives to lithium-ion batteries for six- to twelve-hour electricity storage. Dalian Rongke Power, Sumitomo Electric, Invinity Energy Systems, CellCube, VRB Energy, ESS Tech, VFlowTech, H2 Inc., Delectrik Systems, CMBlu Energy, Jena Flow Batteries and Elestor are competing through vanadium, iron, organic and hydrogen-based technologies. Flow batteries store energy in electrolytes and use electrochemical stacks to convert it into electricity. Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries, their power capacity and energy capacity can be expanded relatively independently. This architecture is attractive for renewable energy integration, grid balancing and long-duration storage. However, manufacturing costs, round-trip efficiency, pumping losses, project financing and maintenance determine commercial competitiveness. 1. Dalian Rongke Power: 1 GWh Vanadium Battery Operating in China Dalian Rongke Power has one of the largest disclosed vanadium redox flow battery portfolios. Its 200 MW / 1,000 MWh CTG Jimusaer project in Xinjiang reached full-capacity operation at the end of 2025. Other references include Xinhua Wushi at 175 MW / 700 MWh and the first 100 MW / 400 MWh phase of Dalian ConCurrent, commissioned in 2022. Rongke also delivered a 12 MW / 60 MWh Panzhihua installation using leased vanadium electrolyte. These four references total 475 MW / 2,160 MWh, although they have different commissioning histories. Electrolyte leasing may reduce initial capital requirements, but customers must evaluate recurring payments and residual-value provisions. 2. Sumitomo Electric: Operating VRFB Projects and 20-Year Service Contract Japan’s Sumitomo Electric has extensive experience in vanadium flow batteries. Its Minami-Hayakita references include a 17 MW / 51 MWh system operating since April 2022 and a separate 15 MW / 60 MWh demonstration system continuing commercial operation. At Kashiwazaki, completed phases total 24 MWh, with another 1 MW / 8 MWh installation scheduled for spring 2027. Sumitomo also secured an 11 MW / 33 MWh Minami-Hayakita project for completion by May 2029, including a 20-year service agreement. The Sumitomo Electric project announcement details its latest contract and operating references. Long-term maintenance commitments are important because flow batteries require pumps, membranes, sensors and stack servicing. 3. Invinity Energy Systems: 77.2 MWh Orders and 12.5 GWh Pipeline UK-based Invinity Energy Systems supplies VS3 and Endurium vanadium flow battery platforms. The company reported 34.2 MWh of customer orders in the first half of 2026. A subsequent 43 MWh Dairyland Power contract increased secured 2026 orders to 77.2 MWh. Its prospective project pipeline exceeded 12.5 GWh, while the global installed fleet had cumulatively dispatched 11 GWh of electricity. The 20.7 MWh Copwood system had been delivered, although grid connection and full commissioning remained pending at the interim reporting date. Invinity targets a 66 percent product-cost reduction for Endurium deliveries in 2027. Its 2026 interim financial results distinguish confirmed orders from prospective opportunities. The main investment considerations are manufacturing costs, gross margins, cash requirements and delivery performance. 4. CellCube: Modular Vanadium Storage and Electrolyte Recovery CellCube, associated with Austrian developer Enerox, provides modular vanadium flow battery technology. Its systems separate electrolyte storage from electrochemical stacks, allowing developers to configure discharge duration. Vanadium electrolyte can retain recoverable material value, potentially supporting end-of-life economics. However, electrolyte tanks, pumps, civil construction and electrical infrastructure increase upfront costs. Customers should verify current manufacturing arrangements, completed installations, stack replacement costs and warranty responsibility. 5. artigo.texto: Duke Energy plans to invest up to $756 million in two massive battery storage facilities in eastern North Carolina, a move the utility says could help keep electricity reliable and reduce costs for customers as demand for power continues to grow. The projects, announced Tuesday, Nov. 17, will be built next to Duke's existing H.F. Lee natural gas plant in Goldsboro. Together, they will provide 410 megawatts of battery storage capacity, more than doubling the amount Duke currently operates across North Carolina. Other WRAL Top Stories The announcement comes one day after the North Carolina Utilities Commission approved Duke Energy's updated long-term energy plan, which calls for major investments in natural gas, solar power, battery storage, and potential new nuclear generation. How could batteries save customers money? Unlike traditional power plants, batteries don't generate electricity. Instead, they store energy when it's available and release it when demand rises. That flexibility could help Duke manage growing electricity needs without relying as heavily on more expensive sources of power during peak periods. In an email to WRAL, Duke Energy spokesperson Bill Norton explained that batteries can store surplus solar energy generated on sunny afternoons and release it during periods of high demand, including cold winter mornings before the sun rises. Norton said that reduces the need to purchase electricity from neighboring utilities or operate less efficient power plants, ultimately lowering fuel costs. Battery storage can also make renewable energy more useful by allowing solar power generated during the day to be used after sunset. The Wayne County facilities will use four-hour lithium-ion batteries, meaning they can deliver their full rated output for up to four hours before needing to recharge. Duke has not provided a specific estimate of how much the Wayne County projects could save customers on their electricity bills. Federal tax credits help offset costs Duke says the Wayne County investment qualifies for a 50% federal tax credit because of its location in an energy community and its use of domestically manufactured components. The company is also prioritizing former coal plant sites for battery storage projects because they already have land and transmission infrastructure, reducing the need for additional construction. "To lower costs for our customers, we're prioritizing former coal plant sites like this, which have available land and transmission infrastructure," Norton told WRAL. The new facilities will be located near the H.F. Lee natural gas plant, on a site with a history of coal-fired electricity generation. While the federal incentives will reduce eligible project costs, the company has not detailed how much of the remaining investment customers will ultimately pay through electricity rates. Part of Duke Energy's larger energy strategy Duke currently operates 308 megawatts of battery storage across 14 facilities in North Carolina. Its largest existing facility is a 100-megawatt installation in Knightdale, which WRAL toured in March. Duke confirmed the Wayne County projects will use the same type of battery containers and technology as the Knightdale facility. "We want more renewables on the grid. We want all of that diverse mix that we have," Duke Energy spokesperson Jeff Brooks said. "It will take all of that, from carbon-free nuclear to natural gas to hydro renewables to battery storage." The newly approved Carbon Plan and Integrated Resource Plan calls for up to 5,400 megawatts of battery storage across Duke's Carolinas system by 2034, including 2,700 megawatts of additional storage beyond previously approved plans. The plan also includes new solar generation, additional natural gas plants, and continued development work on potential nuclear facilities. Environmental advocates have questioned the plan's continued reliance on natural gas, arguing that greater investments in renewable energy and energy efficiency could help reduce costs. Battery storage offers one way to make solar power more flexible, although batteries must be charged using electricity generated elsewhere and cannot replace all the functions of conventional power plants. What's next for the Wayne County project? Construction is expected to begin in early 2027. The first facility will have 260 megawatts of capacity and is scheduled to begin operating in fall 2028. A second, 150-megawatt facility is expected to be completed by the end of that year. The investment could generate up to $2 million in additional annual property tax revenue for Wayne County, according to Duke Energy. The company already pays approximately $5.8 million annually in local taxes for its existing energy infrastructure. Nine permanent jobs are expected to support the new batteries and other regional solar and storage facilities. Duke is also expanding battery storage at the former Allen coal plant near Charlotte, where approximately 400 megawatts of storage is planned by late 2028. The first 50-megawatt installation began serving customers last year. As electricity demand grows across North Carolina, these investments could help utilities make better use of existing power supplies while larger generation projects are developed. For customers already facing rising electricity bills, the question is whether those improvements will translate into measurable savings.

artigo.texto: Elon Musk Tesla’s Powercore could change how data centers get power Tesla unveiled Powercore, a solid-state transformer that could ease one of the grid’s worst bottlenecks. Tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium voltage transformer that also handles the jobs of an inverter and a circuit breaker in a single unit. “Solid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure,” the company’s Tesla Megapack account posted on X Tuesday, adding that the product is “Made in America” and will be “Operating 2027.” Elon Musk followed with his own post: “Advanced solid state transformers at scale from Tesla.” Tesla rates Powercore at 7.4 MW, or 9 MVA, of continuous output at 34.5 kV AC, with grid-forming support for 10 MVA of peak power. Specs shared by Sawyer Merritt list a peak efficiency of 98.86 percent, a DC range of 800 to 2,000 volts and a built-in solid-state breaker that clears faults in about 100 microseconds. Tesla has not announced pricing, a factory location or a first customer. The product fills a gap Tesla left open last year. When it introduced Megapack 3 and Megablock in September 2025, Tesla said it would build its own transformers, but shared almost nothing about them. Megablock groups four Megapack 3 units with a transformer and switchgear into a single medium voltage block, as Teslarati reported. Powercore appears to be that missing piece. A typical battery or solar project today uses low voltage inverters to turn DC into AC, then a large oil-filled transformer to step that power up to grid voltage. A solid-state unit handles both steps with power electronics, which means less equipment, a smaller footprint and no flammable oil. Grid-forming capability lets it actively help hold voltage and frequency steady rather than simply following the grid. Introducing Powercore Solid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure 7.4 MW/9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac w/ grid-forming support for 10MVA of peak power Made in America. Operating 2027 https://t.co/sHxqnpWJrf — Tesla Megapack (@Tesla_Megapack) November 17, 2026 Timing is a big part of the pitch. Lead times for conventional transformers have stretched into years as AI data centers and renewable projects crowd utility interconnection queues. Tesla energy executive Max de Zegher pointed to the problem in a post Musk shared, noting that “transformers have barely changed since the 1890s: copper coils in a tank of oil,” while batteries, solar and compute all run on DC. Powercore, he wrote, delivers “one conversion and about half the losses.” Tesla has also said its Megapack supply for 2027 is nearly sold out. Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage in the third quarter, its second best quarter on record. On Tuesday, the company also said customer solar systems deployed by Tesla Energy now generate more than twice the electricity its global operations consume each year.

artigo.texto: By Oladele Eniola Robin Zeng, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. (CATL), has called for innovation-driven competition rather than price wars in the global battery industry. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that CATL is the world’s largest electric vehicle and energy storage battery manufacturer, headquartered in Ningde, China. In a statement on Thursday, Zeng stressed that competition should be driven by creativity, technological innovation and value creation. He described competition based on continuous price reductions and disregard for intellectual property rights as unhealthy and unsustainable. According to him, genuine competition should encourage companies to develop better products and create more value rather than engage in a race to offer cheaper alternatives. Zeng expressed concern about the sustainability of the global environment, saying the world needed new and clean technologies to address emerging challenges. “It is not sustainable for this world if we don’t have new, clean technology,” he said. On the impact of changing policies across different countries on international business operations, Zeng said the underlying economic interests driving such policies should be understood. He argued that countries and businesses needed to consider whether competition, restrictive policies or cooperation would deliver greater benefits. According to him, cooperation offers better prospects for mutual gains than confrontational approaches that prevent businesses from sharing technological and economic benefits. “Businesses can create greater value and deliver win-win results through cooperation rather than rivalry,” he said. Zeng cited CATL’s technology licensing arrangement with Ford Motor Company as an example of how international partnerships could deliver benefits to different parties. He also highlighted the company’s collaboration with Indonesia, covering activities from mineral mining and refining to battery production. In Europe, Zeng said CATL had made investments and established a joint venture with Stellantis, an automotive manufacturing company. He maintained that such partnerships demonstrated the benefits of sharing technology and economic opportunities instead of engaging in unproductive competition. (NAN) Edited by Folasade Adeniran

artigo.texto: For the second month in a row, the Will County Board on Thursday postponed action on a proposed solar facility and battery storage project in Manhattan Township that local officials oppose. Cultivate Power is asking to build a 5-megawatt commercial solar farm and a battery energy storage system on 153 acres at 15520 W. Baker Road, Manhattan. The solar facility would occupy about 52 acres while the battery storage system, which stores excess energy generated on the site, would take up about 10 acres, county documents said. Angela Feria, a representative with Cultivate Power, said the company has been active in Will County in the last two years, has engaged with neighbors and officials and has agreed to a variety of requests, including increasing the setback from Jackson Creek and performing soil testing over the course of the project. Manhattan Township Supervisor Jim Walsh said the township is against both the solar project and the battery storage system. He said a nearby farmer contacted him because he was concerned about the impact the solar farm would have on his drainage. Manhattan Township officials met with the solar developer Aug. 31 and voted 4-0 at the end of the meeting to object to the plans. The township cited several concerns, including a township policy that states no battery storage facilities are permitted. Another concern was the affect the solar project would have on a planned bike path by the Forest Preserve District of Will County as well as the number of overhead electrical poles that would connect the facility to the ComEd system. The village of Manhattan also voted to object to the proposal, saying it is inconsistent with the village’s comprehensive plan and could “frustrate the orderly development of the village.” County Board member Dan Butler, a Frankfort Republican, said the solar firm’s application is incomplete and the solar company didn’t do enough to engage with the road district and ensure the road commissioner agrees to the plans. Butler said the firm hasn’t provided the proper documents and asked for the board’s legal representation to review the project. “These solar companies should not be taking over eastern and southern Will County,” Butler said. Board member Frankie Pretzel, chair of the county’s Land Use and Development Committee, said the project is “a terrible case” that didn’t get the approval of the committee or the county’s Planning and Zoning Commission. The board on Thursday also approved extensions for five solar projects in Wesley, Channahon, Florence, Joliet and Crete townships. Board member Judy Ogalla, a Monee Republican, said she opposed extending time for the solar projects to commence. With the delays, many residents feel the projects have stopped, but sometimes ownership of the project changed hands. Michelle Mullins is a freelance reporter for the Daily Southtown.

artigo.texto: State environmental regulators have resumed reviewing data center permits, bringing an end to an earlier directive from Gov. Greg Abbott ordering a pause on permit approvals related to data center projects. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality received notice on Friday from Abbott’s office that officials at the state’s electric grid had completed gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers — one of multiple issues Abbott asked grid officials and electricity regulators to evaluate. “The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations,” TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said in a written statement. In August, Abbott had called on the Electric Reliability Council of Texas and electricity regulators to audit all data centers trying to connect to the grid, as well as gather information about tax incentives, power use, water use and potential neighborhood impacts. Abbott at that time paused approval of any grid interconnections for data centers while the audit was completed. In his Sept. 21 letter to TCEQ calling for the environmental permitting pause, Abbott said the agency needed to wait until ERCOT “completes its review.” Environmental advocates at Public Citizen, responding to the news of the resumed permits, called on TCEQ commissioners to resign. “The TCEQ is asserting that ERCOT has concluded its assessment of the community impacts of data centers, and without sharing those results with communities or detailing how the TCEQ will incorporate the findings into permitting decisions, agency leadership has begun unilaterally issuing data center permits,” said Kathryn Guerra, the TCEQ watchdog campaign director for Public Citizen, in a statement. Intense opposition to data centers had been growing all year in communities across the state, where Democrats and Republicans alike fought projects they worried would destabilize the electric grid, lead to more pollution from new gas-fueled power generators and guzzle up water in a state with serious drought concerns. TCEQ handles permits related to air pollution at facilities and stormwater runoff on construction sites. The agency faced criticism in October from Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance. The groups noticed that some data center-related construction permits were being cleared anyway — counter to Abbott’s order. TCEQ said it suspended the permits and then it shut down its entire automated electronic filing system and required physical applications be submitted for staff to review. Then in a staggering upset on Nov. 3, Abbott lost his reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who on the campaign trail vowed to keep data center approvals paused until legislators pass new state laws. Neither Abbott’s office nor Hinojosa’s media team on Tuesday immediately responded to a request for comment. “Texans are tired of this political theatre,” said Sam Law, researcher at FracTracker Alliance, in a written statement shared by Public Citizen. “We need real leadership, transparency, and a true moratorium on data center development.” ERCOT provided an update on its review of community impacts to electric regulators at the Public Utility Commission of Texas on Nov. 5. ERCOT reported receiving responses from 93% of 465 projects, which provided enough information for “a statistically meaningful analysis for the final report.” ERCOT officials plan to report their full findings to the PUC on Dec. 10 and discuss them at the next PUC open meeting Dec. 17.

artigo.texto: A forma de pagar pela energia elétrica poderá mudar nos próximos anos. Em 9 de novembro de 2026, a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL) apresentou a proposta da Tarifa Hora Certa, que prevê valores diferentes para o kWh conforme o horário de consumo. Para quem tem ou pretende instalar […] 19 de novembro de 2026, às 16:42 Para quem tem ou pretende instalar energia solar, a mudança reforça a importância de um projeto que considere não apenas quanto se produz, mas também quando a energia é consumida. É nesse contexto que as baterias e a inteligência artificial ganham espaço. Como funcionará a Tarifa Hora Certa? A proposta divide o dia em três períodos: Os horários e preços efetivos dependem da distribuidora. Assim, dois imóveis com o mesmo consumo mensal poderão ter contas diferentes, conforme os horários de uso de ar-condicionado, aquecimento, piscina e outros equipamentos. Quem poderá ser incluído? A proposta abrange consumidores de baixa tensão residenciais (B1), rurais (B2) e comerciais/industriais (B3), respeitadas as exceções regulatórias. O enquadramento automático poderá alcançar unidades com média mensal a partir de 500 kWh, calculada em 12 meses, de forma gradual: os preparativos são previstos para 2027 e a implementação começa em abril de 2028 pelas faixas de maior consumo. Consumidores abaixo de 500 kWh poderão aderir voluntariamente, quando elegíveis. Para novos projetos de energia solar, há uma regra específica: pedidos de conexão ao Sistema de Compensação de Energia Elétrica (SCEE) apresentados a partir de 90 dias após a publicação da norma deverão entrar na Tarifa Hora Certa, independentemente do consumo e sem opção de saída, segundo o texto proposto. Se a norma for publicada em dezembro de 2026, essa regra poderá alcançar novos pedidos em 2027. A data exata, porém, ainda não está confirmada. Para sistemas já conectados, a transição proposta é distinta, iniciando-se gradualmente em 2028. Por que as baterias ganham importância? Os painéis solares geram energia principalmente durante o dia, enquanto parte relevante do consumo residencial pode ocorrer à noite. Com baterias, é possível guardar energia produzida pelo sistema fotovoltaico e utilizá-la quando a tarifa da rede estiver mais cara. Em certas configurações, também é possível carregar a bateria com energia comprada da rede fora da ponta e utilizá-la na ponta. Essa estratégia é chamada de arbitragem de energia: aproveitar o período mais barato para reduzir compras no período mais caro. Imagine, como exemplo, um kWh a R$ 0,60 fora de ponta e R$ 1,20 na ponta. Armazenar energia no primeiro período para uso no segundo pode gerar economia. Mas o retorno depende da diferença real entre as tarifas, das perdas do armazenamento, da vida útil da bateria e do custo do investimento. Injetar energia armazenada na rede não garante receber um valor maior por isso. A inteligência artificial ajuda a escolher o melhor momento A tecnologia permite ir além de simplesmente guardar energia. Soluções da Sigenergy integram baterias e recursos de inteligência artificial capazes de considerar hábitos de consumo, previsão de geração solar, clima, tarifas disponíveis e nível de carga. Com dados e configurações compatíveis, o sistema pode priorizar o autoconsumo, guardar energia para o horário caro ou manter uma reserva para situações de necessidade. O proprietário define seus objetivos, enquanto o gerenciamento inteligente auxilia na escolha dos momentos de carga e descarga. As funcionalidades dependem do modelo instalado, das informações tarifárias disponíveis e das regras aplicáveis no Brasil. i9 Solar já vinha antecipando essa tendência A i9 Solar já acompanhava a evolução do armazenamento e incorporava ao seu ecossistema tecnologias como as da Sigenergy. Sua proposta é integrar geração fotovoltaica, baterias e gestão inteligente para oferecer mais controle sobre o consumo e ampliar as possibilidades de eficiência e economia. “A energia solar já permite ao consumidor produzir parte da própria eletricidade. Com as baterias e a gestão inteligente, ele também pode escolher melhor quando utilizar essa energia. É uma evolução que pode trazer mais controle e eficiência ao imóvel”, afirma Flavio Abreu, CEO da i9 Solar. Em imóveis de alto padrão, com climatização, piscina aquecida, automação e carregador de veículo elétrico, entender o consumo por horário pode ser especialmente relevante. A mesma análise vale para empresas com demanda concentrada em certos períodos. A empresa apresenta a tecnologia em seu canal no YouTube, que pode ser acessado pelo link https://youtu.be/QN1ooIDF7Yk Instalar bateria será obrigatório? Não. A proposta da ANEEL altera a modalidade tarifária de determinados consumidores, mas não exige baterias. O armazenamento poderá ser mais atraente em alguns perfis; em outros, a conta pode não fechar. A decisão requer um estudo que considere consumo, tarifas, geração solar, necessidades de reserva e investimento. O futuro da energia depende também de quando ela é usada A Tarifa Hora Certa reforça que produzir energia limpa é apenas parte da estratégia. Armazenamento e gerenciamento inteligente podem ajudar proprietários a consumir com mais eficiência, controlar custos e preparar seus imóveis para mudanças no setor elétrico. Para a i9 Solar, investimento inteligente é empregar tecnologia para transformar sustentabilidade em eficiência, conforto e valor no longo prazo. Sobre a i9 Solar A i9 Solar desenvolve soluções sustentáveis para imóveis residenciais e empresariais, incluindo sistemas fotovoltaicos, baterias, aquecimento solar, eficiência hídrica e carregamento de veículos elétricos.
