artigo.texto: Canadian Solar’s energy storage subsidiary, e-STORAGE, has partnered with renewable energy developer X-ELIO to deploy 590 MW/1.43 GWh DC of battery energy storage capacity. This will be spread across five projects in the US and Australia. The projects include four installations in Texas and one in New South Wales. The largest project in the list is a 200 MW/482 MWh project in Texas. For all these projects, e-STORAGE will supply its SolBank 3.0 battery systems built using battery cells manufactured at Canadian Solar’s facilities, along with power conversion systems and plant controls. The projects include 22-year long-term service agreements (LTSA). Shipments are already underway, with commercial operations expected in 2027 and 2028. The duo announced the agreement at RE+ 2026. EDF power solutions Australia, the Australian arm of French energy company EDF, has acquired the Holloway BESS project from SynCo Global. The proposed 250 MW / 1,000 MWh facility will be located near Armidale in New South Wales, within the New England Renewable Energy Zone (REZ). The four-hour battery system will store excess renewable electricity and supply power during periods of peak demand. EDF targets a final investment decision for late 2027 and to commence operations in 2029. Coreshell Technologies has raised $30 million in a Series B funding round. The round was co-led by silicon and specialty alloys producer Ferroglobe and investment firm Access Industries, with participation from ADS, Helios Ventures, Pegasus Tech Ventures, Mana Ventures, and Entrada Ventures. Coreshell said the funding will support technology commercialization, manufacturing expansion, and customer programs as it seeks to scale ‘China-free’ batteries for US industries. A lithium-ion battery producer, Coreshell replaces conventional graphite anodes with US-produced metallurgical silicon (MGS). The company has also secured a $50 million grant from the US Department of Energy to support domestic battery manufacturing. In October 2026, Coreshell announced an eight-year agreement with South Korean cathode materials producer L&F to secure access to lithium for its cathode supply chain. Ferroglobe also supplies its anode materials. US-based NeoVolta has signed a $116 million master purchase agreement with an unnamed energy solutions provider to supply battery energy storage systems (BESS) in 2027. Its majority-owned subsidiary, NeoVolta Power will supply its systems that comply with Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements. The agreement will support the company's manufacturing expansion at its facility in Pendergrass, Georgia, as it scales up domestic battery production. Japanese utility company Kansai Electric Power has agreed to acquire a minority stake in Prospect Power Storage, a 150 MW / 600 MWh battery energy storage project in Rockingham County, Virginia, US. It is making the investment through its US subsidiary, KPIC USA, from infrastructure developer Elevate Infrastructure and investment firm ArcLight Capital Partners. The project is the largest standalone battery storage facility currently operating in the PJM Interconnection region. The project has been operational since May 2026 and is backed by a 15-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Dominion Energy Virginia. The investment marks Kansai’s first battery storage project outside Japan. China’s Envision Energy is partnering with German battery storage developer and operator ju:niz Energy for a 442 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Bavaria, Germany. Named Smareg 13 (Vöhringen II), the project will be the companies’ third collaboration, bringing their combined project capacity to nearly 600 MWh. ju:niz Energy will handle the project’s development, financing, construction and long-term operation, while Envision will supply its Gen 8 BESS platform. The system will offer four-hour storage duration and grid-forming capabilities. It will be located next to ju:niz Energy’s operational Smareg 12 facility. UK-based clean energy developer Pathfinder Clean Energy (PACE) has secured a £68 million portfolio financing facility from Novuna Business Finance. It will use the proceeds to support four solar and battery energy storage projects in the UK, representing a combined of around 140 MW of solar and more than 55 MWh of co-located battery storage. It will initially refinance two operational projects in Norfolk, with the remaining projects included in a second phase. Indian renewable energy company ACME Solar Holdings Limited has signed a 25-year PPA with NTPC Limited for a 150 MW hybrid power project. The inter-state transmission system (ISTS)-connected project was awarded under NTPC’s Hybrid-IV tranche and will combine solar and wind power with energy storage. It has a tariff of INR 3.21 per kWh, with power supply scheduled to begin on June 30, 2028. It will be located across Bhadla, Rajasthan; Jambkhabalia, Gujarat; and Mandsaur, Madhya Pradesh. Separately, ACME Solar commissioned an additional 52.32 MW/209.28 MWh of battery energy storage capacity in Rajasthan at its 300 MW/1,200 MWh firm and dispatchable renewable energy (FDRE) project in Bikaner. With this addition, the cumulative commissioned BESS discharge capacity at the project has reached 247.67 MW/990.68 MWh.

artigo.texto: According to a new SEIA & Benchmark Mineral Intelligence report US energy storage installations have exceeded 200 GWh Utility-scale projects accounted for 12.2 GWh of Q3 additions, led by Texas, Arizona, and California Analysts forecast cumulative installations to reach 708 GWh by 2030 The US energy storage market has crossed 200 GWh of cumulative installed capacity, as battery deployments continue to expand across all segments, as per a new report. The total 215.9 GWh includes 14.3 GWh of new capacity in Q3 2026, taking installations during the first nine months of the year to 48.3 GWh. The figures are from the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 (ESMO), released by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. According to the report, utility-scale projects accounted for the bulk of Q3 installations, adding 12.2 GWh. Three GW-scale projects came online during the quarter, supporting growth in the utility-scale segment. Commercial and industrial (C&I) storage contributed 1.3 GWh, while residential systems added 746 MWh. The report said battery energy storage system (BESS) installations in Q3 at 14.3 GWh remained flat quarter-on-quarter (QoQ), but increased 23% year-on-year (YoY) for the first three quarters of 2026. Overall US installations were up 20% YoY during the January-September period. Texas led utility-scale storage deployment through Q3, adding 12.3 GWh. Arizona followed with 7.7 GWh, while California recorded 6.8 GWh. The report also highlighted the impact of solar and energy storage deployment on electricity prices. According to SEIA analysis, the growth of these technologies helped reduce average wholesale electricity prices by 42% in Texas and 51% in California between summer 2021 and summer 2026 (see Solar & Storage Cut Wholesale Electricity Prices In CAISO & ERCOT). Eleven states had already exceeded their previous annual energy storage installation records by the end of Q3, despite three months remaining in 2026. These included Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois. As states move from targets to centralized procurements, Benchmark Minerals Senior Analyst Pete Tillotson says energy storage pipelines are growing across utility mandates and bulk capacity contracts, thanks to “investment appetite and flexibility requirements”. In 2026, analysts project the annual installed BESS capacity of the US to reach 73.8 GWh, up 26% from 59 GWh installed in 2025 which was an increase of 30% over the previous year, comprising both utility and behind-the-meter (BTM) installations. This implies around 26 GWh of new additions in Q4 2026. SEIA and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence have raised their forecast for cumulative installations by 2030 by 3.7% to 708 GWh across grid-connected and behind-the-meter (BTM) applications. Annual installations are projected to exceed 129 GWh by 2030. Along with installations, domestic manufacturing is also seeing an uptick as per the report. Ultim Cells of LGES and General Motors began Lithium-ion Phosphate (LFP) commenced cell production for stationary storage in Tennessee in July 2026, while Samsung SDI opened LFP production at its StarPlus Energy facility in Indiana in October. This brought the total US battery cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, a 50% increase, according to the report. Battery module manufacturing capacity exceeded 109 GWh following the opening of an additional facility in Q3. Analysts forecast that LFP will account for 92% of lithium-ion BESS deployments in 2026, up from 77% in 2023. Lithium-ion batteries are expected to account for over 97% of all BESS installations in 2026. Other technologies, including flow batteries, sodium-ion and lead acid batteries, continue to lag behind lithium-ion. Recently US flow battery and sodium-ion cell manufacturer ESS Tech filed for relief under Chapter 7 (see US Battery Maker ESS Tech Files For Chapter 7 Bankruptcy). The complete report is available for purchase on Benchmark Mineral Intelligence website. Meanwhile on the policy front, following the results of the mid-term elections in the US, SEIA said more than 300 solar and storage companies recently urged Congressional leaders to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). The industry says the legislation could accelerate storage deployment, reduce project costs, lower prices, and improve access to affordable electricity.

artigo.texto: Empresa suíça apresentou em Londres a estratégia para que a computação de IA deixe de pressionar a rede elétrica e passe a ajudar a sustentá-la. E se o prédio que mais consome energia de uma cidade pudesse, em certos momentos, devolver eletricidade para a rede? É essa a aposta que a Hitachi Energy, empresa suíça de tecnologia para redes elétricas, levou ao seu Investor Day, evento para investidores realizado em Londres em novembro de 2026. A ideia é transformar os data centers de inteligência artificial, hoje vistos como grandes consumidores, em contribuidores do sistema elétrico. O pano de fundo é uma corrida. A computação de IA pode ser instalada em pouco tempo, mas as usinas, linhas e subestações que a alimentam levam muito mais para ficar prontas. Esse descompasso é o problema que a empresa quer atacar. Um consumo que não para de crescer Segundo a Hitachi Energy, a demanda global por eletricidade deve quase dobrar até 2050, empurrada pela eletrificação de transportes, edifícios e indústrias. Os data centers entram como um acelerador extra: a estimativa é que consumam cerca de 950 terawatt-hora por ano até 2030, quase o dobro do nível atual e mais do que o consumo anual de eletricidade do Japão. Para dar conta disso, a Agência Internacional de Energia calcula que o mundo precisará construir ou modernizar aproximadamente 80 milhões de quilômetros de linhas de energia nos próximos 25 anos. É o equivalente a toda a rede global em operação hoje. Como um data center vira fornecedor de energia No modelo defendido pela empresa, o data center não depende só de uma grande conexão com a rede. Ele combina geração no próprio local, armazenamento de energia, eletrônica de potência (equipamentos que controlam e convertem a corrente elétrica) e gestão inteligente de consumo. Quando a geração local supera a demanda dos computadores, o excedente pode ser exportado. Esses sistemas também podem prestar serviços técnicos à rede, como resposta de frequência, regulação de tensão e suporte de potência reativa, o que ajuda a integrar mais energia renovável, que oscila conforme sol e vento. Para quem opera data centers, a empresa vê acesso mais rápido à energia, uso mais enxuto de capital, maior resiliência e novas receitas com venda de eletricidade e serviços de rede, sujeitas às condições de mercado de cada local. A parceria com a Ansaldo e o truque das frequências A solução nasce de uma parceria estratégica recém-anunciada com a Ansaldo Energia. A Ansaldo entra com turbinas a gás e geração; a Hitachi Energy, com transformadores, equipamentos de alta tensão, eletrônica de potência, armazenamento e automação de rede. Uma peça central é o conversor estático de frequência. Ele permite que quem gera e quem recebe a eletricidade operem em frequências diferentes. Na prática, turbogeradores de 50 Hz da Ansaldo poderiam atender mercados de 60 Hz, como os Estados Unidos, sem redesenhar a turbina. Segundo a Hitachi Energy, o princípio já foi testado em larga escala: desde 2014, uma instalação de 413 MW na Alemanha converte energia de 50 Hz em 16 2/3 Hz para a rede ferroviária da Deutsche Bahn. Combinada a armazenamento e controles avançados, a eletrônica de potência também ajuda a lidar com as variações bruscas de carga típicas da computação de IA. As metas financeiras para 2030 Segundo a Hitachi Energy, a empresa busca crescimento anual composto de receita na casa dos 15% entre os anos fiscais de 2024 e 2030, com margem EBITA ajustada de 19% a 21%. A carteira de pedidos deve se aproximar de US$ 100 bilhões, sustentando receitas anuais de cerca de US$ 38 bilhões. Para o ano fiscal de 2026, a projeção é de receita de US$ 23,6 bilhões e margem EBITA ajustada de 15,7%. A companhia estima que clientes industriais e data centers representem uma oportunidade de mercado anual de US$ 130 bilhões até 2030. Para sustentar o crescimento, executa um programa global de investimentos de US$ 9 bilhões em fábricas, engenharia e tecnologia, e persegue retorno sobre o capital investido de 30% a 40%. Elevou ainda a meta de contribuição da IA em suas próprias operações para mais de US$ 350 milhões anuais no EBITA ajustado até 2030, e quer ampliar serviços digitais, como manutenção preditiva, com a plataforma HMAX. O que isso pode significar para a Amazônia A pauta é global, mas o debate chega à região. Data centers exigem energia firme e abundante, e a Amazônia tem rede em que muitas comunidades ainda dependem de geração isolada. A discussão de como integrar geração local, armazenamento e serviços de estabilidade à rede é a mesma que atravessa os sistemas da região, onde fontes renováveis precisam conviver com a necessidade de estabilidade. O material da empresa não cita projetos na Amazônia, mas o modelo mostra uma tendência: quem planeja infraestrutura digital precisará planejar junto a energia que a sustenta, e a forma como isso for feito definirá quem se beneficia, as comunidades do entorno ou apenas o próprio data center. Os próximos passos serão acompanhados nos resultados trimestrais da companhia e na implantação das primeiras soluções integradas com a Ansaldo Energia, que dirão se a promessa de data centers como ativos da rede sai do papel até 2030. artigo.texto: Lawmakers call for national data center construction pause Lawmakers say pause would give Congress time to pass artificial intelligence regulations WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Members of Congress are calling for a national moratorium on data center construction until the artificial intelligence field can be regulated. They said data centers are not helping local communities and, in many cases, are actively harming them. Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) said the White House is not doing enough on artificial intelligence. “The alarm bells are flashing. And the president and the White House are asleep at the switch when it comes to AI,” he said. McGovern said big tech leaders are becoming oligarchs and are enriching themselves at the expense of local communities with data centers. “These billionaires want to come into our communities, tell us what to do, and make a profit by driving up our utility prices, and wrecking our environment,” he said. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Mich.) said data centers do not provide the same community value as an automotive plant. “The value, the billions of dollars that is being raised to build these data centers, is built on the promise that it’s going to put people out of work,” he said. Lawmakers said pausing new construction would give Congress time to pass regulations and protect communities from future construction. Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) said she wants transparency in dealings between big tech and the government. “We don’t want back door deals and secret handshakes between big tech and the government. We want transparency, community engagement, and strong regulations that protect our air, water, climate and communities,” she said. It is not yet clear whether the plan has enough support to pass in the next Congress. The Trump administration has attempted to rename AI - artificial intelligence - as SI - super intelligence. artigo.texto: Regulação Plano da Stockland para um centro de dados de 444 MW em Sydney entra em consulta pública Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveA exposição pública do EIS é uma etapa de revisão e não uma aprovação para construir o… Ver mais - A exposição pública do EIS é uma etapa de revisão e não uma aprovação para construir o campus de Kemps Creek. - O EIS deve demonstrar uma Eficácia no Uso de Energia (Power Usage Effectiveness) de 1,3 ou melhor antes que o projeto possa prosseguir. - O número de aproximadamente 450 MW de plataforma garantida da Stockland é separado da capacidade do campus de Kemps Creek. O Portal de Planejamento de NSW iniciou, em 19 de novembro de 2026, a consulta pública sobre o estudo de impacto ambiental (EIS) do centro de dados proposto pela Stockland Development na Aldington Road. O campus de Kemps Creek, composto por dois edifícios, tem consumo máximo de energia declarado de 444 MW. As contribuições podem ser enviadas até 17 de dezembro de 2026. O empreendimento de importância estadual continua em avaliação; portanto, a consulta pública não autoriza sua construção. A atualização operacional da Stockland de 19 de outubro de 2026 informa que a participação da Stockland em Kemps Creek é de 50% e que o projeto tem como público-alvo clientes de IA e operadores de hiperescala, o que torna a análise de planejamento diretamente relevante para a estratégia da empresa em infraestrutura de IA. Requisitos de energia e refrigeração Os Requisitos de Avaliação Ambiental alterados do Secretário de Planejamento (SEARs), emitidos em 15 de setembro de 2026, estabelecem um consumo de energia de TI de até 360 MW, edifícios para salas de servidores com até 36,4 metros de altura, escritórios auxiliares, sistemas de energia de reserva e armazenamento de diesel, além de uma subestação com capacidade de distribuição de até 1.000 megavolt-ampères. O valor referente à TI é distinto do limite máximo para todo o campus informado no portal, pois separa os equipamentos de computação da infraestrutura de apoio, cuja demanda também deverá ser quantificada no EIS. Na página do projeto, a Stockland localiza a proposta em um terreno industrial na área de Mamre Road, no oeste de Sydney, e informa que o projeto foi concebido em torno de uma tecnologia de refrigeração a ar que não depende de água para resfriar as instalações. Em março de 2026, a Autoridade de Entrega de Investimentos de NSW reconheceu o projeto como um investimento do setor privado em setores críticos, incluindo a infraestrutura digital. A eficiência e o fornecimento de energia fazem parte dos critérios de aprovação. O EIS deve demonstrar que o empreendimento pode atingir um índice de eficiência energética (PUE) de 1,3 ou menos, equivalente a uma classificação de cinco estrelas ou superior no NABERS Data Centre Energy, e abordar as metas estaduais de eficiência no uso da água (WUE). Também deve assumir o compromisso de igualar, em todos os momentos, a demanda operacional de eletricidade ao fornecimento de energia renovável proveniente de NSW. Esses são requisitos da avaliação, não medições de uma instalação em operação. Os sistemas de energia de reserva e refrigeração devem ser modelados para situações de interrupção não programada, testes e manutenção. As avaliações de ruído e qualidade do ar devem incluir os efeitos cumulativos de outros centros de dados propostos e aprovados nas proximidades, além de estudos específicos sobre tráfego, água, biodiversidade e infraestrutura de serviços públicos. Plataforma de desenvolvimento da Stockland A atualização operacional da Stockland descreve sua oportunidade no setor de centros de dados como uma parceria com a operadora global EdgeConneX e informa que cerca de 450 MW de energia foram garantidos para a plataforma, além de identificar quatro locais adicionais em seu portfólio existente de logística. A garantia do fornecimento de energia está sujeita ao projeto final, à documentação e às negociações com os clientes; o valor se refere à plataforma como um todo, não à capacidade de Kemps Creek. Essa distinção é importante porque os documentos de planejamento medem fatores diferentes: a energia garantida em todo o portfólio da Stockland, a carga de TI em Kemps Creek e o consumo máximo total proposto para o campus. Manter essas medidas separadas evidencia tanto a escala da proposta individual quanto o estágio comercial e técnico ainda inicial da plataforma mais ampla. Outros registros de planejamento na região de Sydney O registro do centro de dados de Wetherill Park está na etapa de preparação dos SEARs e descreve um único edifício de quatro andares, em operação 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana, com capacidade total aproximada de 238 MW e carga de TI de 170 MW. As obras também incluem demolição e preparação do terreno, uma subestação no local e uma linha de transmissão. A atualização da Stockland identifica esse local como 100% pertencente à empresa e voltado à mesma categoria de clientes de IA e operadores de hiperescala. Um registro separado do portal para o endereço 192 Narellan Road, em Campbelltown está na etapa de preparação do EIS. Ele descreve a construção e a operação, 24 horas por dia e 7 dias por semana, de um centro de dados de 100 MW, com altura máxima de 30 metros para o edifício. Tanto esse projeto quanto o de Wetherill Park estão em etapas anteriores do processo de planejamento em relação à consulta pública de Kemps Creek. Para a Stockland, Kemps Creek é o teste imediato para saber se um campus voltado a clientes de IA e operadores de hiperescala pode atender aos requisitos de NSW sobre eficiência, energia renovável e impactos cumulativos. A consulta pública e as etapas restantes da avaliação devem ocorrer antes de qualquer decisão sobre a construção; a empresa prevê uma decisão em 2027, mas essa previsão não corresponde a uma data fixa de aprovação.

artigo.texto: A ABDAN (Associação Brasileira para o Desenvolvimento de Atividades Nucleares) e o Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) confirmaram a realização de um workshop técnico internacional nos dias 26 e 27 de janeiro de 2027, na sede da Firjan (Federação das Indústrias do Estado do Rio de Janeiro), focado na inserção de pequenos reatores modulares (SMRs) e microrreatores (MMRs) na matriz energética corporativa. A capacitação técnica, intitulada Powering the Future: Developing an Advanced Nuclear Strategy, direciona sua grade a executivos e especialistas de setores de base e infraestrutura crítica digital, com foco em resolver o iminente gargalo de fornecimento elétrico contínuo demandado pelo avanço acelerado da computação de alto desempenho e da inteligência artificial. Segundo a entidade setorial remetente, a iniciativa responde à urgência de diversificação das alternativas de suprimento firme (baseload) para operações industriais de grande porte e instalações de processamento de dados em hiperescala. A programação no Centro do Rio de Janeiro pretende traçar parâmetros comparativos de custos nivelados de energia (LCOE), requisitos de licenciamento e arquiteturas de integração física direta (behind-the-meter), aproximando os tomadores de decisão nacionais dos parâmetros consolidados pela indústria nuclear global. Pressão de carga da inteligência artificial e gargalos de suprimento contínuo A proliferação de complexos de data centers voltados ao processamento de redes neurais profundas impõe um padrão de consumo energético sem precedentes nas redes elétricas globais e regionais. Diferentemente de plantas fabris tradicionais com perfis de carga variáveis ou previsíveis em turnos, servidores de computação acelerada demandam disponibilidade ininterrupta superior a 99,999%, operando com fator de capacidade praticamente contínuo ao longo de 8.760 horas por ano. Embora o Brasil mantenha uma matriz majoritariamente renovável ancorada na geração hidrelétrica, a expansão acelerada de fontes intermitentes, como a solar fotovoltaica e a eólica, introduz volatilidade operacional e custos crescentes em serviços ancilares para a estabilização de frequência. De acordo com a ABDAN, o esgotamento da capacidade de conexão em subestações centrais e as restrições nas linhas de transmissão do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) colocam a geração dedicada no mesmo local da demanda como uma rota necessária para novos investimentos tecnológicos. Operações industriais eletrointensivas — compreendendo cadeias de óleo e gás, complexos de mineração, plantas de papel e celulose e polos de processamento petroquímico — enfrentam restrições análogas de expansão física quando localizadas em áreas periféricas ou distantes dos troncos de alta tensão, o que amplia o interesse pelo fornecimento modular in loco. Nesse cenário de transição energética, a necessidade de descarbonização dos escopos 1 e 2 das corporações colide frequentemente com a limitação de alternativas térmicas de base livre de emissões de gases de efeito estufa. A tecnologia nuclear de pequeno porte surge, na avaliação defendida pela ABDAN e pelo EPRI, como uma das poucas rotas com densidade energética suficiente para fornecer simultaneamente eletricidade constante e calor de processo em alta temperatura, sem geração de emissões atmosféricas diretas durante a operação. Arquitetura técnica comparativa de reatores avançados A transição conceitual das grandes centrais nucleares convencionais — tipicamente configuradas em potências superiores a 1.000 MW por bloco e caracterizadas por ciclos de construção decenais — para sistemas modulares e microrreatores altera a dinâmica de alocação de capital e mitigação de risco de engenharia. Os SMRs, dimensionados internacionalmente para potências elétricas de até 300 MW por módulo, e os MMRs, limitados a patamares de até 10 MW, baseiam-se em fabricação fabril seriada, transporte rodoviário ou ferroviário padronizado e sistemas intrínsecos de segurança passiva. A conformação dos sistemas de arrefecimento passivo elimina a dependência de fontes externas de energia elétrica de emergência para manter a circulação do fluido refrigerante em situações de desligamento não programado. Essa inovação mitiga substancialmente os requisitos de zonas de planejamento de emergência externa (EPZ), permitindo a proximidade física entre a fonte geradora e as plantas industriais consumidoras ou os campi de data centers corporativos. Além do fornecimento de eletricidade, a ABDAN alega que o aproveitamento do calor de processo gerado pelos fluidos térmicos desses reatores avançados, que podem operar em temperaturas de 300 °C a mais de 750 °C dependendo do refrigerante (água leve, gás hélio, sódio líquido ou sais fundidos), oferece ganhos econômicos para a indústria petroquímica e siderúrgica. Essa integração viabiliza a produção de vapor supercrítico e hidrogênio de baixo carbono via eletrólise de alta temperatura sem queima de combustíveis fósseis. Competitividade industrial e atração de investimentos corporativos A viabilidade de implantação de ecossistemas corporativos baseados em SMRs e MMRs no Brasil pressupõe a evolução de modelos de negócios e arranjos regulatórios. Conforme detalhado na pauta do workshop, a colaboração com o EPRI visa transferir metodologia analítica para que o setor privado dimensione matrizes de custo total de propriedade (TCO), seguros patrimoniais, estratégias de aquisição de combustível e acordos de compra de energia de longo prazo (PPAs) indexados à segurança operacional contínua. O presidente da ABDAN, Celso Cunha, ressalta a relevância da qualificação técnica do ecossistema econômico local frente à corrida internacional pela atração de data centers para modelos de inteligência artificial soberana e hiperescala: “Os pequenos reatores modulares e os microrreatores estão ganhando espaço no planejamento energético de diversos países. artigo.texto: When the dust was still settling after November’s election, Elon Musk posted on X that “data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” This might sound like a crazy idea. But is it? Musk’s post was a reaction to the electorate’s overwhelming rejection of data centers. Voters backed regulations and politicians vowing to halt new construction, concerned about the tremendous energy and water resources needed to power data centers, along with the noise pollution. While it may be technically feasible to someday launch data centers into low orbit to run off of solar electricity — and companies like Google and SpaceX are exploring the idea — for now, this remains science fiction beset by massive technical and financial hurdles. But Musk’s post brings up an interesting discussion: Why not build in the equivalent of the cosmos, meaning in a place with lots of, well, space? The two main components a data center needs are land and energy — the more abundant and cheaper, the better. The other necessity is a welcoming regulatory environment. A small town in North Dakota is the only place where voters supported data centers. The state has plentiful and cheap land and is a major producer of natural gas and wind energy. So why not construct miles and miles of data centers there or in a similar place that’s actually welcoming them? Or what about Canada? Prime Minister Mark Carney is trying to lure technology companies to build there, touting the cooler climate, open spaces, and abundant renewable energy, largely supplied by hydroelectric power. The energy-rich province of Alberta is offering a “concierge service” to ease the approvals process. Meta took the plunge this summer, breaking ground on a $13 billion complex. Even if most Americans don’t want data centers in their backyards, the fact remains that these buildings are the backbone of our modern economy, providing computational power far beyond the needs of artificial intelligence. Data centers enable cloud computing and allow modern financial services, health care, and entertainment streaming to function. To be clear, the editorial board isn’t suggesting thrusting all of our worries onto North Dakota or Canada. Communities there deserve the same protections as any place — developers should pay for their own energy and grid upgrades, and ideally power their centers using renewable energy. Tax incentives should be tied into local economic benefits. Even if a rural place could extract these arrangements, a big if, concentrating large data centers across a place such as the Northern Great Plains would still be a heavy lift. “The difficulty is one of scale and of timelines,” Mohammad Hajiesmaili, who researches carbon-intelligent computing at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, told the editorial board. “Some proposed campuses would draw more than a gigawatt each, and one gigawatt running around the clock is more electricity than the entire city of Boston uses in a year.” That would require new power generation and transmission lines, which could take years to plan, permit, and build, with no guarantees what demand could look like in a few years. Clustering data centers also adds risk — a power outage, severe weather, or a cyber or physical attack could bring a concentrated system to its knees. Just like with an investment portfolio, diversification is key to minimizing the possibility of a catastrophe. Building large data centers in remote areas in conjunction with smaller projects near populated areas, including in Massachusetts, might be the best path forward. From a computing standpoint, there are clear advantages to locating some data centers closer to where computing power is needed, namely better speed and reliability. Transmitting data across vast distances also adds cost. Data travels through fiber-optic cables incredibly fast, about two-thirds the speed of light, but distance can still matter. Autonomous vehicles rely on real-time data. Doctors performing robotic surgery need lightning quick computing. Military operations cannot afford a lag. But for the overwhelming majority of us using a chatbot, or even scientists or businesses doing research, we can afford to wait a few extra milliseconds for our answers. The results of the midterm election present an opportunity to slow down and think through an optimal national strategy. Data centers are also only going to get more energy efficient, so pumping the brakes could be a good thing to control costs, conserve energy, and protect the environment, a win-win-win. Economists have compared the buildout of data centers today to the railroad boom of the late 19th century, when financial speculation and intense competition led to laying far more rails than needed. To be clear, railroads presented a leap forward just as data centers do today. But in 1873, the checks came due, the economy collapsed, and the United States and Europe entered a six-year depression. Let’s hope it doesn’t come to that and we can learn from history’s mistakes. Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board. Follow us @GlobeOpinion.

artigo.texto: Whitley County residents weigh in on data center rules FORT WAYNE, Ind. (WPTA) - The Whitley County Plan Commission just heard from the public Wednesday night on proposed rules for data centers. The debate, which took place at Columbia High School, was over a drafted proposal that addresses where data centers could be built, how far they’d have to be from homes, and requirements for noise and water use. Community members shared their thoughts with the commission, and some speakers want the county to go even farther than the proposed restrictions and ban larger data centers. “I still think there should be a permanent moratorium on class two and three for sure. Class one, I haven’t made up my mind on that, but I still don’t see the benefit and the need for those types of data centers in Whitley County,” one speaker said, Others said that data centers can bring jobs and investment to the area, while still holding developers accountable. “I’m not asking everybody to give a company a blank check. I’m asking everybody to keep an open mind, demand responsible development, look at the actual numbers, and consider the long-term opportunities,” another speaker added. artigo.texto: Alberta put its data center rules and its oil sands emissions policy into one bill on November 18, 2026. Mining Weekly reported that the province unveiled limits on large data centers and dropped the oil sands emissions cap, and Reuters and other outlets ran the same story. The legislation behind both moves is Bill 42, the Energy, Environment and Utilities Statutes Amendment Act, 2026. It is proposed law, not enacted law. The data center half is the part developers will study first. Facilities of 10 megawatts or larger would sit at least 600 metres from the nearest home, stay off the province’s best farmland and its irrigated land, and answer to the Alberta Utilities Commission. The rules arrive as Canadian operators race to add AI capacity, including the Toronto platform we covered in Vertical Data’s 150 MW pipeline. The oil sands half is quieter. Bill 42 would repeal the Oil Sands Emissions Limit Act, a 2016 law that set a 100 million tonne annual ceiling and never took effect through regulation. This analysis walks through what the bill says, what Alberta has left unconfirmed, how the rules stack up against other jurisdictions, and what to watch as the legislature takes it up. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Alberta Bill 42 Changes at a Glance Alberta introduced Bill 42 on November 18, 2026. The title signals a broad housekeeping bill covering energy, environment and utilities statutes, and the contents bear that out. Two items drive the headlines, and a third gets less attention. The province would set new siting and regulatory rules for large data centers, repeal the Oil Sands Emissions Limit Act, and require financial security for closing and reclaiming new oil and gas wells. The province laid out the data center package in its own announcement on new restrictions for data centres. The table below condenses the confirmed provisions and flags what the province has not yet pinned down. Two cautions apply before anyone reads this as settled policy. First, a bill introduced on November 18 still has to move through the legislature, and the sources we reviewed give no passage date or in-force date. Second, several details that matter to builders, such as the water number, are missing from the public material. We flag each gap as we go. The 10 MW Threshold: Which Data Centers Get Caught The line sits at 10 megawatts. Anything at that scale or above faces the new siting rules, and the Alberta Utilities Commission becomes its regulator. Smaller facilities fall outside the package as described. How big is 10 MW? It is large for an enterprise server room and small for a modern AI campus. A single AI-focused project can run far beyond it. Giga Energy’s $1 billion lease for a 60 MW Texas AI site, which we covered on this site, would clear the Alberta threshold six times over. A midsize colocation hall or an edge facility serving a city could land near the line, which is where the drafting will matter most. There is also a wording wrinkle. The province describes the covered facilities as 10 megawatts or larger in the setback and land provisions, while the regulator provision speaks of data centers larger than 10 megawatts. The gap looks like loose phrasing rather than a policy split. Still, a developer sizing a project at exactly 10 MW should read the bill text rather than rely on press summaries, since one word decides whether the project needs commission review. The threshold also shapes behavior. Rules that bite at a fixed capacity invite projects sized just under the line, or phased builds that start small and expand. Large-load rules in other markets face the same design problem, and Alberta has not said how it would treat staged expansions. That silence is worth watching when the committee stage opens. The 600-Metre Setback: 1,970 Feet From Your Front Door The setback rule is the easiest to picture. A covered data center would need a minimum of 600 metres between its site and the nearest home or residential dwelling. For US readers, that is about 1,970 feet, or 0.37 miles. The distance is measured to the nearest dwelling, so a single farmhouse near the edge of a parcel counts. Reports describe the buffer as a response to community effects such as noise and lighting. Large facilities run cooling fans and backup generators around the clock, and lit perimeters add glare at night. A 600 metre gap does not erase those effects, but it moves most of them beyond the property line of a typical residence. Municipal Add-Ons and Reduced Setbacks Reporting on the bill says municipalities could set stricter setbacks than the provincial minimum, and that some projects could win a reduced setback if the affected landowners and the Alberta Utilities Commission agree. We treat both as reported rather than confirmed, because the official release does not carry them. If they hold, they create a floor with local ratchets and a negotiated exit, which is a common pattern in setback law. The landowner-consent route would matter most in rural areas where a single neighbor controls the land around a proposed site. A developer could buy or lease the adjoining parcels, secure agreement, and ask the commission to shrink the buffer. Whether that route stays open in the final bill is one of the first things industry lawyers will test. Here is a simplified screen a developer might run before spending money on a site. artigo.texto: As empresas precisam desenvolver proativamente um plano para reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa. A redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa (GEE) está se tornando uma exigência urgente para as empresas em sua produção e operações, especialmente à medida que as regulamentações sobre inventário de emissões, redução e mercado de carbono são cada vez mais aprimoradas. Em resposta a essa exigência, as empresas na província de Tay Ninh precisam desenvolver proativamente planos estratégicos, inovar em tecnologia e usar a energia de forma eficiente para atender às regulamentações e avançar rumo ao desenvolvimento sustentável. Na indústria cimenteira, a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa exige que as empresas inovem em tecnologia, utilizem matérias-primas e combustíveis de forma eficiente e controlem as fontes de emissão. De acordo com o Sr. Nguyen Viet Thanh, Diretor Adjunto de Gestão da Qualidade da Fico-YTL Cement Joint Stock Company, a empresa planeja mitigar as emissões de gases de efeito estufa durante o período de 2026 a 2030, organizar a implementação e divulgar os resultados conforme necessário. Para atingir esse objetivo, a empresa concentra-se em três grupos principais de soluções: aumentar o uso de combustíveis alternativos por meio do coprocessamento de resíduos; otimizar a proporção de clínquer nos produtos de cimento; e otimizar a operação e a manutenção dos equipamentos. Em particular, o coprocessamento de resíduos em fornos de cimento é considerado uma das soluções importantes para aumentar o uso de combustíveis alternativos, contribuindo para a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa durante a produção. O coprocessamento de resíduos em fornos de cimento apresenta muitas vantagens ambientais em comparação com métodos de tratamento convencionais, como incineração ou aterro sanitário. Essa tecnologia aproveita as altas temperaturas do forno, que variam de 1.450 a 1.800 °C, operando continuamente 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana, em um ambiente oxidante, o que contribui para a completa incineração dos resíduos. Além disso, o ambiente altamente alcalino do forno é capaz de absorver e neutralizar os gases ácidos gerados. O sistema de filtragem de poeira e controle de emissões opera continuamente 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana, com os dados conectados e transmitidos ao Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente para fins de monitoramento. Uma vantagem notável dessa tecnologia é que as cinzas e a escória, após o processamento, são reutilizadas no processo de produção de cimento, visando a reutilização de 100% e reduzindo a quantidade de resíduos que precisam ser tratados por outros métodos. Em termos de capacidade de processamento, o sistema tem capacidade para processar de 2 a 3 toneladas/hora de resíduos líquidos e de 10 a 12 toneladas/hora de resíduos sólidos. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Viet Thanh, além da tecnologia de coprocessamento de resíduos, a Fico-YTL também implementa a solução de gestão de resíduos HEVEA, com o objetivo de fornecer serviços de tratamento de resíduos para organizações e empresas. A HEVEA herda a experiência internacional do Grupo YTL, visando oferecer soluções avançadas que atendam aos padrões internacionais. Os clientes da unidade incluem empresas, incluindo corporações multinacionais e organizações com necessidades de tratamento de resíduos. Você também pode gostar Os tipos de resíduos que a HEVEA aceita incluem resíduos domésticos selecionados; resíduos industriais em geral; e resíduos industriais perigosos. A empresa oferece dois grupos principais de serviços: serviços de descarte de resíduos e serviços de coprocessamento de resíduos, e coordena a implementação com as autoridades e empresas relevantes. No setor de fabricação de aço e chapas metálicas, empresas como a Vina One Steel Manufacturing Joint Stock Company priorizam a eficiência energética para reduzir as emissões. De acordo com o Sr. Duong Hoai Hai, Assistente do Diretor Geral da Vina One Steel Manufacturing Joint Stock Company, a maior fonte de emissões da empresa provém da eletricidade comprada da rede para produção e operação. Em relação às emissões diretas, os fornos e caldeiras que utilizam GNV (Gás Natural Veicular) são as principais fontes. Com base nos resultados do inventário de gases de efeito estufa, a Vina One Steel Manufacturing Joint Stock Company desenvolveu um plano para reduzir as emissões até 2030, visando uma redução de 3% em 2026 e 2027 e de 5% ao ano durante o período de 2028 a 2030. Para atingir essa meta, a empresa concentra-se na otimização da operação de máquinas, na conversão para sistemas de iluminação LED, na instalação de inversores de frequência, na redução do tempo ocioso dos equipamentos e na melhoria da eficiência da combustão. “Além disso, a empresa está estudando a expansão da área para instalação de energia solar em telhados, convertendo gradualmente os processos de produção adequados para o uso de energia renovável. Inventários anuais de gases de efeito estufa, monitoramento de dados de consumo de energia, substituição de equipamentos de refrigeração de baixa eficiência e otimização das operações de transporte também estão incluídos no plano”, informou o Sr. Duong Hoai Hai. Inventário de gases de efeito estufa - a base para uma transição verde. Segundo o vice-diretor do Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, Tran Khac Phuc, responder às mudanças climáticas e cumprir o compromisso nacional de alcançar emissões líquidas zero até 2050 é uma prioridade estratégica máxima. Portanto, juntamente com os esforços das empresas, as agências competentes estão se concentrando em aprimorar os mecanismos, as políticas e as diretrizes para a realização de inventários de gases de efeito estufa. Isso fornecerá uma base para que as instalações emissoras melhorem sua capacidade de gestão, desenvolvam planos de redução de emissões e se preparem para as novas demandas do mercado de carbono. artigo.texto: A Assembleia Legislativa do Paraná (Alep) aprovou na terça-feira (17) o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (Prodatapr), que autoriza o Governo do Estado a conceder benefícios fiscais para atrair data centers. O projeto é dos deputados Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (PP) e Pedro Paulo Bazana (PSD). O Projeto de Lei 55/2026 estabelece diretrizes para a instalação e a expansão dessas estruturas, com foco na economia digital, na atração de investimentos privados e na geração de empregos especializados. A proposta também busca aproveitar a produção de energia renovável e a conectividade do Paraná. Segundo a justificativa, o objetivo é tornar o Estado um polo de data centers na América Latina e fortalecer a cadeia produtiva de tecnologia. Energia renovável e uso racional da água O programa incentiva novos empreendimentos, a ampliação da infraestrutura de telecomunicações e parcerias entre empresas, universidades e centros de pesquisa. Na área ambiental, estimula o uso de fontes renováveis de energia, o aproveitamento do biometano, o uso racional da água e tecnologias sustentáveis de resfriamento dos equipamentos. Os data centers armazenam e processam grandes volumes de informações usadas por empresas, governos, bancos, hospitais, universidades e plataformas digitais. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial, essas instalações ganharam importância na disputa mundial por investimentos em tecnologia. “A inteligência artificial, a computação em nuvem e os serviços digitais dependem de uma infraestrutura robusta de processamento de dados. Temos energia, universidades, profissionais qualificados e um ambiente favorável à inovação. Queremos transformar essas vantagens em investimentos, empregos e oportunidades para os paranaenses”, afirmou Maria Victoria. Formação de profissionais Luiz Fernando Guerra destacou a necessidade de preparar mão de obra para o setor. “Com esse projeto, o Paraná terá diretrizes para planejar a expansão dos data centers, dar mais previsibilidade a quem pretende investir e identificar os empreendimentos estratégicos para o Estado. Para operar e manter essas estruturas, as empresas vão precisar de profissionais preparados”, disse. Para Bazana, a expansão deve beneficiar também o interior. “Defendo que a expansão dos centros de dados fortaleça também as empresas locais, estimule a formação profissional e leve empregos qualificados ao interior”, declarou. Lei federal criou regime especial A aprovação ocorre dois meses depois da sanção da Lei Federal nº 15.504, em setembro de 2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). A legislação federal prevê incentivos tributários condicionados a compromissos de sustentabilidade, investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento e uso de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão.

Moment Energy Unveils Nova, the Next Generation Battery Energy Storage System Made from EV Batteries Moment Energy 6 min read The UL-certified, ITC-eligible system is built at the company's award-winning Megafactory 1, with deployments planned at commercial sites across North America Moment Energy has unveiled Nova, the world's first BESS made with repurposed electric vehicle batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification. Manufactured at the company's Megafactory 1, Nova provides commercial, industrial, and large-scale energy users with resilient backup power, utility savings, and clean energy integration. AUSTIN, Texas and VANCOUVER, British Columbia, Nov. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Moment Energy today unveiled Nova, its next-generation battery energy storage system (BESS). Nova is the world's first BESS made with repurposed electric vehicle batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification. The certifications help support its use in commercial, industrial and large-scale energy storage applications. Nova is now in production at the company's award-winning Megafactory 1 for deployment across North America. The BESS enables commercial customers to reduce energy costs, improve site reliability and uptime, and integrate clean energy into their operations. Moment Energy has already deployed systems powering critical infrastructure including airports, hospitals, agricultural and manufacturing sites. Nova is made in North America and independently verified as fully compliant with Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements. Moment Energy has also been independently verified as a non-Prohibited Foreign Entity. Together, this makes Nova the only third-party verified BESS eligible for the U.S. federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) in 2027 and beyond. "Access to affordable power is a defining factor determining where businesses can grow and what they can build. Today, businesses across North America are being throttled by power capacity constraints," said Edward Chiang, Co-Founder and CEO of Moment Energy. "We see a future where reengineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chain. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering and North American manufacturing to deploy the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid." Designed for Performance, Flexibility and Long-Term Value The Nova platform is designed to integrate batteries from multiple types of EVs into its flexible stationary storage platform. Moment Energy's proprietary AI-powered battery management system (BMS) continuously evaluates and optimizes batteries across different states of health to maximize performance, efficiency and reliability throughout the system's life. Each Nova block delivers 200 kW of power / 500 kWh of energy within a 2.94 m by 1.80 m (9.65 ft x 5.9 ft) footprint. This compact, scalable design brings substantial energy storage capacity to commercial sites where space is an important consideration, while also enabling Nova to deploy in large-scale installations in the tens of MWhs. Nova helps commercial energy users save by supporting grid services and utility bill savings, as well as providing resilient backup power during grid outages. Nova's swappable architecture allows individual battery packs to be replaced as they age over time, instead of replacing the entire system. Durable infrastructure such as the enclosure and concrete pad can remain undisturbed, while the battery packs are serviced and replaced. This design extends the system's lifespan to more than 20 years with Moment Energy's capacity augmentation service. "With Nova, we've solved the engineering challenges that have prevented BESS made with EV batteries from scaling commercially," said Gurmesh Sidhu, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer of Moment Energy. "Every element of the platform has been engineered to maximize flexibility, simplify servicing and give customers confidence that the system will reliably power their critical infrastructure for decades." Batteries Made in North America As battery storage becomes increasingly critical for commercial energy users, battery supply has become a global issue of international trade and national security, with the large majority of batteries currently imported from China. By establishing a new domestic supply chain from the abundant supply of retiring EV batteries, Moment Energy's Nova allows the U.S. and Canada to keep critical minerals and battery software in North America. Repurposing is an important step in the circular economy, unlocking years or even decades of residual value in a battery after its useful life for electric vehicle applications is over, preventing batteries from entering landfills. Nova brings that value into commercial energy infrastructure through a platform engineered, manufactured and supported in North America. Engineered and Certified for Safety Nova is the first BESS built from EV batteries that is certified to UL 9540 by UL Solutions. Nova has achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications, key safety certifications also commonly held by first-life battery systems, and has been tested to UL 9540A for evaluating thermal runaway fire propagation in BESS. With these certifications, Nova meets the listing requirements of electrical codes of the United States and Canada for stationary storage. Additionally, Megafactory 1 is certified to UL 1974, the standard for sorting, grading and repurposing electric vehicle batteries. artigo.texto: The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone. The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Q3 was a little slower: The US installed 14.3 GWh in those three months, down 1% year over year. Texas is in the lead Texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state. Arizona came in second at 7.7 GWh, followed by California at 6.8 GWh. And 11 states had already broken their annual storage installation records with three months to go – Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois. Utility-scale batteries did most of the work in Q3, accounting for 12.2 GWh of new capacity. Businesses and industrial sites added another 1.3 GWh, and residential added 746 megawatt-hours (MWh). That was the best Q3 yet for home batteries, though installs through September were still down 12% year over year. Some homeowners moved up their installations last year before the federal residential clean energy tax credit ended. “States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” said Pete Tillotson, a senior analyst at Benchmark. In September, New York awarded contracts for eight battery projects that can deliver about 950 megawatts (MW) combined. SEIA and Benchmark now expect 708 GWh of storage across the grid, homes, and businesses by 2030, up 3.7% from their previous forecast. The US can also make more battery cells here. A Tennessee factory opened in July and an Indiana factory opened in October, bringing US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, up 50%. What about people’s electric bills? Solar and batteries helped bring down average summer wholesale power prices by 42% in Texas’s ERCOT market and 51% in California’s CAISO market between 2021 and 2026, according to SEIA’s inflation-adjusted analysis. When batteries had power to spare during peak hours, grid operators could call on expensive power plants less often. You wouldn’t know it from looking at the total on residential electric bills. The cost of generating power for households fell in both markets, but the cost of delivering it to homes rose. Overall, residential bills rose 22% at the two California utilities SEIA examined and 3% across its Texas utility sample, driven by higher transmission and distribution costs. California is upgrading its grid to reduce the risk of wildfires. Texas is expanding its grid for rising demand and make it more resilient to storms. artigo.texto: Ohio Becomes the Epicenter of Data Center Backlash After Tax Credits Cost State’s Schools $374 Million Angela Huffman, a sixth-generation farmer, spent 15 years in agriculture policy in Columbus, OH, and Washington, DC. But her focus lately has been 10 miles from her Wharton, OH, sheep farm. On June 4, Huffman picked up her local newspaper, the Daily Chief-Union. The above-the-fold headline revealed a developer was eyeing a $900 million data center in nearby Upper Sandusky. The headline "stopped me cold," Huffman says. The proposal would have planted a 146-acre Smartland Energy data center campus, with a natural gas power plant, on the north edge of town. "We were already worried about a big development coming in and extracting the town's resources," Huffman tells Realtor.com®. Townsfolk were already concerned after another recent proposal for a soybean processing plant. "What does that do to the community?" she says. Huffman, CEO of Farm Action, says her family has owned its nearby farm for six generations. Organizing concerned neighbors, they began filling planning commission meetings and peppering officials with questions about the impact of the development. They also questioned if it should be approved on industrial zoning, as neighbors had hoped. A petition opposing the project drew 1,100 signatures. Many residents worried about how such a major project could change their rural way of life. And Upper Sandusky wasn't alone. Ohio was the heart of data center resistance in the midterms. Voters in 18 of its 88 counties backed 21 bans or restrictions on development of those projects. One of those was in Upper Sandusky, where voters approved a charter amendment blocking large data centers within the limits of the 6,600-person town. "They wanted to use about a third of the water the whole town uses today," Huffman says. "I'm not against AI or development, but can a town of this size absorb a development like that?" Data center tax breaks come into view But the state already hosts dozens of large centers. And they already exact a cost. A new study shows that the state's data center tax break derived its schools of almost $374 million in revenue in 2025 alone. Republican Gov. Mike DeWine paused the tax breaks in May after the state realized developers were exempted from $2.1 billion in taxes in 2024 and 2025, far more than initally projected. Gov.-elect Amy Acton has promised further scrutiny. Good Jobs First and Policy Matters Ohio studied where those missing tax dollars would have gone. The state's Fair School Funding Plan allocates some sales tax to schools. So by exempting data center developers from the 5.75% sales tax, those schools missed out on revenue. "Ohio lawmakers made a choice to give data center companies a blank check, and now Ohio's schools are paying the price," said Hannah Halbert, Policy Matters Ohio's executive director. "In 2025 alone, the state gave up enough revenue from this single tax break to fully update the Fair School Funding plan and close the gap." This comes at a time when homeowners were being asked to make up the difference. Many Ohio schools aimed to raise money through levies this year, but many were unsuccessful. The Ohio Policy Education Institute found just 24 of 66 levies on the May 2026 ballot had passed. Upper Sandusky's school district was one of the losers—missing out on $383,000 in revenue, according to the report. While voters have approved levies for its schools in 2015, 2018, and 2023, it's still been forced to cancel classes this year because it can't install air conditioning in century-old buildings that are too expensive to rebuild. "Our schools were struggling," Huffman says. "It tells you a lot about when these big tech companies come along, and if they are paying their fair share." Wider backlash Voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. NBC exit polls show 76% of voters opposed data center building in their communities, and a majority considered them "crucial" to their votes. Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs, raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas. That's despite a major spending spree by the industry. Ohio was barraged with $1.8 million in data center ads in the fall, Pew Research Center found—more than Texas, Wisconsin, and other large states. AI and crypto political action committees spent an estimated $65 million backing Republican Sen. John Husted, who lost reelection to Democrat Sherrod Brown on Nov. 3. Developers, after all, have big plans in the state, having pitched $168.7 billion in new projects. Regulation of data center developments and AI could be a major factor for new Democratic leaders in Columbus and Washington, DC. Sober to that reality, tech stocks tanked after the election. Acton says she supports a conditional moratorium on data centers. She wants to see them cover their utility costs, build with union labor, and abide by environmental standards. She also says she wants to see incentives "reined in" for the large developments. AI companies address future scrutiny Artificial intelligence companies have spent the days since the election promising they'll work with cities and residents on data centers. OpenAI published a "blueprint for responsible development" promising to slow the technology. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone cited a commitment "to pay our own energy and water costs so they're not passed onto consumers, fund new and upgraded grid infrastructure, and support local communities." Ohio isn't alone, either. Virginia, another data center hot spot, spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. artigo.texto: What happened in Marshall, Michigan Ford said Wednesday it has started U.S. battery cell output for its next wave of electric vehicles using technology licensed from China's CATL. The first cells rolled out last month at the Marshall complex, and they are already shipping for prototype builds of the Fathom small electric pickup that CEO Jim Farley has positioned against Tesla and Chinese competitors. Ford framed this as a step toward wider use of lithium iron phosphate cells - the lower cost LFP chemistry - in U.S. vehicles. The chemistry was developed in the U.S. but reached commercial scale largely in China. Alan Clarke, who oversees advanced development projects as a vice president at Ford, said the CATL license enables Ford to introduce the low-cost chemistry in the United States as rapidly as possible. While guiding visitors through the plant on Tuesday, Clarke said, "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible." "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells." Capacity, pace, and the ramp Ford says the highly automated Marshall operation should be able to turn out 40 battery cells per minute, equating to roughly 20 gigawatt-hours a year for its EV lineup and energy storage business. That goal is below the company's earlier plan that called for up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually, reflecting an EV slowdown at Ford and across the sector. The company also said the site has room to add capacity if needed. Ford remains at an early phase of certifying its processes and plans to ramp cell production next year ahead of the Fathom's expected launch in the fourth quarter of 2027. The automaker said moving faster on throughput will help lower battery costs. When new technologies reshape industries, stay grounded with the free Market Briefs newsletter that explains markets clearly every day The political backdrop and why it matters In Michigan, the decision to build CATL-licensed batteries drew rebukes from certain members of Congress as well as U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who objected to Ford's relationship with the Chinese battery giant. In September, Duffy sent CEO Jim Farley a letter expressing "profound concern" about Ford's relationships with Chinese companies that he said could harm the automaker and the U.S. auto sector. The White House a day later commended the company for its domestic jobs and manufacturing. As the largest producer of U.S. vehicles, Ford has consistently highlighted its American heritage, employment, and factories while both the Biden and Trump administrations press for more domestic production. The bottom line: Ford is anchoring its next EV wave to lower cost LFP cells and a licensed design from the world's biggest cell maker. artigo.texto: Colorado's Elbert County considers rezoning request for large data center The Elbert County Commission spent Wednesday evening and Thursday morning hearing opinions about whether they should approve zoning for a large data center which would be located approximately 15 miles from Agate, 35 miles from Kiowa, and 41 miles from Elizabeth. "This is the biggest thing to hit Elbert County in the history of Elbert County," said Elizabeth resident Danny Wilcox during public comment. The LLC that is seeking approval says if they can build it, the facility will be a financial boon for the rural county. "For the first data center campus alone, Economic and Planning Systems projects an average of about $81 million a year to Elbert County," said Carolynne White, an attorney with Brownstein Hyatt Farber and Schreck who is representing the petitioner during her presentation to the commission. "Plus, an estimated $15 million a year to the two fire districts combined." And they say residents don't have to worry about environmental impacts. "Power will be generated on site, so the residents don't carry any additional power cost," said White. "The closed-loop cooling system will be fueled with imported water. There will be significant buffers to every neighbor and to the Highway 86 scenic corridor." To some residents, that seems like a good deal. "It is a tough economy and a tough market out there. Colorado is ugly. And by God, if I can give somebody 100 employees, a broad span of other people, tons of other trades, an opportunity to keep that foothold here and support our community, I'm going to stand up and say, I think it's the right thing to do," said Shane Jones, an Elbert County resident, during public comment. "Someone who buys property deserves every opportunity to pursue their plans, just like the next person. Whether that means farming, raising cattle, building a home or developing a business," said Kim Herald during public comment. But still others worry about how environmentally friendly it will truly be. "In heavy industrial engineering, you cannot dissipate hundreds of megawatts of heat without continuous loss. Water under constant thermal stress requires regular thermal blowdown, which is a technical way of saying you must constantly dump mineral-heavy water and flush the system with fresh make-up water," said Kaitlyn Mitchell, a Simla resident, during public comment. "My big concern is what are they going to do to generate this power?" asked a man who didn't give his name during public comment. And if the data center will truly bring as much money to the county as they claim it will. "It's been my experience that the truth with proposals (is they) usually come in below that best-case scenario and in some cases far below," said Gary Davis, an Elbert County resident, during public comment. After seven hours of listening and deliberation, the county decided to take more time and take up the issue at a later meeting. The commission will take up this issue once again on Dec 9 at 1 p.m. at the county fairgrounds located at 95 Ute Ave., Kiowa, CO 80117.

artigo.texto: This article is part of the thematic channel The Carbon Observer: subscribe to the newsletter Kigali - I wrote this op-ed from the Carbon Markets Africa Summit in Kigali, a great event that brought together investors, project developers and governments committed to making Africa a major hub for Article 6 carbon markets. One message particularly resonated with me. In her keynote speech, Rwanda's Minister of Environment emphasised that Africa needs bankable projects capable of attracting investment and supporting economic development. And that is exactly the point. Carbon finance could play a central role in mobilising capital, creating jobs and supporting a more sustainable development pathway. But something caught my attention: across discussions, meetings and keynote speeches, plenty about carbon finance and investment opportunities was discussed. Yet, Article 6.4 and its Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM) were almost absent from the conversation. For many of the people actually developing and financing projects, Article 6.4 remains more of a theoretical framework than a practical opportunity. Developers do not really oppose the mechanism, they simply do not see a compelling reason to adopt another complex system in a market that is already extremely difficult to navigate. Developers are already dealing with changing methodologies, host-country authorisations, corresponding adjustments and increasingly demanding buyer requirements. Article 6.4 introduces yet another set of rules and approval processes without demonstrating a clear commercial advantage. After years of negotiations, the mechanism is finally becoming operational. As of October 2026, five methodologies have been approved, including two new clean-cooking methodologies. Meanwhile, 1,512 projects and programmes have requested transition from the old Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), with 418 having received host-country approval by June. Transitioning existing projects, however, is not the same as attracting new investment under the new methodologies. In conversations with experts and developers, one concern kept emerging: methodological conservatism increasingly seems to be treated as synonymous with environmental integrity. Stricter baselines and more demanding monitoring requirements could significantly reduce credit issuance. Developers must also account for mandatory deductions of 5% for the Adaptation Fund and at least 2% for overall mitigation, alongside administrative fees, host-country levies and, where applicable, reversal-risk buffer contributions. To understand the potential economic impact, I ran a quick-and-dirty simulation. This is not a financial model or an Article 6.4 price forecast, just a simple exercise to illustrate how project economics could change. Let's assume a project originally generates 100,000 credits annually, sold at $10 each, generating $1 million in carbon revenue. If more conservative accounting reduces issuance by 40%, and we apply the mandatory 7% UNFCCC deductions, only 55,800 credits remain available for sale. What price would the developer need to charge to maintain the same carbon revenue? In the most demanding scenario, a credit previously sold at $10 would need to sell for almost $30 just to preserve the same carbon revenue. Is the market prepared to pay that difference? The concern is not conservatism itself, but the accumulation of conservative assumptions without sufficiently recognising improvements already made to address historical over-crediting. Conservatism should ensure accurate crediting, not become an objective in itself. Meanwhile, international carbon markets are progressing. According to Sylvera, projected demand for internationally adjusted credits under CORSIA and government purchasing programmes could approach one billion tonnes through 2030. Unlike Article 6.4, these pathways can leverage established standards, methodologies and registries that developers already know, and which are beginning to support deliveries to governments and airlines. Why move to an entirely new mechanism when existing systems are already opening access to compliance markets? The answer may come from future demand. The European Commission has proposed auctioning up to 260 million EU ETS allowances to finance the purchase of international credits between 2036 and 2040. At an illustrative EUA price of €120 in the late 2030s, this could generate approximately €31 billion in purchasing resources. This is not a guaranteed budget or credit price, but it illustrates the scale of the potential opportunity. Such purchasing power could make Article 6.4 more attractive, establish a new market benchmark and potentially encourage other countries to follow a similar approach. But this raises two fundamental questions. Will buyers pay the higher prices needed to make these projects viable, while keeping international credits cost-effective? And perhaps more importantly, will enough eligible and authorised credits be available? Lower issuance per project means more investment is needed to generate the same volume. Host-country authorisation remains a sovereign decision, while credit-vintage eligibility and restrictions across NDC periods create additional uncertainty. For Europe, securing up to 260 million credits between 2036 and 2040 would require a substantial project pipeline developed and financed years in advance. The market cannot wait until 2036 to start developing the projects Europe may need in 2036. This brings me back to the message from Rwanda's Minister of Environment: “Africa needs bankable projects.” Article 6.4's success will ultimately depend on strong demand signals and its ability to reduce risks for project developers and investors. This means simplifying procedures, providing greater regulatory certainty, establishing a clear and transparent pathway for host-country authorisation, and turning regulatory ambition into bankable projects that attract capital and deliver measurab
