artigo.texto: Two companies developing data centers in San Antonio are asking a federal judge to dismiss a lawsuit over alleged air pollution violations, arguing that environmental groups are exercising enforcement powers reserved for the federal government. Vantage Data Centers and energy provider VoltaGrid filed their motion on November 16, 2026, challenging the authority of Public Citizen and the Sierra Club to sue under the Clean Air Act. The companies argue that the law's citizen-suit provision violates the Constitution if it allows private organizations to enforce federal pollution requirements on behalf of their members. The motion follows a September lawsuit accusing the developers of using permits intended for smaller pollution sources to build natural gas power plants and diesel generators serving two data center campuses. Environmental groups contend that the projects require federal permits for major industrial facilities, along with stricter pollution controls and public review before construction. The facilities include approximately 405 megawatts of natural gas generating capacity and another 455 megawatts from 151 backup diesel generators, according to the complaint. Located on San Antonio's west side, the projects could release pollutants that contribute to smog in an area already failing to meet federal air quality standards. Vantage and VoltaGrid maintain that the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality authorized their projects under state permitting procedures. Their defense relies in part on treating the power generation facilities and data centers as separate sources for permitting purposes, a position the environmental groups dispute. The developers are also challenging the legal basis for the lawsuit itself. Congress authorized citizens and organizations to pursue certain Clean Air Act violations through civil litigation, including actions against companies accused of violating federal pollution standards. Vantage and VoltaGrid argue that extending this authority to organizations suing on behalf of their members would improperly transfer executive power to private parties under Article II of the Constitution. A federal judge in Mississippi rejected a similar argument on October 30 in litigation involving Elon Musk's artificial intelligence company xAI. U.S. District Judge Debra Brown ruled that the Clean Air Act allows private groups to pursue enforcement lawsuits without violating the Constitution. Her decision permitted claims over an allegedly unpermitted natural gas power plant supplying an xAI data center to proceed, although the ruling is not binding on the Texas court. The constitutional challenge has also opened the door for federal involvement. On November 18, U.S. District Judge Jason Pulliam notified the U.S. attorney general of the dispute, giving the Justice Department an opportunity to intervene and address the validity of the law. Public Citizen and the Sierra Club are separately seeking a preliminary injunctionA preliminary injunction is a temporary court order issued before a case is finally decided that requires a party to take or stop an action while the litigation continues. Federal courts generally consider the likelihood of success, irreparable harm, the balance of equities, and the public interest before granting one.Read more → to restrict construction and operations at the San Antonio facilities while the lawsuit proceeds. Vantage and VoltaGrid oppose the request, arguing that their projects have state authorization and that the proposed restrictions would disrupt ongoing development. The environmental groups face a November 23 deadline to respond to the developers' opposition to the InjunctionAn injunction is a court order requiring a person or organization to stop specified conduct or, in some circumstances, to take a particular action.Read more → and a December 7 deadline to answer the dismissal motion. artigo.texto: Lawmakers call for national data center construction pause WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Members of Congress are calling for a national moratorium on data center construction until the artificial intelligence field can be regulated. They said data centers are not helping local communities and, in many cases, are actively harming them. Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) said the White House is not doing enough on artificial intelligence. “The alarm bells are flashing. And the president and the White House are asleep at the switch when it comes to AI,” he said. McGovern said big tech leaders are becoming oligarchs and are enriching themselves at the expense of local communities with data centers. “These billionaires want to come into our communities, tell us what to do, and make a profit by driving up our utility prices, and wrecking our environment,” he said. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Mich.) said data centers do not provide the same community value as an automotive plant. “The value, the billions of dollars that is being raised to build these data centers, is built on the promise that it’s going to put people out of work,” he said. Lawmakers said pausing new construction would give Congress time to pass regulations and protect communities from future construction. Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) said she wants transparency in dealings between big tech and the government. “We don’t want back door deals and secret handshakes between big tech and the government. We want transparency, community engagement, and strong regulations that protect our air, water, climate and communities,” she said. It is not yet clear whether the plan has enough support to pass in the next Congress. The Trump administration has attempted to rename AI - artificial intelligence - as SI - super intelligence. artigo.texto: Texas data center permits moving forward again following Abbott pause AUSTIN, Texas - Texas environmental regulators have begun reviewing permits for data centers again just months after outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott issued an order halting the controversial projects. What we know: The Texas Commission of Environmental Quality (TCEQ) said it was notified that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) completed its audit looking at whether these data centers could have an impact on the state’s power grid and natural resources. "The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations," Ryan Vise, director of external relations for TCEQ, said in a statement emailed Tuesday night. A pause on data center permits The backstory: Abbott directed ERCOT to audit all data center projects in August, effectively putting a pause on any pending projects until regulators had gathered the information requested. A letter the governor sent to the TCEQ in September specifically requested that no projects be approved by the agency until the audit was completed. The governor said that, after the review, the TCEQ must only approve audited data centers that follow his directives. SpaceX gets permit What's next: It appears that at least one permit has already been approved since the pause was lifted. Politico reported earlier this week that the TCEQ had issued an air pollution permit to SpaceX for a $24 billion data center project being planned in Starbase, where the company is based. Projects draw controversy Local perspective: These data center projects have drawn concerns from residents across the state who worry about the potential impact on their communities. Some cite worries over noise, light and water pollution, and the closeness of the facilities to their neighborhoods. Activists in Cameron County have previously organized protests against the proposed SpaceX data center, claiming that it and others in the Rio Grande Valley will "use up water" and increase energy bills. Hundreds have popped up in recent years, with Abbott previously welcoming the artificial intelligence agency. Gina Hinojosa, his Democratic opponent in the midterm elections, often criticized him over his attitude toward data center development in the state. Incoming governor promises moratorium Dig deeper: Hinojosa will officially be sworn into the governor’s office in January after defeating Abbott in a stunning upset. Among her campaign promises was an immediate moratorium on data centers. She said she would keep the projects paused until lawmakers could develop stricter regulations. Some state lawmakers have already proposed removing tax breaks and requiring all agreements between data centers and municipalities to be made publicly available. Findings of audit not yet released The findings from ERCOT’s review have not yet been publicly released. The agency last provided an update on Nov. 5 to the Public Utility Commission of Texas, in which it said 93% of companies had responded to its request for information. The Source: The information in this article comes from an emailed statement from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, reports by Politico and previous Fox Local reporting.

artigo.texto: Alan Cooper is CEO of ON.energy, a developer of power infrastructure. On July 22, a mechanical failure forced a 230-kV transmission line in Northern Virginia offline. Within milliseconds, grid protection systems cleared the fault, as they are designed to do. The event would not have been a particularly noteworthy story, had it stopped there. It’s what happened next, though, that pointed to a growing challenge for grid reliability. In response to the fault, data centers that had been drawing nearly 4 GW of energy, close to 4% of PJM’s load, collectively disconnected and switched to their on-site backup generation. The move sent voltage and frequency spiking across the system, a technically wonky but threatening result that caused power flickers as far away as Chicago. Thankfully, the prevailing grid conditions were strong enough to absorb the shock of the fault, so the grid held. But if the same event had hit Texas or even Northern Virginia at a time of higher demand, it could have caused a widespread outage. In West Texas, the Electric Reliability Counil of Texas estimates that a loss of as little as 3.2 GW could threaten grid reliability. The power sector is not unfamiliar with the need for things hooked up to the electricity grid to “ride through” disturbance events. In 2023, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission told the North American Electricity Reliability Corp. to develop requirements that inverter-based supply resources like wind and solar facilities must follow to ensure they “ride through,” i.e., stay online, during certain disturbances. And this time around, NERC, FERC and several grid regions have been quick to identify a similar need for large loads to adhere to analogous standards. In an Oct. 14 presentation to ERCOT, Dominion Virginia confirmed that the disturbance fell within the ride-through parameters that have now been finalized or proposed by NERC and two grid operators (ERCOT and PJM Interconnection). They concluded that if those requirements had been in place, the event would have been avoided. Clear ride-through standards protect the grid, and they protect data centers’ ability to keep connecting to it. The open question for grid operators and regulators isn’t whether to create them, but rather which facilities the rules should cover. Some proposals would exempt projects that aren’t likely to draw grid power for years. Texas took a firmer line and in doing so, gave other operators and regulators an effective blueprint to follow. Texas’s blueprint to grid reliability The Public Utility Commission of Texas approved ERCOT’s ride through rule and it took effect in August. ERCOT made three choices that are key to making it work. It drew the applicability line at energization. Facilities that energize roughly 18 months or more after ERCOT’s first market notice must comply with the rule. That exempts projects that are nearly finished, with equipment already ordered or even installed, and it applies to projects that exist only on paper, which can still change their electrical design for a small share of what a retrofit would cost later. It measured the risk in exempt capacity within a cluster. ERCOT studies ride-through risk in its quarterly stability assessments. Those studies identify the clusters of large load that could trip together and the rule limits the amount of exempted load — i.e., the amount that is not equipped to ride through disturbances within each cluster — to 3,200 MW per single fault. Its latest results flag North Texas and Central Texas as active risk areas, with far West Texas being monitored. It made the risk transparent and predictable. ERCOT watches each load cluster’s combined consumption in real time. When a cluster’s actual demand reaches about 2,500 MW, a mitigation plan kicks in: each utility and scheduling entity gets a “not to exceed” limit based on its share of recent peak use, and ERCOT keeps the authority to curtail non-compliant load. Because ERCOT publishes the study results and updates them over time, developers can see how much headroom is left long before they hit the limit. This transparency gives them time to decide whether to install ride-through capability, change their plans, or accept the risk of curtailment. The result is that existing data centers keep running, and projects under construction generally avoid a forced redesign or need to buy different equipment. Other grid users stay protected. The first facilities built to the new standard will connect in the coming months. How ERCOT’s lessons apply to other grids In general, regulators and regional grid operators across the country are right to be careful about borrowing from ERCOT. Its isolated grid and energy-only market make much of its experience hard to apply elsewhere. This isn’t one of those cases. A data center’s response to a voltage dip is the same in Virginia, Ohio or Texas, and so is the physics of thousands of megawatts disconnecting at once. NERC, PJM and other grid operators should adopt the core tenants of the Texas approach: - Tie the rule’s applicability to energization dates with a firm cutoff, granting exceptions only where grid conditions allow. - Include forward-looking studies that identify where large loads that cannot ride through are concentrated and set limits for how much the grid can safely host in each area. - Provide transparent updates on how much exempt capacity is expected to come online and how close each area is to its limits, by both average and peak consumption. A single large-scale event would change the conversation overnight. Instead of debating exemption criteria, policymakers would be questioning if data centers can remain connected. Clear standards now are the best way to ensure the industry has a path forward. The impact of a major event wouldn’t stop at the fence line: a multistate outage would affect the communities where data centers are concentrated and working to become good grid citizens. artigo.texto: The Churchill County Planning Commission has recommended new rules for data centers and other industrial development, including a requirement that the largest data centers come before the commission for a special use permit. Commissioners voted 5–1 on Nov. 12 to forward the proposed ordinance, with revisions made during the meeting, to the Churchill County Commission, with Commissioner Mark Hyde dissenting. The county commission will make the final decision. The recommendation followed a lengthy discussion about water use, backup generators, industrial chemicals and the amount of public review that should be required as interest in data centers grows. Under the recommendation summarized by county staff before the vote, data centers with a capacity of 100 megawatts or more would require a special use permit in all three industrial zoning districts. Those permits come before the Planning Commission for a public hearing. Facilities under 10 megawatts would require a conditional zoning permit in each of the three districts. For facilities from 10 to 100 megawatts, a special use permit would be required in the I-1 district, while a conditional zoning permit would apply in the I-2 and I-3 districts. Commissioners also agreed to recommend adding battery energy storage systems to the county’s use table, with a special use permit required in the three industrial districts. The permit categories became a central point of debate. Commissioner Dennis Mills argued that the largest data centers should come before the board and receive public attention. Other commissioners said they wanted standards that would give potential investors certainty while preserving the possibility of industrial development. Commissioner Joe Frey questioned whether some of the proposed requirements would duplicate state or federal regulations and whether the county had enough capacity to enforce additional rules. He said the county should remain cautious without allowing fear to drive its approach. The proposed ordinance extends beyond data centers. The draft in the meeting packet would establish standards for new industrial uses and substantial expansions, addressing water, power, chemicals, traffic, noise, building appearance and sanitation. The draft calls for water-efficient cooling methods and annual reporting of operational water use. Depending on the project, applicants could also be asked for information such as estimated power consumption, a power provision plan, traffic studies and emergency planning documents. Commissioners discussed reporting requirements for industrial spills and other incidents. In staff’s summary of the revisions, a state-reportable spill, an explosion or a fire requiring a fire department response would be reported to Churchill County within 10 days. Staff said copies of state reporting forms would be acceptable, and annual reporting would remain part of the recommendation. Commissioners also agreed to remove a proposed requirement that backup generators meet an EPA Tier 4 standard. Staff said that language was specific to diesel generators and could unintentionally limit the types of backup power used. The revisions summarized at the meeting would apply the backup-generator provisions to facilities with more than two megawatts of combined backup-generator capacity. Resident Michelle Anderson raised concerns about public access and the commission’s oversight during opening public comment. She questioned whether replacing some special use permit hearings with administrative approvals would reduce opportunities for public review.

Regra do Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), do Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos, publicada no Federal Register em 19 de novembro de 2026, passa a exigir licença para exportar, reexportar ou transferir chips avançados de IA ao Brasil, à Indonésia, à Malásia, a Singapura e à Tailândia. Vendas a destinatários com sede nos EUA ou controlados de lá, como as donas da AWS, do Azure e do Google Cloud, ficam isentas de licença, desde que o exportador, reexportador ou transferidor envie relatórios mensais ao BIS. Empresas brasileiras precisam de autorização caso a caso. A ABES diz que a regra cria condições desiguais de competição, e o governo brasileiro montou uma força-tarefa para medir o impacto. Os Estados Unidos devem publicar nesta quinta-feira, 19, a regra que passa a exigir licença para exportar chips avançados de inteligência artificial (IA) ao Brasil. A exigência não vale para todos. Se o destinatário for subsidiária de uma empresa americana, como as donas da AWS, do Azure e do Google Cloud, basta que o fornecedor dos chips envie relatórios mensais a Washington. Se for uma empresa brasileira, é preciso pedir autorização ao governo americano e esperar a resposta, caso a caso. A regra foi anunciada na segunda-feira, 16, pelo Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão do Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos que controla exportações de tecnologia. A norma entra em vigor na data de publicação no Federal Register, o diário oficial americano, e vale também para Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia. Para a Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Software (ABES), que representa cerca de 2.000 empresas de software e tecnologia no país, a regra pode "criar condições desiguais de competição entre empresas brasileiras e subsidiárias de companhias norte-americanas". Em Brasília, o governo montou uma força-tarefa para medir o impacto da medida. A regra é uma norma provisória com efeito imediato, o que os americanos chamam de interim final rule. O texto foi disponibilizado para consulta pública prévia no Federal Register na segunda-feira e tem duas partes. A primeira exige licença para exportar, reexportar ou transferir chips avançados de IA aos cinco países da lista. O controle vale também para componentes e servidores fabricados em outros países que usem tecnologia americana. Não se trata de uma proibição de venda ao Brasil: cada pedido será avaliado caso a caso. A segunda parte vale para data centers em qualquer lugar do mundo. Quem oferecer grande capacidade de computação a empresas sediadas na China, ou controladas a partir de lá, precisa de autorização. O objetivo é fechar a brecha que permitia a empresas chinesas usar chips americanos pela nuvem, alugando capacidade em outros países. Data centers que já prestam esse tipo de serviço a clientes abrangidos pela regra e querem continuar têm 90 dias, a partir da entrada em vigor, para obter a licença. A regra também abriu um período de 60 dias para comentários públicos, até 19 de janeiro de 2027, em que empresas e governos podem pedir mudanças. O ponto mais sensível para o mercado brasileiro é a diferença de tratamento entre empresas. A exigência de licença não vale quando o destinatário final tem sede nos Estados Unidos ou pertence a um grupo controlado de lá, como as donas da AWS, do Azure e do Google Cloud. Nesses casos, basta que o exportador, reexportador ou transferidor dos chips envie relatórios mensais ao BIS com informações como as partes envolvidas, os produtos e as datas de embarque. A obrigação é de quem vende ou transfere os equipamentos, não do comprador. Provedores de nuvem e operadoras de data center de capital brasileiro, ou de outros países, não têm essa saída. Para cada operação coberta pela regra, precisam pedir autorização individual, analisada pelas autoridades americanas. Segundo a ABES, empresas que disputam os mesmos clientes passam a enfrentar procedimentos diferentes para comprar equipamentos de IA. Na avaliação da entidade, a exigência de licença "pode elevar custos, dificultar investimentos em data centers" e afetar a atratividade do país para projetos de infraestrutura de IA e nuvem. A associação também chama a atenção para quem fica fora do debate comercial. Universidades e centros de pesquisa que precisam de computação avançada podem ser afetados. E mesmo nas vendas isentas de licença haverá um custo extra de conformidade, com os relatórios mensais que os fornecedores passam a enviar ao governo americano. Segundo o governo americano, o Brasil foi incluído pela expansão acelerada do setor de data centers e pela presença de operações de nuvem da Huawei no país. Washington não acusa o Brasil de desviar chips deliberadamente para a China. Na análise dos pedidos de licença, o BIS considera o regime de controle de exportações do país de destino e o grau de cooperação com os Estados Unidos. Em nota, o governo brasileiro afirmou que "não se trata de proibição, mas de necessidade de autorização" e disse ainda não ser possível avaliar o efeito concreto sobre as importações. A força-tarefa é liderada pelo ministro do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, Márcio Elias Rosa, e pela ministra da Gestão e da Inovação em Serviços Públicos, Esther Dweck. A ABES defende que o governo e o setor privado negociem com as autoridades americanas, com foco na cooperação em controle de exportações e na manutenção das cadeias de fornecimento de tecnologia. Para a entidade, "o Brasil reúne condições para ampliar sua participação no mercado internacional de serviços de data centers", com sua matriz elétrica, disponibilidade de energia, conectividade e políticas de incentivo. artigo.texto: (Photo Courtesy Ida County) A massive battery storage project could be coming to Ida County — and another could follow. MidAmerican Energy is proposing a 200-megawatt battery energy storage facility near Ida Grove, with approximately 180 to 190 large battery containers covering about 20 acres. MidAmerican Associate Project Outreach Manager John Huff and Project Developer Ashley Taylor presented the plans to the Ida County Board of Supervisors Tuesday afternoon. The proposed facility would sit next to MidAmerican’s Ida Grove 2 wind farm substation along Indian Avenue, near the former county landfill. MidAmerican has options to purchase 55 acres, although Huff said the battery installation would occupy less than half that land. The system would store electricity for later use, helping balance power supply and demand when wind generation fluctuates. Taylor explained why MidAmerican selected the location. Before construction can begin, however, the county must establish regulations for the facility. Board Chair Devlun Whiteing said supervisors have discussed incorporating battery storage requirements into the county’s existing wind energy ordinance, rather than adopting a separate ordinance. That approach would treat battery storage as an accessory use to a wind farm, while allowing different requirements for batteries associated with future data centers. MidAmerican hopes to hold a public hearing on the proposed ordinance amendment in December. Board member Creston Schubert questioned the company’s plans for fire protection, security, noise and potential impacts on nearby residents. Taylor said the facility would use lithium iron phosphate batteries, with containers designed to prevent a fire from spreading between units. She said MidAmerican also plans to coordinate with local firefighters and develop an emergency response plan. Another concern involved whether Ida County residents would benefit directly from the stored electricity during power outages. Huff and Taylor said the facility could improve electrical reliability but acknowledged they had not determined exactly how the substation’s transmission connections would affect local service. Supervisors also want answers about the project’s financial benefits. Taylor said the facility would fall under Iowa’s utility replacement tax system, making future county revenue difficult to predict. Schubert stressed the importance of providing that information before a public hearing. Huff and Taylor also indicated MidAmerican could pursue a second battery storage project near another wind farm substation along Orchard Avenue, between Ida Grove and Arthur. Supervisors expressed interest in touring an existing battery storage facility before making a decision. MidAmerican agreed to help explore that possibility. If the necessary state and local approvals are secured, Taylor said construction on the proposed Indian Avenue facility could begin as early as July or August of next year, with operations targeted for May 2028. Supervisors took no action Tuesday. The county plans to have its attorney review MidAmerican’s proposed ordinance changes before moving forward.

artigo.texto: Lansing residents push town board to ban data centers, crypto mining LANSING, N.Y. (WBNG) --More than 20,000 people have signed a petition opposing a proposed AI data center in Lansing. Residents are now taking that opposition to the Town Board and pushing for a ban on data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities. The company TeraWulf has proposed a 300-megawatt facility along the shores of Cayuga Lake. Residents say the potential costs to their community are too high. Resident Renee Vogelsang said, “AI data centers suck up all of our energy, raise our electricity bills, waste our water, and harm our climate and environment.” What the proposal includes The proposed project would include three buildings to house computing equipment. Plans also call for clearing more than 40 acres of forested land and constructing new power infrastructure. Residents worry about the impact on the lake, local wildlife and the region’s tourism industry. Resident John Dennis said, “And in terms of jobs, the Finger Lakes ecotourism and wineries produce 4.6 billion in annual visiting spending a year, and it’s time for the 10 miles of the town of Lansing’s border on the lake to become integrated back into that economy.” Dennis said he believes the region should be focused on protecting the natural resources that already support its economy. Assemblymember raises cost concerns State Assemblymember Anna Kellis, who represents the 125th District, said the concerns go beyond the immediate impact of construction. She said taxpayers could be left paying for the infrastructure needed to power the facility. “But what will still be here is the debt that is then passed on to all taxpayers for paying for the capital infrastructure for the grid, the energy grid that was built up in order to provide those electrons and that energy to those data centers,” Kellis said. “We are the ones who would be stuck with that cost.” Kellis also pointed to potential increases in electricity costs, greenhouse gas emissions and water usage. She said the economic promises made by data center developers do not necessarily guarantee long-term benefits for the communities hosting them. Resident Ken Wolkin, who lives near Cayuga Lake, also shared concerns. “They are bullies who encroach and impinge upon our legislative and democratic processes and they continue to push their development plans even despite our sustained and ongoing refusal to consent to a data center in Lansing,” Wolkin said. Town Board considers zoning change The Town Board is considering a zoning change that would make data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities disallowed uses in Lansing. A vote on the proposal is currently scheduled for Wednesday. The date could change. Residents who have spent months organizing against the project said the decision could help determine the future of their community. Copyright 2026 WBNG. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: UK-EU carbon market plan sparks clash over British energy bills Ahead of Friday's UK-EU summit in Brussels, ministers say linking carbon markets shields £6.5 billion in exports, while critics warn it raises energy bills. Chief editor: Ken Kariuki 0701401086 Britain and the European Union are preparing to link their carbon markets at a Brussels summit on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, prompting a sharp dispute between Downing Street and free-market critics over whether the deal will protect exporters or raise domestic energy bills. In an official factsheet published Tuesday, Nov. 17, the UK Cabinet Office said linking the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) with the EU ETS could add up to £3.8 billion a year to the British economy and shield about £6.5 billion in steel and aluminium exports from the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). Critics at the Prosperity Institute, writing in City AM on Wednesday, Nov. 18, countered that aligning with higher European carbon prices would raise British carbon prices by around 32% and leave the wider economy worse off. The clash highlights a central policy trade-off behind Prime Minister Andy Burnham's European reset: shielding export-heavy manufacturers from EU border tariffs requires accepting higher domestic carbon-price floors across power generation and industry. How Carbon Market Linkage Works Both the UK ETS and EU ETS operate as cap-and-trade systems that require power plants, heavy factories, and airlines to buy permits for their greenhouse gas emissions. Because the UK system has traded at lower carbon prices than the EU's scheme, British exports entering the bloc face CBAM charges designed to equalize carbon costs at the EU border. Linking the two trading schemes would create a shared permit price and secure mutual exemptions from border carbon levies. Beyond emissions trading, the Cabinet Office factsheet outlines a food and drink trade deal projected to add up to £5.1 billion annually by cutting border paperwork, alongside a Youth Experience Scheme for study, work, and travel. Downing Street's economic case rests on protecting export competitiveness. By avoiding CBAM charges on approximately £6.5 billion of steel, aluminium, and related industrial exports, ministers argue the linkage prevents new trade friction while keeping Britain inside its manifesto red lines against rejoining the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement. Competing Cost Estimates and Evidence Limits Critics argue the government's calculation omits the domestic cost of converging toward EU permit prices. Writing in City AM, Prosperity Institute researcher Joseph Dinnage pointed to a 2024 Frontier Economics report cited by ministers, noting that while separate markets could cost British exporters £0.2 billion to £0.8 billion in EU CBAM payments between 2026 and 2030, keeping UK carbon prices lower would simultaneously save the domestic economy £3.5 billion to £8 billion in carbon taxes. Neither side's headline number tells the full story on its own. The Cabinet Office's £3.8 billion figure represents an upper-bound economy-wide projection ("up to") rather than a guaranteed windfall, while the Prosperity Institute's recommendation to abolish the Climate Change Levy, Carbon Price Support, the UK ETS, and the proposed UK CBAM would eliminate domestic carbon pricing altogether, leaving British steelmakers exposed to EU border tariffs and raising Exchequer revenue questions. Brexit Politics and Delayed Long-Term Options The carbon dispute unfolds alongside broader political caution inside Labour ahead of Friday's summit with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and EU leaders. Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet in London on Monday evening, Nov. 16, Burnham declared that "the Brexit we were given has not worked" and said Britain had "lost more than we gained" over the past decade. Yet by Tuesday, Burnham indicated there was "no rush" to set out broader options for Britain's long-term EU relationship, postponing a planned options framework until December amid cabinet unease over reopening Brexit divisions. Meanwhile, former prime ministers Boris Johnson and David Cameron cautioned against moving toward rejoining the bloc, and the Cabinet Office's factsheet stressed that Friday's agreements require no payments into the EU budget beyond proportionate administrative costs for shared databases and IT systems. Whether the summit delivers immediate industrial relief will depend on the final permit-linkage terms published in Brussels on Nov. 20. How did this story land? No sign-in required. Choose up to two. artigo.texto: Os créditos de carbono negociados entre países ganharam um livro-caixa global. A ONU Mudança do Clima lançou na COP31, em Antália, na Turquia, a primeira versão do registro internacional previsto no artigo 6.2 do Acordo de Paris, segundo o secretariado da convenção do clima. O registro vai servir aos países que não têm, ou não conseguem acessar, um registro próprio. Com ele, poderão anotar e acompanhar os chamados ITMOs, sigla em inglês para resultados de mitigação transferidos internacionalmente. O que é o artigo 6.2 O artigo 6.2 do Acordo de Paris permite que um país compre de outro uma redução de emissões e a conte na própria meta climática. Para que a mesma tonelada de carbono não seja contada duas vezes, cada transferência precisa ser registrada e rastreada. É esse o papel do novo sistema. O que já funciona Na primeira versão, os países participantes podem: - abrir seções e contas próprias; - registrar atividades de redução de emissões; - emitir resultados de mitigação e ligá-los às autorizações; - registrar transferência, compra, uso e cancelamento de ITMOs. As funções foram demonstradas num evento na COP31 na segunda-feira (16). Entrada em etapas Os países que pedirem uma seção no registro vão entrar aos poucos. O processo deve incluir uma oficina no início de 2027, seguida de treinamento e testes antes do acesso ao sistema real. Versões futuras vão trazer relatórios e integração com registros nacionais e com o mecanismo de créditos do Acordo de Paris. O desenvolvimento do software começou em janeiro de 2026, e uma versão mínima foi apresentada aos países em maio. Por que isso importa para a Amazônia O mercado de carbono entre países é uma das apostas para levar dinheiro à conservação de florestas. O Peru, vizinho amazônico, já fez a primeira transferência de resultados de redução de emissões da América Latina, para a Suíça, como a Revista Amazônia mostrou. E estados amazônicos brasileiros, como o Pará, pedem que seus programas de REDD+ jurisdicional possam participar desse mercado. Um registro confiável é condição para que esse dinheiro chegue sem fraude e sem dupla contagem. Acompanhe a cobertura diária na página especial da COP 31. Perguntas frequentes O que é um ITMO? É um resultado de redução de emissões transferido de um país para outro, que pode ser contado na meta climática de quem compra. Quem vai usar o registro internacional? Países que não têm, ou não conseguem acessar, um registro nacional próprio. Com informações da ONU Mudança do Clima (UNFCCC). Gostou desta reportagem? Marque Revista Amazônia como fonte preferencial e veja mais conteúdo nosso no Google.

artigo.texto: Oklahoma leaders discuss nuclear power, data centers during State of Business Forum At a State of Business Forum, leaders said Oklahoma is in position to attract new nuclear development and AI data centers. Oklahoma leaders discuss nuclear power, data centers during State of Business Forum At a State of Business Forum, leaders said Oklahoma is in position to attract new nuclear development and AI data centers. Oklahoma is exploring nuclear power and data centers as key industries to drive its economic future, with leaders discussing the state’s potential at the State of Business Forum Tuesday. But to attract the next wave of jobs and investment, Oklahoma will have to compete. The conversations were part of the forum hosted by the State Chamber of Oklahoma, where industry leaders explained why Oklahoma is catching their attention. "Having a state that’s willing to hold its hand up and say, ‘Hey we want to host this stuff here. We have the right infrastructure. We’re an energy state, and we’re hungry for opportunities,’ Oklahoma fits all those in a unique way," Jacob DeWitte, co-founder of the nuclear power company Oklo, said. DeWitte moved to Tulsa last year as Oklahoma submitted its bid for a federal nuclear lifecycle innovation campus. He said the state’s oil and gas history could position it as a leader in nuclear energy. "I think, ultimately, Oklahoma has the potential and positioning to be really the hub for new nuclear development," DeWitte said. >> Video Below: Oklahoma reveals new details of nuclear facility bid, but many questions remain The demand for artificial intelligence is also driving interest in data centers, and Amazon’s Brian Huseman stressed the importance of Oklahoma seizing this opportunity. "Although I work for Amazon, I am definitely on team Oklahoma. I do not want to see our state like in 10 years regret that we were not able to take part in the building of this new kind of interstate highway system," Huseman said. Chad Warmington, president and CEO of the Oklahoma State Chamber, said the state needs to act quickly to attract companies. "The companies that are going to come here are going to come here because we move quickly, and I think we have the regulatory framework in place to do that," Warmington said.

artigo.texto: Data centers – O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos prepara uma regulamentação que exigirá autorização do governo americano para a compra de chips avançados de inteligência artificial por operadoras de data centers de cinco países, incluindo o Brasil. A medida também abrange Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia. A iniciativa pretende impedir que a China e outros países considerados adversários tenham acesso indireto à tecnologia americana por meio do aluguel de capacidade computacional em estruturas instaladas no exterior. LEIA: Novo curso do Sindplay ensina a transformar ideias em soluções inovadoras Segundo o Departamento de Comércio, a norma busca evitar que as restrições existentes sejam contornadas por acordos de computação remota. As empresas afetadas também terão de realizar verificações mais rigorosas sobre seus clientes. A expectativa é que as novas exigências dificultem o uso de chips americanos no treinamento de modelos avançados de IA por organizações de países considerados de alto risco, como China, Rússia e Irã. A regulamentação surge após o escândalo envolvendo a Nvidia e seu ex-CEO, Jensen Huang, que renunciou ao cargo depois de vir à tona seu relacionamento com Alice Huang, ex-executiva de uma companhia de Cingapura investigada por suspeita de envolvimento em espionagem para a China. A empresa nega irregularidades. O episódio aumentou a pressão sobre autoridades americanas responsáveis pela fiscalização das exportações de tecnologia. O secretário do Tesouro, Scott Bessent, criticou a atuação do Departamento de Comércio, comandado por Howard Lutnick, por considerar insuficientes os mecanismos de controle existentes. A discussão também expôs divergências dentro do governo Trump. Enquanto o Departamento de Comércio supervisiona as regras, o Tesouro e o Conselho de Segurança Nacional defendem medidas mais rigorosas para impedir que empresas chinesas obtenham acesso indireto aos processadores. A nova norma, que prevê análise individual dos pedidos de licença, deverá entrar em vigor em até 90 dias. Empresas americanas que operam nos países afetados terão exceções, assim como data centers utilizados em sistemas comerciais de recomendação de varejistas on-line e redes sociais. O anúncio ocorre poucos dias antes da viagem de Donald Trump à China, onde o presidente americano deverá se reunir com Xi Jinping para uma cúpula econômica. As restrições também provocaram reação no mercado financeiro. Na manhã do anúncio, ações da Nvidia recuaram mais de 2%, enquanto Intel e Micron registraram perdas superiores a 6% e 7%, respectivamente. O índice Philadelphia Semiconductor, que reúne empresas do setor, caiu mais de 5%. Fonte de divergências dentro do governo dos EUA A possibilidade de empresas chinesas utilizarem data centers estrangeiros para acessar chips americanos tem provocado disputas internas na administração Trump. Nos últimos meses, Scott Bessent, Marco Rubio e Jamieson Greer defenderam controles mais abrangentes sobre essas estruturas, diante do risco de transferência indireta de tecnologia para a China. O comunicado oficial informou que a regulamentação foi elaborada pelo Departamento do Tesouro, por determinação da própria pasta e do Conselho de Segurança Nacional. A participação dessas instituições reforça a pressão de setores do governo por regras mais rígidas para o acesso internacional à capacidade computacional americana. artigo.texto: This week (2026.11.12-11.19), industry players and professionals continued their efforts. On the pricing front, sulphide electrolytes and core raw material prices showed signs of softening (broad declines), oxide LATP edged up slightly, and solid-state cathode (lithium-rich manganese-based) prices were under pressure, reflecting the ongoing tug-of-war between material-side capacity release and market demand. This week, three threads stood out overall: material-side prices diverged, battery cell pilot production and mass-production preparations continued to advance, and end-user validation began extending to larger capacities and more scenarios. It should be noted that many projects are still in the pilot or validation stage, so single-week data should not be over-interpreted; subsequent developments will depend on actual transactions, yield rates, and equipment commissioning. 1. Material side: sulphide pulled back, oxides edged up, lithium-rich manganese-based remained weak According to SMM quotes on 19 November, the sulphide route pulled back this week. Battery-grade lithium sulphide averaged 1.25 million yuan/mt, down 10,000 yuan; high-purity lithium sulphide held at 2.8 million yuan/mt; SMM sulphide electrolyte LPSC averaged 2.85 million yuan/mt, down 50,000 yuan. Imported lithium sulphide from Japan and South Korea remained elevated, with Japan quoted at $368,000/mt and South Korea at $305,000/mt. Upstream P₂S₅ was at 72,400 yuan/mt, while prices of raw materials such as sulphur and hydrogen sulphide were largely stable this week. Oxide electrolyte demand improved, with prices edging up slightly. LATP averaged 127,500 yuan/mt, up 2,500 yuan; LLZO held steady at 625,000 yuan/mt. Cathode materials were weak this week. High-voltage, medium-voltage, and low-voltage lithium-rich manganese-based cathodes averaged 222,000 yuan/mt, 171,500 yuan/mt, and 153,000 yuan/mt respectively, each down 500-1,000 yuan/mt; conventional 8-series ternary was at 158,100 yuan/mt and 9-series ternary at 158,050 yuan/mt, both flat. Lithium-rich manganese-based materials remain the right direction for solid-state cathodes, but large-scale application still needs time; the near-term view that high-nickel ternary will serve as a transitional solution is more realistic. At the company level, Easpring Technology stated on 17 November that its 60,000 mt high-nickel cathode base in Europe is expected to partially commence production by year-end, with cumulative shipments of all-solid-state cathodes reaching 50 mt and cathode materials for solid-liquid hybrid batteries already achieving kilotonne-level shipments. Hunan Yuneng said on 18 November that it is advancing solid-state cathodes including lithium-rich manganese-based and high-nickel ternary materials. Shanshan Co. clarified on 16 November that capital expenditure over the next two to three years will tilt towards silicon-based materials, hard carbon, and solid-state battery materials. Anode materials are still in the investment phase, with the pace of volume ramp-up depending on actual procurement by downstream battery cell manufacturers. **II. Battery Cells and Terminals: Gotion High-tech Achieves High Pilot Line Yield, Changan Advances Large-Capacity Validation** Gotion High-tech disclosed on November 12 that its 0.2 GWh all-solid-state pilot line is operating stably, with battery cell yield reaching 90%. The process employs warm isostatic pressing (WIP) technology, reducing electrolyte membrane thickness to 35 µm and lowering interfacial impedance by over 99%. A 2 GWh all-solid-state mass production line has been launched, with plans for small-batch vehicle installation in 2027. The 90% pilot line yield is a relatively positive data point this week, but pilot lines and mass production lines differ significantly in equipment, cycle time, and cost control. The key focus going forward will be the commissioning progress and yield ramp-up of the 2 GWh line. Changan Automobile disclosed on November 13 that it has initiated validation of 20 Ah oxygen-polymer composite solid-state batteries, with energy density exceeding 350 Wh/kg and supporting electrolyte conductivity greater than 4.5 mS/cm. The long-term target is 400 Wh/kg, with plans for small-scale demonstration operation in 2027. The 20 Ah capacity is closer to vehicle installation validation than laboratory-scale small cells, but the overall effort remains in the validation stage, with some distance to go before large-scale deployment in vehicles. Application scenarios also saw new developments this week. WELION New Energy signed a strategic cooperation agreement with Yubang Power on November 17 to introduce hybrid solid-liquid and all-solid-state battery technologies into new-type energy storage, grid-side applications, and ex-China markets. Guangdong Nuojia had a 1.8 GWh consumer-grade semi-solid-state battery project filed and approved in Yunfu on November 12, with a total investment of 680 million yuan and construction planned to begin in January 2027. The simultaneous advancement of power, energy storage, and consumer applications indicates that different technology routes are seeking deployment scenarios based on their respective energy density and cost characteristics. **III. Project Implementation: Pilot Projects Lean Toward Asset-Light Models, Mass Production Projects Remain Capital-Intensive** Nanjing Yanpo's 1 MWh-class sulphide all-solid-state battery project entered the public notice stage for environmental impact assessment review on November 16. The project involves an investment of 4.7034 million yuan, leasing a 1,075 m² plant, and deploying 56 sets of domestically produced equipment. It is positioned as a "pilot + small-batch sample" facility, focusing on exploring sulphide process closure, including H₂S prevention and inert atmosphere control. artigo.texto: As LIPA eyes more battery storage, LI developer envisions alternative method As New York State doubles down on large energy-storage plants which could lead to a second wave of lithium-ion based projects and alternative battery technologies before the end of the decade, a Long Island entrepreneur is proposing one of the first plants using an alternative called flow-batteries. Last week, the state announced a second bulk-energy storage solicitation, seeking projects that could add 1,000 megawatts of battery storage plants across the state by 2030. It expands on awards from the first round announced this summer that saw two of eight new projects awarded for Long Island -- in Holtsville and Manorville. All are part of Gov. Kathy Hochul’s plan for 6,000 megawatts of battery storage by 2030, and come as Long Island continues to collectively resist the strategy with moratoriums in nearly all towns. Concerns here are based largely on reports of thermal runaway events at four New York plants in 2023, including one in East Hampton, where high levels of forever chemicals were reported earlier this month at a site dealing with a spreading toxic plume following fire suppression efforts. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority’s competitive solicitation announced on Nov. 12 is “open to a range of eligible storage technologies,” the agency said. Non-lithium batteries are eligible for 25-year contracts in the new solicitation, versus 15-year contracts for lithium-ion battery proposals, NYSERDA said in responses to Newsday. - As New York State doubles down on soliciting for large energy-storage plants proposals, a Long Island entrepreneur is proposing one of the first plants using an alternative called flow-batteries. - Last week, the state announced seeking projects that could add 1,000 megawatts of battery storage plants across the state by 2030. - Meanwhile, Larry Siegel, a businessman from Wantagh with a background in energy finance, said he is in the early stages of developing a non-lithium ion battery storage project for eastern Long Island which would use flow-battery technology to provide 5 megawatts of storage for the grid. NYSERDA’s NY Green Bank will help fund the new battery projects with a “range of financing options” to advance energy storage, the agency said, and its siting team will work “closely with local governments to provide tailored education, technical assistance and model local laws.” LIPA expressed support for the state’s latest battery solicitation, saying in a statement that it “welcomes NYSERDA’s efforts to advance innovation in energy storage and help promising technologies become commercially viable options for meeting New York’s energy needs.” Meanwhile, Larry Siegel, a businessman from Wantagh with a background in energy finance, said he is in the early stages of developing a non-lithium ion battery storage project for eastern Long Island which would use flow-battery technology to provide 5 megawatts of storage for the grid. Siegel, in an interview, said his newly formed Tobay Energy has identified a location for the plant on a site less than an acre. He said he recently met with PSEG Long Island, which runs the grid under contract to LIPA, about connecting his project to the electric grid. It could be ready by 2028, he said. Flow batteries use liquid electrolytes rather than solid lithium-ion cells to store energy, using zinc bromine or vanadium to the store power for up to four hours of discharge onto the grid. Batteries can help stabilize the grid in the face of intermittent energy from solar and wind arrays, one of the reasons they are crucial as LIPA prepares to make way for up to 924-megawatts of wind energy early next year. Siegel said he’s still finalizing a design and specific manufacturer for the project, and that much will depend on the cost of connecting to local power lines. “All over Long Island, there’s a demand for a large number of these batteries, but it’s just very hard to build them because of the moratoriums,” Siegel said, noting that Islip Town recently approved a ban on batteries over a certain size that could nix a LIPA contract for a 79-megawatt battery. “Even Brookhaven is not in a rush to approve them,” Siegel said of the town where multiple projects have been proposed because it has a special zone for batteries and no moratorium. More recently, town supervisor Dan Panico has assured concerned residents nothing will be approved until the town is sure they are safe. Siegel said flow batteries are not subject to thermal runaway fires that lithium batteries are, and said they are already in use in the state and across the country. He pointed to a July contract awarded to manufacturer Eos Energy to build zinc-based battery storage systems for a “Golden Dome for America” defense system for the U.S. Department of War. “It’s going to cost me more” to work with flow-energy batteries, Siegel said. “There’s less profit in it because the costs are higher, but I think it’s the way to go.” The Wantagh resident, who said he previously worked for the U.S. Department of Energy, grew up in Patchogue. “I know the market, I see other site locations that will never get built,” said Siegel, who has attended community meetings where residents have objected to lithium-ion batteries. “I know what’s going on out here. There are a lot of projects that have been abandoned on Long Island.” His proposed flow battery of 5 megawatts has challenges, he acknowledged. “I do have a hurdle to convince investors about these flow batteries,” he said. “They have questions. artigo.texto: Loudoun County leaders approve 10-month pause on data center applications LOUDOUN COUNTY, Va. - Loudoun County's Board of Supervisors voted Tuesday night to put the breaks on future data center development with a 10-month pause on data center applications. What we know: The vote comes after an hours-long meeting where supervisors heard from frustrated residents and industry leaders. Before the decision, some residents were losing hope. The pause is intended to give supervisors time to take a closer look at how much more growth the area can actually handle, including the impact on electricity, infrastructure and neighborhoods. During Tuesday's meeting, supervisors raised concerns about the backlog that could result from putting a halt to all new digital infrastructure projects. The Data Center Coalition argued that these facilities should drive Loudoun County's economy, and generated about $1.3 billion in tax revenue in 2026. They also argued that the county should not abruptly change course in a way that creates uncertainty, invites legal challenges and disrupts investments. On Tuesday night, the coalition warned that developers could take legal action. Certain developers with existing zoning applications, like ZRTD applications, may still move forward, depending on the status of their projects and a case-by-case review. The Source: Information in this article is from a Loudoun County Board of Supervisors hearing and original FOX 5 DC reporting.

artigo.texto: It’s another banner year for batteries in the US See more from Canary Media’s “Chart of the Week” column. Batteries are booming in America. Over the first nine months of this year, the U.S. installed 20% more battery storage capacity than it did in the same period last year, according to a new report by the Solar Energy Industries Association and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Most of that capacity is from utility-scale installations, though it includes residential and commercial installations, too. In the last decade, batteries have gotten exponentially cheaper and have rapidly become one of the most important grid technologies. The systems are relatively speedy to install, and their ability to store inexpensive surplus power for later has captivated utilities, data center developers, and households alike. Even without the final three months of data for 2026, 11 states have already seen battery installations reach record levels this year: Alabama, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Montana, Utah, and Virginia. The bad news is that the report predicts residential installations will drop 8% this year compared to 2025. That sector took a hit after the federal government ripped away incentives for home energy storage at the end of last year, though SEIA and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence say business is recovering faster than expected. Despite the residential dip, the report authors expect overall battery capacity additions in 2026 to surpass last year’s figures by 26%. It’s a testament to the tech’s broad appeal — and a bright spot for the energy transition, which will rely on abundant storage to spread wind and solar power through all hours of the day.

artigo.texto: Sungrow has unveiled a new generation of commercial and industrial energy storage solutions at its Global Energy Pioneer Summit (GEPS) 2026 in Hefei, China, introducing the PowerStack 3.0 alongside an expanded PowerKeeper battery storage family. Held from 10 to 13 November 2026, the summit brought together more than 1,200 attendees from over 80 countries, including installers, distributors and engineering partners. The announcements reflect a growing focus on making energy storage easier to deploy, manage and scale, particularly for businesses looking to improve their use of solar generation, manage electricity costs and maintain operations during grid interruptions. While much of the discussion around battery storage in Australia centres on households, the commercial and industrial sector faces a different set of challenges. Businesses must consider available installation space, peak electricity demand, operational continuity and the financial returns of larger battery systems. Sungrow’s latest developments aim to address these requirements through modular hardware, smarter energy management and greater integration between solar, storage and charging infrastructure. PowerStack 3.0 Brings Modular Energy Storage to Different Business Needs The headline announcement was the global launch of Sungrow PowerStack 3.0, a commercial and industrial energy storage system built around what the company describes as a Scene-in-One architecture. Rather than deploying separate equipment for each application, PowerStack 3.0 uses a Multi-Scenario Dock with four dedicated modules: - PCS Module: Power conversion and standalone battery storage applications. - Solar Module: Integration of photovoltaic generation and battery storage. - Charging Module: DC-coupled integration of solar, batteries and electric vehicle charging. - Microgrid Module: Support for independent power systems and operation during grid outages. This approach allows installers and system designers to configure solutions around the requirements of a particular site without necessarily introducing additional standalone equipment. For example, a commercial facility might begin with battery storage to manage electricity costs, while another installation could require integrated solar generation and EV charging. The standalone storage configuration also supports two-hour and four-hour discharge durations through different power module arrangements. For businesses operating in areas with unreliable electricity supplies, the microgrid configuration supports switching between grid-connected and off-grid operation. Sungrow claims the system can achieve a 0 ms transition without a separate static transfer switch cabinet, potentially helping critical equipment remain operational during outages. Environmental protection includes an IP55 rating and C5-level corrosion protection, with a specified operating temperature range of -30°C to 50°C. Safety provisions include three-level fuse protection and a four-layer fire safety design. These specifications are particularly relevant for industrial locations where space, environmental exposure and system reliability can significantly influence installation decisions. Bubbly AI Takes on Battery Design, Commissioning and Management Artificial intelligence also features prominently in Sungrow’s latest energy storage strategy. PowerStack 3.0 incorporates Bubbly, the company’s proprietary AI assistant, designed to support projects throughout their operational lifecycle. Its capabilities extend beyond monitoring electricity consumption. During planning, Bubbly combines satellite imagery and 3D modelling to produce proposed system designs, including installation layouts and financial calculations. According to Sungrow, this approach can deliver more than 12% higher returns compared with a conventional self-consumption operating mode. The AI platform also monitors operating conditions continuously, identifying more than 30 potential risks and providing diagnostic recommendations. For a 10 MWh installation, Sungrow claims Bubbly can produce a fault diagnosis report with maintenance recommendations in approximately one minute. artigo.texto: O mercado de carbono do Acordo de Paris irá gerar créditos de carbono de alta qualidade? (Jornal Dan Tri) - O novo mecanismo previsto no Artigo 6.4 do Acordo de Paris começou a operar com padrões rigorosos, causando uma redução de até 40% no número de créditos concedidos a projetos e instaurando um processo de triagem mais rigoroso para as empresas vietnamitas. Considerado outrora como uma "tábua de salvação" financeira para ajudar as empresas a adotarem práticas sustentáveis, o mercado de créditos de carbono tem enfrentado recentemente uma onda de ceticismo quanto à sua qualidade real. A tendência de projetos exagerarem os números de redução de emissões e apresentarem falta de sustentabilidade tem dissuadido até mesmo gigantes globais da tecnologia. Por exemplo, em abril, a Microsoft suspendeu temporariamente suas compras de novos créditos de carbono, refletindo a maior cautela dos compradores internacionais. Sob essa pressão, o Artigo 6.4 do Acordo de Paris – o mecanismo centralizado de concessão de créditos supervisionado diretamente pelas Nações Unidas – entrou oficialmente na fase de implementação com o objetivo de restabelecer a ordem no cenário das emissões de carbono. Aperto excessivo na liberação de crédito: queda de 40% na produção. Um ponto de virada importante ocorreu em fevereiro, quando o Órgão de Monitoramento da Convenção-Quadro das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (UNFCCC) aprovou os primeiros créditos, nos termos do Artigo 6.4, para um projeto de fogão a lenha limpo em Mianmar. Notavelmente, esse projeto havia sido originalmente registrado no âmbito do Mecanismo de Desenvolvimento Limpo (MDL) durante a era do Protocolo de Quioto. De acordo com uma análise da Clean Air Task Force (CATF) – uma organização não governamental internacional especializada em pesquisa climática independente – quando comparado usando a nova metodologia e fatores de cálculo mais cautelosos para biomassa não renovável, o projeto recebeu aproximadamente 40% menos créditos em comparação com o sistema MDL anterior. Você também pode gostar A "evaporação" de quase metade dos créditos de carbono é uma clara evidência de que as Nações Unidas estão a tornar a sua fórmula de cálculo mais rigorosa. O novo mecanismo obriga as partes a comprovarem que as reduções de emissões são reais, em vez de se basearem em cenários exagerados. Até à data, o organismo regulador aprovou apenas cinco metodologias, incluindo a captura de gás de aterro, o tratamento industrial de N₂O, as energias renováveis e a cozinha limpa. A transição dos projetos MDL legados para o Artigo 6.4 também está progredindo bastante lentamente. Embora o prazo para os países anfitriões aprovarem as transferências seja 30 de junho, os dados do início de 2026 mostram que apenas cerca de 13% dos créditos MDL submetidos foram aprovados. Isso indica que muitos governos estão considerando reter os créditos para fins de redução de emissões domésticas, em vez de vendê-los internacionalmente em larga escala. O "padrão ouro" em termos de qualidade e o desafio complexo das florestas. Em princípio, um crédito de carbono representa uma tonelada de CO2 equivalente que é reduzida ou removida da atmosfera. No entanto, para que um crédito tenha valor comercial sustentável, o Artigo 6.4 estabelece cinco condições rigorosas: complementaridade (o projeto só sobrevive graças ao financiamento de carbono), longevidade (por quanto tempo o carbono é armazenado), linha de base de emissões precisa, risco de fuga de emissões (não transferir a poluição para outro lugar) e um sistema independente de medição, relato e verificação (MRV). Embora os projetos de engenharia industrial possuam processos de medição relativamente claros, os aspectos de crédito de carbono na silvicultura e no uso da terra representam o maior desafio. As plantações podem ser destruídas por desastres naturais, pragas e doenças, ou o carbono acumulado no solo pode ser liberado quando a propriedade muda de mãos. Uma avaliação realizada pela organização sem fins lucrativos CATF, que analisou 20 regras de créditos florestais na América do Norte, revelou diversas lacunas na determinação da linha de base e na mitigação do risco de retorno de carbono. Embora os créditos florestais já tenham representado quase 40% do mercado voluntário, a metodologia para reflorestamento e recuperação de florestas só foi introduzida no processo de revisão da UNFCCC em outubro, e não há data definida para a aprovação final da estrutura. O dilema entre manter os padrões ambientais e facilitar o fluxo de capital privado é um grande problema. Se as regulamentações forem muito brandas, os créditos de acreditação se tornarão inúteis. Por outro lado, se os procedimentos forem muito complicados e os custos de acreditação muito altos, os países em desenvolvimento terão dificuldades para acessar o mercado. Isso impacta diretamente o roteiro do Vietnã. Você também pode gostar A onda de padronização internacional está impactando diretamente o progresso do Vietnã. Em 1º de abril, o Governo emitiu o Decreto 112/2026/ND-CP (em vigor desde 19 de maio). Este é um importante documento legal que estipula claramente o mecanismo para a troca de resultados de redução de emissões, tanto no âmbito do Artigo 6.2 (acordos bilaterais entre governos), quanto do Artigo 6.4, além de outras formas voluntárias. Anteriormente, em 14 de agosto, o Governo também aprovou a Resolução 235/NQ-CP, formalizando oficialmente o acordo de cooperação do Artigo 6 assinado com Singapura , com vigência a partir de setembro de 2025. Este acordo abre caminho para que empresas vietnamitas vendam créditos internacionalmente reconhecidos para a ilha. De acordo com dados do UNEP-CCC de 5 de novembro, o Vietnã possui 3 acordos bilaterais e 20 atividades registradas no âmbito do Artigo 6.2, embora nenhum crédito tenha sido oficialmente emitido ainda pelo canal do Artigo 6.4. artigo.texto: POWER Act: Clean energy advocates demand data center regulations Lawmakers, advocates hope to pass massive plan before veto session ends SPRINGFIELD, Ill. (WAND) – Clean energy advocates from across the state are pushing lawmakers to pass data center regulations during the second week of veto session. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle agree that Big Tech companies need to bring their own energy sources, pay their fair share for power, and use closed-loop water systems. Advocates say the POWER Act could also establish consumer protection and pollution control policies. “People are tired of waiting for the state to protect our local water supplies and from the dirty fossil fuel plants powering them,” said Springfield environmental activist Lori McKiernan. “People are tired of fighting against backroom deals without a real seat at the table.” The Illinois Environmental Council said the POWER Act would ban NDAs and require full access to any agreements signed. Some argue local governments should decide where data centers can be located and prevent the facilities from being approved within three miles of residential communities. The POWER Act could require data centers to develop energy supply and capacity need plans with renewable and battery storage protections that add new capacity to the power grid. “The protections in the POWER Act are the guardrails we need to protect ratepayers, communities, and our natural resources,” said Sen. Ram Villivalam (D-Chicago). “The impacts of data centers are too large to ignore.” Lawmakers could finalize data center regulations during lameduck session in early January if they fail to pass a bill Dec. 1 to 3. “I think that this has more political power and urgency behind it in getting things done than anything that I’ve ever seen in Springfield,” Illinois Environmental Council CEO Jen Walling said. “I think that people all over the state, bipartisan basis, are pushing legislators to act.” The renewed push comes after the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency and Illinois Power Agency released the 2026 reliability mitigation plan Monday. The joint report proposed extending the 2030 emission limits for gas- and oil-fired power plants under the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act to 2033. Advocates argue data centers haven’t been held accountable for their impact on grid reliability and energy costs. “Data centers claim to be the technology of the future, and yet they’re proposing extending the life of gas and coal plants to operate their facilities,” said IEC’s Cate Caldwell. “They’re operating behind closed doors, ignoring the concerns of local communities. And they’re sucking up our resources to line their shareholders’ pockets. That’s the past. That’s regression, and those days are over here in Illinois.” Copyright 2026 WAND. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: 247 – A COP31 apresentou nesta terça-feira (17) um acordo internacional para diminuir o impacto ambiental dos data centers, estruturas responsáveis pelo processamento de dados e pelo funcionamento de tecnologias digitais. De acordo com a Sputnik, o Brasil e outros oito países aderiram ao Compromisso de Antália sobre Inteligência Artificial nos eventos que ocorrem na Turquia. A iniciativa estimula a redução das emissões, o uso eficiente de água e energia e a adoção de práticas sustentáveis. O pacto não estabelece metas obrigatórias, mas prevê avaliações anuais durante as conferências climáticas até 2030. A presidência turca da COP31 desenvolveu a iniciativa em parceria com a União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT) e a Organização das Nações Unidas para a Educação, a Ciência e a Cultura (Unesco). A proposta busca enfrentar os efeitos ambientais associados à expansão da infraestrutura digital, especialmente diante do crescimento das atividades que dependem de centros de processamento de dados. Acordo busca reduzir consumo de energia e água O Compromisso de Antália estabelece diretrizes para incentivar práticas ambientais nos data centers. Entre as prioridades estão a ampliação da eficiência energética, a redução do consumo de água e o aumento da participação de fontes limpas no abastecimento dessas instalações. A iniciativa também contempla a economia circular, modelo que incentiva o reaproveitamento de materiais e a redução do desperdício ao longo dos processos produtivos. Outro ponto envolve o gerenciamento de equipamentos eletrônicos que chegam ao fim de sua vida útil. O documento defende procedimentos adequados para o descarte desses resíduos, buscando diminuir os impactos ambientais associados à infraestrutura tecnológica. O conjunto de orientações procura estimular mudanças na operação dos centros de processamento de dados, considerando tanto as necessidades energéticas quanto a utilização de recursos hídricos. Brasil participa de compromisso internacional A adesão brasileira coloca o país entre os participantes do entendimento anunciado durante a conferência climática na Turquia. Além do Brasil, outras oito nações assumiram o compromisso de incentivar medidas voltadas à sustentabilidade da infraestrutura digital. O caráter voluntário da iniciativa permite que os governos participantes desenvolvam ações sem a imposição de metas vinculantes de redução de emissões. O acordo estabelece, ainda assim, um mecanismo de acompanhamento anual nas conferências do clima, com avaliações previstas até 2030. A proposta busca manter a discussão sobre os impactos ambientais dos data centers na agenda internacional, permitindo que os países acompanhem as iniciativas implementadas ao longo desse período. Ausência de big techs dos Estados Unidos gera dúvidas Embora o entendimento tenha recebido o apoio de nove países, a iniciativa ainda enfrenta questionamentos sobre sua capacidade de produzir resultados concretos. O principal ponto de incerteza envolve a ausência das maiores empresas de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos, que figuram entre as principais operadoras mundiais da infraestrutura de processamento de dados. Sem a participação dessas companhias, o alcance das medidas dependerá da adesão voluntária dos governos e dos operadores interessados em incorporar as recomendações. O documento também não determina percentuais obrigatórios de redução das emissões, fator que limita sua capacidade de impor mudanças diretamente às empresas do setor. Mesmo com essas restrições, os participantes pretendem acompanhar anualmente o desenvolvimento das ações, mantendo o tema nas próximas conferências internacionais sobre o clima. Inteligência artificial poderá contribuir para soluções climáticas O compromisso não aborda apenas os impactos ambientais associados à operação dos sistemas digitais. A iniciativa também incentiva o desenvolvimento de aplicações de inteligência artificial voltadas ao enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas. Entre os exemplos apresentados está a utilização da tecnologia para melhorar a previsão de eventos climáticos extremos. O acordo também contempla mecanismos de cooperação tecnológica com países em desenvolvimento, buscando ampliar o acesso a instrumentos digitais que possam contribuir para a agenda ambiental. Essa orientação relaciona o desenvolvimento de sistemas de inteligência artificial à necessidade de reduzir seus efeitos ambientais e, simultaneamente, aproveitar suas aplicações no monitoramento e na resposta aos desafios climáticos. Pacto inclui proteção aos trabalhadores diante da automação Outra dimensão do Compromisso de Antália envolve as consequências da automação sobre o trabalho. O documento contempla medidas destinadas à proteção dos trabalhadores diante das transformações associadas à utilização crescente de inteligência artificial. A proposta integra essas preocupações sociais às diretrizes ambientais e tecnológicas, ampliando o alcance das discussões sobre a infraestrutura digital. No Brasil, o conteúdo do acordo apresenta pontos de convergência com iniciativas como o programa Computadores para Inclusão, mencionado entre as ações relacionadas à agenda tecnológica nacional. A proposta brasileira de sediar o Instituto de Inteligência Artificial para Mudanças Climáticas (AICI) também se relaciona aos objetivos do compromisso, especialmente no desenvolvimento de aplicações tecnológicas voltadas à questão ambiental. Com a adesão de nove países, o Compromisso de Antália estabelece uma agenda de cooperação sobre emissões, consumo de energia, utilização de água, resíduos eletrônicos e aplicações climáticas da inteligência artificial. O acompanhamento anual até 2030 permitirá observar os avanços das iniciativas voluntárias, em um cenário no qual as maiores empresas norte-americanas de tecnologia ainda não participam do pacto.
