artigo.texto: Utilities could be left holding the bill for billions in infrastructure spending committed in anticipation of artificial intelligence data centers that are delayed, downsized or canceled, industry observers and experts told Utility Dive. Opposition to data center construction has crossed traditional party lines, while Democratic gains in the midterms are adding pressure on earlier-stage investments across key markets. Together, these dynamics raise the stakes for project approvals and utility cost recovery, they say. “From a financing perspective, prolonged uncertainty will increase the cost of capital, reduce available leverage and make investors more hesitant to commit significant development dollars before power is secured,” said Andrejka Bernatova, managing partner of investment firm Dynamix Capital Partners, which invests in energy infrastructure. Even in regions that theoretically have enough capacity to accommodate new large loads, projects may struggle to secure a credible path to power on the timelines they need. “Interconnection, permitting, and financing all matter, but they are part of the same execution question of whether the team can get reliable power to the site and actually deliver,” Bernatova said. “A customer commitment or a large announced capacity number does not answer that by itself.” Ultimately, Bernatova expects investors to favor markets that offer certainty around power availability and timelines, potentially eroding the competitive advantage of markets like Texas, which until recently attracted substantial data center investment. Over the summer, Gov. Greg Abbott, R, announced a pause on new data center interconnections pending an audit of the queue. In the midterms, he lost his bid for reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who has pledged to maintain pressure on the industry after taking office next year. Ballot-box rebuke puts utility investment safeguards in focus Nearly all of the 46 municipal ballot measures tracked by Bloomberg that addressed data center development resulted in restrictions, moratoriums or bans. That unfavorability extends to a substantial share of the development pipeline. An estimated 191 GW of planned data center capacity faces new risk, with exposure concentrated in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, where incoming Democratic governors campaigned on pausing or restricting construction, according to a report from energy analytics firm Orennia that was shared with Utility Dive. Texas accounts for nearly half of the pre-construction in development in the U.S., so a statewide approval freeze would have an outsized impact on the national buildout, but the “impact of delayed or unrealized data center build-out on power prices varies widely across technologies and markets,” Orennia said. If 20% of projected data center demand in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas region fails to materialize, solar and wind generators could see their average wholesale revenue fall 38% and 37%, respectively, according to the report. Implied heat rates, a measure of the economics of gas-fired generation relative to fuel costs, could decline 39%. In the same scenario, two-hour battery storage arbitrage spreads could fall below new-build break-even requirements. In PJM, delaying half of the planned data center buildout by two years could reduce four-hour battery storage arbitrage spreads by 16% and lower solar and wind capture prices and implied heat rates by about 12% through 2030, the modeling suggests. The election results are unlikely to produce sweeping federal AI legislation but could lead to congressional hearings and greater transparency requirements, according to D.C.-based research and advisory firm Capstone. Its analysts expect much of the policy debate to take place at state utility commissions and local siting boards. Despite a proliferation of large-load tariffs over the past year, safeguards may still leave customers exposed in the event of a slowdown, some say. “Existing tariffs and regulatory frameworks likely won’t fully protect customers because they were designed for a different century,” Louisa Eberle, principal at the Regulatory Assistance Project, warned in a written statement. Eberle also called for reforms to utility business practices “to turn this data center surge into updated infrastructure, cleaner energy and a better deal for average customers.” The push for lower electricity bills is prompting policymakers to look more closely at how utilities use existing grid infrastructure. Richard Caperton, vice president of policy at SPAN, a maker of smart electrical panels, anticipates greater emphasis on data center projects that can be served without major new grid investments. “I’m really thrilled to see governors like Abigail Spanberger [in Virginia] campaign on affordability and then embrace utilization as the solution,” he said. In April, Gov. Spanberger signed legislation requiring Dominion Energy and Appalachian Power to report how effectively they use existing grid infrastructure. The State Corporation Commission can use those metrics to establish improvement targets and evaluate utility spending. “Winning candidates who emphasized lowering electricity prices are already looking for ways to deliver on their promises quickly,” Caperton said. “I expect that will lead to more policies and programs that boost grid utilization being ratified and implemented in early 2027. How those policies affect data center development and utility investments will vary by state.” A ‘necessary’ shakeout puts project commitments to the test Stephen Rose, CEO of infrastructure software provider Render Networks, said he expects to see a “pause and necessary shakeout” in data center development. “Fully permitted projects with real capital will keep moving,” Rose said. “The speculative end takes the hit: developers land-banking without firm power, and the contractors who staffed up for projects that won't break ground.” Rose cited AEP Ohio's large-load tariff,

Associações do setor elétrico defenderam a aprovação do texto original do PL 3.716/2026, que muda o rateio dos custos da contratação de baterias, durante almoço com parlamentares, nesta quarta (18/11). A avaliação predominante, compartilhada pelo autor, deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP), é que incluir outros temas no parecer pode atrasar ou inviabilizar a votação antes dos leilões de baterias de 2 e 4 de dezembro. A manifestação ocorre em meio à expectiava de que o parecer de Danilo Forte (PP/CE), relator do projeto, incorpore outros temas como mudanças na autoprodução e no ressarcimento dos cortes de geração. Participaram do almoço os deputados Joaquim Passarinho (PL/PA), presidente da Comissão de Minas e Energia da Câmara, Evair de Melo (Republicanos/ES) e Heitor Schuch (PSD/RS). A presidente da Associação Brasileira das Empresas Geradoras de Energia Elétrica (Abrage), Marisete Pereira, defendeu a aprovação do texto original, posição também sustentada por Rui Altirei, presidente da Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine). Já o presidente da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae), Fábio Lima, reforçou apenas que a contratação das baterias precisa ocorrer. Bárbara Rubim, da Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar), também defendeu a aprovação “da maneira como proposto pelo deputado Arnaldo Jardim”. Assim como a Associação Brasileira da Indústria de Hidrogênio Verde (Abihv). O presidente do conselho da entidade, Luis Viga, apontou a necssidade de preservar a segurança jurídica do setor elétrico e evitar o encarecimento da energia renovável, com impacto direto sobre os projetos de hidrogênio verde. Para a entidade, a imposição de adicionalidade na autoprodução, ao restringir o uso de usinas existentes e exigir nova geração, compromete a competitividade desses empreendimentos. As manifestações reforçaram a pressão para concentrar o projeto na mudança do rateio, sem reabrir outras disputas da reforma do setor elétrico. Em carta divulgada no evento Abeeólica, Abihv, Abrage, Abragel, Absae, Absolar e Apine não citam a aprovação do texto original, mas pedem ao Congresso a ‘priorização da tramitação e à aprovação da matéria” para garantir a segurança jurídica do leilão. A Abeeólica, entretanto, já entrou com uma ação civil pública para suspender os leilões de baterias, questionando a cobrança dos custos exclusivamente dos geradores. Também estava na mesa da entidade a possibilidade de uma Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade (ADI) no STF. Jardim articula apoio com governo e MME Jardim afirmou perceber uma posição favorável do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) ao texto, mas indicou que a articulação dentro do governo ainda busca uma posição conjunta sobre a proposta. Segundo ele, há um diálogo interno no governo para alinhar uma posição conjunta. Com o debate no Congresso concentrado na agenda fiscal, as associações devem se mobilizar para abrir espaço à votação do PL das baterias. O desafio é transformar o apoio à mudança no rateio em um acordo para aprovar a proposta na Câmara e no Senado nas duas semanas que restam até os leilões. A reforma da reforma O relator, Danilo Forte, não participou do almoço, assim como a Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica) e Associação Brasileira de Geração de Energia Limpa (Abragel). A eixos apurou que o parecer de Danilo Forte deve incorporar mudanças na autoprodução e no ressarcimento dos cortes de geração, o curtailment. O desconto nas tarifas de uso da rede deve ficar fora. O projeto pode se transformar, assim, em uma reforma da reforma do setor elétrico, cerca de um ano depois da aprovação da legislação relatada no Senado por Eduardo Braga (MDB/AM). Foi essa reforma, sancionada em novembro de 2025, que estabeleceu o custeio da contratação de baterias exclusivamente pelos geradores. Agora, o projeto de Jardim busca rever essa escolha, enquanto o parecer de Forte pode reabrir outras disputas enfrentadas na negociação do marco. Forte havia prometido apresentar o parecer na terça-feira passada (10), o que não aconteceu. O projeto tramita em regime de urgência desde 13 de outubro. O próprio autor tenta conter a ampliação do texto. Segundo a MegaWhat, Jardim trabalha para convencer o relator a concentrar o parecer na mudança do rateio, por avaliar que a inclusão de outras pautas pode dificultar a aprovação. “Em vez de você agregar apoio, você torna mais complexa a decisão”, afirmou Jardim na sexta-feira (13), durante evento de setor de energia em Portugal. Adicionalidade e curtailment ampliam a disputa Um dos pontos que deve estar no parecer vincula a autoprodução à adicionalidade — a exigência de nova capacidade de geração para o enquadramento no regime. A adicionalidade é uma disputa recorrente no Congresso. Rejeitada nas discussões do marco do hidrogênio, voltou na MP 1.307/2025, editada pelo governo para as ZPEs e que caducou, e reapareceu na reforma do setor elétrico. Agora, a exigência de nova geração para a autoprodução pode retornar no parecer das baterias, reabrindo o conflito sobre o aproveitamento das usinas existentes, em meio a uma crise de curtailment. O outro ponto trata exatamente do ressarcimento dos cortes de geração, uma das principais pressões sobre o caixa das geradoras renováveis. O governo já abriu um caminho para compensar parte das perdas passadas. A regulamentação publicada em julho alcança cortes por indisponibilidade externa e confiabilidade elétrica entre setembro de 2023 e novembro de 2025. Ficaram de fora os cortes por sobreoferta de energia. Permaneceu também a discussão sobre as perdas acumuladas depois daquele período e sobre o tratamento dos eventos futuros. artigo.texto: Will the Paris Agreement's carbon market generate high-quality carbon credits? (Dan Tri Newspaper) - The new mechanism under Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement has begun operating with stringent standards, causing the number of project credits granted to decrease by up to 40%, opening up a rigorous screening process for Vietnamese businesses. Once seen as a financial "lifeline" to help businesses go green, the carbon credit market has recently faced a wave of skepticism regarding its actual quality. The tendency for projects to exaggerate emission reduction figures and lack sustainability has deterred even global tech giants. For example, in April, Microsoft temporarily suspended its purchases of new carbon elimination credits, reflecting the heightened caution of international buyers. Under that pressure, Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement – the centralized credit granting mechanism directly overseen by the United Nations – officially entered the implementation phase with the goal of restoring order to the carbon game. Tightening the credit disbursement valve: A 40% drop in output. A major turning point occurred in February, when the Monitoring Body of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) approved the first credits under Article 6.4 for a clean cooking stove project in Myanmar. Notably, this project had originally been registered under the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) during the Kyoto Protocol era. According to an analysis by the Clean Air Task Force (CATF) – an international non- governmental organization specializing in independent climate research – when compared using the new methodology and more cautious calculation factors for non-renewable biomass, the project received approximately 40% fewer credits compared to the previous CDM system. You may also like The "evaporation" of nearly half of the credit output is clear evidence that the United Nations is tightening its calculation formula. The new mechanism forces parties to prove that emissions reductions are real, rather than relying on exaggerated scenarios. To date, the regulatory body has only approved five methodologies, including landfill gas capture, industrial N2O treatment, renewable energy, and clean cooking. The transition from legacy CDM projects to Article 6.4 is also progressing quite slowly. Although the deadline for host countries to approve transfers is June 30th, early 2026 figures show that only about 13% of submitted CDM credits have been approved. This indicates that many governments are considering retaining credits for domestic emission reduction purposes, rather than selling them off internationally on a massive scale. The "gold standard" for quality and the challenging problem of forests. In principle, one carbon credit represents one ton of CO2 equivalent that is reduced or removed from the atmosphere. However, for a credit to have sustainable commercial value, Article 6.4 sets out five stringent conditions: complementarity (the project only survives thanks to the carbon funding), longevity (how long the carbon is stored), accurate emission baseline, emission leakage risk (not shifting pollution elsewhere), and an independent measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) system. While industrial engineering projects have relatively clear measurement processes, the credit-based aspects of forestry and land use present the greatest challenge. Crops can be destroyed by natural disasters, pests and diseases, or accumulated carbon in the soil can be released when ownership changes. An assessment by the non-profit organization CATF, reviewing 20 forest credit rules in North America, has revealed a number of gaps in baseline determination and carbon return risk mitigation. Although forest credits once accounted for nearly 40% of the voluntary market, the methodology for reforestation and reforestation was only introduced into the UNFCCC review process in October, and there is no date set for final approval of the framework. The dilemma between upholding environmental standards and facilitating the flow of private capital is a major headache. If regulations are too lenient, accreditation credits will become useless. Conversely, if procedures are too complicated and accreditation costs too high, developing countries will struggle to access the market. This directly impacts Vietnam's roadmap. This is an important legal document that clearly stipulates the mechanism for exchanging emission reduction results under both Article 6.2 (bilateral agreements between governments), Article 6.4, and other voluntary forms. Previously, on August 14th, the Government also approved Resolution 235/NQ-CP, officially formalizing the Article 6 cooperation agreement signed with Singapore , effective from September 2025. This handshake paves the way for Vietnamese businesses to sell internationally accredited credits to the island nation. According to UNEP-CCC data as of November 5th, Vietnam has 3 bilateral agreements and 20 registered activities under Article 6.2, although no credits have yet been officially issued through the Article 6.4 channel. On the domestic stage, the carbon exchange has also been operational since June 29th. According to data from the UNDP, the total pilot quota for the 2025-2026 period is approximately 511 million tons of CO2 equivalent, directly allocated to 110 large facilities in three heavy-emission sectors: thermal power, iron and steel, and cement. artigo.texto: Consumo de eletricidade – A expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) exige uma infraestrutura física cada vez maior, que depende de grandes quantidades de eletricidade para processar dados e manter servidores em funcionamento. O impacto ambiental dessa estrutura, porém, pode ser maior do que se imaginava. Uma pesquisa da Universidade Harvard, nos Estados Unidos, identificou o consumo energético e as emissões de centenas de centros de dados, revelando a dimensão da demanda elétrica provocada por essas instalações. Publicado em 16 de novembro de 2026 na revista científica Nature Sustainability, o estudo analisou 403 instalações classificadas como hyperscale data centers, centros de dados de grande porte utilizados para computação em nuvem, armazenamento digital e inteligência artificial. LEIA: Diferença salarial entre brancos e negros chega a 71% no Brasil Os pesquisadores estimaram que essas estruturas consumiram aproximadamente 82 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, considerando o cenário central de funcionamento. O volume representa cerca de 1,8% de toda a eletricidade consumida nos Estados Unidos no período. Além da demanda energética, o funcionamento dos centros de dados foi associado à emissão de aproximadamente 25,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO₂). O resultado é entre duas e três vezes superior às estimativas anteriores referentes a 2018, embora os períodos e as metodologias utilizadas não sejam diretamente comparáveis. A pesquisa também apontou que aproximadamente 54% da eletricidade atribuída às instalações analisadas foi gerada a partir de combustíveis fósseis. Os dados estão disponíveis no estudo publicado na Nature Sustainability, que apresenta uma avaliação detalhada da relação entre centros de dados, consumo energético e emissões de carbono. Satélites ajudaram a identificar o consumo dos centros de dados A falta de informações detalhadas sobre o funcionamento dessas instalações é um dos obstáculos para avaliar seus impactos ambientais. Empresas de tecnologia divulgam relatórios de sustentabilidade, mas nem sempre disponibilizam dados específicos sobre o consumo de eletricidade de cada centro de dados. Para contornar essa limitação, os pesquisadores utilizaram imagens de satélite para identificar as instalações e estimar sua demanda energética. As informações foram cruzadas com dados da Agência de Proteção Ambiental dos Estados Unidos (EPA), permitindo identificar as fontes de energia utilizadas pelas redes elétricas regionais. A combinação dos dados possibilitou relacionar o funcionamento dos centros de dados às emissões das usinas responsáveis pelo fornecimento de eletricidade. Virgínia, Oregon, Ohio e Iowa concentraram mais da metade do consumo energético analisado. Apesar dos resultados, os cientistas ressaltam que as instalações estudadas atendem a diferentes serviços digitais, e não exclusivamente à inteligência artificial. Por isso, não é possível atribuir todas as emissões identificadas apenas aos sistemas de IA generativa. Emissões também podem afetar a saúde da população Os impactos ambientais dos centros de dados não se limitam ao aquecimento global. Quando a eletricidade utilizada pelas instalações é produzida por usinas a carvão ou gás natural, a geração de energia também pode liberar poluentes como material particulado fino, óxidos de nitrogênio e dióxido de enxofre. Essas substâncias estão associadas a problemas respiratórios e cardiovasculares, o que pode afetar comunidades próximas às usinas, mesmo que os centros de dados estejam localizados a centenas de quilômetros de distância. Francesca Dominici, professora de Harvard e uma das responsáveis pelo estudo, destaca que investigar os efeitos dessas emissões sobre a saúde humana será uma das próximas etapas da pesquisa. O levantamento, entretanto, estimou as emissões de carbono e não mediu diretamente a ocorrência de doenças ou mortes relacionadas às instalações analisadas. Consumo de energia pode aumentar até 2030 O avanço da inteligência artificial deve ampliar ainda mais a demanda por eletricidade. Segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA), o consumo global de energia dos centros de dados poderá dobrar até 2030, enquanto a demanda das instalações especializadas em IA poderá triplicar. Em 2025, os centros de dados foram responsáveis por aproximadamente 1,5% do consumo mundial de eletricidade. A agência também estima que as emissões globais relacionadas à energia utilizada por essas instalações estejam próximas de 150 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ por ano, podendo chegar a 350 milhões de toneladas em 2035, considerando o cenário central. O crescimento da infraestrutura também pode sobrecarregar redes elétricas locais, exigindo investimentos em novas usinas, linhas de transmissão e sistemas de refrigeração. O consumo de água representa outro desafio, especialmente em regiões que já enfrentam escassez hídrica. Energia limpa pode reduzir o impacto ambiental da IA A redução dos impactos ambientais da inteligência artificial não depende exclusivamente do desenvolvimento de computadores mais eficientes. A localização dos centros de dados e as fontes de eletricidade utilizadas também são determinantes. Instalações abastecidas por fontes de baixa emissão, como energia solar, eólica e nuclear, podem apresentar uma pegada de carbono operacional significativamente menor. Alternativas incluem o reaproveitamento do calor produzido pelos servidores, melhorias nos sistemas de refrigeração e o desenvolvimento de modelos de IA que demandem menos energia. Durante a COP31, realizada na Turquia, governos e organizações internacionais apresentaram uma iniciativa voluntária voltada ao incentivo de energia limpa, eficiência energética e maior transparência ambiental no setor tecnológico. A inteligência artificial também pode contribuir para reduzir emissões em áreas como transporte, indústria e gestão de redes elétricas. No entanto, esses benefícios potenciais não eliminam au

A conta começa na coleta Antes de contratar uma solução, a cooperativa pode testar a qualidade dos dados de uma amostra de propriedades. Consumo de energia, combustível e insumos deve ser registrado com período, fonte e responsável. A escolha dos limites do inventário muda o esforço necessário. Para decidir se amplia o projeto, vale estimar o custo de coleta, validação e manutenção dos registros. artigo.texto: Um projeto aprovado pela Assembleia Legislativa do Estado do Paraná (Alep) estabelece diretrizes para incentivar a instalação e a expansão de data centers no estado. O Projeto de Lei 55/2026 cria o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (ProdataPR). Aprovada na terça-feira, 17, a proposta é uma iniciativa dos deputados Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (PP) e Bazana (PSD). O projeto visa ao desenvolvimento da economia digital, à atração de investimentos privados, à geração de empregos especializados e ao aproveitamento das vantagens competitivas do Paraná, especialmente na produção de energia renovável e na conectividade. De acordo com a deputada Maria Victoria, o texto tem o objetivo de criar condições para posicionar o Paraná como um dos principais destinos de investimentos em infraestrutura digital, inteligência artificial e novas tecnologias no Brasil. O deputado Luiz Fernando Guerra destaca a importância do planejamento para que a expansão dos data centers no Paraná seja acompanhada pela formação de profissionais para o setor. Já o deputado Pedro Paulo Bazana (PSD) diz que a proposta busca transformar o potencial tecnológico do Paraná em oportunidades de desenvolvimento para os municípios. Data centers Os data centers são estruturas essenciais para o funcionamento da economia digital. Neles são armazenadas e processadas grandes quantidades de informações utilizadas por empresas, governos, instituições financeiras, hospitais, universidades e plataformas. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial, essas instalações ganharam importância estratégica na disputa mundial por investimentos tecnológicos. Conforme a justificativa do projeto, o ProdataPR tem a finalidade de consolidar o Paraná como polo estratégico de data centers na América Latina, gerando empregos qualificados e fomentando a cadeia produtiva de tecnologia. O texto ainda autoriza o Governo do Estado a conceder benefícios fiscais às empresas beneficiárias do programa. A proposta estabelece diretrizes para estimular novos empreendimentos, aumentar a infraestrutura de telecomunicações e incentivar parcerias entre empresas, universidades e centros de pesquisa. Outro diferencial é a preocupação com a sustentabilidade. O projeto incentiva a utilização de fontes renováveis de energia, o aproveitamento do biometano, o uso racional da água e a adoção de tecnologias sustentáveis de resfriamento dos equipamentos. A aprovação da proposta ocorre em um momento de expansão do setor no Brasil. Em setembro de 2026, foi sancionada a Lei Federal n.º 15.504, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). A legislação federal prevê incentivos tributários condicionados a compromissos de sustentabilidade, investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento e utilização de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão. (Com informações da assessoria de comunicação da Alep)

artigo.texto: O Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos publicará norma que obriga operadoras de data centers no Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia a obterem licença prévia para comprar chips avançados de inteligência artificial destinados a esses centros de dados, produzidos pela Nvidia e por outros fabricantes americanos. A medida visa impedir que a China e outros adversários dos EUA acessem capacidade computacional localizada no exterior que utiliza processadores projetados nos Estados Unidos. A decisão ocorre na esteira do escândalo que levou à renúncia do ex-CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, na semana passada, após revelação de relacionamento com uma executiva chinesa suspeita de espionagem. Os países listados apresentam risco de contrabando acima do normal, segundo o governo americano. A norma foi elaborada para garantir que restrições existentes a tecnologias americanas sensíveis não sejam contornadas por acordos de computação remota envolvendo data centers em terceiros países. A regulamentação fecha brecha que, na visão de muitos em Washington, permitia à China contornar a proibição de compra dos chips de IA mais avançados. Ela estabelece restrições para data centers no exterior que forneçam volumes significativos de capacidade computacional a empresas sediadas em países de alto risco, lista que inclui China, Rússia e Irã. Os centros também deverão realizar verificações rigorosas sobre clientes. A regra, que entra em vigor em 90 dias, deve prejudicar a capacidade dessas empresas de usar chips americanos para treinar modelos avançados de IA. Ações de fabricantes de chips caíram na manhã desta segunda-feira. Papéis da Nvidia recuaram mais de 2%, da Intel mais de 6% e da Micron mais de 7%. O Philadelphia Semiconductor Index caiu mais de 5%, e o Nasdaq também abriu em baixa. O plano surge dias antes da viagem do presidente Donald Trump à China para cúpula econômica, na qual se reunirá com Xi Jinping. A proposta foi divulgada dias após Huang renunciar, após admitir relacionamento extraconjugal com Alice Huang, ex-executiva da Megaspeed International, empresa de Cingapura investigada por possíveis violações de controles de exportação e suspeita de envolvimento em espionagem para a China. A empresa nega irregularidades, e Alice Huang está atualmente na China. Após a queda de Huang, o Departamento de Comércio e autoridades de alto escalão, incluindo o secretário Howard Lutnick, enfrentaram maior escrutínio. O secretário do Tesouro Scott Bessent responsabilizou Lutnick por não ter feito o suficiente para garantir cumprimento das restrições. A norma alinha regras de acesso remoto às restrições já existentes para acesso físico. Há exceção para empresas com sede nos EUA que operam nos países listados, que podem continuar enviando chips sem licença, e para envios a data centers usados como sistemas comerciais de recomendação por varejistas online ou redes sociais. Analistas afirmam que a aplicação ficará a cargo do Departamento de Comércio, e ainda não está claro como será implementada. A minuta estabelece que as exigências entram em vigor com a publicação no Federal Register, que ainda não havia ocorrido até as 9h desta segunda. A possibilidade de a China acessar chips via aluguel de capacidade em data centers do Sudeste Asiático e outras regiões tem sido fonte de divergências no governo Trump. O escândalo da Nvidia elevou o tema aos mais altos escalões, gerando atritos entre o Departamento de Comércio e outros setores. O anúncio afirmou que a norma foi redigida pelo Departamento do Tesouro e por determinação deste e do Conselho de Segurança Nacional, instituições que defendiam regras mais rigorosas. Licenças serão analisadas caso a caso. Nos últimos meses, Scott Bessent, Marco Rubio e Jamieson Greer defenderam restrições abrangentes, enquanto Lutnick resistia a uma versão mais enxuta.

artigo.texto: By Kate Newton of RNZ The government could forgo up to $12 billion in revenue from carbon auctions if it does not overhaul the emissions trading scheme, a new report says. The research, published Friday by policy think-tank Motu, said the current scheme was delaying cuts to New Zealand’s climate pollution and needed major reform. Instead of driving down emissions, the scheme was creating “investment risk for emitters and foresters, climate target risk for the government, and intergenerational risk for New Zealanders”. By the mid-2030s, without changes to the scheme, the government would be forced to bring an early end to its quarterly auctions, and the potential revenue from them, the report found. The country would briefly meet its 2050 net-zero target, but emissions would then rise again, it warned. The incumbent government has said the emissions trading scheme (ETS) should be the main tool for driving down New Zealand’s emissions. Earlier this week at the annual global climate summit, caretaker climate minister Simon Watts noted in his national statement that New Zealand’s ETS, established in 2008, was “the second oldest in the world”. However, the Motu research is the second report in just a few months to declare the scheme “rudderless”, because of design flaws that have encouraged massive forestry planting instead of actual cuts to emissions. In August, the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment called for forestry – which can earn carbon credits – to be removed from the scheme. The scheme requires polluters to surrender one carbon credit – known as New Zealand Units – for each tonne of emissions they create in a year. They can buy units at quarterly government auctions, or receive them for free if their business creates emissions that are difficult or expensive to reduce. The ETS also allows forestry owners to earn and sell units for carbon dioxide stored in trees. There is no limit on forestry units that can enter the scheme, and so no incentive to cut emissions as long as trees continue to be planted and polluters can afford the credits. Modelling in both the Motu and PCE reports concluded that by the mid-2030s, a glut of carbon units from forestry would converge with falling demand for those units as polluters gradually decarbonised anyway. With no extra credits needed from the quarterly auctions, the government would lose control over supply and demand, along with the ability to earn auction revenue. “Deferring policy change beyond 2030 could forgo around $11-12 billion in auction revenue through 2035,” the report said. Like the PCE report, Motu’s suggested “direction of travel” was to take sequestration like forestry out of the scheme altogether – though stockpiled surplus credits could be kept to “honour past investments”. The revamped ETS would encourage polluters to curb their emissions faster, or pay for credits that would steadily increase in cost without unlimited forestry units suppressing the price. Modelling in the report showed the money raised from auctions under that scenario would be enough to fund a separate ‘removals incentive mechanism’ that could include native planting, wetlands restoration and other forms of carbon storage. Lead author and former climate change commissioner Catherine Leining said that would mean carbon removals and emissions cuts could both happen without one being traded off against the other. “They’re actually very different, and New Zealand needs both and the climate needs both,” she said. The UN and other global organisations had now concluded it was inevitable the world would exceed 1.5°C of warming, and was also on track to go past 2°C, making carbon removals to reverse climate change more important than ever, Leining said. “The need for removals is going to rise as temperatures rise, but emitters are going to stop buying as they decarbonise. “That creates a lot of demand uncertainty for foresters in the long-term when we really need their forestry.” Motu’s modelling showed there would be a “net fiscal benefit” even after paying for a removals scheme, Leining said. It showed New Zealand could not only reach and maintain its net-zero target by 2050, but could also reach the Climate Change Commission’s more ambitious net-negative target – a recommendation rejected by the government last year. Nobody involved in the scheme was served well by it at the moment, she said. Price volatility made it hard for both foresters and emitters to plan and invest, the government was already losing revenue through failed auctions, and the scheme’s failure was pushing the costs of climate change onto younger generations. Motu’s report was just a starting point but the organisation wanted to see the government start work on reforms immediately, Leining said. “We’re really encouraging the policy development process to start now, because this is actually a process that’s going to take time to do well.” That process and any changes needed to be carefully staged, with inclusive and transparent consultation, to avoid market disruption. “Our goal here is really to ensure that no one is worse off and hopefully everyone is better off than under the status quo.” This story was first published on rnz.co.nz

artigo.texto: The voluntary carbon market debate we’re having is wrong For several years now, one question has dominated the technical debate over voluntary carbon markets: should host countries be required to apply “corresponding adjustments” — accounting entries that prevent the same emission reduction from being counted twice — when their carbon credits are purchased by foreign companies? The question sounds like a dry accounting matter. It is not. Depending on how it is answered, the result could be either a more credible voluntary carbon market or a smaller and less effective one — with the costs falling disproportionately on the countries and projects that need climate finance most. A new EDF paper, Corresponding Adjustments and the Voluntary Carbon Market makes the case that the debate, as currently framed, is asking the wrong question. What corresponding adjustments are — and where they apply A corresponding adjustment is an accounting entry applied to a host country’s national emission balance when it transfers a mitigation outcome internationally. The logic is simple: If a country sells reductions to a foreign buyer, it should not also count those reductions toward its own Paris Agreement commitment. The same tonne of CO₂ cannot discharge two obligations simultaneously. This accounting obligation is legally clear in two contexts. Under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, CAs are required for government-to-government transfers of mitigation outcomes. Under CORSIA, the international aviation offsetting scheme, CAs are required when airlines use credits to discharge their compliance obligations. Both cases involve legal obligations being discharged through the same transaction — which is precisely why double-counting matters. The contested question is different: Should CAs also be required for purely voluntary transactions, where a company purchases credits to support its own net zero commitment, not to satisfy any legal obligation? Two questions that keep getting conflated The CA debate suffers from a persistent failure to distinguish between two fundamentally different questions. - The accounting question: Are CAs legally required for voluntary corporate transactions under the Paris Agreement? The answer is no. The Paris Agreement and its implementing decisions are entirely silent on what corporate climate claims may or may not be made on the basis of carbon credits. The leap from “sovereign accounting requires CAs for government-to-government transfers” to “corporate offsetting claims require CA-backed credits” is a normative position, not a treaty requirement. - The policy effectiveness question: Would mandating CAs for voluntary transactions, in practice, produce better climate outcomes? This is an empirical question — and the honest answer is that we do not yet have the evidence to resolve it. Conflating these two questions has consequences. When CAs are treated as a matter of accounting integrity, those who oppose them are forced to defend double-counting. When they are treated as a policy instrument with costs and benefits, the burden shifts to proponents to demonstrate that the benefits outweigh the costs. The second framing is the correct one. Do CAs improve climate outcomes? Whether mandating CAs would strengthen or weaken global climate outcomes depends on three empirical parameters that remain poorly understood. - Host country responsiveness: If countries systematically reduce their own domestic climate ambition when private carbon finance flows in — substituting international private money for domestic public commitment — then even additional project-level credits generate no net global benefit. This is the displacement concern at the heart of the pro-CA argument. It is a legitimate concern. But the evidence for it, across the heterogeneous landscape of VCM host countries, does not yet exist at the scale needed to justify a blanket policy response. - Supply sensitivity: World Bank modelling suggests that CA-related fees could exceed $25 per tonne of CO₂ in many host countries — enough to render the most finance-dependent, highest-additionality projects unviable. For projects where carbon revenues are the margin between proceeding and not, this is not a marginal cost. The authorization infrastructure needed to implement CAs efficiently is also, as of today, absent in most potential host countries. Mandating CAs before that infrastructure exists would not reform the market — it would freeze it. - Buyer differentiation: The pro-CA position assumes that CA backing is what makes corporate claims credible. But neither the ICVCM’s Core Carbon Principles, the VCMI’s Claims Code of Practice, nor the SBTi’s framework for beyond-value-chain mitigation currently requires CA backing for valid corporate claims. If buyers and the public do not, in practice, distinguish meaningfully between CA-backed and non-CA credits when the underlying quality is high, the market case for mandating CAs weakens considerably. Who pays when we get CA requirements wrong? The cost structure of CA requirements is not neutral. The most additional projects — those entirely dependent on carbon revenue to proceed — face the steepest barriers from authorization fees. Low-additionality projects, which would happen regardless of carbon finance, are comparatively unaffected. A policy designed to protect environmental integrity should not systematically penalize the most genuinely additional activities. The geographic pattern is similarly concerning. The countries with the greatest mitigation potential and the greatest need for climate finance are typically those with the least authorization infrastructure. The CDM precedent is instructive: Administrative requirements contributed to a heavy concentration of activity in a small number of large, institutionally sophisticated economies, with relatively little reaching least-developed countries. There is no reason to assume CA requirements would produce a different distribution.

artigo.texto: A Assembleia Legislativa do Paraná (Alep) aprovou, nesta terça-feira (17), o Projeto de Lei 55/2026, que cria o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (PRODATAPR). A proposta estabelece diretrizes para estimular a instalação e a expansão de data centers no Estado. O projeto é de autoria dos deputados Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (PP) e Pedro Paulo Bazana (PSD). Entre os objetivos estão atrair investimentos privados, ampliar a infraestrutura tecnológica e incentivar a formação de profissionais para trabalhar no setor. Os data centers são estruturas utilizadas para armazenar, processar e distribuir grandes volumes de informações. Eles atendem empresas, instituições financeiras, hospitais, universidades, órgãos públicos e plataformas digitais. Com o crescimento de serviços de computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial, esse tipo de infraestrutura passou a ter maior importância para o setor de tecnologia. Projeto prevê incentivos fiscais O texto autoriza o Governo do Paraná a conceder benefícios fiscais às empresas que participarem do programa. A proposta também prevê medidas para ampliar a infraestrutura de telecomunicações e estimular parcerias entre empresas, universidades e centros de pesquisa. Outro ponto é a formação de mão de obra especializada. O projeto estabelece diretrizes para incentivar cursos e parcerias voltados à qualificação de profissionais que poderão atuar na construção, operação e manutenção dos centros de dados. Na justificativa, os autores apontam a produção de energia renovável e a estrutura de conectividade do Paraná como fatores que podem favorecer a instalação desses empreendimentos. Proposta inclui medidas ambientais O programa também prevê diretrizes relacionadas à sustentabilidade. Entre elas estão o incentivo ao uso de fontes renováveis de energia, o aproveitamento do biometano, o uso racional da água e a adoção de tecnologias de resfriamento que reduzam os impactos ambientais. A proposta busca ampliar a participação do Paraná no setor de infraestrutura digital e estimular a instalação de empreendimentos em diferentes regiões do Estado. Setor também recebe incentivo federal A aprovação do projeto estadual ocorre após a sanção da Lei Federal 15.504, em setembro de 2026, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). A legislação federal prevê incentivos tributários para empresas do setor, condicionados ao cumprimento de compromissos relacionados à sustentabilidade, aos investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento e ao uso de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão.

artigo.texto: Montrose County drafting data center regulations during moratorium MONTROSE, Colo. (KJCT) - Montrose County is drafting regulations for data centers while a moratorium on data center applications is in place. The Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the regulations Thursday at 6 p.m. Discussion of data centers has grown over the last couple of years. Moratorium in place Montrose County approved a six-month moratorium on data center applications in July. Tallmadge Richmond, Montrose County planning and development director, said the county does not accept applications while a moratorium is in place. “That gives us time to basically research and analyze what these facilities are, what kind of impacts they have,” Richmond said. Draft regulations The county is in the process of drafting data center regulations. Meetings are being held to adjust potential amendments to zoning regulations and to hear from the public. Richmond said the Planning Commission heard public comment the last time the item was heard and then they adjusted the draft based on that. “So it is to continue hearing public comment, but also see if the draft now captures what the Planning Commission was looking for,” Richmond said. The current draft would allow data centers in the general agricultural district and the general industrial district. Both would be allowed by special use. Richmond said that designation means any future data center proposed in Montrose County would have public hearings related to that specific facility and location. Minimum standards Under the draft, all facilities would need to meet minimum standards in several categories. They include energy and water usage, thermal and noise impacts, and others. Richmond said the standards acknowledge potential negative impacts to surrounding properties and identify minimum standards to mitigate them. Next steps The regulations must be finalized by the Planning Commission and approved by the county commissioners before they are adopted. The county is also considering an extension of the moratorium while the regulations are finalized. The moratorium will end when the regulations are finalized. Public hearing details The Planning Commission will hold a public hearing to discuss the regulations Thursday at 6 p.m. The hearing will be held in the Montrose County Public Works Board Room.

artigo.texto: The UL-certified, ITC-eligible system is built at the company’s award-winning Megafactory 1, with deployments planned at commercial sites across North America AUSTIN, Texas and VANCOUVER, British Columbia, Nov. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Moment Energy today unveiled Nova, its next-generation battery energy storage system (BESS). Nova is the world's first BESS made with repurposed electric vehicle batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification. The certifications help support its use in commercial, industrial and large-scale energy storage applications. Nova is now in production at the company’s award-winning Megafactory 1 for deployment across North America. The BESS enables commercial customers to reduce energy costs, improve site reliability and uptime, and integrate clean energy into their operations. Moment Energy has already deployed systems powering critical infrastructure including airports, hospitals, agricultural and manufacturing sites. Nova is made in North America and independently verified as fully compliant with Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements. Moment Energy has also been independently verified as a non-Prohibited Foreign Entity. Together, this makes Nova the only third-party verified BESS eligible for the U.S. federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) in 2027 and beyond. "Access to affordable power is a defining factor determining where businesses can grow and what they can build. Today, businesses across North America are being throttled by power capacity constraints,” said Edward Chiang, Co-Founder and CEO of Moment Energy. “We see a future where reengineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chain. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering and North American manufacturing to deploy the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid.” Designed for Performance, Flexibility and Long-Term Value The Nova platform is designed to integrate batteries from multiple types of EVs into its flexible stationary storage platform. Moment Energy’s proprietary AI-powered battery management system (BMS) continuously evaluates and optimizes batteries across different states of health to maximize performance, efficiency and reliability throughout the system's life. Each Nova block delivers 200 kW of power / 500 kWh of energy within a 2.94 m by 1.80 m (9.65 ft x 5.9 ft) footprint. This compact, scalable design brings substantial energy storage capacity to commercial sites where space is an important consideration, while also enabling Nova to deploy in large-scale installations in the tens of MWhs. Nova helps commercial energy users save by supporting grid services and utility bill savings, as well as providing resilient backup power during grid outages. Nova’s swappable architecture allows individual battery packs to be replaced as they age over time, instead of replacing the entire system. Durable infrastructure such as the enclosure and concrete pad can remain undisturbed, while the battery packs are serviced and replaced. This design extends the system's lifespan to more than 20 years with Moment Energy’s capacity augmentation service. "With Nova, we’ve solved the engineering challenges that have prevented BESS made with EV batteries from scaling commercially,” said Gurmesh Sidhu, Co-Founder and Chief Product Officer of Moment Energy. “Every element of the platform has been engineered to maximize flexibility, simplify servicing and give customers confidence that the system will reliably power their critical infrastructure for decades." Batteries Made in North America As battery storage becomes increasingly critical for commercial energy users, battery supply has become a global issue of international trade and national security, with the large majority of batteries currently imported from China. By establishing a new domestic supply chain from the abundant supply of retiring EV batteries, Moment Energy's Nova allows the U.S. and Canada to keep critical minerals and battery software in North America. Repurposing is an important step in the circular economy, unlocking years or even decades of residual value in a battery after its useful life for electric vehicle applications is over, preventing batteries from entering landfills. Nova brings that value into commercial energy infrastructure through a platform engineered, manufactured and supported in North America. Engineered and Certified for Safety Nova is the first BESS built from EV batteries that is certified to UL 9540 by UL Solutions. Nova has achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications, key safety certifications also commonly held by first-life battery systems, and has been tested to UL 9540A for evaluating thermal runaway fire propagation in BESS. With these certifications, Nova meets the listing requirements of electrical codes of the United States and Canada for stationary storage. Additionally, Megafactory 1 is certified to UL 1974, the standard for sorting, grading and repurposing electric vehicle batteries. “Repurposing electric vehicle batteries for stationary energy storage creates new technical considerations that must be carefully evaluated,” said Jeff Smidt, senior vice president of Testing, Inspection and Certification, Industrial, at UL Solutions. “UL Certification demonstrates that the evaluated battery and energy storage system met applicable safety requirements. This achievement provides important third-party evidence supporting the responsible use of repurposed batteries in commercial and industrial energy storage applications.” Nova combines these UL certifications with integrated safety features and engineering for demanding commercial environments: Nova’s rigorous safety engineering allows the system to be installed in the outdoor built environment, alongside the buildings and facilities it serves. artigo.texto: Trending Although public comment on the proposed amendment to Lycoming County's zoning ordinance pertaining to data centers was light at the hearing held by the county commissioners this week, there were a few suggestions on how to tweak the document which governs data center principal uses and data center accessory uses in the 19 municipalities under the county's zoning. Brown, Bastress, Cascade. Cogan House, Gamble, Jackson, Jordan, Lewis, Limestone, McHenry, McIntyre, McNett, Mifflin, Moreland, Penn, Pine, Plunketts Creek and Porter Townships and Salladasburg Borough are the 19 municipalities that partner with the county. Most of the comments during the public comment section of the hearing came from a resident of Muncy Township, which is not governed by the county's zoning, but rather makes their own planning and zoning decisions. The township is currently seeking to pass their own curative amendment for data center. Earlier this year, the county had declared their zoning ordinance invalid because it did not address data centers, which Jenny Picciano, director of the county's planning and community development department, said was actually unheard of at the time the last amendment to the zoning ordinance was written. "Through this amendment we are now trying to propose and establish clear standards for how and when these facilities will be used," Picciano said. She noted that the amendment only applies to the municipalities in the county zoning partnership. "If you are from a municipality that is not in that, I would encourage you to talk to your own elected officials who manage and operate your zoning ordinance to have this discussion," she said. Picciano explained that the amendment was developed by ENTECH Professional Services PC, who were contracted by the county. "As part of this, we did a lot of research into what other communities were doing," Picciano said. "This was also reviewed by our planning commission solicitor and we also retained secondary legal counsel from an outside legal firm because it is such an important issue in our community," she said. Picciano explained that the amendment establishes clear guidelines, definitions, and performance standards for the development and operations of principal data centers, which is the main data center and the accessory data center uses for the municipality partners. This would include things like generators and backup power. She emphasized that included in the amendment is an extensive definition section about what constitutes a principal data center and data center accessories. "Under our proposed ordinance, it would add data center principal uses and data center accessory uses to the zoning ordinance as specifically regulated industrial uses. So not agriculture, not residential, but specifically industrial uses relegated to the industrial zoning districts...The proposed ordinance would also establish supplemental standards for infrastructure, water, sewer, cooling, power, noise, emergency response, backup power systems, backup power generation, equipment recycling, electronic waste, decommissioning, among other standards," Picciano said. "So together and collectively, these proposed regulations are intended to provide tools to evaluate potential impacts of data centers in these uses, and to protect nearby residents and sensitive areas, conserve our natural resources, and address infrastructure and public safety concerns," she said. Other requirements outlined in the proposed amendment include setback and separation requirements from residential areas and sensitive receptors, which are things like schools and churches. "We include noise and vibration standards that include pre-construction noise studies, noise model, and violation of motion. We require screening and fencing, emergency response planning, industrial-scale battery storage information, industrial-scale power generation standards, operational water meetings, water metering and reporting. We do require extensive coordination with the local water authorities if they are proposing to use public water, and financial security required," she said. She pointed out that those requirements are clearly outlined in the ordinance and all data center development proposals must meet them before they are sent to the zoning board for approval. Picciano said that the proposed ordinance does not guarantee approval of any future development. "At this time, the county. I just want to state that we have not received any applications or development proposals for data centers or similar uses in the 19 municipalities that are under county jurisdiction," she said. artigo.texto: Duke Energy has unveiled plans to invest up to $756 million in its largest battery storage complex yet, adding 410 megawatts (MW) of grid capacity in Wayne County, North Carolina. Announced on November 17, 2026, the two-phase H.F. Lee Battery Storage project is scheduled to begin construction in early 2027 and enter service by late 2028. Situated adjacent to Duke Energy‘s existing H.F. Lee natural gas power plant in Goldsboro, the complex will more than double the 308 MW of battery storage the utility currently operates across 14 North Carolina sites. By building on a former coal plant property using North American-manufactured batteries, the development qualifies for a 50% federal tax credit designed to reduce costs for ratepayers. Two-Phase Buildout Doubles North Carolina Storage Fleet The installation is divided into two four-hour lithium-ion battery systems. H.F. Lee Battery Storage 1 will deliver 260 MW when it comes online in fall 2028, followed by the 150 MW H.F. Lee Battery Storage 2 facility by the end of 2028. At full output, the combined 410 MW complex will supply enough instantaneous electricity to power roughly 300,000 homes during peak demand periods. That capacity is more than four times the size of Duke Energy’s current largest operational battery facility in North Carolina, a 100 MW site in Knightdale. Work on the Goldsboro site will reuse grid interconnections at the H.F. Lee Energy Complex, where a 920 MW combined-cycle natural gas plant replaced a retired 1951 coal-fired station in 2012. How Do Federal Tax Credits and Grid Rules Shape the Deal? Federal clean-energy tax incentives form a central pillar of the project’s economics. Locating the batteries inside a designated energy community alongside domestic content requirements for North American battery manufacturing unlocks a 50% federal tax credit, lowering the net capital cost passed on to utility customers. The announcement arrived one day after the North Carolina Utilities Commission issued a November 16, 2026 order advancing 2,700 MW of new battery storage toward a 5,400 MW fleet target by 2034. Within its broader 2025 Carolinas Resource Plan, the utility has outlined plans for 6,540 MW of battery storage by 2035 as it shifts capital toward dispatchable capacity following Duke Energy’s decision to halt offshore wind plans off North Carolina and advances four planned solar projects in Florida. Local Tax Base and Workforce Impact in Wayne County County officials estimate the two battery facilities could generate up to $2 million in additional annual property tax revenue once operational. Duke Energy is already Wayne County’s largest taxpayer, contributing $5.8 million each year for its existing H.F. Lee generating complex and related local power infrastructure. Nine permanent full-time positions will support operations at the Goldsboro battery complex alongside regional solar and storage assets. Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy’s North Carolina President, said the utility is “reinvesting in our existing power plant communities that have powered North Carolina and South Carolina for decades,” while Wayne County Board of Commissioners Chairman Joe Daugherty noted that the tax revenue and grid reliability will support long-term industrial recruitment across Eastern North Carolina. Across the broader U.S. grid-storage pipeline targeting 2028 delivery, construction is also underway on the 553 MWdc Cold Creek Solar and Storage Project in Texas after developer Doral Renewables closed nearly $900 million in project financing earlier in 2026. artigo.texto: 4 min leitura Viana do Castelo inaugura fábrica de componentes para data centers Grupo CTS vai empregar 2.000 pessoas e prevê iniciar a laboração no final de 2027. 20 Nov 2026 - 08:15 4 min leitura O grupo CTS prevê iniciar a laboração da nova fábrica em Viana do Castelo, para produção de sistemas de refrigeração no final de 2027, altura em que o número de trabalhadores atingirá os 2.000 trabalhadores. A primeira fábrica, com 20 mil metros quadrados, inaugurada nesta quinta-feira, dedica-se à construção de grandes equipamentos de receção, transformação, distribuição e estabilização de energia destinada a Data Centers. Representa um investimento de 50 milhões de euros e, emprega atualmente 250 trabalhadores. O objetivo é chegar os 700. A unidade, entre as freguesias de Darque e Vila Nova de Anha, num ‘campus’com 110.000 metros quadrados, produz desde agosto, Unidades de Distribuição de Energia Elétrica (EPOD), para o mercado mundial de data center. Com o lançamento da primeira pedra, a nova unidade com 17 mil metros quadrados no complexo industrial de Viana do Castelo “será um dos maiores da Europa de produção de EPOD”, com capacidade “para fabricar 900 EPOD por ano”. Atualmente, são produzidos cerca de 450 EPOD por ano, num volume de negócios de 650 milhões de euros anuais, tendo 90% da produção como destino a exportação, focada, numa primeira fase, na Europa e Médio Oriente. Segundo o administrador do grupo em Portugal, Francisco Reis “a procura é tanta”, que o grupo CTS está a crescer muito e precisa de aumentar a capacidade de produção. “Já temos toda a nossa produção de EPOD completa para 2027. Estimamos concluir a fábrica no final do próximo ano. Diria que, seguramente, no final de 2027 e início de 2028 estaremos a produzir”, sublinhou, escusando-se a referir o valor do investimento na nova unidade. Com a conclusão da segunda fábrica, o grupo prevê faturar 1,8 a dois mil milhões de euros. O EPOD “é um estabilizador de energia que transforma a energia em média tensão e em baixa tensão capaz de ser utilizada por um data center”. “Esta fábrica tem todos os componentes eletromecânicos pré-fabricados o que nos ajuda, no nosso modelo negócio, a construir mais depressa e melhor”, frisou o administrador do grupo que tem unidades todo o país. O responsável explicou que a escolha de Viana do Castelo teve a ver com a localização, a 900 metros do porto comercial da cidade, próximo da autoestrada A28 e do aeroporto Sá Carneiro, no Porto. “Hoje não inauguramos apenas uma fábrica, celebramos o emprego e a competência”. Todos usamos ‘data centers’, de uma forma ou de outra. Hoje são considerados, uma infraestrutura crítica, que cria oportunidades e emprego e que precisa de pessoas e de talento”, referiu. Na cerimónia de inauguração da primeira fábrica, o presidente da Câmara de Viana do Castelo, Luís Nobre, salientou que o investimento “é transformador” para o concelho, mas também para o país. “Num primeiro momento pela magnitude da capacidade de exportação que vai ter para o concelho. Desde que iniciamos o processo de instalação desta unidade. Estávamos com uma exportação mil milhões de euros. Este investimento poderá proporcionar dois mil milhões de euros em exportações. Quer dizer que, em dois anos e meio aumentamos as capacidades de exportação em 2/3”, especificou. Além de “transformador” no que se refere à atividade em si, o autarca socialista, salientou “a ação holística que acaba por ter noutras parcerias que são absolutamente fundamentais nesta atividade”. O CTS Group está focado no fornecimento de data centers, contando com escritórios e projetos em 11 países, entre Noruega, Finlândia, Suécia, Dinamarca, Irlanda, Suíça, Portugal, Alemanha, Espanha, França e Itália. É um dos líderes no mercado europeu de data centers e, através da participada CTS Nordics, é a maior empresa de desenho e construção de Data Centers nos países nórdicos. Com uma forte presença em Portugal, o CTS Group dedica-se a implementar soluções inovadoras e sustentáveis. O grupo estabeleceu parcerias estratégicas com empresas nacionais, entre as quais a MecWide, contribuindo para a sua expansão internacional. Agência Lusa Editado por Jornal PT Green

artigo.texto: Luiz Araújo, da Agência iNFRA O governo federal formalizou nesta semana as regras do ProBioQAV (Programa Nacional de Combustível Sustentável de Aviação), que estabelece metas de redução das emissões de carbono para as companhias aéreas. A regulamentação da ANAC (Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil), publicada na terça-feira (17), prevê um período de transição, com redução ou dispensa das metas caso as empresas comprovem a indisponibilidade de SAF (Combustível Sustentável de Aviação). Criado pela Lei do Combustível do Futuro, o programa prevê metas anuais de redução das emissões em voos domésticos, começando em 1% em 2027 e chegando a 10% a partir de 2037. A obrigação alcançará companhias que emitirem mais de dez mil toneladas de carbono por ano em operações de passageiros ou cargas. O cálculo considerará o consumo de combustível de cada empresa e o percentual de redução previsto para o período. O principal instrumento para o alcance das metas é o uso do SAF. Contudo, as regras permitem o cumprimento das obrigações sem abastecimento físico, já que os créditos serão contabilizados a partir dos CS-SAF (Certificados de Sustentabilidade do SAF), documentos que comprovam a redução de emissões e podem ser comercializados. Também admitem o uso parcial de combustíveis de menor emissão, certificados estrangeiros e créditos do SBCE (Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões), limitados a 15% da meta em 2027 e 2028, 10% em 2029 e 5% a partir de 2030. A possibilidade de redução ou dispensa das metas por falta de SAF valerá enquanto não estiver em funcionamento a plataforma de emissão e registro dos CS-SAF. Para obter a flexibilização, as companhias deverão comprovar tentativas de aquisição do combustível, apresentando informações sobre a disponibilidade do produto, respostas dos fornecedores e motivos que impediram o abastecimento. Até a entrada em operação do sistema, o uso de SAF poderá ser comprovado por documentos equivalentes aos exigidos para a emissão dos certificados. A regulamentação também permite que as companhias aproveitem, no ano seguinte, reduções de emissões superiores às metas exigidas. O mecanismo deverá observar as condições estabelecidas pela ANAC e poderá ser utilizado para compensar parte das obrigações futuras. A medida se soma aos instrumentos alternativos previstos para o cumprimento das metas anuais. Fiscalização e penalidades O acompanhamento será feito por três instrumentos, cujos procedimentos foram detalhados em portaria complementar: o PME (Plano de Monitoramento de Emissões), o RE (Relatório de Emissões) e o RC (Relatório de Cumprimento). O primeiro detalhará os métodos de medição do consumo de combustível e das emissões, enquanto os demais apresentarão os dados anuais e a comprovação do cumprimento das metas. O prazo excepcional para entrega do PME será 15 de dezembro deste ano. O RE deverá ser apresentado até 31 de março do ano seguinte ao período de referência, e o RC, até 31 de maio. A ANAC será responsável pela verificação das informações, sem exigir, como regra geral, auditorias independentes. O descumprimento das obrigações poderá resultar em multas de R$ 84 mil pela ausência do PME ou do RE e de R$ 750 por tonelada de carbono que deixou de ser reduzida. O pagamento da penalidade não eliminará a obrigação, e o saldo pendente deverá ser incorporado à meta do ano seguinte. A regulamentação também prevê sanções por inconsistências nos relatórios, ausência de documentos e irregularidades na utilização de certificados ambientais. Embora as regras da ANAC já estejam formalizadas, a implementação integral do ProBioQAV ainda depende da regulamentação e da entrada em operação do sistema de certificados sob responsabilidade da ANP (Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis).

artigo.texto: Bloomberg reported on Nov. 16, 2026, that CATL is considering a China-wide battery-swapping network, citing people familiar with the company’s plans. The proposed system could involve partnerships with automakers, work on vehicle design from the development stage and battery leasing. In battery swapping, a driver exchanges a depleted battery for a charged one instead of waiting for it to recharge. Bloomberg placed the strategy against pressure on CATL’s margins and automakers’ interest in diversifying their battery suppliers. Starting collaboration at the vehicle-design stage would bring automakers into planning for the proposed system, while leasing could make battery ownership part of the model. The reported strategy links CATL’s station network with automaker partnerships and vehicle design. CATL’s reported network in China A Jan. 8, 2026 report by Movilidad Eléctrica put CATL’s Chinese network at 1,325 stations at the end of 2025: 1,020 for passenger cars and 305 truck stations managed by Qiji Energy. The outlet also described a construction plan in which CATL subsidiary Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES) would build the first 1,000 stations, with outside organizations involved in stations 1,001 through 10,000. It reported a separate target of more than 2,500 passenger-car stations in over 120 Chinese cities by the end of 2026.

artigo.texto: The 400 largest data centers in the United States emit more greenhouse gas emissions in one year than the entire nation of Denmark, according to a new report from Harvard University. From May 2024 to April 2025, data centers accounted for nearly 2% of total U.S. energy consumption and produced more than 25 million metric tons of CO2. Amna Nawaz spoke with the study's lead author, Gianluca Guidi. Amna Nawaz: The 400 largest data centers in the United States emit more greenhouse gas emissions into the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark. That's according to a new report from Harvard University. The study found that, from May 2024 to April 2025, data centers accounted for nearly 2 percent of total U.S. energy consumption and produced more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, a level two or three times higher than an earlier estimate in 2018. I'm joined now by the lead author of that study, Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard focusing on AI and public health. Gianluca, welcome to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. Gianluca Guidi: Yes, thank you for having me. Hello, everyone. Amna Nawaz: So, what was most surprising to you from this report? What really stood out to you in the way of the findings? Gianluca Guidi: Yes. So think about it, right? So Denmark is an entire country, and with millions of people, homes, hospitals, and industries. And we're talking about, like, comparable annual carbon emissions from just 403 data centers. So those are just like 400 buildings. And that's an extraordinary scale. And those facilities are just only a fraction of the industry and how the industry looks like right now. Amna Nawaz: You point out in the report too you weren't even able to capture all of the information from many data centers. So what do we not yet know about the impact that they could be having? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, that's a great question. The study dates back like -- it's almost a year-old by now. And since then, there's been, like, an incredible build-out. We have preliminary results of newer studies that tells us there are around 1,000 hyperscale data centers. So that's just more than the double of what we reported in our study. Amna Nawaz: So many more data centers, meaning the numbers in here, in actuality, now the scope of emissions could be much higher than your report suggests. Is that correct? Gianluca Guidi: That is correct. Yes, that is correct. And together with the emissions, you have the water consumption and potentially also public health consequences. So, in a way, we have that a technology that is actually moving faster than our ability to understand its consequences. Amna Nawaz: Tell us more about that, the intersection of the build-out of these data centers and the impact on public health. What are you finding there? Gianluca Guidi: Yes. In this specific study, we haven't addressed yet the public health, but what's happening basically is that, once you have a powered demand and a power that is produced at the power plant level, not only you're producing, we're producing carbon emissions, but we're also producing hazardous pollutants that travel and eventually somebody breathes them, and the effects for the health are pretty dangerous. And there's plenty and ton of scientific research about this. Amna Nawaz: The power pull as well when we talk about the power use in -- of these data centers, there are states you point out, like Virginia, Iowa, Oregon, and Ohio that account for half of the electricity use. Why is that and what kind of downstream impacts does that have for residents in the area? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, that's correct. So, basically, the states offer the infrastructure, the land and the electricity that large data centers need. But there's a catch. So the benefits of these expansion aren't necessarily felt by the same communities that bear its environmental costs. So, more electricity demands can mean more power plans and, therefore, as we're saying, more pollution and more pressure on local infrastructure. So those consequences don't stop at the data center's fence. Amna Nawaz: There are those who will argue, Gianluca, I'm sure you have heard, that we need to build out these AI data centers, that the country has to do it to remain competitive, that it's necessary for our economy, for national security, and that the impact of that on the environment or for residents in the area is a necessary evil, in other words. Would you agree with that? Is that -- can that argument be made? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, I see that, and there's a big backlash happening right now. I wouldn't call them like a necessary evil. I mean, I am an AI researcher myself, and I have to say I'm really excited about this technology and what it can do. but there are better ways to build it, so -- that might cost more, they might take longer. The question is whether we're willing to prioritize doing it right over doing it first. Amna Nawaz: The report, as you mentioned, is now several months old, almost a year-old. There are a lot of things you don't address in it. For the average citizen to understand how this might impact their lives, what are the questions you think need to be answered next? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, here's what concerns me the most. We're building this AI infrastructure faster than we can independently understand its consequences. So, our study, as you were saying, was just published, like -- but the data are already over a-year-old. So scientific evidence shouldn't arrive after the infrastructure, and neither should, I believe, the public participation. And the main concerns would be the water consumption, the electricity, so such that putting the power grid into like -- in strain and potentially therefore, as I was saying before, the public health consequences. Amna Nawaz: That is Gianluca Guidi of Harvard. He's a postdoctoral research fellow there focusing on AI and public health. Gianluca, thank you so much for your time. It's good

artigo.texto: Materials scientists have developed a polymer nanocomposite incorporating an ultra-low loading of zinc oxide quantum dots into polyetherimide, achieving enhanced energy storage properties. In electrostatic energy storage systems, conventional polymer dielectrics are typically constrained by low dielectric constants and insufficient discharge energy densities. While standard methods incorporate high-permittivity inorganic fillers to raise permittivity, this practice frequently introduces internal structural defects that degrade the overall breakdown strength of the host polymer matrix. To address this trade-off, researchers synthesized zinc oxide quantum dot and polyetherimide nanocomposites using a solution casting method. The experimental framework systematically investigated how the particle size of the zinc oxide quantum dots influenced the resulting electrostatic energy storage performance across the matrix. By minimizing filler content down to a fraction of a percent, the preparation sought to enhance dielectric properties while limiting the structural degradation common to high-filler formulations. Testing showed that the composite containing 0.1 weight percent zinc oxide quantum dots reached a dielectric constant of 4.53 at a frequency of 102 Hz. Furthermore, the material achieved a breakdown strength of 553 megavolts per meter and recorded a discharge energy density of 4.63 joules per cubic centimeter. In addition to these primary parameters, the formulated nanocomposite demonstrated stable cycling performance under repeated charge and discharge operations. The observed property improvements are attributed primarily to interfacial polarization generated by the high specific surface area of the zinc oxide quantum dots. Charge trapping—likely related to surface defects on the quantum dots and a widened band gap—was identified as a plausible secondary mechanism contributing to performance. The researchers concluded that this ultra-low loading approach offers a viable route to balance dielectric constant and breakdown strength in dielectric polymer composites.
