artigo.texto: Solving the world’s energy storage problems Advancing energy storage solutions As the world transitions from fossil fuel-based energy systems to renewable energy sources that fluctuate with time and weather, energy storage is becoming increasingly important for maintaining a reliable and sustainable electricity supply. As an electrochemical energy storage researcher, working at the intersection of electrochemistry, materials science and chemical engineering – with considerable experience in working toward commercialising new technologies – UNSW Sydney’s Dr Dipan Kundu focuses on developing safe, reliable and scalable battery technologies. Kundu didn’t set out to work on batteries when he decided to pursue a career in research; he landed in it almost by accident when his PhD supervisor suggested he undertake a battery project with an industry partner. But as someone with almost as much interest in global affairs as he had in science, he quickly recognised the broader implications for energy security and took to the field with enthusiasm. Today, he leads the Laboratory for Battery Research and Innovation at UNSW, where a team of PhD students and postdoctoral researchers work toward unlocking next-generation battery technologies. The group's research spans aqueous batteries, solid-state batteries, battery recycling, and advanced electrochemical and physicochemical analysis of battery materials, with a focus on developing technologies that are safer, more sustainable, and better suited to emerging energy needs. “One of the key challenges we are interested in is developing battery technologies that are inherently safer,” Kundu says. While lithium-ion batteries offer high energy density, they can present safety risks under certain operating conditions or if damaged. To address this, Kundu and his colleagues are investigating aqueous batteries, which use water-based electrolytes and are therefore non-flammable. Much of this work focuses on battery chemistries based on abundant and low-toxicity materials such as zinc and manganese, with the aim of delivering safe, affordable and durable energy storage. “We're interested in technologies that utilise abundant and low-toxicity materials while delivering long cycle life and reliable performance,” he says. The team is also researching solid-state batteries, which replace liquid electrolytes with solid ones. These batteries have the potential to offer improved safety and higher energy density, making them attractive for a wide range of applications where compact, lightweight and high-performance energy storage is needed. At the same time, the team is investigating battery recycling to support a more sustainable lifecycle for energy storage technologies. “I never set out thinking I would change the world,” Kundu says. “What motivates me is the opportunity to contribute to technologies that can make a meaningful difference and help address important societal challenges.”

artigo.texto: More Online: City Budget, Data Center Moratorium, Carbondale Odors Already this week, Dalton’s elected officials have adopted a $50.868 million budget for the 2027 fiscal year, which begins Jan. 1, and voted, in a split decision, to indefinitely table a proposed moratorium on data centers. And there’s plenty more on the calendar. The Whitfield County Commission will hold the first of two work sessions devoted to planning the county’s 2027 budget Wednesday, Nov. 18, at 5:30 p.m., with the second scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 19, also at 5:30 p.m. Both meetings will take place in the Board of Commissioners Meeting Room at the Whitfield County Courthouse, 205 N. Selvidge St., Dalton. According to county officials, the sessions are the initial planning meetings for commissioners to review past spending, anticipated revenues and departmental requests before developing a proposed budget for public review and eventual consideration by the board. The Joint Development Authority also met earlier this week, while residents continue seeking answers and assistance regarding odors associated with Essentia Protein Solutions, a food-grade protein and broth manufacturing plant operating in Carbondale Business Park. Meanwhile, student-athletes are wrapping up the fall sports season as winter sports get underway, and the holiday season is getting into full swing throughout Dalton, Whitfield County and Northwest Georgia. With so much news, so many events and activities taking place across our community, The Dalton Daily Citizen is placing a greater emphasis on timely online reporting, bringing readers local news as stories are completed rather than waiting for the next print edition. Readers can watch daltoncitizen.com in the coming days for reports on these topics and other developments throughout the community. We are also developing an online holiday events calendar, to be hosted on our website through Google Calendar. Residents and organizations will be able to submit events for consideration, helping create a convenient place for readers to find holiday activities throughout the area. Events may also be featured in our print editions as space permits.

artigo.texto: As the world looks for ways to restore degraded land and remove carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere, oasification offers another approach to nature-based restoration. It focuses on improving how drylands capture and retain water, allowing vegetation to recover and ecosystems to become healthier. Beyond its environmental benefits, oasification could also create opportunities for carbon removal projects and nature-based finance. But how does it work, and can it become part of the growing carbon market? What Is Oasification? Understanding the Concept Oasification is a land-restoration approach that aims to reverse desertification by improving how degraded land captures and retains water. It focuses on restoring the natural conditions needed for vegetation to grow, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions where water is limited. The concept was developed by Spanish researchers Andrés Martínez de Azagra, Jorge Mongil, and J. Rojo. Their 2004 paper, Oasification: A Forest Solution to Many Problems of Desertification, describes how small earth structures can collect and infiltrate rainwater and surface runoff, improving soil moisture and supporting vegetation growth. Oasification is closely linked to the fight against desertification, which occurs when land in dry regions loses its productivity due to climate conditions and human activities such as deforestation, overgrazing, and unsustainable farming. The scale of this challenge is significant. According to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), drylands cover approximately 40.6% of Earth’s land area, excluding Antarctica. The UN also reported that 77.6% of the world’s land experienced drier conditions between 1990 and 2020 than during the previous 30 years. Unlike approaches that focus mainly on planting trees, oasification first addresses the land’s ability to capture and retain available water. It can complement reforestation by creating better conditions for vegetation to establish and survive. How Does Oasification Work? Restoring Land by Making Better Use of Water Oasification works by improving how degraded land collects, absorbs, and retains rainwater. Rather than relying on large irrigation systems, it uses relatively small structures and land-management techniques to direct available water toward areas where vegetation can grow. One common technique is rainwater harvesting. Small basins, trenches, terraces, and contour barriers are built along slopes to slow down surface runoff. These structures collect rainwater that would otherwise flow downhill and carry away valuable topsoil. The captured water can then seep into the ground, increasing soil moisture and supporting plant growth. Another important part is soil restoration. By slowing water runoff, oasification helps reduce erosion and allows soil particles and nutrients to settle. This can improve soil conditions and create a better environment for seeds, roots, and microorganisms. Vegetation is then introduced or allowed to recover naturally. Native trees, shrubs, grasses, and other suitable plants help stabilize the soil, provide ground cover, and support local biodiversity. Their roots also help improve soil structure and water infiltration. The process works as a cycle. Better water retention supports plant growth, while growing vegetation protects the soil and adds organic matter. Over time, these improvements can help degraded land recover its productive capacity. However, oasification must be adapted to local conditions. Rainfall, soil type, slope, and available water all influence which techniques will work. It is not a one-size-fits-all solution, but an approach that combines water management, soil protection, and vegetation recovery. Not all carbon added to the soil remains stored permanently. Some organic matter decomposes and releases CO2 back into the atmosphere. Projects must, therefore, measure net changes in carbon stocks over time. Oasification and Carbon Sequestration: How Restored Land Can Capture CO2 Beyond restoring degraded land, oasification could also contribute to climate change mitigation by increasing the amount of carbon stored in vegetation and soil. This is where the approach becomes particularly relevant to nature-based carbon removal and carbon markets. Plants absorb carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere through photosynthesis and store carbon in their trunks, branches, leaves, and roots. When oasification improves soil moisture and supports vegetation growth, it can create better conditions for increasing this natural carbon storage. As trees and other plants grow, they can accumulate more carbon in their biomass. Soil also plays an important role. Fallen leaves, dead roots, and other organic materials break down and add carbon to the soil. Greater vegetation cover can help protect this organic matter from erosion and support the long-term buildup of soil organic carbon. The scale of the opportunity is significant. The IPCC estimates that approximately 20–30 billion tonnes of carbon have been released into the atmosphere through desertification-related processes, including deforestation, overgrazing, and conventional tillage. This highlights the climate value of protecting and restoring degraded land. However, carbon storage does not happen immediately. Vegetation needs time to establish, while soil carbon gains can take years or even decades to become measurable. Results also depend on rainfall, soil conditions, plant species, and long-term land management. The IPCC identifies natural vegetation restoration and tree planting on degraded land as activities that can enrich carbon in topsoil and subsoil over time. It also recognizes that measures to combat desertification can support soil carbon sequestration. For oasification projects, this means carbon benefits could come from two main sources: - increased carbon in growing vegetation, and - additional organic carbon stored in the soil. artigo.texto: Setting ground rules: City of Irondale votes on data center regulations Irondale, Ala (WBMA) - Irondale City Council says it is setting the ground rules for possible future data center developments. Tuesday night, the City voted to adopt regulations for future data center project proposals. City Councilman Aaron Sims says he had been researching data centers for months, and used that information to draft the new ordinance. Under Irondale's new code, if a future data center required upgrades to the power grid, the developer would be fully responsible for funding the upgrades. The code also requires any future data center to use a 'closed loop' water system, that is designed to cut down on excessive water use. Irondale Mayor James D. Stewart, Jr., says as of now, there are no data center projects on the table for the city.

artigo.texto: THE Philippines joined the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, citing the need to expand its own national carbon market framework during the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Environment Secretary Juan Miguel T. Cuna represented the Philippines during the ministerial roundtable, highlighting how the Philippine plans align with the direction set by Executive Order (EO) No. 127. “As we implement Executive Order No. 127 and develop our national carbon market framework, we recognize that private investment must complement public finance to accelerate climate action and sustainable development,” Mr. Cuna said. EO 127 directs the Department of Environment and Natural Resources to act as the national authority in developing a carbon credit market framework. “Government leadership is essential to provide the certainty, transparency, and integrity that give corporate buyers the confidence to invest in credible climate solutions,” he added. Mr. Cuna also said that the Philippines’ participation ensures its commitment in global partnerships to mobilize financing as required by the Paris Agreement and ensuring effective implementations of a carbon market is done in line with sustainable development. Alongside the Philippines, new members to the Coalition include Canada, Egypt and Ireland, bringing the grouping to 18 countries. The ministerial roundtable also introduced the Playbook Policy for developing carbon market regulations. “We are in a race against time to keep the overshoot of the 1.5°C limit as small and as short as possible…High-integrity carbon markets can play a critical role and so can this Coalition,” UNFCCC Executive Secretary Simon Steill said. — Maria Mikaela H. Tormon

artigo.texto: After 17 years at Tesla, Colin Campbell knows a thing or two about solving difficult engineering problems. Now he's helping turn one of those problems into a potentially enormous new business. Campbell is chief technology officer of Redwood Materials, the battery recycling startup founded by Tesla cofounder JB Straubel in 2017. Redwood started by extracting valuable metals and minerals from old EV batteries. It's now expanding into energy storage, using retired batteries to help power AI data centers, factories, and other facilities. Campbell thinks this new business could eventually be even bigger than Redwood's original operation. "It's easily as large as the metals and refining business," he told me during a recent interview, part of Business Insider's AI Insider live event series. "At least as large as the metals business, maybe larger." Finding value in old batteries The original idea came from watching Tesla churn out thousands of electric vehicles. "If you're standing next to like a Model 3 production line," Campbell said, watching battery packs being installed in cars every 30 seconds, you eventually start wondering what happens to all those batteries when the vehicles wear out. The answer: They still contain enormous value. I visited Redwood's sprawling Nevada campus last year and saw firsthand how complicated it is to recover that value. Giant machines process old batteries, extracting materials such as nickel, lithium, and cobalt that can be used again. Campbell said the biggest challenge isn't necessarily the underlying technology. It's making the process work economically at an enormous scale. That requires huge investments in factories and equipment, along with some difficult business decisions. Redwood, for example, paused plans to expand its copper foil manufacturing business after the economics changed. "We are not wedded to the original business plan," Campbell said. "It's very dangerous to just plow ahead regardless of the current economics two or three years later." The AI opportunity Redwood's latest business emerged from another simple observation. Engineers were watching old EV batteries head toward the company's recycling equipment when they realized many could still store substantial amounts of electricity. Why destroy something that might have another five or ten years of useful life? That insight led to Redwood Energy, which repurposes these batteries for large electricity storage systems. The timing couldn't be better. AI data centers are consuming enormous amounts of electricity, and connecting new facilities to the power grid can take years. Redwood has already deployed a large battery installation for AI infrastructure company Crusoe in Nevada. There's a clever piece of engineering behind this business, too. Different electric vehicles use different batteries, with different electrical characteristics and software. Redwood developed a device called the Pack Manager that allows batteries from different automakers to work together in one system. Campbell described it as a "universal translator" for batteries. The company is now scaling production and working on additional technology to make entire power installations cheaper and faster to build. Campbell also isn't overly worried about the recent political backlash against AI data centers. They're important customers, but Redwood's storage systems can serve other industries. The business would still have a strong future even if the current AI boom disappeared, he argued. A lesson for founders Redwood has attracted billions of dollars in funding, including investment from Google and Nvidia. Campbell said the key is finding patient investors who understand that complicated industrial businesses take years to build. The most interesting part of our conversation came when I asked what his experience at Tesla and Redwood had taught him about turning difficult engineering problems into successful companies. "Oh, man, what a great question," he replied. His answer was surprisingly simple: Question how things have always been done. In the data center industry, for example, different companies handle different parts of the electricity supply system. Few have stepped back to consider how everything could work better together, from the power line to the AI chip. For founders, Campbell's advice is to identify these overlooked opportunities, strip away unnecessary complexity, and prove there's a better approach. It's hard work, he acknowledged. Convincing an established industry to change can be particularly difficult. But that's also where some of the biggest opportunities lie. "If you see that kernel of efficiency," Campbell said, "we can do this a different way." Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here. Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com

artigo.texto: Por: Gustavo Estrella* A inteligência artificial deixou de ser apenas uma tendência tecnológica para se tornar uma força concreta de transformação econômica. Por trás dessa revolução, existe uma infraestrutura crítica que tem ganhado protagonismo recentemente: os data centers. E, junto com eles, cresce também um debate inevitável sobre energia, planejamento e competitividade. O avanço acelerado da IA generativa, da computação em nuvem e do processamento de dados está provocando uma corrida global por infraestrutura digital. Hoje, projetos que demandavam consumo de 20 megawatts já dão lugar a empreendimentos de 100 MW ou mais. Segundo projeções da Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação (Brasscom), a capacidade instalada de data centers no Brasil deve triplicar até 2031, passando de 1 GW para 3,1 GW, movimento que pode atrair cerca de US$ 92 bilhões em investimentos no país. Esse crescimento reposiciona o Brasil no mapa global da economia digital. O país já concentra cerca de metade do mercado latinoamericano de data centers e reúne vantagens competitivas importantes, matriz elétrica majoritariamente renovável, disponibilidade de energia limpa, conectividade crescente e capacidade territorial para expansão de infraestrutura. Em um cenário em que grandes empresas de tecnologia assumem metas cada vez mais rígidas de descarbonização, energia renovável deixa de ser diferencial e passa a ser requisito estratégico. O setor elétrico historicamente cresceu em linha com a demanda, acompanhando o desenvolvimento da economia, o aumento da população e a atividade industrial. Com a chegada e o avanço dos data centers, porém, entramos em uma nova dinâmica: o consumo de energia passa a crescer em ritmo muito mais acelerado, impulsionado pela digitalização, pela inteligência artificial e pela crescente necessidade de processamento de dados. Esse movimento representa, ao mesmo tempo, uma grande oportunidade e um desafio para o setor, que precisará acelerar investimentos e modernizar a infraestrutura elétrica para acompanhar esse novo patamar de demanda, garantindo segurança, confiabilidade e competitividade no fornecimento de energia. Diante dessa nova dinâmica, um ponto central permeia essa discussão: o crescimento dos data centers é indissociável do desenvolvimento coordenado da infraestrutura elétrica. Temos debatido este assunto com autoridades, operadores de data centers, investidores e especialistas sobre como alinhar o avanço da economia digital à capacidade energética do país. Nessas discussões, fica evidente que o principal gargalo não é a oferta de energia, mas a conexão à rede elétrica e o prazo de expansão da infraestrutura. Enquanto a demanda por conexão exige respostas em até 24 meses, projetos estruturantes do setor elétrico podem levar de cinco a oito anos. Essa diferença de velocidade desafia a competitividade do Brasil na disputa global por investimentos. Apesar de também desafiador, países da Ásia e os Estados Unidos já avançam em incentivos, segurança regulatória e aceleração de licenças. No Brasil, o debate começa a ganhar força a aprovação do PL 278/2026 (ReData), que prevê isenção de impostos federais para equipamentos de data centers. Nesse contexto, Campinas, uma das cidades de nossa área de concessão, desponta como um dos principais polos estratégicos para essa nova economia digital. A região reúne um ecossistema consolidado de inovação, universidades, mão de obra qualificada, infraestrutura logística e conectividade robusta. Soma-se a isso a disponibilidade energética e a presença de grandes corredores de transmissão, fatores decisivos para operações intensivas em consumo de energia. Para empresas de energia, esse movimento inaugura uma nova agenda estratégica. Na CPFL Energia, entendemos que o avanço dos data centers exigirá investimentos contínuos em redes, subestações, digitalização e planejamento integrado da infraestrutura elétrica. Por isso, ampliamos os investimentos em inovação, redes inteligentes e eficiência operacional para preparar o sistema elétrico para uma demanda cada vez mais intensiva em dados e inteligência artificial. O setor elétrico deixa de ser apenas fornecedor de energia e passa a atuar como viabilizador do crescimento econômico e digital do país. O debate sobre data centers não pode ser tratado apenas como uma pauta de tecnologia. Trata-se de uma agenda de desenvolvimento econômico, atração de investimentos, geração de empregos qualificados e modernização da infraestrutura nacional. O Brasil tem todos os ativos necessários para liderar esse movimento. O desafio agora é transformar potencial em capacidade de execução. Na CPFL Energia, estamos comprometidos em atuar como parceiros estratégicos dessa transformação, porque a nova corrida global da inteligência artificial também será uma corrida por energia. Os países que conseguirem alinhar expansão digital, segurança energética e sustentabilidade estarão mais preparados para liderar o próximo ciclo de crescimento econômico *Gustavo Estrella é presidente da CPFL Energia

artigo.texto: Meta climática de 2040 da UE sob pressão por acordo no mercado de carbono Um documento vazado analisado pela Euronews indica que as reformas do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões da União Europeia, o EU ETS, poderiam enfraquecer a meta climática de 2040 do bloco. A Presidência irlandesa do Conselho da UE suavizou uma proposta que será discutida por embaixadores da UE na quarta-feira, em meio ao aumento da pressão política para conciliar as metas de emissões com a competitividade industrial e os altos custos de energia. O texto de compromisso busca garantir apoio político para o mercado de carbono após 2030, mas defensores do clima alertam que as concessões destinadas a proteger a indústria europeia podem reduzir a contribuição do sistema para a meta de 2040, deixando outros setores econômicos para cobrir a lacuna. Licenças gratuitas e planos de investimento O texto do Conselho mantém a proposta de julho da Comissão Europeia de desacelerar a redução das licenças de carbono, estender as permissões gratuitas para a indústria e trazer créditos de carbono internacionais para o mercado da UE, de modo que as emissões domésticas possam ser compensadas por meio de projetos no exterior. Segundo a proposta da Presidência irlandesa, as empresas industriais manteriam 80 por cento de suas licenças gratuitas se apresentarem um plano de investimento, mesmo que depois não realizem os investimentos de descarbonização propostos. Os 20 por cento restantes dependeriam do início da construção de projetos elegíveis. As licenças gratuitas são permissões que as empresas recebem sem comprá-las em leilão, concebidas para proteger os produtores da UE da concorrência em países com regras climáticas menos rigorosas, como a China e os Estados Unidos. A proposta representa uma concessão política significativa às indústrias preocupadas em perder essas licenças e levanta questões sobre se o ETS oferecerá incentivo suficiente para cortar emissões. Créditos internacionais e a meta de 2040 Sobre os créditos de carbono internacionais, o Conselho manteve a proposta da Comissão de reservar licenças equivalentes a 260 milhões de toneladas de CO2 para financiar sua compra. Também deixa em aberto uma possível fase-piloto entre 2031 e 2035 para testar o sistema antes da implementação plena. O Conselho manteve requisitos rigorosos de qualidade e integridade para os créditos internacionais, tornando a trajetória de redução do ETS cada vez mais dependente de sua disponibilidade. Se as indústrias não puderem comprá-los, a meta climática de 2040 poderá ser comprometida, já que ela exige pelo menos 85 por cento de redução líquida doméstica das emissões, com os créditos internacionais respondendo pelos 5 por cento restantes. Cronograma das negociações e divisões entre os Estados-membros A Presidência irlandesa busca consenso entre os 27 países da UE antes que as negociações avancem para questões politicamente mais sensíveis, como ambição climática e repartição de encargos. Ela espera fechar um acordo no Conselho de Meio Ambiente em 11 de dezembro, enquanto o Parlamento Europeu deve votar durante sua sessão plenária de 14 a 17 de dezembro em Estrasburgo. A presidência enfrenta uma batalha difícil diante das profundas divisões entre os Estados-membros e da complexidade das negociações. Segundo um segundo documento analisado pela Euronews, os países da UE já estão divididos sobre a velocidade com que a oferta de licenças de carbono deve encolher, se as empresas devem usar créditos internacionais para cumprir obrigações e até que ponto os setores industriais devem ser protegidos do aumento dos custos de carbono. Em conjunto, essas demandas correm o risco de diluir o ETS justamente quando se espera que ele impulse grande parte da próxima fase de cortes de emissões do bloco. Os governos em geral querem preservar o ETS como fonte de receita para a descarbonização, mas crescem as preocupações com os custos impostos a indústrias de uso intensivo de energia que competem com fabricantes na China ou nos Estados Unidos. Algumas capitais argumentam que o número de licenças deve cair para elevar o preço do carbono e incentivar o desinvestimento em combustíveis fósseis, enquanto outras temem o impacto da retirada das licenças gratuitas sobre indústrias em dificuldade. Uma redução mais lenta aliviaria a pressão sobre usinas e fábricas, potencialmente moderando os preços do carbono e dando às empresas mais tempo para se adaptar, mas também significaria menos cortes de emissões nos setores cobertos pelo ETS, tornando a meta de 2040 mais difícil de alcançar. Análise questiona compatibilidade da reforma Uma análise recente do Oko-Institut, encomendada pelo grupo ambientalista WWF Alemanha, alertou que a reforma do ETS proposta pela Comissão é incompatível com a meta da UE de cortar as emissões líquidas em 90 por cento até 2040. Lisa Okken, especialista em política industrial do WWF Alemanha, disse que a Comissão está optando por correr riscos na proteção climática em vez de resguardar o futuro da indústria europeia, e argumentou que a reforma proposta carece do sinal de preço do carbono necessário para impulsionar uma modernização urgente. Segundo ela, a lacuna está sendo preenchida com medidas contábeis complicadas e flexibilidade excessiva. Ambientalistas também manifestaram preocupação com uma proposta que permitiria emissões adicionais além do teto existente em troca de futuras remoções permanentes de carbono por meio de tecnologias caras destinadas a capturar CO2 do ar. O estudo observou que ainda não está claro se tais remoções podem ser entregues na escala necessária, já que a capacidade necessária não existe hoje.

artigo.texto: BYD’s next-generation Han will offer up to 875 km of CLTC range (approximately 718 km WLTP estimated), while its most powerful electric version delivers 520 kW (697 hp). The new sedan is expected to debut at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27. It arrives as October domestic deliveries of the outgoing Han fell 68.9% year-on-year to 2,236 units. Three electric versions and a 400 km PHEV The new Han EV comes in three versions, with outputs ranging from 245 kW (329 hp) to 520 kW (697 hp). All three EV versions use LFP Blade batteries supplied by BYD’s FinDreams subsidiary. The entry-level rear-wheel-drive version has a 76.744 kWh battery and a 245 kW (329 hp) rear motor. It delivers 775 km of CLTC range (approximately 635 km WLTP estimated). The Long-Range RWD increases battery capacity to 88.682 kWh and motor output to 300 kW (402 hp), taking the claimed range to 875 km CLTC (approximately 718 km WLTP estimated), according to iFeng. At the top of the range, the Performance AWD uses the same 88.682 kWh battery but adds a 200 kW (268 hp) front motor to the 320 kW (429 hp) rear unit. Combined output reaches 520 kW (697 hp), with a CLTC range of 730 km (approximately 599 km WLTP estimated). It weighs 2,351 kg and has a listed top speed of 270 km/h, compared with 240 km/h for both RWD versions. The Han DM-i plug-in hybrid pairs a 1.5-litre turbocharged engine with a 200 kW (268 hp) electric motor. The engine produces 115 kW (154 hp) maximum power, or 110 kW (148 hp) maximum net power. A 45.36 kWh LFP battery provides 300 km of WLTC or 400 km of CLTC electric range (approximately 328 km WLTP estimated). Listed fuel consumption with the battery depleted is 4.6 L/100 km. The DM-i weighs 2,115 kg and has a top speed of 200 km/h. Chinese media also report that the new Han supports BYD Flash Charging. Compatible vehicles are claimed to charge from 10% to 97% in nine minutes. Larger body and redesigned exterior The new Han is 5,156 mm long and 1,969 mm wide, with a 3,030 mm wheelbase. That makes it 161 mm longer and 59 mm wider than the outgoing car, with 110 mm more between the axles. Depending on the version, height is either 1,507 mm or 1,492 mm. It is also longer than the 5,050 mm Han L, although the 5,256 mm BYD Da Han remains larger. Uncamouflaged photographs show a revised front end, led by a horizontal light bar, illuminated star-diamond elements and a Han emblem on the hood. Recessed door handles and multi-spoke wheels measuring 18, 19 or 20 inches feature along the sides, while the rear retains its full-width Chinese knot-style light bar. Roof-mounted LiDAR is standard on the 300 kW and 520 kW versions and optional on the entry-level EV and DM-i. It supports BYD’s God’s Eye B (DiPilot) driver-assistance system. Inside, photos show a floating central touchscreen, a digital instrument display, a column-mounted gear selector and two 50W wireless charging pads. Sales decline puts pressure on the replacement The Han’s domestic deliveries fell 47.6% year-on-year to 119,821 units in 2025, down from a peak of 274,016 in 2022, according to China EV DataTracker. In October, its 2,236 deliveries represented 1.1% of BYD’s domestic volume. The Xiaomi SU7 sold 12,954 units that month, while the Xpeng P7+ managed 2,247, just 11 more than the Han. BYD has not announced pricing for the new model. The outgoing Han starts at 168,800 yuan (23,700 USD).

artigo.texto: Beril Canakci 19 November 2026•Update: 19 November 2026 Carbon emissions linked to the world’s data centers are projected to rise 70% by 2030 as growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) drives electricity consumption higher, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said Thursday. In its annual World Energy Outlook 2026 report, the Paris-based agency projected that global electricity consumption by data centers would double to about 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030, with AI accounting for much of the increase. Data centers, which house the computer servers used to run AI systems and other digital services, require large amounts of electricity to operate and keep equipment cool. The expansion is expected to increase demand for electricity generated from fossil fuels, particularly in the United States and China, contributing to higher carbon emissions. The IEA projected that natural gas would supply about 60% of electricity used by US data centers by 2030, while coal would account for roughly half of the power consumed by China’s AI data centers. In the European Union, renewable energy is expected to provide about 70% of data center electricity needs by the end of the decade. The agency also warned that rapid growth in electricity demand from AI infrastructure was putting additional pressure on power grids and equipment supply chains, highlighting the need for investment in electricity networks.

artigo.texto: Massive data center proposal faces pushback from Stafford County residents STAFFORD COUNTY, Va. - A massive data center development is putting Stafford County in the spotlight as the proposal goes before the Planning Commission for a vote. What we know: The proposed development, which spans four projects along the Kings Highway corridor near the Rappahannock River, consists of 37 facilities and 14 electrical substations. The scale of the project is larger than 1,000 football fields placed side by side. Stafford County Data Center Proposal More than 100 people signed up to speak when the proposal was introduced to the Planning Commission. While some attendees expressed support for the development, the proposal is already facing significant pushback from residents, with opponents calling it an absolute outrage. Critics argue the development could significantly alter the area and negatively impact local farmland, the Rappahannock River and the historic surroundings near Ferry Farm, George Washington's childhood home. Residents have also raised concerns about construction and its potential impact on the region's water supply. In response, developers told the Planning Commission they are committed to working with the community. They say that if all four projects are approved, the development could generate more than $268 million in revenue by 2036 and create nearly 1,200 jobs. Developers also said habitat rehabilitation along the Oak Creek shoreline and wetland restoration along the Rappahannock River would be prioritized. What's next: If the Planning Commission ultimately recommends approval of the projects, the proposal will still require final approval from Stafford County's Board of Supervisors. The Source: Information in this article is from a Stafford County Planning Meeting and original FOX 5 DC reporting.

artigo.texto: This article is part of the thematic channel The Carbon Observer: subscribe to the newsletter Kigali - I wrote this op-ed from the Carbon Markets Africa Summit in Kigali, a great event that brought together investors, project developers and governments committed to making Africa a major hub for Article 6 carbon markets. One message particularly resonated with me. In her keynote speech, Rwanda's Minister of Environment emphasised that Africa needs bankable projects capable of attracting investment and supporting economic development. And that is exactly the point. Carbon finance could play a central role in mobilising capital, creating jobs and supporting a more sustainable development pathway. But something caught my attention: across discussions, meetings and keynote speeches, plenty about carbon finance and investment opportunities was discussed. Yet, Article 6.4 and its Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM) were almost absent from the conversation. For many of the people actually developing and financing projects, Article 6.4 remains more of a theoretical framework than a practical opportunity. Developers do not really oppose the mechanism, they simply do not see a compelling reason to adopt another complex system in a market that is already extremely difficult to navigate. Developers are already dealing with changing methodologies, host-country authorisations, corresponding adjustments and increasingly demanding buyer requirements. Article 6.4 introduces yet another set of rules and approval processes without demonstrating a clear commercial advantage. After years of negotiations, the mechanism is finally becoming operational. As of October 2026, five methodologies have been approved, including two new clean-cooking methodologies. Meanwhile, 1,512 projects and programmes have requested transition from the old Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), with 418 having received host-country approval by June. Transitioning existing projects, however, is not the same as attracting new investment under the new methodologies. In conversations with experts and developers, one concern kept emerging: methodological conservatism increasingly seems to be treated as synonymous with environmental integrity. Stricter baselines and more demanding monitoring requirements could significantly reduce credit issuance. Developers must also account for mandatory deductions of 5% for the Adaptation Fund and at least 2% for overall mitigation, alongside administrative fees, host-country levies and, where applicable, reversal-risk buffer contributions. To understand the potential economic impact, I ran a quick-and-dirty simulation. This is not a financial model or an Article 6.4 price forecast, just a simple exercise to illustrate how project economics could change. Let's assume a project originally generates 100,000 credits annually, sold at $10 each, generating $1 million in carbon revenue. If more conservative accounting reduces issuance by 40%, and we apply the mandatory 7% UNFCCC deductions, only 55,800 credits remain available for sale. What price would the developer need to charge to maintain the same carbon revenue? In the most demanding scenario, a credit previously sold at $10 would need to sell for almost $30 just to preserve the same carbon revenue. Is the market prepared to pay that difference? The concern is not conservatism itself, but the accumulation of conservative assumptions without sufficiently recognising improvements already made to address historical over-crediting. Conservatism should ensure accurate crediting, not become an objective in itself. Meanwhile, international carbon markets are progressing. According to Sylvera, projected demand for internationally adjusted credits under CORSIA and government purchasing programmes could approach one billion tonnes through 2030. Unlike Article 6.4, these pathways can leverage established standards, methodologies and registries that developers already know, and which are beginning to support deliveries to governments and airlines. Why move to an entirely new mechanism when existing systems are already opening access to compliance markets? The answer may come from future demand. The European Commission has proposed auctioning up to 260 million EU ETS allowances to finance the purchase of international credits between 2036 and 2040. At an illustrative EUA price of €120 in the late 2030s, this could generate approximately €31 billion in purchasing resources. This is not a guaranteed budget or credit price, but it illustrates the scale of the potential opportunity. Such purchasing power could make Article 6.4 more attractive, establish a new market benchmark and potentially encourage other countries to follow a similar approach. But this raises two fundamental questions. Will buyers pay the higher prices needed to make these projects viable, while keeping international credits cost-effective? And perhaps more importantly, will enough eligible and authorised credits be available? Lower issuance per project means more investment is needed to generate the same volume. Host-country authorisation remains a sovereign decision, while credit-vintage eligibility and restrictions across NDC periods create additional uncertainty. For Europe, securing up to 260 million credits between 2036 and 2040 would require a substantial project pipeline developed and financed years in advance. The market cannot wait until 2036 to start developing the projects Europe may need in 2036. This brings me back to the message from Rwanda's Minister of Environment: “Africa needs bankable projects.” Article 6.4's success will ultimately depend on strong demand signals and its ability to reduce risks for project developers and investors. artigo.texto: CATL Chairman Robin Zeng Calls for Innovation and Global Partnerships to Strengthen Battery Industry Competitiveness Company Emphasizes Technology Development, International Cooperation and Long-Term Economic Value Over Price-Based Competition NINGDE, CHINA, November 18, 2026 (Newswire.com) - Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), a global battery technology company, is emphasizing technological innovation, international partnerships and sustainable industry development as key drivers of long-term business competitiveness, according to Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Dr. Robin Zeng. CATL In an interview with CGTN journalist Tian Wei, Zeng discussed the importance of shifting global business competition away from aggressive price reductions and toward technological advancement, research and development, intellectual property protection and collaborative economic growth. "Competition should be driven by innovation, not by price cuts," Zeng said, highlighting the importance of creating sustainable business value through technological improvements rather than relying on short-term pricing strategies. Zeng expressed concerns that excessive price competition could discourage investment in research and development, weaken intellectual property development and create challenges for the long-term growth of industries. He also highlighted the importance of clean technology innovation in addressing global sustainability challenges. International Partnerships Supporting Global Expansion Zeng pointed to CATL's international business relationships as examples of how cross-border cooperation can create economic opportunities and strengthen technological capabilities. Among the examples discussed was CATL's technology licensing arrangement with Ford, which provides the American automaker access to CATL's battery technology expertise. In Indonesia, CATL has pursued cooperation across multiple stages of the battery supply chain, including mining, refining and battery manufacturing, alongside plans for large-scale battery production. The company has also expanded its presence in Europe through a joint venture with Stellantis, reflecting its broader strategy of establishing international partnerships across major automotive markets. According to Zeng, these collaborations demonstrate how companies from different countries can combine technological expertise, investment and industrial capabilities to generate shared economic benefits. Innovation and Cooperation as Long-Term Growth Drivers Zeng further emphasized that economic analysis and practical simulations can help businesses and policymakers evaluate the measurable benefits of international cooperation. Demonstrating the potential economic value of partnerships, he suggested, can encourage stakeholders to prioritize collaborative strategies over restrictive market approaches. His remarks come as the global electric vehicle and battery industries continue to evolve, with technological development, supply-chain resilience, manufacturing efficiency and international market access becoming increasingly important competitive factors. CATL's approach reflects a broader emphasis on building long-term competitiveness through research, advanced battery technologies and international business relationships. The company sees innovation and constructive cooperation as important contributors to sustainable industrial development and global economic growth. For more information, visit the company's official website. About CATL Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL) is a global battery technology company focused on the research, development and manufacturing of battery systems and energy storage solutions. The company works with international automotive manufacturers and industry partners to support the development of electric mobility and clean energy technologies. artigo.texto: Analysts have reset their fair value estimate for American Battery Technology to US$4.38, down from US$6.00, which marks a clear shift in how the stock is being framed. The change lines up with fresh commentary around the black mass export license, as research teams weigh improved regulatory clarity against recent operational headwinds and revenue visibility questions. As you read on, you will see how this revised price target fits into the broader analyst narrative and how to keep track of where sentiment goes next. What Wall Street Has Been Saying 🐂 Bullish Takeaways - Alliance Global highlights that the black mass export license from the U.S. Department of Commerce removes a key regulatory overhang for American Battery Technology and gives the company a defined path to sell output from its Nevada recycling plant. - The firm points to the license capacity of up to US$100m in black mass exports as an important support for near term revenue potential, since American Battery Technology's current customer base is outside the U.S. - Alliance Global has reiterated a Buy rating in recent notes and, as of October 2026, maintained a US$7 price target before trimming it to US$5.75 in November. This still sits above the latest fair value reset in the market. 🐻 Bearish Takeaways - Alliance Global acknowledges that recent fiscal Q1 results were hit by the earlier export restriction on U.S. produced black mass, underscoring execution risk around regulatory shifts for American Battery Technology. - The reduction in Alliance Global's target from US$7 to US$5.75 signals that the firm sees weaker near term earnings visibility even with the export exemption in place. Do your thoughts align with the Bull or Bear Analysts? Perhaps you think there's more to the story. Head to the Simply Wall St Community to discover more perspectives! We've flagged 3 risks for American Battery Technology. See which could impact your investment. How This Changes the Fair Value For American Battery Technology - Fair value estimate is now US$4.38, reduced from US$6.00. - Forecast revenue growth is now 13.82%, reduced from 48.40%. - Forecast profit margin is now 15.14%, increased from 13.96%. - Future P/E multiple is now 197.67x, adjusted from 285.97x. - The discount rate used in models is now 8.88%, up from 8.41%. artigo.texto: Tallahassee's new mayor moves to ban AI data centers, raising stakes in fight TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (FOX 49) — Tallahassee's newly elected mayor is wasting no time taking aim at a rapidly expanding industry, pushing to ban artificial intelligence data centers from operating anywhere within city limits. Mayor Jeremy Matlow won unanimous support from the City Commission Wednesday, Nov. 18, to move forward with exploring an outright ban on AI data centers — a dramatic shift from earlier efforts that failed to gain majority support. The move could put Tallahassee on a collision course with the growing demand for massive computing facilities powering the artificial intelligence revolution. "I'd like to bring an item that defines AI data centers in our land development code and contemplates a ban in every land use category," Matlow told commissioners. The motion passed unanimously, directing city staff to develop a definition of AI data centers and return with a proposal that could prohibit them throughout Tallahassee. The vote does not immediately ban AI data centers. It sets the stage for commissioners to consider restrictions at a future meeting. A dramatic reversal at City Hall The unanimous vote marks a significant political victory for Matlow, who previously pushed for stronger restrictions on AI data centers while serving as a commissioner. During an August meeting, Matlow sought an explicit ban, but the proposal failed 3-2. At the time, city officials argued that existing land development regulations already prevented AI data centers from being built without additional city approval. Now, with Matlow serving as mayor and a newly seated commission in place, the political landscape has changed. What about electricity, water and the environment? AI data centers can consume enormous amounts of electricity, and some facilities require substantial water resources for cooling. Those demands have fueled debates nationwide over whether the economic benefits of artificial intelligence infrastructure outweigh potential impacts on utilities, natural resources and surrounding communities. Tallahassee commissioners are now confronting those questions. Mayor Pro Tem Jack Porter supported Matlow's proposal but raised concerns that Florida lawmakers could eventually prevent cities from imposing outright bans. Porter suggested the city consider backup regulations governing potential impacts, including water consumption and wastewater discharge. "I'm worried ... if it's preempted and we can't have an outright ban, then it's like the wild wild west," Porter said. She emphasized the importance of ensuring Tallahassee retains regulatory authority if state lawmakers intervene. City officials acknowledged that any future restrictions would have to comply with state law. Not all data centers would be targeted Commissioners also emphasized an important distinction: The proposed restrictions would target AI data centers, not necessarily every type of data center. City officials noted that Tallahassee already has data centers operating within its jurisdiction. The proposal directs staff to develop a specific definition identifying which facilities would be subject to the potential ban. That distinction could prove critical in determining how broadly the city can regulate the industry without affecting existing operations. What's next? City staff will return with proposed language defining AI data centers and examining a potential prohibition across all land-use categories. Commissioners would then have to consider and approve any actual changes to city regulations. For Matlow, the unanimous vote represents an early victory for his new administration — and a clear signal that Tallahassee intends to assert greater control over where, and whether, the infrastructure powering artificial intelligence can be built.

artigo.texto: SiTime Addresses $2 Billion Opportunity in Data Center Bandwidth Upgrades with Two New Clock Families FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 Bring 20 Years of Heritage to 2X Faster Ethernet and Connectivity Standards SANTA CLARA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 17, 2026-- SiTime Corporation (NASDAQ: SITM), the Precision Timing company, today introduced FemtoClock™ 4 and VersaClock® 8, two clock families designed for the latest connectivity protocols that double bandwidth over previous generations. The families are designed for networking and computing applications in the data center rack. Together they address a $2 billion serviceable addressable market (SAM) over the next five years. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261117222922/en/ FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 Bring 20 Years of Heritage to 2X Faster Ethernet and Connectivity Standards “Insatiable demand for AI, along with rising performance requirements, is driving the need for greater density and speed,” said Piyush Sevalia, executive vice president and chief business officer of SiTime. “The FemtoClock and VersaClock families have a 20-year heritage and multiple generations of products. Over this period, they have led the industry in performance, density and shipments, and have become the default choice for many customer designs. Engineers know these architectures well. This familiarity enables them to design with confidence, get the most from these programmable clocks and reuse existing software. The result is higher-performance, denser AI hardware that generates revenue sooner. Built on this successful track record, FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 extend SiTime’s lead in Precision Timing.” These clocks are built to solve the bandwidth challenge and the industry is tackling it right now; 224G serializer-deserializer (SerDes) links are being rapidly adopted in data center switches and AI servers to double Ethernet bandwidth, and PCI Express® (PCIe®) 7 is doing the same for interconnectivity between CPUs, xPUs, memory, storage and smart network interface cards (SmartNICs). In faster, denser systems, the margin for error is smaller. FemtoClock 4 delivers resilient clock signals for Ethernet networking with ultra-low jitter and high clock density in a single device. VersaClock 8 serves PCIe interconnectivity with a flexible, compact, low-power design that is ideal for hot and dense compute trays. According to Dell’Oro Group, 1.6 Tbps ports in AI back-end switches are expected to ramp at least five times faster than 800 Gbps, driven by adoption across scale-up, scale-out and scale-across networks. This bandwidth is critical to maximizing utilization of expensive xPU resources. “The AI infrastructure build-out is exposing bottlenecks that go well beyond GPU compute performance,” said Dave Altavilla, president and principal analyst at HotTech Vision and Analysis. “Moving data efficiently across increasingly complex systems is becoming a critical design challenge, particularly as Ethernet and PCIe bandwidth requirements continue to climb. Precision Timing plays an important role here, especially as higher signaling speeds leave less margin for jitter and signal degradation. SiTime’s latest clock families reflect how these underlying technologies are evolving to meet the precise needs of the next generation of AI data center architectures.” Product Features FemtoClock 4 is a jitter attenuator and clock generator for top-of-rack and spine switches built on 224G SerDes. Key features include: - 19 fs RMS phase jitter at 312.5 MHz in clock generator mode (12 kHz to 20 MHz, 4 MHz high-pass filter) - Up to six frequency domains across 18 outputs - Fewer devices for top-of-rack switches that generally need more than 40 clocks VersaClock 8 is a programmable clock generator providing reference clocks for CPUs, xPUs, memory and storage. Key features include: - About 10 fs reference clock jitter for PCIe 7 - 30 fs RMS phase jitter at 312.5 MHz (12 kHz to 20 MHz, 4 MHz high-pass filter) - Low power limits self-heating; operates at up to 105°C - 5-, 9- and 12-output variants in QFN packages from 4x4 mm to 6x6 mm - 12-output variant is about 40% smaller than a comparable solution Availability FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 are in production and available now. FemtoClock 4 part numbers: RC38616, RC38412, RC32418 and RC32412. VersaClock 8 part numbers: RC31312A, RC31309A and RC31305A. Additional Resources About SiTime SiTime is the Precision Timing company. Our people and products help engineers build the impossible. Customers trust SiTime solutions in more than 400 applications, including AI hardware, autonomous vehicles, low Earth orbit satellites and wearables. Built on decades of innovation, our oscillators, clocks, resonators and software deliver higher system performance, greater resilience and better reliability. artigo.texto: How Google's data center investment has impacted Pryor schools While some communities are weighing promises from data center developers, the City of Pryor has already spent years seeing what that kind of investment can mean for local schools. In Pryor, students can end the school day with a paddle in hand through after-school activities the district offers at no cost. Superintendent Lisa Muller said a stronger tax base, boosted by Google’s investment, has helped make programs like that possible. “We're able to provide that as a free program for our students after school,” Muller said. Google’s data center sits inside the Pryor school district, and Muller said the investment significantly increased school revenue. The funding comes in part from property taxes Google pays. In addition, Google has received tax breaks, and the state makes up for that tax revenue and sends it to Pryor schools. Pryor’s original agreement with Google included that money from the company’s tax exemptions going to the district. The impact extends beyond the school district. For the 2025 tax year, the Oklahoma Tax Commission lists about $34.2 million in Google-related reimbursements for Mayes County. That figure is countywide, but Pryor benefits as well. “It’s difficult to separate out, you know, what portion comes from the companies out at the, the industrial park versus what comes from other taxpayers within the district,” Muller said. The laws governing those incentives have changed since Google made its agreement in Pryor. Since 2021, new data centers can’t qualify under the same program. Certain existing facilities can still qualify for breaks on eligible equipment. “And so that's when we end up with these very different structures, that change over time just to fit the needs of the community,” said Trystine Payfer with Google. Payfer said new deals can include company payments in place of property taxes or other negotiated payments to the community, and what reaches schools depends on how each agreement divides those payments. “And this is all separate, of course, from the additional grants and scholarships and sponsorships that we do once we enter a community,” Payfer said. Muller said the additional revenue has helped Pryor keep classes small and pay staff above state minimums. “So just on the sort of the big picture question, like, does money matter? The answer is, is unambiguously yes,” Muller said. Northwestern economist Kirabo Jackson, who studies what happens when schools spend more, said how districts use additional funding is key. “You want to make sure that money is going towards things that improve instruction. You want to make sure that's going towards curriculum, that improves things. You want to make sure it's going towards reducing class size,” Jackson said. Muller said Pryor has seen academic improvement over time tied to the Google investment, and she pointed to staffing and class sizes as part of that progress. “We also maintain small class sizes here in Pryor and are able to pay our, our staff above the state minimums as well,” Muller said. The district’s state report card has continuously improved since the investment began, and the district has funding to provide opportunities and transportation for students and families even after the school day ends.

artigo.texto: SALT LAKE CITY — In response to significant public pushback, a draft policy has been unveiled on Utah's Capitol Hill seeking to regulate data centers. "Utahns have legitimate serious questions about the impacts of data centers," said Rep. Paul Cutler, R-Centerville, who is sponsoring a bill setting up new guardrails on them. Salt Lake City approves temporary data center pause: On Wednesday, the Utah State Legislature's Economic Development & Workforce Services Committee heard a presentation on the draft policy. Senate Majority Leader Chris Wilson, R-Logan, who is co-sponsoring the bill, called the policy proposal a "herculean effort." FOX 13 News reported on pending data center legislation last week. House Speaker Mike Schultz, R-Hooper, has tasked lawmakers with bills on the topic and has said in the past he is not supportive of mass data center development. The policy proposes to cut off some of the tax incentives offered lately to data center developers. It also strips entities like Utah's Military Installation Development Authority of their ability to approve the projects. Instead, decisions on data center approval will remain with local cities and counties. Ready for liftoff? Spaceport idea advances on Utah's Capitol Hill: "I assume when you say local control, that will mean that entities like MIDA and others won’t have super-authority over that?" Rep. Jim Dunnigan, R-Taylorsville, asked during Wednesday's hearing. "That’s the intent," replied Rep. Cutler. "That MIDA or the inland port could support and consult and help provide expertise, but the proposal has to be endorsed and come from a local community, either a municipality or a county. MIDA can’t override those." Elected or appointed officials will not be allowed to enter into nondisclosure agreements around data centers and there will be more disclosures demanded on environmental and energy impacts for the public, Rep. Cutler said. There will be a shift in tax money generated from data centers, earmarking some of it for local schools and environmental impact funds. Data centers will be required to provide "benefits" to water resources, including investments in things like donating water to the Great Salt Lake or Colorado River systems. They must also address air quality, noise, heat and other impacts to the environment. "The intent is to put in place policies to make sure data centers are water responsible in their use," Rep. Cutler told reporters after the hearing. "That only closed loop system or better technologies is allowed for cooling. No evaporative cooling is allowed." Massive opposition to data center projects led to some legislators losing their seats and new lawmakers being voted in. On Wednesday, some new lawmakers who have been data center critics were sitting in the committee with members of the public and lobbyists, watching the presentation. "I think there’s still a question of whether we want data centers at all," said Rep.-elect Kim James, D-Ogden. She told reporters that the proposed bill is "a great start in the conversation" and she appreciated local input, but still had a lot of questions about the proposal as no legislation had been formally introduced. Other environmental groups who sat in the audience watching declined to comment on Rep. Cutler's proposal without seeing additional language. Asked by FOX 13 News about the idea of allowing data center development with guardrails, Rep. Cutler replied: "Data centers will happen. But we can make sure that in Utah, only the best projects that respect our natural resources, that benefit our local communities happen in Utah." Deeda Seed with the Center for Biological Diversity told FOX 13 News the draft proposal is "window dressing" and she did not see substantive changes in how the state incentivizes data center projects. "These are the things that we as community members, people of Utah, need to ask for a statewide moratorium on data center development with real protections," she said. "Because what was described today provides no real protections." Sen. Wilson told reporters that there will be a lot of opportunity for public input on the bill when it's deliberated during the 2027 legislative session that begins in January. "We don’t have the public’s opinion yet, which will be very important as it comes to committee," he said. "We don’t have the input yet."

artigo.texto: SAUGERTIES, N.Y. – Key Capture Energy Development Director Paul Williamson on Tuesday defended his company’s proposed 100-megawatt lithium-ion battery facility and found a core group of supporters willing to stand by the application. During a Nov. 17 public hearing, Williamson said the application addresses the safety questions raised by the Planning Board and the public. “KCE New York 34 has submitted a thorough application for special use permit and (state environmental quality review), including environmental, geotech, sound, visual, and safety studies that address the questions of the Planning Board and members of the public,” he said. “In the very unlikely worst-case scenario of some type of an emergency situation, any impacts of hazardous emissions would mostly be contained within the project limits. Any emissions that go beyond the property boundary would not reach any nearby structures,” Williamson said. Williamson also tried to ward off concerns, saying that the chemistry of Key Capture batteries, as well as the way they are housed, would be different in Saugerties than at sites cited in recurring public comments. “There is no risk at all that emissions from this project, if it were in an emergency situation, would reach public spaces, residential spaces, or commercial spaces,” Williamson said. “There’s absolutely no risk of that at all.” Of the 32 speakers, 12 supported the project, 17 voiced concerns, and three expressed mixed or neutral views. Some supporters — who argued the state electric grid needs industrial-size rechargeable batteries to keep up with goals set by Gov. Kathy Hochul — criticized the opponents who said the application does not adequately address safety or disruptive issues the facility would create. Samantha Dederick, chair of the town Comprehensive Planning Committee, said opponents are not looking at the big picture. “The full power grid belongs to almost everyone in North America,” she said. “I hear a lot of selfishness in this town. …We all benefit from a fully functioning power grid. We all bear responsibility for facilitating it.” Town Climate Smart Task Force member Nicole Roskos told opponents they need to be realistic about how everyday life requires the use of lithium batteries. “If you are afraid of lithium-ion batteries then you should throw all your phones away,” she said, adding that Key Capture proposes to use a generation of batteries developed in response to fire threats. Opponents countered by delving into the application for issues they found troubling, citing an abundance of uncertainty about equipment, emergency response readiness, and the impact on nearby residents. “Technical documents typically associated with final building code approval and detailed engineering review were not available for independent review … including complete proprietary equipment listings, certification documentation, UL 9540A testing reports, project-specific fire and life safety analysis, commissioning documentation, explosion prevention, and control system documentation,” resident Tanya Weiss said. Weiss also pointed to the use of child labor in the lithium mining operations, which has been documented by the U.S. Department of Labor’s Bureau of International Labor Affairs. Resident Janet Greenberg said the application does not address potential problems for homes on Saugerties Manor Road, which is close to the project’s 11-acre facility. “KCE’s emergency plan doesn’t mention our road, sets no evacuation routes, and has no way to notify residents,” she said. “Please require evacuation routes and resident notification in writing before (making) any decisions.” Greenberg added that the application does not reference the potential impact to the homes’ water source. “We’re the only street in the area not on town water,” she said. “We’ve talked about the hazards of runoff…and we’re asking for baseline tests of all 15 wells, ongoing monitoring, and (getting) commitments to containment and replacement water.” Resident Eileen Ryan said recent software failures affecting nationwide air travel, email and banking undermine Key Capture’s safety claims. “Attackers can disrupt lithium battery storage systems by targeting the digital infrastructure that manages their safety and performance,” she said. “Attackers can hijack the…battery management system, override safety protocols by forcing batteries to operate outside safe voltage or temperature threshold. They can…spoof sensor readings, tricking the plant controllers to see normal status while the system is actually failing.” The public hearing was recessed until the Planning Board’s January meeting.

artigo.texto: Good afternoon! It’s Wednesday, and the midterm elections feel both a lifetime ago and like they happened just yesterday. My colleagues want to know your thoughts on our coverage to help shape our future plans. Here’s what you need to know today. 1. AI data centers are blocking pollution reduction and climate efforts in Illinois Under an ambitious law signed by Gov. JB Pritzker in 2021, the state set out to retire all fossil-fuel power plants between now and 2050. But big new data centers require so much electricity that it’s become difficult for the state to shut down all coal, gas and oil sources used to meet demand, a pair of state reports released this week found. As my colleague Brett Chase writes, the findings confirmed fears environmental and climate advocates have had for more than a year. Cleaner sources of power, including wind and solar farms, are not being built quickly enough to keep up with new demands from data centers being used to power artificial intelligence. That’s bad news for the planet because oil, gas and coal create carbon dioxide, the major contributor to global warming. The same pollution causing climate change is also bad for our health, causing respiratory problems and exacerbating a number of other threats. In central and southern Illinois, seven coal plants still operate. The goal has been to shut four of them down by 2030 and that goal remains, according to one of the two reports. Three publicly owned coal-fired plants have longer timelines before they are closed. Eleven so-called peaker plants, which burn oil or natural gas as power backups, were expected to close in 2030 or 2031. But those plants should continue to operate until 2033 to help prevent blackouts when demand peaks, such as on the hottest days of the year, the report recommends. In Chicago, peakers are still active at the long-closed Fisk coal-fired power plant in Pilsen. There are also peakers in Waukegan, where a former coal plant that has operated for more than 90 years will keep operating until 2033 under the state recommendation. [Chicago Sun-Times] After expensive campaigns where voters were pummeled with mailers, digital ads and, for the president’s race, incessant negative commercials, a WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times analysis of Chicago Board of Election voter data shows how the winning candidates managed to rack up votes. Biggs, who won with 49% of the vote, did best in majority-white areas where fewer families send their children to public school. But she also outdid her two opponents in predominately Black areas, though she didn’t get a majority of votes. Biggs did particularly well on the North and Far Northwest sides, where voter turnout was high and people voted overwhelmingly for Biggs. In these areas, which include the wealthy Lincoln Park area and more grassroot liberal areas in Rogers Park, Biggs received more votes than both opponents combined. Black voters may have favored Biggs because, as a former teacher and principal serving on the board, she had the most experience in the education system, said Rufus Williams, a former school board president under Mayor Richard M. Daley and a host on WVON, a radio station that caters to Chicago’s Black community. But in parts of the South Side, West Side and majority-Latino neighborhoods on the Northwest Side, Hilario Dominguez and Victor Henderson combined got more votes than Biggs. Dominguez, who is Latino, alone received almost half of all votes in majority-Latino neighborhoods. [WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times] New Pew Research Center projections show Muslims are poised to become one of the fastest-growing religious populations in North America. In west suburban Berwyn, a Latino-led mosque reflects the changing face of Islam, Christiana Freitag reports for the Chicago Sun-Times. In February, on the first day of Ramadan, Ojala Islamic Center opened as the Midwest’s first Latino-led mosque, offering converts a place to practice Islam while maintaining ties to their cultural heritage. Christopher AbdulKareem Pavlicek, the founder who serves as imam, said the congregation is as much “convert-led” as it is “Latino-led,” with much of its community made up of people from different religious and cultural backgrounds who are embracing Islam for the first time. Nelson Julio-Polanco, born in the Dominican Republic and raised Catholic, found a sense of belonging at Ojala, which offers services in Arabic, English and Spanish. As the only Muslim in his family, Julio-Polanco said speaking Spanish with other Muslims made the community especially welcoming. “When they founded this organization, I felt like, wow, I can speak Spanish to these people and they’re Muslims too,” he said. “We have the same culture.” [Chicago Sun-Times] 4. The David Byrne-backed ‘Theater of the Mind’ will end its Chicago run in January As WBEZ theater reporter Mike Davis writes, the fully immersive show opened in March as an experimental addition to the Goodman Theatre’s 100th season. The production, located in the Reid Murdoch building Downtown, received mostly positive reviews. (Davis wrote in March that the show “exists somewhere in the margins of creepy festival funhouse meets cool high school science experiment. It’s trippy. It’s unique. And somewhere buried in the cool head tricks there is a story about revisiting the pivotal moments of our lives and questioning if we can trust our own recollections.”) An ambitious project created by Byrne and Mala Gaonkar, “Theater of the Mind” takes audiences on a journey through their own memories. Directed by immersive theater aficionado Andrew Scoville, the production features lifelike sets, hands-on experiments and a tour guide named David clad in the fashion of a childhood David Byrne. The production utilized 19,000 square-feet of space to drive home the desired feeling of audiences being transported into another reality. Nearly 50,000 people have seen the 75-minute show, according to the Goodman. [WBEZ] 5. Here’s where to dine in and order

artigo.texto: Ford bets on CATL know-how to bring cheap LFP batteries to U.S. EVs Ford has started making lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells in the United States with technology licensed from CATL, China’s battery giant. The Detroit automaker hopes the cells will help it build cheaper electric vehicles and challenge Chinese rivals. Ford said its first LFP prismatic cells have come off the line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall. They are headed to Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky to power prototypes of the Fathom, Ford’s upcoming midsize electric pickup. Ford says the milestone puts it “in the battery business” and claims it will be the first company to deliver LFP batteries in the U.S. for mainstream consumer vehicles. Cell production at the roughly 3 billion USD plant, about 100 miles west of Detroit, began last month. CATL supplies the technology and manufacturing support, but Ford owns and runs the plant. Why LFP, and why CATL LFP cells contain no nickel or cobalt, which keeps costs down, and they hold up well over many years of charging, according to Ford. The company picked rectangular prismatic cells because they fit directly into the chassis, allowing the battery pack to act as part of the vehicle’s structure and cutting structural costs. Ford said it spoke with battery makers around the world before choosing CATL. It wanted a technology that was “proven in the field, ready to manufacture at scale”, and CATL’s batteries power some 30 million vehicles worldwide. “If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible,” Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced development projects, said during a tour of the plant. “CATL being the biggest in the world means that they’re the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.” LFP chemistry was invented in the U.S. but commercialised mostly in China. CATL staff helped Ford ramp up the Marshall plant by providing training and manufacturing expertise. Capacity and timeline Ford says the Marshall lines can turn out 40 cells per minute, which it calls among the fastest LFP prismatic lines outside China, and that the site has room to expand. Workers use AI-powered image recognition to catch defects, with a goal of measuring the defect rate per billion cells rather than per million. That pace works out to about 20 gigawatt-hours a year for EVs and Ford’s energy storage business. The original plan was up to 40 GWh, but Ford scaled back as it and the broader industry slowed their EV push. Ford says it is still early in certifying its processes. It plans to increase cell output next year, ahead of the Fathom’s expected launch in the fourth quarter of 2027. A battery pack plant in Marshall is due to open in 2027. The Fathom will start at 28,350 USD for the standard-range model, and Ford plans to open preorders in early 2027. What Ford learns in Marshall is also feeding into Ford Energy’s plans for battery energy storage production in Glendale, Kentucky. Political headwinds The project has drawn criticism in Washington. Some lawmakers and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy have objected to Ford’s ties with CATL. In September, Duffy wrote to Ford CEO Jim Farley expressing “profound concern” about the company’s links to Chinese firms. The White House praised Ford’s U.S. jobs and manufacturing the next day. In January, Rep. John Moolenaar, a Michigan Republican who chairs a House committee, asked Ford whether its CATL licensing terms had been “updated, expanded, or otherwise altered” to fit its new focus on energy storage and data centre batteries. Ford replied that expanding domestic LFP production is “an investment in American workers” and said it is confident the batteries meet tax credit requirements. The start of shipments comes the same week President Donald Trump is meeting Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen.
