artigo.texto: German company wpd plans to repower one more of its wind farms in Croatia. The Orlice wind farm will not only have more powerful wind turbines, but also a 10 MW battery energy storage system. Wpd earlier initiated the procedure to repower its Trtar-Krtolin wind farm (11.2 MW), the second-oldest wind power plant in Croatia. In addition, the company has announced plans to convert the Katuni wind farm into a hybrid power plant by adding a solar park. Wpd is one of the pioneers in renewable energy in Croatia. The Orlice wind farm was commissioned in 2009 as the third wind power plant in the country. It comprises 11 Enercon wind turbines with a total installed capacity of 9.6 MW. It is located on the territory of the city of Šibenik, within Šibenik-Knin county. Repowered plant to feature three wind turbines The company plans to dismantle and remove the existing 11 wind turbines and install three new units with an individual capacity of 6 MW. Three new foundations will be constructed for the new turbines at the locations of the existing foundations. The planned total installed capacity of the wind farm upon repowering would reach up to 20 MW, according to the environmental protection study for the repowering project. The investor plans to revegetate, with indigenous flora, approximately 1,500 meters of access roads that will no longer be in use. Wpd’s newest wind farm was commissioned in 2017 The environmental protection study was submitted by the company Vjetroelektrana Orlice to the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition alongside a request for an environmental impact assessment (EIA) screening for the repowering of the Orlice wind farm. In Croatia, wpd also operates the Ponikve wind farm on the Pelješac peninsula. It is its largest one, at 38.6 MW. Wpd’s most recently commissioned facility is the 34.2 MW Katuni wind farm, which came online in 2017.

artigo.texto: Franklin County supervisors discuss holding another data center panel FRANKLIN COUNTY, Va. (WDBJ) - Franklin County supervisors discussed holding another panel on data centers to get more information. At a work session, the board looked back at its October panel, which included a discussion of Mecklenburg County’s experience with data centers. Resident questions balance of first panel Franklin County resident Christine Sizemore said she did not feel the first panel gave a balanced picture. “I think the panel was a little more biased towards, we have a data center and we think they’re a good thing rather than being neutral and saying what can you expect when you have data centers coming,” Sizemore said. Sizemore said location matters. She wants leaders to consider whether a data center would be a good fit for Franklin County. Board discusses who could speak Supervisors discussed hearing from people with experience building and operating data centers, an environmental engineer and representatives from other localities. Board Chair Lorie Smith said the goal is to give the board and residents more information. “It’s my interest in getting our board and the citizens of Franklin County as informed as possible on what the facts are and what is involved with the data center in today’s time,” Smith said. Resident wants questions allowed Sizemore also wants residents to have a chance to question panelists. “I think questions should be allowed. Absolutely. They have to be. And the panelists also have to realize that people are a little bit hot under the collar about data centers, but that should not prevent public input and public questioning when the panels happen,” Sizemore said. Dashboard and ordinance Smith said county staff are working on a data center dashboard. “There will be different controls on that where you can click and look at information, download information, and there’ll be a question and answer portal as well,” Smith said. Smith also said the county is working on its data center ordinance. She said there are no current applications under consideration. Copyright 2026 WDBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Insults, profanity erupt at Massena town board meeting over data centers MASSENA, New York (WWNY) - Massena’s town board meeting erupted into insults and vulgar language Wednesday night over data center development People from communities around Massena voiced anger over the town considering a data center. How the confrontation unfolded The town board has a revised draft of a local law regarding a proposed data center. It could be adopted next month. “I think at the end of the day that’s what we’re all worried about: the safety of all of our people,” said Jacob Thompson, an attendee. Another attendee told the board, “I’m going to come after every one of you when I lose someone I love.” “That’s all you have to say and shake your f*ucking head. You have no moral compass,” another attendee said. Town Supervisor Ray Lancto then said, “This meeting is adjourned.” The attendee continued: “Go f*uck yourself because you don’t give a sh*t about anyone. Where are your f*cking morals? You don’t give a sh*t about anyone but yourself and the money that’s going into your f*cking pockets.” Akwesasne members attend About 60 people from Akwesasne attended the meeting. The community feels frustrated and unheard as North Country Colocation Services’ proposed large-scale data center comes closer to reality. “They’re not going to be able to push our people back. Our people are getting stronger, and our people are standing up,” said Kahentoretha Oakes, who attended the meeting. The proposed data center The data center would be built near tribal land at the former Alcoa East property. Developers say it would expand on services already happening in Massena. The company says it would need 2,000 construction workers to build the project. Developers say 200 full-time jobs would be created and the data center would become the largest taxpayer in the town. Lancto said the town is taking the proposal seriously. “Massena has seen economic opportunities come and go over the years. We’re taking this one very seriously, and we’re taking a look at the upcoming reviews and upcoming review processes,” he said. “We welcome the possibility of new meaningful investment, but we’re also taking this responsibility very seriously.” Environmental and health concerns Lancto said he understands the concerns. Environmental and health concerns continue to dominate opposition from tribal and non-tribal residents. Keith Frey of Colton said he is afraid of what the data center could mean for outdoor enthusiasts. “Massena is world-renowned for bass fishing. This would deplete the fishery and hurt the local economy,” Frey said. The company says its cooling system would have no discharge into local waterways. Massena officials say they want to protect the interests of town residents while creating a framework for reasonable and responsible economic development Copyright 2026 WWNY. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Key Takeaways: - $794 billion: Capital raised by data center developers between 3Q 2025 and 1H 2026 - 56%: Share of colocation financing from private markets in 1H 2026 - 18x: The year-over-year increase in neocloud maturing debt between 2029 and 2030 Executive summary Players driving the global data center buildout have raised around $1.8 trillion in financing since 2020, and capital expenditures are surging alongside demand for artificial intelligence. Firms have tapped new capital sources and deal structures while markets are pricing in higher credit risks, creating refinancing pressure for at least $1 trillion of debt maturing within the next five years. - Volume: Companies developing data centers raised at least $1.8 trillion between 2020 and the first half of 2026 across debt, equity and securitized instruments. Nearly half of that total was raised between 3Q 2025 and 1H 2026, with private markets playing a growing role. Financing for the large group of colocation providers exceeds that of the four hyperscalers. - Refinancing: Rising interest rates, growing concerns around developers’ debt levels and an overreliance on financing support from hyperscalers and chipmakers are placing greater refinancing pressure on firms. Colocation providers and neoclouds, in particular, face steep increases in maturing debt volumes by 2030, with smaller developers like TeraWulf and Crusoe facing higher uncertainties due to large amounts of construction debt. Execution challenges have already affected Firmus and Nscale’s high-valuation IPO plans. - Structure: Deal structures are becoming more complex, leveraging credit support mechanisms from investment-grade backers to enable smaller developers to raise capital at the size and tenor required. Support mechanisms include GPU-backed loans, direct guarantees, residual-value guarantees and prepayments. Nvidia has extended at least $198 billion in direct credit support, committing even more alongside large asset managers. - Banks: Morgan Stanley underwrote the most data center financing, driven in part by its close relationship with Meta. Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase follow. TD Bank and Scotiabank accelerated dealmaking the most in 2026, competing to fund established players. - Approach: BNEF compiled over 2,000 transactions of the largest 125 data center developers across Bloomberg Terminal, third party and news sources, and collected additional sector- and deal-level details through industry interviews and document reviews.

artigo.texto: ICE Launches New Tool to Quantify Data Center Construction Risk ATLANTA & NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 17, 2026-- Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (NYSE: ICE), one of the world's leading providers of financial market technology and data powering global capital markets, today announced the launch of the ICE Data Center Site Analytics Tool. The tool helps developers, investors, lenders, and municipalities assess the feasibility and delay risk of data center projects before capital is committed. Data centers are among the largest components of U.S. private sector investment today, with cumulative global spending projected to reach $7 trillion by 2030 to meet the demand for compute power, according to McKinsey & Company. Although data centers have been a clear driver of U.S. economic growth, local factors such as utility costs, environmental concerns, and community opposition are increasing the probability of halted or delayed projects. Trained on thousands of data center permitting and project outcomes across the U.S., the ICE Data Center Construction Disruption Model, a key part of the ICE Data Center Site Analytics Tool, is designed to estimate the probability that data center construction may face disruption within 24 months. When tested against historical permit outcomes to analyze the probability of disruption, the model achieved 77% accuracy. “Data center capital is moving faster than local permitting and community consensus, and that gap is now a material financial risk,” said Larry Lawrence, Head of the Geospatial Intelligence team at ICE. “On a median-sized $2.7 billion project, a 12-month delay can cost $162 million to $270 million, so giving developers and communities a common, data-driven view of those costs can lead to better-informed agreements.” The ICE Data Center Site Analytics Tool covers more than 3,100 U.S. counties and tracks thousands of existing U.S. data centers across 47 embedded geospatial data layers, estimating disruption probability through three categories of inputs: - County permit history, including past delay and stoppage rates, filing volume and trends, project value, and fees. - Local site characteristics, including nearby electricity and water costs, plus tract-level education, broadband, poverty, and unemployment. - Market conditions, analyzing the ICE U.S . Mortgage Rate Lock Index at the time of filing. The ICE Data Center Site Analytics Tool is part of ICE Geospatial Intelligence, which links location-specific data to financial assets and securities. The platform spans 1.6 billion global building footprints, 13 million corporate asset locations, more than 100 million U.S. properties and more than 50,000 municipal bond issuers. artigo.texto: Proposed Lansing data center ban draws packed hearing, boos and debate A proposal to ban data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities drew a packed auditorium Tuesday night, with supporters urging Lansing officials to protect local resources and opponents warning against closing the door to potential investment. 48 people signed up to speak at the public hearing at Lansing Middle School. Each was given two minutes, with a 9 p.m. cutoff for the proceedings. Many attendees wore red to show support for the ban. Some speakers opposing it, including TeraWulf representatives, were met with boos and shouted interruptions. Board members repeatedly asked the audience to stop shouting and clapping so speakers could continue. The debate comes amid opposition to TeraWulf’s proposed artificial intelligence data center at the former Cayuga Power Plant site near Cayuga Lake. The proposed zoning amendment would define data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities but exclude them from the town’s list of permitted uses, making them prohibited under the zoning code. The change would apply townwide rather than serve as a decision on a single project application. Before the hearing, neighbors and community advocates held a press conference supporting the proposed ban. Speakers stood in front of signs reading “No Data Center on Cayuga Lake.” “We enthusiastically support the board moving forward with a ban on data centers and crypto mining facilities in the town,” said Renee Vogelsang, a member of the FLX Strong coalition. Supporters cited concerns about water resources, electricity demand, noise and the potential effects on nearby neighborhoods. Lisa Lincoln and Mark Zuss said they live approximately 3 1/2 miles from the proposed site. In a joint interview, they raised concerns about how the development could affect the lake and their quality of life, including potential noise from the facility. TeraWulf representatives urged the board to continue considering the project, arguing that development could generate new tax revenue and support schools, public services and infrastructure. One representative also discussed the possibility of a community benefits agreement providing recurring financial contributions toward local priorities. Those contributions were presented as potential benefits, rather than a finalized agreement. Another TeraWulf representative argued that opposing the ban should not be interpreted as endorsing the proposed development. “Voting no to this ban doesn’t mean automatic support of the data center,” the representative said. “It means we should thoughtfully review individual projects as they come along.” A resident speaking against the ban also urged officials to consider potential economic benefits and raised concerns about possible legal challenges. The hearing gave the board sharply differing views on whether Lansing should prohibit the facilities or continue reviewing proposals individually. A vote on the proposed zoning change was tentatively scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 18, at Lansing Middle School.

artigo.texto: NETSCOUT's Sustainability-by-Design Approach Combats Surging Data Center Energy Consumption New M-Series platform delivers 20% improvement in energy efficiency, reducing customers’ operating costs and meeting sustainability goals amid rapid AI data center growth WESTFORD, Mass.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 19, 2026-- NETSCOUT SYSTEMS, INC. (NASDAQ: NTCT), a leading provider of network observability, AIOps, cybersecurity, and DDoS attack protection solutions, today announced that its approach to sustainable design is helping its customers achieve a 20% improvement in energy efficiency in their usage of NETSCOUT® products, reducing operating costs and environmental impact. The overall environmental impact could be further reduced depending upon the energy source utilized. According to recent BloombergNEF research, global data center electricity demand will nearly quadruple by 2035 to 2,354 terawatt-hours, accounting for 7% of the global electricity demand. Forrester blogs note that resource optimization becomes everyone’s business: “Winners will not debate or care whether to label the response ‘sustainability.’ They will be forced to plan AI, energy, water, land, infrastructure, and community impact together, because that is now what resilient growth requires.” NETSCOUT’s sustainability-by-design approach: - Prioritizes resource-efficient design at both the component and platform levels. - Helps organizations mitigate the environmental and financial impacts of rapidly increasing data center and AI energy consumption. - Enables upgrade of older devices with a single appliance to further optimize power efficiency. Demonstrated Energy Savings Performance lab testing of the InfiniStreamNG® 3U appliance measured the M-series platform versus the J-series. The results were reduced power consumption, yielding an estimated 1.3 MWh of annual energy savings per device. When cooling and power distribution losses are considered for the data center, power savings can be even higher. Similar results were observed in a live customer deployment. "NETSCOUT's sustainability-by-design architectural approach means that we select for energy efficiency at the platform and component level," said Jillian James, director of sustainability, NETSCOUT. "We care about our customers' downstream energy and AI impact, not just our own footprint. Our intention is to help customers make their networks and analytics more resource-efficient and better for the environment." Committed to Sustainability The energy-efficient M-series platform reflects NETSCOUT’s broader corporate commitment to environmental responsibility. NETSCOUT is actively integrating sustainability into its operations and product development cycles to support circular economy principles. These product-level energy reductions are a key component of the company's ongoing progress toward its science-based greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets for FY30. By embedding energy efficiency into product design, NETSCOUT helps customers turn infrastructure modernization into lasting business value: lower operational costs, a smaller environmental impact, and greater capacity to support growing digital and AI demands. The M-series platform demonstrates how operational performance and sustainability can advance together, helping organizations make more effective use of power, space, and infrastructure investments. This approach enhances NETSCOUT’s value as resource efficiency becomes an increasingly important driver of technology purchasing decisions. artigo.texto: Installed energy storage capacity in the United States has surpassed 200 GWh, according to the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026, produced by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. During the third quarter of 2026, 14.3 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) entered operation. These additions brought total deployments during the first nine months of the year to 48.3 GWh, representing a 20% year-on-year increase. The volume installed between July and September was 1% lower than in the same quarter of 2025. However, the cumulative results for 2026 reflect growth in both grid-connected projects and behind-the-meter storage. Utility-scale projects account for most deployments Utility-scale projects represented most of the storage deployed during the first nine months of 2026, with 40.8 GWh, while the behind-the-meter segment added 7.5 GWh. In the third quarter alone, the utility-scale market added 12.2 GWh across 45 projects. Three projects with gigawatt-hour-scale capacity began operations during the period. Commercial and industrial storage added 1.3 GWh during the quarter, an increase of 29% year on year. Between January and September, this segment reached 5.4 GWh, exceeding the 4.8 GWh installed during the whole of 2025. SEIA and Benchmark attribute part of this growth to data centre expansion and the difficulties these consumers face in securing sufficient grid capacity. BESS can be combined with on-site solar or wind generation to manage demand, shift renewable output and provide short-duration backup power. Residential storage, meanwhile, added 746 MWh during the third quarter, up 16% year on year and the highest volume recorded for a third quarter. Nevertheless, installations through September remained 12% below the level recorded during the first nine months of 2025. Texas leads state-level deployment Texas led utility-scale energy storage deployment through the end of the third quarter, adding 12.3 GWh of capacity. Arizona ranked second with 7.7 GWh, followed by California with 6.8 GWh. Eleven states had already surpassed their previous annual energy storage installation records by the end of September: Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama and Illinois. The report identifies a shift in state policy from setting storage targets to conducting procurement processes. During 2026, New York awarded contracts to eight projects totalling approximately 950 MW in its first bulk energy storage solicitation, while Illinois secured around 600 MW in its first dedicated procurement. A previous SEIA analysis attributed part of the reduction in average wholesale electricity prices between the summers of 2021 and 2026 to the combined growth of solar and energy storage: 42% in Texas and 51% in California. seia.org 2030 forecast increases to 708 GWh SEIA and Benchmark raised their forecast for cumulative US energy storage capacity in 2030 by 3.7%. The updated outlook expects the country to reach 708 GWh across grid-connected and behind-the-meter systems. The revision reflects the number of projects under development, state procurement programmes and the growing need for flexibility across the electricity system. Energy storage can shift electricity from periods of high production to hours of greater demand, respond to fluctuations in renewable generation and provide grid services. Its deployment can also reduce the need to use additional generation facilities during demand peaks. Battery cell manufacturing capacity reaches 92.4 GWh US manufacturing capacity for energy storage cells also increased during the third quarter. Production of lithium iron phosphate cells for stationary energy storage began at a facility in Tennessee in July. Another facility opened in Indiana in October, increasing total US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, a 50% rise. The report estimates that lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry will represent 92% of lithium-ion BESS deployments in 2026, up from 77% in 2023. Overall, lithium-ion batteries are expected to account for more than 97% of installations. Industry calls for permitting reform The report’s publication coincides with a request from more than 300 solar and energy storage companies for Congress to approve the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). The companies argue that the reform would shorten permitting procedures for energy infrastructure, reduce development costs and accelerate the connection of new projects. SEIA maintains that expanding energy storage infrastructure can increase the capacity available to meet electricity demand growth and support the integration of renewable generation into the US grid.

artigo.texto: Home to digital infrastructure tycoons like Meta, Oracle and Equinix, San Mateo County passed an emergency ordinance Tuesday, Nov. 17, to block data center construction and operation in unincorporated zones of the county. The temporary moratorium, introduced by Board Supervisor Lisa Gauthier, followed a summer inquiry to develop a large data center at the county-owned event center, according to Brian Kulich, the assistant county attorney. “Data centers can place significant demands on electricity, water and infrastructure, and raise concerns about noise, air quality and compatibility with surrounding land uses,” Gauthier said. Urgency ordinances remain in effect for 45 days and may be extended for up to two years. The cloud in the county The county defines data centers as facilities that house computing infrastructure to process, store or distribute electronic data. Kulich said that definition can be refined through stakeholder collaboration in the coming weeks. Rocketing digitalization, especially through artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency, has increased demand for cloud computing infrastructure. U.S. data center electricity consumption nearly tripled from 2014 to 2023, and rose 14% from 2023 to 2024, according to a June report by the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The ordinance prohibits permit applications for data centers in unincorporated San Mateo County. The county’s 20 cities are outside the board’s purview and would have to pass their own policies. Kulich said the city attorney of San Mateo was one of several in the county who are interested in taking similar action to block data centers. Several computing facilities already exist across the county, including an Evoque facility at 3175 Spring St. in Redwood City. Kulich said the electrical capacity of all the proposed data centers across the Bay Area, including in Santa Clara and Alameda counties, would require 1 billion watts — enough to run a mid-sized city. The July inquiry the county received to build a new data facility at the San Mateo County Event Center was part of a larger proposal to construct eight data centers across the Bay Area, according to the ordinance. The company behind the request was Global Stack LLC, a California-based data center developer founded in March, which has been in talks with at least eight fairgrounds in the state, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. At the board’s Oct. 20 meeting, supervisors directed Planning and Building Department staff to work with the County Executive’s Office and County Attorney’s Office to prepare amendments to the county’s zoning regulations. The ordinance takes effect immediately and was enacted in part because the board found it addressed an “immediate threat” to public health, safety or welfare, according to Kulich. “The point of it is to allow a pause, essentially, to allow staff to consider the effects of either acting or not,” Kulich said in a presentation before the board Tuesday. “This particular urgency ordinance, the need arises from the recent proposals to develop data centers across the Bay Area.” Gauthier defended the ordinance as an opportunity to “create space for robust stakeholder engagement” to sculpt a long-term data center policy. Community input, the supervisor said, would involve residents, local organizations, utilities and industry representatives, including Silicon Valley Leadership Group, Bay Area Council and the county’s Economic Development Association, SAMCEDA. The county has passed similar temporary urgent moratoriums before, as recently as Aug. 25, when the San Mateo County Board of Supervisors voted to temporarily stop the development of new detention and correctional facilities in unincorporated areas of the county. The ordinance was in part meant to protect the county from the establishment of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention camps locally. Debate over data facilities Board President Noelia Corzo said she was in favor of blocking data center development in unincorporated San Mateo County due to existing water and electricity “issues.” “Our current zoning was not written with large-scale AI data centers in mind,” Corzo said. “Modernizing our policymaking and making sure that we are staying up to date with how we’re regulating big, impactful industries like this one is important.” Supervisor Jackie Speier was most wary of the ban on data centers. “I’m just concerned that we use this as a means to just not do anything for a period of two years because I don’t think that’s fair for the public or to businesses that may have an interest,” Speier said. All board members present at the meeting ultimately supported the moratorium. Supervisor Ray Mueller was absent for the vote. Public commenters were divided on data centers, as Peter Leroe-Muñoz, a member of the Bay Area Council, which represents almost 400 employers in the region, said the organization would like the county to pursue a “balanced regulatory path, rather than an extended freeze.” He said local data centers help anchor the AI and life sciences economies, generate revenue for schools and county services and create high-wage construction jobs. In response to concerns about resource impacts, he pointed to state laws governing water use, projected energy use and noise levels, and cited San Jose’s community engagement as an example of “clear, uniform standards for data centers.” Dashiell Leeds with the Sierra Club Loma Prieta chapter pushed back, cautioning the board against following San Jose’s approach because its “standards are pretty low.” Leeds, a San Jose resident who has attended many data center meetings in that city, said residents have “overwhelmingly” called for a moratorium over unanswered concerns, including low-frequency infrasound, pollution from diesel generators and the heat island effect. Veja o resumo da notícia - Emissões de carbono dos data centers podem crescer 70% até 2030, impulsionadas pela demanda por inteligência artificial. - Consumo de eletricidade dessas instalações deve dobrar até o fim da década, com cerca de três quartos do aumento ligados à IA. - Centros voltados à IA acrescentarão 350 TWh por ano à demanda mundial, volume superior ao consumo anual do Reino Unido. - Geração por combustíveis fósseis deve crescer, com carvão na China e gás natural nos Estados Unidos como principais fontes. - Capacidade mundial das instalações aumentou dez vezes em dois anos, chegou a 17 GW e pode alcançar 50 GW com obras em andamento. - Parque global soma cerca de 120 GW e deve receber outros 120 GW até 2030, em sua maioria voltados à inteligência artificial. As emissões de carbono dos data centers podem crescer 70% até 2030, impulsionadas principalmente pela expansão da infraestrutura necessária para atender à demanda por inteligência artificial. A projeção consta de relatório da Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE). Segundo a agência, o consumo de eletricidade dos data centers deve dobrar até o fim da década. Cerca de três quartos desse aumento serão provocados pela expansão dos sistemas de inteligência artificial, que exigem maior capacidade de processamento e, consequentemente, mais energia. A AIE estima que os data centers voltados à IA acrescentarão 350 terawatts-hora (TWh) à demanda mundial de eletricidade por ano até 2030. O volume é superior ao consumo anual de eletricidade do Reino Unido. Carvão e gás ganham espaço Apesar dos investimentos das empresas de tecnologia em fontes renováveis, a geração de eletricidade por combustíveis fósseis deve crescer para acompanhar a expansão dos data centers. Na China, aproximadamente metade da eletricidade consumida pelos data centers deverá ser produzida por usinas a carvão até 2030. O restante virá principalmente de fontes renováveis, com participações menores de energia nuclear e gás natural. Nos Estados Unidos, a previsão é que o gás natural responda por cerca de 60% da eletricidade utilizada pelos data centers até o fim da década. Em agosto de 2026, havia planos para aproximadamente 180 gigawatts (GW) de novas usinas a gás associadas a essas instalações. Infraestrutura cresce rapidamente A expansão física dos data centers também acelerou. A capacidade mundial dessas estruturas aumentou dez vezes nos últimos dois anos e chegou a 17 GW. Projetos atualmente em construção podem elevar esse volume para aproximadamente 50 GW. O parque global de data centers soma cerca de 120 GW de capacidade. Até 2030, outros 120 GW devem ser adicionados, sendo que aproximadamente três quartos desse crescimento serão destinados a instalações voltadas à inteligência artificial.

artigo.texto: As ações de empresas americanas de tecnologia óptica subiram na terça-feira, após uma reportagem da Reuters indicar que o governo Trump pretende prosseguir com as restrições à importação de equipamentos chineses para centros de dados, apesar das objeções de várias grandes empresas de tecnologia americanas. As ações da Coherent Corp. (NYSE:COHR) subiram 10%, enquanto as da Applied Optoelectronics Inc. (NASDAQ:AAOI) ganharam 9%. A Lumentum Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:LITE) teve alta de 8% e a Corning Inc. (NYSE:GLW) avançou 3,5%. As medidas propostas restringiriam as importações de novos modelos de transceptores ópticos chineses, componentes usados para transmitir dados em alta velocidade por meio de redes de fibra óptica em centros de dados. As restrições fazem parte de um esforço mais amplo dos EUA para abordar preocupações de segurança nacional associadas à infraestrutura de telecomunicações e informática fornecida por fabricantes chineses. Órgãos reguladores dos EUA expressam preocupação com a segurança dos transceptores ópticos A Comissão Federal de Comunicações (FCC) identificou potenciais riscos à segurança nacional associados aos transceptores ópticos chineses. Segundo as preocupações do órgão regulador, o equipamento poderia ser explorado para acessar informações sensíveis, introduzir software malicioso ou interromper as operações de centros de dados nos EUA. Os transceptores ópticos são usados para converter sinais elétricos em sinais ópticos e possibilitar a comunicação de alta velocidade entre servidores e equipamentos de rede. Os componentes são uma parte importante da infraestrutura que suporta a computação em nuvem e as aplicações de inteligência artificial. As restrições propostas se aplicariam a novos modelos de transceptores ópticos chineses, podendo afetar as decisões de aquisição por parte dos operadores de centros de dados dos EUA. Grandes empresas de tecnologia se opõem às restrições de importação propostas Segundo a Reuters, várias empresas de tecnologia dos EUA fizeram lobby contra as medidas propostas, citando preocupações sobre sua implementação e a disponibilidade de fornecedores alternativos. Amazon, Google, Meta, CoreWeave, Cisco e Microsoft estão entre as empresas que teriam manifestado objeções. Segundo relatos, executivos disseram a funcionários da Casa Branca que o cumprimento da exigência de substituir os equipamentos chineses poderia levar até uma década. Suas preocupações refletem a dimensão dos acordos de fornecimento existentes e os potenciais desafios associados à identificação de fabricantes alternativos capazes de atender à demanda. Apesar da oposição, o governo Trump pretende, segundo relatos, continuar a implementar as restrições. Os fabricantes chineses respondem pela maior parte do fornecimento global De acordo com a empresa de pesquisa Counterpoint Research, a China representa atualmente cerca de dois terços do mercado global de transceptores ópticos. Empresas chinesas, incluindo a Eoptolink e a Zhongji Innolight, estão entre os principais fornecedores desses componentes. Sua posição no mercado reflete a escala da capacidade de produção da China e seu papel consolidado nas cadeias de suprimento globais de equipamentos para data centers. Empresas americanas como a Coherent e a Lumentum competem no mercado de tecnologia óptica, embora sua capacidade de produção atual possa não ser suficiente para substituir imediatamente os fornecedores chineses. Um relatório da Fundação para a Inovação Americana indicou que os fabricantes nacionais atualmente não possuem a escala necessária para atender a todo o volume da demanda atendida pelas empresas chinesas. As restrições propostas podem, portanto, exigir mudanças na capacidade de produção e nos acordos de aquisição em todo o setor. As empresas de tecnologia óptica dos EUA poderiam se beneficiar das restrições? Os desdobramentos políticos relatados podem criar oportunidades comerciais adicionais para os fabricantes de equipamentos ópticos dos EUA, caso os operadores de data centers sejam obrigados a reduzir as compras de fornecedores chineses. As empresas Coherent, Lumentum, Applied Optoelectronics e Corning registraram ganhos no preço de suas ações após a reportagem da Reuters. Os investidores parecem estar avaliando o potencial de mudanças nos acordos de fornecimento para aumentar a demanda por equipamentos fornecidos por empresas sediadas nos EUA. No entanto, a extensão de qualquer benefício comercial dependerá dos requisitos regulamentares finais, dos cronogramas de implementação e da capacidade de fornecedores alternativos de expandir a produção. As limitações de capacidade existentes podem afetar a rapidez com que os fabricantes dos EUA conseguem responder ao aumento da demanda. Indústria alerta para possíveis restrições chinesas às exportações Empresas de tecnologia dos EUA também manifestaram preocupação com a possibilidade de medidas comerciais retaliatórias por parte da China. Segundo a Reuters, representantes da indústria alertaram que Pequim poderia responder restringindo as exportações de fosfeto de índio, um material usado na produção de certos transceptores ópticos. O fosfeto de índio é um importante material semicondutor para equipamentos de comunicação óptica de alta velocidade. Restrições à sua disponibilidade podem afetar fabricantes que dependem do material para a produção de componentes ópticos. A possibilidade de medidas retaliatórias aumenta a incerteza quanto aos potenciais efeitos das restrições de importação propostas pelos EUA nas cadeias de abastecimento globais. FCC mantém restrições mais amplas a equipamentos tecnológicos chineses A proposta mais recente segue outras medidas introduzidas pela FCC ao longo do último ano, relacionadas à importação de certos produtos tecnológicos chineses. Essas medidas incluíram restrições que afetaram novos drones, robôs, inversores de energia e roteadores chineses. artigo.texto: Low Carbon says new UK BESS projects 'demonstrate clear benefits' of co-location with solar PV The 30MW Birch BESS and 35MW Sandon Brook BESS represent the first battery storage projects the company has brought into commercial operation in the UK. UK renewables investment and asset management company Low Carbon has energised two battery energy storage systems (BESS) in Essex with a combined 65MW capacity. The 30MW Birch BESS and 35MW Sandon Brook BESS represent the first battery storage projects the company has brought into commercial operation in the UK. The projects are both co-located with operational solar PV plants owned by Low Carbon. The Birch project shares a 132kV grid connection with the 39MW Birch Solar Farm and 49.9MW Layer Solar Farm, while Sandon Brook has its own connection but is located alongside the 49.9MW solar plant of the same name. Both solar plants secured Contracts for Difference (CfDs) in allocation round 5 (AR5) and are covered by long-term route-to-market (RTM) power purchase agreements (PPAs). Low Carbon said that there is “increasing emphasis” on making smarter use of existing grid capacity and that battery storage is “playing a crucial role supporting market dynamics and enabling more renewable generation to come online”. The company’s managing director of portfolio management, Steven Hughes, said: “Birch and Sandon Brook demonstrate the clear benefits of battery co-location, which is a key part of our business model as we continue to grow our portfolio of operational battery assets across the UK and Europe.” While the two projects are Low Carbon’s first to enter commercial operations, co-located BESS assets feature in many of its plans. That includes its Beacon Fen Energy Park, which was consented by the government in August, which will pair 400MW of solar PV with up to 600MW of batteries.

artigo.texto: Havells India lança sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias na REI Expo 2026 A Havells India apresentou seus sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias na REI Expo 2026, segundo a pv magazine, posicionando o armazenamento dentro de um portfólio mais amplo de energias renováveis que também abrange inversores híbridos, carregadores de veículos elétricos, inversores solares e módulos. A empresa criou uma unidade de negócios dedicada a renováveis em abril para ampliar sua presença no setor. Reshu Madan, presidente e chefe de unidade de negócios da Havells, indicou que a primeira prioridade da empresa são os segmentos residencial e comercial e industrial, com expansão posterior planejada para aplicações em escala de utilidade e agrícolas. A Havells firmou parceria com a norueguesa Pixii para levar à Índia soluções modulares de armazenamento em baterias com controles definidos por software. A linha inicial atenderá aplicações de 3 kW a 125 kW, com sistemas maiores na sequência. A empresa também pretende oferecer pacotes integrados de solar com armazenamento para clientes residenciais, comerciais e institucionais. O portfólio modular incluirá a família PowerShaper, com o PowerShaper XLP nas capacidades de 112 kW e 225 kW, e a família PowerNode, a partir de 125 kW para uso comercial e industrial de maior porte. Aseem Goyal, chefe de unidade de negócios de Renováveis da Havells India Ltd, explicou que o design modular permite adicionar ou substituir unidades individuais com o sistema em operação, de modo que os clientes dimensionem a capacidade de armazenamento conforme suas necessidades, sem subdimensionar nem superdimensionar. A parceria com a Pixii tem o objetivo de levar a tecnologia aos clientes indianos a custos competitivos, aproveitando a rede de distribuição e a base de instaladores da Havells. A Havells também planeja uma futura família de produtos, a MegaNode, voltada ao armazenamento em escala de utilidade. A empresa continua vendo espaço para armazenamento off-grid e em microrredes em áreas remotas, mesmo com a expansão da conectividade à rede. Goyal observou que os mercados off-grid estão encolhendo gradualmente após os esforços do governo para levar eletricidade a todo o país, mas bolsões em estados como Uttar Pradesh e Bihar, além de localidades remotas, ainda apresentam oportunidades. As operações de mineração são outro mercado potencial. No segmento solar, a Havells oferece módulos monocristalinos PERC bifaciais e TOPCon, com produtos TOPCon classificados em até 620 Wp. A empresa fabrica alguns modelos de inversores conectados à rede na Índia e importa unidades de maior capacidade. A Havells também é investidora estratégica da Goldi Solar, que tem 16 GW de capacidade de fabricação de módulos e está entrando na produção de células solares. Goyal descreveu o arranjo como a combinação da força de fabricação da Goldi no mercado de IPP com o alcance de distribuição da Havells. A Havells fabrica e vende módulos não DCR com sua própria marca e espera obter em breve a aprovação na ALMM List-II para seus módulos DCR. A empresa está localizando sua cadeia de suprimentos de armazenamento em baterias em torno de eletrônica de potência, baterias, software e sistemas de rack. Ela começou a localizar o software de gestão de energia e trabalha na localização de racks, com a fabricação local de baterias prevista para começar em breve. A Havells pretende ir além de produtos individuais e avançar para soluções integradas. Madan disse que o objetivo é conquistar a confiança do cliente e melhorar a experiência do consumidor por meio de uma solução completa, e não apenas do produto. A empresa espera se tornar um player relevante em energias renováveis nos próximos três a quatro anos. A confiabilidade dos produtos, as garantias e o suporte pós-venda continuam centrais, com garantia de 10 anos nos inversores, ante as ofertas típicas do setor de seis a oito anos, e garantia mínima de 10 anos nos produtos de armazenamento em baterias, que pode ser estendida por cinco anos. Este relatório fornece uma análise aprofundada do mercado de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias em escala de rede na Índia, cobrindo tamanho de mercado, crescimento, demanda, oferta, fluxos comerciais, preços, cenário competitivo e previsões até 2035. O estudo é projetado para fabricantes, distribuidores, importadores, exportadores, investidores, equipes de compras, consultores e equipes de estratégia que precisam de uma visão consistente e orientada por dados da dinâmica do mercado e de uma definição analítica transparente do escopo do produto. Cobertura do Produto Os Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias em Escala de Rede são grandes instalações estacionárias de armazenamento eletroquímico de energia projetadas para armazenar e descarregar eletricidade no nível de utilidade, transmissão ou distribuição. O escopo abrange sistemas completos turnkey que compreendem racks de baterias, sistemas de conversão de potência, gerenciamento térmico, controles e balance of plant, bem como invólucros containerizados ou construídos para esse fim, classificados tipicamente de vários megawatts a centenas de megawatts e capazes de fornecer serviços de rede, como regulação de frequência, firmeza de capacidade, integração de renováveis e corte de picos. Incluídos - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias de íons de lítio em escala de rede - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias containerizados - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias em edifícios construídos para esse fim - Projetos turnkey de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias com conversão de potência integrada - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias de propriedade de concessionárias - Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias conectados à rede para serviços auxiliares Excluídos - Armazenamento de baterias comerciais e industriais atrás do medidor - S

artigo.texto: Hundreds of residents voice their opinions on data center proposal in Mansfield, Mo. MANSFIELD, Mo. (KY3) - Tempers flared Thursday night in Mansfield, Missouri. Many residents in the area called for transparency during a data center meeting. Mansfield’s Mayor, Derrick Neal, told the crowd at the meeting that the data center was proposed to the city in October by Trent Overhue, and the size of the project would come in at around 80,000 to 100,000 square feet. “I think there are other avenues that would bring revenue without hurting our farmers,” said one resident at the meeting. “We don’t want to industrialize rural America.” Residents from all across the area came to voice concerns over electricity, water, and noise. Only Mansfield residents were allowed to speak, but Ava resident Jeff Leinen says the data center would affect more than just those in Mansfield. “They’ve mentioned that it’s supposed to be a closed loop, but there are all kinds of chemicals that go into that system. And if there’s a spill and it gets into the groundwater, Bryant Creek is just down the road,” said Leinen. “That feeds right into Ava.” More residents are calling for transparency from the board. Mayor Derrick Neal addressed the crowd following the public hearing. “The aldermen and I, we all live in this community. Our families and friends, too. We’ve got friends and family that have cattle, that have farms. We are by no means going to do anything that would impact our city, potentially deplete the water supply, and change the lifestyle that we have here in Mansfield. We don’t want to do that. We are just looking at what has been told to us,” said Mayor Neal. ”I have not signed an NDA, nor would I. And I will not, I don’t think anyone else on this council has been involved in that either. There is no money transferring liens to anyone on this council that I’m aware of. It’s not how we operate. We’re here to do what’s best for this city." After the board left the meeting, more citizens took the microphone, calling for a moratorium and for this discussion to be settled on the ballots. “I want a moratorium until we have an environmental impact study that says what kind of impact this could have, not just on Mansfield, but your underwater groundwater tables go all the way from Seymour to West Plains to Hartville to Ava,” said Mansfield resident Jenifer Johnson. “We want to know how much water is going in. We want it regulated through the city water. I want to know every time you flush it, every time you change your water, where that water goes, where it’s being treated, and that it’s being done right. We need third-party regulation. And if you screw something up, you owe billions to this community.” ”That’s what our governmental basis is founded on; the people have a voice, your vote is supposed to matter,” said Green Mountain resident Adam Spence. ”The people really need to be heard because it’s not good when the people aren’t heard. And everyone knows that government has to work. And we want it to work.” The project developer was not at the meeting. Ahead of the meeting, KY3 asked Mayor Neal if he’d be available for a follow-up interview. He initially agreed to interview following the Board of Aldermen’s closed session at Mansfield City Hall that was scheduled to follow the public meeting. However, following the first meeting, the Board of Aldermen decided to cancel the closed session, and the mayor was not at City Hall following the meeting. artigo.texto: Two City Council members want to place a one-year moratorium on development of data centers in Jacksonville, according to legislation set to appear before Council. The ordinance, which is scheduled for formal introduction on Nov. 22, would create a task force to analyze regulation of data center development. Introduced by Council members Jimmy Peluso and Moné Holder, the legislation states that allowing development of data centers “to proceed without appropriate regulatory standards could create risks to the City’s water resources, electrical infrastructure capacity, land use planning objectives, and long-term community development strategy.” The legislation would also create a task force to study the effects of data centers in Jacksonville. That group would be composed of, at a minimum, the city’s Office of Economic Development, Department of Public Works, Environmental Quality Division and Planning Department. Those effects would include water supply and wastewater treatment capacity, electrical grid capacity and infrastructure requirements, land use compatibility, community impacts, other environmental considerations and best practices adopted by other Florida municipalities. The legislation allows for data centers already operating in Duval County to continue to do so. There are currently six operating in Jacksonville, according to a JEA spokesperson. “JEA does not currently have the electric and water capacity to serve a hyper-scale data center. Hyper-scale data centers run 24/7 with 80 percent or higher load factor and demand 100-500 megawatt (MW) of power. There are not any hyperscale facilities in Jacksonville,” JEA spokesperson Karen McAllister wrote in an email. “We do have six small-scale data centers in Jacksonville. They require less than 5 megawatts of power and do not necessitate major upgrades. Hyper-scale is about 100-500 MW of demand. For perspective, 500 MW equates to energy usage by 280,000 homes. In comparison, a small-scale data center (assuming 5 megawatts) uses as much energy as 2,800 homes.” Phil Perry, chief communications officer for the city of Jacksonville, said the city administration had “concerns about energy and water resources, and our citizens are concerned about their costs. Additionally, JEA has been clear that currently their electric grid cannot support a hyper-scale data center.” Perry said the administration was preparing to review the legislation. In October, Daily Record news partner News4Jax found that several companies had contacted JEA with inquiries about data center build-out. Those requests ranged in demand for power from 10 MW to 1,248 MW. According to News4Jax, a steel company places the largest demand on JEA, drawing a peak of nearly 64 megawatts for its plant’s furnace, plus an additional 18 megawatts for other portions of the facility. JEA also cannot service many of the largest data center requests, News4Jax reported. “Each of these sites would need their own dedicated substation or potentially multiple substations in order for JEA to serve them,” JEA’s interim Chief Administrative Officer Jordan Pope told News4Jax. “With supply chain constraints being a concern, especially because of the growth of data centers, long lead items such as substation transformers can take years to acquire and then install.” The proposal from Peluso and Holder comes as news analysts attributed much of the results of the November U.S. midterms to a “data center revolt.” A Nov. 6 story by the BBC said polling “found 56% of surveyed voters said data centres were a ‘crucial or major’ factor in their vote, while 76% said they would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community.” “Americans in a variety of demographic and partisan subgroups have become more negative in their views of data centers,” the Pew Research Center wrote in a story about its own data center polling. “Men and women alike, as well as adults across age groups and education levels, have become more likely since January to say data centers have a mostly bad impact on the things we asked about.” Proponents of data centers say development of the projects can benefit communities by expanding their tax base, creating jobs and providing infrastructure investment. In a July story, Forbes pointed to Virginia’s Loudoun County as an example of the beneficial impact of data centers to communities. According to Forbes, the county hosts more than 230 data centers, representing approximately 56.5 million square feet that were fully built or under construction at the time of the story. Forbes reported that than 17,000 direct and indirect jobs related to the projects had been created within the county, including in specialized trades, technology, professional services and security. Kerri Stewart, chief administration officer for Miller Electric Co. and a member of the Florida Digital Infrastructure and Security Alliance, said she had no concerns about the moratorium as of its introduction. “This legislation contemplates a task force that allows for thoughtful consideration about community concerns,” she said in a text message. Speaking as a FDISA board member, she said she hoped the city “truly intends to become educated on the impacts — good and bad — that could arise with/without clear regulations that address the public’s hopes for positive economic impact and concerns about strains on the grid and watershed.” "As an executive at Miller Electric, we hope that we will be able to share our experiences building data centers of all sizes around the Southeastern US. And as a Duval County homeowner, I hope that the task force or another City committee will look for ways to minimize the financial impact of Amendment 3." artigo.texto: Trending CHAMPION – Township trustees have placed a three-month moratorium on issuing permits for a data center in the township. Trustee Chairman Doug Emerine said officials want to be prepared is a company does express interest in building a data center in the township. Champion and Warren Township trustees recently came together to discuss the zoning of the former Copperweld Steel site, and part of the discussion was zoning the property for data centers. Officials said 65% of the land on the Copperweld site is in Warren Township and 35% is in Champion. Emerine said there has been no requests for a data center in Champion, but trustees want to be prepared with its zoning guidelines. “No one is going to get away from data centers. Whether it’s the township, the county or the state, they are coming,” Emerine said. Emerine said guidelines would address traffic and noise impacts; responsible economic development and job creation; and preserving public health, safety and welfare. He said officials from both townships want to make sure zoning regulations are the same for both if one is proposed for the site. PROPERTY PURCHASE In other business, trustees approved purchasing property in front of the township administration building off Mahoning Avenue. Trustee Rick York said the township purchased the 1.3-acre site for $178,000 for township use. Emerine said the former Champion Central School property off Mahoning Avenue has been deemed least desirable. The township obtained ownership of the former property from the Champion Local School District when a new elementary school was constructed north of that location. Emerine has said the property needs work on the parking lot, which would cost $100,000 to repair, in addition to other work at the site, which would cost more than $350,000. He said the township also would have trouble getting grants for work there since the local match has requirements the township would likely not be able to meet. York has said that if the trustees decide to sell the property in the future, soccer programs that use the land would be a top priority. Emerine said that when residents were surveyed about what they would like to see at the site, there were suggestions for a swimming pool, splash pad and pickleball courts. Emerine said the idea of having a park in the township has been discussed for years, but residents have said they would not support a levy to cover the costs. The district closed the 100-year-old school in spring 2018 with the opening of the new PK-8 school complex on state Route 45. The township previously sold 22 acres of land north of the cemetery to the school district for $106,000 for the new school complex. In exchange, the district transferred the Central School property to the township. The district did retain a nearby bus garage property. The former school property was discussed by trustees in recent years as a possible location for a park or a new fire station. Emerine said residents have said at past meetings they were concerned about costs to maintain a park, as well as vandalism. Emerine said if the property were to be offered for sale, it would be done through a Realtor or public auction.

artigo.texto: Chesterfield supervisors approve battery energy storage facility CHESTERFIELD, Va. (WWBT) - The Chesterfield County Board of Supervisors on Wednesday approved a proposal to build a 100-megawatt battery energy storage facility off Watkins Centre Parkway. “I think this is going to add to the capacities that we are going to need,” Supervisor Kevin Carroll said. The Munster Battery Energy Storage Facility will store electricity to be used later when demand is high. “It helps keep the lines at more of a constant line, voltage, instead of real highs and lows and that helps in a lot of ways for a lot of reasons,” Supervisor Jim Ingle said. The newly approved facility will be next to another battery energy storage facility. The two facilities will share an electrical substation. Renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind, fluctuate. Battery storage helps make sure none of the energy produced goes to waste. A handful of people spoke during public comment. Multiple speakers pointed to the benefits of the project. “It will actually reduce our electric bills over time and also clean our air,” one man said. Concern was also raised that the extra energy will go to the growing number of data centers being built in the county instead of the people who live there. “Our water, our air, our electricity is meant to be for people, and it’s important that we are prioritizing that,” Billy Davies of the Sierra Club said. Chesterfield currently has nine data center projects. All but two have been approved. Project Loch, one of Google’s sites, is planned to go right by the newly-approved battery energy storage facility. In response to the data center comments, Board of Supervisors Chair Mark Miller pointed to the energy expected to come from the fusion power plant, which should be running by the early 2030s. “I know that I would’ve never approved data center unless we knew that we were having another form of energy coming here. And I believe in fusion,” Miller said. Copyright 2026 WWBT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: RWE constrói bateria de 262,5 MWh na Itália. Sistema de armazenamento de energia poderá atender ao pico noturno de 21 mil residências por quatro horas. A alemã RWE iniciou em Ragusa, na Sicília, a construção de seu primeiro sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias na Itália, com previsão de funcionamento até o final de 2027. A instalação terá 62,5 MW de potência e 262,5 MWh de capacidade, sendo projetada para ajudar a estabilizar a rede elétrica e atender, durante quatro horas, uma demanda equivalente ao pico noturno de aproximadamente 21 mil residências italianas. Como o sistema de armazenamento de energia funcionará em Ragusa Para funcionar como uma reserva de eletricidade, o empreendimento reunirá 42 contêineres com baterias de íon-lítio. A obra, porém, não se limitará à instalação desses equipamentos: a RWE também construirá a infraestrutura elétrica necessária para conectá-los ao sistema italiano, incluindo um transformador de alta tensão que fará a ligação com a rede de 150 kV. É por essa conexão que a energia armazenada poderá ser disponibilizada quando houver necessidade. O funcionamento previsto combina duas etapas. Em momentos de maior oferta, a eletricidade poderá ser retida nas baterias e, quando a procura aumentar, devolvida à rede. Esse recurso ganha importância em sistemas que utilizam energia solar e eólica, pois a produção dessas fontes depende das condições climáticas. O armazenamento permite aproveitar a eletricidade em um horário diferente daquele em que foi gerada, ajudando a ajustar a oferta ao consumo. - Estudo revela como a tempestade geomagnética de maio de 2024 levou à formação inédita de quatro faixas de elétrons nos Cinturões de Van Allen ao redor da Terra - Cientistas criam blocos semelhantes a LEGO usando poeira lunar simulada e impressão 3D a laser, que pode ajudar a construir futuras bases na Lua sem transportar todos os materiais da Terra - China testa avião cargueiro que voa sem pilotos, transporta até 5 toneladas por 2.600 quilômetros e pode reduzir custos logísticos em mais de 60%, com operações comerciais previstas para 2027 - Cientistas do MIT criam microrrobô voador que consegue pousar em um girassol com precisão e pode abrir caminho para futuras máquinas capazes de ajudar na polinização de plantações Além de fornecer energia em períodos de demanda elevada, a instalação prestará serviços de balanceamento para contribuir com a estabilidade da rede. A RWE prevê ainda funções de formação de rede, entre elas a reserva instantânea, também chamada de inércia, como parte dos recursos técnicos oferecidos pelo projeto. A estimativa de atendimento a 21 mil residências deve ser entendida nesse contexto: trata-se de uma demanda equivalente ao pico noturno de consumo, durante um intervalo de quatro horas, e não de abastecimento permanente. Segundo a companhia, os 62,5 MW de potência máxima poderão ser fornecidos durante esse período, enquanto os 262,5 MWh representam a capacidade de armazenamento do sistema. Expansão das baterias acompanha investimentos da RWE em energia renovável A entrada no mercado italiano de baterias ocorre em um país onde a RWE já opera diferentes empreendimentos de geração renovável. Antes da construção em Ragusa, a presença da companhia estava concentrada nas fontes eólica e solar, reunidas em um portfólio composto por: - Três instalações agrivoltaicas; - Uma usina solar; - 18 parques eólicos terrestres. Juntos, esses projetos somam aproximadamente 670 MW de potência instalada. De acordo com a RWE, essa estrutura é suficiente para fornecer eletricidade renovável equivalente ao consumo de mais de 550 mil residências italianas. O conjunto continuará crescendo: a empresa também constrói outros 200 MW em projetos de geração solar e eólica no país, ao mesmo tempo que planeja instalar novos sistemas de baterias. A iniciativa de Ragusa faz parte de uma expansão que ultrapassa as fronteiras italianas. Atualmente, a companhia mantém cerca de 1,7 GW de potência instalada em sistemas de armazenamento por baterias ao redor do mundo e outros 3 GW estão em construção. O novo empreendimento na Sicília será o primeiro dessa modalidade da RWE na Itália. Sopna Sury, CEO da RWE Renewables para a Europa e a Austrália, relacionou o investimento à necessidade de tornar a rede mais estável à medida que cresce o uso de fontes renováveis. A executiva também sinalizou a intenção de ampliar a presença da companhia em armazenamento de energia no país.

artigo.texto: - Singapore has signed carbon credit implementation agreements with Kenya and Zambia at COP31, bringing its total bilateral agreements to 14. - The partnerships establish frameworks for Article 6 carbon credit transfers, with proceeds supporting climate adaptation and a portion of credits set aside for cancellation. - A separate memorandum of understanding with Bangladesh lays the groundwork for a future implementation agreement. Singapore is expanding its international carbon market network, signing implementation agreements with Kenya and Zambia at COP31 in Antalya while beginning a separate carbon credit cooperation initiative with Bangladesh. The agreement with Zambia, signed Wednesday, is Singapore’s 14th bilateral Implementation Agreement under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and its fourth with an African country, following Ghana, Kenya and Rwanda. The Kenya agreement, which was the 13th overall, was signed earlier this week. Both agreements establish legally binding frameworks for generating and transferring carbon credits from eligible mitigation projects. Project developers will be able to pursue activities aligned with Article 6 rules, with Singapore and its partners expected to publish authorization procedures and eligible methodologies. Partnerships Target Climate Finance And Project Development Singapore allows eligible international carbon credits to cover up to 5% of companies’ taxable emissions under its carbon tax framework. Credits can also be used toward national climate commitments and other international obligations, including the aviation sector’s carbon offsetting scheme CORSIA. Under both the Kenya and Zambia agreements, Singapore will direct 5% of proceeds from authorized credits toward climate adaptation in the host countries. It has also committed to cancelling 2% of authorized credits at first issuance, preventing those units from being traded or used toward emissions targets. Relevant: Zambia Sets Stage For International Carbon Trading With Digital Registry Separately, Singapore signed last week a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Bangladesh to explore Article 6 carbon credit cooperation, identify potential projects and exchange expertise. The countries will work toward a legally binding implementation agreement in the following months. According to S&P Global, more than 120 bilateral agreements have been signed under Article 6.2, reflecting rising interest in using carbon trading to finance emissions reductions and mobilize private investment. The partnerships are intended to direct investment to mitigation projects while supporting sustainable development and local communities. artigo.texto: University of Dubuque forum explores benefits, risks of AI and data centers DUBUQUE, Iowa — The University of Dubuque hosted a public forum Tuesday night to explore the potential benefits and drawbacks of artificial intelligence and data centers, giving community members an opportunity to learn about the technology and ask questions. Students spent the semester researching data centers from several perspectives, including their potential impact on water use, energy demand, land use and the environment, as well as ethical and public policy concerns. Donovan Tann, an English professor at the University of Dubuque, said the forum was designed to challenge the idea that technological changes are inevitable and demonstrate that communities have choices about how those changes affect them. In a statement to Iowa's News Now following the event, Tann emphasized that he does not believe technological change is inevitable. “I said that the event is designed to respond to people who say ‘this is inevitable’ and that instead, we show the options available to communities,” Tann said. Tate Glaspie, who examined the potential environmental impacts of data centers, said communities must weigh the benefits of the technology against its potential consequences. “It could be a huge beneficial thing to overall improve the quality of life. But the main concern that I know for people is, are we sacrificing a huge aspect of our quality of life in order to basically make our life simpler and, you know, more convenient,” Glaspie said. Several academic divisions across the university collaborated on the event, including aviation and flight, computing and applied technology, humanities, natural sciences and theology. In addition to student research presentations, the forum featured a 90-minute panel discussion and question-and-answer session with three journalists from across the region. The panelists included Dubuque-based freelance journalist Benjamin Fisher, Wisconsin Watch reporter Tom Kertscher and The Gazette's Linn County local government reporter Grace Nieland. The forum aimed to help community members better understand the technology and make informed decisions about data center development. “It is more of a moral obligation that we take into account all factors that could potentially harm our quality of life in order to make sophisticated and educated decisions,” Glaspie said.

artigo.texto: Appear Inc Begins Pre Production of Solid-State Battery, Targets Mid-2027 Launch Field trials complete across motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters. Pre-production underway. Limited production on track for mid-2027, with full-scale production in 2028. SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Appear Inc., a San Francisco-based developer of next-generation solid-state battery technology, today announced that it has moved from proving its technology to producing it. The company has completed field trials on three types of electric vehicle: motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters. It has also completed advanced manufacturing trials and started pre-production manufacturing with a manufacturing partner. Alongside this technical progress, Appear has added new distributors and strategic partners in selective established and emerging markets. The company remains on track to begin limited commercial production in mid-2027, followed by full-scale production in 2028. The technology Most electric vehicles today run on lithium-ion batteries, which use a liquid electrolyte to move charge between the electrodes. Solid-state batteries replace that liquid with a solid material. This is widely seen as a path to safer batteries, with no flammable liquid to leak or ignite, and to more energy in a smaller, lighter cell. Appear’s solid-state technology is built around three priorities: safety, performance and manufacturability. For motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters, where weight, range and safety matter on every ride, that combination is especially valuable. From the lab to the production line Following its advanced manufacturing trials, Appear has moved into pre-production with its manufacturing partner and is refining its processes for volume manufacturing. Building a route to market New distributors and strategic partners in selective established and emerging markets are expected to give Appear regional market access and distribution channels at launch. Partner details remain confidential. Prashant Rurs, Founder & CEO of Appear Inc, said: We are moving beyond development and validation and into commercialization, “We remain on track to begin limited production in mid-2027 and to scale up to full production in 2028.” READ the latest Batteries News shaping the battery market Appear Inc Begins Pre Production of Solid-State Battery, Targets Mid-2027 Launch, source

artigo.texto: Canadian EV battery re-engineering company Moment Energy has launched a new battery energy storage system (BESS) called Nova. Nova is the first BESS made from repurposed electric vehicle batteries that achieves UL 1973 and UL 9540 safety certifications from US testing and certification company UL Solutions. Nova has also been tested to the UL 9540A standards for the evaluation of thermal runaway, Moment Energy says. Jeff Smidt, senior vice president of testing, inspection and certification, industrial, at UL Solutions said, "UL Certification demonstrates that the evaluated battery and energy storage system met applicable safety requirements." Nova is now in production at Megafactory 1 in British Columbia, the company's facility that's certified to UL 1974, a standard determining the sorting, grading and repurposing of EV batteries. Moment Energy has been verified as a non-Prohibited Foreign Entity by the US government, so investments in Moment Energy battery systems are eligible, therefore, for the federal Investment Tax Credit from 2027. Related:Veolia to recycle EV batteries in the EU, calls for regulation of domestic strategic metals Moment Energy takes end-of-life EV battery packs from vehicles at around 70% state-of-health (SoH), then removes underperforming cells and reconfigures them to form units specifically designed for utility-grade battery storage systems. Each Nova 2.94m x 1.80m (9.65 ft x 5.9 ft) block provides around 200kW/500kWh, and individual battery packs can be replaced as they reach end-of-life without altering the overall BESS enclosure, producing a projected lifespan of the Nova of around 20 years. The Nova BESS comes in a Type 3R enclosure with an ISO 12944-complaint C4 coating, operates in temperatures from -25°C to 50°C (-13°F to 122°F), functions at altitudes up to 2,000 metres (6,500 ft) and has an IEEE 693 high seismic rating. Edward Chiang, co-founder and CEO of Moment Energy, said: "We see a future where re-engineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chain. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering and North American manufacturing to deploy the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid." Moment Energy's battery storage systems are used in data centres, airports, hospitals, factories and micro-grids, the company says. First deliveries of Nova are planned for Q1 2027. In January 2024 Moment Energy received US$15 million in Series A funding from the Amazon Climate Pledge Fund and Voyager Ventures. Series B funding of US$40 million for the company came in May this year from Evok Innovations, Liberty Mutual Investments, the W23 Global Fund and Acario, the latter the wholly-owned subsidiary of natural gas supply company, Tokyo Gas.
