artigo.texto: Ecobiz.asia – The ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF) is seeking a more formal role within ASEAN and closer alignment with global carbon market standards as it moves into a new two-year phase focused on turning regional cooperation into practical outcomes. The framework’s 2026–2028 strategy includes expanding its membership, strengthening coordination with international carbon market initiatives and establishing an ASEAN Community of Practice to facilitate knowledge-sharing and consultations on longer-term projects. The priorities follow the renewal of the ACCF’s Memorandum of Collaboration at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 12, 2026. The five founding signatories extended their cooperation for another two years, while the Philippines-based Aboitiz Foundation Inc. joined as an observer. The ACCF was established at COP29 in November 2024 to support the development of high-integrity and interoperable carbon markets across Southeast Asia. Its founding members are the Malaysia Carbon Market Association (MCMA), ASEAN Alliance on Carbon Markets (AACM), Singapore Sustainable Finance Association (SSFA), Indonesia Carbon Trade Association (IDCTA) and Thailand Carbon Markets Club (TCMC). Under the chairmanship of SSFA, which began in the second half of 2026, the ACCF will focus on three areas: strengthening carbon credit supply and demand, improving market infrastructure and building regional capacity. On the demand side, it plans to develop an interim pathway for corporate use of high-integrity carbon credits and a due diligence framework to help financiers assess carbon project investments. On market infrastructure, it will seek greater clarity on the legal status of verified carbon credits and explore ways to reduce cross-border barriers to harmonisation and the fungibility of credits across ASEAN markets. The framework will also work with international partners to provide technical and advisory support for carbon finance and bring its work to ASEAN forums. Oi-Yee Choo, ACCF co-chair, co-lead of SSFA’s Carbon Markets Workstream and chief executive of Climate Impact X, said the organisation would work closely with Singapore as it assumes the ASEAN chairmanship in 2027, complementing regional market-building efforts from the private sector. The framework also aims to broaden its regional representation through new members, including Aboitiz Foundation, which joined as an observer. “By plugging in to initiatives such as the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, we will also bring ASEAN’s perspective to the global agenda and help ensure carbon markets develop more equitably,” Choo said. The renewal also marks a step towards aligning ASEAN’s carbon market development with global efforts to promote credible corporate use of carbon credits. All five founding signatories now support the Shared Principles developed by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, a government-led initiative co-chaired by Kenya, Singapore and the United Kingdom. Launched at the COP30 Business and Finance Forum in November 2025, the principles set out six pillars for companies to use carbon credits credibly alongside deep emissions reductions within their own operations. Renard Siew, president of MCMA, said the ACCF had originated as a priority deliverable under Malaysia’s ASEAN chairmanship, championed through the ASEAN Business Advisory Council Malaysia to advance regional carbon market cooperation. He said the next phase should move beyond dialogue towards tangible outcomes that build market confidence, strengthen institutional capacity and unlock cross-border opportunities. “The ambition should not simply be to grow carbon markets, but to ensure they deliver meaningful climate impact, mobilise investment and create lasting value for the region,” Siew said. Dharsono Hartono, permanent chair of AACM, said closer coordination, knowledge-sharing and joint efforts to address common challenges would help strengthen confidence in carbon credits originating from ASEAN and create more opportunities for cross-border cooperation. Riza Suarga, president of IDCTA, said the framework should now translate its commitments into concrete action, particularly by supporting the development and implementation of carbon projects that meet high standards of quality, transparency, credibility and environmental integrity. Gloyta Nathalang, chair of TCMC, said cooperation between governments and businesses could strengthen credit quality and market interoperability while respecting the different priorities of ASEAN member states. She said TCMC would contribute by sharing knowledge and bringing the practical experience of project developers and buyers into the framework’s work. Aboitiz Foundation President Ana Margarita Hontiveros said the foundation’s participation as an observer would allow it to share experience and learn from regional partners, representing the Philippines’ nature-based solutions industry and carbon coalition groups. She said regional carbon market cooperation should deliver benefits beyond the generation of credits, including opportunities for communities and the protection of natural resources. Since its establishment, the ACCF has gained recognition in several regional policy platforms, including the joint media statement of the 57th ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting and the ASEAN Joint Statement on Climate Change to COP30. Its work has also been cited in the ASEAN Capital Markets Forum’s guidance for an ASEAN voluntary carbon market. Over the past year, the framework has supported national and independent carbon standards aligned with benchmarks set by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM) and the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), according to the initiative. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no AIE aponta que consumo de energia em data centers pode duplicar até 2030 Publicado 19/11/2026 • 20:00 | Atualizado há 19 horas KEY POINTS Foto: Unsplash A expansão da inteligência artificial e dos serviços digitais aumenta a demanda por infraestrutura de processamento de dados em todo o mundo. Esse crescimento também amplia a pressão sobre o setor elétrico, que precisará acompanhar o crescimento do consumo de energia. A Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE) alerta que os data centers podem dobrar o consumo de eletricidade até 2030, alcançando aproximadamente 1.000 terawatts-hora por ano. A agência também aponta obstáculos que ameaçam o avanço dos projetos, como limitações nas redes elétricas e dificuldades nas cadeias de abastecimento. Leia também: CEO interina da Nvidia defende diálogo com comunidades para expansão de data centers De acordo com a CNBC, a projeção da AIE integra o Cenário de Políticas Declaradas, que considera medidas anunciadas pelos governos. Dessa forma, o aumento da demanda dos data centers pode exigir investimentos maiores para garantir o fornecimento de energia. A agência destaca que a capacidade limitada das redes elétricas representa um dos principais desafios para a expansão dessas estruturas. A falta de equipamentos e componentes nas cadeias de abastecimento também pode atrasar empreendimentos. Com isso, pelas estimativas da AIE, os gastos com redes de transmissão e distribuição podem crescer 75% na próxima década, colocando o setor entre as principais frentes dos investimentos em energia. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Mesmo com o aumento da demanda no setor elétrico, a agência prevê um crescimento positivo das fontes renováveis. A geração de energia limpa poderá crescer 85% a mais na próxima década em comparação com os dez anos anteriores. Além disso, o setor de energia solar também deve ampliar sua participação na matriz internacional e se tornar a maior fonte de eletricidade do mundo a partir de 2030. Nos últimos meses, diversos países têm investido milhares de dólares no setor de energia renovável. Além de auxiliar na demanda por energia, a fonte renovável pode ajudar a reduzir a dependência de combustíveis poluentes. Leia também: Por que empresas de inteligência artificial estão investindo bilhões em data centers? A instabilidade atual no mercado internacional de combustíveis também pode acelerar a transição para sistemas elétricos. Segundo a AIE, a crise energética de 2026 deve incentivar países a reduzir a dependência de petróleo e gás importados. Com isso, novos projetos de eletricidade podem diminuir as oscilações no fornecimento de combustíveis. artigo.texto: Empresas interessadas em instalar ou ampliar data centers no Brasil ainda aguardam a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) para acessar os benefícios fiscais previstos na Lei 15.504/2026. Embora a legislação tenha sido sancionada em setembro, a utilização dos incentivos depende de um decreto do governo federal, que deverá estabelecer os critérios de habilitação, as condições técnicas e os procedimentos para adesão ao programa. Segundo informações divulgadas pelo UOL nesta segunda-feira (16), a expectativa é que o decreto seja assinado após o retorno do governo da Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31), possivelmente por volta de 27 de novembro. Até a publicação das regras, as empresas não conseguem utilizar os benefícios do regime. O Redata foi criado para estimular investimentos em infraestrutura digital, computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial no país. O programa prevê a suspensão de tributos na aquisição de equipamentos de tecnologia da informação e comunicação utilizados na implantação, modernização e ampliação de centros de processamento de dados. Quais benefícios estão previstos no Redata A Lei 15.504/2026 prevê a suspensão de PIS/Pasep, Cofins, Imposto sobre Produtos Industrializados (IPI) e Imposto de Importação, observadas as condições estabelecidas para cada tributo. No caso do Imposto de Importação, o benefício alcança equipamentos e componentes sem produção nacional equivalente. A suspensão dos tributos poderá ser convertida em isenção definitiva após o cumprimento das contrapartidas e a entrega dos produtos aos empreendimentos habilitados. O atraso na regulamentação, porém, reduz o período disponível para aproveitar parte dos incentivos. Segundo o UOL, a suspensão de PIS/Pasep, Cofins e IPI tem efeitos até 31 de dezembro de 2026, em razão da transição da Reforma Tributária sobre o consumo. Já o benefício relativo ao Imposto de Importação permanece previsto por cinco anos. Regulamentação deve definir critérios técnicos Um dos pontos que ainda precisam ser esclarecidos é o enquadramento das fontes de energia consideradas de baixa emissão de carbono. A legislação exige que os data centers atendam à demanda de energia elétrica com fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, mas não detalha quais alternativas serão aceitas nessa segunda categoria. A possibilidade de inclusão do gás natural está entre os temas em discussão no governo. Segundo o portal Eixos, há divergência entre os ministérios da Fazenda e de Minas e Energia sobre o enquadramento do combustível. A definição deverá constar das regras complementares. Outro ponto envolve a definição de quais equipamentos importados poderão receber o benefício. A lei restringe a suspensão do Imposto de Importação aos produtos sem produção nacional equivalente, mas a regulamentação deverá esclarecer os procedimentos para essa avaliação. A discussão envolve interesses de fabricantes instalados no Brasil e empresas de tecnologia que dependem da importação de equipamentos específicos para seus projetos. Empresas terão contrapartidas para acessar o regime A adesão ao Redata não será automática. As empresas precisarão obter habilitação junto ao Ministério da Fazenda e cumprir compromissos relacionados a investimentos, fornecimento de serviços ao mercado interno e sustentabilidade. Entre as principais exigências previstas na lei estão: - Destinar pelo menos 10% da capacidade efetiva de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados ao mercado brasileiro; - Investir o equivalente a 2% do valor dos produtos adquiridos com os benefícios fiscais em projetos de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação no país; - Utilizar fontes de energia renováveis ou de baixa emissão para atender à demanda contratual de eletricidade; - Apresentar índice de eficiência hídrica para resfriamento dos equipamentos igual ou inferior a 0,05 litro de água por quilowatt-hora. Para empreendimentos instalados nas regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste, a legislação prevê redução de 20% em duas das contrapartidas: o percentual destinado ao mercado interno e o investimento em pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Com a regulamentação ainda pendente, empresas do setor continuam sem acesso efetivo ao regime. A publicação do decreto será necessária para esclarecer as condições de habilitação e permitir que os investimentos planejados considerem os benefícios fiscais e as exigências definitivas do programa.

artigo.texto: UK hotel operators face growing pressure from electricity network charges that can remain high even when energy consumption falls. For multi-site hotel groups, these fixed costs are becoming an important factor in energy procurement, property investment and long-term financial planning. One charge attracting attention is the Transmission Network Use of System (TNUoS) charge. It helps fund the high-voltage electricity network that moves power across Great Britain. Although it is less visible than wholesale electricity prices, it can have a significant effect on the total cost of supplying large commercial properties. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. The challenge for hotel businesses is that lower electricity consumption does not always lead to a proportionate reduction in bills. Some network costs are based on a property’s connection and charging category rather than the amount of electricity it uses. This is prompting a closer look at commercial battery energy storage systems, on-site generation and smarter electricity management. Yet the financial case for these investments depends on how each hotel is charged. Battery storage can reduce some electricity costs, but it cannot automatically remove fixed TNUoS charges. Why electricity network charges matter for hotels Electricity bills contain more than the cost of generating or purchasing power. They also include charges for transporting electricity through transmission and local distribution networks, alongside other regulated costs and supplier charges. For hotels, this distinction matters because electricity demand is difficult to eliminate. Guest rooms, kitchens, lifts, ventilation, lighting, refrigeration and digital systems all require reliable power. Many properties operate around the clock, while demand can change considerably with occupancy, weather and the use of conference or leisure facilities. The UK’s electricity network charging arrangements create different cost pressures depending on a property’s location, voltage connection and supply agreement. TNUoS charges recover the costs of the national transmission network. Distribution Use of System (DUoS) charges fund the local networks that deliver electricity to individual premises. These charges can be passed through to commercial customers by electricity suppliers, although the way they appear on bills varies between contracts. For international hotel groups, understanding these distinctions is essential. Two properties with similar electricity consumption may face different network costs because of their connection arrangements, location or charging classification. How TNUoS residual charges affect hotel operating costs TNUoS charges have two broad elements: a locational component and a residual component. The locational element reflects differences in the costs associated with using the transmission network in different areas. The residual element recovers transmission costs that are not collected through locational charges. Under reforms introduced by the UK energy regulator Ofgem, residual transmission charges for final electricity demand are recovered through fixed charges rather than being linked directly to electricity consumed during particular periods. For non-domestic customers, the charging framework uses bands determined by relevant site characteristics, including historical consumption or capacity measures, depending on the connection category. This creates an important distinction for hotel energy managers. Reducing electricity use during a winter evening can help control certain consumption-related charges. However, it does not directly eliminate the fixed TNUoS residual charge. The distinction is particularly relevant when assessing investment proposals for batteries or other technologies intended to reduce exposure to network costs. A hotel may reduce the amount of electricity purchased during expensive periods without achieving an equivalent reduction in its fixed transmission charges. For multi-site operators, the financial exposure can be substantial in aggregate. It also creates a need for property-level analysis rather than assuming that every hotel will benefit equally from the same energy-saving measures. Why winter evening electricity demand remains important Winter evenings are a challenging period for electricity management in Great Britain. Demand across the electricity system can be high as homes and businesses use more lighting, heating and other electrical equipment. Hotels may also experience overlapping demand from guest services, restaurants, kitchens, leisure facilities and building systems. Although fixed TNUoS residual charges are not avoided by reducing consumption during these hours, other elements of electricity pricing can still make peak demand expensive. Some commercial electricity contracts expose customers to time-varying wholesale prices, network charges or peak-demand costs. Local distribution network tariffs may also vary by time of day and connection type. For hotels with suitable contracts, reducing electricity imports during costly periods can therefore deliver savings. The financial opportunity depends on the structure of the electricity agreement, the relevant network tariff and the hotel’s actual demand profile. This makes it important to distinguish between avoiding expensive electricity imports and avoiding fixed network charges. The two objectives require different calculations and may justify different investments. artigo.texto: Solar energy has emerged as one of the fastest-growing sources of renewable energy globally. How do you see its role evolving in the coming decade as countries work towards their clean energy and net-zero targets? The amount of electricity generated worldwide from solar photovoltaics surpassed that from nuclear and wind in 2025 and is destined to surpass that from coal in the early 2030s. Past then it will be our largest source of electricity generation, with electricity supplying an increasing portion of our total energy needs. How significant is the contribution of solar power in reducing global carbon emissions, and what more needs to be done to accelerate the shift from conventional energy sources? There are now over 3 terawatts of solar photovoltaics installed worldwide that will generate 3.5 petawatt-hours of electricity in 2026. If displacing coal from electricity generation or oil from transport, this will have reduced global CO2 emissions by over 3 gigatons. Solar is being installed at over 0.5 terawatts per year, but this needs to be increased to at least twice this. The more that is installed now, the lower will be global temperature rise Solar technology has advanced considerably over the years. What have been the most significant breakthroughs in solar cell efficiency, and what innovations can we expect to see in the coming years? Over the last decade, solar panel efficiency has increased from about 16% to values as high as 25%. We have made a solar system in our lab that converts sunlight with over 40% efficiency. This is by using a stack of four cells, each specialised for a different colour range in sunlight. If this approach can be commercialised at low cost, we would expect commercial panels to operate at such efficiencies at some time in the future. Despite the rapid growth of solar energy, what are the key challenges that continue to limit its wider adoption, particularly around energy storage, grid integration, efficiency and reliability? The availability of low-cost Li-ion storage batteries has overcome earlier barriers to large-scale integration. Solar plus batteries are now providing a more reliable electricity supply than traditional coal generators, not only in Australia but in countries like Pakistan and many African countries with notoriously unreliable electricity supply. How can next-generation solar technologies, including advancements in PERC and TOPCon cells, help improve the performance, affordability and scalability of solar power? Improving solar cell performance not only lowers the costs of solar panels not only by lowering the amount of glass, cover sheets, frames and terminals required but also costs of transport, support structures and wiring required when being installed. As solar energy becomes more cost-competitive, what steps are needed to make it a reliable and accessible energy source for both developed and emerging economies? The International Energy Agency announced in 2020 that solar was now providing “some of the cheapest electricity in history,” but because it used to be expensive, this has taken time to become more widely known. Private citizens in emerging economies have only recently realised this and are now taking the initiative in procuring solar to provide a reliable electricity supply. Looking ahead, which countries or regions do you believe have the greatest potential to drive the next phase of solar innovation, and how important will international research collaborations be in achieving this? Australia pioneered both the PERC and TOPCon cell technologies that have dominated recent solar production, so it is likely to play a major role in leading progress here. China and India are the two countries likely to dominate solar production, helped by the strong demand in their local markets. artigo.texto: A leaked compromise proposal seeks to shield European industry from rising carbon costs, but environmental groups warn that concessions on free emissions allowances and international carbon credits could undermine the bloc's 2040 climate ambitions. The European Union's 2040 climate target risks being undermined by reforms to the bloc's carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS), according to a leaked document seen by Euronews. The Irish Presidency of the EU Council has softened a proposal, to be discussed by EU ambassadors on Wednesday, amid growing political pressure on the ETS as national governments struggle to reconcile emissions targets with industrial competitiveness and high energy costs. The compromise text seeks to secure political support for the bloc's carbon market beyond 2030. However, climate advocates warn that concessions to protect European industry could weaken the system's contribution to the 2040 target, leaving other sectors of the economy to make up the shortfall. The Council text retains the European Commission's July proposal to slow the decline in carbon allowances, extend free permits for industry and introduce international carbon credits into the EU carbon market, allowing emissions at home to be offset through projects abroad. But negotiations are further reshaping the plan, especially around how much flexibility governments and industry will have to avoid domestic emissions cuts. Free allowances and international credits Under the Irish Presidency's proposal, industrial companies would retain 80% of their free allowances if they submit an investment plan, even if they subsequently fail to carry out the proposed decarbonisation investments. The remaining 20% would be conditional on starting construction of eligible projects. Free allowances are permits that companies receive without having to buy them at auction. They are designed to protect EU producers against competition from countries with less stringent climate rules, such as China and the US. The proposal marks a significant political concession to industries concerned about losing free allowances, raising questions about whether the ETS will provide sufficient incentives to cut emissions. The compromise would shield industry from carbon costs for longer, while leaving governments to ensure that this protection translates into investment in European production and clean technologies. On international carbon credits, the Council has retained the Commission's proposal to set aside allowances equivalent to 260 million tonnes of CO2 to finance their purchase. It also leaves open the possibility of a pilot phase between 2031 and 2035, allowing the EU to test the system before implementing it in full. The Council has also maintained stringent quality and integrity requirements for international credits, making the ETS emissions reduction trajectory increasingly dependent on their availability. However, if industries can't buy them, it could jeopardise the 2040 climate target, since it requires at least an 85% domestic net emissions reduction, with international credits accounting for the remaining 5%. The Irish Presidency is seeking to build consensus among the 27 EU countries before negotiations turn to more politically sensitive questions of climate ambition and burden-sharing between member states. It hopes to secure an agreement at the Environment Council on December 11. The European Parliament is expected to vote during its December 14-17 plenary session in Strasbourg. Fragmentation at national level The Irish Presidency faces an uphill battle given the depth of divisions among member states and the complexity of the negotiations. EU countries are already divided over how quickly the supply of carbon permits should shrink, whether companies should be allowed to use international carbon credits to meet their obligations and how far industrial sectors should be shielded from rising carbon costs, according to a second document seen by Euronews. Taken together, the demands risk diluting the ETS when it is expected to drive a large share of the bloc’s next phase of emissions cuts. In general, governments want to preserve the ETS as a source of revenue for decarbonisation, but concerns are mounting about the costs it imposes on energy-intensive industries competing with manufacturers from China or the United States. EU capitals are split over the total number of emissions permits available to companies — some argue they should decline to increase carbon pricing and encourage divestments in fossil fuels. Others fear the impact of withdrawing free allowances on their struggling industries. A slower reduction would ease the pressure on power plants and factories to cut emissions, potentially tempering carbon prices and giving companies more time to adapt. But it would also mean fewer emissions cuts in the sectors covered by the ETS, making the 2040 target harder to reach. Environmental groups sound the alarm A recent analysis by the Öko-Institut, commissioned by environmental campaign group WWF Germany, warned that the Commission's proposed ETS reform was "incompatible" with the EU's target of cutting net emissions by 90% by 2040. “The Commission would rather gamble on climate protection than safeguard the future of European industry," said Lisa Okken, industrial policy expert at WWF Germany. "Its proposed reform lacks the carbon price signal needed to incentivise the urgent modernisation of European industry. This gap is being filled with complicated accounting tricks and excessive flexibility.” Another key concern cited by the environmentalists is the proposal to allow additional emissions beyond the existing emissions cap in exchange for future permanent carbon removals through expensive technologies designed to capture CO2 from the air. "It remains unclear whether these removals can be delivered at the scale required, as the necessary capacity simply does not exist today," reads the study.

artigo.texto: Data center developer provides free water during boil water advisory SPARTANBURG COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - Northmark Compute and Cloud is providing free water at the Piedmont Interstate Fairgrounds as a boil water advisory across Spartanburg County continues. The line for free wrapped around the fairgrounds Thursday. Once it ended for the day, crews at the fairgrounds started preparing for another round of distribution. Crews unloaded a truck after truck of water. People said they are grateful for the water. “I’m just thinking God they’re able to give us some water for the situation,” one resident said. “It helps out tremendously and we truly appreciate it,” another resident said. Residents describe water loss Many people said they have not had water from the tap since Wednesday morning. “Everybody’s out of water,” one person said. Others said they have only a trickle. “We have a little water just don’t got any pressure,” another person said. Company brings in trucks of water Northmark Compute and Cloud is behind the free water. The company is also the developer of the South Pine Street Data Center. Sarah Knox, director of external affairs for Northmark Compute and Cloud, said the company stepped up to help. “I am a lifelong South Carolinian. I know that when your neighbor needs help, if you can, you step up. If you see a need, you fill a need. It was super important to us the moment that we heard this crisis was happening, we sprung into action,” Knox said. Northmark said it brought in 15 trucks of water from North Carolina and Georgia. People arrived in cars, on bikes and on foot to pick up two cases each. artigo.texto: Deputados do Paraná aprovam projeto de lei que incentiva instalação e expansão de data centers no estado — Foto: Divulgação/Gov.br Deputados estaduais da Assembleia Legislativa do Paraná (Alep) aprovaram, nesta quarta-feira (18), em segunda discussão, uma política estadual para incentivar a instalação e a expansão de data centers no estado. O projeto autoriza o Poder Executivo a classificar datas centers como empreendimentos de interesse estratégico estadual, dar prioridade administrativa a estes projetos, firmar parcerias com universidades e centros de pesquisa e regulamentar benefícios fiscais. Os autores da proposta, os deputados Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (PP) e Bazana (PSD), apontam que o Paraná reúne condições favoráveis para atrair grandes centros de processamento de dados, como matriz energética predominantemente renovável, disponibilidade de energia, redes de fibra óptica de alta capacidade, ecossistema de inovação consolidado e capital humano qualificado. Segundo a justificativa, a proposta pode estimular a economia digital, a pesquisa tecnológica, a inteligência artificial e a geração de empregos especializados. Conforme o texto da proposta, o objetivo é atrair investimentos de infraestrutura digital para o estado, consolidar o Paraná como polo estratégico de data centers na América Latina, entre outros. Na versão original, o projeto criava o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (PRODATA-PR) e autorizava benefícios fiscais de ICMS (Imposto sobre Circulação de Mercadorias e Serviços) para empresas do setor. Entre eles estavam suspensão, isenção ou redução do imposto. Porém, no substitutivo aprovado pela Comissão de Constituição e Justiça, o texto passou a ser mais genérico. Com a mudança, ele apenas autoriza o Poder Executivo a regulamentar eventuais benefícios fiscais, respeitando a legislação federal e a disponibilidade orçamentária, sem conceder incentivos específicos diretamente na lei. LEIA TAMBÉM: - Política: Sergio Moro anuncia ex-procurador da Lava Jato como secretário Anticorrupção do Paraná - Final feliz: Bilhete com telefone de contato ajuda idoso com amnésia a voltar para casa após se perder - Vídeo: Motorista joga caixas de cigarros contrabandeados pela janela enquanto foge da PRF com carro sem um dos pneus Data centers são alvos de discussões Os data centers são grandes instalações que abrigam servidores responsáveis por armazenar e processar informações, inclusive para sistemas de inteligência artificial. Como funcionam continuamente, esses equipamentos precisam de muita energia e de refrigeração para evitar o superaquecimento. Em setembro de 2026, foi sancionada uma lei federal que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). Na prática, o programa reduz a cobrança de impostos sobre equipamentos usados na instalação e na expansão de data centers, desde que as empresas cumpram uma série de requisitos. No entanto, a instalação desses empreendimentos também tem gerado controvérsias. Nos Estados Unidos, por exemplo, moradores de regiões que concentram grandes centros de processamento de dados relatam impactos como ruído permanente gerado pelos sistemas de refrigeração e pelos geradores de energia de emergência, além de preocupações com o aumento do consumo de água e energia elétrica. Em algumas regiões do país norte-americano, comunidades afirmam que a chegada dos data centers altera a dinâmica urbana sem necessariamente trazer benefícios proporcionais em empregos. O debate também envolve questões ambientais e de planejamento urbano. No Brasil, os problemas são semelhantes. Em São Paulo, o Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente de Campinas (Comdema) convidou três instituições de ensino e pesquisa para avaliar os possíveis impactos da construção de um mega data center na Fazenda Pau d'Alho, em Barão Geraldo. Também naquele estado, o Ministério Público abriu um procedimento para apurar a instalação de dois data centers na cidade de Salto. A representação menciona o receio do potencial aumento no consumo de água na cidade, que tem problemas constantes no abastecimento. No Pará, o primeiro data center de IA na Amazônia gera debate por risco de formação de "ilhas de calor" em uma região já castigada por temperaturas extremas. artigo.texto: Duke Energy customers across North Carolina are facing higher electricity bills starting in January, but new rules will require large data centers to shoulder more of the financial risks associated with their growing energy demand. After opening in downtown Raleigh one year ago, Alejandro Leon Jr., owner of Olé Sports Bar and Lounge, said a new challenge is on the horizon for his establishment: Higher electricity bills. Other WRAL Top Stories “We’ve been eating that up and now unfortunately with that spike its obvious that the consumers are going to have to pay all that up front. Very unfortunate," Leon said. Leon says the rate hike would put business owners like himself in a crunch. “I was pretty disappointed that North Carolina approved the spike," Leon said. For Durham resident Midori Brooks, who recently received a $900 electricity bill, the prospect of another rate increase means she may need to take on a second job. Brooks has lived in the same home since 1995 and has watched her electricity bills climb. She recalls paying about $225 to $250 a month in previous years. Now, even with her husband working full time and Brooks working part time, the family is struggling to keep up. “I have to figure out whether I'm gonna pay at least a portion of the light bill and still be able to feed my three grandkids,” Brooks said. About $200 of her recent $900 bill was a past-due balance, she said, reflecting how difficult it has already become for her family to keep up with electricity costs even before the new rate increases take effect. The North Carolina Utilities Commission on Monday approved two-year rate plans for Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress, largely accepting negotiated settlements that reduced the utility's original requests. Residential electricity rates are projected to rise about 9.5% over the next two years for Duke Energy Carolinas customers and 9.3% for Duke Energy Progress customers. Duke released new figures Tuesday detailing how those increases will translate into monthly electricity bills. The increases will begin Jan. 1, 2027, in the middle of the winter heating season. How much more will customers pay? According to projections released Tuesday by Duke Energy, a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity per month would see the following increases: Duke Energy Carolinas (Charlotte, Durham, the Triad and much of western North Carolina): - January 2027: $6.53 more per month - January 2028: An additional $4.66 per month - Total monthly increase by 2028: $11.19 Duke Energy Progress (Raleigh, much of eastern North Carolina and the Asheville region): - January 2027: $9.62 more per month - January 2028: An additional $5.89 per month - Total monthly increase by 2028: $15.51 That amounts to approximately $134 to $186 in additional annual electricity costs by 2028 for a typical household, based on Duke's projections. Actual bill impacts will vary depending on electricity usage and other charges. Under the settlements, Duke would collect approximately $834 million in additional annual revenue across all customer classes by the second year of the rate plans. Regulators authorized a 9.8% return on equity for both utilities, down from Duke's initial request of 10.95%. That figure represents the authorized return on shareholder equity invested in the utility, not the percentage increase in customers' electricity bills. The rate plans include approximately $7.2 billion in capital investments over two years, along with a mechanism to refund customers for certain infrastructure projects that are delayed or canceled. Duke also agreed to contribute a combined $20 million in shareholder funds to support electricity bill assistance and home repairs that help low-income households access weatherization programs. Duke said it worked with customers and other stakeholders to reduce its initial rate increase requests while maintaining investments needed to strengthen the power grid and accommodate North Carolina's growth. “We listened to our customers and worked closely with stakeholders to find a more cost-effective way forward,” said Kendal Bowman, Duke Energy's North Carolina president, in a statement Tuesday. “This outcome keeps affordability at the forefront while allowing us to make the investments needed to strengthen reliability and support North Carolina's continued growth.” For some low-income customers, however, the financial impact could be significantly greater. A $42 monthly credit available to qualifying customers through Duke's Customer Assistance Program is scheduled to expire at the end of December, just as the new rates take effect. Brooks said some of the programs that Durham families have relied on for help with utility bills have lost funding. “I know I'm struggling, so I can imagine how the seniors are going to be struggling with a fixed income,” Brooks said. The commission directed Duke to submit revised revenue calculations within 10 days of its orders and updated rate schedules for approval within 30 days. New rules for data centers For the first time, regulators established a separate electricity rate schedule for large data centers with power demands of at least 50 megawatts. The decision comes as artificial intelligence and cloud computing drive unprecedented growth in electricity demand across the Carolinas. Between March 2024 and April 2026, Duke signed contracts to provide 6.7 gigawatts of electricity capacity to new large customers in North Carolina and South Carolina. Data centers account for 92% of that contracted demand, according to the commission. Meeting that demand will require billions of dollars in new power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure. Regulators found that Duke's existing and proposed billing structures did not adequately address the financial risks associated with that expansion. artigo.texto: Geral COP31 propõe controle de emissões de data centers O crescente impacto ambiental dos data centers entrou na mira de um novo pacto global lançado durante a COP31, em Antália, na Turquia. Batizado de Compromisso de Antália sobre Inteligência Artificial e articulado pela presidência turca junto à União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT) e à Unesco, o acordo, anunciado nesta terça-feira (17), busca frear a pegada ecológica da infraestrutura digital, exigindo maior eficiência energética e hídrica dos centros de processamento de dados. Articulado pela presidência turca em parceria com a União Internacional de Telecomunicações (UIT) e a Unesco, o acordo conta com a adesão do Brasil e incentiva o uso de energias limpas, a eficiência no consumo de água e energia, a economia circular e o descarte adequado de lixo eletrônico nos centros de processamento de dados. Embora tenha caráter voluntário e não estabeleça metas obrigatórias de corte de emissões, o pacto prevê acompanhamento anual nas conferências do clima até 2030. Além do Brasil, oito países aderiram ao pacto, incluindo Coreia do Sul e a gigante chinesa Alibaba. Entretanto, o acordo enfrenta dúvidas sobre seu alcance prático por não ter atraído as principais big techs dos Estados Unidos, maiores operadoras globais dessa infraestrutura. A iniciativa incentiva ainda o uso da própria IA para soluções climáticas, como previsão de eventos extremos, prevê apoio tecnológico a países em desenvolvimento e inclui medidas de proteção aos trabalhadores diante da automação — ponto alinhado a ações brasileiras como o programa Computadores para Inclusão e a proposta de sediar o Instituto de Inteligência Artificial para Mudanças Climáticas (AICI). Brasil é o 4º país a apresentar novo relatório de transparência do Acordo de Paris Também nesta terça-feira (17), o Brasil tornou-se a quarta nação do mundo a cumprir a etapa das regras de prestação de contas do Acordo de Paris. O principal destaque do levantamento é a queda de 27% nas emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa entre 2022 e 2024, resultado extraído da série histórica analisada desde 1990. Coordenado pelo Ministério da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação (MCTI) e aprovado pelo Comitê Interministerial sobre Mudança do Clima, o material integra dados científicos e resultados de políticas públicas em uma única publicação para dar mais agilidade aos processos. Além de detalhar o cumprimento das metas climáticas brasileiras, o relatório traz um diagnóstico sobre os riscos do aquecimento global e as estratégias de adaptação do país, reunindo também informações sobre educação ambiental, pesquisas científicas e as necessidades de financiamento e transferência de tecnologia. De acordo com a pasta, o documento, que foi submetido em inglês — idioma oficial da ONU —, terá em breve versão em português no portal do ministério e o conteúdo enviado passará pelo crivo de especialistas internacionais e por um fórum multilateral da convenção para revisão técnica. artigo.texto: Technology First Read An Electrician's Tale: Working on Data Center Projects Before Drawings Exist Mission critical schedules bring electrical contractors on before the design is close to construction ready, the first thing you contribute isn’t labor, but information. We get onboarded to data center projects that barely have drawings. Not bad drawings; no drawings at all. What exists may be early concepts or an intent somebody wrote down: we want a 300-MW facility, we think this area is going to be where the data halls are, these are the systems we’re thinking we’re going to leverage. No equipment spec. Architectural design isn’t figured out, either, so you can’t even start coordinating where things are going to go. And we’re on the project anyway. So, what are you contributing at that point? Not installation. Capacity, and people in the room. Where the Decisions Ultimately Get Made I think about in relation to the software development life cycle. A solution architect sits down with the customer and comes up with a grand idea. If all you do is hand that off to a developer, it’s really challenging for the developer to build it unless the documentation is phenomenal. A lot of these projects are at exactly that stage. You have an owner with high demands and a budget. You can’t just hand everything off to an engineer, and the engineer can’t just hand everything off to a contractor. There isn’t time for that. So, you bring everybody into the discussion upfront. That’s awareness of capacity. Awareness of lead times on material. Logistics. All the expertise a contractor can bring to steer a decision the right way — before the drawings get created, so those things don’t hit later. Because that’s what goes wrong on these jobs. Too many decisions get made without all the proper data or information that would have been valuable at the time, and they end up biting the project later. Get the stakeholders into the big-room discussions early and they can make what would have become an issue down the road nonexistent. Coordination Isn't a Project Phase Anymore Think about building a house. You don’t want the plumber and the tile guy scheduled in the bathroom at the same time. It’s sequenced. Put people on top of each other and you end up with more issues. Coordination used to run the same way: this group does their stuff in an area, then the next group gets that area, then the group after that. Installation still works that way. Coordination doesn’t. It’s moved to everybody getting all of their stuff in, coordinated together, in live models, and it all happens at the same time. You’re working the drawings side by side with the other groups, sharing continuous iterations of what can, should and shouldn’t be, and the answer keeps moving because the design is still moving. So being on the same platform, on the same file, is critical. You need the history tracked and the metadata attached, so you can see what changed and who changed it. That’s the piece a lot of tools in this space are thin on. We Moved This Off Paper 10 Years Ago About 10 years ago we recognized that field practice was printing out drawings and laying out the electrical scope with pens, paper and highlighters. That markup lived on that sheet. Drawing gets revised, you start over. So we moved that effort into the office, onto a digital platform — Bluebeam, in our case — and made it scalable. Drawing gets revised now, you slip sheet it and all your markups are retained. That became our single source of truth. The people doing it were field guys. We brought them into the office, and now they’re the pros at it. The Risk Lives in the Handoffs Follow the data through our process. It comes out of our building information modeling team. It hits the fab floor as a PDF: a sheet with the map of everything, and on the next page a 3D view they can spin without opening a model — Okay, this conduit’s on this side of the strut, it looked funny on the build sheet and here’s why. Then it goes to the crew receiving those assemblies in the field. At every one of those handoffs, somebody could be looking at the wrong version. We also just established a sister company focused on modular electrical construction. That makes all of this more critical, not less. The BIM team, the fab floor and the crew receiving the kit all have to be on the same set of files. Where it still falls short: our heavy use is on PC. When you want to hand a guy a set of drawings on a tablet and let him walk around, there isn’t a great solution yet that retains all the metadata. That’s a real gap. What the Technology is For Earlier this year I was at an AI and robotics conference, and the whole theme was the opposite of what people expect. It’s not replacing people. It’s the things humans can’t do, or shouldn’t do, for safety reasons. In our trade, think about energization: The gear is installed, commissioned, and now it’s getting turned on, and a human has to get into an insanely big suit that is hopefully going to protect their life. My safety director wouldn’t appreciate the word “hopefully,” but it’s a huge risk. Nobody wants to do that, and nobody should have to, if there are other options. Technology in construction should be the same idea. It should increase productivity or increase the availability of the right information. That second one is where this industry has had a lot of its issues — getting the right information to the point of installation when it’s needed. That’s where technology helps, if it’s done the right way. It Isn't One Thing People ask what I’d tell another electrical contractor before their first data center job, like there’s one thing. There isn’t. Is your local labor force ready for the scale of the project? Are you set up for modeling and prefab? because these jobs typically require it. Can your schedule hold? artigo.texto: Copel mira leilão de 2027 para transformar hidrelétricas em baterias Projetos em estudo somam 9,1 GW de potência; companhia defende disputa com baterias químicas nos mesmos certames A Copel (Companhia Paranaense de Energia) detalhou na 5ª feira (19.nov.2026), em Nova York, projetos de hidrelétricas reversíveis que somam aproximadamente 9,1 gigawatts de potência. A companhia pretende aproveitar a infraestrutura de suas usinas para armazenar energia e fornecê-la nos horários de maior demanda. Os planos foram apresentados durante o Copel Day, encontro com investidores realizado na Bolsa de Valores de Nova York, e em entrevista a jornalistas depois do evento. A empresa quer disputar um possível leilão de armazenamento no 2º semestre de 2027. Leia a apresentação da companhia (PDF – 9,6 MB). COMO FUNCIONA As hidrelétricas reversíveis funcionam como grandes baterias de água. Quando há excesso de geração, como nos períodos de elevada produção solar, o sistema usa eletricidade para bombear água de um reservatório inferior para outro situado em uma altitude maior. Quando a demanda aumenta, especialmente no início da noite, a água do reservatório superior é liberada para movimentar turbinas e gerar eletricidade. Há perdas nesse processo: o sistema consome mais energia no bombeamento do que devolve na geração. A companhia apresenta a tecnologia como alternativa para aproveitar excedentes de eletricidade e reduzir a necessidade de cortes de geração, conhecidos como curtailment. Essas restrições são determinadas pelo ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico). PROJETOS DA COPEL Segundo o vice-presidente de Estratégia, Novos Negócios e Transformação Digital da Copel, Diogo Mac Cord, a prioridade são projetos que aproveitem a infraestrutura das hidrelétricas existentes. A companhia estuda 3 configurações: - circuito semiaberto – reúne cerca de 6,6 GW dos projetos. Combina um reservatório conectado a um curso d’água com outro isolado, geralmente artificial; - circuito aberto – inclui 2 projetos, nas usinas Foz do Areia e Segredo. Os reservatórios são conectados a cursos d’água naturais; - circuito fechado – contempla um projeto piloto de 200 MW, com reservatórios isolados dos cursos d’água naturais. “São vários tipos de projeto. A gente tem 3 tipos de projeto: aberto, semiaberto e fechado. O que a gente acredita mais são os projetos semiabertos”, afirmou durante conversa com jornalistas depois do Investor Day da Copel. Nos projetos semiabertos, o reservatório de uma hidrelétrica existente pode ser aproveitado como parte do sistema. A empresa busca, assim, reduzir os custos e as dificuldades de implantação em comparação com empreendimentos construídos integralmente do zero. “Então a gente está falando em projetos sempre como sendo novas casas de força em usinas existentes”, declarou Mac Cord. Segundo o executivo, o projeto mais avançado é o de uma nova casa de força reversível na usina de Segredo, no Paraná, com potência estimada em 2,2 GW. A companhia já solicitou à Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) a aprovação do projeto básico. LEILÃO E INVESTIMENTOS A Copel trabalha com a expectativa de contratação de hidrelétricas reversíveis no 2º semestre de 2027. O cronograma estimado do Ministério de Minas e Energia inclui sistemas de armazenamento hidráulico nos leilões de reserva de capacidade de 2027 a 2029. O formato da contratação e as condições do eventual certame ainda precisam ser definidos. Caso consiga contratar seus projetos, a empresa estima aproximadamente 5 anos para construir as instalações. Os valores necessários para executar os empreendimentos não foram divulgados. Segundo os executivos, esses investimentos seriam adicionais ao plano de R$ 21,1 bilhões para o período de 2027 a 2030, anunciado na 5ª feira (19.nov). DISPUTA COM BATERIAS A companhia defende leilões em que diferentes tecnologias de armazenamento possam competir, com critérios que considerem suas características operacionais. “A nossa defesa é que seja um leilão agnóstico com todas as fontes”, afirmou o presidente da Copel, Daniel Slaviero. Segundo a empresa, as reversíveis podem ter autonomia de 15 a 20 horas de geração. A companhia argumenta que essa duração permite aproveitar grandes excedentes de eletricidade acumulados durante os fins de semana. Mac Cord considera as reversíveis e as baterias químicas complementares. Na avaliação do executivo, as usinas podem oferecer vantagens em aplicações que exigem armazenamento de grandes volumes de energia por períodos mais longos. O jornalista viajou a Nova York a convite da Copel.

artigo.texto: Resumo - Data centers nos EUA oferecem vagas com salários acima de US$ 100 mil por ano - Faltam técnicos para refrigeração, racks, parte elétrica e fibra óptica - Treinamentos de dois dias já terminam com cerimônia de diploma - Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft oferecem cursos gratuitos e acelerados - Falta de mão de obra supera qualquer freio na construção civil do setor - Muitos americanos nem sabem que esses empregos existem Nos Estados Unidos, a construção da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial criou um gargalo inesperado: faltam técnicos. Na disputa por profissionais, empresas de tecnologia já oferecem vagas com remuneração acima de US$ 100 mil por ano. E parte dessas contratações recai sobre pessoas que acabaram de concluir cursos relâmpago. A trajetória pode ser rápida: bastam dois dias de formação para que os alunos recebam seus diplomas numa solenidade. Mal o certificado fica pronto e as companhias, sedentas por mão de obra, já brigam pelos novos profissionais. Por que faltam técnicos Para dar conta da demanda disparada pela tecnologia, as companhias precisam de gente capaz de montar os sistemas de refrigeração, instalar racks de servidores, lidar com equipamentos elétricos e puxar os cabos de fibra óptica que sustentam os data centers. O problema é que encontrar profissionais com essas habilidades virou um desafio. Ainda que o ambiente político em torno da IA venha se transformando, sobretudo após as últimas eleições de meio de mandato, a falta de trabalhadores pesa mais do que qualquer eventual desaceleração nas obras. Diante disso, o setor vem se organizando para formar e contratar quem possa preencher essas vagas. Cursos gratuitos e salários de seis dígitos Diferentes origens respondem pela qualificação desses trabalhadores. Para capacitar nas habilidades técnicas que a edificação de data centers requer, cursos rápidos e sem custo são oferecidos por entidades sem fins lucrativos, por plataformas de ensino digital e pelas quatro gigantes da nuvem com inteligência artificial: Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft. Há posições nesse setor cuja remuneração chega à casa dos seis dígitos. Mesmo assim, a maioria dos americanos nem imagina que empregos assim estejam disponíveis. Javonntae Hill é um exemplo de quem entrou nesse universo. Formado em design de videogames e na casa dos 30 anos, ele procurava uma carreira, mas não tinha clareza de por onde começar.

artigo.texto: Ford has started producing lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for its Fathom electric pickup truck at a Michigan plant. InsideEVs reported on Nov. 18, local time, that Ford has begun manufacturing mass-production-grade LFP battery packs at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall, Michigan, a few hours west of Detroit. The batteries produced this time will first be installed in Fathom prototypes. Full-scale mass production is expected to begin next year. For Ford, it marked a turning point in bringing the battery supply chain into the United States alongside development of a new electric pickup. The plant was presented as the first case in the United States of local production of LFP batteries used in vehicles for mass-market consumers. LG Energy Solution also produces LFP batteries in the United States, but its supply is for stationary energy storage systems for GM and Tesla. Ford’s 2 million-square-foot facility is dedicated to automotive LFP batteries. Production capacity was also spelled out. Annual capacity is 20 gigawatt-hours, and the plant can make 50 battery packs per hour. It has a vertically integrated structure in which finished battery packs come out after lithium and iron phosphate powder are fed in. Key processes, including production of anode and cathode materials, are carried out inside the plant. Ford sees the plant as a core facility directly tied to the Fathom launch schedule. Allan Clarke (앨런 클라크), vice president of Ford Advanced Development Projects, said at a media briefing, "Ford is moving quickly to launch the Fathom." He said Ford built a new universal EV platform, a new production system at the Louisville assembly plant and a U.S. LFP battery production system in a short period. He said building a battery plant, a unicastings plant and a highly automated vehicle production facility in less than five years is faster than the pace in China. A licensing deal with China’s CATL underpins the plant’s technology. Ford established the production system by adopting CATL’s battery technology. Ford owns and operates the plant, while CATL engineers supported setup of complex production equipment, worker training and establishment of a quality-control system. Ford explained that the prismatic LFP cells for the Fathom are Ford-specific specifications, not CATL’s existing global product lineup. Ford said the plant also meets requirements under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). It said raw materials used for battery production are not sourced from entities designated by the U.S. government as a foreign entity of concern. It said that while the technology came from CATL, the core materials are structured not to rely on sources of concern to the United States such as China, Russia and North Korea. Meng Wang (멍 왕), head of battery cell industrialisation and chief engineer at Ford, said of the background to cooperation with CATL, "To reduce time to market, we decided to learn from a top-tier partner." He added that CATL transferred key knowledge to Ford, including equipment functions, manufacturing processes and quality control. A future timeline was also laid out. Fathom preorders will begin in early 2027, and production and deliveries are expected to begin by the end of next year. Ford will therefore put to the test both commercialisation of an electric pickup backed by lower-cost batteries and localisation of battery production in the United States.

artigo.texto: Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today! The 2026 midterms didn’t only swell the ranks of progressives and green economic populists in Congress — they also ushered in a stunning number of Native American leaders in down-ballot races across the country. Among the state legislative races involving Indigenous candidates that have been called so far, Native American candidates won 83 percent of the time, according to ICT. Montana led the way: 12 of 13 Indigenous candidates there, all Democrats, won legislative seats, including Natalie Weeks-O’Neal (Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux) in House District 31 and Katie Fire Thunder (Oglala Lakota) in House District 59. In Nevada, Brian Wadsworth, a former Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribal Council member, won a seat on the Washoe County Commission representing the county’s rural north, becoming the first tribal member from any of the county’s tribal nations to serve on it, Wadsworth told Truthout. Native Republicans won too, including Emily McIntire (Muscogee) in Oregon and Heather Ellison (Navajo) in New Mexico. In Alaska, Mary Peltola defeated the incumbent to became the first Native person to represent the state in the U.S. Senate. Many of these candidates spoke to voters’ concerns on the campaign trail about the affordability of groceries and health care. In Northern Nevada, voters also raised concerns about water, land, and unchecked growth. And the offices these candidates won are increasingly in locales where fights over land, water, and AI data centers get decided, as the federal government weakens its obligation to consult tribes. “We have about 120 proposed hyperscale data centers for Indian Country,” said Krystal Two Bulls, executive director of environmental advocacy group Honor the Earth. Locally, “these fights are currently being fought and won,” Two Bulls told Truthout. A U.S. Senate permitting bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, despite its name, focuses on narrowing environmental review processes and threatens tribal consultation on projects affecting tribal water, land, and cultural sites. “That’s pretty much going to gut any kind of protections or legs that tribes can stand on to push back against these corporations,” said Two Bulls. The bill passed a preliminary vote on November 9 but has yet to clear the next hurdle in the Senate. National wins among Native politicians could augur change at the state level, especially in states with multiple Indigenous candidate victories. Montana’s wins were historic: “It’s not lost on us that we’re making history, being the largest American Indian caucus in the United States at the state level,” said Weeks-O’Neal, adding that the state’s main media has yet to cover this fact. Two Bulls expressed hope that the Indigenous bloc will be able to exert real leverage, saying: “They can actually throw a lot of wrenches into the fast tracking that’s currently happening.” Despite Two Bulls’ forward-looking ambitions for the new class of Native politicians, especially around AI, Weeks-O’Neal faces extant costs to her district: The Zortman mines, which extracted gold from the Little Rocky Mountains in the 1980s and ’90s, contaminated Montana’s water and still cost $3 million a year to treat. “The water is devastated. It is tainted in perpetuity. That means forever,” she said. “Whatever profit was made from the mine, I mean, I can’t imagine.” The site has been re-listed for $52.5 million with geologists estimating “that only 20% of the gold and silver [was] harvested, leaving plenty of reserves for investors or operators,” the listing states. House District 31 includes much of the Fort Peck Reservation, whose median age is 30 and median household income is roughly $53,000, far below the national median of around $87,000. It’s no surprise then that voters’ primary concern is affordability, especially groceries. “They were struggling to even feed their families,” said Weeks-O’Neal. Trump’s administration has moved to slash the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which could cut off access for 6.3 million people nationally. Meanwhile Katie Fire Thunder’s constituents in South Bozeman, which is one of the wealthiest areas in the state, are also worried about affordability: Rising property taxes, driven by soaring land values, are creating a crisis for retirees on fixed incomes who are being priced out of homes they’d expected to keep for life. “That tax burden is being shifted on to residential and property owners,” she said, joining the call alongside Weeks-O’Neal. Rep. Thedis Crowe (Blackfeet), reelected in House District 15, which borders Canada and includes part of the Blackfeet Reservation, said protecting the water compacts negotiated by the Blackfeet Nation and the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes is a top priority, because both are “headwaters tribes.” He said data center bills expected in the coming session will force lawmakers to weigh impacts on rural and tribal communities, and on water quality. Weeks-O’Neal said too many of those decisions in Montana have been left to counties, which she said “is just way too much power given to county entities,” and that it was part of why she ran for the Montana House of Representatives. In northern Nevada, that county power is exactly what Brian Wadsworth just won. Wadsworth lives in Nixon, on the Pyramid Lake Paiute Reservation, about an hour from Reno. Rush-hour traffic along I-80 by the area’s industrial center was once quite rare, he said. Now, “it’s literally a daily occurrence,” something “that we haven’t seen in our lifetimes.” Wadsworth told Truthout that voters are fed up with unchecked growth and have been asking cities to examine the area’s economic growth and really grapple with infrastructure issues. “We definitely have a lack of adequate roads here in Washoe County,” said Wadsworth. artigo.texto: The San Joaquin County Board of Supervisors has extended its moratorium on the development of hyperscale data centers in the unincorporated County for an additional 10 months and 15 days. The move allows time for a comprehensive review of potential environmental and economic consequences and opportunities for community input. “We owe our residents answers before allowing development that could have negative consequences for our environment and economy,” said Chair and Third District Supervisor Sonny Dhaliwal. “This extension gives us the time needed to thoroughly evaluate the potential effects of these large-scale facilities and ensure that any future decisions reflect the best interests of our communities.” Traditional data centers store, manage, and process digital information, while artificial intelligence (AI) data centers are designed to support the intensive computing demands of developing and operating AI systems. These facilities can require substantial electricity, water, and infrastructure resources, raising important questions about their long-term effects on surrounding communities. Last month, the Board adopted an interim urgency ordinance establishing a temporary moratorium and directed the Community Development Department (CDD) to conduct an initial 10-day review of AI data centers. Following that review, CDD presented its preliminary findings and recommended extending the moratorium to allow for a more comprehensive evaluation. During the extension, CDD will examine the experiences of other jurisdictions, conduct community outreach with stakeholders, assess potential demands on local resources, and explore regulatory options. The department will also work with a consultant to prepare a more detailed analysis to help guide future policy decisions. “We simply don’t have enough information to make an informed decision on something that could have lasting consequences for our community,” said CDD Director Jennifer Jolley. CDD is expected to present its comprehensive report to the Board in June 2027.

artigo.texto: Monticello data center proposal leaves homeowner, buyer facing big losses MONTICELLO, Minn. (FOX 9) - A proposed hyperscale data center in Monticello has one homeowner ready to leave and another buyer starting over. Homeowner says proposed project changed everything What we know: Kathy Cohen said she moved into her Monticello house in February, not long after her husband died, so she could be closer to her grandchildren after moving from Hopkins. She said she did not know that a proposed 3 million-square-foot hyperscale data center was planned blocks away and said her realtor never brought it up. "It never even occurred to me that they would have this in the works, or I would’ve never bought this house," she said. Cohen said possible future construction would be too disruptive, and she said she also worries about the environmental impact. She said she has been told she could lose as much as $50,000 if she sells, but she still plans to move. Cohen also said she plans to disclose the project to prospective buyers when she lists the house. Buyer says backing out could cost $30,000 What they're saying: Rebecca Webeck said she and her two sons recently signed a purchase agreement for a brand-new house in Monticello. But after they learned it was near the proposed data center site, they pulled out of the sale and now expect to lose as much as $30,000. "With me being disabled and my boys helping with my medical stuff, it took us a while to get to this point, and so it’s devastating for us to have to completely start over again and lose all that money," she said. Webeck also said her realtor never said anything about the proposed project. She said the experience will make her ask much more directly about data centers in future home searches. Attorney says disclosure rules are limited What's the law: Rob Shainess, an Edina-based real estate attorney, said there is no law that specifically requires realtors to tell buyers about proposed data center projects. But he said state law does require them to share anything they know that could adversely affect a buyer’s use and enjoyment of a home. That leaves key questions about whether either realtor knew about the proposal and whether they knew it would negatively impact the property. Shainess said buyers probably do not have any legal recourse because proposed projects are not final and "any impact on the property is amorphous and only potential." The Source: FOX 9's Mike Manzoni interviewed Kathy Cohen and Rebecca Webeck and spoke with a real estate attorney.

artigo.texto: Advanced graphene architectures have demonstrated an enhancement of 30 to 50 percent in energy storage performance compared to conventional electrode materials, addressing long-standing limitations in device capacity, charge kinetics, and operational longevity. In an extensive technical review published in the Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Energy, researchers Jahanvi Thakur and Shreya systematically evaluated the synthesis methodologies, intrinsic physical characteristics, and device implementations of graphene-based materials. The investigation encompasses electrochemical storage platforms including supercapacitors, lithium-ion batteries, sodium-ion batteries, and solid-state systems. Conventional energy technologies frequently encounter severe engineering trade-offs, such as limited energy densities, slow charge and discharge rates, restricted cycle lives, and material degradation caused by mechanical stress during prolonged cycling. Graphene, structured as an atomically thin two-dimensional honeycomb sheet of carbon atoms, provides a versatile physical foundation capable of mitigating these technical bottlenecks across multiple commercial and industrial sectors. The extraordinary baseline physical characteristics of graphene provide the foundational rationale for its electrochemical efficacy across diverse energy conversion and storage platforms. Monolayer graphene possesses a theoretical specific surface area of approximately 2630 square meters per gram, establishing an expansive interface for electrostatic charge accumulation and active electrochemical species interaction. In terms of electronic transport, the delocalization of pi-electrons across the hexagonal carbon lattice facilitates ballistic carrier movement, yielding electrical conductivities as high as 10 to the sixth power Siemens per meter, which exceeds that of metallic copper by more than a factor of one hundred. Graphene also displays an exceptional thermal conductivity of approximately 5000 Watts per meter-Kelvin, allowing devices to dissipate high thermal fluxes generated during intense charge and discharge cycles, alongside a thermal stability that resists degradation at temperatures exceeding 3000 degrees Celsius in inert environments. Mechanically, graphene exhibits a tensile strength reaching 130 gigapascals and an elastic strain tolerance of 20 percent, ensuring robust mechanical resilience against the destructive stresses that typically accompany repeated electrochemical cycling. Synthesis methodologies strongly dictate the structural integrity, sheet morphology, defect distribution, and final electrochemical capabilities of graphene-derived materials. Chemical vapor deposition stands as the premier fabrication route for growing continuous, large-area monolayer and bilayer graphene films characterized by high crystalline order and minimal defect concentrations. Operative at temperatures between 800 and 1000 degrees Celsius, chemical vapor deposition decomposes carbon-bearing precursors such as methane, ethylene, or acetylene over catalytic transition metal substrates, notably copper and nickel foils. The resulting films achieve sheet resistances as low as 20 ohms per square, electrical conductivities between 10 to the fifth and 10 to the sixth Siemens per meter, and Raman intensity ratios of the defect-induced D-band to the graphitic G-band below 0.1. However, the requirement for high thermal budgets, specialized catalyst substrates, and delicate post-growth metal etching processes introduces mechanical defects that complicate cost-effective, large-scale industrial device manufacturing. To overcome throughput limitations inherent to vapor deposition, wet-chemical, mechanical, and thermal exfoliation techniques provide scalable pathways for bulk graphene manufacturing. The chemical reduction of graphene oxide derived through modified Hummers oxidation of graphite remains one of the most accessible approaches, producing functionalized reduced graphene oxide flakes. This route relies on reducing agents such as hydrazine, sodium borohydride, or ascorbic acid to restore conjugated carbon networks, though incomplete reduction often leaves residual oxygen-containing functionalities that modulate electrical conductivity. Complementary hydrothermal and solvothermal approaches treat graphene oxide dispersions in sealed autoclaves at temperatures between 150 and 250 degrees Celsius, where reactive organic solvents provide elevated reduction degrees, yielding highly conductive powders suitable for ink formulation and composite manufacturing. The transition toward environmentally sustainable manufacturing has motivated the development of biomass-derived graphene and green synthesis protocols utilizing agricultural waste and organic residues. Thermal processing routes, including high-temperature pyrolysis in inert atmospheres and hydrothermal carbonization in aqueous media, successfully convert forestry and agricultural wastes into functional carbon structures. Quantitatively, biomass-derived graphene materials exhibit electrical conductivities ranging from 10 to the second to 10 to the fourth Siemens per meter, specific surface areas spanning 500 to 1800 square meters per gram, and Raman defect ratios between 0.8 and 1.3. Although these values reflect greater disorder than pristine chemical vapor deposition films, the resultant hierarchical porosity, structural vacancies, and heteroatom sites accelerate ionic diffusion pathways and generate additional electrochemically active charge storage centers. Sustainable synthesis strategies also incorporate the direct electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide and the utilization of biodegradable solvents, establishing circular production paradigms that reduce reliance on toxic reagents. artigo.texto: New Delhi/Mumbai: The Maharashtra Government on Tuesday announced the country's first sulphur dioxide (SO2) emissions trading scheme to improve air quality. The scheme will be implemented by the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB) in collaboration with Emissions Market Accelerator, Environment and Climate Change Minister Pankaja Munde said. Speaking at an event in Mumbai, Munde said the government wanted to develop, in collaboration with industries, solutions that balance environmental protection with economic development. Under the emissions trading scheme, participating industrial units will be given permits specifying their permissible sulphur dioxide emissions. Industries that can reduce emissions at a lower cost will be able to make additional reductions and sell their surplus permits, while those facing higher costs of emission reduction can purchase them, an official release said. Michael Greenstone, professor of economics at the University of Chicago, director of the Energy Policy Institute and co-chair of Emissions Market Accelerator, said research had shown that market-based schemes could achieve effective emission reductions while lowering the cost of pollution control for industries. The MPCB and the University of Chicago Trust also signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to use artificial intelligence and machine learning in environmental regulation and industrial inspections. The initiative will be implemented through the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago India. Under the agreement, the two institutions will jointly develop and pilot an AI-based framework for environmental inspections. The system will analyse data available with the MPCB to identify industrial units that are more likely to violate environmental regulations, the release said. Training programmes will also be organised for MPCB officials and field inspectors on AI, environmental data analysis and the use of modern technologies. A decision on expanding the system across Maharashtra will be taken based on the findings of the pilot project.
