artigo.texto: - Salt Lake City paused new data centers for six months to review regulations. - The City Council voted unanimously, addressing concerns over a proposed Northpoint project. - Mayor Mendenhall supported the pause to reassess zoning and environmental impacts. SALT LAKE CITY — Utah's capital city quickly pushed through a new ordinance pausing all new data centers within city limits for up to six months so it can better review a proposed project on its west side. The Salt Lake City Council voted unanimously on Tuesday to approve the measure after quickly adding it to its agenda this week. It essentially creates a moratorium on new data centers, allowing the city and potentially the state to adopt new data center regulations. "While policy would be the best protection for everyone in the long term — and I will advocate for that at any level of government — I'm also going to use any amount of soft power I have to influence whoever can make a decision to back off plans that can hurt people or the land out there," Salt Lake City Councilwoman Victoria Petro told KSL before the vote. The measure popped up on the City Council this week in an apparent response to a proposed data center that recently made headlines. A San Francisco-based architect filed a commercial building permit with the city for a one-story data center in June. Little else is known about the project, which would be located at 2258 W. 2950 North in Salt Lake City's Northpoint neighborhood. Qlevr LLC, a Florida-based digital infrastructure company, then applied for an air quality permit at the same site with the Utah Division of Air Quality on Sept. 30. That, too, only provided vague details, only saying it would run on grid power with fuel storage tanks and diesel-fired emergency generators. "That particular development is a thorn in my side," said Petro, whose district covers the Northpoint area. She explained that the development flew under the city leadership's radar until recently, and the developer hasn't provided much readily available information. The location is particularly vexing for her and the city. Salt Lake City recently completed a new plan for the Northpoint area to map out developments within the city's final rural edge. That came as residents pleaded with the city to help stop massive warehouses that wreaked havoc on them. It would potentially create a new challenge with noise and environmental concerns. "This is just heaping trauma upon trauma on one community," she said, adding that many residents aren't anti-data center but against the impacts they can have without any type of regulation. What the city voted on Tuesday follows a similar moratorium that Salt Lake County leaders approved in September, but that measure only applied to unincorporated land within the county, not Northpoint. It's also similar to a six-month pause the city approved in March to cap nonresidential water to 200,000 gallons per day. What started as a temporary measure to potentially thwart an immigration detention center on the west side ended up in a permanent ordinance approved in September. The new pause would give the city time to craft a new policy to address data centers, as the concerns over them mount. It would also carry through mid-May, potentially allowing the state to craft new data center policies that could go into effect by the time Tuesday's order expires. State leaders suggested making improvements to data center policy earlier this month after it seemed to be one of the key local issues during this year's election cycle. It's a "healthy pause" for the city, Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall said earlier on Tuesday, asserting that the city's technology plans and zoning never considered data centers at the scale that has been proposed in recent years. Many vary in how they use water, which is something the city is very interested in, so she believes it makes sense to review new centers before approving them. "I think it's appropriate for our city and any other city that does land use to reconsider and take a hard look at zoning that's out there so that we can make sure what happens here is reflective of our capacity," she said.

artigo.texto: How GPUs Are Changing the Colocation vs. Private Data Center Debate GPUs are shifting the colo vs. private data center decision toward power, speed, utilization, and sustainability – not just location, scale, and cost. Traditionally, the main factors in deciding between colocation and a private data center were relatively straightforward: location, the scale of the infrastructure to be deployed, and future growth plans. By weighing those considerations, businesses could determine whether it made more logistical and financial sense to lease colocation space or invest in a data center of their own. In an era when GPUs have become a common component of data center infrastructure, however, the colocation-versus-private-data-center calculus has changed in important ways. Traditional considerations still matter, but organizations must now also account for factors that are unique to GPU-equipped environments. Here’s a look at how GPUs are reshaping the colocation decision, along with guidance on when colocation or a private data center may be the better fit. How GPUs Reshape the Colocation Decision GPUs, especially the high-performance accelerators used to support AI workloads, introduce several challenges that traditional data center infrastructure does not. One is power density. Historically, a typical data center rack consumed no more than about 10 kW. GPU-enabled servers can push that figure dramatically higher, often by a factor of 10. That shift creates demands around power delivery, cooling, energy sourcing, and utility interconnection timelines. Another is cost. GPU-equipped servers are significantly more expensive than standard servers, which makes utilization rates much more important from an ROI perspective. Idle or underused GPUs are costly assets. Speed to deployment is also a major factor. Many organizations pursuing AI training or inference initiatives are working on aggressive timelines. They cannot afford to wait years for a new facility to be built, commissioned, and connected to sufficient power. These are not the only considerations. Traditional factors such as total CapEx and OpEx, geographic requirements, and long-term capacity planning still matter. But in many cases, the power, cost, and deployment realities associated with GPUs outweigh the older decision framework, forcing businesses to reassess how they weigh colocation versus private infrastructure. How to Choose Between Colocation and Private Infrastructure for GPUs The right answer depends on several key questions. How Many GPUs Does the Business Need? The scale of GPU deployment matters. If only a small share of the organization’s infrastructure will require GPUs, GPU-specific concerns may not drive the overall decision. For example, if only 10% of planned servers will include GPUs, the choice between colocation and a private data center may still hinge primarily on broader considerations such as cost structure, location, and expansion capacity. If GPUs will make up a substantial portion of the environment, however, their power and cooling requirements become central to the decision. What Are the Business’s GPU Use Cases? How the organization plans to use GPUs is critical. For workloads such as AI model training, where GPU demand may be bursty rather than constant, colocation can make more financial sense. It may be more cost-effective to deploy in a facility already equipped for high-density infrastructure than to invest in a GPU-ready private data center that will sit idle for long stretches. By contrast, a private data center may prove more economical over time for organizations running GPU-intensive workloads continuously, such as large-scale AI inference. In those cases, the higher upfront capital investment can translate into lower long-term operating costs, especially if the organization can secure power more cheaply than a colocation provider, which may build a markup into power pricing. How Long Will It Take to Source Power for a New Data Center? If speed is a priority, colocation is usually the faster route. Building a new private data center can take years, especially if permitting delays emerge. Even after construction is complete, obtaining enough utility power to support a dense GPU deployment can take considerable time. In many markets, grid interconnection timelines have become a major constraint. Colocation providers, by contrast, may already have the power capacity, cooling systems, and operational readiness needed to bring GPU infrastructure online much sooner. How Important Is Energy Sustainability? Because GPUs consume far more power than conventional infrastructure, they also raise the stakes around sustainability. Colocation can offer an easier path to renewable energy, at least in the near term. Many providers already operate facilities backed by renewable energy contracts, low-carbon power mixes, or offsets. Achieving the same result in a private data center can be difficult, particularly in regions where renewable energy is limited or where building on-site generation is financially or logistically impractical. For organizations with aggressive sustainability targets, the difference may significantly influence the decision. Why GPUs Change More than Capacity Planning GPUs have not eliminated the traditional considerations involved in choosing between colocation and a private data center, but they have shifted the relative importance of these options. Power availability, deployment speed, utilization rates, and sustainability now play a much larger role in infrastructure strategy than they did in the past. The key is to evaluate not just how much infrastructure a business needs, but how GPU-driven workloads change the cost, timing, and operational realities behind that infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Converting renewable agricultural byproducts into silicon-bearing anodes for lithium-ion batteries requires balancing pore preservation, irreversible lithium inventory consumption, and intensive processing resources, according to a mini review published in Frontiers in Chemistry. Researchers Shuxin Yan, Qinglian Wang, and Hongwei Wei evaluated current chemical, physical, biological, and thermal pretreatment routes designed to prepare biomass-derived carbon hosts and silicon composites. Their synthesis indicates that simply boosting host porosity or raising silicon loading does not reliably guarantee superior practical electrode durability. Excessive reactive surface area, pore occlusion by subsequent coatings, and diminished electrode packing density frequently negate nominal gravimetric capacity improvements, highlighting structural and chemical trade-offs inherent to biomass anode fabrication. Silicon provides an attractive alternative to conventional graphite due to its high theoretical lithium storage capacity, yet its implementation is severely hindered by substantial volume expansion during lithiation and delithiation cycles. This severe mechanical deformation fractures active particles, disrupts critical electrical conduction pathways, and repeatedly exposes fresh silicon surfaces to liquid electrolytes, accelerating capacity fading. Introducing conductive carbon matrices and protective interfacial coatings mitigates particle pulverization, but enhanced gravimetric capacity at the isolated material level does not inherently yield elevated energy densities inside fully assembled battery cells. Natural biomass offers an accessible source of porous carbon frameworks and transport channels, while silica-rich feedstocks such as rice husks provide inherent silicon precursors that can be integrated or chemically reduced. The sequence and severity of feedstock pretreatments dictate both mineral retention and final organic structure. Common unit operations, including hot-water washing, mechanical milling, chemical leaching, biological digestion, and thermal carbonization, fundamentally alter mineral distribution, pore accessibility, overall carbon yield, and surface reactivity. In feedstocks such as rice husk, inherent biological silica architectures can be preserved to support reversible lithium insertion, decoupling the process from blending synthetic carbon with commercial nanosilicon. However, retaining unreduced silicon oxides introduces significant electrochemically active oxygen phases that react irreversibly with lithium during the initial charging cycle, permanently depleting cyclable lithium ions from the cell system. Managing internal void geometry remains essential because protective pores created during early processing can easily be compromised during subsequent composite synthesis and electrode manufacturing. While micropores under two nanometers substantially elevate interfacial surface area and accelerate initial electrolyte decomposition, mesopores spanning two to fifty nanometers host active silicon but remain vulnerable to entrance blockage during chemical vapor deposition or protective carbon coating. Larger macropores exceeding fifty nanometers provide mechanical buffer space for silicon volume expansion, yet their presence drastically decreases electrode volumetric tap density. Prior synthetic benchmarks, including yolk-shell and pomegranate-like configurations, illustrate the necessity of maintaining internal void space beneath outer carbon boundaries, but translating these physical principles into naturally irregular biomass architectures requires rigorous stage-by-stage structural verification. Experimental examinations across distinct agricultural sources demonstrate that natural porosity requires deliberate modification and careful tracking. In investigations utilizing bamboo leaves, sequential acid leaching, magnesiothermic reduction, and hydrofluoric acid etching yielded macroporous silicon coated with a thin conductive carbon layer. Although gas-adsorption measurements recorded specific surface area shifts from 204 square meters per gram down to 86 square meters per gram alongside stable half-cell cycling, the microscopy alone did not quantify the precise internal volume remaining after final electrode calendering. Similarly, when depositing silicon from silane gas onto biomass-derived hard carbon, high deposition densities risk sealing outer pore entrances, restricting mechanical expansion buffering and hindering electrolyte transport regardless of total measured silicon content. Chemical and physical processing techniques also introduce stark operational compromises regarding energy efficiency and reagent consumption. Molten-salt reduction routes using calcium hydride and aluminum chloride convert raw rice husks into structured core-shell silicon-carbon composites, whereas leaching combined with electrodeposition isolates silicon nanowires alongside porous carbon. Although both pathways circumvent basic direct carbonization, they incur extensive chemical washing, neutralization, and salt recovery burdens. Conversely, physical methods involving extended mechanical agitation, such as sequential rocking milling and ball milling of washed rice husk, disperse silica agglomerates down to uniform sub-micron distributions and enhance first-cycle delithiation capacity from 329 to 421 milliampere-hours per gram, yet milling demands substantial mechanical energy and leaves substantial irreversible first-cycle capacity losses. Alternative preparation routes employing biological treatments or rapid thermal processing highlight further divergences between material properties and energetic requirements. Fermentation-assisted digestion and enzyme treatments selectively dissolve specific organic fractions, such as starches or non-cellulosic fibers, to open internal diffusion pathways under ambient temperatures, but these biological steps require extended processing duration

artigo.texto: SEATTLE, Wash. — A bill moving quickly through U.S. Congress would bring permitting reform for energy and data center projects, while also rescinding input from tribal nations and walking back environmental protections. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), sponsored by four bipartisan senators, was introduced on Sept. 30, but was never heard or read in committee hearings where stakeholders typically give feedback. Instead, it went straight to the Senate floor for a procedural vote Tuesday. Washington Senator Maria Cantwell said she didn’t get the bill until Sunday night. “This process has been one in which we didn’t have hearings, didn’t have a markup, [and] basically came to the Senate floor without much notice and debate,” Cantwell said. “Right at the aftermath of an election, and, so, I just feel like it hasn’t gotten the attention that it deserves.” The bill would reform the permitting process for projects related to the electricity grid to accommodate an increasing load of electricity. The goal is to speed up approval for energy projects to develop renewable energies like solar and wind, as well as traditional oil, gas, and coal projects. It does this by limiting the scope of several review processes designed to protect environments, endangered species, and sensitive historical sites. “While Washington Wild supports infrastructure for energy transmission and future solutions, bedrock environmental laws and tribal consultation should not be held hostage to do so.” Washington Wild executive director Tom Uniack said. BAAJA would prioritize ensuring the certainty of a project moving forward, rather than revisit legal, analytical, or clarity errors in the original permit, making them difficult for future administrations to reverse course. It would limit the Endangered Species Act (ESA) by changing the definition of “best available science” that ensured agencies and developers must prioritize protection of endangered species. It also requires states to take on the review project to ensure federal projects meet ESA standards, something the organization Earth Justice says few states, if any, have the resources to do. “This is really concerning, because it is legislation and there’s a finality to that, if they make the wrong choice,” Uniack said. BAAJA also changes the National Environmental Review Act processes by altering the best available science requirement and exempting many projects from the review completely. It changes the Clean Water Act by doubling the length of water pollution permits, limiting state and tribes’ ability to protect waters in its jurisdiction, and makes it easier for developers to fill in wetlands -- regardless of flooding or wildlife concerns. “I’m for building transmission, but last I checked, that was not the problems with transmission. It wasn’t because, oh my god, we had to run over the Clean Water Act, because we couldn’t get transmission,” Cantwell said. The bill aims to lower electricity costs by requiring data centers to pay for electricity and projects that require increasing electrical capacity, and, with shorter review periods, lowering the cost of projects. Sovereign Indigenous Tribes are speaking out, because both the National Environmental Policy Act process and the National Historic Preservation Acts have ensured a seat at the table for feedback and consultation on projects that directly or indirectly impact tribal nations. “My people have already paid far too much for this country’s energy development,” Yakama Nation tribal councilmember John Washines said. “We should not be asked to sacrifice our salmon and our treaty rights yet again.” ©2026 Cox Media Group

artigo.texto: Tarifa Hora Certa coloca as baterias em foco Proposta da ANEEL prevê preços diferentes ao longo do dia e enquadramento obrigatório para novos pedidos de conexão de energia solar. Entenda o papel do armazenamento inteligente. A forma de pagar pela energia elétrica poderá mudar nos próximos anos. Em 9 de novembro de 2026, a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL) apresentou a proposta da Tarifa Hora Certa, que prevê valores diferentes para o kWh conforme o horário de consumo. Para quem tem ou pretende instalar energia solar, a mudança reforça a importância de um projeto que considere não apenas quanto se produz, mas também quando a energia é consumida. É nesse contexto que as baterias e a inteligência artificial ganham espaço. Como funcionará a Tarifa Hora Certa? A proposta divide o dia em três períodos: - Ponta: três horas consecutivas, geralmente no início da noite, com a tarifa mais alta. - Intermediário: normalmente uma hora antes e uma depois da ponta, com preço intermediário. - Fora de ponta: demais horários, com a tarifa mais baixa. Aos sábados, domingos e feriados nacionais, vale durante todo o dia. Os horários e preços efetivos dependem da distribuidora. Assim, dois imóveis com o mesmo consumo mensal poderão ter contas diferentes, conforme os horários de uso de ar-condicionado, aquecimento, piscina e outros equipamentos. Quem poderá ser incluído? A proposta abrange consumidores de baixa tensão residenciais (B1), rurais (B2) e comerciais/industriais (B3), respeitadas as exceções regulatórias. O enquadramento automático poderá alcançar unidades com média mensal a partir de 500 kWh, calculada em 12 meses, de forma gradual: os preparativos são previstos para 2027 e a implementação começa em abril de 2028 pelas faixas de maior consumo. Consumidores abaixo de 500 kWh poderão aderir voluntariamente, quando elegíveis. Para novos projetos de energia solar, há uma regra específica: pedidos de conexão ao Sistema de Compensação de Energia Elétrica (SCEE) apresentados a partir de 90 dias após a publicação da norma deverão entrar na Tarifa Hora Certa, independentemente do consumo e sem opção de saída, segundo o texto proposto. Se a norma for publicada em dezembro de 2026, essa regra poderá alcançar novos pedidos em 2027. A data exata, porém, ainda não está confirmada. Para sistemas já conectados, a transição proposta é distinta, iniciando-se gradualmente em 2028. Por que as baterias ganham importância? Os painéis solares geram energia principalmente durante o dia, enquanto parte relevante do consumo residencial pode ocorrer à noite. Com baterias, é possível guardar energia produzida pelo sistema fotovoltaico e utilizá-la quando a tarifa da rede estiver mais cara. Em certas configurações, também é possível carregar a bateria com energia comprada da rede fora da ponta e utilizá-la na ponta. Essa estratégia é chamada de arbitragem de energia: aproveitar o período mais barato para reduzir compras no período mais caro. Imagine, como exemplo, um kWh a R$ 0,60 fora de ponta e R$ 1,20 na ponta. Armazenar energia no primeiro período para uso no segundo pode gerar economia. Mas o retorno depende da diferença real entre as tarifas, das perdas do armazenamento, da vida útil da bateria e do custo do investimento. Injetar energia armazenada na rede não garante receber um valor maior por isso. A inteligência artificial ajuda a escolher o melhor momento A tecnologia permite ir além de simplesmente guardar energia. Soluções da Sigenergy integram baterias e recursos de inteligência artificial capazes de considerar hábitos de consumo, previsão de geração solar, clima, tarifas disponíveis e nível de carga. Com dados e configurações compatíveis, o sistema pode priorizar o autoconsumo, guardar energia para o horário caro ou manter uma reserva para situações de necessidade. O proprietário define seus objetivos, enquanto o gerenciamento inteligente auxilia na escolha dos momentos de carga e descarga. As funcionalidades dependem do modelo instalado, das informações tarifárias disponíveis e das regras aplicáveis no Brasil. i9 Solar já vinha antecipando essa tendência A i9 Solar já acompanhava a evolução do armazenamento e incorporava ao seu ecossistema tecnologias como as da Sigenergy. Sua proposta é integrar geração fotovoltaica, baterias e gestão inteligente para oferecer mais controle sobre o consumo e ampliar as possibilidades de eficiência e economia. "A energia solar já permite ao consumidor produzir parte da própria eletricidade. Com as baterias e a gestão inteligente, ele também pode escolher melhor quando utilizar essa energia. É uma evolução que pode trazer mais controle e eficiência ao imóvel", afirma Flavio Abreu, CEO da i9 Solar. Em imóveis de alto padrão, com climatização, piscina aquecida, automação e carregador de veículo elétrico, entender o consumo por horário pode ser especialmente relevante. A mesma análise vale para empresas com demanda concentrada em certos períodos. A empresa apresenta a tecnologia em seu canal no YouTube, que pode ser acessado pelo link https://youtu.be/QN1ooIDF7Yk. Instalar bateria será obrigatório? Não. A proposta da ANEEL altera a modalidade tarifária de determinados consumidores, mas não exige baterias. O armazenamento poderá ser mais atraente em alguns perfis; em outros, a conta pode não fechar. A decisão requer um estudo que considere consumo, tarifas, geração solar, necessidades de reserva e investimento. O futuro da energia depende também de quando ela é usada A Tarifa Hora Certa reforça que produzir energia limpa é apenas parte da estratégia. Armazenamento e gerenciamento inteligente podem ajudar proprietários a consumir com mais eficiência, controlar custos e preparar seus imóveis para mudanças no setor elétrico. Para a i9 Solar, investimento inteligente é empregar tecnologia para transformar sustentabilidade em eficiência, conforto e valor no longo prazo. artigo.texto: O Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) já credenciou 11 empresas para o fornecimento de equipamentos destinados a projetos de armazenamento de energia no Brasil. Entre as empresas já credenciadas pelo BNDES estão as brasileiras WEG, Moura, You.On e SecPower, além das empresas Canadian, BYD, Gotion, TBEA e Trina. A lista também passou a contar com a Windey Brasil, que está implantando uma fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento em Camaçari, na Bahia. O banco também reconheceu a Windey entre empresas para o desenvolvimento de software e firmware dos sistemas de gerenciamento de energia (EMS), que ainda conta com Moura, Automa e Reivax. O credenciamento permite que os fabricantes avancem na habilitação de seus equipamentos para acesso às linhas de financiamento do BNDES. A movimentação ocorre às vésperas dos leilões de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência (LRCap) com participação de baterias, previsto para 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. Uma das modalidades do certame, o Produto A, prevê a contratação de sistemas de armazenamento com exigências de conteúdo local, vinculadas ao credenciamento no CFI. Windey na Bahia A fábrica da Windey em Camaçari receberá investimento anunciado de R$ 100 milhões e ocupará uma área de aproximadamente 25 mil metros quadrados. A unidade terá capacidade produtiva prevista de 2 GWh por ano e deverá iniciar as operações em 2027. Será a primeira base de manufatura de sistemas de armazenamento da companhia fora da China, com produção destinada aos mercados brasileiro e latino-americano. A iniciativa também representa um movimento de entrada de fabricantes estrangeiros na cadeia industrial brasileira de baterias, em um momento em que o país busca ampliar a participação da indústria nacional no fornecimento de equipamentos para o setor elétrico. Em nota, o CEO da Windey Brasil, Ricardo Galvão, afirmou que a escolha da Bahia para sediar a primeira fábrica da companhia fora da China considerou a localização, a estrutura industrial e a presença de empreendimentos de energias renováveis no estado.

artigo.texto: Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology have developed a structural lithium-sulfur battery cathode capable of maintaining stable electrical performance inside curved and hollow structures. Led by Professor Il-Kwon Oh from the Department of Mechanical Engineering, the research team fabricated the electrode by growing ultrafine nanowires directly onto woven carbon cloth, creating a monolithically integrated scaffold designed to serve simultaneously as a mechanical support and an energy storage medium for drones and robotic systems. In robotics and unmanned aerial vehicle engineering, maximizing energy storage capacity while minimizing device weight and occupied volume remains a primary design constraint. Conventional vehicle architectures rely on separate structural airframes and discrete, rigid battery packs, restricting the extent to which overall platform weight can be reduced. Structural energy storage addresses this challenge by converting load-bearing airframe parts, such as landing gear or robotic limbs, into functional battery components. Implementing multifunctional structural batteries in practice requires energy storage cells that conform to non-planar structural geometries. Unmanned aerial vehicle landing legs and robotic support frames frequently incorporate curved, hollow, or tubular surfaces that cannot accommodate conventional flat battery configurations. To resolve this geometric restriction, the KAIST team focused on engineering an electrode architecture capable of conforming to tightly curved, three-dimensional enclosures without sacrificing mechanical durability or electrochemical activity. The engineering team selected a lithium-sulfur electrochemical system, which utilizes sulfur as the active cathode material. Lithium-sulfur chemistries provide theoretical potential for high energy storage capacity at a relatively low material weight compared to traditional alternatives. Within this system, the cathode acts as a critical functional electrode that governs the redox reactions occurring during electrical charge and discharge cycles. Despite these theoretical storage advantages, lithium-sulfur systems encounter operational obstacles that hinder long-term performance. Elemental sulfur has poor electrical conductivity, and intermediate compounds termed lithium polysulfides dissolve into the electrolyte during operation. The migration of these dissolved polysulfides away from the cathode disrupts the reversible electrochemical reactions required for efficient energy retention, accelerating capacity loss over repeated cycling. Conventional electrode fabrication techniques introduce additional structural vulnerabilities when subjected to physical movement. Active materials are typically applied as a surface slurry coating onto a conductive substrate, making the layer susceptible to cracking or complete delamination under repeated bending or external mechanical stress. When active material detaches from the underlying current collector, the electrical pathways are severed and the electrode degrades rapidly. To overcome delamination and polysulfide migration simultaneously, the KAIST researchers grew nickel cobalt selenide nanowires directly on the surfaces of interwoven carbon fibers. Nanowires are ultrafine structures with dimensions measured on the scale of nanometers, where one nanometer represents one billionth of a meter. The nickel cobalt selenide compound, consisting of nickel, cobalt, and selenium, catalyzes sulfur-related redox reactions while chemically anchoring lithium polysulfides to limit their dissolution and migration away from the reaction zone. Because the nickel cobalt selenide nanowires are grown directly out of the woven carbon cloth substrate rather than spread as a secondary surface coating, the cathode establishes firmly anchored, continuous electrical conduction pathways. In cyclic mechanical deformation tests, the monolithic electrode underwent 1,000 bending cycles at a tight curvature radius of 2.5 millimeters. Following testing, the nanowires remained intact and securely attached to the carbon fiber surfaces, displaying no structural collapse, cracking, or material detachment. To verify the practical viability of the electrode within non-planar enclosures, the researchers assembled the material into functional lithium-sulfur pouch cells. They incorporated the resulting cells into multiple curved and angular housings, including oval, square, and drone-leg structural components. In each configuration, the integrated lithium-sulfur battery successfully powered a light-emitting diode, demonstrating reliable electrical discharge across varied structural contours. The team also subjected the integrated structural battery to external mechanical load testing to evaluate electrical stability under severe mechanical strain. When installed within a cylindrical housing, the battery retained 99.8 percent of its initial operational voltage even under external mechanical forces sufficient to fracture the surrounding structural frame. In a parallel loading evaluation, a connected light-emitting diode maintained steady illumination without flickering or interruption during structural failure. Looking toward practical deployment, the authors noted that the electrode architecture could eventually be paired with load-bearing composite materials, such as carbon fiber and resin matrices, to construct multifunctional drone legs and robotic airframes. However, the researchers emphasized that further experimental research remains necessary to quantify precisely how much structural weight can be eliminated and the degree to which operational flight times or robot mission durations can be extended in operational conditions. The study, titled “Monolithically integrated NiCo2Se4 nanowire–carbon cloth cathode scaffolds for non-planar lithium-sulfur structural-battery integration,” was published in the journal Advanced Composites and Hybrid Materials

artigo.texto: – Collaboration to assess next-generation ultralight solar cells for space-based computing infrastructure – Partnership brings together Korean space energy technology and French orbital infrastructure expertise Bremen, Germany – Flexell Space, a space energy company, announced that it has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with ALATYR, a French company developing orbital data centers, to explore solar power solutions for space-based computing infrastructure. The collaboration will assess the potential application of Flexell Space’s next-generation solar cell technology to orbital infrastructure designed for large-scale computing and data storage. The companies intend to exchange technical requirements relating to power demand and operating conditions and explore opportunities for future joint development and validation. ALATYR develops orbital data centers designed to support artificial intelligence (AI) computing and mission-critical workloads. Its CITADEL modular infrastructure architecture and BYLD robotic system are designed to enable assembly, maintenance, and upgrades in orbit. The architecture separates the service life of the supporting infrastructure from the replacement cycle of computing hardware, enabling computing modules to be renewed in orbit while retaining the infrastructure that powers, cools, and supports them. Reliable power generation is essential to making orbital data centers viable. As these facilities grow, solar power systems must address not only electrical performance but also mass, launch and deployment efficiency, manufacturing costs, and long-term reliability. Flexell Space is developing next-generation space solar cells based on CIGS (copper indium gallium selenide) and perovskite technologies. With a focus on lightweight, flexible designs and large-area manufacturing, the company aims to provide power solutions for satellites and larger space infrastructure. Through the collaboration, Flexell Space intends to gain a clearer understanding of orbital data center requirements and assess how its technology could support this emerging application. “This MoU marks an important milestone in strengthening cooperation between Korea and Europe, particularly France, in space energy and infrastructure,” said Kyumin Lee, Business Development Manager at Flexell Space. “By combining our next-generation solar cell technology with ALATYR’s orbital infrastructure expertise, we aim to build a lasting partnership and lay the groundwork for joint development and validation of power solutions for future orbital data centers.” He added, “By bringing together our complementary capabilities, we aim to establish a practical foundation for future development and validation.” “Our orbital infrastructure is designed to serve successive generations of computing hardware,” said Emeric Lhomme, Chief Executive Officer of ALATYR. “That makes solar cell efficiency and longevity central to our approach: our power systems must continue to deliver reliable performance as computing modules are replaced and upgraded. With Flexell Space, we will explore how next-generation lightweight solar technologies could meet the demands of that extended service life.” The companies plan to begin by exchanging information on their technologies and development priorities, followed by a phased assessment of solar cell and power system compatibility. Specific development activities and validation approaches will be discussed through subsequent technical consultations. About Flexell Space Flexell Space is a space energy company that originated as an internal venture at Hanwha Systems. The company develops next-generation space solar cells and power solutions based on CIGS and perovskite technologies, with a focus on low-cost, large-area, ultralight products. Through collaboration with global partners, Flexell Space is advancing the commercialization of solar cell technologies for satellites and a broad range of space infrastructure. About ALATYR ALATYR is a French company developing a new layer of critical digital infrastructure in space. The company designs orbital data centers that evolve with computing technology, rather than being replaced with each hardware generation. Its infrastructure is designed to remain productive over the long term and expand with demand, creating a lasting extension of the cloud in orbit to increase computing capacity and strengthen the resilience of essential digital services worldwide.

artigo.texto: Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. O setor elétrico brasileiro vive um momento de profundas transformações. A expansão acelerada das fontes renováveis, especialmente solar e eólica, associada ao crescimento da micro e minigeração distribuída, vem alterando a dinâmica de operação do sistema e ampliando a necessidade de flexibilidade, armazenamento e disponibilidade de potência nos momentos de maior demanda. Nesse cenário, o armazenamento de energia assume um papel cada vez mais estratégico. Tecnologias como baterias e usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis permitem aproveitar melhor os recursos energéticos disponíveis, ampliar a segurança do abastecimento e contribuir para uma operação mais eficiente do sistema elétrico. O Brasil reúne condições privilegiadas para avançar nessa agenda. Conta com uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável, um expressivo parque hidrelétrico e oportunidades para integrar diferentes tecnologias de armazenamento, aproveitando a infraestrutura existente e atraindo novos investimentos. É nesse contexto que ganha relevância a discussão sobre a distribuição dos custos da contratação de baterias no âmbito da reserva de capacidade. A legislação estabeleceu um tratamento específico para esses sistemas, determinando que os custos de sua contratação sejam rateados exclusivamente entre os agentes de geração, diferentemente da regra geral aplicável às demais tecnologias contratadas para prestar o mesmo serviço. Essa distinção merece uma reflexão. A reserva de capacidade tem como finalidade assegurar a disponibilidade de potência e flexibilidade acompanhando as necessidades do sistema. Trata-se de um serviço essencial à segurança e à confiabilidade do abastecimento, cujos benefícios alcançam todos os consumidores. Não parece razoável, portanto, que tecnologias contratadas para atender à mesma necessidade do sistema estejam submetidas a critérios tão distintos de custeio. Além disso, atribuir exclusivamente aos geradores os custos da contratação de baterias não significa que esses valores deixarão de alcançar os consumidores. Parte desses encargos será incorporada aos preços e tarifas da energia e, consequentemente, aos custos de produção de bens e serviços, de forma menos transparente e potencialmente mais onerosa. Há ainda outro aspecto relevante. A imprevisibilidade desses encargos amplia os riscos dos empreendimentos, pode elevar os custos de financiamento e comprometer a atratividade dos investimentos, justamente quando o país precisa expandir sua infraestrutura de armazenamento. Nesse contexto, o Projeto de Lei nº 3.716/2026, de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim, apresenta uma solução objetiva. Ao propor a revogação de um único dispositivo legal, busca restabelecer para as baterias a regra geral de custeio da reserva de capacidade, promovendo tratamento isonômico entre tecnologias contratadas para prestar o mesmo serviço. A proposta não elimina custos nem cria benefícios adicionais. Seu objetivo é assegurar coerência regulatória e maior transparência na distribuição de um encargo associado à segurança de todo o sistema elétrico. O momento dessa definição também é fundamental. Com os leilões de armazenamento previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro, é importante que a questão seja solucionada antes de sua realização, reduzindo incertezas, prevenindo questionamentos administrativos e judiciais e preservando a segurança jurídica necessária à contratação e à implantação dos projetos. Para aproveitar essa oportunidade, precisamos de um ambiente regulatório estável, previsível e coerente com a natureza dos serviços prestados. A segurança energética é um benefício coletivo. As regras de custeio devem refletir essa realidade, com transparência, isonomia e responsabilidade. Mais do que viabilizar os próximos leilões, trata-se de estabelecer bases sólidas para que o armazenamento de energia contribua efetivamente para um sistema elétrico mais seguro, eficiente e competitivo. Marisete Pereira, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Empresas Geradoras de Energia Elétrica (Abrage)

artigo.texto: Spotsylvania County residents call on officials to scrap 'sweetheart deal' for data center SPOTSYLVANIA, Va. (7News) — Stafford and Spotsylvania counties are moving ahead with plans to approve more data centers, according to recent actions by their boards of supervisors. In recent years, both counties have approved data center developments. On Tuesday, the Spotsylvania County Board of Supervisors voted 4-3 to approve the Crossroads Technology Campus, a massive data center project planned for a 550-acre site near neighborhoods. SEE ALSO | Jawando’s pick for Montgomery County police chief faces scrutiny over past audit When she introduced the motion to approve the project in her district, Spotsylvania County Supervisor Lori Hayes said the developer agreed to noise mitigation, generator emissions standards and setbacks from homes. She said the developer also agreed not to use groundwater for cooling. Hayes told 7News that 66% of the site would remain forested. Supervisors Tim McLaughlin, Hayes, Drew Mullins and Deborah Frazier voted to approve the special use permit. Supervisors Chris Yakabouski, Jacob Lane and David Goosman voted against it. Despite more than 50 guarantees and the developer’s promise of $30 million in annual tax revenue for the county, dozens of homeowners told the board they don’t want to be surrounded by data centers. SEE ALSO | Fares as high as $8.25 a ride? Metro seeks to address $132M budget gap Spotsylvania County resident Kelly Shaeffer told 7News reporter Nick Minock that she doesn’t want to see data centers from her home, hear their constant hum and generator noise, or see her home’s value decrease because of the facilities’ proximity to her neighborhood. Her neighborhood is surrounded by several proposed data center sites. “Do you fear Spotsylvania County is going to become Loudoun County data center alley?” Minock asked. “Oh yeah, I absolutely do, especially with the tax rate that they're giving,” Shaeffer said. Spotsylvania County offers one of the lowest tax rates for data centers in Virginia. “Our board decided to put in place an Amazon local performance agreement [for Amazon data centers] that provides them $1.25 per $100 of computer and peripherals,” said Cindy Staats. “On top of that, they get 60% back of the generated tax revenue for ten years, and then they get 20% back for the next ten years. On top of that, they get an accelerated depreciation schedule.” “Would you call this a sweetheart deal?” Minock asked. “Oh, it is a very much a sweetheart deal,” said Staats. Both Spotsylvania County homeowners who spoke with 7News said they were disappointed that the board approved the Crossroads Technology Campus. “Disappointed because I feel like the residents have brought up some really valid concerns and unanswered questions that we still have on this project,” said Staats. “And a lot of residents just even ask them to pause or to defer the vote until we could get answers on those questions and the fact that they chose not to do that and to kind of push forward was really disappointing.” “It feels like we can't even catch up with how quickly they're [data centers] popping up,” said Shaeffer. “Like last night was the public hearing for Crossroads. And then tonight is the public hearing for the one across the river. And it's just back-to-back. And it's like we can't fully get our feet underneath us to try and fight. I know they've made the argument that they've kind of zoned all the data centers to be here. But my issue with that is why would you then spend the money to have all these residential areas pop up? Like, if I knew that this was specifically zoned [for] all these data centers my husband and I wouldn't have bought here and I think all of our neighbors wouldn't have bought here.” Stafford County also has a data center tax rate of $1.25 per $100 of assessed value, less than one-third of Loudoun County’s rate for data center computer equipment. Now, one developer is proposing four data centers near George Washington’s boyhood home. The project, off Kings Highway, spans more than 1,400 acres and would put data centers on the Rappahannock River. The proposed data center and substation would tower over Arlene’s home, as 7News previously reported. "It makes me very sad and I am praying it doesn't come about,” said Arlene. The developer’s attorney said the project, if approved, would generate $245 million in total tax revenue, about 20% of Stafford County’s total budget. The attorney said it would provide funding for schools, local roads and other public services, which he said is needed because residents’ taxes have increased 57% over the past five years. Spotsylvania and Stafford counties, King George County and the city of Fredericksburg have some of the region’s lowest tax rates on data center equipment, at $1.25 per $100 of assessed value. Fairfax, Fauquier, Prince William and Loudoun counties charge higher rates. Fairfax County charges $4.57 per $100 of assessed value for data center equipment. Prince William County’s rate is $4.50, while Fauquier and Loudoun counties charge $4.15. Loudoun County Supervisor Kristen Umstattd said the Fredericksburg-area localities should raise their tax rates so they can see the same tax revenue benefits as Loudoun County. “What we get out of a $4.15 tax rate is money for our schools, 100% of our general fund covered by data center tax revenues,” Umstattd said. “And it's 45% of our entire budget, including the schools.” While Spotsylvania and Stafford counties continue to approve data centers, Loudoun County is beginning to pump the brakes. After years of allowing dozens of data centers and substations near homes, the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted Tuesday night to pause new substations for data centers. Loudoun County currently has more than 230 data centers, with 100 more planned. artigo.texto: On the afternoon of Thursday, Nov. 19, an estimated 200 students and community members protested outside of the Alexander G. Ruthven Building on the University of Michigan's campus in Ann Arbor. As the regents voted to approve the Textile Road facility in collaboration with Los Alamos National Laboratory, some Ypsilanti residents raised signs and yelled chants to voice their dissent. U-M describes this project as a high performance computing center and has purchased 144 acres in Ypsilanti Township for the building. Beginning an hour before the regents meeting, protesters from ypsidatacenter.org began lining the street and sidewalk with posters and chants fighting against the proposed data center. Data center protest Editor and researcher from ypsidatacenter.org and resident of Ypsilanti Township Andy Melichar told The Echo, "We built a website that has all the information about this project that the university does not want us to know. We're here to protest the vote that they're holding today ... We don't want that in our backyard, and I don't think most of the people in Michigan want that in Michigan." Juliet Heinley, another resident of Ypsilanti Township, said that she came to protest the data center because it affects her, as well as her friends, neighbors and people she doesn't even know directly. "I don't want them to have to live in the fallout of living next door, across the street or down the river from this data center," Heinley said. She described her fears of air, water and noise pollution: "The negative health outcomes of communities that have data centers put in them are outrageous." Frustration with U-M's communication While much of the protesting was aimed toward the data center as a whole, many community members expressed frustration with the lack of communication from the university about the project proposal. Ypsilanti Township Supervisor Brenda Stumbo carried a "Hail no Los Alamos data center" sign and told The Echo, "I'm shocked that they added this to the agenda so quickly without notifying the host community, which is Ypsilanti Township. The University of Michigan Board of Regents are elected by the people, for the people and they are funded by the taxpayers of the state of Michigan." Stumbo is in her 10th term as township supervisor and said that in her 37 years of leadership, she has "never met elected officials that treat people and other elected officials the way we have been treated. It's really gross to me ... This project is clearly a partnership with the University of Michigan and the Department of War, and if you'd have asked me in my lifetime, would the University of Michigan be a supporter of war? I would have said 'Hail no.'" Stumbo said that she warns everyone she meets not to trust U-M, specifically the Board of Regents and vice presidents. She mentioned her gratefulness for the support of Regent Paul Brown, who has expressed opposition to the project and voted against it Nov. 19. Heinley explained her frustrations with the U-M leaders to The Echo, "There has been zero meaningful community engagement about it. There has been a miniscule amount of going through the motions of listening, but not really listening." U-M hosted two town halls in Ypsilanti regarding the project in September, as well as some previous community engagement events. Educating students and community members Ypsilanti may be hotspot for data center information, but protesters at U-M said they came, in part, to educate students who have no idea what their university is doing. U-M student Lou Ridgeway told The Echo, "The U-M community really doesn't know about this data center or that it's being built with their tuition money. We've been tabling at a whole bunch of campus events to try to both spread awareness and really drill the message every day for these people that we don't want this data center." Melichar also noticed the lapse in information just one town over from the data center site. "I was here for like two minutes, and a student came up to me and said: on behalf of the students, I'm sorry that they are doing this to you guys. It does not reflect what the students believe — that made all of the effort worth it, " Melichar said. He said that most of the U-M students walking by had no idea that their school had a data center proposed in Ypsi, and that his goal was to educate those who do not know what is going on. Ridgeway had a table set up offering postcards for peace for people to write. "We've been doing these postcards for months and just letting people who are building this data centers at all levels [know] that we do not want this. We're writing to the people at Los Alamos and U-M, but also the Smith group, who is the architecture firm designing this data center," Ridgeway said. Marching dissent Once the regents meeting began, protesters gathered together to walk through Ann Arbor. They chanted "5, 6, 7, 8, we will fight the AI state," and "We don't want no data center: not in Ypsi, nowhere, never," for the duration of the meeting. The U-M regents formally approved the project 7-1, with Brown voting no.

artigo.texto: In a recent study, researchers investigated biodegradable polymer electrolytes engineered for use in green electric double-layer capacitor devices. The research examined solid polymer blend electrolytes composed of chitosan and methylcellulose paired with potassium thiocyanate salt and modified using glycerol as a plasticizing agent. The development addresses the implementation of environmentally friendly biopolymer matrices capable of supporting functional electrochemical storage systems, with an emphasis on establishing sustainable materials for capacitor applications. Impedance spectroscopy evaluations demonstrated that the addition of glycerol plasticizer effectively enhanced the overall electrical properties of the chitosan/methylcellulose/potassium thiocyanate electrolyte system. By incorporating glycerol into the ternary biopolymer blend, the investigators identified clear modifications in electrical response compared to unmodified formulations. These impedance findings confirmed that plasticization served a critical functional role in optimizing the bulk electrical characteristics required for practical solid polymer electrolyte performance. Structural and morphological analyses confirmed that glycerol incorporation induced measurable physical alterations within the solid polymer blend. X-ray diffraction measurements showed a reduction in diffraction peak intensity alongside noticeable peak broadening, indicating structural reorganization in the polymer electrolyte network. Furthermore, scanning electron microscopy revealed a homogenous dispersion of glycerol throughout the solid polymer electrolyte matrix, demonstrating uniform integration of the plasticizer across the combined chitosan and methylcellulose structure. The dielectric behaviour of the electrolyte system provided additional insights into the internal charge transport dynamics. The loss tangent peaks exhibited a systematic shift toward higher frequencies, which the authors identified as direct evidence that the time required for ion transport decreased as plasticizer concentration increased. Complementing these observations, an electric modulus study was performed to suppress electrode polarization phenomena and enable clear observation of the relaxation peaks associated with ionic motion. Conductivity testing revealed that the plasticized polymer electrolyte reached a maximum ionic conductivity of 2.305 x 10^-4 S/cm, a performance level deemed adequate for device production. To clarify the transport mechanism, transference number measurements were performed on the electrolyte. The measurement confirmed that the dominant fraction of conducting species consisted of ions, establishing that ionic mobility governs the electrical conductivity of the plasticized polymer blend rather than electronic transport pathways. Electrochemical stability assessments using linear sweep voltammetry confirmed the capacity of the electrolyte to resist electrical breakdown under applied voltage. Furthermore, cyclic voltammetry was conducted to examine ion storage and interface reactions at the boundary between the electrodes and the electrolyte. The resulting cyclic voltammograms displayed a characteristic rectangular pattern, while galvanostatic charge-discharge testing produced an almost ideal profile, confirming that the fabricated capacitor operates through non-faradaic charge storage processes. Overall performance testing of the assembled electric double-layer capacitor demonstrated low equivalent series resistance and high specific capacitance as key experimental outcomes. The resulting energy storage device achieved energy densities ranging from 9.6 to 7.61 Wh/kg and power densities ranging from 1791 to 1475 W/kg across testing conditions. The researchers noted that these combined structural and electrochemical results substantiate the operational viability of biodegradable solid polymer electrolytes in advancing green capacitor storage technology. artigo.texto: St. Joseph County Council advances proposal to ban non-legacy hyper-scale data centers The Area Plan Commission voted unanimously against the proposal earlier on Tuesday SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU) - The St. Joseph County Council took the next step Tuesday on a proposal that would ban non-legacy hyper-scale data centers, hours after the Area Plan Commission voted unanimously against it. Tuesday was the first reading of the proposal, which would prohibit future hyper-scale data centers in unincorporated parts of St. Joseph County that exceed one million square feet. County Council President Bryan Tanner sent the proposal to the Land Use Planning Committee. Tanner said the proposal also creates definitions that are not currently in the county’s development code. “It is institutionalizing a new definition that hasn’t historically existed in our development code for what a hyper-scale data center is,” Tanner said. “There will also be a new definition for what is considered a legacy data center.” Officials said a meeting focusing on public comment and discussion of the proposal will be held in December. artigo.texto: Alep aprova programa de incentivos fiscais para atrair data centers ao Paraná Projeto prevê benefícios tributários para empresas de infraestrutura digital e aposta em energia renovável; proposta levanta discussões sobre renúncia fiscal, consumo de água e energia e contrapartidas dos empreendimentos 🎧 Ouça esta matéria — narrado por IA A Assembleia Legislativa do Paraná (Alep) aprovou, em 17 de novembro, o Projeto de Lei 55/2026, que cria o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (PRODATAPR). A proposta autoriza o Governo do Estado a conceder benefícios fiscais para atrair empresas do setor de infraestrutura digital, estimular investimentos privados e ampliar a geração de empregos especializados. O projeto é de autoria dos deputados Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (PP) e Pedro Paulo Bazana (PSD). A iniciativa busca posicionar o Paraná como um polo estratégico para a instalação e expansão de centros de dados, estruturas fundamentais para o armazenamento e processamento de informações utilizadas em serviços digitais, instituições financeiras, computação em nuvem e aplicações de inteligência artificial. A proposta considera como diferenciais competitivos do Estado a disponibilidade de energia renovável, a infraestrutura de conectividade e a capacidade de integração com universidades e centros de pesquisa. A expectativa é atrair novos empreendimentos, fortalecer o setor de tecnologia e ampliar oportunidades de trabalho qualificado. Sustentabilidade e consumo de recursos Um dos eixos do programa é o estímulo à adoção de práticas sustentáveis. O texto prevê incentivos ao uso de fontes renováveis de energia, aproveitamento do biometano, utilização racional da água e tecnologias de resfriamento com menor impacto ambiental. A discussão é relevante porque os data centers funcionam continuamente e exigem grande capacidade de fornecimento de energia elétrica. Dependendo da tecnologia de refrigeração utilizada, também podem apresentar elevado consumo de água. Por isso, a atração desses empreendimentos exige planejamento e acompanhamento dos impactos ambientais. A expansão da infraestrutura digital precisa considerar a disponibilidade de recursos naturais e a capacidade de atendimento da rede elétrica. Renúncia fiscal e contrapartidas A aprovação do projeto também abre espaço para o debate sobre o custo dos incentivos tributários para os cofres públicos. Embora a proposta tenha como objetivo estimular investimentos e empregos, a concessão de benefícios fiscais exige transparência sobre os valores envolvidos e os resultados esperados. Entre os pontos que devem ser acompanhados estão os investimentos efetivamente realizados, a quantidade de empregos criados, a qualificação de profissionais, o consumo de energia e água e o cumprimento das exigências ambientais. A proposta também prevê aproximação entre empresas, universidades e centros de pesquisa, com o objetivo de estimular a inovação e a formação de mão de obra especializada. O programa estadual acompanha o movimento nacional de incentivo ao setor de data centers. Em setembro de 2026, o governo federal sancionou a Lei 15.504, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), com benefícios tributários condicionados ao cumprimento de compromissos pelas empresas. Com a aprovação do PL 55/2026, o Paraná avança na criação de uma política própria para atrair empreendimentos de infraestrutura digital. A efetividade da iniciativa, entretanto, dependerá da regulamentação, dos critérios para concessão dos incentivos e da fiscalização das contrapartidas. O desafio será conciliar a atração de investimentos, a geração de empregos e o desenvolvimento tecnológico com a responsabilidade fiscal e a preservação dos recursos naturais. artigo.texto: Article Summary - Hundreds rallied at the state Capitol Wednesday for passage of the POWER Act, which would regulate data centers. - The bill’s Senate sponsor said the bill is a “big solution” for a “big problem.” - The legislation would, among other things, require big tech companies to pay for the energy used to power giant data centers. This summary was written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story. SPRINGFIELD — Hundreds of residents and environmental advocates rallied at the state Capitol Wednesday to urge lawmakers to regulate data centers. The residents came via bus, car and Amtrak from around the state to call for passage of the POWER Act, a bill that would require data centers to pay to create the energy they consume, mandate transparency around water use, limit noise levels and diesel generator use, ensure local community benefit agreements, and more. The bill failed to progress during the spring legislative session, but advocates hope to see it passed during the veto session. “Illinoisans are tired of fighting alone for basic protections without help from the state legislature,” said Lori McKiernan, a local Springfield community organizer and Sierra Club member. “Time is up. Our legislators must take action on data centers.” Over the summer break, lawmakers have been meeting with environmental advocates, organized labor, and representatives of the data center industry to negotiate the details. The Senate Energy and Public Utilities Committee was set to hold a hearing on the POWER Act at 4:30 p.m. Wednesday. Sen. Ram Villivalam, D-Chicago, is the lead sponsor of the Senate bill. He called the roughly 1,000-page bill a “big solution” for a “big problem,” and described the legislation as the “most comprehensive data center legislation in the nation.” “You’re here because this matters,” Villivalam told the crowd. “When something affects your families, your homes, your neighbors, and of course our bills, your voices deserve to be heard.” Battling big tech Data centers have existed for years in Illinois, housing servers and hardware that store data and power the digital world, supporting email, video streaming and other web services. But in recent years, as major technology firms race to create generative artificial intelligence, they have begun to build hyperscale data centers — massive buildings and campuses that sometimes consume the energy of a small city. Their actual and projected energy consumption have driven up energy costs for regular residents and small businesses. The rally comes shortly after the release of two reports from state agencies proposed delaying the planned closures of 11 fossil fuel plants, as required under the state’s landmark energy bill, in order to guarantee enough energy supply to meet the growing demand. But environmental advocates don’t want to see the state’s landmark climate goals delayed in order to power hyperscale data centers. “Big tech, they’re counting on us to be intimidated by their big money. They’re counting on us to be overwhelmed by the fight in front of us,” Illinois Environmental Council organizer Cate Caldwell said at the rally. “But as I look at this crowd today, I think big tech should be intimidated by us.” There won’t be a vote this week, but lawmakers could take up the issue when they return for their final days of the veto session next month. It is funded primarily by the Illinois Press Foundation and the Robert R. McCormick Foundation.

artigo.texto: A inteligência artificial se consolidou como uma promessa irrefreável de conveniência e produtividade. Mas perto dos data centers que fazem essa tecnologia funcionar, a percepção é outra. Enquanto a maioria experimenta respostas instantâneas nas telas, alguns se preocupam com algo muito mais básico, como a ameaça à água e ao território, à própria sobrevivência e ao direito de decidir sobre seu futuro. Na semana passada, visitei o território Anacé, nas proximidades do Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém, no Ceará. Até então, eu conhecia os impactos dos data centers por estudos, reportagens e debates. Mas estar diante das pessoas que vivem lá deu rostos e histórias aos números e às projeções, revelando uma dimensão que nenhum relatório consegue expressar. Segundo o cacique Roberto Ytaysaba Anacé, a história dos Anacé envolve a agricultura, a pesca, a caça e a coleta, além de uma cultura marcada pela espiritualidade e pelos "encantados", seres espirituais vinculados à ancestralidade e à natureza. Para eles, a terra não é apenas o lugar onde vivem, mas parte de uma história, de uma identidade e de uma relação com o mundo que atravessa gerações. Os Anacé souberam pelas redes sociais que um data center chegaria à região. "A gente não sabia nem o que era data center", disse Roberto. Lideranças e moradores começaram então a estudar essa infraestrutura e a inteligência artificial, enquanto o empreendimento, que será usado pelo TikTok, avançava nas proximidades. - Assine gratuitamente minha newsletter sobre IA, experiência do cliente, mídia e transformação digital - Inscreva-se no meu podcast (escolha a plataforma): Spotify, Deezer, Apple Podcasts ou Soundcloud Para ele, o problema não se limita aos possíveis impactos do empreendimento sobre a água e o território. Estaria também em não terem sido ouvidos sobre decisões que podem afetar sua cultura, sua espiritualidade e seu futuro. "A gente não quer dinheiro, a gente quer direitos", afirmou. Entre suas reivindicações, está a demarcação da terra onde vive seu povo. O cacique ilustrou os riscos com a expressão "aguacídio". "Uma água morta não se repõe mais, não tem dinheiro no mundo que pague", detalhou. A frase expõe o limite das compensações financeiras, porque há perdas ambientais e culturais que não podem ser reparadas. Para uma comunidade, a água não é um recurso negociável, mas condição para a vida. Na tela, nada disso aparece. As respostas instantâneas da IA não revelam os territórios e as comunidades afetados pela infraestrutura que as produziu. E não se trata de querer frear essa facilidade, mas de reconhecer que a distância entre quem usa e quem convive com os equipamentos dificulta a percepção desses custos. "Quanto mais a gente conseguir traduzir esses impactos, que são complexos, em uma linguagem acessível, mais a gente aproxima os dois grupos", sugere Cynthia Picolo, diretora-executiva do Lapin (Laboratório de Políticas Públicas e Internet). Ela observa que há quem desconheça os riscos, não acredite neles ou os imagine distantes. Mas alerta que os efeitos podem aparecer antes do que se imagina até para quem está longe dos data centers, como em aumentos na conta de eletricidade. Thalita Verônica, defensora pública do Estado de São Paulo, defende que as comunidades sejam ouvidas antes das decisões e que os benefícios sejam repartidos de forma justa. "Zona de sacrifício é um território onde algumas pessoas pagam com a sua saúde e seu modo de vida o preço do desenvolvimento, como está acontecendo na regulamentação dos data centers no Brasil", explica. Para ela, benefícios efetivos devem acrescentar oportunidades novas, e não rebatizar obrigações do Estado como generosidade empresarial. "Muitas pessoas não têm a compreensão real do impacto desse tipo de tecnologia e infraestrutura", afirma Edson Prestes, professor da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul, ao criticar a ênfase de empresas e governos nos benefícios, sem dar a mesma visibilidade aos riscos. Dessa forma, não cabe culpar quem não recebeu informação clara, mas criar condições para discutir custos e escolhas, sem exigir adesão ou rejeição à IA. Afinal, quando usamos a IA, raramente pensamos no que foi necessário para isso acontecer. O ponto não é aceitar ou rejeitar a tecnologia, mas entender que a comodidade que ela proporciona pode vir acompanhada da precarização da vida de outras pessoas. E não cabe aos usuários resolverem sozinhos o problema. Empresas devem responder pelos impactos, governos precisam proteger direitos e a sociedade não pode deixar comunidades como os Anacé fora das decisões que afetam sua vida. Vivemos no mesmo planeta, mas não sentimos da mesma forma os efeitos da transformação tecnológica. O que para alguns representa avanço e conveniência para outros significa insegurança hídrica, perda territorial e ameaça à sua cultura. O progresso não pode ser medido apenas pela capacidade computacional ou pelos negócios que a IA viabiliza. Nenhuma inovação merece esse nome se exigir que os direitos de algumas pessoas sejam sacrificados para beneficiar tantas outras. Vídeo relacionado:

artigo.texto: OLYPHANT — More than 200 people cheered on 27 Lackawanna County residents who urged council Tuesday not to settle a data center developer’s lawsuit and forgo the public hearing process for Project Triboro in exchange for $101 million. Council chose not to listen. Olyphant Borough Council voted 5-2 during a special meeting to approve the settlement with ERCOR Triboro LLC allowing it to move forward with plans to develop seven 420,000-square-foot data centers and a substation within the footprints of four previously approved warehouses off Marshwood Road and Route 247. Council President Jimmy Baldan and council members Beth Frushon, Eric Hartshorn, Tony Delfino and Fred Hartman voted in favor of the settlement. Council Vice President Robert Hudak and Councilman Mike Abda dissented. In an identical 5-2 vote, the council members approved a 15-year, $101 million community benefits agreement with ERCOR Triboro that was widely opposed by the community. Project Triboro will still be subject to the land development process under Olyphant’s planning commission as they modify their plans from warehouses to data centers — a detail project representatives stressed Tuesday night. But Project Triboro will not be required to navigate the conditional use hearing process, where residents would have had the opportunity to cross-examine data center representatives at public hearings and present their own evidence. Victor, New York-based ERCOR sued Olyphant in June in a bid to sidestep that process and develop its data centers as principal permitted uses. People crowded the Rescue & Restore Church sanctuary during the nearly three-hour meeting that culminated in council’s decision. As furious residents shouted at council and data center officials, half a dozen Olyphant police swarmed the front of the sanctuary after a hasty adjournment following the votes. “Give us each a million dollars for our house, then you could have our freaking town you dirtbags,” a woman yelled as the meeting adjourned. “I hate you all.” Borough police maintained a heavy presence throughout the night, including shutting down Willow Avenue and surrounding streets for the duration of the meeting. Police received credible threats of violence; officers arrested a Taylor man Tuesday, charging him with terroristic threats and harassment, Police Chief James DeVoe said. The man’s name was unavailable Tuesday night. Following a brief presentation by ERCOR Triboro and Emergent Data Centers, who partnered with ERCOR to design and develop the data centers, residents addressed council. Every speaker opposed the settlement and CBA, either asking council to table its decision or to outright deny it. Lifelong resident Nicole Pasko, 27, one of the first speakers Tuesday, stood before council and described her pride in Olyphant and its small-town charm. “By allowing this corporation to buy you and your cooperation, you are directly sewing shut the mouths of your constituents,” Pasko said. “Grow a backbone and say, ‘No.’ Listen to those that voted you into these positions. Your vote tonight shows exactly what you think about the people of our town, our opinions and our futures.” As residents discussed the night’s proceedings on the sidewalk in front of Rescue & Rescue Church after the decision, Lackawanna County Commissioner Bill Gaughan said council’s complete disdain for public comment was embarrassing. Gaughan, who also spoke during the meeting, criticized council members for failing to explain their decision. “For them again not to explain their vote is a complete dereliction of duty on their part,” Gaughan said, calling it their basic responsibility. “They didn’t even do that, and it just shows a complete lack of respect for the people.” Check back for updates.

artigo.texto: LEBANON, OH -- Warren County commissioners are preparing to take another look at regulations governing data center development when they meet Dec. 1, as the county continues evaluating how large-scale facilities could affect local communities and resources. During the commissioners' Nov. 17 meeting, county officials reported that planning and zoning staff are developing proposed regulations for discussion at an upcoming work session. The discussion follows the commissioners' Sept. 29 decision to establish a temporary moratorium on data center development in areas governed by county zoning. The moratorium provides time for officials to examine potential impacts and establish appropriate regulations before considering new development proposals. County Preparing New Regulations During Tuesday's meeting, county officials reported attending a recent Ohio-Kentucky-Indiana Regional Council of Governments (OKI) symposium focused on data centers. The gathering included representatives from government agencies and the data center industry, including Amazon. According to the discussion, an Amazon representative indicated that the company welcomes clear zoning regulations because uncertainty about local requirements can make development planning more difficult. County officials also reported that Warren County has not received a data center development application. The county's current moratorium includes a provision for periodic review every 60 days, with the next review scheduled for Dec. 1. At that meeting, planning and zoning staff expect to present draft regulations for commissioners to evaluate and discuss. Water, Power and Community Impacts Commissioners previously raised concerns about the potential demands large data centers could place on water supplies, electricity and other infrastructure. Unlike traditional commercial buildings, large data centers can require substantial electrical capacity and cooling systems to support computer equipment operating around the clock. Officials have been considering how zoning regulations could address these facilities while protecting surrounding communities. The commissioners discussed several potential regulatory approaches during their September work session, including conditional-use approvals, site plan requirements and the creation of a separate zoning classification for data centers. What Happens Next? The Dec. 1 meeting is expected to provide commissioners with an opportunity to review proposed regulations and offer additional direction to county planning staff. No final zoning regulations were adopted during the Nov. 17 discussion. For now, the temporary moratorium remains in place as Warren County continues determining how future data center proposals should be evaluated.
