artigo.texto: HILLSBORO, Texas (KXXV) — The proposed Provident data center has now pulled out of its agreement to come to Hillsboro. - “They’re taking a lot of the farmland, and I’m not happy about that," said Sheila Brazil. - In August 2026, the city announced that Provident no longer had the property under contract. “We’re going to have to pay their water and their electric bill, and I don’t think that’s fair," said Shelia Brazil, a Hill County resident. In this case, Sheila Brazil thinks less is best. Brazil, a Hill County resident, said that with Provident Data Centers backing out of coming to Hillsboro, she’s completely okay with it. “They’re taking a lot of the farmland, and I’m not happy about that," said Brazil. According to the City of Hillsboro, the city's economic development corporation entered into a contract with Provident in September 2024 for the potential sale of approximately 300 acres. In August 2026, the city announced that Provident no longer had the property under contract. “That contract on the land, everything before close is a matter of due diligence. So they were going through their processes to see whether the project could come to fruition. There’s a lot of uncertainty, statewide, around data centers, and at the time they were in a month-to-month contract extension period and decided to terminate," said Jessica Trew, the executive director for the Hillsboro Economic Development Corporation. Trew explained that the initial contract for Provident was for nine months to complete its due diligence. Afterwards, she said the company started asking for contract extensions. Trew said she’s unsure why Provident ended the contract. 25 News reached out to Provident Data Centers, but we have not heard back. TA Smith, the founder of the Texas Coalition Against Data Centers, said he’s not sure what to believe. "Everyone keeps saying Provident is backing out… are they? They might have backed out on paper; they may have publicly backed out, but have they actually left?" said TA Smith, founder of the Texas Coalition Against Data Centers. But Provident may not be the only data center backing out on projects. Data Center Watch reports at least 75 data center projects worth billions were blocked or delayed in the first quarter of 2026. Smith said regardless of the reason, this is good news. “At the moment it gives you a sigh of relief, but again next month it’s a different story and that same company…there’s nothing against them coming back...here’s a new proposal with a new zoning board committee," said Smith. Trew said the EDC isn’t for or against data centers, and the property once sought by Provident cannot be used for farmland. Brazil said whatever comes to Hill County can impact many people. “And we care about what comes up, what comes here, and what’s going to affect us," said Brazil.

artigo.texto: As developers pursue new data center projects in SF, the Board of Supervisors voted Tuesday to extend a moratorium on new facilities, citing unanswered questions about their environmental impacts and demands on the city's power grid. San Francisco supervisors voted unanimously Tuesday to extend the temporary ban for 10 months and 15 days, as the Chronicle reports. The extension, recommended by the Land Use and Transportation Committee on Monday, gives the Planning Department more time to examine the facilities' potential effects and develop regulations before the city considers approving additional projects. The vote follows a report released last week by the Planning Department that identified significant gaps in the city's understanding of existing data centers, including their electricity and water consumption, pollution, and effects on surrounding neighborhoods, as SFist reported previously. The department stopped short of recommending whether San Francisco should allow more facilities, but outlined several policy changes officials could consider, including restricting standalone data centers in residential and commercial areas and requiring developers to assess impacts on nearby communities. According to Mission Local, the report also recommended updating the city's definition of a data center, which currently relies on language dating back to 2001, to better align with the state's definition. The department's assessment examined the city's three standalone facilities but acknowledged that San Francisco does not maintain a complete inventory of smaller data centers operating inside other buildings. Data Center Map, meanwhile, identifies 15 potential facilities throughout the city, many of them downtown. Two of the larger standalone facilities are located along Paul Avenue in Bayview Hunters Point, a neighborhood that has experienced disproportionate air pollution for decades due to industrial operations, truck traffic, and a former PG&E power plant that closed in 2006. District 10 Supervisor Shamann Walton, who represents the neighborhood and introduced the original moratorium in October, said the city needs to understand how the facilities affect residents before allowing additional development. “We really don't know the impact of data centers to our communities,” Walton said before Tuesday's vote. The Planning Department's report also warned that larger facilities could place substantial demands on an electricity grid already approaching its transmission capacity. A 50-megawatt data center could use as much electricity as 25,000 new homes, potentially competing with housing, hospitals, and businesses for limited power resources, as previously reported. Other concerns include air pollution and noise from backup generators. Developers have explored potential data center projects at the shuttered SF Centre mall downtown and in Dogpatch. NOVVA, an existing facility at 400 Paul Ave. in Bayview, had also planned to expand from nine to 36 megawatts by 2028, but those plans are now on hold. The moratorium comes as San Francisco attempts to balance its ambitions to remain a center of the AI industry against the infrastructure demands of the facilities needed to support it. As the Chronicle notes, Mayor Daniel Lurie has made attracting tech investment part of his economic strategy, while labor groups have argued that data centers could create union construction jobs and help fund needed infrastructure improvements. In a letter Monday, Building and Construction Trades Council leader Rudy Gonzalez, who ran Supervisor Connie Chan’s campaign for US Congress, opposed a permanent ban, arguing that developers should have a path to approval if they meet enforceable environmental and labor standards and cover the costs of the infrastructure they require. He also urged the city to distinguish large commercial facilities from smaller research and development sites. Walton acknowledged the union's concerns and said he intends to involve labor and community groups in developing future restrictions. Per the Chronicle, public speakers at Monday's committee hearing, meanwhile, questioned whether data centers would deliver meaningful employment benefits, given the relatively small number of workers needed to operate them. Others raised concerns about pollution and the concentration of facilities in communities already facing environmental burdens. San Francisco now joins Oakland and Seattle in extending temporary restrictions while officials work on regulations. As SFist reported last week, Oakland supervisors also voted unanimously to extend that city's moratorium for another 10 months and 15 days, through October 5, 2027. Oakland is reviewing potential effects on its electricity grid, water supply, and air quality after receiving inquiries from developers, including Behring Companies, which proposed putting a data center inside a downtown office building. artigo.texto: ACME Solar Holdings Limited has announced the commissioning of an additional Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) component with a capacity of 52.32 MW / 209.28 MWh for its firm and dispatchable renewable energy project in Bikaner district, Rajasthan. The newly commissioned storage component is scheduled to achieve its commercial operation date (COD) on November 19, 2026. Following this latest development, the cumulative commissioned capacity of the project’s battery energy storage component has reached 247.67 MW / 990.68 MWh. The overall installed storage capacity of the project stands at 247.67 MW / 1,321 MWh, marking further progress in the company’s efforts to strengthen its renewable energy and storage portfolio. The project is being developed through a wholly owned subsidiary of ACME Solar Holdings Limited. The company has also entered into a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with SJVN Limited for the supply of electricity generated under the firm and dispatchable renewable energy project. The commissioning of the additional BESS capacity represents an important step towards improving the project’s energy storage capabilities and supporting the reliable supply of renewable power. Battery storage systems play a significant role in managing the intermittent nature of renewable energy generation by storing electricity and making it available when required. With the latest addition, ACME Solar continues to advance its integrated renewable energy development strategy, combining solar power generation with battery storage solutions. The project also highlights the growing importance of energy storage infrastructure in supporting India’s transition towards a more reliable and flexible renewable energy system. artigo.texto: SPRINGFIELD, Ill. (CAPITOL NEWS ILLINOIS) — Hundreds of residents and environmental advocates rallied at the state Capitol Wednesday to urge lawmakers to regulate data centers. The residents came via bus, car and Amtrak from around the state to call for passage of the POWER Act, a bill that would require data centers to pay to create the energy they consume, mandate transparency around water use, limit noise levels and diesel generator use, ensure local community benefit agreements, and more. The bill failed to progress during the spring legislative session, but advocates hope to see it passed during the veto session. “Illinoisans are tired of fighting alone for basic protections without help from the state legislature,” said Lori McKiernan, a local Springfield community organizer and Sierra Club member. “Time is up. Our legislators must take action on data centers.” Over the summer break, lawmakers have been meeting with environmental advocates, organized labor, and representatives of the data center industry to negotiate the details. The Senate Energy and Public Utilities Committee was set to hold a hearing on the POWER Act at 4:30 p.m. Wednesday. Sen. Ram Villivalam, D-Chicago, is the lead sponsor of the Senate bill. He called the roughly 1,000-page bill a “big solution” for a “big problem,” and described the legislation as the “most comprehensive data center legislation in the nation.” “You’re here because this matters,” Villivalam told the crowd. “When something affects your families, your homes, your neighbors, and of course our bills, your voices deserve to be heard.” Battling big tech Data centers have existed for years in Illinois, housing servers and hardware that store data and power the digital world, supporting email, video streaming and other web services. But in recent years, as major technology firms race to create generative artificial intelligence, they have begun to build hyperscale data centers — massive buildings and campuses that sometimes consume the energy of a small city. Their actual and projected energy consumption have driven up energy costs for regular residents and small businesses. The rally comes shortly after the release of two reports from state agencies proposed delaying the planned closures of 11 fossil fuel plants, as required under the state’s landmark energy bill, in order to guarantee enough energy supply to meet the growing demand. But environmental advocates don’t want to see the state’s landmark climate goals delayed in order to power hyperscale data centers. “Big tech, they’re counting on us to be intimidated by their big money. They’re counting on us to be overwhelmed by the fight in front of us,” Illinois Environmental Council organizer Cate Caldwell said at the rally. “But as I look at this crowd today, I think big tech should be intimidated by us.” There won’t be a vote this week, but lawmakers could take up the issue when they return for their final days of the veto session next month. Capitol News Illinois is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news service that distributes state government coverage to hundreds of news outlets statewide. It is funded primarily by the Illinois Press Foundation and the Robert R. McCormick Foundation.

artigo.texto: China is targeting 300 million kilowatts (300 GW) of installed new energy storage capacity by 2030, with an average storage duration of approximately three hours, under its latest policy roadmap. The target is part of the 15th Five-Year Plan New Energy Storage Implementation Plan, released on November 13 by the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) and the National Energy Administration (NEA). The plan aims to move the energy storage sector from policy-driven expansion towards market-oriented development and operation. The blueprint builds on the rapid growth achieved during the 14th Five-Year Plan period. China’s installed new energy storage capacity increased from around 3 million kilowatts at the end of the 13th Five-Year Plan to 136 million kilowatts. This expansion has strengthened the country’s ability to integrate renewable energy, improve power system stability and maintain electricity supplies during periods of peak demand. Under the new framework, authorities will focus on expanding storage applications across different parts of the electricity system while improving market mechanisms, industry management, industrial development and international cooperation. The plan identifies three major application areas: power generation, electricity grids and innovative business models. On the power generation side, energy storage will support large-scale renewable energy bases and improve the ability of renewable projects to participate in electricity markets. On the grid side, storage systems will help strengthen regulation capabilities, balance electricity supply and demand, and improve overall grid stability. The plan also encourages coordination between storage projects and emerging electricity business models. Grid-side energy storage currently accounts for more than 50% of China’s total installed new energy storage capacity. It is expected to remain a major contributor to additional capacity during the 15th Five-Year Plan period. According to an NEA official, future deployment will prioritise electricity supply security, renewable energy absorption and grid stability. To support these objectives, authorities plan to improve inventory management, introduce capacity-based electricity pricing mechanisms and guide the appropriate location of storage projects. These measures are intended to ensure that storage facilities are developed according to regional electricity requirements. Improving project profitability is another major priority. China’s energy storage industry has gradually developed a three-part revenue model based on capacity payments, electricity market transactions and frequency regulation auxiliary services. However, the government plans to strengthen these mechanisms to ensure more sustainable financial returns for project developers and operators. The implementation plan proposes better recognition of energy storage capacity value, including capacity tariff mechanisms for independent grid-connected storage projects. It also calls for improved charging and discharging price signals and more flexible peak-and-valley electricity tariffs that reflect actual supply and demand conditions. Industrial and commercial consumers, along with industrial parks, will also be encouraged to invest in energy storage solutions. The government will align the pace of capacity expansion with regional grid requirements, electricity price affordability and market absorption capacity. Through these measures, China aims to establish a commercially sustainable energy storage industry by 2030, with market mechanisms playing a greater role in investment decisions, project development and operational performance. artigo.texto: NTIA Adviser Floats Data Center Guidance for States; AT&T Executive on Permitting Bill With local resistance sinking data center projects, panelists weighed state guidance and federal preemption Akul Saxena NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 19, 2026 – The Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration has explored guidance states could adopt for data center development, a senior agency adviser said Thursday. NTIA’s senior adviser for strategy, Matthew Plaster, suggested states should ease reporting requirements for developers that invest in communities where they build. He did not mention a specific requirement. One benefit residents could retain after construction ends is training in a skilled trade, Plaster said at the Broadband Nation Expo here. Workers could use those skills on another project or start a business, such as an HVAC company, he said. Some developers already pay for that kind of training. In September 2025, 20 trainees finished a paid, four-week Amazon Web Services pre-apprenticeship at Hinds Community College in Mississippi, learning HVAC, electrical work, plumbing and fiber optics. AWS is investing $10 billion in two data centers in nearby Madison County, Miss., and thousands applied for the program. President Donald Trump’s July 2025 executive order, “Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure,” directs federal agencies to speed up permit reviews for qualifying projects. Each state would decide whether to adopt the guidance Plaster described. Federal permitting rules that supersede conflicting state requirements across all 50 states would let developers know before they apply which documents to file and when to expect a decision, said Giulia McHenry, senior vice president for public policy at telecommunications carrier AT&T. A clear permitting schedule would have the added benefit of notifying residents when they can comment. One potential bright spot, McHenry said, is the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a permitting overhaul that pairs electricity rate changes with reforms that would help carriers build “the level of connectivity we need to support AI,” she said. The bill would require data centers to pay the full cost of the transmission upgrades they need, and it cleared a Senate procedural vote on Nov. 9. Pre-zoned tech parks could speed local approvals States compete for data centers, but data center developers often reach a town without knowing what local officials will require to approve a site, said Lance Alvarez, vice president of development at NTT Global Data Centers, which builds and operates the facilities. Texas, for example, exempts qualifying data center equipment from its 6.25 percent state sales tax. Eligibility requirements include investing at least $200 million over five years and creating at least 20 qualifying jobs in the county. In Elk Grove Village, northeast Ill., Mayor Craig Johnson proposed setting aside several hundred acres for a technology park, Alvarez said. The land already had industrial zoning and power, water and sewer service, with no homes nearby. Developers evaluating a site would know at the outset which utilities were in place and which entitlements, the zoning approvals and permits a project needs, remained outstanding. The model suits smaller facilities, Alvarez said, but offers limited value for campuses that require a gigawatt of electricity. The Chicago suburb’s records show what local review can involve. Its plan commission scheduled a public hearing on a proposal from developer Prime Data Centers, which lists 13 campuses in North America and Europe. A separate application from Dallas-based Aligned Data Centers, which an investor group including BlackRock’s Global Infrastructure Partners bought for $40 billion in July, went before the village board for a special-use permit to operate at a particular site. Loudoun's $1.3 billion in tax revenue hasn’t won over residents Loudoun County, Va., projects $1.3 billion in local tax revenue from data centers in fiscal 2027. Residents considering another facility want to know what the county will do with the revenue, said Parker Slaybaugh, vice president at LINK Public Affairs, which advises developers seeking local approvals. He cited a new school, better emergency services or a lower property tax bill as benefits residents could judge for themselves. In March 2025, Loudoun supervisors amended the county’s zoning ordinance to require a special exception for data centers in three industrial districts. A developer proposing a facility in one of those districts now needs a vote from the county board even when the land already has industrial zoning. That wealth has not bought goodwill. Loudoun hosts 233 data centers, more than any other place in the world, and has the highest median household income of any U.S. county, $181,765. Supervisor Juli Briskman, who oversees the board’s land, zoning and economic policies, proposed a moratorium on new data centers in July. “We’ve become addicted to the data centers,” she said. Residents remain skeptical despite the benefits, said Slaybaugh, whose firm conducts public opinion polling. “Data centers are pretty well despised in Loudoun County,” he said.

artigo.texto: Loudon County Is the Data Center Capital of the World. Now It's Paused Building New Ones. Data centers have cut residents’ tax rates and funded schools. Loudoun’s board paused new approvals anyway. The nationwide data center backlash has reached the industry's home turf. On Tuesday night, the Board of Supervisors for Loudoun County, Virginia—the data center capital of the world—voted to pause approval for new data center projects for the next 10 months. The pause was passed in a 7–1 vote, with one supervisor abstaining. The measure will halt board approval for new data center and substation applications potentially until next September while the county develops new rules. Projects in the Route 28 tax district, a special commercial tax district in eastern Loudoun, are exempt. In the meantime, pre-approved projects can continue. The vote comes amid mounting concerns from residents over developments near residential areas, noise disturbances, air quality, and impacts on the electrical grid. "The fact of the matter is that this development of data centers has moved a lot faster than the board has been able to respond," said Supervisor Juli Briskman, who proposed the pause, according to reporting from Bisnow. "And we did have a lot of missed opportunities to respond and get this under control, as our constituents have been begging us to do, and this is a golden opportunity to do that tonight." Loudoun County has the highest concentration of data centers in the world, with around 233 of these facilities already up or under construction. As industry advocates pointed out during the meeting, this has brought immense economic benefits to the county. According to county data, data centers are expected to generate around $1.3 billion in tax revenue in FY 2027. Data center revenue alone is expected to make up roughly 40 percent of the county's total budget. This revenue has contributed to a steady decrease in the county's real property tax rate over the past decade. The rate has fallen to $0.805 per $100 of assessed value from $1.145 in 2016, making it the lowest rate in northern Virginia, according to the county. At the same time, the county increased funding for the school system by $105 million this year, thanks in large part to data centers. Board Chair Phyllis Randall, who voted in favor of the pause, acknowledged the economic benefits, but stressed that her duty to her constituents comes first. "I'm also an elected official, and I'm supposed to move to some degree with the constituents, so when constituents have switched, I'm not supposed to just say well three years ago you weren't saying that so I'm not going to do anything different," she said, according to reporting from local CBS affiliate WUSA9. Not everyone on the board was so convinced. Supervisor Caleb Kershner, who abstained from the vote, had some choice words for the measure. "This, ladies and gentlemen, is a pure political vote to try to win votes," he said. "This is really bad governance to do it this way. We expose ourselves to litigation." He argued that if developers successfully challenge the resolution in court, it could cost the county big time, citing a potential estimate of up to $60 million in legal costs. Even though he called the pause "legally defensible," the county attorney echoed Kershner's warnings about the potential threat of litigation. Despite their benefits, data centers have recently faced staunch opposition from local communities in the United States. On election night, localities across the country considered at least 40 ballot measures to rein in the industry, most of which passed. In the third quarter of 2026, construction of these facilities slowed down for the first time in a year, according to Cleanview, a data center research firm. Now, Loudoun County, which has felt the benefits of data centers firsthand arguably the most in the country, has voted to slow down the industry. If the data center capital of the world is having second thoughts, this could spell even more trouble for the rest of America's AI buildout.

artigo.texto: Oregon has more hyperscale data centers than all but one U.S. state, study finds Only Virginia beat the Beaver State for its number of “hyperscale” data centers and the demand they put on the power grid, a recent Harvard University study found. Oregon is home to the second-highest number of hyperscale data centers in the country, according to a consortium of researchers led by Harvard University. That means Oregon is also home to the second largest concentration of energy demand from the industry’s largest server farms. The team published its findings Monday in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Sustainability. It focused on hyperscale data centers because they are the largest, most powerful class of data centers designed to handle the largest computing and data storage loads, and are growing in number as the era of artificial intelligence unfolds. Analysts at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimate that hyperscale data centers will account for more than 90% of all data center electricity consumption by 2028. Researchers identified more than 400 total hyperscale facilities in the U.S. between May 2024 and April 2025, including 56 in Oregon. The researchers generally defined hyperscale facilities as housing several server-filled buildings of roughly 2,000 square meters each — about one-third of a football field — with an average energy capacity of 40 MW, meaning at any given hour they can use as much power as five American households use annually. Only Virginia, with 142 facilities, had more hyperscale data centers than Oregon. Ohio is close behind Oregon with 38 facilities. Hyperscale data centers in Oregon, almost entirely in the eastern half of the state, required 11.1 terawatt-hours of energy to operate, equivalent to the amount of electricity that could power more than 1 million American homes for a year. Oregon’s hyperscale data centers contributed to 1.3 million metric tons of greenhouse gas pollution, equal to the pollution from more than 300,000 gas-powered cars in an average year, according to the study. That’s less pollution than hyperscale data centers caused in Ohio or Iowa, which have fewer facilities but rely more on electricity powered by coal and natural gas. Rising energy demand from data centers and rollbacks in federal clean energy policies have knocked Oregon off track on meeting state-mandated climate goals, the Oregon Department of Energy shared in March. The study’s lead author, Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard University’s Department of Biostatistics, called the findings in a news release a “snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry.” “The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow,” he said. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.” Data center growth became a central issue in local and statewide political races during the last year, and several communities issued temporary moratoriums on new facilities. Oregon lawmakers and Gov. Tina Kotek are expected to propose new data center regulations during the 2027 legislative session that starts in January. Proposals could require more transparency around the facilities’ energy use, water consumption and on data centers’ access to property tax incentives meant to spur job growth in the state, according to Kotek and state lawmakers. Kotek in October also mandated state agencies cease issuing environmental permits for new and expanded data center construction, effectively putting a halt to projects for the time being. Umatilla County in eastern Oregon, where the state’s largest concentration of large and hyperscale data centers are located, has sued in response with the goal of restarting the permitting process. A September analysis from the consulting firm ECOnorthwest found that most of Umatilla County’s 22 data centers are hyperscale centers. Both the city of Umatilla and the county’s attorneys have asked a local judge to step in and overturn Kotek’s order pausing permitting. The team behind the Harvard study will examine the health effects of large-scale data centers on local communities, according to the news release, given concerns over data centers’ massive energy demand driving up greenhouse gas pollution and water consumption in many states. “When data centers draw heavily on fossil fuel power, the people living near and downwind of those power plants may bear health costs, even if they’re far from the data center itself,” said Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science initiative. This article was originally published by Oregon Capital Chronicle and used with permission. Oregon Capital Chronicle is part of States Newsroom and can be reached at info@oregoncapitalchronicle.com.

The partnership provides scope for further investment opportunities across Revera’s UK portfolio, including the 400 MW Kincardine BESS, and supports the UK's Clean Power 2030 Action Plan. The A&O Shearman team was led by partner Dan Graham and senior associate Arabella Robinson, with support from associates Ine Deblaere and Livia Gauntlett. The team also included energy, natural resources and infrastructure partners Edward Moser and Alexander Chenery, senior associates Saskia Volhard Martin and Arvindh Rai, and associates Kamilla Marianayagam and Aidan Swietochowski; tax partner James Burton, counsel Sorsha Taylor and associate Maria Clezy; antitrust partner Thomas Masterman and associate Amol Vani; and environment and sanctions partner Matthew Townsend and senior associate Danae Wheeler. Mas o quadro está mudando rapidamente. “Portanto, não é uma parcela grande das exposições, mas, é claro, vem crescendo relativamente rápido nos últimos tempos e também está contribuindo com uma parcela relativamente grande… dos novos empréstimos”, disse Buch em uma coletiva de imprensa ao apresentar o relatório anual do BCE sobre a situação do sistema bancário.

artigo.texto: Irondale sets rules for data centers before any are proposed, but resident raises loophole concerns Irondale is putting rules in place for potential data centers before any companies come knocking. The City Council voted unanimously to approve an ordinance regulating data center development after a second reading and a chance for residents to comment. Mayor James Stewart Jr. said no data centers have been proposed in the city, and no companies have expressed interest in building one. The regulations follow a six- to seven-month study led by a city councilor. Stewart said the goal is to prepare for potential development while protecting residents. Under the ordinance, data center companies must pay for any necessary power grid upgrades, keep noise within a specified limit and use a closed-loop cooling system. The ordinance also establishes a community benefit agreement intended to support schools, infrastructure and nonprofit organizations and requires the data center company to complete a certification every year to hold it responsible. Stewart said he hopes the ordinance will help residents make informed decisions about data centers while providing safeguards for the community. “A lot of this has to do with education,” Stewart said. “We’re hoping that the ordinance provides that information. It gives you the opportunity to be able to educate our citizens more, but then it also, at the end of the day, protects our community.” The mayor said three residents spoke during the meeting, and one opposed bringing data centers to Irondale. That resident didn’t want to go on camera but expressed concerns about specific language data centers can use to find loopholes around the established regulations. She also feels like the six-to seven-month study is outdated and so much has changed with data centers since it was done. She said she felt like a moratorium on data centers would’ve been better, but Stewart said that would only allow for the city to do more research, which it's already done.

artigo.texto: Georgetown panel recommends denial of rezoning for northeast data center after outcry GEORGETOWN, Texas — Georgetown's Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended denying a rezoning request Tuesday night for a proposed data center in northeast Georgetown, following opposition from residents concerned about the project's proximity to neighborhoods and future development. More than 100 people signed up to speak at Tuesday's meeting as commissioners considered a request to rezone approximately 28 acres near East University Avenue and Northeast Inner Loop. Commissioners ultimately voted unanimously to recommend denying the proposal, citing concerns about how close the data center would be to nearby neighborhoods and its potential impact on future development. Residents raised concerns about potential light and noise pollution, as well as how the project could affect the surrounding area. The proposal includes a data center, on-site generators and closed-loop cooling systems. A representative of the developer, Phillip Niels, said the project would use low-level lighting and was designed to limit noise compared to larger artificial intelligence data centers. ALSO| More camp safety law changes could be on their way in Texas Niels also said the project could generate millions of dollars in property tax revenue for the city. "If this project is built as planned, it will be the largest taxpayer in Georgetown," Niels said. "Should deliver 10 to 15 million dollars a year in property taxes." The rezoning request would increase the maximum allowed data center building footprint from 5,000 to 290,000 square feet. Among those opposing the location were Judy Fabry and Kerry Brun, who said they have lived about half a mile from the proposed site for more than 30 years. "It's too close to houses. It will ruin any other development in that area. And we need a grocery store out there," Fabry said. "There's a lot of downsides, I think. I don't even know what an upside of having a data center would be," Brun said. Despite the commission's unanimous recommendation to deny the rezoning request, the proposal is not yet officially rejected. Georgetown City Council is expected to consider the rezoning request and the commission's recommendation on Dec. 8. Because the Planning and Zoning Commission recommended denial, the City Council would need a 6-1 vote to overturn that recommendation and approve the rezoning request. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

artigo.texto: At their Nov. 19 board meeting, members of the University of Michigan’s Board of Regents have voted proceed in building a research computing center in collaboration with Los Alamos National Laboratory in Ypsilanti Township, amid outcry from community members. Regents approved the proposal 7-1, with Regent Paul Brown, who has previously emphasized the need for community consent of the project, against it. Brown said he believes U-M can identify a community that will welcome the project and asked regents to take pause before proceeding. As the regents approved the project, about 150 members of the community gathered outside Alexander Ruthven Building in Ann Arbor to protest the facility, which they describe as a data center. U-M categorizes the facility as a high-performance computing center. The vote took place during U-M President Domenico Grasso’s last board meeting before President-elect C. Cybele Raver will begin her five-year term Dec. 1. The board also approved a resolution to build a community partnership and $5M investment program intended to benefit residents of Ypsilanti Township. The partnership focuses on investments in education, parks and recreation, community organizations, infrastructure, environmental enhancement and public safety. Despite the resolution’s intent, Ypsilanti Township Supervisor Brenda Stumbo told The Eastern Echo that it does not represent true partnership with the community. Stumbo, the township trustees and other local leaders have been vocal in their disapproval of the data center, with formal opposition through resolutions and a utilities moratorium. As a public institution, U-M is exempt from local zoning laws, meaning the project doesn't require township approval to proceed. "I do not think this will meet the needs of our community because what our community needs is not to have Los Alamos, the research and development and brains of nuclear war," Stumbo previously told The Echo. "Because that will be the brand that we will forever be known for." Los Alamos National Laboratory, a research laboratory within the United States Department of Energy, is known for its central role in developing the atomic bomb. This association has been a point of concern for some residents. The inclusion of the community partnership resolution by the university was largely the result of community advocacy, Brown told The Echo after the meeting. So far, however, there hasn't been a good partnership between the university and the community, Brown said, so he understands frustration from residents and Stumbo. "I'm hoping we can do something that the community wants," Brown said. Part of the problem, Brown said, is both sides have raised meaningful points, be it the real benefits of the project voiced by the university or the valid concerns raised by the community. "Instead of acknowledging both of those facts, the university, I think, has kind of pretended like there are no negative consequences," Brown said. "I think if both sides acknowledge those things, then you can start to have a dialogue of ... Is there a way to do this project? And there might not be that is appropriate." Brown, who campaigned on the issue during his reelection bid in which he kept his seat on the board, said it can be difficult to be the lone voice of opposition on the board, but he hopes to advocate the position of Ypsilanti Township residents. "I don't begrudge my colleagues. There was massive pressure put on me ... the president came straight out and said: I want everybody to vote yes on this," Brown said. "You get alienated when you don't, but they respect my decision as I would theirs — as I do theirs." Regent Sarah Hubbard voted yes on the project, but said U-M needs to proceed alongside the local community, which is what she said the partnership resolution commits the university to doing. "Partnership works both ways, and to be a partner you have to both give something," Hubbard told The Echo after the meeting. "What we continue to hear from some in the community — not everyone — is just [opposition], and it's tough to have a discussion about a partnership when one side won't actually engage in the facts and the project." Through the partnership, U-M would also look to work with Eastern Michigan University, Hubbard said. She said even though U-M is in Ann Arbor, not Ypsilanti, the two cities are neighbors and there are joint benefits for both. Still, he acknowledged that tech companies need to âdo it better and partner more closely with our communities.â Given Nvidia is so central to the AI buildout, Jassy said he didnât think Jensen Huangâs departure would impact Amazon and pledged to continue working closely with the chipmaker. The growth in AI stems from âmore than one company,â he said. Nvidia GPUs help power AWS data centers and Amazon works with the chip giant on infrastructure and robotics. âTheyâll have to work out how they move forward as a company, but weâll be partners with them either way.â Jassy also said that Amazon, which currently doesnât let Metaâs Muse and other consumer agents access its site, is still talking to companies like Meta about how to open up the e-commerce giant to consumers who want to use the agents. He said the company would open up the site to agents if it could find a âgood exchange of valueâ and a positive experience for customers, which isnât happening at the moment.

artigo.texto: The data center capital of the world is pressing pause on legislative approvals for the digital infrastructure facilities through as late as September of next year. The Loudoun County Board of Supervisors voted 7-1, with one abstaining, Tuesday evening to halt consideration of legislative applications for data centers and substations, with a retroactive effective date of Sept. 15. Thirty-three legislative applications are currently active, according to the resolution. Supervisor Kristen Umstattd, who represents the Leesburg District, voted against the motion, and Supervisor Caleb Kershner, who represents the Catoctin District, abstained. "Just the fact of the matter is that this development of data centers has moved a lot faster than the board has been able to respond," Supervisor Juli Briskman, who proposed the review that culminated in the resolution, said just before the vote. "And we did have a lot of missed opportunities to respond and get this under control, as our constituents have been begging us to do, and this is a golden opportunity to do that tonight," added Briskman, who represents the Algonkian District. Loudoun County is in the second phase of its impact study that would establish new guidance and standards for data centers and substations. The result of that study is expected to be released next spring. The county's pause comes as communities across the U.S. are fighting to slow down the rapidly spreading asset class. Next door to Loudoun, Prince William County in September drastically shrank its map for data centers that are allowed by right. Montgomery County instituted an 18-month data center freeze in July. New York instituted a yearlong moratorium for large-scale data centers, also in July, and at least seven more states are considering similar measures, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Loudoun’s halting of legislative applications includes rezonings and special exceptions that need to be approved by the board. Administrative applications for things like site plans and subdivision plans would still be allowed to proceed. Data center moratoriums are not allowed in Virginia. But since the board has one year to review legislative applications under Loudoun's zoning ordinance, it's using that length of time to effect the pause. At Tuesday night's board meeting, Loudoun County Attorney Leo Rogers confirmed the legality of the pause that the county is undertaking, but said he does believe there is a "real threat of litigation" from data center applicants. The legislative effort dates back to July, when the supervisors asked county staff to look into whether instituting such a pause would be permissible. In September, after getting the green light from the county's attorney, the board voted to direct staff to draw up a resolution for the final vote. In March 2025, Loudoun took its first step in limiting data center development when it stripped by right zoning, requiring all data centers to go through a special exception process. Under that legislation, data centers in the works that had already been approved — 15 projects in the pipeline totaling 10.5M SF of development — can still proceed without going through that process. In 2025, Loudoun had about 53M SF of data centers, a 100% increase from five years earlier, according to county officials.

artigo.texto: Sistema OCB apresentou em Antália os inventários de emissões de 27 cooperativas agropecuárias; projeto de redução de metano em dejetos de suínos e aves está entre os exemplos Cooperativas lançam guia para o mercado de carbono na COP31 O Sistema OCB lançou na segunda-feira (16), na COP31, em Antália, na Turquia, o Guia para a participação de cooperativas no mercado de carbono. O material explica as diferenças entre os mercados regulado e voluntário, as oportunidades para cada ramo do cooperativismo e o que avaliar antes de desenvolver um projeto, como custos, exigências técnicas, certificação e viabilidade econômica. O lançamento ocorreu durante um painel sobre transparência climática no agro, no Pavilhão Brasil. Segundo o gerente de Relações Institucionais da OCB, Eduardo Queiroz, medir as emissões é o primeiro passo para a gestão climática no campo. A entidade já ajudou 27 cooperativas agropecuárias a elaborar inventários de gases de efeito estufa. No ciclo de 2026 do programa Neutralidade de Carbono, 13 cooperativas inventariaram 344 unidades e reportaram cerca de 190,3 mil toneladas de CO₂ equivalente. Doze desses inventários foram publicados no Registro Público de Emissões. “Não conseguimos melhorar o que não conseguimos medir. Precisamos avançar nos estudos, nas metodologias e nas certificações nacionais que reconheçam as particularidades da agricultura brasileira”, afirmou Queiroz. Leia também no Agrimídia: - •Brasil pode gerar 85 bilhões de m³ de biogás com resíduos agroindustriais - •ABPA celebra 50 anos da criação da ABEF e destaca trajetória das exportações brasileiras de carne de frango - •Inscrições para o Concurso de Qualidade de Ovos Capixaba terminam nesta sexta-feira - •Itamaraty busca reverter exclusão do Brasil da lista de fornecedores de carne de aves e mel da UE Exemplos no cooperativismo O guia traz casos já em andamento. Um deles é o programa do Sicredi para evitar emissões de metano no tratamento de dejetos da produção animal, com produtores do Paraná e de Santa Catarina, que evitou cerca de 45 mil toneladas de CO₂ equivalente entre junho de 2024 e novembro de 2025. Também são citados um projeto de cafeicultura regenerativa da Cooxupé, que sequestrou cerca de 650 toneladas de carbono com 12 cooperados, e o Projeto Carbono Reca, na Amazônia, que conserva cerca de 5 mil hectares de floresta e gera renda para cerca de 130 pequenos agricultores. O presidente da Frente Parlamentar da Agropecuária (FPA), deputado Pedro Lupion (PR), também participou do painel. “Precisamos superar narrativas que não representam a realidade da nossa agropecuária e apresentar os avanços do setor na produção de alimentos, na preservação ambiental e na responsabilidade com o meio ambiente”, disse. Fonte: Sistema OCB

In another development earlier this year, Juniper Green Energy fully commissioned its 150 MW wind-solar hybrid project awarded by Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited (GUVNL), following the commissioning of the final 5 MW wind turbine at the project site. The company had secured the project from GUVNL under a 500 MW tender through the greenshoe option. artigo.texto: Shelby Co asthma ER visits decline, as citizens question data center health impact Colossus One data center is not among the county’s major emitters, according to new health department data MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - Emergency room visits for asthma in Shelby County have declined from more than 20,000 in 2024 to just under 11,000 so far in 2026, the Shelby County Health Department announced during a meeting on pollution in Westwood on Wednesday night. The latest health department statistics also show Colossus One, the first SpaceXSI data center built in Memphis, is not considered one of the city’s biggest polluters. Data center critics have consistently cited worsening asthma in the community as their biggest health concern as gas turbines produce energy and pollution for Elon Musk’s data centers. The statistics presented at the meeting only apply to Colossus One in South Memphis. They do not apply to Colossus Two in Whitehaven, which is the world’s most powerful data center and is still expanding. Residents seek answers in Westwood Westwood is a community near the Colossus One data center in South Memphis. Residents have many questions since the data center boom in Memphis began in 2024. “Well, the biggest concern is pollution...,” Westwood resident Bettye Lewis told Action News 5. Clifford Lewis, also a Westwood resident, said, “It’s hard to tell whether some of the smells are coming from xAI or whether it’s coming from the waste treatment plant or another facility.” “First of all, I would say your concerns are legit,” said Dr. Bruce Randolph, interim director of the Shelby County Health Department, “I rode around yesterday along Stateline Road, Holmes Road and Tulane. I went through Boxtown and went by White’s Chapel. I rode through all of that to see for myself and you have reasons to be concerned. You’re right to voice your opinion. When I drove by TVA, I smelled the chemicals.” Major emitters named The health department listed these companies as the major emitters of pollutants in 2025: - Valero - Covoro Mining - Nucor Steel - The Allen Combined Cycle Plant - Mitsubishi Chemical The Colossus data center is considered a minor emitter. SCHD said the facility puts out less pollution than Kellog, Owens Corning, JM Smucker, Hershey and Exxon. “Yes, you should be concerned. But you need to be concerned about all of these major emitters, not just one,” Randolph said. Monitoring and testing Shelby County Mayor Mickell Lowery said the health department follows Environmental Protection Agency guidelines for measuring pollution. SCHD currently has 27 monitors at five locations. “But as the world changes…as technology changes…things may need to change as far as testing emissions, so we have to be on top of that,” Lowery said, “because if we don’t have a healthy community and we’re not protecting our water, our aquifer and our air, it’s for naught.” ZIP codes with most asthma ER visits These are the five ZIP codes with the highest number of emergency room visits for asthma year-to-date in 2026, according to SCHD: - 38127 – Frayser - 38109 – Southwest Memphis - 38128 – Raleigh - 38116 – Whitehaven - 38106 – South Memphis Poor communities are hurting the most. “We deserve to be healthy, wealthy, and wise,” said Dr. Karen Streeter, a newly elected Shelby County Commissioner now representing District 9. She organized the pollution meeting. More data centers planned The health impact of multiple data centers is still being studied. By the end of the year, SpaceXSI will operate six data centers in the Memphis metro area. “I’m not sure their pollution will be greater than what we already have...but hopefully, it will not,” Bettye Lewis said. How to report a concern Residents with a complaint or concern about something in their neighborhood can report it directly to the Shelby County Health Department at 901-222-9000. SCHD said it will send someone to investigate. To read the most recent SCHD report on environmental disparity, view it here: Click here to sign up for our newsletter! artigo.texto: The Hillsboro City Council voted Tuesday night unanimously to adopt Resolution 2941, extending the city’s temporary moratorium on new and expanded data centers and battery energy storage systems (BESS) for six more months. The vote came after a large crowd gathered at City Hall to be heard, with all testifying that the Moratorium passed nearly 4 months ago must be extended. Many of the same residents who have been boots on the ground all year showed up and spoke passionately, many holding nothing back. The extension extends the initial 120-day pause enacted in July—set to expire Nov. 24—and gives city staff time to complete environmental and economic impact studies before drafting a second phase of permanent land-use regulations. The council previously approved Phase 1 code amendments in October, restricting standalone data centers primarily to Industrial Park and Industrial Sanctuary zones and establishing a temporary 1,000-foot buffer from schools. While the 6–0 vote was unanimous—with Council President Rob Harris and Councilors Olivia Alcaire, Saba Anvery, Elizabeth Case, Cristian Salgado, and Kipperlyn Sinclair all voting in favor—the debate emphasized several policy questions and tensions on the dais. State Action vs. Local Protection: Councilor Salgado questioned whether extending the local moratorium was an unnecessary use of staff resources given Gov. Tina Kotek’s recent pause on certain state environmental permits and Enterprise Zone applications. City Attorney Chad Jacobs and planning staff clarified that state permits typically occur later in the development process and may not apply to smaller facilities. Without a local land-use moratorium, staff explained, a developer could still submit an application now to lock in Hillsboro’s current development code and wait out state-level pauses. Hillsboro’s Data Center Moratorium Overview: Funding and Study Timelines: City Manager Robby Hammond noted that the upcoming environmental impact study is expected to cost roughly $500,000 and will return to the council for contract approval within the next one to two months. Following a question from Council President Harris, Hammond confirmed that no General Fund dollars will be used; the vast majority of the cost will be covered by Enterprise Zone Community Service Fee reserves, supplemented by water funds for water-quality analysis. Staff said they are targeting four to five months for draft study deliverables to allow for public engagement within the six-month window. Salgado urged staff to include firm deadlines in the consultant contracts so residents do not have to repeatedly return to City Hall to advocate for further extensions. View this post on Instagram Battery Storage, Ethics, and Dais Tensions: Several councilors raised concerns that battery energy storage systems could be overlooked as consultants focus primarily on data centers. Councilor Sinclair requested that a BESS fire safety study and utility capacity data from PGE, Hillsboro Water, and Clean Water Services be incorporated into the process. Councilors Harris and Case also expressed interest in potentially decoupling BESS from data centers if battery storage regulations are completed sooner. Staff said they plan to evaluate BESS using national building code standards and in-house analysis, and confirmed the council could separate the two issues in the future. Sinclair also asked about ethics firewalls regarding the now-dissolved Silicon Forest Partnership, as well as the absence of a formal definition for “artificial intelligence” in the city’s development code. Economic and Community Development Director Dan Dias stated that while there could be overlap among regional consulting firms, the entities and scopes of work are separate and present no legal conflict of interest. View this post on Instagram Before the vote, Councilor Alcaire—noting it was likely her final official opportunity to address the issue—delivered a pointed rebuke of several colleagues on the dais, accusing them of failing to listen to residents and citing Forest Grove as a warning of siting data centers near wetlands. City staff will bring the environmental study contract back to the council for final budget approval in the coming weeks, with public review and Phase 2 code amendments expected to follow in 202

artigo.texto: ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov 19: Nepal is seeking to turn its institutional preparations for participating in the carbon market into actual carbon credit transactions and climate finance by expanding cooperation with international buyers, investors and development partners. A discussion held at the Nepal Pavilion on Wednesday during the UN Climate Conference (COP31) explored ways to attract investment through the National Carbon Registry and implement Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The event, titled 'Mobilising Climate Finance through Carbon Markets: Country Experiences, Challenges and the Way Forward', was jointly organised by the Ministry of Forests and Environment and UNDP Nepal. Government officials and carbon market experts from Nepal, Bhutan and the Philippines attended. Nepal launched its National Carbon Registry in March 2026 with technical and financial support from UNDP. The digital platform is designed to register carbon projects, record emission reductions, issue and transfer carbon credits, and ensure transparency in transactions. The registry provides the institutional foundation for Nepal's participation in international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which allows countries to cooperate and exchange emission reduction outcomes to help limit global warming. COP31 launches platform to track cross-border carbon credits Presenting Nepal's policy and institutional arrangements, Ministry Undersecretary Dr Prakash Singh Thapa explained the registry's operational procedures, requirements for project developers and potential participation of international buyers. However, participants cautioned that establishing an institutional framework would not automatically attract investment. Nepal needs a credible pipeline of carbon projects, stronger institutional capacity, transparent benefit sharing and international partners willing to purchase high quality carbon credits. Deepak KC, climate change and resilience programme analyst at UNDP Nepal, said establishing the registry was only the first step towards developing a carbon market. "The priority now is to operate the system effectively, develop a strong pipeline of high quality carbon projects, attract private investment and create a supportive policy and regulatory environment," he said. He added that carbon finance should be viewed as a means of mobilising investment for Nepal's climate and development priorities and implementing its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0, rather than simply trading carbon credits. Bhutan's experience also featured in the discussion. Yeshi Lhendup, deputy chief of Bhutan's Ministry of Finance, presented the country's progress in developing domestic carbon market regulations, policies and a national registry. Bhutan is working to connect its carbon market with international systems and increase participation by local communities and the private sector. Building on its experience under the Clean Development Mechanism, the country has moved some projects under the Paris Agreement framework and established bilateral carbon market cooperation with Singapore. It has also developed a separate platform to ensure transparency in carbon market activities and transactions. Another major challenge discussed was securing upfront financing for carbon projects. Their preparation, implementation, monitoring and verification require substantial investment. However, revenue comes only after emission reductions are independently verified and carbon credits issued, making initial financing difficult. Nasif Sofiane, regional lead for carbon pricing at the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), said innovative financing arrangements were needed to address the problem. Banks and investors are reluctant to commit capital without sufficient certainty about future project revenues. He also proposed combining smaller projects into larger investment portfolios. Nepal could, for instance, bring together brick industries, clean cooking technologies and small hydropower projects to attract investors and fund managers. Providing grants for project preparation, technical documentation and verification could also reduce investment risks and encourage private sector participation, he said. Representatives from the Philippines and international organisations, including Sandy Recabar of the country's Climate Change Commission and federal parliamentarian Kamal Subedi, also shared their views. Forestry, renewable energy, clean cooking technologies, electric transport, waste management and industrial energy efficiency are among the sectors with potential to generate carbon credits and attract investment in Nepal. Nepal's immediate challenge, however, is to move beyond institutional preparations and establish actual carbon transactions and investment partnerships through projects that deliver emission reductions alongside economic and social benefits.

artigo.texto: Imagem ilustrativa Documento cita risco para o abastecimento de água e questiona o protocolo de R$ 10 bilhões assinado com a Atlas Renewable Energy Moradores, trabalhadores e entidades da sociedade civil de Uberaba lançaram uma petição pública que exige transparência e a realização de audiências públicas antes de qualquer licença, outorga ou benefício municipal para a instalação de megadata centers na Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) da cidade. O documento é uma reação ao anúncio da Prefeitura de que assinou um protocolo de intenções com a Atlas Renewable Energy para um megacomplexo de data centers, com investimento previsto de R$ 10 bilhões. Segundo os autores, poucas semanas antes do anúncio, o telejornal MGTV 2ª Edição noticiou o fechamento frequente de reservatórios e o pedido oficial para que a população economizasse água diante da crise hídrica. Choque de datas O principal argumento da petição é o descompasso entre dois cronogramas. Comunicados da Prefeitura, divulgados por veículos como o JM Online e o Regionalzão, projetam o início da operação do data center para 2028. Já a Resolução ARISB-MG nº 298, do Codau, prevê a conclusão das operações do Sistema de Abastecimento do Rio Grande apenas em 2030. Ao cruzar dados de consumo médio de água de Uberaba, do SINISA, com levantamentos técnicos divulgados pelo The Intercept Brasil, os autores calculam que o consumo diário de um megadata center equivale ao de 2.200 até mais de 36 mil residências. Para eles, operar a estrutura antes da conclusão da obra do Rio Grande colocaria em risco o abastecimento das moradias durante a estiagem. Protocolo não garante obra A petição também ressalta que o documento assinado é uma carta preliminar, sem obrigação de execução. Segundo os autores, citando o The Intercept Brasil e a BNamericas, a Atlas já divulgou anúncios bilionários semelhantes em Paracatu (R$ 35 bilhões), no Norte de Minas e no Rio de Janeiro, em disputa por clientes globais que ainda não fecharam contrato. Empregos e capital Com base em estudo da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV), o texto afirma que 85% das vagas geradas seriam temporárias, restritas à construção civil, e que menos de 4% seriam empregos permanentes em galpões altamente automatizados, beneficiados por isenções fiscais da ZPE e do regime federal Redata. A petição afirma ainda que cerca de 80% do capital investido não permanece na cidade, sendo destinado à compra de servidores e chips importados. Conta de luz e precedentes Os autores citam levantamentos da CBS News e da NPR segundo os quais o custo de obras de expansão da rede elétrica para atender centros de dados costuma ser repassado à tarifa dos consumidores residenciais. Afirmam também que, em cidades vizinhas como Paracatu e Uberlândia, projetos semelhantes avançaram sem audiências prévias e hoje são alvo de questionamentos na Assembleia Legislativa de Minas Gerais (ALMG) e de investigações do Ministério Público Federal (MPF). O que os signatários pedem - Transparência total: divulgação da íntegra dos protocolos de intenções e das estimativas de consumo de água e energia, sem cláusulas de sigilo comercial sobre recursos públicos e naturais. - Audiências públicas amplas: convocação pela Câmara Municipal e pelo Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente (Comam), com participação de moradores, sindicatos, universidades, produtores rurais e especialistas independentes. - Condicionante hídrica: proibição de licença ou operação de data centers de alto consumo antes da entrada em operação efetiva do Sistema Rio Grande, com exigência de refrigeração em circuito fechado, sem perda de água por evaporação. - Contrapartidas reais: definição clara de benefícios sociais, ambientais e de qualificação profissional para a população local. “Uberaba não pode decidir o futuro da sua água e da sua energia a toque de caixa”, conclui o texto, que convida a população a assinar e compartilhar. A Folha Uberaba solicitou um posicionamento da prefeitura e assim que for atendido, será inserido na matéria O link da petição: https://www.peticao.online/data_centers_na_zpe_de_uberaba_debate_publico_imediato?utm_source=whatsapp A prefeitura de Uberaba respondeu ao questionamento, veja a resposta na íntegras: A Prefeitura de Uberaba respeita o direito de manifestação do cidadão e está à disposição da comunidade para prestar esclarecimentos e dialogar. Nesse sentido, o Município informa que o projeto foi concebido desde a origem para promover o uso eficiente e responsável dos recursos hídricos, adotando soluções que reduzem a demanda por água e evitam a utilização da rede pública de abastecimento. O fornecimento de água ocorrerá por meio de fontes independentes, sem demanda direta sobre o sistema público de distribuição que atende à população e estando de acordo com todos os requisitos e formas de controle da legislação aplicável. Durante a operação, o sistema de resfriamento funcionará em circuito fechado, permitindo a recirculação contínua da água e reduzindo significativamente a necessidade de reposição. O projeto também prevê o reaproveitamento de água proveniente da Estação de Tratamento de Esgoto (ETE) para atividades de serviços gerais, como limpeza e manutenção, reduzindo ainda mais a necessidade de utilização de água potável. A combinação dessas soluções demonstra o compromisso do empreendimento com a eficiência, o reaproveitamento e o uso racional da água. Além disso, a instalação do empreendimento depende, entre outras etapas, do licenciamento ambiental, processo durante o qual o Conselho Municipal do Meio Ambiente (Comam) se manifestará por meio dos seus membros, que representam diferentes setores, incluindo a sociedade civil.

artigo.texto: University of Dubuque students present semester-long data center research at community forum DUBUQUE, Iowa (KCRG) - As Dubuque County communities draft new zoning rules for data centers, University of Dubuque students shared semester-long research on the facilities with the public Tuesday night. The Data Center Community Forum at the Peter and Susan Smith Welcome Center featured projects from seven classes spanning aviation, environmental science, public policy, computing and theology. Junior Roland Preston, a flight operations and politics major from Des Moines, focused his research for his public policy and environmental ethics classes on the data center campus in Altoona, a facility he passes regularly on his drive home from college. “I chose the one in Altoona because I drive to and from Dubuque and back home in Des Moines, so I drive by that data center all the time,” Preston said. “So I wanted to actually take a look at that one specifically and kind of gather why was it built, what’s the impact on the local community, how’s the local community feel about it.” During his trips near the Altoona campus, Preston said he experienced firsthand one of the most common complaints raised by nearby residents. “If I get close to that campus in the Altoona area, you can hear it,” Preston said. “And I understand why people have concerns about it because it’s just this constant droning sound you hear. And I can imagine why it’s quite the inconvenience.” Dubuque County, the City of Dubuque and the City of Peosta all currently have temporary moratoriums halting data center construction while officials write ordinances governing water use, power demand and noise. Preston said those local pauses reflect how quickly the industry is moving compared to municipal policy. “This technology is outpacing our ability to regulate it,” Preston said. “And we need to stall it in its tracks right now, come up with a comprehensive way to regulate it, and then we can maybe allow it to keep happening.” “When Dubuque County, for example, talks about doing a moratorium on data centers, it is from that perspective that we have all these companies trying to come in ... and for them (the local governments) it feels like it’s the only way that they can put in meaningful regulation before companies start building,” he added. While Preston said he entered the semester with a favorable view of data centers, researching a specific facility gave him a more detailed understanding of community pushback. “When we talk about noise, talk about water issues, the impact on the community, I have a better understanding as to why people feel that way, especially now that I’ve taken a specific data center and looked at it very intentionally,” Preston said. Christine Darr, an associate professor of philosophy at the university, helped organize the forum after watching public meetings across the area grow increasingly heated. “We wanted to work together to help students understand a local issue, both locally and kind of nationwide,” Darr said. “We thought it would be a great opportunity to do some interdisciplinary work, so thinking about such a complex issue from a variety of perspectives, and then a great opportunity to kind of showcase our students and the great work that they do and offer something to the community.” Darr said combining fields like theology, aviation and environmental science was deliberate. “We thought it was an exciting opportunity to show how complex even something seemingly as simple as a data center might be,” Darr said. “And by bringing as many different disciplinary lenses, I think we did really kind of lift up all of the different ways that you can think about a particular issue, that nothing is one way or another way.” Following the student showcase, regional journalists Benjamin Fisher, Tom Kertscher of Wisconsin Watch and Grace Nieland of The Gazette held a panel discussion and Q&A on data center coverage and local policy. For Preston, presenting months of research to community members fulfilled a goal he set when he started college “It’s very nice researching something for months and then being able to talk to the public about it,” Preston said. Darr said she hopes attendees left the forum with a broader view of the debate. “I hope that people see that the issue is actually pretty complex, and also, I hope they walk away feeling as though they are part of a community that really cares about understanding issues, and trying to work together to understand things in a more nuanced way,” Darr said. The deal is a sign that, despite slowing demand for electric cars and the automotive industry’s shift toward low-cost cathode chemistries, high-performance silicon-based anode materials are finding niches in the battery market. Silicon is almost necessary to achieve the performance required for batteries used by the defense industry, electric aircraft, and data centers, says Charlie Parker, principal consultant and founder of the battery intelligence firm Ratel Consulting. “Silicon is driving these emerging applications.” Silicon anode materials can store more energy than the same amount of graphite, the material typically used in the anodes of lithium-ion batteries. They also allow batteries to charge faster and pump out energy at a higher rate. The main disadvantage is that silicon costs more than graphite.

artigo.texto: The “blue wave” election this month was not just a nationwide success for Democratic candidates at all levels of government, but also local candidates who stood up against hyperscale data centers — the high-energy usage facilities that fuel big tech’s artificial intelligence services. This was true in several local races around Kentucky where specific data center projects have been proposed over the past two years, as companies and developers sought to take advantage of generous new tax breaks passed in Frankfort. One key example was in Cave City, the small tourist city along I-65 in Barren County where locals have fought a company’s proposal for a data center using 1.2 gigawatts of power. Over the objections of two-term Mayor Dwayne Hatcher, the city council voted 4-1 for a moratorium on data centers, drawing a lawsuit from the developer. Clifton Parsley, one of the city council members who voted for that moratorium, decided to run against Hatcher on that issue and won by a wide margin, despite large ad spending by a mysterious PAC supporting the incumbent mayor. The lone council vote against the moratorium also lost his office by not finishing among the top six candidates. Just a half hour down I-65, Bowling Green saw a similar result, as its city commission had voted down a proposed data center moratorium this summer. The two commissioners who voted for the moratorium finished with the most votes, while a pro-moratorium candidate finished third to replace a member voting against it. Comparable scenarios played out in local elections near proposed hyperscalers in Mercer, Simpson and Mason counties, with pro-data center incumbents losing out to candidates either outright opposing them or calling for more transparency. One of those successful candidates was Beth Corea from the tiny city of Burgin in Mercer County. She was a local organizer opposing the city’s efforts to annex a large area of farmland for a hyperscale data center who decided to run for city council and won — swept into office along with a new mayor and council fully opposed to annexation. Corea, a first-time candidate, said these local election results should send a bipartisan message to elected officials, including state lawmakers in Frankfort. “People aren't buying into this two-party, Hate Inc., us-versus-them anymore,” Corea said. “The us-versus-them now is the community, the public, versus the multimillion-dollar developers, the multimillion-dollar corporations coming in trying to get these tax breaks and lax regulatory frameworks for what they're bringing in.” The Kentucky General Assembly’s new session begins in January, where they are expected to take up legislation to put regulatory guardrails on data centers and consider repealing their 50-year exemption from use and sales taxes. House Bill 593 from this year’s session was an effort to put regulations in place to protect existing ratepayers from data centers’ increased energy demands and uphold local rules on where they can be located. The bill, sponsored by GOP Rep. Josh Bray of Mount Vernon, passed the House by a wide majority, only to stall in the Senate after opposition from Louisville Gas & Electric and Kentucky Utilities, the state’s largest private utility company. At the Kentucky Chamber of Commerce’s legislative preview conference this week, Bray said he plans to push “a more robust version” of HB 593 in the 2027 session. Legislative candidates, including some in the GOP supermajority, even campaigned on repealing data centers’ tax breaks — a position promoted by U.S. Rep.
