artigo.texto: W.Va. Treasurer prioritizing teacher pay, data center tax distribution for legislative session CHARLESTON, W.Va. (WSAZ) - West Virginia Treasurer Larry Pack presented his legislative priorities Tuesday, ahead of the state legislative session that begins in January. Pack’s priorities include: - More tax revenue from data centers going to county commissions and school boards, rather than the state, as laid out in H.B. 2014 - Pay raises for public school teachers - Eliminating the business inventory tax - Term limits for Board of Public Works officers, which include the Treasurer, Attorney General, and Secretary of State. Data center tax revenue Pack began highlighting the issue that county school boards don’t receive revenue from data centers in the lead-up to the 2026 general election. “The only money the Board of Education can get, any Board of Education can get, with respect to these data centers, is if they have an excess levy in the county,” Pack told WSAZ in October. “If the excess levy goes away, then the Board of Education does not get any of the money, with respect to the data centers.” Pack’s focus on the issue was concentrated in Mason County, who stood to gain or lose $90 million per year from its two data centers depending on whether its school board tax levy passed. It did. Tuesday, Pack said he’s advocating for the state policy to change, so county school boards don’t have to worry about a levy passing to benefit from data centers. “What [H.B.] 2014 does is take money away from county school boards, takes money away from county commissions, and puts it into the general fund for the state,” he said. “At a time when our school boards are struggling, why would we take money away from school boards?” Under the current bill, the data center’s host county receives 30 percent of the tax revenue, while 10 percent goes to all other counties, and the rest goes to the state - 50 percent of the tax revenue goes to the state’s Personal Income Tax Reduction Fund. “We don’t have a county that has water to every household, or sewer to every household. We don’t have a county that doesn’t complain about EMTs or having enough sheriffs. Why would we take money away from county commissions? They’re on the front lines,” he said. Sen. Eric Tarr (R-Putnam) told WSAZ he supports that change, and that the money could be “transformative” for a county. “It can have generational impact for the families that are there now and the great-great-grandchildren of those counties,” he said. “You can go in and say, ‘OK, well, now that we have our needs met, what are our wants?’ ” Tarr believes the money from the data centers could allow counties to decrease taxes for their residents. “When you have such a significant tax base being constructed with outside money coming into West Virginia, the opportunity to reduce all that taxation is significant,” he said. “And you can really create a competitive environment for businesses coming in to locate into those counties. And then you can grow out from that.” Tarr added: “You’re going to see county after county figuring out ‘how can we get one here? How can we get one in our county?’” Del. Sean Hornbuckle (D-Cabell) agreed that the proposal could be a good idea, emphasizing his belief that local control is crucial in the data center debate. “If we’re going to even have data centers, [counties] need to make sure they have their fair share,” he said. “The way that [H.B. 2014] was written was that the majority of it goes back to Charleston. That’s just unacceptable.” Pay raises for teachers Tuesday, Pack offered his proposal for pay raises for all public school teachers: the new minimum salary would be $50,000, and any teacher already making that amount would receive a $2,000 pay bump. “We have to attract new teachers, we have to retain our teachers we have, and we have to be competitive with our surrounding states,” Pack said. “You can drive across the line in the Eastern Panhandle and make $10,000 or $15,000 more. What person wouldn’t do that to bring more money into their family? We need to make sure that we’re competitive.” Eliminating the business inventory tax Pack said Tuesday he wants lawmakers to propose a constitutional amendment that would phase out the state’s business inventory tax over five years. According to Pack, West Virginia is one of few states that have a business inventory tax, which he called a “job killer” and a “growth killer.” “If we want manufacturing jobs, if we want small business to grow, we need to get rid of this business inventory tax,” he said. Pack said the phase-out would cost $100 million, but believes the investment that would come as a result of the elimination would make up for the cost. “We think the county commissions and boards of education can absorb that because we’ll get more growth,” he said. “We’ll get more jobs. We’ll have more investment in West Virginia.” Copyright 2026 WSAZ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: O senador Márcio Bittar (PL-AC) questionou, nesta terça-feira (17), nas redes sociais, o impacto ambiental provocado pelo deslocamento de milhares de pessoas para participar da COP 31. Em manifestação sobre a conferência, ele criticou o que considera uma contradição entre o objetivo do evento, que é discutir medidas de combate às mudanças climáticas, e as emissões de carbono geradas pela própria realização. “Você não acha uma contradição milhares de pessoas viajarem até a Turquia, emitindo toneladas de CO₂ para participar da COP 31, exatamente uma conferência que pretende combater as mudanças climáticas?”, questionou o parlamentar. Para dimensionar o impacto, Bittar apresentou uma estimativa hipotética considerando cerca de 93 mil inscritos presenciais. No cálculo, ele considerou que 70% dos participantes teriam viajado de avião e que cada pessoa emitiria, em média, 1,5 tonelada de CO₂ nos trajetos de ida e volta. Com esses parâmetros, o senador estimou que as viagens aéreas poderiam gerar quase 100 mil toneladas de emissões. Para compensar esse volume, seriam necessários aproximadamente 100 mil créditos de carbono, considerando o valor hipotético de US$ 20 por crédito. A conta chegaria a quase US$ 2 milhões. Bittar ressaltou que a simulação considera apenas o deslocamento aéreo dos participantes. Ele também levantou questionamentos sobre as emissões geradas pela estrutura necessária para receber o público, incluindo circulação de veículos, funcionamento de hotéis, consumo de energia, alimentação e produção de resíduos. LEIA TAMBÉM: Marcio Bittar critica agenda do Acre na COP31 e dispara: “É uma humilhação” “Quanto carbono tudo isso representa? Quanto foi efetivamente compensado? Quantos créditos de carbono foram comprados e quem está pagando essa conta?”, perguntou. O senador também questionou a necessidade de reunir presencialmente milhares de pessoas e defendeu que parte das atividades poderia ocorrer pela internet, considerando os recursos tecnológicos disponíveis. Ele reconheceu, porém, que as negociações diplomáticas presenciais têm importância. Na avaliação de Bittar, os organizadores de eventos voltados ao enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas também precisam demonstrar compromisso com a redução das próprias emissões. “Se um discurso exige sacrifício da população, mas não vem acompanhado do mesmo compromisso por parte de quem cobra, como chamar isso, senão de hipocrisia?”, declarou. Ao final da manifestação, o senador afirmou que a responsabilidade ambiental deve começar pela transparência e pelo exemplo, cobrando informações sobre o impacto da conferência e as medidas adotadas para compensar as emissões.

Existing data centers tend to be much smaller than the massive ones being built for AI, and repurposing old infrastructure will require the industry to be âmuch more energy-efficient in the chips that we build,â Liang said. Still, he said, itâs good for the industry to get more value out of what it has available now. âTo distribute the data center into existing environments where power already exists, the infrastructure already exists, the cooling already exists and fits within the ecosystem â itâs not a bad way to do it,â he said. Compute is a precious resource for companies right now. Voice AI company ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski told Rappaport that âcompute constraintâ in the near term is a real possibility.

artigo.texto: An Indianapolis group tasked by city officials to draft zoning regulations for data centers announced its meeting schedule, including a Dec. 5 kick-off meeting. The Indianapolis Data Center Advisory Committee was created when the city approved a temporary moratorium earlier this year on new data center developments through the end of 2027. Three data centers have already been approved for Marion County despite community opposition. Data centers can be the size of a warehouse or multiple facilities filled with servers that store, process and transmit digital information. The developments are a controversial issue in Indiana and across the country because of concerns over water and energy consumption. As of last month, over half of Indiana counties have passed some form of local restriction on their development. The Marion County zoning rules are intended to regulate where data centers can be built, such as how close they can sit to homes and how much noise a building can generate. The Committee will hold five meetings and three “open houses” through next summer and focus on public health, cost of utilities, environmental impact and other issues related to data centers. The goal is for a draft zoning ordinance to be available for public feedback in June 2027. The first meeting will focus on Indiana’s regulatory environment and legal requirements for data centers. The committee, which is overseen by the Department of Metropolitan Development, wants the public to provide input throughout the process. The committee will use community feedback from the first meeting to shape later conversations. Last month, the department announced the committee’s makeup, including representatives from academic, community and industry groups. The membership expanded to include Megan Lapa from Protect Indy, a collective that includes groups of concerned citizens like Protect Pike Township. The committee’s final ordinance recommendation will go to the Indianapolis City-County Council and the Metropolitan Development Commission for consideration before the moratorium expires. Most of the committee’s meetings will be held on the second floor of the Indianapolis City-County Building. The meetings will be recorded and uploaded on the city’s website. DMD expects they will be livestreamed. Consulting and planning firm MKSK will lead the committee. The firm has previously done work on the Lebanon Leap Innovation District, which includes Meta's $10 billion data center campus. Indianapolis Data Center Advisory Committee schedule Saturday, Dec. 5, 2026, 11:00a.m. – 1:00 p.m. — Community Open House, John Boner Neighborhood Center, 2236 E. 10th St. Topic: Current Regulatory Environment and Existing Requirements. Register here. Tuesday, Dec. 15, 2026, 4-5:30 p.m. — Advisory Committee Meeting. Topics: Zoning Authority and Industry Innovation Wednesday, Feb. 24, 2027, 4-5:30 p.m. — Advisory Committee Meeting. Topics: Public Health and Sound Saturday, Feb. 27, 2027 - TBA — Community Open House. Topic: Public and Environmental Health Wednesday, April 28, 2027, 4-5:30 p.m. — Advisory Committee Meeting. Topic: Draft Ordinance Recommendations Wednesday, July 28, 2027, 4-5:30 p.m. — Advisory Committee Meeting. artigo.texto: Jasper residents get a crash course on data centers, but some say the presentation leaned one-sided JASPER, Ind. (WFIE) - Dubois County residents got a closer look at data centers Tuesday night, but some who attended said the event wasn’t as neutral as advertised. Officials and developers gave a presentation Nov. 17 at Jasper’s Thyen-Clark Cultural Center. They explained what data centers are and how they work, and they weighed the pros and cons. Nancy Eckerle, executive director of the Jasper Chamber of Commerce, said she hoped people came with open minds. “I hope people are just educated and informed that they come here with an open mind that they are not biased in their opinion, but maybe they learned something. Maybe they learned something. They didn’t know if they were against data centers maybe they’ll learn something that will just open their eyes a little bit and if they’re definitely for them, they may learn something that says you know maybe we don’t need that here or whatever it might be.” Presentation focused on property values, water and power The night’s main speaker was Paul Wyman, owner of The Wyman Group, a full-service real estate firm in north central Indiana. He went into detail on how data centers affect property values, water and power. Officials said the event was meant to be a neutral learning experience. Many in the audience said it wasn’t. They said they felt a bias in favor of data centers. Jasper resident Maggie Stimming said she agrees data centers are coming, but she questioned some of what she heard. “I agree with him that we are going to have data centers. I don’t think there’s any doubt about that. We’re not gonna turn the clock back. The horse is out of the barn and we will have data centers, but how we do them is I think what he was trying to get across how we do them and that’s a good point to make however, some of his examples I felt were not really very good.” Environmental questions dominate Q&A After the presentation, many in the audience asked questions. Many of them focused on how data centers would affect the environment. Others asked why demand for data centers is so high in the area. Some residents left concerned. They said many environmental topics were not addressed. Jasper resident Rock Emmert said diesel pollution was his biggest concern. “He touched on a lot of reasons and methods how communities can demand the best possible like the best practices or the best available control technology but he didn’t address about the pollution aspect of diesel. That was my biggest concern about the whole presentation. Absolutely zero concern for public health and pollution.” Now again, this was just meant to be an educational experience, and no plans for a data center were discussed. But if one ever comes, we will keep you updated. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: AUBURNDALE, Fla. — The city of Auburndale is considering a pause on future data centers. This comes after the city received major pushback from the community over a proposed facility near Florida Polytechnic University. The project, known as the Auburndale Technology Center, would be housed inside two existing warehouses at 810 and 820 Pace Road. Since news broke about the data center earlier this month, Audrey Meadows and her husband, Daniel, have been focused on learning what could happen to their home. “Because we’re retired, we don’t get to leave every day and go away somewhere else. We have to live in it,” Audrey said. The Army veteran says she moved back to the rural area in 2018 to help take care of her mother. Her property has been passed down through generations, like many of the other homes along Marker Road. “Everything is all at least third generation. So, they’re not homes that ever come up for sale out there,” she said. “They get passed down through the family.” Meadows says her sons are supposed to be next in line, but she’s concerned the Auburndale Technology Center could move into the warehouses less than a mile away. “In five years from now, are they even going to want to live in it? And then can you sell it? Nobody else will buy it if it’s too noisy for you to live in,” she said. Texas-based development company Hillwood says the data center would have lower sound levels than a typical warehouse of its size. The facility is also expected to use less water than originally approved and have its own power supply through TECO. But after hearing from residents, Auburndale City Manager Jeffery Brown says leaders are considering a moratorium on future projects. “It would give us time to strengthen any shortcomings we find in our policy,” he said. “It would give us time to look at other places that have ordinances in place and pick the best of those to bring into an ordinance here.” Brown says that pause wouldn’t apply to the Auburndale Technology Center. The project is already in the permitting process, and the property is zoned to allow a data center. But Brown says the city will continue to make sure developers comply with local and state regulations. “One of the things we still have to do, we have to review the site plan, work with Hillwood on any deficiencies that are in that site plan,” he said. “We still have to get a consumptive use permit and approval through SWFWMD based upon the Florida statutes that show that it’s encumbering the city’s water system, or if it was, then what improvements have to be made to the water system that would be on Hillwood’s dime.” But Meadows believes the project should be put on hold until leaders come up with additional guidelines before it’s too late. “They’re rapidly hitting the point of no return,” she said. “Once that’s in, you can’t go back to make it a warehouse.” The city expects the moratorium to come before commissioners by the end of December, with a potential final vote in January. The public will have an opportunity to comment during both meetings.

artigo.texto: Swedish private markets fund manager EQT is acquiring US battery energy storage firm Flatiron Energy from Hull Street Energy (HSE). EQT said it has agreed to acquire Flatiron through its EQT Transition Infrastructure fund without disclosing financial terms. Flatiron, which was founded in 2021, develops and operates utility-scale energy storage projects across New England, New York and Mid-Atlantic power markets. Since HSE’s initial investment in 2022, Flatiron has expanded its portfolio nearly tenfold to 24GWh of capacity, been awarded 6GWh of long-term contracts and has 2GWh of batteries under construction. Flatiron joins an existing EQT battery storage platform that comprises Statera Energy in the UK and Ju:niz Energy in Germany. Benjamin Bygott-Webb, partner at EQT, said: “Battery storage has become essential to keeping the grid reliable and electricity affordable, as an ageing grid, a changing generation mix and rapidly growing power demand continue to put the system under strain. Flatiron has secured scarce, well-located sites and built a strong record in the communities where it operates. “Building on EQT’s deep experience investing in critical infrastructure, our expertise in scaling energy platforms and the opportunities for collaboration across the EQT infrastructure portfolio, we look forward to supporting the Flatiron team as they deliver their projects and bring more firm capacity to the region.” Sarah Wright, founder and managing partner at HSE, said: “This transaction underscores HSE’s approach to identifying attractive opportunities and creating long-term value in a rapidly growing and decarbonising power sector. “HSE is highly selective about the management teams we back, and Flatiron is an excellent illustration of why this matters. Because the Flatiron team has a strong track record in the sector and a rigorous, fundamentals-driven approach to setting strategy, they have been able to deliver material growth and value accretion.” Rob Brink, CEO of Flatiron Energy, said: “We started Flatiron with the mission to bring reliable energy where it’s needed most, in the communities that rely on it every day. “EQT is an exceptional firm with a strong track record of scaling platforms in the energy transition, and we couldn’t be more excited to partner with them on our next stage of growth.” Simpson Thacher & Bartlett and Santander served as legal and financial advisers to EQT, respectively, while Kirkland & Ellis and Guggenheim Securities advised Flatiron Energy. Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath acted as legal counsel to HSE. To read the latest IPE Real Assets magazine click here.

artigo.texto: PowerX, Averroes to explore BESS opportunities in the Gulf region November 20 (Renewables Now) - Japanese battery systems maker PowerX Inc 485A will partner with Dubai-based tech company Averroes Tech Manufacturing to explore supplying its battery energy storage systems (BESS) to the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) market. Under the agreement, the two companies will jointly identify BESS projects and offer PowerX’s containerised battery solutions, including the 10-foot Mega Power 2500 and 20-foot Mega Power 4000, along with the Grid Connector package, which combines a power conversion system, transformer and switchgear. The configuration will depend on each project's requirements, PowerX announced on Thursday. The Japanese manufacturer will provide the equipment and design and technical specifications. Averroes will be in charge of customer engagement, local permitting, installation and after-sales service. “This partnership brings advanced Japanese battery energy storage technology and engineering to the GCC. For Averroes, it is the first step in long-term Japanese–GCC industrial cooperation, supporting the region’s energy security, grid resilience and the integration of renewable energy,” said Abdullah Ahmad AlFarhan, Co-Founder & Executive Director of Averroes. PowerX noted that the collaboration will start with joint sales activities and, if proven successful, can include a joint venture and local assembly in the region.

artigo.texto: Tobay Energy Development announced plans to create Long Island’s first utility-scale battery energy storage project not using lithium-ion. The compamy made the announcement on November 19. This project will employ a 5-megawatt (MW) flow battery that will not be subject to thermal runaway. To date, all similar projects proposed or operating on Long Island rely on lithium-ion battery systems. The proposed grid-connected facility, located on eastern Long Island, is designed for 5 MW of AC power capacity and four hours of discharge, equivalent to 20 megawatt-hours (MWh) of energy storage. The project may qualify for New York’s Value of Distributed Energy Resources (VDER) compensation mechanism, subject to applicable requirements and project-specific review. Tobay has begun preliminary project development, beginning with an evaluation of the interconnection with the grid, a key first step. The company said that there are many safety concerns around lithium-ion battery systems, particularly in densely populated communities. Tobay is proposing an alternative battery technology intended to address those safety concerns with a product not subject to thermal runaway, while providing the potential grid benefits of energy storage, including support for the reliability and flexibility of Long Island’s electric system. Many parties have objected to battery projects because of their large size and impact on the community. At 5 MW, the project contemplated by Tobay would have a much smaller footprint than proposals in the 40-100-plus MW range. This project is expected to sit on about one-quarter of an acre. While there has been opposition to battery projects and moratoriums in many townships across Nassau and Suffolk counties, this new technology option is designed to address the ongoing public and local government safety concerns while complying with applicable interconnection, zoning, permitting, and fire-safety standards. “We realized that community groups and town zoning boards will want to learn more about this project and how they differ from lithium-ion batteries.” Tobay President Larry Siegel said, “We look forward to working with all parties to advance this project to support the Long Island grid and the environment in a safer way.” “We are looking forward to advancing other projects on Long Island and are actively seeking landowners interested in lease revenue,” Siegel added. “We are working with not-for-profits and commercial owners who want to monetize unused space.”

artigo.texto: Publicidade As novas restrições impostas pelos Estados Unidos à exportação de chips avançados para inteligência artificial adicionaram uma nova fonte de preocupação para os planos de expansão de data centers no Brasil e podem representar um obstáculo para a WEG (WEGE3), na avaliação do Bradesco BBI. A partir de 16 de novembro, fornecedores passarão a precisar de autorização do governo americano para exportar ao Brasil determinados processadores utilizados em data centers. A medida também alcança chips fabricados fora dos Estados Unidos quando desenvolvidos com tecnologia americana e faz parte dos esforços de Washington para evitar que empresas chinesas utilizem operações em terceiros países para contornar restrições tecnológicas impostas à China. Segundo a regulamentação do Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), Brasil, Singapura, Tailândia, Malásia e Indonésia foram classificados como países com risco acima do normal de desvio ilegal desses componentes para a China e Macau. Para o BBI, a notícia tem leitura negativa para a WEG, embora o banco não veja, por enquanto, necessidade de alterar suas estimativas, recomendação equivalente à compra ou o preço-alvo de R$ 62 para a ação. Na avaliação dos analistas, as restrições podem desacelerar a implementação de alguns projetos de data centers justamente em um momento em que o governo brasileiro tenta atrair investimentos para o setor por meio do programa ReData. Como a companhia fornece uma ampla gama de equipamentos para esse mercado, eventuais adiamentos poderiam postergar parte da demanda por seus produtos. O banco ressalta, contudo, que o impacto ainda é incerto e dependerá de fatores como a estrutura societária dos projetos, os usuários finais dos chips e as aplicações pretendidas. Além disso, a regulamentação prevê exceções para operações ligadas a empresas americanas e não representa uma proibição total das exportações para o Brasil. Continua depois da publicidade A preocupação surge em um momento de forte expansão do mercado local. Dados da Abinee citados pelo BBI mostram que as importações brasileiras de semicondutores somaram US$ 6,8 bilhões entre janeiro e setembro, alta de 51% na comparação anual. JPMorgan vê fundamentos intactos Apesar das preocupações de curto prazo envolvendo data centers, o JPMorgan segue otimista com a tese de investimento da WEG e reiterou recomendação overweight, equivalente à compra, elevando o preço-alvo para R$ 66 ao fim de 2027, ante R$ 56 anteriormente. O novo alvo implica potencial de valorização de cerca de 30% em relação aos níveis atuais. Para o banco americano, a empresa continua bem posicionada para acelerar o crescimento nos próximos anos, com expectativa de expansão da receita de 23% em 2027 e de 21% em 2028, depois de um crescimento estimado de apenas 3% em 2026. A tese é sustentada principalmente pelos negócios ligados a transformadores, sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS) e motores elétricos. Continua depois da publicidade Outro ponto destacado pelo JPMorgan é a proteção natural que a companhia possui contra a desvalorização do real. Mais de 60% das receitas da empresa são geradas fora do Brasil, sendo cerca de 30% provenientes da América do Norte. Segundo os cálculos do banco, cada depreciação de 5% do real acrescenta aproximadamente 4% ao EBITDA (lucro antes de juros, impostos, depreciações e amortizações) projetado da companhia. O JPMorgan também revisou para cima suas projeções financeiras após incorporar um cenário de câmbio mais depreciado. O banco elevou suas estimativas de EBITDA para 2027 em 6% e passou a trabalhar com crescimento de 27% nessa linha, além de prever lucro líquido e receitas acima do consenso de mercado para 2027 e 2028. Na visão dos analistas, a ação ainda negocia a múltiplos considerados atrativos, com desconto de cerca de 15% em relação à média histórica do período pós-pandemia. O banco argumenta ainda que a empresa tende a se beneficiar do atual ambiente doméstico por ser vista pelos investidores como uma companhia de alta qualidade, forte exposição ao dólar e menor dependência do ciclo econômico brasileiro. artigo.texto: SUBTULO: Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente busca análise do CNPEM, CPQD e PUC-Campinas sobre consumo de recursos e interferências em pesquisas científicas O Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente de Campinas (Comdema) publicou ofícios no Diário Oficial para convidar o CNPEM, o CPQD e a PUC-Campinas para avaliarem os impactos ambientais e nas atividades científicas do projeto de um mega data center na Fazenda Pau d'Alho, em Barão Geraldo. O empreendimento, da empresa Terranova, tem previsão de início em 2027 e pode alcançar 400 megawatts de capacidade até 2029, o que representaria 40% da capacidade atual de processamento de dados no Brasil. A Unicamp também participa das discussões por meio de pesquisadores. O Comdema está organizando um grupo de trabalho com especialistas em tecnologia, energia, recursos hídricos, legislação e saúde para apresentar um relatório técnico em até 90 dias. O conselho busca esclarecimentos sobre o consumo de até 3,24 milhões de litros de água por dia, a demanda de eletricidade, o aumento da temperatura no entorno, ruídos e vibrações que possam afetar equipamentos científicos sensíveis, além do descarte de resíduos eletrônicos e impactos urbanísticos. A Terranova informou que utilizará um sistema de refrigeração em circuito fechado para reduzir o consumo hídrico. A proximidade com o CNPEM, onde funciona o acelerador de partículas Sirius, motivou a consulta específica sobre vibrações e interferências. O CPQD foi convocado para avaliar eficiência energética e descarte de resíduos, enquanto a PUC-Campinas colaborará em análises ambientais e urbanísticas. Em agosto, o Comdema solicitou a suspensão dos licenciamentos da subestação de energia devido às preocupações com os recursos hídricos e elétricos. O Ministério Público de São Paulo (MP-SP) instaurou um inquérito civil em setembro para apurar a regularidade do projeto após denúncias. A Prefeitura de Campinas informou que apenas a subestação recebeu autorizações até o momento, seguindo a legislação municipal. artigo.texto: Coalizão Direitos na Rede contesta PL que prevê incentivos a data centers no Norte e Nordeste PL 305/2026 prevê redução de tributos e prioridade em linhas do BNDES. Entidade cobra avaliação dos impactos sobre as comunidades. A Coalizão Direitos na Rede (CDR) manifestou-se hoje, 19 de novembro, contra o Projeto de Lei 305/2026, que prevê incentivos fiscais e prioridade no acesso a financiamento público para data centers de médio e grande porte nas regiões Norte e Nordeste. Em nota, a entidade pede que o Congresso debata as contrapartidas exigidas dos operadores e a proteção das comunidades afetadas antes de avançar com a proposta. Apresentado em 4 de fevereiro pelo deputado Duda Ramos (Pode-RR), o projeto cria o Programa de Desenvolvimento de Data Centers Regionais (Prodata Brasil). A proposta tem entre seus objetivos atrair investimentos, reduzir desigualdades regionais e fortalecer a soberania digital. Para a CDR, a instalação dos servidores, por si só, não assegura empregos duradouros, pesquisa científica ou desenvolvimento de tecnologia no país. “Não somos contra o desenvolvimento tecnológico nem contra investimentos em infraestrutura digital. Somos contra um modelo que oferece benefícios ao setor privado antes de garantir direitos, proteger os territórios e assegurar que a riqueza e o conhecimento gerados permaneçam no Brasil”, afirma Alexandre Arns Gonzales, integrante do DiraCom, entidade que compõe a coalizão. Projeto vincula benefícios a metas de investimento e emprego O PL prevê redução temporária do Imposto de Renda da Pessoa Jurídica (IRPJ) e da Contribuição Social sobre o Lucro Líquido (CSLL), regimes diferenciados de PIS/Pasep e Cofins sobre bens de capital e depreciação acelerada de ativos. O artigo 6º condiciona os incentivos ao cumprimento de metas de investimento, operação, geração de empregos e manutenção da atividade econômica na região. Caberá ao Executivo definir os parâmetros mínimos de investimento e os mecanismos de avaliação. Os empreendimentos enquadrados teriam prioridade de acesso a linhas de financiamento do BNDES e a instrumentos de apoio à inovação da Finep. A União também poderia priorizar a expansão de redes de fibra óptica, cabos submarinos, redes de transporte de dados e pontos de troca de tráfego para atender aos polos. Coalizão cobra avaliação de impactos e consulta às comunidades O artigo 10 prevê uso prioritário de fontes renováveis de energia, adoção de sistemas para reduzir o consumo de água e gestão de resíduos e equipamentos. A CDR considera essas diretrizes insuficientes e cobra avaliação dos impactos cumulativos dos empreendimentos, participação das comunidades afetadas e consulta prévia, livre e informada aos povos indígenas, quando aplicável. A entidade relaciona a manifestação à sua oposição ao Redata, objeto do PL 278/2026. Na avaliação da coalizão, as duas propostas levantam a mesma questão para o Congresso ao prever incentivos ao setor antes da definição de salvaguardas socioambientais que a entidade considera necessárias. O PL 305/2026 foi distribuído para apreciação conclusiva pelas comissões de Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação, de Integração Nacional e Desenvolvimento Regional, de Finanças e Tributação e de Constituição e Justiça e de Cidadania da Câmara.

artigo.texto: UK steel set to gain from EU carbon market link, but UK border rules lag EU – analysis Linking the UK and EU emissions trading scheme will benefit the UK steel industry, according to a new report commissioned by the ECIU drawing on analysis provided by CBI Economics. By Tom Cantillon info@eciu.net Share Last updated: Around two-thirds of UK steel exports, by value, go to the EU and successfully linking the schemes would exempt UK steel exports to the EU from carbon border charges, helping to protect approximately £3 billion of steel exports each year and avoid costs that the Government estimates could reach £800 million annually across affected sectors. It may also mean that carbon charges on UK steel production would continue to be paid into the UK ETS, and could fund public services, rather than part of them being collected at the EU border through the EU CBAM. In turn, the UK would not apply its own CBAM to steel imported from the EU. The report analyses the UK’s own Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which is due to start on 1st January 2027, and identifies several ways in which its design differs from the EU’s, including default emission values that do not vary by country of origin until 2029. This could better protect the UK steel industry from competition from higher-carbon steel imports Tom Cantillion, Senior Analyst, at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, said: “Not only would linkage of the UK and EU emissions trading schemes benefit UK industry by reducing red tape, it would also mean more of the carbon charges would stay in the UK – and could fund schools and hospitals. “The UK CBAM should arguably have been put in place years ago, is already running a year behind the EU’s and is simply not as strong. But both policies will provide protection to domestic steel production from cheaper, dirtier imports while pushing other countries to clean up to compete. It’s just one of the many ways, like leading the world on offshore wind, that the UK can have impact on climate change beyond its borders. “As the UK switches to electric arc furnaces, powered by ever more renewables, it gives our steel a clean competitive advantage as demand for green steel rises. Carbon pricing is spreading rapidly and is increasingly the norm with South Korea, China, Japan, India, Vietnam and California all having introduced or introducing schemes. [2]” Globally, commitments to reach net zero emissions cover around 84% of GDP [3]. Previous analysis has found the UK could develop many more electric arc furnace (EAF) steel plants to process UK scrap - that would otherwise be exported to places such as Turkey - to meet our own growing demand in housing, renewables and pylon construction [4]. ENDS Notes to editors: - The report was prepared by ECIU drawing on analysis by CBI Economics. The views and conclusions are those of ECIU. CBI Economics is the independent economic consultancy arm of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), providing independent, data-driven research and analysis to public and private sector clients. Its work applies robust economic methodologies tailored to client objectives, while operating independently from the CBI’s member-led policy and advocacy functions. CBI Economics delivers objective analysis and insights, with findings and conclusions reflecting its own evidence-based assessment. For information about this analysis or enquiries about carrying out similar research, contact cbieconomics@cbi.org.uk. - https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/64c7e4b9-bdd4-4761-9f3f-35fcccb4b7ef - https://zerotracker.net - https://eciu.net/media/press-releases/taxpayer-owned-steel-faces-ticking-clock-to-capture-britains-green-steel-boom

artigo.texto: As Electorate Rejects Terrestrial Data Centers, Satellite Industry Considers Space Compute Small onboard computers could analyze satellite imagery to flag crop problems for farmers and identify potential threats for defense agencies Akul Saxena NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 18, 2026 – Voters in 10 states backed restrictions on data center development on Nov. 3. Satellite executives say those restrictions strengthen the case for putting some computing equipment in orbit. Executives at the Broadband Nation Expo and Data Center Excellence event here took up what that rebuke means for computing in space Wednesday. Early compute applications Satellites collect more imagery than their radio links can send to Earth, said Rick Ward, founder and chief technology officer of OrbitsEdge, a Central Florida startup developing small computers that other companies can carry aboard their satellites. Processing the imagery in orbit and sending down only the results gets around that bottleneck. For a farmer, it’s the information that’s useful. “They need the information, not necessarily the pictures,” Ward said. Defense agencies are likely early customers, Ward said. Builders cannot start with gigawatt data centers, he said, so the first computing tasks have to be small ones where processing on board pays off. Early warning is another use case. A satellite that analyzes its own sensor data can send down an alert instead of raw imagery, skipping the wait to move the pictures to the ground first. "If you're doing something like Starshield, you need early warning protection first," Ward said. Starshield is SpaceX’s satellite line for government agencies. OrbitsEdge’s Edge1 design weighed less than 4.4 pounds and required 10 watts from its host satellite, Payload reported in June 2025. Meanwhile, Elon Musk’s rocket company applied to the Federal Communications Commission in January to operate up to one million data center satellites. That is about 59 times the 16,910 satellites the European Space Agency counted in orbit at the time, Broadband Breakfast reported. Moving from small onboard computers to facilities serving customers on Earth requires overcoming three major constraints: Cooling, launch costs and transmission delays. The case for orbit starts with scarce power on the ground A data center brings modest value to the town that hosts it, even when its value to the country is large, Ward said. That mismatch has made the facilities a hard sell locally, and it is the case for orbit, he said. Power is the other terrestrial bottleneck. A data center goes up in about two years, Ward said. Two nuclear reactors, by contrast, took close to 20 years, he said. For example, the two reactors at Georgia Power's Plant Vogtle took 15 years and $36.8 billion before entering service in 2024, took 15 years and $36.8 billion before entering service. Until new plants arrive, data centers on the ground rely on gas turbines and large solar arrays while their demand for electricity continues to surge, Ward said. Heat caps how big a machine can get Data centers on the ground often draw on local water to cool their servers while a spacecraft uses none. On Earth, servers shed heat three ways, through conduction, convection and radiation, Ward said. In space it’s only through radiation. Cooling 1 megawatt of computing takes about 13,000 square feet of panel, according to SatNews. That is nearly a quarter of a football field for 1 megawatt. Large data center campuses on the ground run to a gigawatt, 1,000 times more. Launch sets the price, and supply just tightened However, computing in orbit costs far more today than on the ground, Ward said. But the launch is a one-time bill, and hardware with few moving parts can run for decades. He called orbital compute a closed-loop system since “it's just mass." A Vulcan rocket failed Sunday, Nov. 15, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites, and could stay grounded for months. Falcon 9 launches from Florida paused for at least six weeks after Oct. 20 to make room for Starship. Altitude determines which computing tasks can go up The farther a satellite sits from Earth, the longer a signal takes to make the round trip. That delay, called latency, determines which computing tasks can run in orbit at all. A round trip to a geostationary satellite, about 22,236 miles up, runs 600 milliseconds or more. Low Earth orbit cuts that to 25 to 60 milliseconds. That gap matters for TCP, the protocol that carries most internet traffic. "There's no TCP-based network application that works better with more latency," said Grant Kirkwood, chief executive of Contrivian, which routes traffic across satellite and ground networks. Space traffic management Space traffic management matters more as the technology outruns policymakers, Ward said. The FCC has a role through licensing while civil traffic coordination moves from the Defense Department to the Commerce Department, said Tom Stroup, president of the Satellite Industry Association. A 2022 FCC rule requires low Earth orbit satellites to deorbit, or reenter Earth's atmosphere, within five years of mission end, replacing a 25-year guideline. The turnover in Congress With United Launch Alliance's Vulcan grounded and SpaceX's Falcon 9 paused in Florida, there are few rockets to go around. SpaceX can sell room on a launch to another company or fill it with its own satellites. Computing in orbit could easily take up all available capacity, Stroup said, which raises competition issues. New members of Congress take office in January. With that significant turnover, he said, policymakers will have a lot of questions about the industry. Some have called for breaking up SpaceX, which builds both the rockets and the satellites they carry. The model is working, Ward said, and splitting it would serve no real benefit because the pieces would very likely still be each other's customers.

artigo.texto: Conquista representa mais uma etapa na consolidação do investimento de R$ 100 milhões em fábrica de baterias em Camaçari A Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Econômico da Bahia (SDE) celebra mais um avanço na consolidação de investimentos estratégicos no estado. A Windey Brasil, empresa chinesa que está implantando uma fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) no Polo Industrial de Camaçari, foi oficialmente cadastrada no Credenciamento de Fornecedores Informatizado (CFI) do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES). A conquista representa um passo importante para a estruturação da operação da companhia no Brasil e o fortalecimento da indústria baiana de energias renováveis. Para o secretário da SDE, João Carlos Oliveira, o avanço demonstra a capacidade da Bahia de atrair empreendimentos internacionais e ampliar sua participação em setores estratégicos. “Esse avanço da Windey demonstra que a Bahia está no caminho certo ao apostar na atração de investimentos que agregam tecnologia, inovação e desenvolvimento industrial. A fábrica em Camaçari representa um passo importante para ampliar a participação da Bahia na cadeia de energias renováveis, gerar oportunidades de emprego e renda e consolidar nossa posição estratégica na transição energética”, destacou. O cadastro no CFI permite à empresa avançar no processo de habilitação de seus equipamentos para acesso às linhas de financiamento do BNDES. A Windey já submeteu a documentação necessária para o credenciamento do sistema de armazenamento VOLTPACK L5015, que segue em análise pelo banco. O avanço ganha relevância diante do Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de 2026, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Uma das modalidades, identificada como Produto A, prevê a contratação de sistemas de armazenamento com exigência de conteúdo local e está vinculada ao credenciamento no CFI. “O cadastro da Windey Brasil no BNDES representa uma conquista muito importante para nossa operação e reforça o compromisso de longo prazo da companhia com o Brasil. A escolha da Bahia para sediar nossa primeira fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia fora da China foi uma decisão estratégica, considerando sua localização privilegiada, sua vocação industrial, seu protagonismo no setor de energias renováveis e o potencial de desenvolvimento de toda essa cadeia produtiva”, destaca Ricardo Galvão, CEO da Windey Brasil. O gestor também destacou a parceria com o Governo da Bahia. “Quero registrar nosso agradecimento ao Governo do Estado da Bahia, especialmente ao governador Jerônimo Rodrigues, pelo apoio, pela confiança e pelo compromisso com a atração de investimentos e o desenvolvimento industrial. Estamos construindo aqui não apenas uma fábrica, mas uma plataforma industrial e tecnológica com potencial para atender ao Brasil e à América Latina” Será a primeira base de manufatura de sistemas de armazenamento de energia da Windey fora da China, com produção voltada aos mercados brasileiro e latino-americano. A fábrica de Camaçari receberá investimento anunciado de R$ 100 milhões e ocupará uma área de aproximadamente 25 mil metros quadrados. Com capacidade produtiva prevista de 2 gigawatt-hora (GWh) por ano, a unidade tem previsão de iniciar as operações em 2027. A implantação da unidade integra a expansão da cadeia produtiva de energias renováveis na Bahia. O armazenamento permite guardar a energia produzida em períodos de maior geração para utilizá-la quando necessário, contribuindo para a estabilidade e a eficiência do sistema elétrico, especialmente diante da expansão das fontes eólica e solar. A presença da Windey no estado também envolve pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação. Em 2025, a empresa firmou memorando de entendimento com o SENAI CIMATEC e o Ministério de Minas e Energia para cooperação nas áreas de energia eólica, hidrogênio verde e armazenamento. No mesmo ano, foram inaugurados o escritório nacional da companhia e seu Centro de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento, em Salvador. Com o avanço no BNDES e a implantação da fábrica em Camaçari, a Bahia amplia sua participação em uma cadeia industrial estratégica para a transição energética, reunindo investimentos, tecnologia e novas oportunidades para a economia estadual.

artigo.texto: Principais destaques - Blue Origin foi escolhida: a empresa de Jeff Bezos utilizará seu foguete New Glenn para lançar os satélites de computação do Project Suncatcher, do Google. - Chips de IA em órbita: cada satélite será equipado com unidades de processamento Tensor Processing Unit (TPU), com capacidade computacional equivalente à de um rack de servidores de um data center convencional. - Energia solar quase contínua: a iniciativa pretende aproveitar a luz solar diretamente no espaço para alimentar sistemas de inteligência artificial e reduzir a pressão sobre a infraestrutura terrestre. O Google está preparando uma aposta ambiciosa para o futuro da inteligência artificial: levar parte da infraestrutura que alimenta seus modelos para fora da Terra. A empresa escolheu a Blue Origin, de Jeff Bezos, para realizar o lançamento de satélites de computação do Project Suncatcher, iniciativa experimental que pretende transformar a órbita terrestre em uma nova fronteira para data centers. A primeira missão dedicada ao projeto está prevista para o primeiro trimestre de 2029. 🚀 Bezos ganha uma missão importante do Google O foguete escolhido é o New Glenn, veículo de lançamento pesado desenvolvido pela Blue Origin. A missão transportará vários satélites equipados com processadores especializados em inteligência artificial desenvolvidos pelo próprio Google. O contrato representa uma oportunidade importante para a Blue Origin ampliar sua presença no mercado de lançamentos comerciais, especialmente enquanto busca consolidar o New Glenn após atrasos e dificuldades técnicas. Para o Google, a parceria oferece capacidade de lançamento para uma iniciativa que pode redefinir a maneira como grandes empresas de tecnologia pensam sobre infraestrutura computacional. Mas por que colocar servidores no espaço se já existem enormes data centers na Terra? ☀️ O Sol pode resolver um dos maiores problemas da IA A expansão da inteligência artificial está criando uma demanda gigantesca por capacidade computacional. Modelos cada vez maiores exigem mais processadores, eletricidade e sistemas de refrigeração. Os data centers também precisam de terrenos, conexões elétricas robustas e grandes estruturas de distribuição de energia. O Project Suncatcher tenta contornar parte desses desafios utilizando uma vantagem disponível em abundância na órbita terrestre: a energia solar. Os satélites serão posicionados em uma órbita que oferece exposição quase contínua à luz do Sol. Isso permitiria alimentar os processadores diretamente com energia solar, reduzindo a dependência das redes elétricas convencionais. 💡 A proposta é transformar satélites em verdadeiros computadores orbitais, capazes de executar cargas de trabalho de inteligência artificial utilizando energia solar. 🧠 Cada satélite terá poder computacional de um rack de servidores O projeto utilizará as Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), chips desenvolvidos pelo Google especificamente para executar operações de inteligência artificial. Segundo a Reuters, cada satélite terá capacidade computacional aproximadamente equivalente à de um rack de servidores utilizado em um data center convencional. Isso significa que o Google não está simplesmente enviando equipamentos para o espaço. Está testando uma infraestrutura computacional distribuída em órbita. A ideia é investigar se esses equipamentos conseguem executar operações intensivas de IA em condições muito diferentes das encontradas em instalações terrestres. 🛰️ O primeiro teste já saiu da Terra O Project Suncatcher não está começando do zero. Em outubro de 2026, Google e Planet Labs lançaram o primeiro protótipo do projeto utilizando um foguete da SpaceX. Após estabelecer contato, as empresas informaram que o satélite estava operando conforme o esperado. Esse primeiro experimento tem uma missão fundamental: descobrir se os chips conseguem sobreviver às condições extremas do ambiente espacial. Entre os principais desafios estão: - Radiação: partículas energéticas podem danificar componentes eletrônicos e corromper dados. - Temperaturas extremas: os equipamentos precisam suportar grandes variações térmicas. - Resfriamento: sem o fluxo de ar disponível nos data centers terrestres, o calor precisa ser transportado por tubulações e dissipado por painéis. - Lançamento: os componentes precisam resistir às forças e vibrações durante a viagem até a órbita. 🔬 O problema não é apenas fazer a IA funcionar no espaço: é conseguir manter os processadores operando de maneira confiável durante longos períodos. 🌎 Google, SpaceX e Blue Origin estão olhando para o mesmo destino O Google não está sozinho nessa corrida. Outras empresas também investigam a possibilidade de construir data centers em órbita, aproveitando energia solar e novas arquiteturas de computação. Entre os nomes que aparecem nesse mercado estão: Google | Project Suncatcher Desenvolve uma arquitetura experimental de satélites equipados com TPUs para executar inteligência artificial no espaço. SpaceX Participa dos primeiros testes do Project Suncatcher e também explora possibilidades de infraestrutura computacional orbital. Blue Origin Fornecerá o foguete New Glenn para a missão dedicada ao projeto em 2029. Starcloud Startup que também trabalha no desenvolvimento de data centers em órbita. A disputa mostra como a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial está aproximando dois setores que historicamente evoluíram de maneira relativamente independente: computação em nuvem e exploração espacial. 💰 Ainda estamos longe de aposentar os data centers terrestres Apesar do potencial, transformar satélites em instalações comerciais de computação não será simples. Os custos de lançamento continuam elevados, a fabricação de satélites em escala representa outro obstáculo e a engenharia necessária para manter processadores funcionando no espaço ainda precisa amadurecer. artigo.texto: Data Center na Virgínia, EUA • 17 de março de 2025 REUTERS/Leah Millis Dois dias de treinamento culminam em uma cerimônia de entrega de diplomas. Empresas ansiosas para contratar os recém-formados já estão oferecendo vagas com salários superiores kmja US$ 100.000 por ano. Bem-vindo à economia dos centros de dados. Na corrida para construir a infraestrutura de IA dos Estados Unidos, as empresas de tecnologia estão com dificuldades para encontrar técnicos com as habilidades necessárias para instalar os sistemas de refrigeração, racks de servidores, equipamentos elétricos e cabos de fibra óptica essenciais para atender à demanda altíssima por essa tecnologia revolucionária. Mesmo com as mudanças no cenário político da IA — principalmente após as recentes eleições de meio de mandato — a falta de mão de obra disponível para dar continuidade aos projetos de data centers certamente superaria qualquer possível desaceleração na construção civil. Assim, o setor está se empenhando ao máximo para capacitar e contratar pessoas para preencher essas vagas cruciais. Diversas organizações sem fins lucrativos, empresas de ensino online e os quatro grandes gigantes da computação em nuvem com inteligência artificial — Amazon, Google, Meta e Microsoft — oferecem vários tipos de cursos de treinamento acelerado e gratuito para as habilidades técnicas necessárias para a construção de data centers. Algumas dessas posições podem pagar salários de seis dígitos. E muitos americanos nem sequer sabem que esses empregos existem. Formatura na sexta-feira. Orientação na segunda-feira. Javonntae Hill estudou design de videogames. Ele está na casa dos 30 anos e buscava uma carreira, mas não sabia bem por onde começar. A namorada dele viu um anúncio da America's Workforce Academy, um novo programa de treinamento que a Meta lançou em agosto para ajudar a suprir a falta de mão de obra qualificada. A empresa se dispôs a pagar a ele durante as quatro semanas de treinamento e garantiu a ele um emprego em um data center após a conclusão do curso. Hill resolveu tentar. Ao longo de um mês, em uma sala de aula com 30 pessoas, ele participou de uma combinação de aulas teóricas e treinamento prático, aprendendo como instalar e passar cabos de fibra óptica e de cobre, e o que cada cor de isolamento do cabo indicava. Ele estava nervoso: esperava conseguir reter todas aquelas informações para o novo emprego. “A formatura foi na sexta-feira”, disse Hill. “Comecei o período de integração na segunda-feira.” A Meta fez uma parceria com a Associated Builders and Contractors, uma associação comercial do setor da construção civil que treina trabalhadores há décadas. Ao contrário dos métodos de treinamento tradicionais, como escolas técnicas ou estágios, os cursos acelerados da ABC não são projetados para serem abrangentes; eles são projetados para colocar o maior número possível de pessoas para trabalhar em data centers. “É como no exército”, disse Joel Thames, chefe do grupo de segurança e força de trabalho da ABC. “O treinamento básico os prepara para qualquer cenário? Não. Mas oferece uma formação fundamental antes de começarem a trabalhar no local de trabalho.” Hill disse que seu nervosismo era infundado: ele chegou ao local de trabalho em Ohio superpreparado. E grato. "Eu poderia fazer isso pelo resto da minha vida", disse Hill. "Já vi anúncios de vagas disponíveis, mas tenho muita lealdade à Meta." O problema Apesar da crescente oposição pública e de uma onda de novos legisladores prometendo regulamentar sua expansão, a construção de centros de dados é praticamente imparável. De acordo com o economista Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, da Columbia Business School , espera-se que os gastos com infraestrutura de IA se aproximem de US$ 1 trilhão por ano , anualmente, num futuro próximo. Mas a construção enfrenta muitos obstáculos logísticos , incluindo licenças de construção, garantias de energia, materiais e financiamento. Mesmo as empresas de IA com os maiores recursos financeiros, capazes de superar esses obstáculos, encontram um problema constante: os Estados Unidos têm muito poucos profissionais qualificados para construir centros de dados — principalmente em algumas das localidades remotas ou rurais onde estão sendo construídos. Os Estados Unidos enfrentam uma escassez de 1 milhão de engenheiros necessários para atender às estimativas de construção de data centers, segundo estimativas da PwC. Muitos projetos, que já estavam prontos para serem iniciados, sofreram atrasos de meses enquanto as empresas reúnem equipes qualificadas para construí-los. De acordo com o Goldman Sachs, apenas cerca de metade da capacidade de computação de IA prevista para entrar em operação entre agora e 2028 deverá ser concluída dentro do prazo. Essa espera tem um custo elevado: para grandes centros de dados de IA, um mês de atraso pode custar desde algumas dezenas de milhões de dólares até bem mais de 100 milhões de dólares, dependendo da localização, da escala e dos termos do contrato, afirmou Mona Dajani, copresidente da área de infraestrutura, energia e imobiliário da Cooley. Assim, as empresas de IA estão enfrentando esse desafio abandonando a exigência de cursos técnicos de vários anos ou estágios remunerados, em favor de cursos acelerados e de alta intensidade, projetados especificamente para vagas na construção de data centers. Muitas oferecem os cursos gratuitamente. Um número crescente delas chega a pagar aos alunos para participarem dos cursos. As aulas podem durar de 15 semanas a apenas dois dias, dependendo da vaga. A demanda por mão de obra é tão grande que empresas de IA estão contratando alguns dos melhores graduados logo no dia seguinte à obtenção de suas certificações. artigo.texto: Juniper Green brings live 109 MWp of solar, 95 MWh of BESS in India November 20 (Renewables Now) - Indian independent renewable energy power producer (IPP) Juniper Green Energy (544853:BOM) has expanded its operational portfolio with the commissioning of a 109-MWp solar plant in Maharashtra and a 95-MWh battery in Rajasthan. The company, which completed its INR-18-billion (USD-193.9m/EUR 176.7m) initial public offering this summer, said on Friday that it now has roughly 2.95 GWp of renewables energy assets in its installed fleet, as well as 698 MWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS). In Maharashtra, Juniper Green has brought online the photovoltaic (PV) component of its solar-wind hybrid project in the town of Tuljapur in Dharashiv district. The solar plant is connected to a 132-kV substation and will be operated under a 25-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (MSEDCL). Meanwhile in Rajasthan, the company has hooked to the Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) an additional 95 MWh of BESS capacity at its integrated renewable energy and storage facility in Barmer. “As we continue to scale our operations, our focus remains on building a resilient energy platform that can deliver reliable, sustainable power and contribute meaningfully to India’s clean energy ambitions,” said CEO Ankush Malik. He noted that the new additions to Juniper Green’s portfolio are aligned with the company’s commitment to applying a more integrated approach that combines renewable generation with storage and flexibility. Juniper Green’s total portfolio of operational, under-construction, contracted and awarded projects includes over 11 GW of generation and 8.9 GWh of BESS capacity. (INR 10 = USD 0.0108/EUR 0.098)

A vitória democrata abre uma nova frente de incerteza para os investimentos em inteligência artificial (IA), com perspectiva de maior regulação sobre o setor e restrições à construção de data centers. A executiva comandou sua primeira webcast para comentar os resultados da gigante de chips de inteligência artificial nesta terça-feira, após assumir o posto principal da Nvidia interinamente diante da renúncia do ex-CEO Jensen Huang. A CEO interina ressaltou que a empresa continuará sendo “cautelosa” e “disciplinada” na forma como aloca capital daqui para frente. A Nvidia está “avaliando rigorosamente” futuros investimentos, compromissos e garantias, acrescentou. Kress, contudo, afirmou que a companhia seguirá dando apoio aos seus fornecedores, o que é uma prioridade, citando que alguns precisam de ajuda financeira para desenvolverem suas capacidades. artigo.texto: Chesterfield board punts again on what to do with data center taxes, potential Midlo Middle site Chesterfield’s Board of Supervisors deferred two key agenda items for a third time each Wednesday night: One would have used data center revenue to reduce the car tax rate, and the other sought to rezone a property that’s been in limbo for seven years. The decision on where to put data center taxes was pushed to December. The board introduced it in August, then deferred it to September, then to November. “We’re trying to get all our ducks in a row,” Board Chair Mark Miller said Wednesday before again motioning to postpone. As for the property rezoning — 12 lots along Coalfield Road being considered for Midlothian Middle School — that will come up again in March 2027. One of its owners, Joseph Beauchamp, said in September that the property was first considered for the new facility in 2021. After this project initially fell through, Beauchamp and his fellow owners decided to develop a senior community on the site. This updated rezoning case was first on the agenda in May, then was pushed to August, and finally to November. Miller has previously earmarked this property as his favorite of the three proposed Midlothian Middle locations — the others being 500 Old Hundred Road and 1101 Otterdale Road. As of September, an anonymous donor also offered $1 million to help the county purchase the area for the school. Contact Eleanor Shaw at eshaw@richmonder.org. She is a Report for America corps member.

artigo.texto: A Assembleia Legislativa do Estado do Paraná (Alep) aprovou, nesta terça-feira (17), um projeto de lei que estabelece diretrizes para incentivar a instalação e a expansão de Data Centers no Estado. A iniciativa foi proposta pelos deputados Luiz Fernando Guerra (Novo), Maria Victoria (PP) e Bazana (PSD). O Projeto de Lei 55/2026 cria o Programa Paranaense de Incentivo a Centros de Dados (PRODATAPR) e reúne propostas voltadas ao desenvolvimento da economia digital, à atração de investimentos privados, à geração de empregos especializados e ao aproveitamento das vantagens competitivas do Paraná, especialmente na produção de energia renovável e na conectividade. A deputada Maria Victoria explica que o texto tem o objetivo de criar condições para posicionar o Paraná como um dos principais destinos de investimentos em infraestrutura digital, inteligência artificial e novas tecnologias no Brasil. “A inteligência artificial, a computação em nuvem e os serviços digitais dependem de uma infraestrutura robusta de processamento de dados. Temos energia, universidades, profissionais qualificados e um ambiente favorável à inovação. Queremos transformar essas vantagens em investimentos, empregos e oportunidades para os paranaenses”, ressaltou. O deputado Luiz Fernando Guerra destaca a importância do planejamento para que a expansão dos Data Centers no Paraná seja acompanhada pela formação de profissionais para o setor. “Com esse projeto, o Paraná terá diretrizes para planejar a expansão dos data centers, dar mais previsibilidade a quem pretende investir e identificar os empreendimentos estratégicos para o Estado. Para operar e manter essas estruturas, as empresas vão precisar de profissionais preparados. Por isso, a proposta incentiva parcerias com universidades e centros de pesquisa para qualificar mão de obra e ampliar as oportunidades de trabalhar com tecnologia em diferentes regiões do Paraná”, afirma o deputado Luiz Fernando Guerra. Segundo o deputado Pedro Paulo Bazana (PSD), a proposta busca transformar o potencial tecnológico do Paraná em oportunidades de desenvolvimento para os municípios. “Queremos que o Paraná aproveite seu potencial em energia renovável e conectividade para atrair investimentos que gerem oportunidades para a população. Como coautor desse projeto, defendo que a expansão dos centros de dados fortaleça também as empresas locais, estimule a formação profissional e leve empregos qualificados ao interior. É uma forma de preparar o estado para as novas demandas da economia e ampliar as possibilidades de desenvolvimento dos nossos municípios", defendeu Bazana. Estratégico Os Data Centers são estruturas essenciais para o funcionamento da economia digital. Neles são armazenadas e processadas grandes quantidades de informações utilizadas por empresas, governos, instituições financeiras, hospitais, universidades e plataformas. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial, essas instalações ganharam importância estratégica na disputa mundial por investimentos tecnológicos. De acordo com a justificativa do projeto, o PRODATAPR tem o objetivo de consolidar o Paraná como polo estratégico de Data Centers na América Latina, gerando empregos qualificados e fomentando a cadeia produtiva de tecnologia. O texto autoriza o Governo do Estado a conceder benefícios fiscais às empresas beneficiárias do Programa. A proposta estabelece diretrizes para estimular novos empreendimentos, ampliar a infraestrutura de telecomunicações e incentivar parcerias entre empresas, universidades e centros de pesquisa. Outro diferencial é a preocupação com a sustentabilidade. O projeto incentiva a utilização de fontes renováveis de energia, o aproveitamento do biometano, o uso racional da água e a adoção de tecnologias sustentáveis de resfriamento dos equipamentos. Expansão A aprovação ocorre em um momento de expansão do setor no Brasil. Em setembro de 2026, foi sancionada a Lei Federal nº 15.504, que instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). A legislação federal prevê incentivos tributários condicionados a compromissos de sustentabilidade, investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento e utilização de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão. artigo.texto: Researchers have developed a hybrid machine learning framework that formulates carbon price forecasts as reliable numerical ranges rather than deterministic single-point projections, improving uncertainty quantification across regional and national trading systems in China. Traditional analytical models for emissions markets have overwhelmingly concentrated on point forecasting, an approach that predicts a singular future price value but fails to capture the full statistical distribution of market fluctuations or communicate the boundaries of forecasting error. In an investigation evaluating daily trading records, a research team demonstrated that combining variational mode decomposition with a mathematically refined interval estimation architecture generated bounds that captured over ninety-eight percent of empirical closing prices while preserving narrow interval boundaries. Tracking the trajectory of carbon allowance valuations has become a central priority within modern energy market economics, as market-based emissions trading programs directly shape industrial capital allocation, low-carbon technology investments, and national environmental compliance frameworks. Since the establishment of early emissions trading systems such as the European Union carbon market in 2005, comparable regional and national programs have expanded across multiple jurisdictions. The Hubei pilot carbon market exemplifies the heightened volatility characteristic of these trading environments, exhibiting an upward valuation trajectory from 2017 onward that eventually reached approximately sixty yuan per ton. The inherent volatility and regulatory adjustments surrounding carbon allowances introduce considerable financial exposure for market participants, emphasizing the necessity of predictive tools that explicitly quantify price uncertainty rather than obscuring potential variance behind single deterministic points. Methodologies designed for interval prediction have traditionally followed three distinct paths: direct interval-valued data modeling, the generation of point forecasts augmented with assumed error distributions and predetermined confidence levels, and direct lower-upper bound estimation known as LUBE. The conventional LUBE framework utilizes a dual-output neural network designed to simultaneously maximize prediction interval coverage probability and minimize normalized average width. However, traditional LUBE implementations rely on a non-differentiable coverage-width criterion, precluding direct parameter optimization through standard gradient descent and forcing researchers to depend on heuristic search algorithms such as particle swarm optimization. Furthermore, conventional formulations combine coverage and width through heuristic weighting mechanisms that lack rigorous statistical derivation, frequently causing optimization conflicts that lead to either excessively wide bounds or substantial under-coverage. To overcome these computational and theoretical constraints, the authors formulated Quality-Driven Lower Upper Bound Estimation, designated as QD-LUBE, which re-engineers the objective formulation into a differentiable loss function grounded in maximum likelihood principles. Drawing inspiration from likelihood-driven neural estimation, the system replaces the discrete coverage indicator with a smooth, continuously differentiable sigmoid approximation. This mathematical transformation permits gradient propagation even for target observations that temporarily fall outside the predicted boundaries. Under this statistical framing, the coverage of each individual observation corresponds to an independent Bernoulli trial governed by a target nominal confidence level, allowing the cumulative coverage across an evaluation sample to follow a binomial distribution. The composite loss function penalizes coverage shortfalls relative to the specified confidence threshold while simultaneously minimizing interval width computed exclusively over successfully captured observations. To prevent error accumulation and model over-specification across multi-scale price dynamics, the forecasting architecture integrates a divide-and-conquer signal processing pipeline centered on Variational Mode Decomposition. Financial price series typically embed both sustained structural trends and high-frequency transient shocks. Applying a single complex recurrent network directly to the raw, unseparated price series frequently introduces noise into learned parameters or leads to overfitting. Variational Mode Decomposition resolves these challenges by decomposing the original daily closing price sequence into two distinct sub-sequences: a smooth, low-frequency component representing underlying structural trajectories and seasonal patterns, and a volatile, high-frequency residual component reflecting short-term market disturbances and stochastic fluctuations. The study selected Variational Mode Decomposition following rigorous statistical benchmarking against alternative decomposition techniques, including Empirical Mode Decomposition and Complete Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition with Adaptive Noise. Evaluation of Pearson correlation coefficients and associated significance values revealed that Variational Mode Decomposition successfully decoupled the time series, yielding a low-frequency mode that captured dominant market variance alongside a weakly correlated, statistically distinct high-frequency mode. For instance, in national carbon market records, the low-frequency mode produced an association coefficient of 0.9966 with raw prices, whereas the high-frequency component registered an association of 0.1248. In contrast, alternative mode decomposition techniques exhibited persistent mode mixing, generating high-frequency series that shared virtually no statistically meaningful independent information with original market trajectories. artigo.texto: Elysia BESS Copilot for mines: dispatch, degradation and revenue notes for engineers Reviewed by Joe Ashwell First reported on International Mining – News 30 Second Briefing Elysia, Fortescue Zero’s battery intelligence division, has launched Elysia BESS Copilot to manage large, multi-site battery energy storage system portfolios at mines that are expanding faster than operations teams. The software ingests high-frequency BESS data to optimise dispatch, state-of-charge windows and degradation, targeting higher revenue capture from arbitrage and ancillary services while protecting cell life. For mine power engineers, it aims to cut manual portfolio tuning effort as installed MWh scale up, reducing chronic underperformance and operational complexity across hybrid diesel–renewables systems. Technical Brief - Elysia BESS Copilot is developed by Fortescue Zero’s dedicated battery intelligence division, Elysia. - Chronic underperformance is framed as compounding with every additional MWh of storage deployed. Our Take Fortescue Zero’s role in both this Elysia BESS Copilot piece and the recent Pilbara decarbonisation strategy shift (2025-12-03) suggests the software may be aimed at integrating with, or at least complementing, Fortescue’s evolving battery-electric haul fleet architecture rather than standalone grid projects. In our Software category, relatively few of the 43 stories intersect directly with mine haul electrification, so a Fortescue Zero–linked energy management product signals that mine-site BESS optimisation is moving from pilot tools into operational fleet-scale systems. The earlier installation of a Fortescue Zero battery-electric system into a Liebherr T 264 haul truck (2026-05-23) implies that any BESS Copilot deployment will need to handle highly transient, high-C-rate duty cycles, which is a more demanding optimisation problem than typical stationary industrial storage. artigo.texto: Texas resumes data center permit reviews before ERCOT community impact report is out SAN ANTONIO - Texas is resuming its review of permits tied to data center projects, a move that is drawing criticism from opponents who say the state is pushing ahead before a promised study on community impacts is finished and before residents have a meaningful chance to weigh in. In September, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered a pause on issuing data center-related permits while the Electric Reliability Council of Texas gathered information about how the facilities affect communities. Abbott reversed that pause on Nov. 13, directing the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to resume its normal permit review process even though the full report on data centers’ community impacts is not expected until Dec. 10. Across Texas, data center projects are moving forward, raising concerns about how much water and electricity they will require and how they could affect the communities where they are built. For rancher Joseph Reznicek, the growth of data centers is not only a debate over utilities. He said it is putting pressure on the ranching lifestyle his family has built over generations. “to be effectively pushed out of a market and a lifestyle that I've had for 61 years is sobering,” Reznicek said. Reznicek said two data centers are being developed now, including one about two miles from his ranch. He said rising land prices and developers buying up property have made it harder to find land for his cattle. “We're gonna be done with cattle production probably within maybe a year, two possibly, maybe three at the max,” he said. Asked whether residents have been given enough information about the projects and what they could mean for communities, Reznicek said, “Absolutely not. There's the one thing that is in spades is the lack of communication, the lack accountability, the lack transparency.” Those concerns are shared by Public Citizen, an environmental and consumer advocacy group that is questioning the state’s decision to resume permit reviews before the public can see the results of the ERCOT study on the impact of data centers on communities. The study was ordered by Abbott. “And so the public doesn't have a seat at the table in deciding whether or not they want to host these data center facilities in their communities. That means that environmental health impacts, public health impacts including air quality,” said Kathryn Guerra, Public Citizen’s TCEQ watchdog campaign director. Guerra called for stronger protections for communities as the industry expands. “we need real meaningful guard rails on the data center industry that protects Texans instead of protecting corporations' bottom line. And ultimately, it's the will of the people that will be heard,” she said. The governor’s office was contacted for comment and directed questions to TCEQ. The agency said it “will resume its normal permit review process and evaluate applications under state and federal law.”
