artigo.texto: Tazewell County approves 500MW solar project, delays decision on battery storage facility TAZEWELL COUNTY (25News Now) - After weeks of public hearings and debate, the Tazewell County Board has approved a large-scale solar energy project while postponing a decision on a separate battery storage facility amid concerns about its potential impact on nearby water supplies. During Wednesday night’s meeting, the board approved a special-use permit for Mackinaw Solar LLC, allowing the development of a 500-megawatt commercial solar facility spanning approximately 3,400 acres in Cincinnati and Spring Lake townships in Manito. Previously, the county’s zoning board of appeals had made no recommendation, while the land use committee recommended approval, with conditions. However, a separate proposal for a 300-megawatt battery energy storage facility by Lumina Energy Storage LLC in Elm Grove Township will have to wait until December for a final decision. Previously, the zoning board of appeals had recommended denial, while the land use committee concurred. Both projects faced opposition from residents during hearings before the county’s Zoning Board of Appeals earlier this month, with concerns ranging from property values to the potential environmental impacts of the developments. Mackinaw Solar receives approval The approval marks a major step forward for Mackinaw Solar, a proposed $400 million development that has been in the planning stages since 2022. According to the developer’s website on the project, the facility would generate enough electricity to power approximately 100,000 homes and is expected to begin operating in 2029. It is also predicted to have a life cycle of 30+ years. The project would be built primarily on privately owned agricultural land, with plans to incorporate agrivoltaics, a practice that combines solar energy production with agricultural activities, including grazing livestock between solar panels. The county’s approval includes conditions allowing grazing on the property. Other conditions included requiring the facility to have a decommissioning plan, agree that water may not be drawn from any operational well within the facility for uses outside of it, and limited hours of construction. Battery storage decision postponed While Mackinaw Solar received approval, the future of a proposed battery energy storage facility remains uncertain. The Tazewell County Board voted to postpone a decision on Lumina Energy Storage LLC’s special-use permit until December, allowing additional time for the developer and neighboring property owners to address concerns involving water, particularly if a battery fire were to release toxic substances. The proposed facility, developed by Strata Clean Energy through Lumina Energy Storage LLC, would be located in Elm Grove Township near Ameren Illinois’ Tazewell substation. According to the company’s application, the facility would store excess electricity during periods of lower demand and release it back into the electrical grid when demand increases or during emergencies. During Wednesday’s meeting, county officials discussed the possibility that a denial could allow the developer to appeal to the Illinois Commerce Commission, potentially moving the final decision outside the county’s authority. The developer said its experts found no risk of contamination or reduced water volume but offered alternatives: a deep well or a tank supplied with hauled-in water. The postponement gives both the developer and neighboring residents additional time to address outstanding concerns before the board takes up the proposal again. artigo.texto: AI infrastructure is increasing demand for high-speed connectivity, compact components, and reliable manufacturing at scale. As data rates rise and component dimensions shrink, high-speed connector manufacturing faces tighter tolerances and greater challenges in achieving consistent weld quality and production yields. Precision laser processing and automated inspection are becoming increasingly important to data center component manufacturing. Laser Processing for Next-Generation Data Center Components examines how green laser copper welding addresses the challenges of joining highly conductive copper, while ultrashort pulse laser wire stripping prepares conductors for reliable welds without damaging the underlying material. This interview feature covers how AI machine vision laser welding can improve weld consistency by identifying component positions and gaps, and how automated laser welding supports repeatable, high-volume manufacturing for AI infrastructure. These technologies offer practical approaches to manufacturing challenges that grow as connector designs become smaller and production volumes increase. Discover how the latest laser technologies can help manufacturers improve process control, weld quality, and production consistency as connectivity demands grow.

artigo.texto: The United States has surpassed 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of cumulative installed energy storage capacity, highlighting the rapid expansion of battery storage across the country. The industry added 14.3 GWh of new capacity during the third quarter of 2026, taking total installations for the first nine months of the year to 48.3 GWh, according to the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 released by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. The growing deployment of energy storage is helping improve electricity grid reliability, manage energy costs and support the integration of renewable energy. The report also increased its forecast for cumulative U.S. energy storage deployment by 3.7%, projecting total installations of 708 GWh by 2030 across grid-scale and behind-the-meter applications. Installations during the first nine months of 2026 increased 20% compared with the same period last year. The industry is also calling on Congress to accelerate permitting reforms and support the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). More than 300 solar and energy storage companies recently sent a letter to Congressional leadership urging the legislation’s swift passage. The proposed measures are expected to accelerate storage deployment, reduce project costs and expand access to affordable and reliable electricity for households and businesses. SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty said increasing energy storage deployment is helping address electricity affordability concerns. He urged lawmakers to pass the legislation to strengthen America’s energy infrastructure and put downward pressure on electricity prices. Texas led the country in utility-scale energy storage deployment through the third quarter, adding 12.3 GWh of capacity. Arizona followed with 7.7 GWh, while California recorded 6.8 GWh. According to recent SEIA analysis, the expansion of solar and energy storage helped reduce average wholesale electricity prices by 42% in Texas and 51% in California between summer 2021 and summer 2026. The report also highlighted strong growth across state markets. Eleven states, including Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama and Illinois, surpassed their previous annual energy storage installation records during the third quarter, with three months remaining in 2026. Manufacturing capacity is expanding alongside project deployment. New battery cell manufacturing facilities opened in Tennessee in July and Indiana in October, bringing total U.S. battery cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, representing a 50% increase. Utility-scale projects accounted for most installations during Q3, with 12.2 GWh deployed. Commercial and industrial installations contributed 1.3 GWh, while residential storage added 746 MWh, demonstrating the expanding role of energy storage across different electricity market segments. artigo.texto: Amazon pode comprar R$ 1 bilhão em créditos de carbono do Pará; negócio é questionado pelo MPF Negociação envolve 12 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ equivalente, mas acordo firmado em 2024 é alvo de ação judicial por possíveis irregularidades e falta de consulta a comunidades tradicionais. Adicione o Estado do Pará Online como fonte preferencial no GoogleSiga o Estado do Pará Online no Google NotíciasNa página que abrir, toque em ☆ Salvar O governo do Pará pode concluir uma operação de aproximadamente R$ 1 bilhão com a venda de créditos de carbono para empresas internacionais, entre elas a Amazon, multinacional fundada pelo bilionário Jeff Bezos. A negociação envolve 12 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e), avaliadas em US$ 15 por tonelada. No entanto, o contrato firmado pelo estado está sendo contestado pelo Ministério Público Federal (MPF). A informação sobre o andamento do programa foi divulgada nesta sexta-feira (13), em entrevista do pesquisador norte-americano Daniel Nepstad, presidente do Earth Innovation Institute, à revista Veja. Segundo ele, o Pará está próximo de concluir a validação do programa estadual de créditos de carbono, procedimento necessário para avançar na comercialização dos ativos ambientais. A operação está vinculada à Coalizão LEAF, iniciativa internacional que reúne empresas e governos interessados em financiar a redução do desmatamento em países e regiões de florestas tropicais. A participação da Amazon pode representar um negócio de US$ 180 milhões, valor equivalente a cerca de R$ 1 bilhão. O acordo foi firmado em setembro de 2024, durante o governo de Helder Barbalho (MDB), com a organização Emergent Forest Finance Accelerator, responsável pela intermediação da Coalizão LEAF. Em abril de 2025, o MPF e o Ministério Público do Estado do Pará recomendaram a anulação do contrato. Posteriormente, o MPF ajuizou uma ação civil pública para questionar a validade do negócio. Entre os pontos levantados pelos órgãos estão possíveis irregularidades na comercialização antecipada de créditos referentes a períodos futuros e a ausência de consulta prévia, livre e informada aos povos indígenas, quilombolas e demais comunidades tradicionais potencialmente afetados pelo programa. A contestação envolve também a aplicação da Lei Federal nº 15.042/2024, que instituiu o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa. Segundo o entendimento apresentado pelo Ministério Público, a legislação impede a venda antecipada de créditos de carbono relativos a resultados ambientais ainda não alcançados. O programa paraense utiliza o mecanismo conhecido como REDD+, sigla para Redução de Emissões por Desmatamento e Degradação Florestal. Nesse modelo, os resultados de redução de emissões são contabilizados em uma escala territorial abrangente, considerando o estado como um todo, e não apenas iniciativas específicas em propriedades individuais. A proposta é transformar resultados ambientais comprovados, como a redução do desmatamento e da degradação florestal, em créditos que possam ser negociados com empresas e governos interessados em financiar ações de conservação. Apesar desse objetivo, o modelo é alvo de críticas de organizações e movimentos ambientalistas. Uma das preocupações é que a preservação da floresta seja convertida em um ativo financeiro negociado por grandes corporações, inclusive por empresas cujas atividades também provocam impactos ambientais. Críticos apontam ainda o risco de greenwashing, prática em que uma companhia divulga iniciativas ambientais para construir uma imagem de sustentabilidade sem promover mudanças proporcionais aos impactos de suas operações. A Amazon é citada nesse debate por seus indicadores ambientais. De acordo com os dados apresentados no levantamento, a empresa registrou aumento de aproximadamente 16% nas emissões de gases de efeito estufa, que chegaram a 80,9 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ em 2025. A companhia também foi associada à geração de 94 mil toneladas de resíduos de embalagens plásticas nos Estados Unidos em 2022 e ao impacto ambiental de centros de dados que demandam grandes volumes de água e energia. Além das questões ambientais, a participação de territórios tradicionais no programa levanta preocupações sobre os direitos das populações que vivem na região. Para o Ministério Público, a ausência de consulta adequada pode comprometer a autonomia de povos indígenas, quilombolas e comunidades que desempenham papel histórico na proteção da floresta. A conclusão da negociação, portanto, depende não apenas da validação dos créditos, mas também dos desdobramentos das ações judiciais que discutem a legalidade do contrato e o respeito aos direitos das populações envolvidas. artigo.texto: Siga Reset no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Siga Reset no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. A Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (Abeeólica) entrou com uma ação civil pública na segunda-feira (16) para suspender os leilões de reserva de capacidade de baterias de grande porte, marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro. É um novo capítulo do principal ponto de disputa em relação aos certames: o rateio dos custos de funcionamento dos sistemas de armazenamento. A legislação atual define que o custo seja dividido entre as empresas geradoras de energia, mas a Abeeólica defende que a conta seja repassada aos consumidores, o que já acontece com outros tipos de reserva de capacidade como as termelétricas. Na ação, a Abeeólica questiona a constitucionalidade da regra, que foi definida pela lei 15.269, sancionada em 2025, e argumenta que a diferenciação em relação às termelétricas viola a ordem econômica e os princípios de isonomia, legalidade e segurança jurídica. Para a entidade, que reúne grandes empresas geradoras de energia, as baterias vão beneficiar todo o sistema, e por isso seu custo não pode recair apenas sobre as geradoras. Elbia Gannoum, presidente-executiva da Abeeólica, diz que manter o custo sobre as empresas de geração pode inviabilizar investimentos em renováveis, em um momento em que enfrentam prejuízos devido ao curtailment. Esses cortes são realizados pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema (ONS) para evitar o risco de apagão por excesso de geração. “A ação é uma forma de nos proteger de um custo que não temos condição de pagar. É um remédio amargo, e deixamos para tomá-lo por último”, diz Gannoum. A associação segue tentando mudar a regra de divisão no Congresso, com o projeto de lei 3.716/2026, e pretende retirar a ação caso o texto seja aprovado antes do leilão. O PL propõe repassar o custo para todos os consumidores, como acontece com as termelétricas hoje. O texto foi apresentado pelo deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP) e tramita em regime de urgência, com relatoria de Danilo Forte (PP-CE). A presidente da Abeeólica tem expectativa de que o texto avance na Câmara nesta semana. Jardim afirmou em um evento que o projeto pode ser votado de forma mais rápida se outros temas do setor elétrico não forem incorporados ao texto como “jabutis”. A mudança no rateio enfrenta resistência de associações de distribuidores e de consumidores. Os grupos afirmam que a conta de luz já tem encargos para apoiar a expansão de fontes renováveis, que geraram a necessidade de sistemas de armazenamento. Uma boa parte da energia que causa o excesso de geração vem da geração distribuída, que cresceu nos últimos anos por meio de incentivos. O segmento inclui painéis solares individuais e em usinas, e não é controlado pelo ONS — portanto não sofre cortes de curtailment e não pagará pelos encargos das baterias. Em busca de uma liminar A ação da Abeeólica, que corre na 17ª Vara Federal Cível do Distrito Federal, foi apresentada contra a União e a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). Na noite de segunda-feira, o juiz Diego Câmara intimou a Aneel a se manifestar em até três dias. Procurada, a agência afirmou que vai apresentar esclarecimentos nos prazos do processo. O Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), responsável pelos leilões, não se pronunciou. De acordo com a lei atual, cabe à Aneel determinar a divisão exata dos custos das baterias entre os geradores. A agência propôs que a divisão seja proporcional ao nível de flexibilidade de cada usina: hidrelétricas e termelétricas, mais flexíveis, pagam menos, enquanto solares e eólicas, menos flexíveis, pagam mais. A proposta ficou em consulta pública até o início de novembro, mas a norma final ainda não foi publicada. A falta de publicação a poucas semanas dos leilões também é citada pela Abeeólica como argumento para o adiamento. A Aneel tentou adaptar o edital do leilão para acomodar incertezas sobre o rateio do custo, mas o diretor-geral da agência, Sandoval Feitosa, já afirmou que uma mudança na lei antes das datas do leilão provavelmente faria a agência republicar editais e adiar a data dos certames. A tendência é que a decisão sobre o mérito da ação demore a sair e seja alçada a instâncias superiores como o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), na visão de Eduardo Evangelista, sócio da área de infraestrutura e direito público do Madrona Advogados. A dúvida agora é se a Justiça vai conceder uma liminar a tempo de suspender os leilões. Para o advogado, o pedido de manifestação feito pelo juiz sinaliza que ele deve ouvir as partes antes de decidir por uma liminar. Evangelista considera que, em termos jurídicos, não há tanta evidência do “perigo de demora”, que indicaria forte risco se o leilão ocorrer sem uma decisão final sobre o mérito da ação. “Não se discute se o serviço de armazenamento será pago, e sim por quem”, diz o advogado. Os sistemas precisam estar em funcionamento até meados de 2028 para inserir potência no sistema elétrico e mitigar riscos de falhas e apagões — um cronograma visto como apertado pelo setor, mesmo sem adiamentos. O governo vem prometendo leilões de bateria desde 2023. Ainda assim, Evangelista diz que há tempo até a celebração dos contratos que vão incluir a divisão de custos — esses não ocorrem imediatamente após os certames, mas posteriormente, entre a Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE) e os agentes envolvidos. Esse ponto, além da pressão para que os leilões aconteçam, pode contribuir para que a Justiça hesite em suspender os certames por meio de uma decisão liminar, diz o advogado.

artigo.texto: Pesquisa científica e datacenter do Serpro terão mais R$ 48,1 milhões Da Agência Senado | 19/11/2026, 17h39 O governo federal autorizou a abertura de créditos orçamentários que somam R$ 48,1 milhões para pesquisa e desenvolvimento científico e para demandas de datacenter. Os recursos estão previstos nas Leis 15.531 e 15.544, sancionadas pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva e publicadas no Diário Oficial da União (DOU) nesta quinta-feira (19). A Lei 15.531 abre crédito suplementar de R$ 13,2 milhões para o Ministério da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação. O objetivo é ampliar os valores destinados ao apoio à pesquisa e ao desenvolvimento científico e tecnológico no país, com atenção especial às áreas de ciências biotecnológicas, agrárias e da saúde. A ação faz parte do programa de Consolidação do Sistema Nacional de Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação (SNCTI). Os recursos devem vir do cancelamento de verbas destinadas ao Ministério da Integração e do Desenvolvimento Regional. A abertura do crédito foi proposta pelo Executivo por meio do Projeto de Lei do Congresso Nacional (PLN) 3/2026. A proposta foi aprovada em sessão conjunta do Congresso Nacional, sem passar pela Comissão Mista de Orçamento (CMO). O relatório do deputado Luiz Gastão (PSD-CE) teve parecer favorável. Processamento de dados Já a Lei 15.544, de 2026, abre crédito suplementar de R$ 34,9 milhões para a manutenção e a adequação de imóveis do Serpro. O crédito deve ser usado para atender necessidades contratuais do centro de processamento de dados, o Datacenter Modular de São Paulo. A medida também foi proposta pelo governo federal, na forma do PLN 22/2026. O projeto recebeu parecer favorável do deputado Jilmar Tatto (PT-SP) na CMO e foi aprovada em sessão conjunta do Congresso Nacional. artigo.texto: A qualidade e a confiabilidade do fornecimento de energia elétrica são fatores importantes que travam a eletrificação na indústria, já que eventuais interrupções no suprimento podem causar efeitos novos à produção. Por isso, sistemas de armazenamento de energia são solução importante para acelerar a substituição de combustíveis fósseis por eletricidade na indústria, mas a demanda industrial ainda precisa de novos modelos regulatórios e de mercado que permitam o empilhamento de receitas de sistemas de armazenamento utilizados como reserva pelo consumidor, a partir da prestação adicional de serviços para a rede. A conclusão consta em relatório sobre entraves e soluções para impulsionar a eletrificação no Brasil. O documento foi produzido pela Coalizão do Setor Elétrico, que é liderada pelo Conselho Empresarial Brasileiro para o Desenvolvimento Sustentável (Cebds) e articulada pela PSR. O relatório também indica que a maior oportunidade de eletrificação industrial está na geração de energia térmica, e menciona a nova tecnologia de ‘bateria de calor’, que permite gerar calor em altas temperaturas quando a eletricidade está mais barata, e posteriormente utilizar o calor no processo produtivo. Outras tecnologias já consolidadas, como as bombas de calor e as caldeiras elétricas, também são importantes, e já são aplicadas no país, como caldeiras elétricas já em operação na fábrica de alumina da Hydro Alunorte, no Pará, além de novos equipamentos que devem entrar em operação ainda neste ano em plantas da Braskem e da BASF, em São Paulo. Segundo o relatório, dados da Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA, na sigla em inglês) indicam que cerca de 40% da energia usada em calor de baixa e média temperatura na indústria pode ser eletrificada com custo competitivo, com potencial mais imediato nos setores têxtil, de alimentos, de papel e celulose e químico. Além dos ganhos com menores emissões a custo competitivo, executivos identificam maior proteção contra choques de preço e menor dependência de energia importada como vantagens da eletrificação, de acordo com pesquisa apresentada pelo relatório. A percepção de maior segurança energética é ainda maior no Brasil, onde 97% dos executivos identificam a vantagem, do que no mundo, onde a prevalência é de 91%. 190 milhões de toneladas de CO2 evitadas por ano no Brasil De acordo com o estudo do Cebds e da PSR, a substituição de combustíveis fósseis por eletricidade no transporte e na indústria pode evitar a emissão de até 190 milhões de toneladas de CO2 por ano no Brasil em 2050. No transporte, o estudo mostra que a mobilidade elétrica já avança no país, mas sobretudo entre veículos leves, cujas vendas passaram de 7% em 2025 para 16% em setembro de 2026, na comparação com as vendas totais de veículos. Já entre veículos pesados, ônibus elétricos são apenas 6% das vendas, e caminhões elétricos representam apenas 0,3% do total vendido em 2026. “Os desafios de custo e de autonomia ainda estão maiores para essas categorias, requerendo apoio de políticas para sua adoção”, diz o relatório. Sinal de preço e redução de subsídios Para todos os segmentos, o custo final da energia é um dos desafios. O relatório indica que, somente em 2025, os subsídios na conta de luz somaram R$ 57 bilhões, sendo R$ 16,1 bilhões como desconto às fontes incentivadas e R$ 14,5 bilhões em subsídios à geração distribuída. “Alguns subsídios se justificam, como a tarifa social. Outros perderam a razão de ser, como o desconto às fontes incentivadas”, avalia o relatório, que sugere a extinção de subsídios dispensáveis e o desincentivo à criação de novos subsídios, além de maior clareza ao consumidor sobre o que é pago na conta de luz. Para subsídios sociais, a proposta é deslocá-los da tarifa para o orçamento da União. Outro gargalo importante para a eletrificação, e que atinge todos os segmentos na medida em que sobrecarrega a rede, é a ausência de sinal de preço. Por isso, o Cebds e a PSR recomendam aprimorar os sinais de preço nas tarifas de todos os níveis de tensão, mas fazem a que isso só será possível com a adição de medidores inteligentes.

artigo.texto: Decisão exige definição prévia de quem financiará energia, manutenção e atualização tecnológica da nova infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. A Anatel formalizou nesta quarta-feira, 18 de novembro, a destinação de R$ 375 milhões para construir um data center de inteligência artificial que será operado pela Telebras. A decisão amplia as responsabilidades da estatal justamente quando seu balanço revela dificuldades para alcançar a independência financeira: nos primeiros nove meses de 2026, a companhia acumulou prejuízo de R$ 90,7 milhões e recebeu R$ 169,9 milhões em subvenções governamentais. Sem esse apoio, seu EBITDA ajustado teria sido negativo em R$ 32,9 milhões. O contraste entre a nova missão e a situação financeira da empresa está no centro do Acórdão nº 325/2026 (Nº 325 – Processo nº 53500.088928/2021-76), aprovado pelo Conselho Diretor da Anatel no último dia 4 e publicado agora no Diário Oficial da União. Embora autorize o investimento para construir a infraestrutura, a agência determina que, antes de qualquer contratação, seja formalmente identificada a fonte de recursos que financiará sua operação permanente. A exigência não é secundária. O governo informou dispor de até R$ 375 milhões para implantar a infraestrutura. O que ainda não foi demonstrado publicamente é quanto custará mantê-la funcionando e se as receitas da Telebras serão suficientes para sustentar essa nova responsabilidade sem ampliar sua dependência financeira da União. Ficou claro que o dinheiro proveniente dos saldos remanescentes do leilão do 5G poderá ser utilizado para implantar o empreendimento, mas não para custear sua operação. Caberão à Telebras as despesas com energia elétrica, manutenção, atualização tecnológica, segurança e suporte. A Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz (EAF), responsável pela implantação, deverá transferir a infraestrutura à União e não poderá continuar financiando seu funcionamento. Nova infraestrutura O empreendimento aprovado pela Anatel terá configuração inicial composta por dois módulos: um dedicado à inteligência artificial e outro destinado à infraestrutura tradicional de tecnologia da informação. A carga elétrica inicial prevista é de 2 megawatts (MW), com possibilidade de expansão condicionada a nova análise técnica e financeira. O orçamento máximo autorizado é de R$ 375 milhões, com prazo-alvo de implantação de 12 meses. A EAF (entidade que opera os recursos do 5G para infraestrutura do setor de telecomunicações) será responsável pela implantação, mediante processo competitivo de contratação, propostas vinculantes e validação independente de engenharia. A agência também estabeleceu etapas obrigatórias de aprovação, incluindo confirmação do terreno e da conexão elétrica, validação dos projetos de engenharia, requisitos térmicos, disponibilidade dos equipamentos e testes de integração, segurança e desempenho. A contratação de uma etapa não poderá gerar compromisso automático com as seguintes. Qualquer expansão além da configuração inicial ou aumento do orçamento dependerá de nova proposição do Gaispi e aprovação do Conselho Diretor da Anatel. O acórdão também proíbe que a EAF explore comercialmente a infraestrutura, preste serviços de inteligência artificial ou hospedagem a terceiros, ceda capacidade a empresas privadas ou obtenha receitas decorrentes do empreendimento. Prejuízo persistente A decisão foi tomada poucos dias antes da divulgação do balanço do terceiro trimestre da Telebras, no dia 13 de novembro. Os resultados oferecem uma dimensão mais concreta do desafio financeiro que a estatal enfrentará ao assumir uma instalação de processamento de dados intensiva em energia e equipamentos de alto desempenho. A Telebras registrou receita operacional líquida de R$ 125,4 milhões entre julho e setembro, crescimento de 18,1% sobre o mesmo período de 2025. O EBITDA ajustado avançou 67,7%, alcançando R$ 45,5 milhões. Apesar desses indicadores positivos, a companhia encerrou o trimestre com prejuízo líquido de aproximadamente R$ 30,4 milhões, aumento de 18,7% em relação à perda registrada um ano antes. No acumulado de janeiro a setembro, a receita líquida alcançou R$ 403,6 milhões, expansão de 22,1%. O prejuízo, entretanto, chegou a R$ 90,7 milhões, contra R$ 83 milhões no mesmo período do ano passado. O indicador mais revelador da dependência financeira da companhia está nas subvenções orçamentárias. Nos nove primeiros meses de 2026, a Telebras reconheceu R$ 169,9 milhões desses recursos. Considerando as subvenções, o EBITDA ajustado acumulado foi positivo em R$ 137 milhões. Excluindo seus efeitos, o resultado seria negativo em R$ 32,9 milhões. Isso significa que, apesar do crescimento comercial, a geração operacional medida por esse indicador ainda não seria positiva sem o apoio orçamentário da União. Não significa, porém, que a companhia esteja sem disponibilidades financeiras ou incapaz de honrar seus compromissos imediatos. A estatal também apresenta melhora em algumas atividades. A receita bruta dos Serviços de Valor Adicionado (SVA) cresceu 233,2% no terceiro trimestre, alcançando R$ 23,1 milhões. A receita de Serviços de Comunicação Multimídia (SCM) chegou a R$ 92,8 milhões no período, com expansão apoiada por novos contratos e reajustes, inclusive no programa Gesac. O problema é que o crescimento das receitas ainda não se converteu em resultados líquidos positivos e sustentáveis no conjunto das operações. A situação ganha relevância porque a Telebras está submetida a um plano de transição para deixar a condição de estatal dependente do Tesouro Nacional. Em setembro de 2025, a empresa assinou com o Ministério das Comunicações um contrato de gestão, com duração de cinco anos, para implementar seu Plano de Sustentabilidade Econômico-Financeira. O processo foi regulamentado pelo Decreto nº 12.500/2025 e pela Portaria Conjunta MGI/MPO/MF nº 57/2025. artigo.texto: ‘Data centers thrive in silence’: Southwest Michigan residents voice concerns against data centers Township officials say no developer has contacted them about the 285-acre property BENTON TOWNSHIP, Mich. (WNDU) - Dozens of Benton Charter Township residents filled a township board meeting on Tuesday, Nov. 17, to oppose a possible data center at the corner of Meadowbrook Road and Yore Avenue. Residents attend regular board meeting Board members said this was a regular business meeting and data centers were not on the agenda. “Our meetings are for taking care of business,” said Township Clerk Carolyn Phillips. “It’s not to have a debate or a question and answer about something you just brought to us at the last minute or you heard something on social media.” Phillips recommended these types of discussions during office hours. Residents who spoke during public comment said they want to get ahead of the action before anything gets approved. “I don’t understand this mentality of waiting and seeing,” said Benton Township resident Triana Ward. “I see a possible data center site and I see no buyers, so for me I see opportunity for us to do something now.” Township officials said no one from a data center project or the land developer has contacted them. “We assured them that we knew nothing about a data center,” said Township Supervisor Cathy Yates. “No one has been here or approached us because there is steps to be taken before anything like that takes place, and the public would surely be part of the process.” Yates and Phillips said there is a lengthy process that includes talking to residents and experts before anything is approved. The property The property up for discussion is 285 acres near I-94. It is represented by Advantage Commercial Real Estate, an agency based in Grand Rapids. The agency’s website listing says the land “offers an optimal location for high-powered data center development.” WNDU reached out to the agency for clarification and has not heard back. Chris Siriano, an Eau Claire resident and real estate agent, is worried about homeowners and their property values. He believes officials know more than they are letting on. “There’s a lot more to it. It’s very, very secretive, which makes my stomach hurt,” Siriano said. He does not want a data center in southwest Michigan and doesn’t believe the current infrastructure and natural resources could handle it. “Elon Musk says, ‘Put it in space.’ Some people say, ‘Put it on the ocean.’ That’s fine. Don’t put it in southwest Michigan,” Siriano said. Homebuyer backs out, nonprofit across the street cites concerns Triana Ward was about to close on her dream property when she looked into 2274 Yore Avenue. She said she and her family immediately backed out of the sale when she learned of a possible data center. “I can’t commit to this huge investment knowing that this might be going up less than a mile away,” she said. Ward said the possibility has changed how she views farmland. “It’s no longer like this promise of a peaceful life. It’s like, ‘Well, it’s peaceful right now.’ You don’t know what’s going to go up next week or next month,” Ward said. Ward believes data centers “thrive in silence,” so she is taking steps to say no now, while there is still time. Michael Petlick is the executive director of nonprofit Lucky Dog Ranch, which is directly across from 2274 Yore Avenue. He is worried about a data center’s impact on the ranch’s rescue dogs, wildlife and environmental effects. He is especially worried about noise pollution, citing noisy construction when highway and roadwork was recently done. “We’d have to pack up on day one with the construction noise and the busyness around here, as well as the noise,” Petlick said. “Once that structure is built, it’ll absolutely destroy everything that we’ve built here for the last 10 years on this 40-acre property.” He said he didn’t look into data centers until the possibility of one landed in his backyard. Now he wants others to consider the same. Township says it will wait The township said it will not take action until a developer or data center company approaches them and they hear from residents on all sides of the debate. Residents said they want officials to act now, such as by amending zoning ordinances or enacting a moratorium. Stay up to date on local news with WNDU on-air and online. artigo.texto: The Chickasaw County Board of Supervisors appear to have the appetite to put together an ordinance dealing with data centers in the county. However, it appeared Monday that board members aren’t willing to enact a moratorium on allowing the facilities that have generated controversy and opposition in other parts of Iowa. Assessor Ray Armel, who also serves as the county’s land-use administrator, asked supervisors to look over examples of what other counties have done when it comes to rules governing data centers in the county. “They include in their moratoriums everything from bit drives to battery storage to solar … The majority [that I have] are just for data centers,” Armel said, “but I think if you want to get ahead on this, you should look these over.” Board Chairman Jake Hackman pointed out that some data center sites can take up between 500 and 600 acres of land, and opponents of data centers point out the use of natural resources — especially water — make them unattractive. Armel said that state lawmakers, who have passed property tax limitation laws in recent years, have expressed their frustrations that “counties and jurisdictions are passing some of these moratoriums and limitations, yet not accepting some of these facilities — whether it be solar, whether it be battery power, whether it be the bitcoin or what have you.” County Attorney David Laudner echoed Armel, and said it was important for supervisors to have a clear reason for enacting an ordinance or a moratorium. “I know a lot of people are against wind and were upset that the wind [turbines] came here,” Laudner said, “but they have provided quite a boon for some of the development and some money. Would the data centers do the same thing or would they not have much of an impact financially?” He emphasized that he “was not weighing in on” the issue, but that those questions need to be answered by supervisors. Armel said a data center would have a financial impact. “In my reading, what it showed and that wouldn’t necessarily be the case here, but [some places, there’s] up to a 30 percent reduction in property tax,” he said. Hackman said he would support an ordinance so that “we can make sure the current residents, county right-of-ways and intersections are protected,” and asked fellow board members how they felt about proceeding with putting an ordinance together. “I think we should have a couple weeks to look these over and make that decision,” Supervisor Steve Breitbach said. Fellow board members Travis Suckow said he was OK with adopting some kind of ordinance, but he also indicated he was firmly against a moratorium. “I don’t feel like we can — or should — tell property owners what they can and can’t do with their property,” he said. In the end, board members said they will look over the examples Armel provided and take up the issue again in the near future.

artigo.texto: SAN DIEGO (KGTV) — Plans for what could be by far the largest data center in California are being considered in rural East County, and while the developer stresses it's only an early proposal, many who live there are already fighting against it. County records obtained by our media partners at KPBS, which ABC 10News has since reviewed, reveal a proposed data center called Project ECO with an electrical load of up to 500 megawatts — roughly four times the reported capacity of California's largest existing data center in Santa Clara County. It would be placed on 177 acres of land, less than a mile away from the home of Greg Curran, vice president of the Jacumba Sponsor Group which is leading the resistance. Jacumba is about 70 miles east of the city of San Diego, near the U.S.-Mexico border. You might recognize the unincorporated community from its well-known oasis, the Jacumba Hot Springs. In fact, that's part of what drew Curran there in the first place. "I just love soaking in the mineral hot springs and, you know, the area out here in the high desert," he said. "I just fell in love with it." Curran calls Jacumba the "perfect place to get away," but he and others fear this potential new development would change that. "This is the time to nip it in the bud," Curran said. Curran's neighbor Tanya Aiau, who lives in the Jacumba area even closer to the proposed site, shared her frustration as well. "If they start to build that, I'll literally have to move. I've got 30 acres. It's terrifying," Aiau said. IGNIS, a renewable energy company based in Spain, is the developer behind the project. ABC 10News spoke with a representative over the phone, Tahir Fazal, who made it very clear this is nothing more than a proposal to see if it's even feasible. Fazal said "pushback is very reasonable" and added that the company wants to stress "(we) will be very engaged with the community once (we) make the decision to move forward, if (we) make it." Curran knows what he would like the leaders of San Diego County's decision to be. "I think that we should put a moratorium on them. It's just too massive. It takes — it's mind-boggling the amount of energy that it needs," Curran said. Earlier this year, the City of San Diego and Escondido already approved moratoriums on large-scale data centers, and the City of Poway passed an ordinance to ban them outright. The county has already flagged water availability as a major concern and wants the electrical infrastructure to be reviewed. Residents tell ABC 10News they're also worried about air quality and noise, and more than anything, say it would be an industrial eyesore in an otherwise natural landscape. artigo.texto: In the midterm elections, voters gave America’s data center industry a beating. In 40 of 41 local ballot contests across 10 states, they backed restrictions or rejected measures favoring these sprawling developments. In Boulder City, Nevada, nearly 71% voted against allowing data centers in a large area of city-owned land. But now, the Trump administration is opening federal land to the same industry, including places where residents have spent months fighting to keep it out. In May, after fierce public opposition, Boulder City’s planning commission recommended rejecting a developer’s proposed data center on city land. But the company had also sought permission from the Bureau of Land Management to replace a solar project with a data center on nearby federal land. In June, BLM approved the change without a new environmental review, treating a massive data center as substantially the same project as a solar farm. “We were not consulted,” city attorney Brittany Walker told reporters. As one resident warned at a packed meeting, “Even if the project is now on adjacent BLM land, the impact does not stop at a property line.” An Interior appeals board halted the approval in September, and in October, the decision was set aside for further BLM review. The project remains alive, while meaningful environmental review and public participation remain unresolved. This is one project in a much larger building spree. The nonprofit More Than Just Parks has mapped more than 2,000 large data centers operating, under construction or proposed across the country, along with hundreds halted or delayed by community opposition. Each appears as a local land-use decision. Together, they represent a national transformation. In Utah, one company is seeking roughly 9,000 acres of BLM land for a nuclear-powered data-center complex. The Energy Department has selected four of its own federal sites for potential private data-center development. The buildings are just the beginning. They require power plants, substations, transmission lines, pipelines and water. A 2025 Energy Department report projects data centers could consume nearly 12% of America’s electricity by 2030. We’ve seen what happens when Washington embraces a colossal building spree — the last one to build as many federal dams as possible — without reckoning with the costs. In 1957, the federal Dalles Dam drowned Celilo Falls on the Columbia River, where Native families had fished for thousands of years. Treaty-protected fishing grounds vanished beneath the reservoir. Forty-nine years later, Google built its own data center in The Dalles, drawn partly by the region’s power infrastructure. Today, the Bonneville Power Administration markets electricity from 31 federal dams across the Northwest. The machinery of one great building spree is helping power the next. Those dams powered cities and irrigated farms. They also drowned Glen Canyon and more than 350,000 acres across seven Indian reservations on the Missouri River. The benefits spread far and wide. The people whose homes, fisheries and sacred places disappeared bore the cost. David Brower, who helped spare Dinosaur National Monument from another dam, later regretted his part in Glen Canyon’s destruction. He hadn’t even seen the place before its fate was sealed. “When we began to find out, it was too late,” he wrote. The secrecy is familiar, too. Google’s initial land deal in The Dalles was negotiated under “extreme confidentiality,” according to The Dalles Chronicle. In Tucson, officials and a utility signed nondisclosure agreements over a proposed data center. Residents did not learn what was coming until later, though packed public meetings helped to stop it. The Trump administration is working to speed up permitting for data centers. A 2025 executive order directed the Army’s civil-works leadership to examine a nationwide permitting pathway. The same Corps of Engineers that built The Dalles Dam is being enlisted to accelerate the next boom. Congress has an opportunity to intervene. Bills from Senator Ron Wyden, D-Oregon, and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Michigan, would ban data centers on federal land. Rep. Dina Titus, D-Nevada, has proposed stronger environmental review and public participation for such developments. Midterm election voters made their wishes plain. Before Washington commits more public land, water and electricity, communities deserve a say in what gets built and who pays for it. Once the land is sacrificed, no public hearing can bring it back. Will Pattiz is a contributor to Writers on the Range, an independent nonprofit dedicated to spurring lively conversation about the West. He co-founded More Than Just Parks, a public lands advocacy and media organization.

artigo.texto: Siga Folha BV no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Siga Folha BV no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. A WEG apresentou o W30Slim Smart EC, motor com inversor integrado e 175 milímetros de comprimento axial destinado a aplicações como ventilação e refrigeração de data centers. Divulgada pela fabricante em 10 de novembro de 2026, a solução reúne acionamento eletrônico e ventilação própria para facilitar sua integração aos equipamentos que mantêm os servidores em condições adequadas de operação. A família oferece potências de 1,5 a 10 hp, equivalentes a aproximadamente 1,1 a 7,5 kW. Esses números representam potência mecânica de acionamento, não capacidade de refrigeração. O catálogo posiciona o modelo em aplicações com ventiladores radiais: ele movimenta o conjunto responsável pela circulação de ar, dentro de um sistema térmico mais amplo. O que os 17,5 centímetros representam A medida destacada corresponde ao comprimento ao longo do eixo. Portanto, não descreve o diâmetro nem todas as dimensões externas do equipamento. Para fabricantes de sistemas de ventilação, essa característica pode ampliar as possibilidades de montagem em espaços restritos, embora o resultado dependa da geometria do conjunto. A WEG classifica o produto como o mais compacto, leve e eficiente de sua categoria. Entretanto, os documentos consultados não apresentam uma comparação reproduzível com concorrentes, identificando modelos, condições de ensaio e diferenças percentuais. A afirmação permanece atribuída à fabricante, sem validação independente apresentada nesses materiais. Inversor integrado controla a velocidade O inversor incorporado permite ajustar a rotação conforme o comando recebido, reunindo motor e eletrônica de acionamento em uma solução integrada. Isso oferece ao fabricante do equipamento uma forma de controlar a movimentação de ar conforme as necessidades operacionais, em vez de trabalhar exclusivamente com uma velocidade fixa. Entre as interfaces especificadas estão sinais de 2–10 V, corrente de 4–20 mA e PWM, além de comunicação Modbus. Na prática, esses recursos permitem receber comandos e integrar o acionamento à automação da instalação. A documentação também relaciona proteções contra sobrecarga, sobretemperatura, sobretensão, subtensão e rotor bloqueado. O catálogo apresenta alternativas de rotação nominal que chegam a 3.600 rpm, com faixas ajustáveis conforme a versão. A seleção precisa considerar simultaneamente potência, velocidade e alimentação elétrica; o limite de 10 hp não deve ser entendido como disponível em qualquer configuração. Ventilação própria e proteção opcional Outro diferencial é a construção TEFC, com ventilação própria. Segundo a WEG, o motor não depende do fluxo de ar produzido pela aplicação para manter seu desempenho térmico. Essa independência é relevante quando o posicionamento do acionamento dificulta a passagem de ar sobre sua estrutura. O catálogo informa operação em ambientes de −25 °C a 50 °C e regime S1, destinado ao funcionamento contínuo. A proteção padrão é IP55; IP66 aparece como opção. Assim, a resistência ampliada a poeira e jatos fortes de água precisa ser confirmada na configuração adquirida. A documentação menciona níveis de eficiência IE5 e IE6, mas não fornece, na apresentação geral do W30Slim, uma tabela completa de rendimento por carga e rotação. Por isso, essas classificações não permitem calcular diretamente a redução da conta de eletricidade de uma instalação. Demanda energética cresce, mas economia exige medição O contexto comercial é global. No relatório Key Questions on Energy and AI, de 2026, a Agência Internacional de Energia estima que os data centers consumiram 485 TWh em 2025 e projeta aproximadamente 950 TWh em 2030. Os valores abrangem o setor inteiro, incluindo instalações que não são dedicadas à IA. Para avaliar o impacto dessa tecnologia na infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, ainda faltam resultados operacionais do modelo: economia medida sob condições comparáveis, efeito sobre a eficiência total da instalação, preço e retorno do investimento. Os materiais consultados descrevem especificações e aplicações previstas, mas não apresentam esses indicadores em um data center identificado nem detalham prazos de fornecimento para projetos no mercado brasileiro. artigo.texto: Tulsa, Broken Arrow leaders weigh data center regulations amid growing public concerns As debate intensifies across Green Country over hyperscale data centers, Tulsa and Broken Arrow, the region’s two largest cities, have voted to pause consideration of any new data center proposals while they work on regulations. Broken Arrow City Manager Michael Spurgeon said the city’s decision followed packed City Hall meetings and concerns that have surfaced in other communities. Broken Arrow leaders halted data center discussions through the end of the year while the city develops an official plan for how to handle developers. “I know the council shares the same concerns that I have that the public has about the detrimental effect that a data center could have on a community when it comes to for example, our utilities, the water usage, utility rates,” Spurgeon said. He said the city wants to take a deliberate approach before moving forward. “We need to go about this in a very methodical way to look at every aspect of of what the impact would be, whether it's financial, whether it's environmental, whether it's long term,” Spurgeon said. In Tulsa, city leaders raised similar concerns, including the prospect of data centers being built near neighborhoods with limited ability for elected officials to weigh in. During discussion, Tulsa City Councilor Laura Bellis said, “I totally agree with you 100 percent about putting a data center next to large subdivisions. It's just nonsense to me.” Councilors also pointed to zoning rules that could allow data centers in multiple areas near neighborhoods with little to no need for city leaders to provide input. Tulsa City Councilor Vanessa Hall-Harper said, “I'm just raising a question that we have some kind of say in it or not. Where it's already zoned, I don't think we do.” As more cities and towns face data center proposals, a push is growing at the state Capitol to establish statewide guardrails. Tulsa state Rep. Amanda Clinton said communities can feel pressured by promises of economic benefits while lacking the resources to negotiate with major tech companies. “They're between a rock and a hard place. You know, they have this carrot being dangled out of there that they're going to get better schools, better sidewalks, better roads. And that's very tempting. But they also know that they share a city attorney with, say, 4 or 5 other towns. So they're not really quite equipped to go up against, you know, a Google or an Amazon. And they just feel like they're outgunned,” Clinton said. At Clinton’s request, the Legislature held its first-ever interim study on data centers last fall. Then last spring, lawmakers passed the first bill placing a limit on data centers by requiring them to produce their own electricity rather than drawing from the grid and increasing demand. “If these large tech companies want more electricity, fine. You pay for it. We shouldn't have to pay for it,” Clinton said. Clinton said lawmakers still need to address issues including water use, potential impacts on property values, and residents’ ability to learn about proposals. She also said data companies have realized that using non-disclosure agreements to advance projects in Oklahoma has not helped. “I think that people just don't feel like they have any say so they don't have any buy in. Like these decisions are being made for them and around them,” Clinton said. Clinton said she plans to file new bills on data centers in the coming legislative session. She also said that in multiple states, exit polling of midterm voters showed data centers ranked just under the war in Iran and inflation as a top concern. “This is not a Republican or Democratic issue. This is an issue about what we want for our future and for our communities,” Clinton said. Tulsa and Broken Arrow leaders are expected to finalize data center regulations in the coming months. City leaders say it is not a matter of if a new proposal comes, but when. “Sometimes it can seem like you're a little bit behind, but eventually you start to see the cities will catch up and start having regulations and ordinances in place that will actually govern how you how those businesses can move forward,” Spurgeon said.

artigo.texto: Trending WHEELING - City officials in Wheeling have consistently heard from vocal opponents of data centers in recent months, but some of those same individuals stepped forward Tuesday night to express gratitude for comprehensive data center regulations introduced as new legislation before city council. Council heard the first reading of an ordinance to create Article 1365 of the city’s planning and zoning code, which outlines several pages of rules and regulations on data centers in Industrial districts. The legislation will establish a rigorous application process, requirements for development and performance standards, regulations for electrical power demands and water consumption, and guidelines on water reuse for closed-loop cooling systems. It additionally outlines rules for noise and air emissions, wastewater guidelines and regulations pertaining to other potential impacts associated with data center operations. For several months, local data center opponents have vocally stood against a planned development at the former Centre Foundry & Machine Company facility in the Wheeling neighborhood of Warwood along River Road. Silicon Foundation plans to redevelop the Centre Foundry site into a phased data center and energy technology campus. While opponents over the past several months have expressed criticism about the way the city has handled the situation surrounding the planned data center in Warwood, a handful of vocal community members came forward during Tuesday night’s meeting to acknowledge they view the new legislation as a step in the right direction. "This ordinance is a good effort to control if not prevent data centers in the city of Wheeling," said Warwood resident Polly Barks. "This effort to halt or mitigate Silicone Foundation’s disastrous effects on Warwood would not have happened without the sustained effort of our community, without coming together almost unanimously against data centers. I challenge any of you to find something that has been so uniquely unifying to the community, for better or for worse." Barks is among several Warwood residents who earlier this summer filed a civil lawsuit against Silicon Foundation in an effort to stop or at least pump the brakes on the development of the Centre Foundry site. She and others have been outspoken on the matter during public informational gatherings as well as during city council meetings. Barks and fellow colleagues have called for the city to pass a moratorium on data center development within the city - a move that Wheeling’s city solicitor maintains cannot be done legally. Officials have noted the Center Foundry site is properly zoned for data center use in an Industrial location. "Although it’s not a moratorium, I’m pleased that this provides a stop-gap that makes the city far less appealing to those coming in to exploit us for their own benefit to our detriment," Barks said. "Although I do disagree with the opening statement that, ‘the city recognizes that facilitating the development of data center service technology can be an economic development asset to the city and of significant benefit to the city and its residents. That’s subjective - we can agree to disagree on that." Barks applauded Ward 1 Councilman Tony Assaro, who represents the Warwood neighborhood, for listening to his constituents and representing their voice. "Tony has shown himself to be a faithful steward of the will of the people," Barks said. "For that we thank him and look forward to working with him further to make our community even better." Members of the Rules Committee of Council, the city administration, the city’s legal department and other council members all worked on the development of the data center regulations for several weeks. A draft of the document was made available on the city’s website, and city leaders welcomed suggestions from the public to make any adjustments to the regulations that may be deemed necessary or beneficial. The regulations were viewed as a result of community action, Barks noted, indicating the regulations attempting to address concerns expressed by vocal residents who do not want noise, higher utility bills, pollution or any other potential side effects data centers have reportedly brought to communities in other parts of the country. She credited people who wore anti-data center T-shirts, posted yard signs, signed petitions, attended events and let their voices be heard. "Residents have become activists," she said, noting this was the beginning of a fight against data centers throughout West Virginia, an effort unfolding "in a state that does not support the will of the people." Barks asked council to make a public statement about anticipated impact on the proposed data center at Centre Foundry. "Take credit for being the first city in West Virginia, to our knowledge, to adopt an ordinance against data centers, and lend your expertise elsewhere," she said. Amanda McWhorter of Triadelphia said she represents Ohio County on a statewide panel known as the West Virginia Data Center Accountability Project. "Thank you for listening to the community and working on this ordinance," McWhorter said. "I would love to be able to connect you to other communities, as well, with our group." McWhorter and Barks encouraged city leaders to work with other communities in the state and with Ohio County on similar efforts to regulate data centers on a local level. In West Virginia, House Bill 2014 - known as the Power Generation and Consumption Act of 2025, establishes state jurisdiction and outlines regulations on the state level for data centers planning to operate at 90 megawatts, which would be deemed as a "high impact data center." Wheeling’s new Article 1365 of the city planning and zoning code, could be used as a template for other communities faced with regulating the development of data centers below the "high-impact" threshold. "Thank you guys, sincerely," Wheeling resident Vincent DeGeorge told city leaders Tue

artigo.texto: India is building its domestic carbon market under which agricultural carbon credits can finance climate-friendly farming. In this post, Suthar and Jangra highlight the importance of transparent prices, timely payments, data rights, and strict limits on corporate offset claims – without which there is a risk of greenwashing and transfer of climate risk from large polluters to the country’s smallest cultivators. A carbon-credit pilot involving 3,500 mango farmers in Karnataka’s Koppal district appeared to offer a useful bargain. Farmers would plant trees and manage biomass. The carbon stored through these activities would be measured, converted into credits, and sold. Farmers would earn additional income from land they were already cultivating. The payments did not arrive as quickly as expected. Officials attributed the delay to complex auditing, biomass assessment, and carbon-credit calculations. Farmer organisations questioned whether cultivators properly understood the system or knew when they would be paid. The pilot may eventually deliver benefits. Yet its early difficulties expose a central weakness in agricultural carbon trading: farmers must act before they know how much they will receive, when they will receive it, or how the value of their environmental work will be divided. This problem deserves attention as India builds its domestic carbon market. Carbon trading is not inherently greenwashing. A credible market can direct finance towards activities that genuinely reduce emissions. It becomes greenwashing when a company buys inexpensive credits, avoids difficult changes in its own operations, and then presents itself as environmentally responsible. For marginal farmers, the distinction is crucial. Their fields must not become places where corporations purchase reputational relief while leaving the agricultural and financial risks behind. The two markets must not be confused India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme contains two distinct parts: (i) The compliance mechanism applies to designated industries that must meet government-set emission-intensity targets. Companies performing better than their targets may earn certificates while those falling short may need to purchase them. (ii) The offset mechanism allows eligible projects outside the compliance system to generate carbon credits from verified emission reductions or removals. Agriculture is included within this emerging framework. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency has already listed an offset methodology for reducing emissions through improved management practices in rice cultivation. These mechanisms raise different questions. A compliance market can compel industrial facilities to meet regulated targets. Agricultural offsets allow corporations or other buyers to purchase reductions generated elsewhere. The greatest greenwashing risk arises when these offsets are treated as substitutes for reducing emissions within factories, transport networks, and supply chains. A farmer’s climate-friendly practice may be real. The corporate claim built upon it may still be excessive. Marginal farmers enter with weak bargaining power According to the government’s Situation Assessment Survey, 89.4% of India’s agricultural households own less than two hectares of land. These households enter carbon markets with limited savings, fragmented holdings, and little capacity to survive a failed crop or delayed payment. They do not negotiate with corporate buyers as equal market participants. A project developer generally designs the programme. A technical agency establishes the carbon baseline. An auditor verifies the claimed reduction. A registry issues the credit. An aggregator combines credits from hundreds or thousands of farms and negotiates with prospective buyers. The farmer changes the cultivation practice, supplies the land and provides the information needed to create the credit. But the farmer may never know the final selling price. Aggregation is often necessary because measuring and verifying carbon on each small plot would be expensive. It also creates an information imbalance. The intermediary knows how many credits were generated, what deductions were made, and what the buyer paid. An individual farmer may know only the amount transferred to their bank account. India risks recreating a familiar agricultural problem in a new market. Farmers produce the underlying value while intermediaries control the information, pricing, and final transaction. The company purchases a claim. The farmer accepts a constraint Agricultural carbon projects may require farmers to reduce tillage, alter water management, change fertiliser use, retain crop residue, plant trees, or adopt prescribed cultivation practices. Many of these changes can improve soil health and conserve resources. Their effects are not identical across farms. A method that works in one district may perform differently under another soil type, rainfall pattern, or pest regime. The farmer bears this uncertainty directly. A change in cultivation may require additional labour or machinery. It may alter weed management or increase costs during the transition. If the crop underperforms, the loss affects household income. If the activity fails verification, the expected carbon payment may disappear. The corporate buyer faces no comparable agricultural risk. It purchases a certificate and may use it in a sustainability report, advertisement, or net-zero claim. The environmental credit travels upwards. The production risk remains in the village. This imbalance is particularly troubling when carbon income is described as assured revenue. A payment that depends on future measurement, verification, market prices, and deductions is not assured income. It is a contingent claim the conditions of which are largely controlled by organisations outside the farm. Measurement can become another source of dependency A carbon market needs credible measurement. Buyers should not receive credits for reductions

artigo.texto: A Greenline, multinacional brasileira de tecnologia climática, passará a exigir cobertura securitária para todos os créditos de carbono mensurados e emitidos em suas operações. Desenvolvida com o apoio da corretora internacional Marsh e comercializada pela AKAD Seguros, a solução busca atender à crescente demanda de compradores corporativos por maior segurança jurídica, financeira e reputacional no mercado voluntário de carbono. Segundo a Greenline, a companhia será a primeira do setor a estabelecer a contratação de uma apólice como condição indispensável para a emissão de créditos na modalidade ex-post, na qual os ativos são gerados após a verificação dos resultados ambientais dos projetos. A iniciativa se dá em paralelo a questionamentos sobre a qualidade dos créditos negociados internacionalmente, a efetividade das iniciativas de conservação florestal e os riscos associados ao greenwashing, prática que consiste em atribuir a produtos ou atividades benefícios ambientais que não correspondem à realidade. A apólice contempla quatro modalidades de risco: descumprimento da entrega dos ativos contratados, falhas estruturais nos projetos, perda permanente de utilidade dos créditos, incluindo a desqualificação de metodologias ou autorizações governamentais, e despesas adicionais para a aquisição de títulos substitutos em caso de sinistro. Também estão previstas coberturas para gastos emergenciais destinados à contenção de danos ambientais, como operações de combate a incêndios florestais e auditorias realizadas após desastres naturais. Considerando o limite inicial de US$ 25 milhões por projeto e um preço de referência de US$ 10 por crédito, a proteção financeira corresponderia ao valor de ativos representativos de 2,5 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO2). “Controvérsias sobre a qualidade dos créditos, regularidade fundiária e o risco reputacional do greenwashing tornaram-se tópicos centrais em nossas negociações com grandes compradores corporativos”, afirmou Lucio Lopez, fundador e CEO da Greenline. “Tornar o seguro obrigatório em 100% das nossas operações não é apenas uma garantia financeira. É uma declaração de maturidade do setor. Estamos transformando ativos ambientais em instrumentos financeiros verdadeiramente bancáveis.” A contratação poderá ser estendida a projetos que já integravam a carteira da companhia antes da formalização da parceria, mediante avaliação individual da seguradora. Segundo a empresa, a padronização dos processos de mensuração e o uso de tecnologias de sensoriamento remoto favorecem a inclusão dessas operações. Concebido inicialmente para iniciativas de preservação de florestas nativas e redução do desmatamento, o produto também estará disponível para outras empresas do segmento de ativos ambientais, observados os critérios de aceitação de risco da AKAD.

artigo.texto: Two Nevada scientists tried figuring out how much water data centers use. It got complicated. Estimates of how much power Nevada's swelling number of data centers need have grown astronomically over the past two years. But the amount of water needed to cool and power them is opaque, even to scientists attempting to finalize a number. There are more than 75 data centers operating, under construction or planned across the state, primarily in the Las Vegas and greater Reno areas. And because little is known about site-specific cooling operations at each center, "We don't know how water-efficient these places are going to be," Sean McKenna, former director of the division of hydrologic sciences at the Desert Research Institute (DRI), told The Nevada Independent. McKenna and Erik Henzl, a research scientist and environmental economist at DRI, have spent more than a year correlating projected power needs to water usage for yet-to-be-built data centers in the state. The pair issued a report early this year, but their numbers were immediately rendered obsolete when NV Energy announced it had grossly underestimated how many power-hungry data centers were looking to come to Nevada. Henzl and McKenna reworked their numbers in a new report issued today. Their findings? How much water is needed depends on whether the data centers coming into Nevada utilize newer, water-efficient cooling technologies and how the power to run them is produced. Individual facility water usage is largely opaque, forcing the pair to instead base their projections on water estimates. "The energy demand has surged," Henzl said. "The water demand is more difficult to assess because of a dearth of information." With data centers moving toward more efficient technologies, the pair assumed medium or low water consumption by the centers, finding that under the updated power forecast put out by NV Energy, Nevada would require an additional 4,200-to- 12,800 acre-feet of water per year on top of existing consumption. At the higher end, that would be roughly how much Carson City's businesses and 58,000 residents use annually. "We're just kind of making our best guess on what we know," McKenna added. New power estimates blow old forecasts out of the water DRI's original report, which it issued in January, was the first Nevada-specific comprehensive analysis of data centers' water and power needs in the state. The report's findings were based on projections made by NV Energy in its 2024 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP), a roadmap outlining the utility's upcoming projects and needs. In that plan, NV Energy outlined 12 data center projects seeking power by 2033 with 5,900 megawatts (MW) of requested capacity, according to the report. But then NV Energy released an updated IRP this spring with drastically higher energy projections, largely driven by data center power needs, which are coming in much faster than NV Energy had previously anticipated. In its 2026 IRP, the utility outlined more than three dozen data centers seeking 16,530 MW of requested capacity by 2036. Projects range from smaller developments, such as BlueSky AI's planned 2.7 MW facility in Elko to Tract's 2,500 MW Virginia Highlands development. Various agencies and groups offer differing opinions on how many houses can be powered with one MW of power, but the general consensus is around a few hundred. Looking even further out, data centers, which currently account for 5 percent of NV Energy's sales, are expected to account for 64 percent of the utility's power sales by 2046. "NV Energy recognizes they will have to serve loads approximately 2.5 times current levels by 2046," according to the report. The big unknown Data centers are cooled differently depending on their age, local regulations, such as Southern Nevada's ban on evaporative cooling and other variables. Novva's 100 MW Las Vegas data center, for example, uses a closed-loop system. In 2025, it consumed less than 2 acre-feet of water. Google's data center in Henderson, however, uses an evaporative cooling system and consumed about 636 acre-feet of water in 2024. Henzl and McKenna had limited access to site-specific water usage, which McKenna said was "really a frustration with this report." What they do know is that direct and indirect water consumption — how much is used on site and how much is used offsite to generate power for the centers — are expected to increase under NV Energy's forecasts. Henzl and McKenna estimate that direct water use by data centers requesting to come into Nevada but not yet built, under a medium-usage model, could grow to nearly 12,800 acre-feet per year and indirect water usage could increase to nearly 22,000 acre-feet. "The big unknown is really this indirect or grid water use?" McKenna said. "Where does our power come from and how efficient are those generating sources? That's a big question." Behind-the-meter power In its 2026 IRP, NV Energy proposed adding nearly 12,000 MW of new power generation, primarily through solar, battery storage and natural gas, with some geothermal. But that isn't enough to meet the company's power demands plus the data centers' requested capacity. In response, impatient data center developers are turning to what is known as behind-the-meter power — power that is generated and consumed on-site. Behind-the-meter power allows data centers to produce the amount of energy they need without waiting in a queue with other large-load customers for NV Energy to have capacity to serve them. But because they aren't connected to NV Energy's system, the behind-the-meter systems bypass many state regulatory requirements. "The allure is speed to power," Henzl said. But with that speed comes uncertainty, including the amount of water needed to produce that power. "It's just a two-sided coin and it depends what that behind-the-meter source is," he said. artigo.texto: Ford has begun shipping battery cells made in Michigan using technology licensed from China's CATL, moving its next electric pickup from battery planning into prototype testing. The cells are destined for vehicles being developed at the company's Louisville plant in Kentucky. The announcement on 18 November concerns lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, cells from BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall. Ford owns the factory; CATL provides licensed technology and manufacturing expertise. That distinction sits at the centre of a project facing scrutiny over its Chinese connections. For Ford, the immediate customer is its own development programme. The shipments do not mean the Fathom pickup is on sale, or that the battery operation has reached its intended production rate. Michigan cells head for Kentucky prototypes Reuters reported that the first cells will support Fathom prototypes. CNBC said production at the roughly $3 billion Michigan facility started in October, with shipments now underway. Fathom is being developed on Ford's Universal Electric Vehicle platform. The company expects the pickup to reach customers in the fourth quarter of 2027, according to CNBC and Electrek, leaving further testing and manufacturing work before launch. The cells have a prismatic shape. Electrek reported that Ford chose this format to fit into the vehicle's structure and lower structural costs. It also said the company has not yet disclosed the pickup's battery specifications or driving range. LFP brings a different cost calculation Lithium iron phosphate avoids the nickel and cobalt used in other battery chemistries. Reuters described lower cost and durability as reasons carmakers are adopting it, while Ford links its choice to the effort to build less expensive electric vehicles. That is a manufacturing argument, not a promise that every cost saving will reach buyers. The new shipments establish a supply milestone for the development vehicles; they do not settle the final specification or ownership cost of a production truck. Ford's Alan Clarke told reporters that working with CATL offered a faster route to making affordable EVs in the United States. His comments describe why Ford chose a licensing arrangement rather than developing the manufacturing process entirely on its own. Planned output is not today's production The Marshall factory is designed for a rate of 40 cells per minute. CNBC reported an annual capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours for vehicles and Ford's energy-storage business, below the original plan of as much as 40 gigawatt-hours. The same report said Ford is still certifying processes and expects to increase output next year. Those qualifications matter when comparing a newly operating line with its planned capacity. The technology arrangement remains politically contentious. Reuters reported criticism from US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, while Ford has defended the domestic production and its decision to license CATL's expertise. A Ford spokesperson told Reuters the company still expects eligibility for a federal battery-manufacturing tax credit. The bottom line Ford now has Michigan-made LFP cells moving towards Fathom prototypes, an important step before its planned 2027 pickup launch. The next test is turning early shipments into repeatable production, while showing that licensed technology can deliver the lower costs behind the programme.
